c64.name: Commodore 64 (breadbin, ASSY 250407)
c64.description: A home computer sold from 1982. This tree traces every physical component back through the industrial processes of the early 1980s to the ore, crude oil and quartz sand it began as. Roughly 320 discrete parts from about twenty distinct manufacturing industries. The chips were designed in Pennsylvania and fabricated there; the board was populated and the machine was boxed in Hong Kong, with some runs contract-manufactured in Japan.

c64.bottoms-out.name: Where every branch terminates
c64.bottoms-out.description: Everything above ends in one of three trunks: refined metals, petrochemicals, and the utilities and factories that supply both. Most component subtrees inline their own copy of the relevant chain — a capacitor really does carry its own aluminium, and an ABS case really does carry its own acrylonitrile — so these are the canonical, deepest versions of those same chains, kept together so you can read one end to end.

unlinked.catalogue.name: Published but unlinked materials
unlinked.catalogue.description: These 9 nodes were written as canonical, reusable subtrees — a fragment's "made from" chains in full detail — but no other branch ended up referencing them, so nothing linked them into the tree. They are collected here rather than deleted. Where a component subtree inlines its own shorter version of the same material chain, this is the long one.
unlinked.catalogue.note: Generated by scripts/build.mjs. Nothing in the tree points here; the connection exists only in prose, in each node's own branch.

metal.zinc.ingot.name: Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995%
metal.zinc.ingot.description: Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. This is a deliberate convergence node with four branches: the electrowinning route, the die-cast alloy branch, the electroplating and chromate branch, and the brass branch.

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~65% galvanising, ~15-20% die casting, ~10% brass, rest chemicals

metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.name: Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp
metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.description: The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: ZnO with 0.5-2 mol% each of Bi2O3, CoO, MnO and other dopants

facts.label: Clamp voltage
facts.value: ~240 V for a mains disc, ~700 V for a DC-side disc

facts.label: Energy handling
facts.value: 10 J to over 1 kJ per disc, set by diameter

metal.zinc-oxide-powder.name: Zinc oxide powder from high-purity zinc
metal.zinc-oxide-powder.description: Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.
metal.zinc-oxide-powder.note: The exact powder route for a given varistor is proprietary; medium confidence. The atmospheric oxidation of zinc metal is the bottom of this branch and is a certainty.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: combustion or calcination; vapour-phase oxidation for the best powder

metal.zinc.brass.name: Brass (Cu-Zn) and the alloying of zinc
metal.zinc.brass.description: Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

facts.label: Common grades
facts.value: C26000 cartridge brass (70/30), C36000 free-machining brass (62/38 with 0.5% Pb)

facts.label: Zinc share
facts.value: brass takes roughly a third of refined zinc

facts.label: Famous problem
facts.value: dezincification of alpha brasses in seawater; the cartridge brass avoids it

metal.zinc.electroplate.name: Electrolytic zinc plating of steel
metal.zinc.electroplate.description: For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.
metal.zinc.electroplate.note: Trivalent chromium passivation arrived in the 1990s-2000s; hexavalent chromate was the 1982 norm.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: alkaline cyanide zincate, or acid chloride, or sulphate

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 5-25 um for passivated decorative and EMI shielding work

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or olive chromate conversion coating

metal.chromate-passivation.name: Chromate conversion coating
metal.chromate-passivation.description: A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sodium dichromate plus nitric acid, 5-30 s at room temperature

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) in the film, which is why the dried chromate coating itself is not toxic

facts.label: Applicable to
facts.value: zinc electroplate, tinplate, cadmium, and aluminium anode foil formation treatments

metal.zinc.die-cast.name: Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster
metal.zinc.die-cast.description: Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.
metal.zinc.die-cast.note: Zinc die casting lost share to aluminium and to engineering polymers during the 1980s-90s, and the alloy names (Zamak, ZA, ZA-8) are supplier-dependent. High confidence on the chemistry and the process, medium on the specific alloy for any Commodore part.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Zamak 3: Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5; Zamak 5: Zn 95 / Al 5 / Cu 0.5

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 1-5 s per shot; 400-700 shots per hour on a small machine

metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.name: Zinc alloy melting furnace
metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.description: The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air. A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.
metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.note: Furnace design varies widely; medium confidence on capacities.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 100-500 kg crucible, resistance or oil-heated, 380-430 C, held under a cover flux

facts.label: Occupational hazard
facts.value: zinc oxide fume from disturbed surfaces; metal-fume fever

metal.zinc.galvanising.name: Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip
metal.zinc.galvanising.description: Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.
metal.zinc.galvanising.note: Zinc-aluminium and zinc-nickel coated sheet for automotive was a 1980s development, not a 1982 consumer-electronics one.

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: 45-85 g/m2 for sheet; 300-600 g/m2 for fabric

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: a continuous strip line uses 50-300 t of zinc a day, of which the dross is a real loss

facts.label: Coating form
facts.value: pure zinc for general use; Zn-Al alloy for high-drip lines; Zn-Ni for automotive sheet

metal.zinc.dross-recovery.name: Ashes and dross recovery from the galvanising kettle
metal.zinc.dross-recovery.description: The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.
metal.zinc.dross-recovery.note: Recovery efficiency varies with dross age; medium confidence.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 70-90% of the dross metal is recovered

metal.rosin.name: Rosin (colophony) from pine
metal.rosin.description: The flux, and it is not synthetic: it is the sticky, yellow-brown, semi-solid fraction of pine resin tapped from living trees or distilled out of pine stumps and mill residues. Chemically it is a mixture of resin acids - abietic acid and its relatives - which at soldering temperature decompose to a mild organic acid that dissolves the copper and tin oxides and floats them away in a non-conductive film. Electronics rosin is gum or wood rosin, bleached pale, dissolved in the flux. It is one of the few places in the electronics chain where the feedstock is a forest product rather than a mine, and it is combustible, which is why rosin-fluxed boards must be cleaned before conformal coating.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: tapped pine resin (gum) and pine-stump distillation (wood rosin)

facts.label: Acid content
facts.value: abietic acid and dehydroabietic acid, about 70-90% of rosin

facts.label: Behaviour
facts.value: at 180-250 C the acids break down into non-corrosive, non-conductive residues

metal.rosin.activator.name: The halide activator in the flux core
metal.rosin.activator.description: Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.
metal.rosin.activator.note: Flux grade nomenclature and the activator levels are standard; medium confidence on which grade Commodore specified in 1982.

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: zinc chloride at 0.1-2%, or zinc-ammonium chloride

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: RA (rosin-ammonia), RMA (rosin mildly activated), MA, A

facts.label: The trade
facts.value: more activator means better oxide removal and worse corrosion of copper if residues remain

metal.pine-resin.name: Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill
metal.pine-resin.description: The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.
metal.pine-resin.note: By the 1980s the pulp-mill (wood rosin) route supplied the majority of industrial rosin; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between gum and wood rosin.
places: Kraft pulp mill, southeastern United States

metal.turpentine.name: Turpentine from the same stump
metal.turpentine.description: When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.
metal.turpentine.note: Medium confidence on the order-of-processing; the distillation sequence is standard.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene, by steam distillation of the stumps

facts.label: First fraction
facts.value: turpentine, then rosin as the residue

metal.quartz.name: Natural quartz crystal
metal.quartz.description: Vein and pegmatite quartz, of which Brazil's Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry. Only used where natural material beat synthetic on Q - high-stability resonators - and as the seed for hydrothermal growth. Included because it is a genuine geological leaf for the clock crystal branch, unlike the industrial silica sand and the silicon-grade quartzite, which are both processed rocks.

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: vein quartz in a granitic pegmatite or a hydrothermal vein

facts.label: Use
facts.value: resonator-grade seed and, for high-Q parts, natural crystal

metal.hex-chrome-plating.name: Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath
metal.hex-chrome-plating.description: The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.
metal.hex-chrome-plating.note: Hexavalent chromium plating is essentially unchanged since the 1980s except for the trivalent and hex-free alternatives developed after 2000; high confidence on the chemistry.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: an automatic catalyst based on sulphate, in the 1980s

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: OSHA standard on airborne hexavalent chromium, 1971

metal.cryolite.name: Cryolite (Na3AlF6), the electrolyte solvent
metal.cryolite.description: The white, insoluble, water-repellent mineral that makes aluminium electrolysis possible at all. Pure alumina melts at 2072 C; a bath of cryolite with excess aluminium fluoride and some calcium fluoride is liquid at 950-970 C, and the alumina dissolves in it at 6-10%. The other crucial property is that cryolite is not consumed stoichiometrically - it is a solvent - and only the fluorine lost as HF and in the fume has to be replaced. Correcting the brief: consumption was roughly 0.5-1.0 t of cryolite per tonne of aluminium in 1980s practice (theoretical about 0.5 t, higher in practice because of fluoride loss), not 'four tonnes of aluminium per tonne of cryolite'.
metal.cryolite.note: Explicit correction of the 4 t Al per t cryolite figure in the brief: cryolite is a solvent, not a stoichiometric reactant, so consumption is roughly a tonne per tonne of metal, not a quarter of that. High confidence on the mechanism; medium on the exact consumption range, which varies with the fluorine recovery practice.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 1012 C pure; the bath runs at 950-970 C because of the excess AlF3 and CaF2

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.5-1.0 t per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: Ivittuut, Greenland - the only commercial natural cryolite deposit - was still being mined in 1982 and closed in 1987; every other tonne was synthetic

metal.aluminium-fluoride.name: Aluminium fluoride and the bath
metal.aluminium-fluoride.description: The excess AlF3 in the bath is not a deliberate additive so much as the consequence of the water and the fluorides in the alumina; smelters add it back to hold the bath at the composition that gives the best current efficiency, which is somewhere between 8 and 14% excess AlF3. Too little and the bath's freezing point rises and the pot freezes; too much and the current efficiency falls and the crust gets hard. Getting this balance right is the potline operator's entire job, and it is checked by sampling the frozen bath and analysing it in a laboratory.
metal.aluminium-fluoride.note: The 8-14% excess AlF3 window is well documented in the aluminium literature; medium confidence because smelter practice varied.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: made by reacting alumina and hydrofluoric acid

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: freezing-point depression of a sample of frozen bath

metal.cryolite.synthesis.name: Synthetic cryolite from hydrofluoric acid
metal.cryolite.synthesis.description: Because natural cryolite was one mine in Greenland, the industry made its own. Sodium carbonate or caustic soda reacts with hydrofluoric acid and aluminium hydroxide at 60-90 C: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O. So the electrolyte solvent of the aluminium pot is manufactured from fluorspar, caustic soda and alumina - three of this file's other endpoints in one reaction.

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the sodium cryolite is a constituent of the EPA-registered rodenticide and insecticide 'cryolite' - a genuinely different market

metal.chromium.metal.name: Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum
metal.chromium.metal.description: Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.
metal.chromium.metal.note: The hydrometallurgical chromium route is well documented; I have medium confidence on the exact 1982 process parameters.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 500-700 C with soda ash, to water-soluble sodium chromate

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: sodium metabisulphite to Cr(III) as chrome alum

facts.label: Electrowinning
facts.value: lead cathode, low voltage, to 99.9% Cr

metal.chromium.metal.cell.name: Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm
metal.chromium.metal.cell.description: Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.
metal.chromium.metal.cell.note: Low confidence on the cellroom details; this part of the industry is poorly documented outside the chrome plating literature, where the figures for chromium metal electrowinning are not commonly given.

metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.name: The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance
metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.description: The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.
metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.note: Low confidence on the specific 1982 chromium cell diaphragm practice; the asbestos overlap with chlor-alkali is real but I am inferring the chromium side of it.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: asbestos cloth, replaced by synthetic fibre and PTFE-lined designs through the 1980s

metal.chromium.aod.name: Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel
metal.chromium.aod.description: The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: ~78% Ar / 22% O2 initially, rising to pure O2, then back to Ar

facts.label: Chromium loss
facts.value: some chromia goes to the bath, recovered from ferrochrome dust

metal.chromium.aod.lance.name: The AOD lance and its tuyere block
metal.chromium.aod.lance.description: The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.
metal.chromium.aod.lance.note: Medium confidence; the lance geometry and injection depth are standard practice.

facts.label: Argon flow
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 Nm3 per minute per tonne of steel

metal.refractory-ladle.name: The refractory ladle lining
metal.refractory-ladle.description: The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.
metal.refractory-ladle.note: Medium confidence; the magnesia supply chain is well documented but is not part of this subsystem's requested scope.

metal.chromium.stainless-use.name: Chromium in the C64's stainless parts
metal.chromium.stainless-use.description: AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.
metal.chromium.stainless-use.note: The passivation chemistry is standard; whether Commodore's specific parts were passivated in manufacture is medium confidence.

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, room temperature or 50 C, 30 min

chem.glass-fiber.name: Glass fibre (E-glass) for laminate and filter media
chem.glass-fiber.description: Continuous drawn glass filaments a few microns thick, bundled into strand and woven into cloth. A C64 needs it twice: as the reinforcing cloth in the FR-4 mainboard laminate, and — if you follow the machine out to a television — as the fine filter media in an air-cleaning system. E-glass is the workhorse composition, named for its electrical resistivity, and it is made in enormous tonnage.
chem.glass-fiber.note: Soda ash (Na2CO3) came from Solvay-process soda, and boron from imported borax — both are pure inputs in the historical sense.

facts.label: E-glass composition
facts.value: ~54 wt% SiO2, 15% Al2O3, 16% CaO, 8% B2O3, small Na2O/K2O, Fe2O3 under 0.4%

facts.label: Typical filament diameter
facts.value: 3-10 um continuous; 0.1-3 um for fine filter grades

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: ~800 C; fibres soften in a flame

chem.glass-fiber.filter-media.name: Fine and ultrafine grades for air filtration
chem.glass-fiber.filter-media.description: Air-purification media use a much finer fibre than the 5 micron laminate grade: 0.1-1 micron fibres are produced by reducing the number and size of bushing holes and, for HEPA grades, by a flash or steam-blowing process that collapses the fibre into mats. This branch exists because a semiconductor fab and a television both need filtered air, and the same silica-and-limestone feedstocks are involved.
chem.glass-fiber.filter-media.note: Owned in detail by the industry fragment's cleanroom branch; recorded here so the material chain to the sand is continuous.

chem.glass-fiber.packaging.name: Spinning to strand, roving and woven cloth
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.description: The attenuated strand is wound onto a rotating package at high traverse speed — a single package can hold tens of kilometres of strand — then combined into rovings and woven on a air-jet loom into plain-weave cloth. The loom matters: a plain weave with square fill is what gives an FR-4 laminate its isotropic behaviour, which is why PCB cloth is woven rather than chopped.
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.note: The agent's brief specified long-fibre softwood for the kraft liner; that is the paper, not the glass.

facts.label: Cloth weight for FR-4
facts.value: 100-300 gsm; 120-200 gsm typical for 1.6 mm two-layer board

facts.label: Weave
facts.value: plain, or crow/twill for higher stiffness

facts.label: Yarns per cm
facts.value: about 13 x 13 per cm for 100-200 gsm

chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.name: Attenuation and sizing
chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.description: Air jets at high velocity and constant pressure stretch the molten filament to 3-10 microns. As it passes a sizing apron a thin film of starch or oil is applied; for laminate grade this is usually replaced after weaving by a silane or acrylate coupling agent, which is what lets the glass bond chemically to the epoxy instead of merely sitting in it.

facts.label: Sizing
facts.value: starch or oil on the strand; silane/acrylate after weaving

chem.glass-fiber.bushing.name: Forehearth and bushings
chem.glass-fiber.bushing.description: Glass travels from the furnace through a refractory forehearth to a bushing plate — a small alloy block drilled with 200 to several thousand holes of 10-40 microns, usually gold-platinum alloy because it resists corrosion at 1400 C. Pressure pushes the melt through each hole; surface tension then draws it out, and gravity plus attenuation stretches it to a fiber diameter a fiftieth of the hole.

facts.label: Bushing material
facts.value: Au-Pt alloy, or rhodium-plated nickel in the cheapest grades

chem.glass-fiber.melt.name: Melting in a regenerative tank furnace
chem.glass-fiber.melt.description: The batch is charged into a regenerative furnace held around 1400-1500 C. The glass is not just melted: it must then be refined (bubbles larger than a few microns rise out or are broken by a rotating mechanical stirrer) and conditioned (held just above the liquidus so beta-eucryptite crystallises, which is what stops the finished fibre devitrifying into a crystalline, brittle, unusable mass). Conditioning is slow — tens of hours — and it is the step that makes continuous fibre possible at all.

facts.label: Conditioning time
facts.value: 10-40 h, the slowest step in the plant

chem.glass-fiber.batch.name: Batch mixing
chem.glass-fiber.batch.description: The raw oxides are weighed and dry-mixed in a batch charger to about +/-1% on each constituent. A modern batch is tens of tonnes; the tolerance matters because the melt is what fixes the composition, and composition fixes the viscosity, which fixes whether 5 micron fibre can be drawn at all.

industry.name: Foundries, factories, utilities and logistics
industry.description: The plant and the plumbing behind the Commodore 64: who made the chips, who assembled the box, what burned to light the lights, where the water came from, where the waste went, and how many hands and hours it took. A C64 is an artefact of eleven industries, not one.

facility.test-equipment.name: Factory and engineering test equipment
facility.test-equipment.description: Short branch. Every C64 that left the Hong Kong line had been through a functional test, and the boards had been tested electrically before population and after soldering. In-circuit testers and flying probes were the technology of the era; the ATE and flying-probe industry of the 1990s did not exist yet.

facility.test-equipment.bare-board.name: Bare-board test and flying probe
facility.test-equipment.bare-board.description: Bare PCB test came first: a bed-of-nails grid fixture to prove every net was etched and plated correctly, catching a shorts-heavy board before it was populated and therefore before the parts were on it. The flying probe - a robot or CNC head with a moving needle that touched nets individually without a fixture - existed by the early 1980s as an engineering diagnostic, and only later became the standard production tester once it got fast enough.
facility.test-equipment.bare-board.note: Today the flying probe has largely displaced the bed-of-nails in production, which removes the per-revision fixture cost - a genuine change in the economics of board design between 1983 and now.

facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.name: Spring probe and tungsten needle
facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.description: The bed-of-nails is a field of sprung tungsten-rhenium or beryllium-copper pins on a 2.54 mm grid, each pressing a few grams onto a pad to make contact. The 1980s fixtures were drilled and wired by hand or on a numerical-control machine from the Gerber artwork - which is why a board layout change meant a new fixture.
facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.note: Tungsten-rhenium was the common needle alloy in this era; beryllium copper became the standard later, and both carry real occupational-exposure caveats for the operators who handled them.

facility.test-equipment.burn-in.name: Burn-in oven and sockets
facility.test-equipment.burn-in.description: A forced-air oven at 70-100 C with burn-in sockets, holding hundreds of boards for 24-72 hours so that early-life component failures - bad solder joints, marginal ICs, leaky capacitors - showed up on the line instead of in the customer's house. Commodore's 1982-83 quality record suggests it was not always run long enough.

facility.test-equipment.test-rom.name: Test ROM in the final-test fixture
facility.test-equipment.test-rom.description: A dedicated test ROM - the '501' diagnostic ROM is the one most C64 owners meet - loaded into the machine's own ROM socket during factory final test so the machine could self-test its own RAM, character ROM, CIA timers and VIC registers. It is the same object a user later used to prove the machine worked.

facility.test-equipment.functional.name: Functional tester
facility.test-equipment.functional.description: A powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM. On a Commodore line this was a dedicated fixture with a monitor and a keyboard, and the operator's job was to load, run, read the result, box or quarantine.

facility.test-equipment.ict.name: In-circuit tester (ICT)
facility.test-equipment.ict.description: A bed-of-nails fixture pressing 1000 or so spring-loaded probes onto the bare board's pads, measuring resistance, capacitance, diode voltage and, at an increasing share, functional signatures at each node - all in a few seconds. By 1983 the analogue resistance-only tester was giving way to the analogue-plus-functional 'in-circuit functional tester' that could catch an unpopulated IC or a wrong-orientation part without a board-level functional test.
facility.test-equipment.ict.note: The bed-of-nails fixture itself is bespoke per board revision - which is one of the reasons a new motherboard revision was expensive to introduce and why the 250407 revision mattered.

logistics.people.name: The labour content of a C64
logistics.people.description: Two labour populations with almost nothing in common: a tiny, very senior, very expensive American engineering team in Pennsylvania and Japan, and a large, low-paid, mostly female production workforce in Hong Kong and Japan. The design labour is amortised over millions of units and is invisible in the $35-40 BOM; the assembly labour is a few dollars per unit and is the reason Commodore could hit a $135 production cost.

logistics.people.qa-defects.name: The labour cost of the quality problems
logistics.people.qa-defects.description: Commodore's labour did not just build machines, it found and reworked other people's mistakes. The 'sparkle' defect was traced after three weeks to a ROM - not the VIC-II - with a pre-charging circuit that was sensitive to a bus contention spike; three million such ROMs were already in service. A logic error put 64 clock cycles on a scanline instead of 65 and took about five months into production to fix. Assembly-line workers over-adjusted the colour potentiometer until it saturated the colour and wiped out the luma. Electric screwdrivers cut traces on the disk-drive connector, and because those traces went to a connector nobody tested, they passed final inspection. Charles Winterble: 'It takes a very tough person to say I'm not shipping these because they're not as good as they could be - especially when people are clamoring to buy them.'

facts.label: ROMs affected
facts.value: 3 million already in service when the sparkle cause was found

facts.label: Cost of the C64A redesign
facts.value: a substantial redesign was required to fix the Santa Clara build

logistics.people.production-engineering.name: The production engineers who fixed it
logistics.people.production-engineering.description: The unsung labour in Commodore's story: David Ziembicki (production engineer, then Commodore West Chester), Bruce Crocket and Charles Winterble, who had to debug the project and bring it into production, and Robert H. Lane, who became president of Commodore Business Machines Inc in November 1982 and was fired by Tramiel after the June 1983 CES. Kentron's 150 Japanese engineers and technicians - brought in specifically because Commodore Japan's production engineering had worked on the VIC-20 - are the documented reason the C64 was eventually manufacturable at all.

logistics.people.development-cost.name: Nobody knows what the C64 cost to develop
logistics.people.development-cost.description: Winterble's answer to the question was direct: 'I had no formal budget accountability, other than Jack watching me. Jack said that budgets were a license to steal.' The reason the answer was 'nothing much' is that the fab was not running at full capacity and the design chips were absorbed into existing overhead with no supplier margin at all. Ziembicki: 'We were using people who were there anyway.' Software, per Charpentier, 'wasn't tangible - you couldn't hold it, feel it, or touch it - so it wasn't worth spending money for.'

logistics.people.c64-system-team.name: The C64 system design team
logistics.people.c64-system-team.description: After Tramiel decided in late November 1981 that the VIC-II and SID would go into a 64 KB home computer rather than a game console, the machine itself was designed in about five weeks. The architecture was laid out on paper in two days; five working prototypes were finished just before the new year. The team was Bob Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki, with Yash Terakura of Commodore Japan involved on the Japanese variant. They worked over Thanksgiving and Christmas. Charlie Winterble had set the deadline; Tramiel had decided the machine had to be at the January 1982 CES.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: laid out on paper in two days

facts.label: Prototypes
facts.value: five working units in under five weeks

facts.label: Show
facts.value: January 1982 Consumer Electronics Show, Las Vegas

logistics.people.design-team.name: The C64 chip design team
logistics.people.design-team.description: A team of about seven people, working in parallel on two chips, in nine months. Al Charpentier designed the VIC-II with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Bob Yannes designed the SID with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Charles Winterble, then director of worldwide engineering, authorised and managed the project. The whole effort began in January 1981, spent about two weeks studying the Mattel Intellivision, the TI 99/4A and the Atari 800, and finished with first-pass silicon in November 1981 that worked except for one bad sprite. The chips were designed in a modular, deliberately uncompact style - Yannes built one oscillator module and repeated it rather than multiplexing - because design time was the scarce resource, not die area. Neither designer had a modern CAD workstation; logic was simulated by hand.
logistics.people.design-team.note: The brief's 'six months' is not what the sources say: Charpentier and Yannes both worked the full nine months from January 1981 to November 1981. The nine-month figure is documented in IEEE Spectrum's 1985 case history and in the C64 design histories; I have used it. The system-level C64 (architecture on paper in two days, five working prototypes in under five weeks) was a different and much shorter effort by Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki in December 1981.

facts.label: Team size
facts.value: about 7 (2 designers, 4 draftsmen, 1-2 CAD operators, plus a manager)

logistics.people.hk-headcount.name: Commodore's Hong Kong workforce
logistics.people.hk-headcount.description: The Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd employed approximately 2,500 people when mass production of the production-redesigned C-64A began there in March 1983. That is the single best-documented headcount in the whole Commodore manufacturing story.

logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.name: The worker at the wave-solder line
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.description: The single most recognisable job in a 1980s electronics factory. She stood or sat at one end of a 2-3 m wave-solder machine, fed pre-inserted boards into the conveyor, watched for bridging and dry joints, pulled the rejects, and often did the visual inspection and the component-insertion handwork at the same station. Almost always female, usually in her twenties or thirties, on a piece rate or a small hourly premium for yield, and living within an hour's bus ride of the plant in a New Territories squatter village or a public housing block. Hong Kong's 1983 wage survey listed 'soldering worker' as a distinct occupational category for exactly this reason.
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.note: The 1980s photographs of the Commodore Hong Kong line show a robotised through-hole populating machine followed by a long line with bench test desks, consistent with this description, but they date from December 1992, not 1983.

logistics.people.wage-index.name: The international wage gap that placed the work in Hong Kong
logistics.people.wage-index.description: The cleanest comparative number available: ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics hourly compensation costs for production workers in electronic and electrical equipment (SIC 36), indexed to the United States at 100. In 1975 Hong Kong was 15-16, Korea 16, Taiwan 18-19, Japan 84, Israel 75. By 1984 Hong Kong was 19, Korea 23, Taiwan 22, Japan 82. The Asian plants ran at roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of American labour cost, and that gap - not the technology - was the reason the assembly was where it was.

logistics.people.hk-wages.name: Hong Kong electronics wages, 1983
logistics.people.hk-wages.description: The Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's Quarterly Report of Wages, Salaries and Employee Benefits Statistics carried explicit occupational breakdowns for the electronics industry in 1983 - assembler, soldering worker, tester/aligner, quality control operator, packer, machine operator - with average daily wages and normal hours, and it separately flagged that piece rates were common in manufacturing and that the survey therefore reported them on a time basis. Operative daily wages across manufacturing generally sat around HK$60-100 in 1983, so an assembler earned roughly HK$9-14 per hour at a 7-8.5 hour day. Hong Kong had no statutory minimum wage at all in 1983.
logistics.people.hk-wages.note: The scanned 1983 Census and Statistics Department tables are OCR-garbled; the HK$60-100 daily figure is read off the reported range across manufacturing occupations and should be treated as a range, not a single number.

logistics.people.direct-labour.name: Direct assembly labour per machine
logistics.people.direct-labour.description: Roughly 0.5-1.5 person-hours per machine across population, insertion (automated), wave-solder, assembly, test and packing, plus a share of the test and rework. At 1983 Hong Kong and Japanese electronics wage levels of roughly HK$9-14 or JPY 500-700 per hour, that is about US$1-3 per machine of direct labour - between 3% and 8% of the $35-50 production cost. Direct labour is genuinely tiny compared with the IC content, which is exactly the point Commodore's vertical integration strategy rested on.
logistics.people.direct-labour.note: I could not find a documented Commodore standard time for C64 assembly. The person-hour estimate is my own reasoning from the process steps (insertion is automated; a wave-solder pass plus test plus pack is on the order of 30-60 minutes of attended time) and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measured value.

logistics.people.bom.name: The bill of materials (1983 estimate)
logistics.people.bom.description: Brian Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks gave the most-cited contemporaneous breakdown, used as a production cost of $35-50 by 1985: three ROMs at $1 each; eight 64K DRAMs at $1.85 each; SID and VIC-II at $4 each; RF modulator $3; 6510 at $1-2; TTL, buffers, regulators and capacitors together $5; keyboard under $10; PC board $1-2; plastic case $1-2; power supply and connectors $5-10; packaging and manual $1-2. Note what this says: the eight DRAM chips alone were $14.80, more than the case, the board and the modulator combined.
logistics.people.bom.note: These are Dougherty's estimates, not Commodore's accounts - Commodore never confirmed them. The $135 initial production cost is a Commodore figure.

logistics.shipping.name: Moving 100,000 C64s
logistics.shipping.description: The C64 was assembled in East Asia and sold in North America and Europe. In 1983 that was containerised cargo on liner services, not break-bulk: a 40-foot box holds 250-350 C64s depending on how they were packed, and the whole industry's economics were shaped by the 1966-1980s transition from weight/measurement cargo to box rates.

logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.name: Customs valuation and the paper trail
logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.description: US customs value was the transaction value - the price actually paid or payable - which is why Commodore's transfer-pricing between Commodore Electronics Ltd (Bahamas), Commodore Japan Ltd and the Hong Kong branch became the subject of a US Tax Court case that ran from 1991 and shifted $116 million of income between entities. The same transfer prices determined the duty. The documentation for a 1983 shipment would have included a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and, in a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal, a certificate of origin.

facts.label: Section 482 adjustment
facts.value: $65.6 M for 1985 and $50.5 M for 1986 added to CBM income

logistics.shipping.import-duty.name: US import duty on a computer in 1983
logistics.shipping.import-duty.description: The C64 entered the United States under the Tariff Schedules of the United States (the TSUS - the HTS did not exist until 1989), classified as an accounting, computing and other data processing machine incorporating a calculating mechanism, item 676.15, dutiable at 5.5% ad valorem. Separately, item 807.00 gave a duty allowance for the US components shipped out for assembly abroad - which for Commodore meant a deduction for the value of the MOS chips and the case shipped to Hong Kong, so only the value added in Hong Kong paid duty.
logistics.shipping.import-duty.note: The 5.5% figure for TSUS 676.15 is verified from a 1987 Court of International Trade decision. I could not verify the exact 1983 rate for item 676.15; it is flagged as medium confidence for that reason. Note also that in 1983 the HTS did not exist (it was introduced in 1989) and the Customs Tariff Index, not a searchable database, was the practical reference.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 5.5% ad valorem (rate confirmed for 1987; 1983 rate not directly verified)

facts.label: Assembly relief
facts.value: TSUS 807.00: duty on full value less US component value

logistics.shipping.demurrage.name: Demurrage, detention and the inventory cost
logistics.shipping.demurrage.description: Two separate costs. Demurrage is the charge for leaving a container on the terminal beyond the free time; in 1983 free time was commonly four to five days and the daily charge escalated. Detention is the charge for keeping the container beyond the time allowed at the other end. On top of both sat the real cost: eight to twelve weeks of sea transit each way meant Commodore had to hold inventory in transit and in the destination warehouse, which is exactly the cost structure that rewarded the 'just-in-time' port-to-port discipline and punished Commodore's famous spotty availability in 1983.
logistics.shipping.demurrage.note: Modern practice: much longer contractually-guaranteed free time (7-10 days), published terminal tariffs and time-and-demurrage clauses that convert demurrage into a rental. The published per-day figures quoted today ($65-$315/day at LA/LB) are anachronistic for 1983.

logistics.shipping.air-freight.name: Air freight for the high-value parts
logistics.shipping.air-freight.description: Customs values tell the story: a box of 300 C64s entered at, say, $150-200 declared value each would carry $45,000-60,000 of electronics inside a container whose ocean freight was a few hundred dollars. The ICs were the opposite case: a 6510 and a VIC-II at internal transfer value were a tiny fraction of the customs value of the finished case, so nobody flew the chips - the chips came by sea inside the container, and the container moved once. Air freight was for prototypes, for a replacement part in an emergency, and for the tape and the spares.
logistics.shipping.air-freight.note: Air freight in 1983 was priced by weight with a minimum weight, so the economics made it essentially unusable for consumer electronics inbound freight; it was used for sample and prototype shipments and for urgent replacement parts.

logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.name: The bill of lading
logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.description: The negotiable document that made containerised trade possible: a carrier-issued contract of carriage naming the shipper, the consignee, the port of loading and discharge, the freight terms, and the description of the goods. Without it the goods did not move; with it, the bank paid on presentation. The 1983 electronic BOL did not exist - the paper document was the mechanism.

logistics.shipping.routes.name: Route times: transpacific and Europe-Asia
logistics.shipping.routes.description: Kaohsiung or Hong Kong to Long Beach is about 4,500-5,000 nautical miles via the Luzon Strait and the great circle; at 16-18 knots that is roughly 12-14 days port to port, plus 3-7 days in the terminal on each end. Hong Kong to Rotterdam via the Suez Canal is about 11,000 nautical miles, 22-26 days, with 5-7 days of canal transit and waiting. These were the numbers that set Commodore's inventory position: eight weeks of sea transit each way on the Pacific route, eleven to twelve weeks each way on the Europe route.
logistics.shipping.routes.note: These are order-of-magnitude figures derived from distances and 1980s liner speeds; I did not find a published 1983 schedule for a specific Commodore carrier service.

logistics.shipping.ports.name: The ports
logistics.shipping.ports.description: Kaohsiung was Taiwan's largest container port and was ranked the world's fifth-largest container port in 1982; its first container terminal was built 1969-70 and Container Terminal No. 4 in the Zhongxing Commercial Harbor Area was built from 1983. Keelung, on the northern approach to Taipei, opened the first Taiwanese container ship movements in January 1972 and worked on a filled jetty because of the terrain. Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour terminals, Rotterdam, and Long Beach or Oakland on the US West Coast, plus New York and Newark on the East Coast, completed the set.

logistics.shipping.c64-count.name: The volume Commodore was moving
logistics.shipping.c64-count.description: By March 1983 the C64 was shipping at about 25,000 units a month and had passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales; roughly half a million had sold in the first six months. At 300 units a 40-foot box, that is about 83 TEU a month - about four to five ships' worth of containers a month, which sounds trivial until you remember it was compounding 20-30% a month.

logistics.shipping.containerisation.name: Containerisation (40-foot box)
logistics.shipping.containerisation.description: ISO 40-foot general purpose container: 12.192 m x 2.438 m x 2.591 m internal, holding up to about 32-36 tonnes. One TEU is a 20-foot box; a 40-foot box is two. Box rates had replaced weight rates on the main east-west lanes by the end of the 1970s, so a low-density, high-value cargo like a C64 paid per box rather than per tonne.
logistics.shipping.containerisation.note: The C64 weighed roughly 4 kg boxed; a 40-ft box at 32 t payload would in principle hold hundreds, but in practice the limit was volume and the fact that C64s were not stackable with the packaging of the day, so 250-350 is a working estimate, not a documented figure.

facility.foundries.name: The Commodore supply-chain geography
facility.foundries.description: Where a C64 physically came from. Commodore owned one fab, in Pennsylvania. The boards were printed in Hong Kong. The boxes were assembled in Hong Kong, Japan, West Germany, the United States and - from 1984 - Britain. The corporate records that survived the bankruptcy are unusually detailed and are the best source for this branch.

facility.foundries.subcontract-network.name: The sub-contractor geography: Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines
facility.foundries.subcontract-network.description: Commodore's own factories were few; its supply base was enormous. Japan supplied the disks and a great deal of the precision mechanics and passives. Taiwan and Korea supplied the display-grade passives, the transformers, the coils, the keyboards and the power supplies, through the export processing zones. The Philippines and Malaysia supplied the switching power supplies and the magnetics by the late 1980s. Hong Kong was the assembly and test node, sitting between them, with the boards printed locally and the chips arriving from Pennsylvania.
facility.foundries.subcontract-network.note: ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics, hourly compensation costs for production workers in US SIC 36 electronic and other electrical equipment. This index is the cleanest single measure of why the work was in Hong Kong and Taiwan: roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the American cost per hour.

facts.label: Hourly compensation index (US=100), electronic equipment
facts.value: 1975: Hong Kong 15-16, Korea 16, Taiwan 18-19; 1984: Hong Kong 19, Korea 23, Taiwan 22

facility.foundries.other-sites.name: The rest of the manufacturing map, 1983
facility.foundries.other-sites.description: By 1983 Commodore described itself as an international company with manufacturing in Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany, the UK, Pennsylvania and California in the United States, and Scarborough in Metropolitan Toronto. C64 units carried the MADE IN HONG KONG, West Germany or England marks, and were assembled in at least 11 factories worldwide over the model's life. Commodore did not, at this stage, have a Commodore Taiwan plant - the Taiwanese supply chain in this story is the sub-contractor base, not a Commodore factory.
facility.foundries.other-sites.note: Commodore Taiwan as a subsidiary is a later-1980s development; I found no 1983 evidence of a Commodore-owned Taiwan factory. A Philippine assembly operation definitely existed by the 1990s (the Philippine government seized Amiga and CD32 stock after Commodore's 1994 bankruptcy over a debt to a factory there), but that is outside the 1982-84 window.

facility.foundries.corby.name: Commodore Business Machines (UK), Corby
facility.foundries.corby.description: The British end. Commodore UK's head office was in Slough and it built calculators at a factory on Teesside; in 1983 it announced a new GBP 20 million home computer factory at Corby, Northamptonshire, as the European manufacturing and distribution centre for the C64 and VIC-20, expecting 300 jobs by the end of 1984 and 700,000 units a year by then. The Corby plant was in place by September 1984 with 850 jobs on a ten-acre site, ran flat out sixteen hours a day, and was closed as a manufacturing base in January 1986.
facility.foundries.corby.note: Corby post-dates the C64's 1983 peak, so it belongs here as the European logistics and finishing node rather than as a 1983 production source.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: GBP 20 million announced 1983; a little over GBP 2 million of UK grant

facts.label: Jobs
facts.value: 300 planned for 1984; 850 by opening; 170 retained at closure

facility.foundries.braunschweig.name: Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH, Braunschweig, West Germany
facility.foundries.braunschweig.description: The European production base. Commodore launched production for the European market in Braunschweig in 1980 and it once employed up to 2,000 people. Commodore GmbH also designed products. The PET had been imported from Braunschweig, and Commodore UK in the 1970s bought calculators at a factory on Teesside. After the 1983 Corby decision, the more expensive business systems stayed in Braunschweig.

facility.foundries.japan-vendors.name: Japanese assembly vendors for the VIC-20
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.description: The VIC-20 - the machine whose case, board size and BASIC the C64 inherited - was first built in Japan by Shinwa Electric Company, then by Japanese Cash Register (JCR), both assembling and manufacturing to Commodore Japan Limited's specifications and under its direction. Japanese Cash Register also owned a factory on Ina road; CJL's engineering headquarters was at Isaka.
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.note: The C64-Wiki list of Commodore entities includes 'Commodore Japan Limited in Japan (Isaka)'; the Tax Court record confirms Shinwa Electric and Japanese Cash Register as the VIC-20 assemblers but does not give their locations.

facility.foundries.kentron.name: Kentron Co., Ltd., Ina, Japan
facility.foundries.kentron.description: The small Japanese production-engineering company that Commodore Japan acquired in October 1982 and that actually fixed the C64. Kentron had about 150 employees at its height and expertise in production engineering, quality control, work standards, purchasing and materials control. Commodore Japan substantially redesigned the machine into the 'C-64A' with Kentron's help; Kentron produced prototypes in late 1982 and began mass production in January 1983. Kentron was a CJL subsidiary from October 1982 to June 1986, when it was sold to an unrelated party.

facility.foundries.hong-kong.name: The Hong Kong operation (CE(HK)L and the CEL Hong Kong branch)
facility.foundries.hong-kong.description: Where the C64 really got built. Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd had been making watches and calculators since 1979, and manufactured VIC-20 units from April 1982; later the Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd took over. Mass production of the production-redesigned 'C-64A' began at the Hong Kong branch in March 1983, and that branch employed approximately 2,500 people. Commodore's Hong Kong operation bought or produced watches, calculators and computers, and by 1983 it was the assembly centre for the whole company's output. Commodore had Hong Kong subsidiaries listed as Commodore Business Machines Ltd (Hong Kong) and Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd.
facility.foundries.hong-kong.note: The exact street address of the Commodore Hong Kong plant is not established in the sources I found; it is not confirmed as Kwai Chung, Tsuen Wan or Kwun Tong. Photographs of the plant taken in December 1992 by Robert Baker, a Commodore production engineer sent from West Chester PA for the Amiga 600 pilot run, show a robotised through-hole insertion machine, a long assembly/test line and bench test desks.

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: ~2,500 persons at the Hong Kong branch of CEL

facility.foundries.psu-maker.name: Power supply / transformer sub-contractor
facility.foundries.psu-maker.description: The linear power supply inside the C64 - the big orange or black transformer, the rectifier and the linear regulators - came from outside suppliers, cost an estimated $5-10 including connectors, and one of Ziembicki's complaints was that a supplier that had passed engineering approval then quietly changed the design without telling anybody.

facility.foundries.hk-injection.name: Hong Kong / Taiwan injection moulding sub-contractor
facility.foundries.hk-injection.description: The ABS case, the keyboard keycaps and the cassette-port door were moulded by a sub-contractor, not by Commodore. Hong Kong and Taiwan each had hundreds of small toolrooms and presses in 1983, and Commodore used both. The case cost an estimated $1-2 in 1983 prices.
facility.foundries.hk-injection.note: The identity of the moulder is not documented in the sources I found.

facility.foundries.hk-pcb.name: Hong Kong PCB fabricator
facility.foundries.hk-pcb.description: All sixteen versions of the C64 motherboard were manufactured in Hong Kong. Hong Kong in the early 1980s was a genuine centre of bare-board fabrication - dozens of small plants doing gold-impregnated or tin-lead plated FR-4 double-sided boards on a 0.3-0.4 mm grid with the pads drilled and plated by a subcontractor. Commodore did not own one; it bought them.
facility.foundries.hk-pcb.note: The bare-board manufacturer is not named in any source I found; 'manufactured in Hong Kong' is the documented claim.

facility.foundries.santa-clara.name: CBM Santa Clara, California
facility.foundries.santa-clara.description: Commodore's US assembly line, where production of the C64 began in late summer 1982. It had automated component-insertion equipment. It went badly: excessive video and audio noise, excessive heat, and semiconductors incompatible with the design, so yield was low, cost high and returns came back. Only a limited number of units came out of Santa Clara before responsibility was shifted to Commodore Japan in the autumn of 1982.

facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute.name: The automated-insertion board layout fight
facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute.description: Commodore's US plant used automatic component insertion; the Japanese plant did not, and the two wanted different component spacing. Charpentier's group won: the C64 board was laid out for automated insertion, and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools. This single decision is why every C64 motherboard was made in Hong Kong.

facility.foundries.mos.name: MOS Technology / Commodore Semiconductor Group fab, Norristown PA
facility.foundries.mos.description: The fab that made the 6510, the 6567/6569 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, the 6526 CIA and the ROMs. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 by John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin as a second source for Texas Instruments' calculator chips, was majority-owned by Allen-Bradley from 1970, and built its own plant on 14 acres of the Valley Forge Corporate Center, 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania. It was a 1-micron NMOS fab running 4-inch wafers, and it is the only place the C64's silicon came from - none of the five custom chips could ever be second-sourced. Commodore bought MOS outright for a 9.4% stake in CBM in November 1976 and merged it in 1981. The fab was closed in 1992 after Commodore's bankruptcy.
facility.foundries.mos.note: Sources variously call the location Norristown, Valley Forge or Lower Providence; the EPA documents put the plant at 950 Rittenhouse Road in Lower Providence Township, Norristown PA, in the former Valley Forge Corporate Center.
places: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania

facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor.name: After Commodore: GMT Microelectronics
facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor.description: The fab was bought out of bankruptcy in December 1994 for about $4.3 million plus $1 million of liabilities (including the EPA licence), reopened in 1995, ran a 1-micron process for third parties, and was shut down by the EPA in 2000-01. 183 employees and $21 million of revenue in 1999. It is a rare, well-documented instance of a 1970s fab surviving the death of its owner.

facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototypi.name: The captive fab as a prototyping advantage
facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototypi.description: The reason Commodore could design a chip in nine months: the fab was not full, the mask shop and the processing line were on site, and a designer could pull a test chip in a few weeks - or, in an emergency, four days. Ziembicki's line is the whole story of Commodore's speed: 'We were using people who were there anyway... You waste a little bit of silicon, but silicon's pretty cheap. It's only sand.'

facts.label: Turnaround
facts.value: a few weeks; 4 days in an emergency

facility.foundries.corporate-structure.name: The corporate chain that owned all of it
facility.foundries.corporate-structure.description: From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top; Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas); Commodore Electronics Ltd (CEL, Bahamas) as the principal operating corporation; Commodore Business Machines Inc (CBM, West Chester PA) as the US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division; Commodore Japan Ltd (CJL); Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd (CE(HK)L) and, after April 1982, the Hong Kong branch of CEL; Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH (West Germany); and CBM International Sales Inc, the DISC. MOS Technology was merged into CBM on 1 January 1981 and carried on as a division - which is why all the chips were still stamped with the MOS logo until 1989.

facts.label: MOS acquisition
facts.value: CBM agreed to buy MOS in November 1976 for a 9.4% equity stake in CBM; merged into CBM 1 January 1981

facility.foundries.vertical-integration.name: Vertical integration as a strategy
facility.foundries.vertical-integration.description: Tramiel's thesis, and the reason the whole tree looks the way it does: if you own the chip, you do not pay a merchant supplier's margin, you control the schedule, and nobody can raise your price. The concrete results: a $135 initial production cost against a $595 retail price, and a production cost driven down to $35-50 by 1985.

facility.cleanroom.name: The semiconductor fab building
facility.cleanroom.description: Where the C64's five custom chips were made. A 1-micron NMOS fab: a raised access floor over a service plenum, a ceiling of HEPA filters feeding laminar-flow hoods and open cleanroom, Class 100 in the process bays and Class 1000 in the support areas, and a yellow-lit room for photolithography. Air changed 100-1000 times an hour and consumed most of the plant's electricity.
facility.cleanroom.note: The 1980s standard was US Federal Standard 209E (1963), which is why everyone said 'Class 100' rather than ISO Class 5. ISO 14644 only arrived in 1995.

facts.label: Class definition
facts.value: Class 100 = <=100 particles >=0.5 um per cubic foot of air

facts.label: Fab capital cost
facts.value: roughly $4 M in 1970 (a small fab) rising through $100-300 M for a full 1980s 100-300 mm fab

facility.cleanroom.workforce.name: Fab workforce, 1980s
facility.cleanroom.workforce.description: A large 1983 fab ran 5,000-10,000 employees, of whom the majority working on the wafer lines were women - the largest single female industrial workforce in many of the regions where the plants went, because the tool operators and the wafer handling were culturally coded as women's work even though they were skilled and tightly controlled.
facility.cleanroom.workforce.note: Commodore's own Norristown fab was far smaller; the reference here is to the industry-wide pattern the brief describes, which I could not verify with a firm number for a single named 1983 plant.

facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.name: Wafer handling and shipping hardware
facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.description: In 1983 a wafer still travelled in a quartz boat inside a plastic carrier, or hand-carried in a PTFE-wafer cassette from process to process. The SMIF FOUP - the sealed nitrogen-purged single-wafer container that made the whole modern fab possible - arrived with SEMI E10 in the early 1990s. Before that, every transfer was an opportunity for a particle, and a large fraction of the total defect budget.
facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.note: Modern practice is the 300 mm FOUP in a minienvironment with automatic material handling; the 1980s practice was a person carrying a cassette.

facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat.name: Fused-quartz wafer boat
facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat.description: A slotted quartz holder that carries 25-50 wafers through the diffusion furnace. Fused quartz is used because it survives 1000 C, expands predictably, and is chemically inert to the dopants. Made from high-purity synthetic quartz rod, ground and flame-polished.

facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.name: Garment and consumable supply
facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.description: Garments were not laundryable in the era - a hooded coverall was worn once and destroyed. The plant bought enormous quantities of spun-bonded polypropylene garments, hoods, overshoes, gloves, wipes and tacky mats, and washed nothing. One 1980s 5,000-person fab burned something like a million garments a year.
facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.note: The garment figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate; I did not find a published 1983 consumption figure. Modern fabs launder and reuse garments and use more reusable materials, which was one of the first sustainability targets in the industry.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order of 1 million garments per year at a large fab

facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.name: Spun-bonded polypropylene
facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.description: Polypropylene melt-spun into continuous filaments and laid down in a random web, then bonded by heat or needle punching. Cheapest possible cleanroom garment material, and the raw material for the 'tacky mat' that caught shoe-borne particles at every airlock.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter.name: Pre-filter bank
facility.cleanroom.prefilter.description: Bag or panel filters (2-5 micrometre) ahead of the HEPA units, on the make-up air ducts and on the return air. The 1980s standard pre-filter was a 5-ply disposable bag of coarse glass fibre in a steel frame, or a V-bank of 1-inch washable aluminium-header panels. It existed because a HEPA that gets loaded with dust is an expensive mistake.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.name: Coarse glass-fibre filter media
facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.description: Glass melted and blown into coarse fibres and felted into a mat. The same glassfibre technology as the HEPA medium but 100-1000x coarser and far cheaper. Ends at the glass batch.

facility.cleanroom.cost.name: What the building cost (1983 dollars)
facility.cleanroom.cost.description: For scale: a small 4-inch fab cost about $4 million in 1970 (about $31 million in 2024 money); a full production fab in 1983 ran from roughly $100 million to several hundred million dollars - National Semiconductor announced a $100 million, 290,000 sq ft plant in August 1983, and UMC spent about $200 million on a 1.2 micron fab in the same year. That is why owning a fab was only ever available to very large firms.
facility.cleanroom.cost.note: The '$100-300 M' figure in the brief is right for a 1980s production fab; the $4 M figure is right for an early small 4-inch fab like MOS's.

facility.cleanroom.airlock.name: Gowning and airlock
facility.cleanroom.airlock.description: A two-stage airlock - a 'dirty airlock' for incoming components and personnel in street clothes, and a 'clean airlock' with a cross-over bench for gowning. The costume of the era was a hooded coverall plus boots; in the amber room a yellow-coated garment as well.

facility.cleanroom.hvac.name: Temperature and humidity control
facility.cleanroom.hvac.description: 20-22 C and 40-60% relative humidity, tighter than any other building of the era, and the single most expensive thing in the building to get right. The 1980s control was a system of pneumatic controllers and a mechanical chart recorder; a modern fab uses thousands of sensors and a BMS.

facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.name: Make-up air and air change rate
facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.description: The fab's single largest utility load. Because the Class 100 rooms were almost entirely recirculating, the make-up air was only the leakage plus the exhaust: the acid and solvent fume hoods, the furnace exhaust, the ion-implant exhaust. Even so, a 1980s fab typically ran 100-1000 air changes per hour in the clean bays and 20-60 in the support areas, and the air-handling plant cost tens of millions of dollars and dominated the energy bill.
facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.note: Modern practice is roughly the same air-change figure but with far better heat recovery, a 6-second air exchange in Class 1 areas, and much higher total electrical intensity per square foot because the process tools now dominate.

facility.cleanroom.passivation.name: Passivation and packaging areas
facility.cleanroom.passivation.description: Passivation (the final silicon nitride or phosphosilicate glass over the completed aluminium) and then the back-end: wafer probe, dice, die attach, wire bond, and the moulding of the ceramic or plastic package. The back end in 1983 was Class 10000 to Class 1000, not Class 100 - the contaminating work (bonding, moulding compound) happened there.

facility.cleanroom.litho-area.name: Photolithography area
facility.cleanroom.litho-area.description: Mask aligners, coat/develop tracks, bake ovens and the mask storage cabinets. In a 1980s 1-micron NMOS fab the lithography bay was Class 100 with the amber lighting, the operators wore yellow-room coats and face shields, and the photoresist was spun from a solvent (Shipley AZ1350, based on a novolak resin sensitised with a diazonium salt) with xylene or cellosolve acetate.

facility.cleanroom.amber-room.name: Amber (yellow) room for photolithography
facility.cleanroom.amber-room.description: The lithography bay was lit only through yellow filters - either yellow-lens fluorescent fixtures or, later, a laminated film - so that no light below about 500 nm reached the photoresist. The 1980s specification was that irradiance from 350 to 500 nm should stay below roughly 0.5 W/m2 at the work surface, with the rest of the spectrum unrestricted. Resists of the period were sensitive to the mercury g-line (436 nm), h-line (405 nm) and i-line (365 nm).
facility.cleanroom.amber-room.note: The classic 1980s yellow room was a room with yellow fluorescent tubes. That alone was often not enough - later measurement work has shown legacy 'yellow' tube lighting can still expose resist within an hour - so good fabs added a second, external filter film. Modern practice is to run the room in white light and rely on the area's low-actinic-UV requirement plus dosimetry.

facts.label: Actinic lines
facts.value: g 436 nm, h 405 nm, i 365 nm (mercury lamp)

facility.cleanroom.classes.name: Class 100 and Class 1000 zoning
facility.cleanroom.classes.description: Federal Standard 209E Class 100 in the lithography, etch and metallisation bays; Class 1000 in the diffusion, cleaning and packaging areas; Class 10,000 in the corridors, the airlock and the material store. The class was maintained by air pressure differentials - the Class 100 room slightly positive to the Class 1000 room, which was positive to the corridor - which is why the doors of a 1980s fab always felt like they were being blown open.
facility.cleanroom.classes.note: Modern practice: ISO 14644-1/2, ISO Class 5 (equivalent to the old Class 100) and Class 7 (Class 1000), with ISO Class 8 corridors and much tighter pressure control.

facility.cleanroom.ffu.name: Fan filter unit and laminar flow
facility.cleanroom.ffu.description: A 2.4 x 1.2 m fan-filter unit or a fan coil with an integral HEPA, blowing filtered air down through perforated ceiling tiles at 0.3-0.5 m/s to give unidirectional ('laminar') flow. Open cleanroom used ceiling FFUs over the whole floor; the 1980s move was to a 'minienvironment' - a small FFU box over each process tool inside a Class 1000 room - which was the direct ancestor of today's SMIF pods.

facts.label: Filter bank
facts.value: typically 5-10% of floor area in FFU ceiling

facility.cleanroom.hepa.name: HEPA (absolute) filter
facility.cleanroom.hepa.description: Deep pleated borosilicate glass-fibre media in a galvanised steel casing, rated 99.97% efficient at 0.3 micrometres - the most penetrating particle size, hence 'most penetrating diameter'. A 2.4 m x 1.2 m filter was the ceiling module of every 1980s fab, ceiling and laminar-flow bench alike.
facility.cleanroom.hepa.note: HEPA rated at 0.3 um is the number quoted then; it is a worst-case penetration figure, not the true 0.5 um count the class designation used.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: borosilicate glass microfibre on aluminium separator

facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.name: Borosilicate glass microfibre
facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.description: Glass melted at 1400 C and blown into fibres a few micrometres across, then laid into a paper and fired at 800-900 C to set a bonding agent, and chopped into slivers. Every 1980s fab consumed tens of thousands of these filters a year and changed them on a schedule rather than on condition.

facility.cleanroom.silica.name: High-purity silica
facility.cleanroom.silica.description: The same raw material as the fused-quartz diffusion tube, the photomask substrate and the ceramic package: high-purity SiO2. In 1983 most came from Brazil or from the US inland deposit, and by the mid-80s the industry moved to synthetic vapour-deposited silicon tetrafluoride because natural high-purity quartz was getting scarce.

facility.cleanroom.access-floor.name: Access floor panel
facility.cleanroom.access-floor.description: A 600 mm square steel or aluminium-frame panel with a steel or cast-iron skin, on adjustable pedestals with seismic and electrical bonding. The panel had to be load-rated for a 1000 kg diffusion furnace cart and still be light enough for two people to lift.

facility.cleanroom.raised-floor.name: Raised floor and plenum
