facility.cleanroom.raised-floor.description: A 600 mm or 900 mm void under a load-rated pedestal floor, with all the process exhaust, the cold water, the nitrogen, the vacuum and the electrical cabling running underneath. The whole architectural idea of the fab is that the floor is a duct. This is also why the 1980s fabs needed full basements and 4.5-6 m ceilings.

facility.hazardous-waste.name: Hazardous and industrial waste, 1980s practice
facility.hazardous-waste.description: The part of the story usually left out. A 1980s electronics plant generated, per fab, tens of thousands of gallons of spent acid, spent solvent, cyanide-bearing rinse, and metal-bearing sludge a year, plus a smaller amount of contaminated equipment and packaging. What happened to it was loosely governed - in the US by RCRA, which had only been in force for three years in 1983 - and often not well.

facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.name: Commodore's own solvent site: the CSG Superfund case
facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.description: The clearest documented example in this whole story. A 250-gallon underground concrete tank at the MOS Technology site at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania - installed with the building in 1970 - leaked in 1974. It stored the trichloroethene and other solvents used to clean silicon wafers. MOS replaced it with an unlined steel tank, which leaked too. In 1978 the Audubon Water Company, which supplied the public water system, detected trichloroethene in its wells. PADER concluded by 1979 that the contamination could not be excavated. A ground-water recovery well and a spray/treatment system began in November 1981; an air stripper began in February 1984. The site went on the Superfund National Priorities List on 4 October 1989 and the fab was closed in 1992.
facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.note: The site history is documented in unusually fine detail because it was litigated for 15 years: the tanks, the replacement, the recovery well VFCC-4, the stripper, and the 1981 practice of spraying pumped groundwater onto surrounding fields to volatilise the VOCs. All of that is in the public record.

facts.label: Leak
facts.value: 1974; TCE found in public wells in 1978

facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.name: Trichloroethene (TCE)
facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.description: A chlorinated solvent, 1,1,2-trichloroethene, once the standard vapour-degreasing and wafer-cleaning solvent in the semiconductor industry. A suspected carcinogen; a common groundwater contaminant; the specific reason the Norristown site is on the National Priorities List.

facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.name: Ethylene from the steam cracker
facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.description: The chlorination of ethylene, or the oxychlorination of 1,2-dichloroethane, which is itself from the chlorination of ethylene. The ethylene came from naphtha steam cracking - the same petrochemical chain as everything else on this tree. Ends at the crude oil still.

facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.name: Ocean outfall
facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.description: In the coastal Far East - Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines - dilute effluent was and is discharged through a permitted outfall diffuser into the sea, often at a designated ocean disposal zone beyond the territorial limit. The dilution argument is real; so is the fact that the 1980s outfalls had almost no metals monitoring.
facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.note: The offshore dumping of raw sludge - not diluted effluent - was also common in the Far East until the early 1990s and was progressively banned.

facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.name: The RCRA manifest
facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.description: A multi-part paper form - the shipping paper, the generator certification and the transporter and facility certifications - carried with the load from generator to treatment, storage or disposal facility, with signed copies returned to the generator. This is the paper trail that later made it possible to reconstruct where Commodore's waste went.

facts.label: Copies
facts.value: at least 4 (generator, transporter, TSDF, and the returned copy)

facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.name: Incineration of solvent vapours
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.description: Vapour incineration (afterburner / thermal oxidiser) for the xylene, toluene and trichloroethane vapour from the resist track and the degreaser, plus a wet scrubber or a carbon absorber on the cool side. By the time the air came out it passed an oxidiser at 800-1000 C with a residence time of about one second.
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.note: Solvent recovery by activated-carbon adsorption and distillation was increasingly preferred for cost reasons even in 1983 - recovery plant cost money to buy but paid back in solvent.

facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.name: Acid neutralisation with lime
facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.description: The cheapest and by far the most common treatment: slaked lime or limestone slurry is dosed into a reaction tank, the acid is neutralised, the metal hydroxides precipitate out, and the tank is then settled and the supernatant discharged. It converts an acid into a sludge - which is still a hazardous waste, just a solid one.

facility.hazardous-waste.landfill.name: Hazardous waste landfill
facility.hazardous-waste.landfill.description: In 1983 a hazardous landfill was typically a clay-lined cell with a leachate collection system and groundwater monitoring wells, licensed under RCRA or operating under interim status. Because the Land Disposal Restrictions did not yet exist, most of it received untreated sludge and incinerator ash.

facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond.name: Settling pond / lagoon
facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond.description: An unlined or clay-lined earthen basin into which treated effluent was discharged and solids allowed to settle, with the supernatant decanted to a stream or a municipal sewer. Thousands of these existed in 1983; the liner requirements came later. The pond was often the plant's cheapest and worst idea.

facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.name: Heavy-metal hydroxide sludge
facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.description: A wet, low-solids sludge of iron, aluminium, chromium, copper, nickel, zinc and cadmium hydroxides, filtered on a plate-and-frame or belt press to 15-25% solids and trucked to a hazardous landfill in a lined, covered cell. In 1983 this was the default destination and the reason so many US sites are now Superfund sites.

facility.hazardous-waste.generation.name: What a plant actually generated
facility.hazardous-waste.generation.description: Spent sulfuric and hydrochloric acid from etching; spent developer (tetramethylammonium hydroxide from positive photoresist) and stripper; acetone, xylene, toluene, IPA and cellosolve acetate; arsenic-containing waste from the diffusion furnaces; cyanide-bearing waste from the gold and tin plating; and copper/nickel/chromium-bearing rinse. Small generators - which in 1983 was most of Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base - had almost no obligations at all beyond a monthly manifest.

facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.name: RCRA: the cradle-to-grave regime
facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.description: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act became law on 21 October 1976. Its Subtitle C hazardous waste regulations were promulgated 26 February and 19 May 1980 and took effect 19 November 1980 - so in 1983 the whole American electronics industry was three years into the most consequential change in waste handling since the Clean Air Act. Generators must determine whether a waste is hazardous, accumulate it in a closed, labelled, inspected area for no more than 90 days, describe it on a manifest, and ship it only to a permitted treatment, storage or disposal facility.
facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.note: The 1984 Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments (HSWA) tightened this substantially, including the ban on land disposal of untreated hazardous waste; in 1983 that ban did not yet exist and land disposal of untreated sludge was routine and lawful.

facility.compressed-air.name: Instrument air and plant air
facility.compressed-air.description: Every factory ran on compressed air. Instrument air was dried, oil-free air fed to the air-line and to the logic valves; plant air was for the pneumatic tools, the automated insertion machines and the ejectors. The classic 1980s split was a dedicated compressor for instrument air and one or more dirty machines for everything else.

facility.compressed-air.fab-exhaust.name: Process exhaust (fab wet-bench and furnace)
facility.compressed-air.fab-exhaust.description: A separate, larger system from the instrument air: a scrubbed chemical exhaust ducting the acid, base, solvent and furnace exhaust out of the building, usually to an alkaline scrubber on the roof. See facility.hazardous-waste for the emissions and liquid side.

facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.name: Alkaline scrubber packing
facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.description: A packed column of plastic Raschig or saddle rings on a support grid, fed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate, stripping acid mist and the base-mist equivalent out of the exhaust. Discharge is a neutral brine sent to the effluent system.

facility.compressed-air.caustic-soda.name: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
facility.compressed-air.caustic-soda.description: Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH, with the hydrogen and chlorine sold and the caustic sold. The most-used industrial chemical on the site. Ends at salt and electricity.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: roughly 2,200-2,500 kWh per tonne of NaOH (as Cl2)

facility.compressed-air.salt-brine.name: Brine (concentrated sodium chloride)
facility.compressed-air.salt-brine.description: Either evaporated sea salt or a solution of mined rock salt, brined to saturation and clarified with lime and salt cake. Ends at the salt field or the sea.

facility.compressed-air.rock-salt-mine.name: Rock salt mine
facility.compressed-air.rock-salt-mine.description: Bedded evaporite salt (halite) mined by room-and-pillar in shafts or by solution mining in the brine field, in Permian or Silurian formations. Ends at the salt body in the rock.

facility.compressed-air.membrane-cell.name: Chlor-alkali membrane cell
facility.compressed-air.membrane-cell.description: From the late 1980s the diaphragm cell gave way to the cation-exchange membrane cell, which makes caustic soda pure enough to go straight into a transistor wet bench instead of being evaporated. In 1983 most plants still used diaphragm or mercury cells, which made their caustic soda full of salt - a real problem for a photoresist developer.

facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.name: PVC / PP packing media
facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.description: Moulded plastic ring or saddle packing, chemically inert to acid and alkali where ceramic or metal would be attacked. The same vinyl chloride monomer chain that makes the conduit and the cable in the plant.

facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.name: Nitrogen purge of the air system
facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.description: Before opening a vessel, a line, or a tank that had held flammable or reactive material, it was purged with nitrogen and tested with an oxygen analyser. The purge itself was fed from the nitrogen header or, in a small plant, from a bottled cylinder.

facility.compressed-air.ring-main.name: Ring main and distribution
facility.compressed-air.ring-main.description: Black steel pipe - galvanised or, better, painted steel - in a ring around the plant with drop-legs to each machine. A ring rather than a spine so that a single closed valve could isolate a section for maintenance. Drops went through a service unit with a tap, a pressure regulator, a filter and a flowmeter at each bench.

facility.compressed-air.receiver.name: Air receiver (accumulator)
facility.compressed-air.receiver.description: A vertical ASME code air vessel, 1-10 m3, acting as a buffer so the compressor could unload on a pressure switch. It also stored enough air to ride through a power cut for a few minutes - which in a fab meant keeping the wet-bench exhaust and the compressors together.

facility.compressed-air.dryer.name: Air dryer
facility.compressed-air.dryer.description: Two chemistries in 1983. Refrigerant (absorption or adsorption, e.g. a zeolite unit chilled to 1-3 C) gave a pressure dew point of about 2-10 C, good enough for most pneumatic machinery and marginal for instrument air. Desiccant (two alternating towers of silica gel or molecular sieve with a heatless regeneration on the off-line tower) got the dew point down to -40 to -70 C, which was what a pneumatic logic valve or a moisture-sensitive process needed.
facility.compressed-air.dryer.note: Modern practice is a zero-pressure-change desiccant dryer with a heated purge and dew-point controlled switching; in 1983 the purge air was thrown away, which is why instrument-air plants were noisy and hot.

facility.compressed-air.refrigerant.name: Refrigerant (CFC-11/12, or ammonia)
facility.compressed-air.refrigerant.description: The refrigeration for an absorption dryer. CFC-11 and CFC-12 were the universal choices and are the ozone-depleting gases the 1987 Montreal Protocol eventually banned - so this node is both a 1983 fact and a direct cause of later environmental regulation.

facility.compressed-air.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) for the HF needed to make CFCs
facility.compressed-air.fluorspar.description: Metallurgical-grade fluorspar for the anhydrous hydrofluoric acid that reacts with chloroform to make the chlorofluorocarbons. A large share of the 1980s HF demand, and a distinct little industry with its own mine (Fluorspar, Derbyshire; Kerimsi, Turkey; San Luis Potosi, Mexico). Ends at the fluorite vein.

facility.compressed-air.fluorspar-mine.name: Fluorspar mine
facility.compressed-air.fluorspar-mine.description: Vein or replacement deposit of fluorite in limestone, often with a metre-scale overburden, worked by open pit or by shallow shaft. Ends at the ore body.

facility.compressed-air.separator.name: Water (and oil) separator
facility.compressed-air.separator.description: An automatic drain pot or cyclone knock-out that removes the condensed water and, in an oil-injected screw machine, the injected oil. This vessel was the source of most of the 'the air is wet' complaints in the shop.

facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.name: Aftercooler
facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.description: A water-cooled or finned-air heat exchanger that takes the discharge air from ~100 C down to ~40 C. Without it the machine would not hold pressure in a hot climate and the separator would not work.

facility.compressed-air.compressor.name: Air compressor
facility.compressed-air.compressor.description: Reciprocating or, from the 1960s onward, oil-injected rotary screw machines. A large electronics plant ran several 100-300 kW screw units; a small sub-contractor ran one 30 kW reciprocating machine under a concrete acoustic enclosure.

facility.compressed-air.motor.name: Drive motor
facility.compressed-air.motor.description: A TEFC or, in a corrosive coastal plant, an explosion-proof motor. 400 V three-phase induction motor with a direct-on-line or star-delta starter; speed control only by pole changing.

facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer.name: Intake silencer and inlet filter
facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer.description: An intake filter-silencer combination that kept the machine from eating the dust and the unfiltered outside air. In a coastal site (Kaohsiung, Hong Kong, Long Beach) the sea salt went straight onto the rotors if this was neglected.

facility.gases.name: Industrial gas supply
facility.gases.description: The bulk gases a 1980s electronics plant bought by the tanker load: nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen, plus the specialty gases. Supplied either by an on-site air separation unit, an on-site PSA/membrane/electrolyser, or delivered as liquid from a merchant producer in a road tanker.

facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.name: Carbon dioxide (dry ice)
facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.description: Used in the plant for refrigerant cargo, for the dry-ice shipping of perishables, and - in the electronics plant - for nothing much; the two dry-ice applications in a 1980s C64 supply chain were chilling the shipped goods and cleaning moulds of frost. Skipping the beverage-carbonation story as instructed.

facility.gases.co2-ammonia.name: Ammonia-synthesis CO2 (fertiliser plant)
facility.gases.co2-ammonia.description: A large part of the 1980s merchant CO2 came from hydrogen- and ammonia-based fertiliser plants, where the shift reactor CO2 is captured and dried. Ends at natural gas and air.

facility.gases.nitrogen-purge-system.name: Bulk liquid storage and tube trailers
facility.gases.nitrogen-purge-system.description: The logistics layer of the gases: a merchant ASU on the edge of the industrial park with bulk tanks, or a fleet of tube trailers on a shift schedule, delivering 24 hours' supply into a customer's own cryogenic tank.

facility.gases.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen
facility.gases.hydrogen.description: Three routes in 1983: (a) bulk hydrogen from a merchant plant by tube trailer or by liquefaction; (b) on-site steam methane reforming of natural gas, the standard for anything above about 100 Nm3/h; and (c) electrolysis of demineralised water for the last, and highest, purity.

facility.gases.hydrogen.uses.name: Where hydrogen went in a 1980s electronics plant
facility.gases.hydrogen.uses.description: Hydrocarbon and silicone greasing, hydrogen annealing of the copper and the metallisation, the reducing atmosphere in the diffusion furnace and the epitaxial reactor, and - for the tie-in with this story - the hydrogen atmosphere in the case of a lamp or a nickel/plated through-hole fill was not yet standard practice.

facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.name: Electrolysis of demineralised water
facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.description: In a diaphragm or, from the 1970s, an alkaline cell, a nickel-plated or activated-titanium cathode makes hydrogen while a nickel anode makes oxygen. Fed with conductivity-grade water at 20-25 C. Output purity is 99.99% once the cell gas is passed over a palladium diffuser or an oxygen getter - the 'deoxo' step that killed the last 0.1% of oxygen.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: about 50-55 kWh per kg of hydrogen

facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.name: Steam methane reforming
facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.description: Natural gas is desulphurised to under 0.5 ppm sulphur, mixed with steam at 3:1 and passed over a nickel-molybdenum or chromite catalyst at 800-850 C and 15-25 bar. This gives hydrogen plus CO, and the CO is shifted over an iron-chrome catalyst to CO2 and more hydrogen. Then CO2 is removed by amine scrubbing or molecular sieve.

facility.gases.nickel-catalyst.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
facility.gases.nickel-catalyst.description: Nickel oxide on alumina, or the classic nickel-molybdenum on alumina, formed by impregnating a porous pellet with nickel nitrate and calcining. Ends at the laterite and the bauxite.

facility.gases.laterite.name: Nickel laterite ore
facility.gases.laterite.description: The dominant world nickel ore in 1983 - a limonite/garnierite blanket over ultramafic rock in New Caledonia, Cuba, the Philippines and Indonesia, usually smelted in a ferronickel plant. The Philippines connection is the direct one to the C64's subcontractor geography.

facility.gases.laterite-mine.name: Laterite open pit
facility.gases.laterite-mine.description: Weathered ultramafic mantle rock, strip-mined by shovel and truck. Ends at the saprolite profile in the ground.

facility.helium.name: Helium
facility.helium.description: In 1983 helium was a genuinely scarce, genuinely odd commodity. Most of the world's supply came from a handful of natural-gas fractionation plants in Texas, Wyoming, Kansas and New Mexico, which extracted the 0.0005-0.005% helium in the gas as a crude 50-75% mixture. The rest came from four dedicated underground helium fields - the hug gas of Amarillo, Texas, and the Dixon and Harley fields in Kansas. Cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s.
facility.helium.note: Helium was rationed and price-controlled in the US until the 1996 helium policy change; a factory that needed it in 1983 wrote to a supplier, waited, and paid whatever was quoted.

facility.helium.supply-constraint.name: The 1980s helium shortage
facility.helium.supply-constraint.description: US Bureau of Mines and then BLM administered the supply; the Cliffside field ran out in the mid-1970s and production was rationed, so helium became genuinely rationed and expensive for laboratories and for leak testing. This is a real constraint on the 1980s helium supply chain, not a later phenomenon.

facility.helium.hug-gas.name: Hug gas from an underground helium reservoir
facility.helium.hug-gas.description: The Permian Basin of west Texas and the southwest Kansas gas fields hold helium that never migrated out of the crust, trapped under impermeable salt and anhydrite since geological time. These are drilled specifically for helium, at tiny volumes - Amarillo field production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year even in its peak.

facts.label: Fields
facts.value: Cliffside, Amarillo and Bush, Texas; Hugoton, Kansas

facts.label: Age of the source
facts.value: helium accumulated since Precambrian radiogenic decay

facility.helium.cryo-separation.name: Cryogenic helium separation from natural gas
facility.helium.cryo-separation.description: The gas is chilled to -190 C through a train of plate-fin heat exchangers; helium, having the second-lowest boiling point, stays in the vapour phase and is drawn off from the top of the cold box as a crude 50-75% helium stream. Then purified by cryogenic adsorption, catalytic dehydrogenation of the residual hydrogen and activated-carbon adsorption of the nitrogen.

facility.helium.liquid-helium.name: Liquid helium dewar (4.2 K)
facility.helium.liquid-helium.description: A double-walled stainless vessel with a superinsulating vacuum jacket, holding 4.2 K liquid helium for a cryostat or a superconducting magnet. Expensive, evaporating at about 0.5-1% a day, and topped up by truck in a dewar that looked like a scaled-down rocket stage.

facility.helium.activated-carbon-adsorbe.name: Activated carbon helium purification
facility.helium.activated-carbon-adsorbe.description: The last step: nitrogen is adsorbed on a char bed at 77 K to give 99.995% (5N) or 99.9999% (6N) helium. The same activated-carbon adsorption principle as the water-treatment carbon, run at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

facility.argon.name: Argon
facility.argon.description: Argon is not made; it is separated out. It is the third component of air and comes off the top of the ASU's nitrogen column, either as an argon-nitrogen mixture from a simple unit or as 99.99% pure from a dedicated argon column. Most 1980s plants bought it by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant.

facility.argon.uses.name: Where argon actually went in 1983
facility.argon.uses.description: TIG welding of the sheet metal and the transformer laminations, the inert blanket over the 1800 C silicon melt in the crystal puller, and - increasingly - argon sputter deposition of the aluminium interconnect in a fab.

facility.argon.argon-column.name: Argon recovery column
facility.argon.argon-column.description: A second, smaller column that separates the nitrogen-argon mixture from the top of the nitrogen column into pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops. Installed when the oxygen plant needed the argon value or the customer paid for it - usually in a semiconductor or welding-wire plant, not in a steelworks.

facility.gases.oxygen.name: Oxygen supply
facility.gases.oxygen.description: Supplied as liquid oxygen from a merchant AS U or from the site unit. Used for the oxy-acetylene flame of the mechanical and maintenance shops, the gas-shielded welding of the metal frames, and increasingly for the oxygen plasma strip in a fab.

facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.name: Acetylene cylinder
facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.description: Dissolved acetylene at 15 bar in a porous monolithic mass (calcium carbide + acetone), in a steel shell. Calcium carbide came from the electric arc furnace carbide plant, i.e. ultimately from coal coke and quicklime.

facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.name: Oxy-acetylene flame for tool and frame welding
facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.description: Oxygen plus a locally generated acetylene from calcium carbide (in the Far East, imported cylinder acetylene was common). This is the flame that welded every sheet-metal chassis, rack and jig in the factory.

facility.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen supply
facility.nitrogen.description: The single largest bulk gas. Used for inerting storage tanks and vessels, blanketing, purging, and as the carrier gas in diffusion furnaces and plasma etchers. Small plants bought a few tonnes a month of liquid N2; a furnace-loaded fab wanted tens of tonnes a day and built its own ASU.

facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.name: Tube trailer (bulk gas road delivery)
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.description: A tractor-trailer carrying 30-40 high-pressure cylinders or a single multi-compartment tube bundle of 6,000-15,000 litres, delivering liquid nitrogen, oxygen or argon from a merchant plant. In 1983 this was how a factory without an on-site ASU got its gases; the driver's unload was a vent line that fogged the yard and alarmed the neighbours.
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.note: Oxygen road tankers in that era were often marked with a diamond placard and were the single most dangerous vehicle in the industrial park.

facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage.name: Bulk cryogenic liquid storage
facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage.description: A double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless tank on a skirt, with a vacuum-insulated transfer line (a double pipe with perlite or multilayer reflective insulation between) from the ASU or the delivery tanker. The tank is a pressure vessel rated to about 700-1000 kPa on the inner shell.

facts.label: Tank sizes
facts.value: 5-60 m3 merchant tankers; 50-500 m3 on-site bulk tanks

facility.nitrogen.membrane.name: Membrane nitrogen generator
facility.nitrogen.membrane.description: Hollow-fibre asymmetric polyimide or cellulose acetate membranes in a pressure vessel, 20-40 bar feed, with N2 diffusing through the wall faster than O2. Cheap, silent, no regeneration heat, and limited to about 90-95% nitrogen - which is fine for blanketing and not fine for a furnace. By 1983 membrane units were new and uncommon; they took the small-plant market from PSA in the 1990s.

facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.name: Hollow-fibre polyimide membrane
facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.description: A thin-walled asymmetric fibre, about 0.1-0.2 micrometre wall, with a selectively permeable outer skin. Making a defect-free fibre over a 1 m length was, and is, the hard part.

facility.nitrogen.psa.name: PSA / molecular-sieve nitrogen generator
facility.nitrogen.psa.description: Pressure swing adsorption: compressed air is adsorbed on beds of zeolite molecular sieve at 7-10 bar, then dropped to near atmospheric and purged with a slice of product to release the nitrogen. Gave 90-99% nitrogen cheaply at small scale; the 1980s workhorse for factories of under a few hundred kW load.
facility.nitrogen.psa.note: The user asked for 4000-6000 kPa: a PSA will not deliver oxygen at that pressure. That number is a liquid-oxygen or high-pressure-pipeline convention and belongs to the ASU branch, not here.

facility.nitrogen.zeolite.name: Zeolite molecular sieve (synthetic)
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.description: Crystalline hydrated aluminosilicate with a uniform 3-5 angstrom pore, made by hydrothermal crystallisation of bentonite, kaolin or synthetic gels. Uniform aperture size is what makes PSA possible - a zeolite with 3A pores excludes N2 and adsorbs only O2 and H2O; the 4A and 5A grades are used elsewhere in gas drying.
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.note: The same chemistry gives the 4A sieve that fills the R-2400 filter's perforated shell in the C64's power supply, if the cartridge was the zeolite type rather than the coil type.

facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.name: Cryogenic air separation unit (ASU)
facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.description: Air is filtered, compressed in a large multi-stage compressor to about 6-7 bar, cooled against the cold product streams until it liquefies, then fractionally distilled in a low-temperature column to make oxygen and a nitrogen-argon mixture. A unit also making argon has a separate argon column fed from the top of the nitrogen column. Typical small unit: 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h of oxygen.
facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.note: The prompt's '4000-6000 kPa' is the high-pressure liquid oxygen delivery case (pumped at 50-100 bar before the warm end of the vaporiser); a plant that piped oxygen directly would normally run at 400-600 kPa.

facts.label: Oxygen delivery pressure
facts.value: typically 0.5-0.6 MPa at the battery limit, piped up to 3-4 MPa

facility.nitrogen.expander.name: Expansion turbine (expander)
facility.nitrogen.expander.description: A turbine in the cold box that recovers the enthalpy drop of the expanding nitrogen and uses it to generate power, offsetting part of the ASU's compression energy. Standard from the 1960s onward.

facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.name: Fractionating columns
facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.description: Insulated stainless-steel columns 5-10 m tall with trays or packing, holding the low-temperature distillation that separates oxygen (bottoms, warmer) from nitrogen and argon (top, colder). A common 1980s arrangement was a single low-temperature column producing oxygen plus a nitrogen-argon mixture, with a side argon column.

facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.name: Cold box (plate-fin heat exchanger)
facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.description: A stack of aluminium brazed plate-fin exchangers, some 10-20 m tall, in which the compressed air is progressively cooled to -196 C by the outgoing oxygen and nitrogen. The heart of every ASU.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.name: Atmospheric air
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.description: 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, plus water and CO2. The single source of every bulk industrial gas. Delivered to an ASU intake through a windowless, acoustically baffled multi-bay intake so it arrived at a steady temperature, humidity and free of the dust that would plug a cryogenic plant.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.intake.name: Air intake stack
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.intake.description: A tall concrete or brick stack with louvres facing away from the prevailing wind, feeding a plenum and the air compressor. Intakes were sited so that no two of them - for air, for cooling water, for the coal yard - were close enough to contaminate each other.

facility.water.name: Water for a factory
facility.water.description: Every 1980s electronics and metals plant drank more water than it realised. Two distinct demands: ordinary industrial water (cooling, rinsing, process, human) and, in the fab, water pure enough to grow an oxide on silicon without introducing a defect.

facts.label: Industrial process water
facts.value: hundreds of m3 per day for cooling; tens of m3 per day of ultrapure

facility.water.industrial.name: Ordinary industrial water
facility.water.industrial.description: The 99% of the plant's water use: cooling, washing, rinsing, boiler feed, human use. Deliberately not ultrapure, deliberately recycled.

facility.water.leach-plant-water.name: Water in the leaching plants
facility.water.leach-plant-water.description: Where this tree passes through the metal and silicon trees, the water system is completely different: an agitated heap or tank leaching circuit with a counter-current rinse, a pregnant-liquor clarifier and a counter-current decant (CCD) wash, using acidic sulfate or alkaline cyanide liquor. The cyanide circuit consumed a large water volume and generated a cyanide-bearing tailings pond.
facility.water.leach-plant-water.note: This node exists to connect the water branch to the metals/silicon branches; the specific leaching chemistry belongs to those files.

facility.water.chiller.name: Reciprocating chiller
facility.water.chiller.description: A compressor, condenser and evaporator in a packaged unit, cooling water or air cooled. The alternative to evaporative cooling wherever the wet-bulb was too high. 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11, and therefore both a refrigerant-ozone problem and a safety problem.

facility.water.evaporative-cooling.name: Evaporative (swamp) cooler
facility.water.evaporative-cooling.description: A finned coil with water sprayed over it and an induced-draft fan. Far cheaper than a chiller and it worked well in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore, where the wet-bulb temperature was already low; useless in a humid July in Pennsylvania.

facility.water.cooling-tower.name: Induced-draught cooling tower
facility.water.cooling-tower.description: A 20-60 m concrete or steel shell packed with fill, with fan blades in the base drawing air up through the falling film of circulating water. Water evaporates, concentrates the dissolved solids, and is purged to the drain or the recovery plant.

facts.label: Evaporation loss
facts.value: ~1% of circulating flow per 10 C of wet-bulb depression

facility.water.chem-treatment.name: Cooling-water chemical treatment
facility.water.chem-treatment.description: Chromate-based corrosion inhibitors (the dominant, and environmentally toxic, 1980s chemistry), or the newer phosphate/phosphonate/zinc formulations, plus biocide (chlorine or an organomercurial/isothiazolinone blend) and an antiscalant acid. This is where a large share of the plant's chemical consumption went.
facility.water.chem-treatment.note: Chromate inhibitors were being phased out across the industrial West in the 1980s - the same decade Commodore's own site was a Superfund listing because of chlorinated solvent handling.

facility.water.chromate.name: Sodium chromate inhibitor
facility.water.chromate.description: A dichromate/chromate film former that passivates the steel of the cooling system. Enormously effective, and the reason thousands of 1980s cooling towers are a chromate source in the groundwater.

facility.water.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4)
facility.water.chromite.description: The only economic source of chromium. Mined by underground stoping in the Bushveld Complex of South Africa and elsewhere, then smelted to ferrochrome.

facility.water.chromite-mine.name: Chromite mine
facility.water.chromite-mine.description: A stratiform chromite seam (UG2 in the Bushveld) worked by stoping or by open pit. Ends at the chromitite layer in the ground.

facility.water.tower-filling.name: Tower fill and eliminator
facility.water.tower-filling.description: Cellulose (Kraft), PVC or polystyrene film fill media in a lattice or dendritic pack, plus a drift eliminator of PVC chevron sheets at the top. Cellulose fill was being replaced by flame-retardant PVC in the mid-1980s for fire reasons.

facility.water.ultrapure.name: Ultrapure water for the fab
facility.water.ultrapure.description: The water that rinses a silicon wafer between every process step, and the water in which the thermal oxide grows. Target in 1983 was 10-15 MOhm-cm (roughly 1 ppb total ionic impurities) held at 20-25 C, distributed in 304 stainless or PVDF-lined piping.
facility.water.ultrapure.note: The 1980s 'yellow room' photolithography step and the wet chemical benches were the biggest consumers; the C64 itself was an assembly operation, not a fab, but every IC on its board came from a plant running exactly this chain.

facts.label: 1983 practice
facts.value: 10-18 MOhm-cm; modern fabs specify 18 MOhm-cm at 25 C as a minimum

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: TOC <5 ppb in modern practice; 1980s practice often 50-100 ppb

facility.water.effluent.name: Effluent treatment and discharge
facility.water.effluent.description: Neutralisation, settling and (where the acidity and fluoride demanded it) lime neutralisation with fluoride precipitation, then discharge to a municipal sewer under a permit or to an outfall. See facility.hazardous-waste for the solid side.

facility.water.reclaim.name: Water reclaim and recovery loop
facility.water.reclaim.description: Acid and solvent rinses, dump rinses and cooling-tower blowdown collected, neutralised, filtered and fed back to the pretreatment inlet. Water conservation in a 1983 fab was a cost decision, not an environmental one, and typically recovered 50-70% of the plant's demand.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 50-70% of demand in a mature plant

facility.water.di-loop.name: Ultrapure distribution loop
facility.water.di-loop.description: Slotted 316L stainless or PVDF-lined pipework in a continuous recirculating loop, running hot at 60-80 C to suppress bacteria, with take-off points at each wet bench. A loop that is not constantly moving will grow biofilm within a day - the single hardest problem in 1980s ultrapure water.
facility.water.di-loop.note: Modern fabs run the loop cold and sterilise it; running hot was the 1980s answer to bio-growth.

facts.label: Loop temperature
facts.value: 60-80 C (1980s practice); 20-25 C (modern practice, with UV/UF)

facility.water.pp.name: Polypropylene piping
facility.water.pp.description: Polypropylene was the cheapest acid- and chemical-resistant pipe for wet-bench waste lines and reclaim, and (as spun-bonded fabric) the material of the 1980s 'class 100' air filter pre-filter.

facility.water.pvdf.name: PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride)
facility.water.pvdf.description: A fluoropolymer from vinylidene fluoride, chemically inert to ultrapure water and to most process acids, used as a liner or as solid pipe in ultrapure service. Melting point about 170 C, and it will not support microbial growth.

facility.water.ultrafiltration.name: Ultrafiltration
facility.water.ultrafiltration.description: Hollow-fibre or dead-end membranes with a 1-100 nm cut-off, pressurised at 1-4 bar, stripping colloids, bacteria and endotoxin from the DI loop and from the reclaim stream. Rare in the 1980s; the state of the art then was a 0.2 micrometre-rated 'final filter' on the last loop, or nothing.
facility.water.ultrafiltration.note: Modern fabs use UF as the terminal barrier before the distribution loop; 1980s fabs used 0.2 um PTFE or nylon membrane cartridges.

facility.water.uv.name: UV sterilisation
facility.water.uv.description: A 254 nm germicidal lamp in a stainless vessel, dosing typically 30-40 mJ/cm2, to kill bacteria and oxidise the last of the organics. Added in the late 1980s onward, mostly for the reclaim loop, because a 1970s fab did not sterilise its ultrapure water at all.
facility.water.uv.note: 1948-1983 practice: no UV, no ultrafiltration in most plants; bacteria were managed by keeping the loop hot (60-80 C for hot DI water) or by chlorination upstream.

facility.water.uv-lamp.name: Low-pressure mercury lamp
facility.water.uv-lamp.description: A quartz envelope with a low-pressure mercury vapour discharge emitting 254 nm, immersed in a quartz sleeve in the water. Same lamp chemistry as the germicidal fittings in hospitals.

facility.water.ro.name: Reverse osmosis
facility.water.ro.description: Cellulose acetate or thin-film composite spiral-wound elements in 6-inch pressure vessels rejecting 90-99% of dissolved ions, 95-98% of organics and, importantly for the 1980s plant, most of the silica and hardness. The first RO units were installed at plants like this from the mid-1970s; by 1983 they were displacing two beds of ion exchange ahead of the polishers.
facility.water.ro.note: Modern practice is two-pass RO with antiscalant dosing and a final UV and ultrafiltration; the 1980s plant had a single pass and no antiscalant.

facility.water.ro-membrane.name: Cellulose acetate / TFC membrane
facility.water.ro-membrane.description: A 0.2-1.5 micrometre-thick selective layer on a polysulphone support, wound into a spiral and potted with epoxy. This is the same membrane family as the 1541 floppy's read/write head gap in spirit - a nanoscale selective barrier - but the RO element was 1 m long.

facility.water.mixed-bed.name: Mixed-bed deioniser
facility.water.mixed-bed.description: A resin bed with cation and anion beads thoroughly mixed, polishing the effluent to sub-ppb. It was the top of the 1980s purity curve and was standard offtake to the wet benches.

facility.water.ion-exchange.name: Demineralisation by ion exchange
facility.water.ion-exchange.description: Strong-acid cation then strong-base anion exchange, then a mixed-bed polish. Removed >95% of the ionic load of the filtered water and got to 10-15 MOhm-cm. It could not remove silica, organics or colloids, and the resin was a huge organic load in itself.

facility.water.pretreatment.name: Pretreatment for the ultrapure plant
facility.water.pretreatment.description: Coagulation, clarification, multimedia filtration and activated carbon, all in one reinforced-concrete block that dominated the plant footprint. The purpose is to strip the water of the things that would poison an ion-exchange resin or foul an RO membrane: suspended solids, colour, hardness, chlorine, organics and silica.

facility.water.activated-carbon.name: Activated carbon adsorption
facility.water.activated-carbon.description: A tall bed of coconut-shell, coal or lignite carbon catalytically activated in a furnace, removing humic colour, trihalomethane precursor, pesticide and industrial organics. In the ultrapure plant it was the last chance to remove organics before the ion-exchange resin and the RO membrane.

facility.water.coconut-carbon.name: Coconut-shell activated carbon
facility.water.coconut-carbon.description: The premium grade, made in Sri Lanka, India or the Philippines by carbonising shell and steam-activating. The same material appears in the 8-bit filter section of a home computer.

facility.water.coconut-shell.name: Coconut shell (husk)
facility.water.coconut-shell.description: The waste husk of the coconut palm, dried in the sun and carbonised. Ends at the coconut plantation.

facility.water.multimedia-filtration.name: Multimedia (sand) filtration
facility.water.multimedia-filtration.description: Pressure filters in lead/catalysed iron tanks, 3.5-4.5 m diameter, containing 600-700 mm of graded media - typically 100 mm anthracite on 50 mm sand on 25 mm garnet. Backwashed with air scour plus water at 20-40 m/h.

facility.water.anthracite.name: Anthracite filter coal
facility.water.anthracite.description: Hard, coarse anthracite crushed to 1-2 mm as the coarse top layer. Same material as the boiler fuel, just graded differently.

facility.water.filter-sand.name: Silica filter sand
facility.water.filter-sand.description: Washed, graded, nearly pure SiO2 sand with effective size 0.5-0.7 mm. A large, unglamorous, and genuinely scarce mineral input to any waterworks.

facility.water.sand-quarry.name: Sand and gravel extraction pit
facility.water.sand-quarry.description: Sand and gravel pit, usually a river dredging operation. Ends at the sand deposit.

facility.water.coagulation.name: Coagulation and clarification
facility.water.coagulation.description: Alum or ferric chloride plus lime and a coagulant aid is flash-mixed, then the floc is grown in a flocculation bay and settled out over 2-4 hours in a clarifier. Residual turbidity had to be under about 1-2 NTU for the sand filters to be worth having.

facility.water.alum.name: Alum (hydrated aluminium sulfate)
facility.water.alum.description: The workhorse coagulant. Made from bauxite (or domestic low-grade bauxite/clay) digested in sulphuric acid and crystallised. Ended at the bauxite mine by way of the same chain that makes the aluminium in the grid conductor.

facility.water.sulphuric-acid.name: Sulphuric acid
facility.water.sulphuric-acid.description: Made by burning sulphur or roasting pyrite and absorbing the SO2 in a contact plant to 93-98% oleum-free acid. The single most-produced industrial chemical in the world, and the raw material for lead-acid batteries, phosphates and most water treatment.

facility.water.sulphur.name: Sulphur (from recovered petroleum gas)
facility.water.sulphur.description: By 1983 nearly all of the world's sulphur came from desulphurising high-sulphur crude and natural gas with Claus converters - i.e. it came out of the same crude oil that made the fuel oil.
facility.water.sulphur.note: Frasch-process sulphur from the Texas Gulf caprock rock had already been largely displaced by this point.

facility.power.bauxite-mine-alum.name: Bauxite ore for the alum plant
facility.power.bauxite-mine-alum.description: High-digestion alumina-grade bauxite, crushed and digested. The same input as the Bayer process. Ends at the ore body.

facility.water.raw-intake.name: Raw water intake
facility.water.raw-intake.description: Either a surface intake from a river or reservoir, or a deep well into a confined aquifer. Surface water for cooling, well water for the ultrapure plant - because groundwater is already filtered by geology and low in organics.

facility.water.surface-intake.name: River / reservoir intake and pump house
facility.water.surface-intake.description: A screened intake structure with travelling-bar screens, coarse screens and a low-lift pump house on the bank. In practice many 1980s plants - including Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones - bought municipal or industrial-zone water from the local authority and paid a tariff, rather than taking their own.

facility.water.river-intake.name: The river or reservoir
facility.water.river-intake.description: Turbid, hard, seasonally variable. The Schuylkill at Norristown, the Sham Chun at Hong Kong, the Tamsui at Taipei, the Keelung river, and the many dams that supplied Hong Kong from the 1960s (Plover Cove, 1973).

facility.water.well.name: Deep well and well pump
facility.water.well.description: A 150-300 mm steel or PVC casing to 100-300 m with a deep-turbine or submersible pump. In the Lehigh Valley the sand-and-gravel aquifer gave soft, iron-bearing water that had to be degreased; in Taiwan the wells hit 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel.

facility.water.well-screen.name: Well screen and gravel pack
facility.water.well-screen.description: Wire-wound or slotted screen with a graded silica-sand or garnet gravel pack, wrapped in geotextile. Stops the well pumping sand and the aquifer silting up the pump.

facility.water.aquifer-gravel.name: Aquifer sand and gravel
facility.water.aquifer-gravel.description: Glacial outwash and alluvial gravel forming the confined aquifer; the raw material of the well itself and the source of the hardness and iron.

facility.water.aquifer.name: Confined sand-and-gravel aquifer
facility.water.aquifer.description: The buried glacial and alluvial gravel bed saturated under pressure. Ends at the ground.

facility.steam.name: Industrial steam plant
facility.steam.description: Process steam for soldering, cleaning, degreasing, autoclaving and heating the building. Most industrial steam plants of 1983 were coal- or oil-fired package/field-assembled water-tube boilers, often with their own turbo-alternator so that the site exported some of its own electricity.

facts.label: Typical pressures
facts.value: 6-10 bar saturated for process; 25-45 bar / 250-400 C for turbo-alternator schemes

facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.name: Boiler feedwater treatment
facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.description: Two chemistries: lime-soda softening for the low-pressure plant, and ion-exchange demineralisation for anything above about 20 bar. By 1983 the whole industry standard was sodium-cycle cation plus strong-base anion demineralisation with a mixed-bed polish.

facility.steam.demineralisation.name: Ion-exchange demineralisation
facility.steam.demineralisation.description: A cation exchanger in the sodium form swaps Ca/Mg for Na; a strongly basic anion exchanger then swaps the bicarbonate/sulphate/chloride anions for OH; CO2 is degassed between the two beds; the effluent is then polished in a mixed bed to sodium chloride equivalent of a few tens of ppb. Resin is regenerated with 10-20% caustic and 6-12% hydrochloric or sulphuric acid.
facility.steam.demineralisation.note: Modern practice adds a second pass of RO/mixed bed and typically achieves 18 Mohm-cm; the 1980s benchmark for a good mixed bed was 10-15 Mohm-cm.

facts.label: Demineralised water
facts.value: typically 0.1-1.0 us/cm (10-100 Mohm-cm) after a mixed bed

facility.steam.brine-regen.name: Brine regeneration and waste
facility.steam.brine-regen.description: Regeneration blew a large slug of acidic or alkaline brine once or twice a day, which had to go somewhere. In 1983 the answer was usually a lined lagoon, a settling pond and then a discharge permit.

facility.steam.co2-degas.name: CO2 degasser
facility.steam.co2-degas.description: A packed or bubble column that strips dissolved carbon dioxide from the water between the cation and anion beds. Skipping it overloaded the anion resin with carbonic acid and shortened its life.

facility.steam.ion-resin.name: Ion-exchange resin (polystyrene-DVB)
facility.steam.ion-resin.description: A gel-type cation resin (sulfonic acid groups) or an anion resin (quaternary ammonium groups) on a cross-linked polystyrene-divinylbenzene bead. Beads of 0.3-1.0 mm, sieved into size fractions so the fine resin could be kept out of the top of the bed.

facility.steam.divinylbenzene.name: Divinylbenzene crosslinker
facility.steam.divinylbenzene.description: A small fraction of a C10H10 comonomer added to the styrene so the bead does not dissolve in the caustic used for regeneration. This crosslinking is what makes the resin insoluble and gives it its capacity.

facility.steam.styrene.name: Styrene monomer
facility.steam.styrene.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene or by cracking benzene, both from the aromatic fraction of an oil refinery. A C8H8 molecule - the same feedstock family as the styrene in the ABS case of the C64.

facility.steam.lime-soda.name: Lime-soda softening
facility.steam.lime-soda.description: Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 and soda ash Na2CO3 are dosed into a hot reaction basin, converting the scale-forming calcium and magnesium hardness into calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide sludge, which settles in a clarifier. This is the classic 1900-1960 process, still running at small industrial plants in 1983. Produces a lot of sludge.

facility.steam.hardness-sludge.name: Calcium carbonate / magnesium hydroxide sludge
facility.steam.hardness-sludge.description: The lumpy waste from lime-soda softening, pumped to a thickener and then to a drying bed or trucked to landfill wet. This is the sludge that fills the lagoons around old steel and chemical works.

facility.steam.soda-ash.name: Soda ash (sodium carbonate)
facility.steam.soda-ash.description: Solvay or Leblanc-process sodium carbonate for the lime-soda process. Ends at salt and limestone.

facility.steam.lime.name: Slaked lime (calcium hydroxide)
facility.steam.lime.description: Quicklime CaO burnt in a vertical or flash calciner to 1000 C, then hydrated. Ends at the limestone quarry.

facility.steam.limestone.name: Limestone (CaCO3)
facility.steam.limestone.description: Carboniferous and Permian limestone, crushed to 20-40 mm for the kiln. Ends at the quarry face.

facility.steam.condensate-return.name: Condensate return
facility.steam.condensate-return.description: Steam traps in every steam-consuming process returned hot condensate to the hotwell. Recovering it saved both fuel and water-treatment chemical, and the copper condensate pipework of a 1980s plant was a continuous, weeping mess of unions and gaskets.

facility.steam.trap.name: Steam trap
facility.steam.trap.description: A thermostatic (bimetallic or liquid-expansion) or mechanical bucket trap with a strainer upstream. Failed-open traps cost fuel; failed-closed traps flooded the plant. Every steam system of the era leaked at a few percent of its steam load, largely from these.

facility.steam.header.name: Steam header and distribution
facility.steam.header.description: A large-diameter steel pipe - 300-800 mm - with flanged or socket-welded branches to each user, insulation lagged in magnesium-block or calcium-silicate, and a trap at every low point. Steam was distributed at constant pressure from a header rather than generated at each machine.

facility.steam.insulation.name: Steam pipe insulation
facility.steam.insulation.description: Moulded magnesium-block sections, calcium silicate or, on hot surfaces, an asbestos-based rope and canvas wrap. Asbestos lagging was utterly routine on a 1980s steam line and is the reason so many power and chemical plants have mesothelioma claims decades later.

facility.steam.asbestos.name: Asbestos (chrysotile) mineral
facility.steam.asbestos.description: Fibrous magnesium silicate mined from open pits and shafts in Quebec, South Africa, Italy and the Soviet Union, and spun, carded and woven into rope, cloth and board. This is the single most under-acknowledged raw material in any 1980s industrial plant.

facility.steam.asbestos-mine.name: Asbestos mine and mill
facility.steam.asbestos-mine.description: A serpentinite or chrysotile orebody worked by open pit or underground, then crushed, graded and carded. Ends at the serpentinite rock in the ground.

facility.steam.turbo-alternator.name: Industrial turbo-alternator
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.description: Where a plant burned coal continuously it made sense to take steam past 300 C and put it through a small turbine to make some of its own electricity. A 2-6 MW pass turbine driving a 480 V alternator, exporting a few hundred kW and buying back the rest at peak rates, was a standard arrangement in Taiwan, Korea and Britain.
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.note: These units were called 'pass turbines' or 'back-pressure turbines' and were the main cogeneration technology before the 1980s gas-engine programme; natural-gas-fired turbine-generator sets took over from about 1980.

facility.steam.turbine-governor.name: Speed governor and overspeed trip
facility.steam.turbine-governor.description: A flyball or hydraulic governor on the turbine shaft plus a mechanical overspeed trip and, in larger sets, a turbine protective device that tripped the generator breaker. The overspeed trip was the last line of defence against a runaway.

facility.steam.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler
facility.steam.boiler.description: Two-drum or three-drum evaporators with a superheater. Industrial boilers of 4-20 t/h fired coal at about 6-9 bar saturated, directly into the plant's heating and process network. Economisers and feedwater heaters recovered heat; blowdown controlled the dissolved solids.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 2-20 t/h industrial; 50-300 t/h for power-house duty

facility.steam.safety-valves.name: Safety valves and drum level control
facility.steam.safety-valves.description: Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator on the drum, and the refractory-lined sight-glass port that operators actually looked at. A steam plant is a place where the concrete is usually older than the manager.

facility.steam.blowdown.name: Blowdown and demineralised make-up
facility.steam.blowdown.description: A fraction of boiler water is blown down to keep total dissolved solids and alkalinity inside limits; the make-up has to be soft or demineralised or the cycles of concentration collapse. Blowdown is sent to a flash tank for heat recovery and then to the cooling-water basin.

facility.steam.fuel.name: Industrial boiler fuel
facility.steam.fuel.description: Anthracite, bituminous coal, fuel oil or - very commonly in Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan - coal briquettes pressed from imported anthracite fines in a ring-die or pillow press.

facility.steam.briquette.name: Coal briquette (hongsha / pressed coal)
facility.steam.briquette.description: Binderless or starch-bound anthracite fines pressed at 200 bar into egg-shaped briquettes about 100 g each, fired on a grate. Hong Kong's thermal power and much of its industrial boiler load ran on exactly this fuel.

facility.steam.anthracite.name: Anthracite fines
facility.steam.anthracite.description: Hard, high-carbon coal, largely imported to the Far East from South Wales, Vietnam and China. Ends at the anthracite seam.

facility.steam.boiler-house.name: The boiler house
facility.steam.boiler-house.description: A tall, heavily built single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, the boilers in a row, coal bunkers or an oil day tank alongside, and the chimney outside. Even in 1983 it was the tallest building on most industrial sites.

facility.steam.fuel-handling.name: Fuel handling and bunker
facility.steam.fuel-handling.description: A conveyor, a hopper and a boiler feed screw, or an oil tank and a pump skid. Manual barrow-and-shovel coal handling was still normal at plants below about 10 t/h.

facility.power.name: Industrial electricity supply (1983)
facility.power.description: The electricity that ran every press, oven, wave-solder machine, conveyor and test rig. In 1983 the world's grids were coal, oil, gas and hydro - not the gas-turbine-dominated grids of today - and industrial customers bought it on a two-part tariff with a demand charge.

facility.power.tariff.name: The industrial electricity tariff (1983)
facility.power.tariff.description: Industrial customers never paid a simple price per kWh. The tariff was two-part: an energy charge per kWh plus a demand charge per kW of measured maximum demand over a 15 or 30 minute interval. The demand charge rewarded flat load and punished a factory that ran its ovens and its wave-solder line together. Tariff classes ('medium general service', 'large power and light') were negotiated against contract demand and often a five-year commitment.
facility.power.tariff.note: Modern practice is the same two-part structure, but with hourly and time-of-use pricing and, in some markets, deregulated retail suppliers; the 1980s tariff was a regulated cost-of-service tariff set by a public utility commission.

facility.electricity.name: Electricity at the factory wall
facility.electricity.description: The chain from the utility's service drop to the machine tool. This is the branch other subsystems should reference whenever they need 'mains power': the substation, the transformer, the low-voltage switchboard, the motor control centre, and finally the cord and plug.

facts.label: Factory service voltage
facts.value: 11-13.8 kV into the plant, 480 V three-phase or 220 V single-phase out of the transformer in the US; 380-415 V in HK/Europe

facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.name: Busbar trunking and cable
facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.description: Copper or aluminium busbar in an epoxy-impregnated sandwich ('busway') for high-current runs, and PVC/PVDF-insulated copper or aluminium cable in conduit or tray for the rest. Flexible conduit was still common above machine tools.

facility.electricity.substation.name: Customer substation
facility.electricity.substation.description: Where a large factory bought at transmission or sub-transmission voltage: a fenced yard with the utility's metering, an incoming circuit breaker, a main transformer, a secondary switchgear line-up and the plant's own protection relays.

facility.electricity.switchgear.name: Low-voltage switchboard
facility.electricity.switchgear.description: Air-circuit-breaker switchboards at 480/415 V, with bolted busbar, fuses/MCCBs per outgoing way and a transformer tap-selector. Most factory power for small machines was tapped off the board at 120/230 V through a plug.

facility.electricity.earthing.name: Earthing grid and lightning protection
facility.electricity.earthing.description: Copper rod or bare conductor bonded under the floor and up the steelwork, plus air terminals and down conductors to earth rods. In a fab with a raised floor, the earth grid and the electrostatic-dissipative floor were often the same conductor.

facility.electricity.power-factor.name: Power factor correction capacitors
facility.electricity.power-factor.description: Motor loads are inductive, so a big factory runs at 0.7-0.85 power factor and gets penalised by the utility. Banks of switched capacitor kVAr corrected it. A capacitor is the cheapest industrial electronics ever made - a polypropylene film between two aluminium foils.

facility.electricity.mcc.name: Motor control centre
facility.electricity.mcc.description: A vertical lineup of combination starters and contactors with a fused disconnect per motor, feeding the compressors, injection-moulding presses, conveyors and extract fans. The 1980s unit had no variable-frequency drives at all - speed control was a pole-changing or slip-ring motor.
facility.electricity.mcc.note: Adjustable-frequency drives only became normal in the late 1980s-90s, and the first-generation IGBT VFDs cost more than the motor.

facility.electricity.contactors.name: AC contactors and overload relays
facility.electricity.contactors.description: Silver-alloy contacts on a moulded phenolic base with a shading ring to stop contact chatter, plus a bimetal or electronic overload. The bimetal overload relay, unchanged since the 1920s, was the industrial motor's main protection.

facility.electricity.transformer.name: Distribution transformer
facility.electricity.transformer.description: A laminated silicon-steel core with copper or aluminium windings on pressboard and paper insulation, immersed in mineral oil or Askarel. Oil-immersed units dominated until the 1980s-90s fire codes and the economics of dry-type began to change the picture in Europe and Japan.

facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing.name: Porcelain bushings and standoff insulators
facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing.description: Glazed porcelain sheds, cemented with epoxy onto the winding ends, to bring the winding out to a terminal. These are the tall ribbed 'sheds' you see on any pole-top transformer.

facility.electricity.feldspar.name: Feldspar
facility.electricity.feldspar.description: A potassium-sodium aluminosilicate used as a flux in porcelain and in the electrolytic alumina bath. Ends at the pegmatite quarry.

facility.electricity.insulating-oil.name: Transformer insulating oil
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.description: Mineral oil (naphthenic or paraffinic), a by-product of vacuum distillation of crude. Also Askarel (PCB-filled chlorinated dielectric) in older units - a PCB source that explains part of the PCB contamination of the Hudson/Superfund sites.
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.note: Askarel transformers were phased out in the US after the EPA began classifying PCBs as hazardous in 1979; by 1983 new units were mineral-oil or dry-type.

facility.electricity.askarel.name: Askarel (PCB-filled transformer dielectric)
facility.electricity.askarel.description: A chlorinated biphenyl dielectric used from the 1930s until the 1980s ban. Ends at the chlorinated benzene/aromatics stream.

facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.name: Chlorinated aromatic feedstock
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.description: Chlorobenzene and biphenyl feedstock for the askarel blend, itself from the chlorination of benzene over a chloride catalyst. Ends at the aromatic hydrocarbon still.
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.note: Not verified for a specific 1980s askarel producer.

facility.electricity.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented silicon steel (GOES)
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.description: 3.2% silicon steel rolled so its crystallographic grain lies parallel to the flux direction, giving a core loss an order of magnitude lower than hot-rolled steel. Made in a special continuous-annealing line. This is the same material used in the C64's switch-mode transformer and in every mains transformer in the world.
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.note: Deliberately stiff magnetically so it laminates easily and does not ring when punched - 'GOES' is stamped on the laminations.

facility.electricity.grain-oriented-mill.name: Grain-oriented steel rolling mill
facility.electricity.grain-oriented-mill.description: Hot band rolled to 2 mm, cold rolled to 0.3 mm, decarburised in a hydrogen atmosphere and given a final magnetic anneal. Ends at the ore and the coke oven.

facility.electricity.service.name: Utility service and metering
facility.electricity.service.description: A pad-mount or pole-mounted transformer on the utility side of the fence, with revenue metering and a fused cut-out. The customer owned everything downstream of the meter.

facility.power.generation.name: The 1983 generating mix
facility.power.generation.description: Coal, oil, gas and hydro carried the whole industrial world in 1983. In Taiwan, the grid that powered the subcontractors' factories was still mostly oil (58.8% of supply in 1980) with coal at 17.1% and hydro at 13.9%; by 1990 coal had taken over at 38.4% and oil had fallen to 25.6%. Korea and Hong Kong had almost no indigenous fuel at all.
facility.power.generation.note: Natural gas barely existed as a grid fuel in 1983; the first LNG cargo (Algeria) reached Kaohsiung in 1983 and Hong Kong's town gas came from manufactured coal gas, not natural gas.

facility.power.grid.name: Transmission and distribution network
facility.power.grid.description: High-voltage transmission from the plant's switchyard to the city, then medium-voltage distribution to the industrial park, then the service drop to the customer. This is the piece almost nobody thinks about: roughly 8% of generated electricity is lost in transmission and distribution before it reaches the meter.
facility.power.grid.note: Losses have fallen by only a few percentage points since 1983 because the physics of I2R dominates; a modern grid still loses 5-8%.

facts.label: Transmission voltage
facts.value: 230-765 kV AC, some 500 kV DC by 1983

facility.power.grid.distribution.name: Medium-voltage distribution feeder
facility.power.grid.distribution.description: Overhead or underground 11-13.8 kV feeders with reclosers, sectionalisers and fuses. Underground feeders were standard in the new Hong Kong industrial estates and in Japanese and Korean industrial parks; overhead was normal in the US outside cities.

facility.power.grid.substation.name: Utility substation
facility.power.grid.substation.description: Transformer bays, circuit breakers, buswork and the control house that steps transmission voltage down to the 11-34.5 kV distribution level. Utility substations outnumbered the plants; a 1980s industrial park typically had one primary substation feeding a ring of unit substation transformers.

facility.power.grid.line.name: Overhead transmission line
facility.power.grid.line.description: Steel lattice towers or wooden H-poles carrying three phases on aluminium conductor, with shield wires and porcelain or glass suspension insulators. The thermal rating of the conductor, not the voltage, is the limit.

facility.power.insulator-porcelain.name: Porcelain suspension insulator
facility.power.insulator-porcelain.description: Glazed (glassy) or unglazed (ceramic) insulator strings, 10-20 discs to hold a 230-500 kV line up in the air. Replaced later by composite polymer strings, which is why the classic transmission silhouette disappeared after 1990.

facility.power.kaolin.name: Kaolin (china clay)
facility.power.kaolin.description: A white kaolinite clay from a kaolin pit, washed and beneficiated for the ceramic and paper trades. Ends at the clay pit.

facility.power.acsr-conductor.name: Aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR)
facility.power.acsr-conductor.description: Aluminium strands around a steel core for tensile strength, twisted and stranded on the line. Ends at an aluminium smelter fed by alumina.

facility.power.alumina-bauxite.name: Bauxite -> alumina (Bayer process)
facility.power.alumina-bauxite.description: Aluminium exists as bauxite ore -> alumina -> aluminium. The Bayer process leaches alumina from bauxite with hot caustic soda under pressure, then precipitates aluminium hydroxide. 4 tonnes bauxite give 2 t alumina give 1 t aluminium.

facility.power.bauxite-mine.name: Bauxite mine
facility.power.bauxite-mine.description: Residual laterite capping on old limestone terrain, stripped by shovel and truck or by cable-sbucket wheel excavator. Ends at the bauxite body.

facility.power.coal-plant.name: Coal-fired steam power plant
facility.power.coal-plant.description: The workhorse baseload of the 1980s. Coal from a mine or a rail/barge unloading dock is crushed, pulverised to talcum fineness, blown into a furnace with preheated air, burned under a boiler, and the resulting steam drives a turbine-generator. Net efficiency typically 33-38% thermal to electricity on a unit built in the 1960s-70s.

facility.power.nuclear-plant.name: Nuclear power plant
facility.power.nuclear-plant.description: Not a 'coal/oil/gas/hydro' machine, but it was 10.2% of Taiwan's electricity in 1980 - the first reactor at Chinshan came on line in 1978, followed by Chinshan 2 (1979), Chinshan 3, Feitsui and Lungmen. Any 1983 power bill in northern Taiwan could legitimately be traced to a uranium fuel rod.

facility.power.uranium.name: Uranium fuel
facility.power.uranium.description: Uranium concentrate converted to UF6 and enriched from natural 0.71% U-235 to 2.5-3.5%, then fabricated into ceramic UO2 pellets 8 mm across, sintered, ground to length, clad in zircaloy and made into a fuel assembly. In 1983 the US HEU was being phased down and the world's enrichment market was switching to centrifuge cascades.

facility.power.uranium-ore.name: Uranium ore (U3O8)
facility.power.uranium-ore.description: Graded and leached in the 1970s-80s, largely from the Colorado Plateau (Uravan) and New Mexico, plus Namibia and Canada. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.name: Vanadiferous uraninite ore
facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.description: The US Colorado Plateau ore was processed mainly for vanadium with uranium as a by-product, in mills that roasted the ore with salt and soda ash and leached it with chlorine.

facility.power.gas-plant.name: Gas-fired power plant
facility.power.gas-plant.description: Two different things share this name. For the 1983 industrial economy the honest answer is that almost none of the grid came from natural gas - gas turbines ran mainly for peak load, standby and cogeneration. Taiwan's first LNG cargo arrived in 1983 and natural gas did not become a grid fuel until the 1990s.
facility.power.gas-plant.note: In the US the big gas-fired build-out came after 1990, with the EPA NOx rules; in 1983 a gas turbine plant was an unusual and expensive thing to run on a peak-load schedule.

facility.power.natural-gas.name: Natural gas
facility.power.natural-gas.description: Methane with ethane and propane, delivered by pipeline or (from 1983 in Taiwan and Japan) as LNG. Western Europe's gas was North Sea and Groningen; the US grid burned domestic Appalachian, Texas and Louisiana gas.

facility.power.natural-gas.us-domestic.name: Appalachian / Gulf Coast gas
facility.power.natural-gas.us-domestic.description: In the US - which is where the Commodore fab and the assembly lines in Pennsylvania and California were - electricity generation burned natural gas mostly on the Gulf Coast and in Texas, plus Appalachian gas in Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia.
places: Marcellus and Black Mountain shales, Pennsylvania

facility.power.natural-gas.lng.name: LNG cargo
facility.power.natural-gas.lng.description: Liquefied at -162 C in one of the big North African/Middle East trains and shipped in a 125,000 m3 membrane or Moss-type tanker. Taiwan's first LNG landed at Kaohsiung in 1983 from Algeria.
facility.power.natural-gas.lng.note: Japan's LNG programme (from 1969) and Taiwan's first imports (1983) predate the gas-turbine power boom; both burned the gas in gas-heated boilers and industrial plants, not mostly in turbines.

facility.power.natural-gas.liquefier.name: LNG liquefaction train
facility.power.natural-gas.liquefier.description: A cascade of propane and mixed-refrigerant heat exchangers that chill the gas to -162 C. The 'missing link' for helium also hangs off this kind of plant.

facility.power.natural-gas.northsea.name: North Sea gas field
facility.power.natural-gas.northsea.description: Permian Zechstein gas reservoirs beneath the southern North Sea - the source that made Netherlands and UK power stations coal-light in the 1970s and 80s. The gas arrives at the platform's own gas turbines over a 30-40 km undersea pipeline.

facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.name: Gas turbine
facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.description: A compressor, a combustor at 1400-1600 C and a turbine in a single shaft or two. Open-cycle efficiency only 25-35% in 1983 - the poor number that made gas peakers expensive until combined cycle became standard in the 1990s.

facility.power.oil-plant.name: Oil-fired steam power plant
facility.power.oil-plant.description: The 1980s default in much of Asia and the Middle East, and the reason Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. Residual fuel oil and fuel oil burned in a boiler instead of coal - cheaper to handle, dirtier, and dead on arrival once the 1979 oil shock and OPEC reset prices.

facility.power.oil-plant.stack.name: Tall chimney
facility.power.oil-plant.stack.description: A 150-250 m concrete or steel chimney to get the plume above the inversion layer and disperse sulphur dioxide over a large area. Not a pollution control device - a dilution device.

facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.name: Oil-fired boiler
facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.description: Same water-tube boiler as the coal plant, but with oil burners instead of a pulveriser and an induced-draft fan sized for the lower flue-gas volume. Two to four boilers typically share one stack.

facility.oil.name: Crude petroleum and fuel oil
facility.oil.description: The liquid fuel of the whole industrial world in 1983. Kuwait and Saudi Arabian Light for the Far East, plus North Sea Brent and US domestic crude for Europe and the US East Coast.

facility.oil.refinery.name: Refinery
facility.oil.refinery.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation plus hydrotreating to make fuel oil and, in a complex refinery, the naphtha feed for the hydrogen and ethylene crackers. Ali Qaido in Kuwait (1945) or Amuay in Venezuela (1962) typified the scale.

facility.oil.lpg.name: LPG (propane/butane)
facility.oil.lpg.description: The liquid the Hong Kong and Japanese industrial estates burned for process heat and factory heating, and the feedstock for the 1980s alkylation route to isobutylene. Ends at the well or the refinery.

facility.oil.well.name: Oil and gas well
facility.oil.well.description: A rotary or cable-tool hole completed into sandstone or carbonate. In 1983 the Far East's oil was largely onshore (Gawair in Kuwait, Ghawar-equivalent fields) with growing offshore production.

facility.oil.reservoir.name: Sandstone or carbonate oil reservoir
facility.oil.reservoir.description: Porous sedimentary rock (typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate) saturated with oil under pressure. This is where the story actually ends for oil.

facility.power.hydro-plant.name: Hydroelectric power plant
facility.power.hydro-plant.description: Genuinely important for the 1980s Far East: Taiwan took 13.9% of its supply from hydro in 1980 and 24.5% by 1990 (Sun Moon Lake, Tachia, Feitsui, Wujie), and Taiwan's run-of-river stations are exactly the kind of small plant Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors drew from. Elsewhere hydro was the cheap baseload of Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Canada.

facility.power.hydro-plant.tailrace.name: Tailrace and reservoir
facility.power.hydro-plant.tailrace.description: Where the water goes back to the river - and, downstream of the dam, the river itself is the raw water intake for the industrial park that the dam's power attracted.

facility.power.river.name: The river itself
facility.power.river.description: A glacial or monsoonal river carrying suspended sediment, hardness and organic colour. This is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water in this tree.

facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.name: Francis turbine
facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.description: The standard medium-head machine: water enters the spiral casing, turns a runner on a vertical or horizontal shaft at 100-750 rpm, and exits into the draft tube.

facility.power.hydro-plant.penstock.name: Concrete penstock and headrace tunnel
facility.power.hydro-plant.penstock.description: A 3-6 m diameter steel or concrete conduit carrying water from the intake at head to the turbine, usually several hundred metres and dropping 50-300 m of head.

facility.power.cement-portland.name: Portland cement
facility.power.cement-portland.description: Limestone plus clay, fired in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, ground with gypsum. The universal structural binder of the 1980s industrial plant: dams, cooling towers, substation foundations, effluent tanks, the fab's raised floor.

facility.power.cement-kiln.name: Rotary cement kiln
facility.power.cement-kiln.description: A 60-150 m inclined steel tube rotating 1-2 rpm, burning coal or oil at 1450 C to drive off CO2 and drive the reaction forward. Ends at the limestone and clay pits.

facility.power.rockfill.name: Rockfill dam and riprap
facility.power.rockfill.description: Dams of the era were built of quarried rock tipped into the river and compacted, faced with concrete or asphaltic membrane. Ends at the quarry face.

facility.power.aggregate-quarry.name: Aggregate and riprap quarry
facility.power.aggregate-quarry.description: Granite/gneiss quarried, crushed and screened for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material. Ends at the rock in the hillside.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.name: Steam turbine
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.description: A multistage expansion turbine: high-pressure, intermediate-pressure and low-pressure sections, the last with the long bladed rotor of a wet-steam half-pressure machine. Exhaust goes to the condenser at about 0.05 bar. Steam rate for a 1980s unit was roughly 9-11 MJ/kWh.

facility.power.coal-plant.switchyard.name: Switchyard and circuit breakers
facility.power.coal-plant.switchyard.description: Outdoor busbars, disconnectors, dead-tank and live-tank oil circuit breakers and surge arresters, on a steel lattice gantry. The step-up point where the plant connects to the transmission network.

facility.power.coal-plant.stepup-transfo.name: Generator step-up transformer (GSU)
facility.power.coal-plant.stepup-transfo.description: A single-phase or three-phase bank of 240-500 kV oil-filled transformers that takes 21 kV from the alternator to the transmission line. This is the piece of iron that makes the whole grid possible, and it is why every power station has a lumpy, oil-filled, bunded yard next door.

facility.power.coal-plant.generator.name: Generator (turbo-alternator)
