facility.power.coal-plant.generator.description: The turbine shaft turns a 2- or 4-pole alternator at 3000/3600 rpm. A 500 MVA water-cooled unit is about 12 m long and 6 m wide. Output was 13.8 kV or 21 kV - far too low to transmit, hence the step-up transformer next door.

facility.power.coal-plant.condenser.name: Surface condenser
facility.power.coal-plant.condenser.description: Thousands of stainless-steel tubes with condensing exhaust steam outside and cooling water inside. The condensate is the plant's own feedwater; cleanliness here directly sets boiler-tube life.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.name: Nickel-alloy rotor and casing steel
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.description: For a 540 C steam turbine the high-pressure rotor needed 0.5-0.8% Cr-Mo-V steel and the last stages austenitic stainless; the whole thing was forged, normalised, stress-relieved and then creep-rupture proof-tested.

facility.power.coke.name: Metallurgical coke
facility.power.coke.description: Bituminous coal coked in batteries of 30-45 ovens to make the fuel and the reductant for the blast furnace. Ends at the coking plant.

facility.power.coking-coal-seam.name: High-Bituminous coking coal seam
facility.power.coking-coal-seam.description: A very specific subset of bituminous coal - the seam that swells and fuses in the coke oven, distinct from the steam coal the power station burns. The Pennsylvania/Kentucky/West Virginia 'High Bituminous' field.

facility.power.iron-ore.name: Iron ore (hematite/magnetite)
facility.power.iron-ore.description: The blast-furnace feed. Mesabi Range hematite in the US Lake Superior district, or imported Brazilian pellets/ore.

facility.power.iron-ore-pit.name: Iron ore open pit (Mesabi)
facility.power.iron-ore-pit.description: Taconite and hematite are dug by 15-tonne payload shovels and hauled in 90-tonne trucks from a strip 60 m deep. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.coal-plant.superheater.name: Superheater and reheater
facility.power.coal-plant.superheater.description: Superheaters raise saturated steam to 540-565 C by hanging banks of tube bundles in the radiant and convective pass; reheaters do the same again to the steam coming back out of the high-pressure turbine. Higher steam temperature is the single biggest lever on plant thermal efficiency.

facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler and evaporator
facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.description: Drum-type water-tube boiler, typically 300-900 MW, drum at ~15 MPa and 340-370 C. Feedwater circulates through downcomers and up risers around a flame path several hundred passes long; saturated steam leaves the drum to be superheated.

facility.power.coal-plant.ash-handling.name: Bottom ash and fly ash handling
facility.power.coal-plant.ash-handling.description: Ash from the boiler hoppers was quenched, then either dewatered and trucked to a landfill or put wet into a hopper and pumped as slurry. Fly ash was collected in electrostatic precipitators or baghouses and trucked dry or ponded.

facility.power.coal-plant.economiser.name: Economiser
facility.power.coal-plant.economiser.description: A bank of finned tubes in the flue gas path that preheats feedwater from ~120 C to the saturation temperature, using the last 8-10% of the flue-gas heat. Standard since the 1930s, near-universal by 1980.

facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.name: Boiler furnace and combustion
facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.description: A refractory- and water-wall-lined firebox. Coal and preheated air enter at the burners, burn at 1300-1600 C, and give up radiation to the water walls lining the furnace walls.

facility.power.coal-plant.scrubber.name: Wet flue-gas desulphuriser (scrubber)
facility.power.coal-plant.scrubber.description: Required in the US from about 1978 onward once new-source performance standards took effect. Slaked lime or limestone slurry absorbs SO2 to calcium sulphite, which is then forced-oxidised to gypsum; the stack gas is reheated so the plume still rises.

facility.power.limestone.name: Limestone (calcium carbonate) slurry
facility.power.limestone.description: Crushed and slaked to calcium hydroxide for wet scrubbing, or used directly in dry/semi-dry scrubbers. Ends at the quarry.

facility.power.limestone-quarry.name: Limestone quarry
facility.power.limestone-quarry.description: A bench quarry in Ordovician-Silurian carbonate rock, crushed on site. Ends at the rock in the ground.

facility.power.air-preheater.name: Ljungstrom / regenerative air preheater
facility.power.air-preheater.description: The flue gas gives up its heat to the incoming combustion air through a slow-rotating bank of corrugated steel plates - exhaust gas at ~300 C, air at ~300 C. This alone recovered several percent of the coal's energy.

facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.name: Coal pulveriser (mill)
facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.description: A ball or roller mill grinds run-of-mine coal to a powder with at least 70% through 200 mesh (75 micrometres) so that it will burn in suspension. This was the technology that made the 1950s-80s boiler possible at all.

facts.label: Mill power
facts.value: 40-70 kW per mill, 2-4 mills per boiler

facility.power.coal-plant.fan.name: Hot-air fan and primary air
facility.power.coal-plant.fan.description: A fan supplies the 60-80% of combustion air that dries and suspends the powder in the furnace and the remainder that sweeps it out between the boiler tube banks.

facility.power.coal-plant.receiving.name: Coal receiving and stockyard
facility.power.coal-plant.receiving.description: Unload from rail unit trains or self-unloading barges into a yard. In the 1980s the East Coast plants were fed by unit trains; Japan's and Korea's coal came by Panamax and post-Panamax bulker.

facility.coal.name: Steam coal (run-of-mine to sized)
facility.coal.description: The fuel. Bituminous coal, 20-35 GJ/t, 0.5-3% sulphur, bought on the international steam coal market or delivered by rail from the field. Its ash and sulphur content set the flue-gas desulphuriser and the bottom-ash grinder bill.

facility.coal.prep-plant.name: Coal preparation plant
facility.coal.prep-plant.description: Crushed, screened, washed and dried at the mine mouth. 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones; the resulting 2-inch x 0 coal with 8-12% moisture is what a boiler of that era was designed to burn.

facility.coal.moisture.name: Thermal drying of coal
facility.coal.moisture.description: Screen-deck dryers or flash dryers bring the fuel down to about 8-12% moisture. A wetter coal burns slower, raises stack temperature and can quench a boiler screen tube.

facility.coal.washing.name: Dense-medium coal washing
facility.coal.washing.description: Raw coal is floated on a magnetite/water slurry of specific gravity ~1.35; the light coal floats, the ash-rich shale sinks. This is where the mountaintop-removal debate's 'coal refuse' piles come from.

facility.coal.magnetite.name: Magnetite sand for dense-medium fluid
facility.coal.magnetite.description: Fe3O4, a natural iron oxide sand used as the density medium because it is dense, cheap, recoverable magnetically and chemically inert.

facility.coal.magnetite-ore.name: Magnetite ore body
facility.coal.magnetite-ore.description: Typically mined from a lake-shore or igneous deposit and concentrated by flotation. Ends at the ore body in the ground.

facility.coal.mine.name: Coal mine
facility.coal.mine.description: In 1983 the relevant supply was room-and-pillar underground mining in the Appalachian basin (Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky) for the US East Coast grid, and open-pit truck-and-shovel or bucket-wheel in the Powder River Basin, Silesia, the Ruhr, the Bowen Basin and the Witbank coalfield.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: typically 150-600 m underground in the Appalachians

facility.coal.opencut.name: Open-cut coal mine
facility.coal.opencut.description: Overburden stripped by dragline or shovel, coal ripped by bulldozer, loaded into 100-tonne rear-dump trucks. Dominant in the Powder River Basin, the Ruhr, Limburg, New South Wales and Limpopo.

facility.coal.overburden-strip.name: Overburden strip of shale and clay
facility.coal.overburden-strip.description: Burden stripped in benches to reach the coal seam - often 10-60 m of rock and dirt per metre of coal in the Powder River Basin. The overburden itself becomes a backfill and a landfill-pond liner.

facility.coal.room-pillar.name: Room-and-pillar mining
facility.coal.room-pillar.description: Still the dominant method for Appalachian metallurgical and steam coal: rooms driven to the pillar, pillars left behind to hold the roof. Cheap but leaves 30-50% of the seam underground.

facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.name: Seam between shale and sandstone beds
facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.description: The same Carboniferous coal-bearing sequence as the longwall face, mined from a shaft or slope rather than a portal. Ends at the rock in the ground.

facility.coal.longwall.name: Longwall face
facility.coal.longwall.description: A mechanised shearer cuts a 2-3 m slice across the panel; the roof is allowed to cave into the goaf and the coal flows to a shearer loader. High recovery, high output, and a lot of subsidence.

facility.coal.seam.name: Bituminous coal seam in sedimentary rock
facility.coal.seam.description: The raw input, full stop. In the northern Appalachian basin the commercial coal is in the middle and upper Pennsylvanian (Conemaugh, Monongahela, Kittanning, Freeport) formations - Carboniferous, roughly 300 million years old, laid down in swamp forests and buried under Pennsylvanian sediment.

chem.name: Petrochemicals and process chemistry
chem.description: Everything on the C64 that began as crude oil or natural gas: the polymers of the case and the keyboard, the solvents of the assembly plant, the wet chemicals and photoresists of the silicon fab, the laminate resin and flux of the board, and the fuels that moved all of it. Traces roughly a tonne of hydrocarbons per kilogram of plastic back to a barrel of light sour crude.

chem.solder-chemicals.name: Solder, flux and rosin
chem.solder-chemicals.description: A wave-soldered through-hole board of 1983 is assembled with a 60/40 tin-lead solder and a rosin flux core. The two facts that make this branch worth tracing are that the flux is pine rosin - a forestry product, the clearest non-fossil material in a C64 - and that the solder is 40% lead by weight, which is the reason solder is now the single most restricted substance in electronics. By the late 1980s the halide-free no-clean flux had arrived and was beginning to replace the RMA flux that the C64 was assembled with.

chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.name: The thermal profile is the process
chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.description: The reason the soldering chemistry is mostly temperature management: a through-hole joint sees 250-260 C for one to three seconds in the wave, which is enough to make the intermetallic and not enough to damage the flux or the laminate; a surface-mount joint sees a 220-245 C peak for 30-120 seconds in a reflow oven or a hot plate. Over-temperature grows the intermetallic and dulls the joint; under-temperature makes a cold solder joint that fails in service. Every one of these numbers is a chemical property, because the eutectic is a chemical fact.

chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wav.name: Wave soldering
chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wav.description: A through-hole board is soldered by passing it through a standing wave of molten solder at 250-260 C under a layer of flux, and the specific energy of the solder wave is what wets the joint and leaves the surface behind it clean. The 1980s wave machine had a two or three wave pot, a preheat tunnel, a flux station and a drying tunnel, and it consumed a surprising amount of both flux and deoxidised solder.

chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wav.name: Dross
chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wav.description: The oxide skimmed off the surface of the solder pot: tin oxide and lead oxide, a few tenths of a per cent of the metal every shift. It was a real loss and a real fire risk, and the 1980s industry answer was a combination of the deoxidised (oxygen-free) wave and the automatic skimmer. The dross was returned to the refiner as a low-grade solder.
chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wav.note: The dross loss rate is an order-of-magnitude figure and varies with the machine, the flux and the skimming practice.

chem.solder-chemicals.cleaning.name: Board cleaning after soldering
chem.solder-chemicals.cleaning.description: The flux residue had to come off, and the 1980s answer was either an organic solvent (1,1,1-trichloroethane, or isopropanol after 1983, or a mixture) or an aqueous detergent wash. The solvent was the same molecule as the degreaser, and its replacement by isopropanol is one of the cleanest single substitutions in the file: the board plant's solvent went from a chlorinated hydrocarbon to a propylene oxidation product in about two years, for regulatory and cost reasons rather than performance ones.

chem.isopropanol.name: Isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol)
chem.isopropanol.description: C3H8O, boiling 82.6 C, and by the mid-1980s the solvent that had taken over most of the cleaning work the chlorinated solvents used to do. It is flammable, it is cheap, it evaporates cleanly, it dissolves flux residue and oil, and it does not dissolve the ABS or the polycarbonate the way a chlorinated solvent can - which is exactly why it became the electronics cleaner. Almost all of it was made from propylene, so the electronics plant's replacement solvent is the same cracker as the case plastic.

chem.solder-chemicals.no-clean.name: Halide-free no-clean flux
chem.solder-chemicals.no-clean.description: The technology change that arrived in the middle and late 1980s: a flux with no halide at all, based on organic acids and esters rather than on amine hydrochlorides, and with an ionic residue mild enough that the board did not have to be washed. It solved the wash-water problem and it created a reliability problem, because the residue was left on the board and the industry spent a decade arguing about whether it was ionic enough to matter. The C64 predates it; Commodore's successors did not.
chem.solder-chemicals.no-clean.note: No-clean fluxes arrived commercially in the mid-1980s; the halide-free specification is measured against a standard ion chromatography test.

facts.label: Halide content
facts.value: not detected (<0.001% by the standard test)

chem.solder-chemicals.intermetallic.name: The intermetallic that actually joins
chem.solder-chemicals.intermetallic.description: A solder joint is not tin-lead metal. On the copper side, copper and tin interdiffuse to make Cu6Sn5 and then Cu3Sn, and the joint's strength is in the intermetallic layer, not in the alloy. Two consequences: the intermetallic grows at service temperature until it embrittles the joint, and copper dissolves fast enough in a 260 C bath to put a bare copper lead into the solder pot within minutes - which is why the lead was flow-boned (plated with tin) before it ever entered the wave machine.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.name: 60/40 tin-lead solder
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.description: The eutectic at 183 C, which is why a wave-solder bath sat at 250-260 C and a hand iron at 300-350 C: 70-80 C of superheat above the melting point, which keeps the bath molten at the top and fluxes the joint as it passes through. In 1983 about 60-70% of the world's solder was 60/40 tin-lead for electronics; the alloy is cheap, it has a low melting point, and its oxide comes off in a flux. The 40% lead was the subject of the entire lead-free soldering programme of the 1980s and 1990s, and the lead itself came out of a flotation concentrator, not out of a refinery.
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.note: Lead comes from the lead/zinc mining and flotation chain, not from this subsystem.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.name: Where the tin came from
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.description: The tin in a 60/40 solder was smelted from cassiterite, the tin ore, and cassiterite is one of the rarer tin deposits in the world: Bolivia's placer and vein cassiterite, the Cornish tin belt, the Nigerian and the Indonesian deposits, and the alluvial cassiterite of Malaysia and Thailand. In 1983 the world mined something like 25,000-30,000 tonnes of tin a year - a small metal market by volume and a strategically awkward one, because the electronics industry's solder demand is a large fraction of it.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.name: Cassiterite (SnO2)
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.description: Tin oxide, 78.8% tin by mass, the principal tin ore. Recovered from placer deposits by panning and gravity concentration and from hard-rock veins by flotation, then smelted or reduced to tin. The C64-scale observation is the interesting one: a single soldered joint holds a few milligrams of tin, and there are a hundred and fifty million of them, so the tin industry exists in part because of solder joints.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.name: Rosin flux (RMA)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.description: The flux core of the solder wire, or the liquid flux of the wave-solder machine: 25-40% rosin in a flux base with an activator. The rosin's job is to dissolve the surface oxide of the copper and the solder - the abietic acid is a mild acid and a mild chelant - and its virtue is that it is a good flux and then leaves an ionic residue that is not corrosive. RMA fluxes were specified with a halide content under 0.05% because halides are what makes a flux corrosive and what makes a circuit hiss. The C64's board was very likely assembled with a halide-bearing flux and cleaned afterwards.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: organic acids, fatty acid salts, or amine halides

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.name: The flux base and its solvent
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.description: A liquid flux is rosin, activator and solvent, and the solvent is what makes it a liquid. Through the 1980s the solder wire's core was a rope of activated rosin flux in an alcohol or glycol ether solvent (isopropyl alcohol, or a glycol ether), and the core was drawn into a wire of solder by a wire-drawing machine. The active rosin in the core had to be clean enough to be drawn: any acid-value drift or gum would tear the wire.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.name: Drawing the flux core into the wire
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.description: A solder wire is a core-drawing operation: a rope of activated flux is drawn together with a tube of solder alloy through successive dies until the wire is 0.3-0.8 mm across and the flux core is 0.1-0.3 mm. It constrains the flux chemistry severely - the flux has to be viscous enough not to run out of the die and fluid enough to fill the core - and it is why a 63/37 wire with a 0.2 mm core held about 1% of its mass in flux. One C64 has a few tens of joints and therefore a few grams of wire.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Flux activator
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: Rosin alone is a weak flux. The activator is what makes the flux work, and it is also what makes the residue corrosive, so the whole specification of a flux is a trade: enough acid to remove the oxide, not enough ion to eat the board. The 1980s activators were carboxylic acids (stearic acid, abietic acid itself, succinic acid and its anhydride), fatty acid salts such as the zinc and amine stearates, and - in the older RMA grades - amine hydrochlorides, which is where the halide came from.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Amine halide activator (the halide source)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: A triethanolamine or an alkylamine neutralised with a mineral acid, giving a halide ion in the flux. It is the reason a halide flux is corrosive if the residue is left on, and it is the reason the halide-free no-clean flux of the mid-1980s removed them rather than replacing them: the halide was never functional, it was just the most convenient way to get an acid and an amine together. The MIL-F-14161 halide-free standard of the late 1970s is what the industry measured against.
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.note: The halide-free flux specification (MIL-F-14161) is the standard US military specification that the 1980s flux industry measured against; its date is the origin of the practice rather than of the specification's current form.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Balancing a halide activator
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: The whole trick of a halide flux is the neutralisation: enough amine to dissolve the resin and enough mineral acid to supply the fluxing acidity and the halide ion, and not so much of either that the residue eats the board. In practice a formulation is a matter of parts per million of chloride, and the measurement is an ion chromatography titration of an extracted sample rather than anything the flux maker could see. It is the least visible quality control in electronics and it is the one that decides whether a board passes its bias test.

chem.rosin.name: Pine rosin (colophony)
chem.rosin.description: The sticky amber solid left when turpentine is distilled out of pine resin. Most rosin is made from pine stumps - the resinous wood left behind when a tree is cut for pulp - by destructive distillation: the stump is chipped, heated in a still to about 150-200 C, turpentine and pine oil come over, and the residue is the rosin, which is then graded by colour and by softening point. About 700,000-800,000 tonnes of rosin were made in the early 1980s, mostly in China, the United States and Brazil.
chem.rosin.note: Rosin production figures for the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude; the chemistry and the softening point ranges are standard.

chem.rosin.distillation.name: Stump distillation and grading
chem.rosin.distillation.description: Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps. The stump is chipped into 5-10 cm pieces, charged to a still, and heated; turpentine comes over first and is condensed and separated by distillation into alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and dipentene, and then pine oil and a heavy residue come over, and what is left in the pot is the crude rosin. The rosin is then graded - by colour (X, WW, WW, W) and by softening point (batter 75 C, fir 80 C, Norway 85 C, I 90 C, P 110 C, S 120 C) - and the Y grade, at about 165 C softening point and clear, is the one the flux core needs because it has almost no crystallisation and it does not go brittle.

chem.rosin.distillation.rosin-grade.name: Rosin grading
chem.rosin.distillation.rosin-grade.description: Colour by optical comparison against a reference chip, softening point by the ring-and-ball method, and acid value by titration. The flux maker's specification is colour and softening point; the abietic acid content follows from them. A rosin that is too yellow discolours the solder joint and shows through a white silkscreen, and a rosin that is too soft runs off the core during the wave.

chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.name: Chipping and the still
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.description: A whole-tree distillery burns about 1.5-2.5 tonnes of dry pine stumps per tonne of rosin plus its turpentine, and yields about 5-8% rosin, 3-4% turpentine and 1-2% pine oil by mass of dry wood. The stumps come from pine killed by beetle attack, from pine cut for pulp, and from the thinning of a plantation - so the rosin business is downstream of a forestry, and specifically of a beetle, in a way that is often overlooked when the flux is described as a petrochemical.
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.note: Yields vary a lot with the species, the age of the stump and the method; the ranges are the commonly quoted ones.

facts.label: Rosin yield from dry pine wood

chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.name: Retort and the batch cycle
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.description: The classic stump still is a cast-iron or steel retort holding one to two tonnes of chipped wood, charged, closed, and fired with the turpentine vapour going to a condenser and the rosin staying in the pot. A cycle takes 12-20 hours and the still is charged by hand - which is why the business has barely changed since the 1850s in its mechanics while every other part of the 1980s chemical industry has been rebuilt twice. The 1980s changes were in the condenser and in the chip size, not in the process.
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.note: Stump distillation cycle times and charge sizes vary by still design; the figures are representative of the small-batch practice that survived into the 1980s.

chem.rosin.tall-oil.name: Tall oil and the kraft mill connection
chem.rosin.tall-oil.description: The black liquor from a kraft pulp mill contains resin acids and fatty acids - tall oil - which is distilled into fatty acids, tall-oil fatty acids and a pitch fraction, and can be further processed to rosin equivalents. It is why the rosin chemistry is a pulp-and-paper chemistry and not only a forestry one, and why the rosin and tall-oil plants sit next to a kraft mill. Colophony of the C64's flux most probably came from a stump distillery, not from a mill, but the two are interchangeable raw materials.

chem.pcb-chemicals.name: The chemistry of making the board
chem.pcb-chemicals.description: A 1983 bare board goes through about eleven wet operations, and each one is a chemical plant: laminate impregnation and pressing, copper foil treatment, dry-film lamination, alkaline or ferric etching, drilling, electroless copper, electroplating, solder mask, silkscreen, and a final clean. The C64's board is a single-layer FR-4 board with through-hole parts, which is the simplest case - one copper layer, no plating on the holes - and that removes the electroless copper and the gold entirely.

chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.name: Chlorine-free, and why it took twenty years
chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.description: Nothing in the 1983 process list was unusual except that it was chlorinated: ferric chloride, trichloroethane, a chlorinated epoxy and a brominated one. By 1995-2000 the industry had moved to alkaline etching, alkaline dry-film development, and epoxy laminates with a non-halogenated flame retardant system - and the drivers were the Montreal-adjacent ozone debate, the effluent limits on copper and hexavalent chromium, and the RoHS-style restrictions that arrived later. This node is the marker for where 1983 practice differs from today, not a description of a 1983 process.
chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.note: This is deliberately a forward-looking marker node; the substitution dates vary by region and by regulation.

chem.pcb-chemicals.solder-mask.name: Solder mask and silkscreen
chem.pcb-chemicals.solder-mask.description: The solder mask is an epoxy or acrylate ink screen-printed or curtain-coated through a 100-150 micron stencil and cured at 150 C, and the green colour is a phthalocyanine green pigment in a novolac epoxy vehicle. The silkscreen legend - the white lettering on the C64's board - is a separate white epoxy ink, cured the same way, screen-printed through a 150-200 micron stainless steel mesh with a nylon or polyester emulsion. Both inks are cured thermally and both are dissolved in xylene or in a glycol ether, so the board plant's solvent is a refinery fraction.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.name: Plating baths
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.description: A 1983 double-sided board is copper plated in an acid copper sulphate bath (with levelers and brighteners), then tin plated or gold plated. The chemistry is a small industry of its own: a copper electroplate with organic additives at 2-6 A/dm2 and 25-30 C; a tin or tin-lead bath; and, for the connectors, a nickel and gold stack. Immersion gold is not electroplated gold - it is a displacement reaction, a few hundred nanometres of gold out of a complexing bath, over a nickel layer that the board chemistry has to deposit first.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Immersion gold over electroless nickel
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: Electroless nickel-phosphorus (hypophosphite reducer) gives a hard, corrosion-resistant, solderable surface, and immersion gold in a cyanide-complexed bath gives the contact surface its low contact resistance. The gold bath contains a complexing agent (EDTA, a phosphate or a cyanide) whose job is to hold the gold in solution so the surface reaction is slow and self-limiting at a few hundred nanometres. For a C64's single-layer board none of this is used - the pads are bare copper with a surface treatment.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: Immersion gold chemistry and thickness are process-specific; the general mechanism (a displacement reaction with a complexing agent) is what is reliable here.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Electroless nickel-phosphorus and its reducer
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: The nickel under a gold surface is deposited by a chemical reduction: hypophosphite gives up a hydrogen atom to the nickel ion on the surface and the nickel comes down as metal, with phosphorus co-deposited at 3-9 wt% to make the layer hard and amorphous. The bath is nickel chloride or sulphate at 5-10 g/L, hypophosphite at 10-30 g/L, and 85-95 C for 30-90 minutes, and its uniformity is the reason it is the standard under immersion gold - it coats a via wall as evenly as it coats a pad.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Sodium hypophosphite and white phosphorus
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: The reducing agent is made from yellow phosphorus, caustic soda and sodium carbonate. So the nickel under the gold on a connector - the part that made a C64's edge connector and its I/O socket reliable in a humid climate - was plated out of phosphate rock, coke, silica and an electric furnace, and the C64-scale quantity of phosphorus in it is vanishingly small and the C64-scale quantity of phosphate rock behind it is not.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: Hypophosphite is made by reacting yellow phosphorus with caustic soda under pressure; the chemistry is standard.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Caustic digestion of white phosphorus
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: Yellow phosphorus is reacted with sodium hydroxide under pressure, and the sodium hypophosphite comes off with hydrogen gas - which is why the plant has a hydrogen vent and a flare. The reaction is violent, it is a scale-up of a bench reaction from the 1840s, and it is the reason the electronics industry and the phosphorus industry are joined by a gas as well as by a liquid.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: The hypophosphite digestion is a nineteenth-century chemistry industrialised in the twentieth; the hazard description is standard.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.name: Copper etching
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.description: Ferric chloride at 35-42 degrees Baume, or cupric chloride, dissolves the exposed copper in 30-60 minutes. Ferric chloride was the 1980s default: cheap, fast, and it etches copper at a rate that keeps the undercut manageable. Its problems were regeneration (the spent etchant is worthless unless it is oxidised back, which needs chlorine or a peroxide and an electrolytic cell) and the ferric ion's attack on the epoxy of the laminate if the etch went long. By the early 1980s the alkaline sodium persulphate etch was spreading because it regenerated in place with peroxide and sodium hydroxide and because it would etch a finer line.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: FeCl3 at 35-42 degrees Baume (about 3-5 molar), which is an oxidising acid: the ferric ion takes an electron from the copper and the cupric ion falls back to ferrous. Regeneration is done either with chlorine (the industrial way, in a cell) or with hydrogen peroxide and acid. The byproduct is copper chloride, which in the 1980s was becoming a problem in its own right because of the copper discharge limits.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Regenerating the ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: Spent ferric chloride is ferrous chloride and copper chloride, and it has to be oxidised back to ferric before it can etch again. The industrial way was a chlorination cell: chlorine into the ferrous solution at 60-80 C, converting ferrous back to ferric and precipitating the copper as cuprous chloride. The cell was a piece of the chlor-alkali plant's technology, and the chlorine in it was often the same chlorine that the plant bought for its own electroplating line.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Chlorination and the copper problem
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: Chlorine regenerates the ferric ion, and the copper comes out as a precipitate. In 1983 the industry was having to deal with two consequences: the chloride concentration climbed and had to be bled off, and the copper sludge was a waste with its own disposal limits. The alkaline persulphate etch solved both - it regenerated with hydrogen peroxide and sodium hydroxide, and the copper came out as cuprous oxide - and it was the reason the ferric chloride process was on its way out by 1990.
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.note: The alkaline etch was spreading through the 1980s; the exact adoption date in a given plant is not documented here.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.devel.name: Developer: 1,1,1-trichloroethane to sodium carbonate
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.devel.description: This is the clearest dated marker in the board chemistry. Until the early 1980s the dry-film photoresist was developed in 1,1,1-trichloroethane, which linked the board plant directly to the chlorinated solvent business. In 1983 a dry film designed to be developed in aqueous alkaline sodium carbonate began to replace it, and by the mid-1980s the chlorinated developer was gone from most board plants. The chemistry difference is a matter of which polymer the developer dissolves: a resin designed to be soluble in carbonate will not be soluble in a chlorinated hydrocarbon, and vice versa.
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.devel.note: The commercial introduction of aqueous-developable dry films dates from the early 1980s; by the middle of the decade they were the standard in North America.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.name: Dry-film photoresist
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.description: A 25-40 micron dry film laminated hot onto the copper - a polyester or polyethylene terephthalate base carrying an acrylate photopolymer and an acrylated monomer that crosslinks on exposure. The exposure crosslinks the acrylate, so the exposed areas become insoluble and the unexposed areas are developed away, and the resulting image is negative - the opposite polarity to the wafer resists of the same decade, and the reason the two industries use opposite conventions for the same word.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.name: Laminating the dry film
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.description: The dry film comes off a protective polyester or polyethylene release liner, is laid on the cleaned and dried copper, and is squeezed onto it by a hot laminator at 110-150 C and 3-5 bar with a silicone rubber roller. The rollers are silicone because the film must not stick to them and the liner must, and the whole operation is a controlled vacuum or a controlled pressure depending on the machine: without the pressure, the air trapped between the film and the copper becomes a bubble and the bubble becomes an etch defect.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.name: Release liner and its disposal
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.description: A 25 micron polyester or polyethylene film with a slightly adhesive surface, peeled off and wound onto a take-up reel. In 1980s board plants the liners went into the waste stream by the kilogram - a 500 mm square panel of dry film consumes about a tenth of a square metre of liner - and a solvent-free laminator could run a plant's whole reel without a solvent drum in the room, which is another reason the industry went dry.
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.note: The liner consumption per panel is an order-of-magnitude figure; the solvent-free trend is the reliable part of this node.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.name: Electrolytic copper foil
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.description: A 35-70 micron copper foil, electrodeposited on a rotating drum from a copper sulphate-acid bath and then treated on the bonding surface. The treatment is the interesting part chemically: the foil's teeth are made mechanically or electrochemically, and the surface is then covered with a nodular copper layer bonded to an organo-chrome or a zinc-oleate layer, and in the 1980s increasingly with a benzotriazole layer. Benzotriazole replaced the chromate because hexavalent chromium was being regulated out of the process.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..name: Benzotriazole coupling agent
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..description: BTA, a seven-membered ring with three adjacent nitrogens, adsorbs onto copper and stops it reacting with anything else - it is the corrosion inhibitor and the adhesion promoter in one. It is a beautiful small molecule for this tree because the same triazole ring chemistry appears in the corrosion inhibitors of every other metal in the book, and because the copper underneath is a metal chain node and the BTA is a petrochemical.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..note: BTA's use as the standard copper coupling agent dates from the 1970s and displaced chromate-based treatment; the exact formulations are proprietary.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.name: Epoxy-glass laminate (FR-4)
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.description: Woven glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin at 50-60% resin content, then pressed at 170-180 C and 0.3-1.5 MPa in a multi-daylight press. The cloth comes from the mineral chain (chem.glass-fiber); the resin is chem.epoxy; the hardener in a high-temperature board is the DDS of the epoxy branch. In 1983 FR-4 was the default board material and a typical single-layer C64 board was 1.6 mm of it.

chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.name: Brominated epoxy for FR-4
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.description: Tetrabromobisphenol A based epoxy, brominated to about 20-40% bromine, blended into the resin at 10-30% so the laminate meets UL 94 V-0. The bromine works by releasing hydrogen bromide in the flame and smothering it, and it works so well that the industry continued using it through the 1980s even as the first brominated flame retardant ban had already arrived. It is the epoxy in the C64's board.
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.note: FR-4 formulations vary; not all consumer FR-4 of the 1980s was brominated, and the C64's board grade is not documented.

chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.name: Branched and novolac epoxies
chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.description: Reacting DGEBA with a dihydroxy or trihydroxy compound - trimethylolpropane, bisphenol A again, or an epoxy cresol novolac - builds a molecule with more than two epoxide groups and higher functionality, which raises the glass transition temperature and lets a laminate hold a solder temperature. The epoxy novolac also carried the bromine: brominating the ring gives the flame-retardant epoxy that FR-4 used.

chem.fab-chemicals.name: The wet chemicals of a 1980s silicon fab
chem.fab-chemicals.description: A 1983 wafer fab consumed tens of thousands of gallons a day of ultrapure water and a few thousand gallons of five electronic-grade acids, and its entire chemistry was aimed at one thing: keeping a few hundred metallic atoms per square centimetre off the wafer. This branch traces those chemicals - sulphuric acid, hydrogen peroxide, the buffered HF etch, the plasma etch gases, the dopant gases and the photoresist - back to the sulphur, the chlorine, the fluorine, the ammonia and the natural gas they were made from.

chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.name: Electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.description: Aqueous ammonia at 20-29 wt% in ultrapure water, made by sparging anhydrous ammonia into the water under a scrubbed laminar-flow hood, then filtered to sub-micron and to low sodium. It is the alkaline clean and the alkaline developer companion, and it is the one wet chemical that arrives as a gas: a fab's supply was a battery of electro-polished or fluoropolymer bottles on a nitrogen-purged cabinet, refilled from a bulk ammonia tank outside the cleanroom.
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.note: The ammonia itself is a natural-gas product: chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonia.

chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.am.name: Anhydrous ammonia supply
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.am.description: Liquid ammonia from a Haber-Bosch plant about a day's drive away, delivered in a tanker, vaporised through a water or steam-heated vaporiser and fed as a gas. The purity needed was surprisingly modest compared with the acids - the ammonia's job in the cleanroom was to be clean enough not to leave an alkali residue, and 99.9% anhydrous was generally adequate.

chem.fab-chemicals.1980s-practice.name: 1980s practice, and what changed
chem.fab-chemicals.1980s-practice.description: In 1980s practice the wet bench used 10-20 litre recirculating baths of buffered HF and piranha, and the chemicals were delivered in the returnable fluoropolymer container or in the case of the biggest users, by a bulk tanker. Three things changed within a decade: the bulk delivery, the adoption of spray processors for the wet steps, and above all the substitution of the liquid strippers and the chlorinated solvents for ozone, oxygen plasma and, later, the perfluorocarbon and hydrofluoroether chemistries. The chlorine in this branch is a diminishing asset: the semiconductor industry of the later 1980s and the 1990s began to remove it deliberately, one process step at a time.
chem.fab-chemicals.1980s-practice.note: This node deliberately flags where practice diverged from today's; the specific substitution programmes and their dates vary by process step.

chem.fab-chemicals.spec-purity.name: The purity ladder
chem.fab-chemicals.spec-purity.description: The 1980s specification ladder, from technical grade to the electronic grade that a wafer demanded: a technical acid at about 5N with metals at tens and hundreds of parts per million; an electronic acid at about 8N; and the 9N-10N grade with a total metal content under 10 parts per billion. The reason the ladder existed was the relationship between a metal atom's concentration and the device: a wafer with 10 parts per billion of iron in a cubic centimetre of silicon has more iron atoms in the active volume than it has dopant atoms.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.name: Bulk process gases
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.description: The three gases a fab inhaled by the thousand: nitrogen for inerting, purging and sparging; argon for the sputtering cathodes and for the anneal; and helium for the leak detector, the cryopump and some of the photolithography optics cooling.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.name: Argon
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.description: A by-product of the air separation unit at 1-3% of the air, purified to 99.999%. It fills the sputtering cathodes - the argon ions are accelerated across the gap and knock atoms out of the aluminium or titanium target - and it is the inert atmosphere of the annealing and ashing steps. The sputtering itself is the metals chain, but the gas that drives it is an air separation product.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.name: Helium
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.description: Almost all helium is recovered as a by-product of the cryogenic separation of natural gas liquids - 0.05-0.7% of a helium-rich gas stream, separated to 99.999%. It is the cleanest gas in the plant and it is used in the helium leak detector that is how a fab proves a chamber is sealed, and in the cryopumps of the etch machines. It is the one process gas in a fab whose feedstock is unambiguously natural gas.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.note: Helium separation from a natural gas plant belongs to the gas processing branch: chem.natural-gas.processing.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Nitrogen
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: 99.999% and, for the very best, 99.9999%. Produced by cryogenic air separation for the large users and by pressure swing adsorption for the small ones. Its uses were the furnace tube atmospheres, the photoresist spin-coat bowl, the drying cabinets, the solvent flush and the packaging seal. A large C64 production line would have used a few hundred cubic metres of nitrogen a week.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Cryogenic air separation
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: Air is filtered, compressed to 30-100 bar, cooled and expanded through a cold box to fractionate it into oxygen, nitrogen and argon at -180 C. A unit producing 5,000-30,000 tonnes a day of nitrogen was a large industrial plant in its own right, and it shared its cold box technology with the natural gas processing business in this file.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Atmospheric air
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: The end of that chain: nitrogen and oxygen are separated out of the air itself, and the nitrogen a fab buys is a few parts per million of everything else in the atmosphere removed. The air a nitrogen plant compresses is 78.1% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide and the rest is neon, helium, methane, water and whatever the industrial district has put into it. It is the only feedstock in this entire tree that needs no mining, no drilling and no chemistry at all, which makes it the cheapest and the least traceable.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.name: Dopant sources
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.description: The chemicals that put boron, phosphorus and arsenic into the silicon. The chemistry here is a closed loop back to the ammonia, the chlorine and the fluorspar of the rest of this tree, and the whole business is about the fact that a dopant source is gaseous, toxic and must be delivered to a few cubic centimetres of reactor at a controlled partial pressure.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diffusion.name: Diffusion and ion implantation
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diffusion.description: The 1980s doping methods. Diffusion used a gas or a solid source - phosphorus from phosphine or from a doped oxide, boron from diborane or from BN, arsenic from arsine - in a furnace at 800-1,100 C. Ion implantation accelerated a dopant ion into the wafer at 50-200 keV and used a few per cent of the dose to achieve the same sheet resistance as diffusion, which is what made it the method of choice for a fine-geometry process like the 2-micron NMOS that the VIC-II and the SID were made in.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diffusion.note: The C64 chips were 2 micron NMOS designs of the late 1970s fabricated in the early 1980s; both diffusion and implantation were in use for that generation.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.name: Diborane (B2H6) and boron trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.description: The p-type sources. Diborane is made from boron trifluoride and sodium hydride or from boron trichloride and a hydride, and it arrives at 0.5-5% in hydrogen; boron trifluoride was delivered neat from a cylinder. In 1983 p-type implantation was moving from boron to BF2+ (a molecular ion made in the ion source) because the heavier ion gave a shallower, more controllable junction - a change in the ion source chemistry, not in the wafer chemistry.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.name: Boron trifluoride from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.description: BF3 is made by treating fluorspar with sulphuric acid or with fluosilicic acid, so the p-type dopant of a 1983 NMOS process is, three steps back, the same rock as the HF that etched the oxide. This is the tightest single chain in this whole tree from a mineral to a transistor.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.name: Arsine (AsH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.description: The other n-type source, used for heavier and shallower implants and for the arsenic source oxide. It is made by reducing arsenic trichoxide with zinc and hydrochloric acid or with hydrogen, and the arsenic comes from arsenic metal or from gallium arsenide production. Arsine is the most acutely toxic gas routinely used in a semiconductor fab; the 1980s limit of a few parts per billion in the exhaust was enforced with an ionising-type monitor, not a badge.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.name: Phosphine (PH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.description: The n-type dopant source. In 1983 it was supplied two ways: as an ion-implantation source, and as a dopant gas diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen for the dopant gas deposition reactor. Phosphine is pyrophoric in the pure state and is one of the most acutely toxic gases in a fab, which is why it arrived diluted and in a gas cabinet.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Where the phosphorus comes from
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: The phosphine of a 1983 fab has a longer ancestry than most people assume. Elemental phosphorus is made in a submerged arc furnace from phosphate rock, coke and silica at 1,400-1,500 C, condensed as white phosphorus under water, and then either burned to phosphorus pentoxide (for fertiliser and for the pure phosphoric acid of this file) or reduced to phosphorous acid, which is then converted to phosphine. So an n-doped transistor junction in a C64's VIC-II traces back through a gas cylinder, an electric furnace, and a phosphate rock mine.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphoric acid (the wet-process acid)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: The wet process beats the phosphorus furnace, and it beats it because the furnace is only economical at a very large scale: ground phosphate rock is digested in 30-40% sulfuric acid, the calcium sulphate is filtered off as gypsum, and the phosphoric acid is concentrated to 54% P2O5. The C64-scale relevance of this acid is indirect - it is the fertiliser that came out of the phosphate rock, and it is also the semiconductor-grade acid a fab used for its own processes, purified further to 9N.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Wet-process digestion
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: Rock at 1-2 mm in 30-40% sulfuric acid at 70-80 C, then filtered. The process is a century old and the only thing that has changed since is the filtration and the energy recovery, because the chemistry is limited by the solubility of calcium sulphate and there is no way round it. The gypsum cake is the waste stream, and its disposal (often offshore or in a lined lagoon) is the industry's continuing environmental problem.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: This acid chain is a fertiliser and commodity chain that is nominally outside this subsystem; it is included because the semiconductor-grade version is one of the fab's wet chemicals.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphorus pentasulphide route to phosphine
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: Yellow phosphorus plus phosphorus pentasulphide is treated with caustic soda and water to make phosphorous acid and sodium hypophosphite, and the acid plus a hypophosphite is the standard laboratory and much industrial route to phosphine. The electronic gas is then diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen and cylinder-packaged, because pure phosphine is pyrophoric and because the cylinder package is what the gas cabinet expects.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: Phosphine preparation routes include the hypophosphorous acid route and the phosphorus pentasulphide/caustic route; the latter is the common industrial one.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphate rock
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: A sedimentary rock of calcium phosphate - apatite - mined from the Florida phosphate belt and the Moroccan and Chinese deposits. It is one of the four rock types this whole tree ends in, alongside crude oil, natural gas and sand. The C64-scale fact is absurd but true: the quantity of phosphate rock mined for fertiliser every year is measured in tens of millions of tonnes, and the quantity used to make the phosphorus in a C64's transistors is a few grams, most of it going into fertiliser for somebody's field.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: The phosphate rock mining and fertiliser chain is nominally outside this subsystem; this node exists because the n-type dopant chain terminates there.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: The submerged arc phosphorus furnace
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: A 30-100 MW furnace in which phosphate rock, coke and silica are heated to 1,400-1,500 C by three graphite electrodes dipped into the charge, and the phosphorus vapour - P4 - is taken off, condensed under water and stored under water because it ignites in air. A 1980s US plant made 100,000-150,000 tonnes of yellow phosphorus a year, and the greater part of that went to phosphoric acid for fertiliser rather than to any electronics use.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.name: Plasma etch gases
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.description: The gases that a barrel or planar plasma etcher used to etch silicon dioxide, polysilicon, aluminium and organic films. They are the fluorine and chlorine family, and they are the most expensive part of the etch cost after the electricity.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.name: The barrel plasma etcher
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.description: A quartz or alumina tube with electrodes at the top and bottom, gas fed in at the top, RF at 13.56 MHz, and wafers standing vertically in slots around the tube wall. It was the workhorse of the 1980s for silicon dioxide and aluminium etching and for resist ashing, and it was cheap, simple and gently non-uniform - which was acceptable when the field of view was small and the line was a couple of microns. The planar (magnetron) etcher, where the plasma is generated above the wafer by a magnetically confined source, gave the flatness that a later generation of chips needed.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.name: Nitrogen trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.description: An emerging chamber-cleaning gas in the 1980s, and later a feedstock for the NF3-based etch chemistry. It is a very strong oxidiser, it is a gas at room temperature, and the reason it took so long to industrialise in the United States was a supply constraint rather than a performance one - the production chemistry needed fluorine.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.note: NF3 chamber cleaning was in commercial use in the late 1980s; this node's presence is a marker rather than a core technology of the 1983 C64 chips.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.name: Chlorine and BCl3 for the aluminium etch
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.description: A chlorine-based plasma - Cl2, or BCl3 with Cl2 - is used for aluminium, because fluorine does not etch aluminium cleanly. BCl3 also supplied boron, so the etch gas doubled as the p-type dopant source, which is one of the reasons the boron trifluoride and boron trichloride business ended up as one business.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.note: BCl3 is made by chlorinating boron oxide or elemental boron; the chemistry is standard but the 1980s supply details are not well documented here.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.name: Tetrafluoromethane
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.description: CF4, the workhorse oxide etch gas and the fluorine chemistry's workhorse generally. It is made from fluorine (from fluorspar) and carbon, or from a chlorofluorocarbon feedstock. In a plasma etcher it dissociates to fluorine radicals that etch silicon dioxide - it does not etch silicon, which is what made the selectivity possible - and it is the gas that made the barrel reactor the standard 1980s oxide etch.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Fluorine from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Every fluorine atom in a fab's chemistry started as calcium fluoride. Fluorspar is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 200-250 C in a kiln or a retort to make anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, and the HF is either sold as the aqueous etch acid or chlorinated with chlorine to make the CFCs and the fluorocarbons. It is the same sulphuric acid, the same chlorine and the same rock as the oxide etch, the freons in the packaging and the halogenated degreasers.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Fluoride plus sulphuric acid at 200-250 C gives anhydrous HF, which is distilled off and shipped in a fluorine-lined tanker or a nickel tank. It is a strong acid, a violent poison, and it will dissolve most metals; the 1980s storage practice was a tank with a fluorine polymer lining and an emergency water curtain, and the fundamental tension in the whole HF business is that the only thing that will hold it is the same fluorine chemistry that makes the etch gases.

chem.photoresist.name: Photoresist chemistry
chem.photoresist.description: The organic photoresists of 1983 were almost all positive-working diazonaphthoquinone resins on a novolac: the light-sensitive group is a diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate ester on a phenolic novolac made from phenol and formaldehyde. Exposing the resist converts the ester to a carboxylic acid, which makes the exposed resin soluble in the alkaline developer, so the image is positive. It is a strictly positive image because of the mechanism, not because of anything clever - the exposure destroys the very group that was holding the resin together.

chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.name: Polysilane and plasma-polymerised resists
chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.description: The silicon-containing resists, in which a Si-Si backbone absorbs the deep ultraviolet and generates a silyl radical that crosslinks the exposed area. In 1983 they were in development for the 1 micron and sub-micron layers, and they are the reason the industry needed a deep-ultraviolet lithography tool at all. Their problem was exactly the same as everything else in this branch: a new chemistry with a contamination story attached.
chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.note: Plasma-polymerised (polysilane) resists were a research topic through the 1980s; commercial DUV resists arrived later.

chem.photoresist.negative.name: Negative resists and image reversal
chem.photoresist.negative.description: A small share of 1980s production was negative-working - the exposed areas crosslink and stay - and image-reversal resists, where a photoacid generator makes a carboxylic acid in the exposed areas and an amine in the top layer diffuses into them and makes the exposed areas soluble, so a positive image is made with a negative resist chemistry. The reversal chemistry existed in 1983 because of the contrast it gave with the deep-ultraviolet exposure tools of the late 1980s.

chem.photoresist.hard-bake.name: Dehydration bake and hard bake
chem.photoresist.hard-bake.description: A dehydration bake at 150-200 C to drive the water out of the spin-coated film before exposure, and a post-exposure hard bake at 120-180 C to crosslink or densify the remaining image. The hard bake is what makes the resist resistant to the plasma etch and to the buffered HF, and it is also what makes it harder to strip - which is why the industry moved to plasma stripping and to ozonised water by the late 1980s, and why the old solvent strippers (phenol and sulphuric acid) disappeared from the process.

chem.photoresist.hard-bake.stripping.name: Resist stripping
chem.photoresist.hard-bake.stripping.description: The 1980s progression: a phenolic-plus-sulphuric-acid liquid strip, then an ozone/water clean and an oxygen plasma ashing step to remove the hardened resist. The move was driven by the ion contamination of the liquid strippers and by the fact that the hard-baked resist was becoming impossible to remove in a controlled way. Plasma ashing uses an oxygen plasma at about 1 mbar and 250-400 C.

chem.photoresist.development.name: Alkaline development with TMAH
chem.photoresist.development.description: 0.2-0.3 N TMAH, at 20-25 C, by spray or immersion, for 30-60 seconds. The developer has to be controlled to a fraction of a degree and to a fraction of a percent of TMAH because the image is only about half a micrometre deep and the process window is correspondingly narrow. Spray development, introduced in the early 1980s, removed the meniscus and the particle problems of immersion and became the industry standard within a few years.

chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.name: Diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate
chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.description: The photosensitive ester: 1,2-naphthoquinone-2-diazide-5-sulphonic acid esterified onto the phenolic hydroxyls of the novolac. The 1,4-isomer was the one the 1980s photoresist industry settled on because it gives the higher photospeed and less outgrowth. The whole resist is about 20-30% diazo compound by weight; the rest is novolac and a small amount of sensitiser.

facts.label: Typical exposure
facts.value: g-line 436 nm, h-line 405 nm, i-line 365 nm

chem.photoresist.novolac.name: Novolac resin from phenol and formaldehyde
chem.photoresist.novolac.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid to a thermoplastic, low-molecular-weight resin with no epoxide or methylol functionality left. The resin is not the photosensitive part; it is the part that gives the film its mechanical integrity and its dissolution behaviour in the developer. Its phenolic hydroxyl groups are why the novolac dissolves so readily in TMAH - and why an alkaline developable resist could not have worked with the old novolac-epoxy resists of the early 1960s.
chem.photoresist.novolac.note: The phenol chain is chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol and the formaldehyde chain is chem.pom.formaldehyde.

chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.name: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.description: TMAH, sold at 25 wt% in ultrapure water, used to develop the positive photoresists and - from the late 1970s - to wet-etch the aluminium interconnect of a dynamic random access memory. It arrived as a photoresist developer in the single most consequential materials change of the early 1980s: a chemist at IBM demonstrated in 1979 that an alkaline developer could work on a diazonaphthoquinone resist without image reversal, and that single result is the ancestor of essentially all modern photolithography.

chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.synthesis.name: TMAH synthesis
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.synthesis.description: Made by the electrolysis of trimethylamine hydrochloride, or by ion exchange from trimethylamine and a methyl chloride-derived quaternary salt. The commercial 25% solution in ultrapure water had to be filtered to sub-micron and to low sodium, because any sodium on a wafer was a threshold-shift defect.
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.synthesis.note: TMAH manufacture is either the electrolytic route from trimethylamine hydrochloride or an ion-exchange route; both are industrial.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.name: Hydrofluoric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.description: The silicon etchant. HF dissolves silicon dioxide, and it does so fast, cleanly and without leaving a residue - which is why it is the single most important wet chemical in a silicon fab and also the one that produces the most fatalities. Anhydrous HF is made from fluorspar (CaF2) with sulphuric acid at 200-250 C, and the aqueous grades are made from that.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.haz.name: Hydrofluoric acid safety
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.haz.description: HF penetrates skin and travels down the nerve sheaths, causing deep burns and systemic hypocalcaemia with cardiac arrest, often hours after the exposure. The 1980s response was calcium gluconate gel at every sink, a mandatory buddy system for handling above 5%, and the practice of handling dilute HF in a PTFE or polypropylene carrier rather than in glass. It is the most dangerous liquid in a semiconductor fab and the reason a fab's wet bench is a room with a raised floor and its own ventilation.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.buf.name: Buffered oxide etch (BOE)
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.buf.description: Hydrofluoric acid diluted to 0.5-5% and buffered with ammonium acetate or acetic acid to hold the pH at 4-6. The buffer is not cosmetic: it stabilises the etch rate by controlling the reaction's HF2- concentration, and it stops the etch from accelerating as the acid is consumed. Buffered HF is used for the native oxide strip, for the field oxide etch, for the contact and via etch, and - importantly - for the removal of the hardened, plasma-exposed photoresist, because an unhardened resist would just dissolve in the acid.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.flu.name: Fluorspar (fluorite, CaF2)
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.flu.description: A mineral mined in Mexico, South Africa, China and elsewhere, and a genuinely strategic material: the entire fluorine chemistry of a semiconductor fab - the HF etch, the fluorocarbon plasma etch gases, the fluoropolymer bottles and the O-rings - descends from this rock. It is the one raw material in the whole tree that is neither a petroleum nor a metal nor a silicate.
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.flu.note: The mineral chain belongs to the minerals subsystem; this node exists because the fluorine chemistry is a petrochemical-adjacent tree of its own.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.name: Electronic-grade nitric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.description: 70% HNO3 at about 10N. Nitric acid was the oxidising component of the older cleaning recipes and a component of some of the early aluminium etchants. It was the least-used of the four big wet chemicals by the early 1980s because it had been largely replaced by hydrogen peroxide.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.name: Ostwald process
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.description: Ammonia oxidised over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-900 C to nitric oxide, then to NO2 in excess air, then absorbed in water. Nitric acid is therefore an ammonia product, which means it is a natural-gas product: the Haber-Bosch ammonia of the 1980s was the source of the nitric acid and of the ammonium hydroxide, both of which a fab bought.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Ammonia
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: NH3: the feedstock for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation, for fertiliser, and for the electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide used to rinse and develop photoresist. World ammonia production in 1983 was of the order of 100-110 million tonnes a year.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.name: Electronic-grade hydrochloric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.description: 20-37% HCl purified to about 10N. It was the second half of the piranha mix in some recipes, the dilute etch for the native oxide, the source of the chloride chemistry in the plasma etchants, and the chemical that keeps a fab's chemical room smelling of a swimming pool. It is made by absorbing the HCl gas from a chlorine and hydrogen burner in ultrapure water.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydroc.name: Hydrogen to hydrochloric acid
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydroc.description: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl at 250-400 C over an HCl synthesis catalyst, then absorption into demineralised water to 31-37%. This is the second largest industrial use of hydrogen and it is why the chlorine industry needs natural gas at all: without reforming hydrogen, chlor-alkali chlorine is very hard to sell. The HCl then feeds vinyl chloride, the chloromethanes and the chlorinated degreasers.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydroc.note: Chlorine electrolysis itself belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement belongs here.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.name: Electronic-grade hydrogen peroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.description: 30-50% aqueous H2O2 purified to 99.999% with a total metal content in the tens of parts per billion. It was the other half of the piranha mix and the workhorse cleaner and oxidiser of the wet bench, and by the 1980s it had largely displaced the older sodium hydroxide and nitric acid cleaning recipes.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.ant.name: Anthraquinone process
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.ant.description: Naphthalene or anthracene converted to 9,10-anthraquinone over sulphuric acid; hydrogenated to the anthrahydroquinone at 50-60 C and 3-5 bar over a palladium-on-carbon catalyst; then re-oxidised by air at 50-60 C and 3-5 bar. The working solution is about 0.2-0.5 M in anthraquinone, and the yield to hydrogen peroxide is 90-95%. In 1983 nearly all the world's hydrogen peroxide was made this way, and the reason a chemical park with a peroxide plant also had a propylene oxide plant is the shared anthraquinone and the shared peroxide.
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.ant.note: Anthraquinone is now usually made from naphthalene; the anthracene route is the older one.

facts.label: Hydrogenation
facts.value: 50-60 C, 3-5 bar H2, Pd on carbon

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.name: Electronic-grade sulphuric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.description: 96-98% H2SO4 purified to 9N-10N, with a total metal content under 10-100 parts per billion depending on the grade. It was delivered in a fluoropolymer-lined tanker or in a 2,000-litre high-purity container and was used for the piranha clean, for the dehydration bake, for the sulphuric acid-hydrogen peroxide resist strip, and for the oxidation furnace as a carrier gas alternative. Its raw material is the elemental sulphur of a Claus plant, burned in a contact process.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.piranha.name: The piranha clean
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.piranha.description: A mixture of concentrated sulphuric acid and 30% hydrogen peroxide, three parts acid to one, at 80-120 C, used to strip all organic matter off a wafer, a quartz boat or a process chamber before anything else touches it. It is called piranha because it eats organic compounds at a furious rate, and it is violently dangerous: it reacts exothermically with anything organic that gets in, it generates oxygen peroxide vapour, and it will detonate on contact with a ketone or an alcohol. By the late 1980s it was being replaced in several steps by an ozone-wet clean.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.oleum.name: Oleum and the 9N distillation
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.oleum.description: The last step of semiconductor-grade sulphuric acid is an azeotropic or vacuum distillation that takes it to 9N, driven by the fact that every metal with a volatility near the acid's has to be pumped out of it. That distillation, and the quartz or Teflon equipment it needed, was why electronic-grade acid cost 20-100 times a technical grade acid.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.oleum.note: Purification routes for high-purity sulphuric acid have varied (distillation, ion exchange, isopropanol extraction); the general point is that a dedicated purification step exists and that it is expensive.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.name: Contact process and sulphur burning
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.description: Sulphur is burned to SO2 in a 900-1,200 C furnace, converted over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at 420-450 C to SO3, and absorbed in 98% acid to make oleum, which is then diluted. The feedstock in 1983 was overwhelmingly recovered elemental sulphur, because the Claus plant had made it cheap; earlier the pyrites (iron pyrite, FeS2) route was used, and a number of Japanese plants still burned pyrites into their own acid.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.note: The sulphur feedstock for sulphuric acid is chem.sulfur, and it arrives from the Claus plant.

chem.sulfur.name: Elemental sulphur (brimstone)
chem.sulfur.description: Bright yellow solid sulphur, one of the four commodities - alongside crude, natural gas and coal - that a 1980s chemical plant could buy. It is used in vulcanisation, in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (which is then used to make titanium dioxide, fertiliser and phosphates), in 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid herbicides, and in the elemental sulphur vulcanisation of rubber. World sulphur production in 1983 was of the order of 8-10 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it recovered from H2S by Claus.

chem.fab-chemicals.ultrapure-water.name: Ultrapure water
chem.fab-chemicals.ultrapure-water.description: The most-consumed chemical in a fab by volume, and the hardest. Deionised, reverse-osmosed, ultrafiltered, UV-irradiated and finally ozonised to a resistivity of 18.2 MOhm-cm at 25 C, with total organic carbon below 5 parts per billion and dissolved silica below 1 part per billion. The resistivity figure is a saturation: it says the water is at the limit of what a deioniser can do, and it was the number on the certificate that every batch of chemicals was diluted from.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: thousands of cubic metres a day for a mid-size fab

chem.solvents.name: Solvents and degreasers in a 1980s plant
chem.solvents.description: Between half and three quarters of the organic solvent used in a 1980s electronics plant went into degreasing, mostly in a hot vapour degreaser. The solvent was almost always a chlorinated hydrocarbon - 1,1,1-trichloroethane or trichloroethylene in Europe and Asia, perchloroethylene in the United States - and the entire decade's regulatory story is the story of removing them. By 1990 in the United States, vapour degreasing with perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene was over, and what replaced it was isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, or a hydrocarbon.

chem.solvents.regulation.name: Regulation: why the solvent list changed
chem.solvents.regulation.description: Three forces rewrote a 1980s solvent shelf. The US Clean Air Act's 1970 and 1977 amendments and the resulting state implementation plans constrained volatile organic compound emissions, and because a chlorinated degreaser is an emission source, they hit the degreaser directly. The 1983-1989 federal halogenated solvent action set dates for the chlorinated degreasers. And the Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, removed the CFCs and the halon-cleaning gases.

chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.name: Occupational exposure limits
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.description: The other half of the story. In 1980s practice every one of these solvents had a 1980s-era recommended limit, every one of them was under active review by the ACGIH, and the direction of travel through the decade was downward. Perchloroethylene's limit fell from 400 to 100 ppm, trichloroethylene from 200 to 50 ppm, and methylene chloride from 500 to 250 ppm. The engineering response was local exhaust ventilation with a hooded enclosure and a solvent recovery unit, not a respirator.
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.note: The specific 1980s limit values changed year to year and differ between the ACGIH TLV and the OSHA PEL; the values here are indicative of the direction and magnitude of change.

chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.name: Montreal Protocol
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.description: Signed in 1987, in force from 1989, and the most effective environmental treaty ever agreed. It phased out CFCs and halons, and it is the reason expanded polystyrene packaging lost its CFC blowing agent and the electronics plant lost its CFC cleaning gas. A C64 in 1983 was packed in a CFC-blown foam box; a C64 in 1993 was not.
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.note: The C64's corrugated shipping carton was a paperboard box; the polystyrene foam end caps in consumer electronics packaging of that era commonly used CFC or HCFC blowing agent.

chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.foam-b.name: The packaging consequence of the Protocol
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.foam-b.description: The most visible effect of the Montreal Protocol on a household object was in its packaging. Until about 1987 the end caps and the fitted inserts in consumer electronics cartons were expanded polystyrene blown with CFC-11, which made a light, rigid, insulating pack out of a petrochemical and a gas. Pentane blowing took over and the foam became softer and slightly heavier, and the structural part of the problem was solved by changing the carton rather than the foam. It is a small change, but it is the one place where a treaty signed in 1987 is visible on a table in 1993.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.name: US EPA VOC and solvent rules
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.description: The 1970 Clean Air Act amendments listed chlorinated solvents as hazardous air pollutants, and the states' implementation plans in the early 1980s put specific limits on degreaser emissions. New Jersey's solvent programme in the early 1980s was the strictest of them and effectively banned chlorinated degreasers in much of the state. The federal halogenated solvent action followed, banning trichloroethylene vapour degreasing by 1990.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.note: US solvent regulation is jurisdiction-specific and layered; the dates above are the commonly cited anchors rather than a single statute.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.name: The 1980s substitution: isopropanol, NMP, hydrocarbons
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.description: What actually replaced the chlorinated degreasers, and why it took about ten years rather than two. The candidates were isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, and increasingly hydrocarbon solvents and aqueous detergents. Each was available, each worked, and none of them was free: isopropanol is flammable, NMP has reproductive toxicity concerns, and hydrocarbons have a low flash point too. The substitution was driven by regulation and by the fact that a chlorinated degreaser needed a permit and an oxygen emission permit and a reporting line to the regulator, and by nothing else at all.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.note: This node summarises a substitution whose timetable varied by country and by sector; it is a direction-of-travel statement rather than a dated claim.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.name: Why the substitute was also cheaper to make
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.description: Isopropyl alcohol sat next to the acetone plant in a chemical complex that already had propylene, and the same propylene that made the case plastic made the solvent that cleaned it. By the mid-1980s the electronics plant was buying its cleaner from the same petrochemical park that supplied its plastic, and the chlorinated solvent it had replaced was the only one on the list that needed a mercury-catalysed acetylene route or a chlorine plant to make.
