That is the deepest reason the substitution was easy: it was a move along an existing supply chain.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.name: Xylene, toluene and hexane
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.description: The hydrocarbon solvents. Xylene is the classic silkscreen and coatings solvent and it is what the screen printing ink of a PCB is thinned with. Toluene was the coatings and adhesive solvent. Hexane (extracted from the light ends by solvent extraction with furfural or NMP) was the degreaser for precision metalwork and the extraction solvent for the edible oils. All three are refinery fractions, and they are also the most flammable solvents on the shelf.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.name: White spirit and mineral spirits
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.description: A petroleum distillate boiling 150-200 C - roughly C8-C12 - sold as the standard paint and stencil solvent. It was the cheapest coating solvent there was and it was used in the silkscreen shop, in the stencil shop and in the assembly shop's fixture cleaning. Its defect was the same defect as xylene's: flash point around 30-40 C, which means it belongs in a room with no open flame and a bonded-earth tank.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.note: White spirit definitions vary by standard; the 150-200 C range and the flash point are representative.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.solve.name: Solvent extraction of aromatics with furfural or NMP
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.solve.description: Furfural (161 C) and NMP (202 C) were the two classical solvents for separating aromatics from paraffins in a refinery, and both were displaced from most of their other duties in the 1970s and 1980s by better solvents and by the pressure-swing and adsorption processes. NMP is the survivor: it went from refinery aromatics extraction to butadiene extraction to the electronics degreasing market within twenty years.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.solve.note: The same two solvents appear in chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby and in the solvent replacement business.

chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.name: Ketones, esters and glycol ethers
chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.description: The rest of the 1980s solvent shelf: methyl ethyl ketone and methyl isobutyl ketone (the latter made by condensing acetone to diacetone alcohol and then hydrogenating), ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate, propylene glycol ethers, and dimethylformamide. Each had a niche - the ketones for coatings, the esters for cleaning, the glycol ethers for the controlled evaporation of a coating, DMF for the film and fibre industries.

chem.solvents.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.solvents.acetone.description: Propanone, boiling 56 C. It was the general cleaning solvent for glass, for the epoxy residues of a coil winding operation, and for some stencil and screen operations, and it is the solvent in the acetylene absorption step of the acetylene process and in the electrophotography of copying. It came out of the cumene process and the acetone cyanohydrin process, both of which are propylene plants.

chem.ethanol.name: Ethanol
chem.ethanol.description: C2H6O, boiling 78.4 C. In 1980s electronics it was a solvent and a cleaning fluid for a few specialist applications, and it was the fuel additive competing with MTBE for the octane that lead had given up. Chemically it can be made either by hydrating ethylene over phosphoric acid at 300 C and 60-70 bar, or by fermenting sugar. Both routes existed in 1983; the fermentation route made most of the world's ethanol in that decade because it was cheaper.

chem.ethanol.fermentation.name: Fermentation route (the biomass route)
chem.ethanol.fermentation.description: Sugar from cane, beet or starch fermented by yeast at 30-35 C for two to three days, then rectified to 95% or dehydrated to absolute. In 1983 this made most of the world's fuel ethanol and it is the one large ethanol supply in the tree that does not begin with crude oil. It is also the honest boundary of this subsystem: a C64's plastics begin in petroleum, but a C64's fuel ethanol begins in a field.

chem.ethanol.ethylene-hydration.name: Ethylene hydration (the synthetic route)
chem.ethanol.ethylene-hydration.description: Ethylene plus steam over phosphoric acid on silica at 280-330 C and 60-70 bar gives 4-6% ethanol per pass, so the off-gas is recycled. The selectivity limit is thermodynamic: the reaction is an equilibrium, and the industry spent decades on better catalysts and on pervaporation and extractive distillation to get around it.

chem.isopropanol.acetone-route.name: Acetone hydrogenation route
chem.isopropanol.acetone-route.description: Acetone plus hydrogen over a copper or a nickel-zinc catalyst at 100-150 C and 5-20 bar gives isopropanol with 95-98% selectivity. It is the older, simpler route and it was still fully in use in 1983. Both routes end at the same molecule; they differ in whether the plant has to own a propylene oxide unit.

chem.isopropanol.kpo.name: KPO process (from propylene)
chem.isopropanol.kpo.description: Propylene plus acetone gives propylene oxide; propylene oxide isomerises to acetone over a base catalyst; acetone plus hydrogen is hydrogenated to isopropanol. The isomerisation-hydrogenation loop is the unit that makes the process economical, and the 1970s introduction of the low-temperature isomerisation catalysts was what made the KPO route beat the older acetone-hydrogenation route on the balance sheet.

chem.isopropanol.kpo.acetone-loop.name: The acetone loop
chem.isopropanol.kpo.acetone-loop.description: About 0.6 t of acetone per tonne of isopropanol is circulated and needs to be bought in or made on site, so an isopropanol plant without an acetone source was not viable. This is the reason the isopropanol business grew up attached to cumene plants, and it is why the electronics cleaner's supply chain in 1983 went back through cumene, phenol and the cracker.
chem.isopropanol.kpo.acetone-loop.note: The KPO acetone circulation ratio is commonly quoted around 0.6 t/t; exact values depend on the loop design.

chem.solvents.cfc.name: CFCs and HCFCs (halons and freons)
chem.solvents.cfc.description: Trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11, boiling 23.8 C) and trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane (CFC-113, boiling 48 C) were the 1980s cleaners, refrigerants and foam blowing agents, and CFC-11 was the blowing agent in expanded polystyrene packaging until the late 1980s. In 1983 there was no regulation on them at all; by 1987 the Montreal Protocol had been signed and by 1989 the phase-out of the developed countries had begun.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.name: CFC synthesis from chloroform
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.description: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) is chloroform plus hydrogen fluoride in an antimony halide catalyst at 50-100 C; CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) is carbon tetrachloride plus hydrogen fluoride. Both therefore start from the chlorination of methane - the same methane the plastics industry buys - and both end in the ozone layer. The chain from a gas field to a chlorofluorocarbon is four steps long and it took twenty years of argument before anything was done about it.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.name: Methane chlorination
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.description: Chlorine plus methane at 250-400 C gives chloromethane, and further chlorination gives chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. The chlorination is a free-radical chain reaction in a fluidised bed, and the product is a mixture that has to be distilled. The chloroform route to CFC-11 is therefore a natural gas route: methane, chlorine, fluorine - and fluorine is from fluorspar, the same rock as the HF that etched a silicon wafer.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.name: The chlorine in every chlorinated molecule
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.description: Methylene chloride, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, the trichloroethane degreaser, the vinyl chloride monomer and the epichlorohydrin all start from the same brine electrolysis. One electrochemical cell in a chemical park produces the chlorine atom that appears in a dozen different industrial molecules, and it is the single most useful reason to think of the 1980s chemical industry as one connected thing rather than thirty.

chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.name: Dichloromethane (methylene chloride)
chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.description: CH2Cl2, boiling at 40 C, made by chlorinating methane to chloromethane and then to dichloromethane, or by the chlorination of formaldehyde. It was the fastest-evaporating chlorinated solvent and was used for paint stripping, for the epoxy and flux residues that a slow solvent would not remove, and in place of perchloroethylene in some cleaning operations. Its 1980s regulatory moment came at the end of the decade, when the US EPA designated it a hazardous air pollutant and set a phase-out of its use in degreasing and in the aerosol propellant market.

chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.name: Tetrachloroethylene (perchloroethylene)
chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.description: Cl2C=CCl2, boiling at 119 C, made by chlorinating ethylene to 1,2-dichloroethane and then to tetrachloroethane followed by chlorination and dehydrochlorination, or by the oxychlorination route. It was the American electronics degreaser of choice because it dissolves grease and flux residue and does not evaporate as fast as 1,1,1-trichloroethane. It is the clearest case in this file of a solvent killed by regulation rather than by performance: the US EPA's 1984 halogenated solvent rule set a phase-out schedule for vapour degreasing - all sources by 1989, with the smaller degreasers going first - and perchloroethylene was also being restricted as an air pollutant.
chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.note: The exact sub-schedules of the US halogenated solvent rule (1984) had tiered deadlines by source size; the 1989 completion date is the one usually quoted.

facts.label: US EPA phase-out of vapour degreasing
facts.value: small sources from 1985-1986, all sources by 1989

chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.name: Trichloroethylene (1,1,2-TCE)
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.description: Boiling at 87 C, made from acetylene by chlorination to tetrachloroethane followed by dehydrochlorination. It has excellent solvency for grease and for the epoxy and phenolic residues of an electronics line, and it is also a solvent for the vapour degreaser that handles the cleaned parts. It is a suspected carcinogen, and the United States removed it from vapour degreasing in 1990 under the federal halogenated solvent rule; by then the replacement across the industry was largely done.
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.note: The US prohibition dates: the halogenated solvent rulemaking began in 1983 and the prohibition on TCE vapour degreasing took effect in 1990. Trichloroethylene remained widely used outside the US into the 1990s.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane from acetylene
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: The synthesis that links a degreaser to a natural gas field. Acetylene plus HCl over a mercuric chloride catalyst gives vinylidene chloride, CH2=CCl2, and chlorinating that with chlorine gives 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Both steps are the same chemistry, and the same catalyst, as the vinyl chloride process - and therefore so are the same upstream, the same natural gas and the same mercury liability.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Chlorination to 1,1,1-trichloroethane
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: Vinylidene chloride plus chlorine at 20-50 C gives 1,1,2-trichloroethane first and then 1,1,1-trichloroethane, which is separated by distillation. The 1,1,2 isomer is the more valuable one because it dehydrochlorinates to trichloroethylene, so a plant could swing between a degreaser and a vapour degreaser solvent depending on where the chlorine went - the same swing as in the oxychlorination plant, and the reason both plants were built with the flexibility.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Mercury catalyst and its recovery
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and acetylene adds across it. The catalyst is what makes the chemistry work and what makes the plant a mercury emitter, and the 1980s answer was a mercury recovery system: the reactor effluent was stripped with an acid stream, the mercury concentrated to a recoverable 10-20% solution, and that solution taken back to the catalyst maker. It is the same engineering problem and the same answer as the PVC plant's, for the same reason.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Activated charcoal support
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: A 2-4 mm charcoal pellet, impregnated with mercuric chloride and dried. Activated charcoal is made by carbonising wood or coal at 800-1,000 C and steam activating it, so it is - like the rosin in the solder flux - a forestry product. The charcoal support in the degreaser's ancestor chemistry is therefore, like almost everything else in this file, something dug up or grown and then refined.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.note: Activated charcoal manufacture by steam activation of a carbonised precursor is standard; the specific precursor used for this catalyst is not known here.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane (methyl chloroform)
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.description: CH3CCl3, boiling at 74 C, a non-flammable solvent that was the standard degreaser for precision metalwork and electronics through the 1950s to the 1980s. It was made from acetylene by hydrochlorination to vinylidene chloride and then chlorination to 1,1,1-trichloroethane - so it shares its whole upstream with vinyl chloride and with natural gas. It is toxic to the liver and kidney, mildly carcinogenic, and it was banned as a non-essential aerosol propellant in the United States in 1987 and phased out as a degreaser through the late 1980s and 1990s.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.note: The flammability of 1,1,1-trichloroethane is a special case: it is non-flammable in air but burns in oxygen-enriched atmospheres, which is a hazard in a large open vapour degreaser. Exposure limits in the early 1980s were under active revision.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: non-flammable in the usual range (flammable limits ~6-13% with an oxygen-rich atmosphere)

facts.label: 1980s occupational limit
facts.value: 200 ppm 8-hour TWA (ACGIH), with a 300 ppm ceiling

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.name: The vapour degreaser
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.description: A tank of boiling solvent with a cold condenser coil above it. Parts are lowered into the vapour, the vapour condenses on the part and washes the grease off, the condensate runs back into the boil tank, and the distilled clean solvent is pumped to the sump. It was astonishingly effective and astonishingly cheap, and it filled a plant with vapour - which is why it was also the plant's largest solvent loss and its largest occupational and air-emission exposure. A large plant had three or four machines with 20-40 litre tanks.

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.name: The condenser and the tank
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.description: The machine has two working parts: a boiling sump at the bottom that supplies the vapour, and a water-cooled coil above it that condenses the vapour and drips it back clean. The whole design depends on the vapour being kept out of the room, so the machine had a lid and a draught, and the lid was opened to put the parts in - which is exactly when the vapour left. A 20-40 litre tank boiled away 1-3 litres of solvent a day in a well-run plant, and that vapour was the emission the regulator was measuring.

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.name: How fast the solvent went
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.description: Three losses: evaporation out of the open tank, drag-out on the parts, and carry-over into the room ventilation. The 1980s engineering answers were a lid that stayed shut, a water-cooling coil with more area, a parts basket that dripped over the tank rather than over the floor, and - at the largest sites - a condenser on the vapour that ran the condensate back into the distilled reservoir so it never left the machine. A well-designed 1980s plant recovered most of its solvent; a badly designed one replaced 20% of its tank a month.

facts.label: Worst-case make-up
facts.value: up to 20% of tank charge per month

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.ultrasoni.name: Ultrasonic cleaner
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.ultrasoni.description: A tank of hot solvent or water with a 20-80 kHz transducer. In 1983 the electronics plant used ultrasonic cleaning before the vapour degreaser for fine work - the watch crystals, the gears, the small press-fit parts - because a vapour degreaser will not clean a crevice and an ultrasonic tank will. It is also the machine that put solvent into the ultrasonic cleaner market, where 1,1,1-trichloroethane and perchloroethylene were the usual fills.

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.sump-and-.name: Sump, return and the solvent loss
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.sump-and-.description: The tank works continuously with a boiling sump and a distilled solvent reservoir. In practice 5-20% of the solvent charge had to be replaced each month because of dragout, evaporation and the azeotroping of oil and water back into the tank - the solvent loss was the largest cost and the largest emission, and it is the number the whole regulatory campaign was aimed at.

chem.abs.name: ABS resin plant, and the C64 case
chem.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene is not a copolymer but a polymer blend: a SAN matrix with a grafted polybutadiene rubber phase dispersed in it as 0.1-10 micron particles. Making it is four separate unit operations - make the rubber, graft styrene and acrylonitrile onto it, make the matrix, blend and pelletise - and then a fifth that most people forget, drying. The C64's case, its keyboard surround and the beige plastic of its keys are this material.

chem.abs.other-polymers.name: The other polymers in and around a C64
chem.abs.other-polymers.description: A 1983 consumer electronic device used perhaps eight different engineering plastics and two rubbers. This branch traces each of them to its monomer, because they all come out of the same crackers, the same benzene and the same phenol. Each is a node with its own subtree; chem.pvc, chem.epoxy, chem.rubber, chem.polyester and chem.silicone are the ones other parts of this tree reference.

chem.thermosets.name: Phenolic and amino thermosets
chem.thermosets.description: The two oldest synthetic plastics, still in a 1983 machine in the places where a thermoplastic will not do: phenolic for the switch and socket housings and the old-style bakelite knobs, and urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde for the white insulating parts, the plug bodies and the coil-formers. Both are condensation networks: once cured they do not melt, and they are made from phenol or from urea, which comes from the same cumene and ammonia chain as everything else in this file.

chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.name: Urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde
chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.description: Urea condensed with formaldehyde gives a thermoset used for the white insulation of plugs, sockets and coil formers, and melamine gives the tougher, heat-resistant version used for the panel fittings. Both are white, both are cheap, and both are moisture-sensitive, which is the defect that kept them out of anything structural. The urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide - the Haber-Bosch product - so this is a nitrogen branch rather than a hydrocarbon one.

chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.ammoni.name: Urea from ammonia and carbon dioxide
chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.ammoni.description: 2NH3 plus CO2 at 180-220 C and 15-25 bar gives ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea. Ammonia comes from the Haber-Bosch loop fed by steam-reformed natural gas, so the white plug body of a 1983 appliance is, four steps back, natural gas.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.name: Phenolic resin (phenol-formaldehyde)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid (novolac, with hexamine as the curing agent) or under base (resol, self-curing). Bakelite, patented in 1907, was the first wholly synthetic plastic. In 1980s electronics it was in the switchgear, the relay covers and the phenolic laminate (paper or cotton cloth in phenolic resin) for the low-cost circuit boards and for the insulating barriers in a power supply.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.name: Hexamethylenetetramine (hexamine)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.description: Formaldehyde plus ammonia, and it does double duty: it is the curing agent for novolac phenolic and it is a slow accelerator and a decomposition source of formaldehyde in rubber compounds. It is one of the few molecules in this file that reaches into three unrelated chemistries.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.name: The formaldehyde in a phenolic
chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.description: Methanol oxidised to formaldehyde over silver at 600-700 C. The same formaldehyde as the acetal plastics, from the same methanol, from the same synthesis gas. Phenolic resin and POM sitting a few hundred metres apart in a 1980s chemical park is not a coincidence; both are formaldehyde chemistry.

chem.pom.formaldehyde.name: Formaldehyde from methanol
chem.pom.formaldehyde.description: Methanol plus a controlled amount of oxygen over silver at 600-700 C, giving 25-35% formaldehyde in air (the Formox process), then concentrated to 60-70%. The methanol comes from synthesis gas, so this is a coal-or-gas-to-methanol-to-formaldehyde chain rather than a direct petroleum one - although in a 1980s plant the methanol would typically have been made from natural gas.

chem.pom.formaldehyde.methanol-oxidation.name: Formox partial oxidation
chem.pom.formaldehyde.methanol-oxidation.description: CH3OH plus about 0.4 mol O2 per mol methanol over silver gauze at 600-700 C gives 25-35% formaldehyde with 90%+ selectivity. Silver is the only catalyst that works cleanly, and the reactor is a thousands-of-tubes packed bed. The oxygen is the whole control problem: too little and you get methyl formate, too much and you oxidise to carbon dioxide.

chem.pom.name: POM (acetal homopolymer and copolymer)
chem.pom.description: Polyoxymethylene, made by polymerising formaldehyde - from the oxidation of methanol - either with an acetic anhydride chain transfer (giving the homopolymer, Delrin) or with a small amount of a diacetate comonomer (giving the Celcon-type copolymer). It is the 1980s precision engineering plastic: gears, cams, hinges, tolerance rings and the moving parts in a mechanism.

chem.pom.uses.name: Where POM sat in a 1983 machine
chem.pom.uses.description: Small precision parts: the gear and cam of a fan, the hinges and catches, the insulator of a switch mechanism, the arm of a relay. In a 1983 home computer it was present in tens of grams at most, but it was there because nothing else moulded to a 0.05 mm tolerance with a low friction coefficient.
chem.pom.uses.note: POM use in a C64 is likely but small and not documented in the sources used here.

chem.pom.polymerisation.name: Acetal polymerisation
chem.pom.polymerisation.description: The homopolymer route runs formaldehyde with acetic anhydride: the growing chain's hydroxyl end reacts with the anhydride to give an acetoxy end, which stops further polymerisation. The copolymer route instead uses formaldehyde with a 2-4% fraction of a methylol-substituted diacetate (methyl formal or a diacetate monomer) so that the chain stops at an inert C-O-C end. In both cases the polymer has to be stabilised with an antioxidant, because formaldehyde polymerisation reversibly gives back formaldehyde at temperature.
chem.pom.polymerisation.note: Acetal chemistry is standard; the exact comonomer loadings vary by grade.

chem.rubber.name: Elastomers: natural rubber, neoprene, EPDM
chem.rubber.description: Three rubbers for three different jobs in and around a 1983 machine: natural rubber for the feet and plinths and the moulded grips, neoprene for gaskets and the flexible cable jacket, and EPDM for the cable's weather-resistant insulation. The C64's case feet are elastomer pads stuck to the underside of the case, and they are the only rubber on the outside of the machine.

chem.rubber.epdm.name: EPDM
chem.rubber.epdm.description: Ethylene copolymerised with a diene (norbornene or a cyclic diene), the diene content giving the vulcanisable double bonds. It has no unsaturation in the main chain, so it is ozone-resistant and will not crack in sunlight, which is why it replaced natural rubber in weather-exposed cable insulation and in the C64's power cord as the flexible jacket material of preference.
chem.rubber.epdm.note: The ethylene comes from the cracker: chem.ethylene.

chem.rubber.neoprene.name: Neoprene (polychloroprene)
chem.rubber.neoprene.description: Chloroprene polymerised in emulsion at 40 C. It is oil-resistant, weather-resistant and flame-resistant, which makes it the rubber for gaskets, for the flexible jacket of a power cord, and for the cable's outer sheath when the cable is not PVC. It is made from acetylene and chlorine through vinylacetylene and dichloroacetylene - one more route that ends in acetylene, and therefore in natural gas.

chem.rubber.neoprene.chloroprene.name: Chloroprene from acetylene
chem.rubber.neoprene.chloroprene.description: Acetylene dimerises to vinylacetylene, which chlorinates to 1,2-dichloro-2-butene; dehydrochlorination gives chloroprene, which polymerises in emulsion at 40 C to neoprene. The process is hazardous in a way that is instructive: chloroprene is a carcinogen and the dichloroacetylene intermediate is an extremely toxic pyrophoric gas, so the plant runs at low partial pressure with a fast quench.
chem.rubber.neoprene.chloroprene.note: Neoprene's process chemistry is standard; the intermediate toxicity warnings are well established.

chem.rubber.natural.vulcanisation.name: Vulcanisation and the role of sulphur
chem.rubber.natural.vulcanisation.description: Heated with sulphur and an accelerator (a thiuram or a sulphonamide), the cis double bonds get a short sulphur bridge between neighbouring chains: crosslinked, so the chains can no longer slide. The C64's case feet are a filled, carbon-black-reinforced natural or SBR compound cured in a mould at 140-170 C for 5-20 minutes. Elemental sulphur here came out of a Claus plant.

chem.rubber.natural.prevulcanisation.name: Prevulcanised rubber and latex goods
chem.rubber.natural.prevulcanisation.description: Before the 1930s the only way to make a rubber article was to vulcanise the whole thing in the mould. By the 1930s the industry could prevulcanise the compound in a mixer first - deliberately introducing some crosslink - so the compound was a flowable, uncured-on-the-surface material that could be shaped, then cured in the mould. That development is what made rubber mouldings mass-produced and is the direct ancestor of the ABS pellet.

chem.rubber.natural.tapping.name: Tapping and coagulation
chem.rubber.natural.tapping.description: A quarter-spiral cut into the bark's tapping panel is made about every other day, and the latex is collected in a cup. Thirty per cent of a mature tree's latex can be taken without killing it over a 25-30 year tapping life. The latex is preserved with ammonia, coagulated by adding formic acid or acetic acid to bring it to the isoelectric point, pressed into sheets, and then smoke-dried.
chem.rubber.natural.tapping.note: Tapping yield of about 30% of latex content is the standard agronomic figure.

chem.rubber.natural.name: Natural rubber (cis-1,4-polyisoprene)
chem.rubber.natural.description: Field latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis, coagulated, smoked and pressed into bales. In 1983 world production was of the order of 3.0-3.5 million tonnes a year, two thirds of it in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. It is cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a glass transition near -70 C, so it is the most resilient rubber at room temperature, and it needs vulcanisation with sulphur because the cis double bond is what makes it elastic.
chem.rubber.natural.note: World natural rubber production in the early 1980s was around 3 million tonnes a year; the figure is approximate.

chem.silicone.name: Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane)
chem.silicone.description: The only engineering polymer whose backbone is not carbon. Built from chlorosilanes made by the Rochow direct process - silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C - then hydrolyzed and condensed. In 1983 silicones were everywhere in electronics: as RTV sealing gaskets, as conformal coatings and encapsulants, as dielectric greases for the variable capacitors, and as the flexible key domes.

chem.silicone.polymer.name: Silicone rubber and fluids
chem.silicone.polymer.description: The chlorosilane is hydrolyzed to a silanol and condensed with a silanol-terminated chain stopper, giving a silicone oil (low viscosity) or, with reinforcing silica and peroxide cure, a silicone rubber (elastomer). The 1980s mix in electronics was dominated by room-temperature-vulcanising silicone - a moisture-cured acetoxy or hydroxyl-terminated compound - because it cures in a fixture without heat, and by the fluorosilicone mould releases.

chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.name: Conductive elastomer key domes
chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.description: A switch contact made of a silicone or neoprene elastomer filled with carbon black - or with metal-plated hollow glass spheres - so that the rubber itself conducts. When the dome is pressed it shorts to a printed conductor beneath; the dome's force curve (about 0.5-2 N operating, 8-12 mm travel) is the feel of the keyboard. The conductive filler is a petroleum carbon black or a silvered microsphere, and the elastomer is usually a peroxide-cured silicone or a neoprene, chosen for its fatigue life in millions of actuations.
chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.note: The C64 keyboard used elastomer-dome membrane technology; the exact elastomer and filler for a given revision are not documented here.

chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.name: Conformal coating
chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.description: A 20-100 micron film of room-temperature-vulcanising silicone brushed or dipped over a populated board, cured in humid air, to keep water, dust, sulfur dioxide and salt off the conductors. In 1980s practice it was used on power supplies and on automotive electronics rather than on consumer boards, and the industry debate was whether a conformal coating is better than a conformal coating removed badly - the rework risk is the problem. The C64's mainboard is generally described as uncoated.
chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.note: Whether a given board was conformal-coated is a plant practice, not a material fact; most consumer boards of this era were not.

chem.silicone.rochow.name: Rochow direct process
chem.silicone.rochow.description: Metallurgical silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C gives dimethyldichlorosilane. The silicon comes from the quartz and coke reduction that the whole semiconductor industry depends on, so the silicone business and the chip business share an upstream - and share the same four-nines purity problem in their own way. The methyl chloride comes from the natural gas chlorination business, so the silicone plant and the semiconductor plant are both fed by chlorine and by methane.

chem.silicone.rochow.metallurgical-silic.name: Metallurgical silicon
chem.silicone.rochow.metallurgical-silic.description: 98-99.5% silicon made in submerged arc furnaces from quartz and petroleum coke. The 1980s trade fed two very different industries: the ~100,000 tonne a year silicones and chlorosilanes trade, and the far smaller but far purer semiconductor-grade silicon trade, which used the same furnaces with nine-nines purification. Coke, silicon and chlorine are three inputs that appear in both branches of this tree.
chem.silicone.rochow.metallurgical-silic.note: The silicon chain itself belongs to the silicon subsystem; this node exists because the silicone business shares its first two steps.

chem.polyester.name: Polyesters: PET, PBT and unsaturated polyester
chem.polyester.description: Three families that share the same two feedstocks - ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, and a terephthalic or maleic/fumaric acid. PET in 1983 was overwhelmingly a fibre and bottle business, PBT was the engineering thermoplastic, and unsaturated polyester was the resin of the glass-reinforced mouldings. In a 1983 electronic assembly, the polyester was the transformer bobbin insulation, the relay base, the film capacitors, and any glass-filled moulding.

chem.polyester.unsaturated.name: Unsaturated polyester resin
chem.polyester.unsaturated.description: Maleic anhydride plus propylene glycol condensed to about 1,000-2,000 molecular weight and dissolved in styrene; the crosslinker is styrene itself and the cure is a peroxide (usually methyl ethyl ketone peroxide) at 20-80 C. In the 1980s it was the resin of glass-reinforced moulding compound and of the cast reinforced parts - and it is the resin family most associated with the styrene emission complaints of boat building, which is the same styrene that the ABS matrix uses.
chem.polyester.unsaturated.note: The styrene comes from chem.styrene; the propylene glycol from the propylene and ethylene oxide chains.

chem.polyester.pbt.name: PBT (polybutylene terephthalate)
chem.polyester.pbt.description: Polymerised by transesterification then polycondensation like PET but with butanediol, giving a lower melting point (about 225 C against 260 C) and a faster crystallisation, which is why it is the engineering grade: it sets in a 5-10 mm wall in 5-10 seconds where PET needs a minute. It went into connectors, relay and transformer bobbin mouldings, and into the small gears and cams of the power supply mechanism.

chem.polyester.pet.name: PET from ethylene glycol and dimethyl terephthalate
chem.polyester.pet.description: Dimethyl terephthalate plus ethylene glycol transesterified at 180-280 C over an antimony or titanium catalyst, then polycondensed at 270-290 C under 1-50 mbar. The bottleneck is the transesterification methanol coproduct, which is recovered and returned to the terephthalate plant, so the plant is a big methanol recovery column. The route through dimethyl terephthalate rather than terephthalic acid was chosen in the 1970s and 1980s because the acid route's oxidation step had the corrosion and the purity problems; by the late 1980s the acid route had caught up.

chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.name: Ethylene glycol side
chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.description: About 2.2 tonnes of ethylene glycol per tonne of PET resin, from the ethylene oxide hydration branch. The glycol is purified to 99.9% because the water it carries ends up as a hydrolysis chain terminator and it is the single largest cause of high-acid-value polyester.

chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.name: Para-xylene and terephthalic acid
chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.description: Para-xylene is separated from the C8 aromatics by adsorptive separation (UOP Parex, 4A zeolite) or by crystallisation, then oxidised with air over a cobalt-manganese-acetate catalyst at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar in acetic acid. The para isomer must be more than 99.5% pure because the meta and ortho isomers cannot be polymerised into a useful fibre.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: 175-225 C, 15-30 bar, Co/Mn/Br in acetic acid

chem.polyamide.name: Nylon 6 and nylon 6,6
chem.polyamide.description: The two polyamides that a 1980s machine used for its precision parts. Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, or nylon 6 from caprolactam which itself comes from phenol. Both are condensation polymers of a diamine and an acid or of a lactam, and both need the phenol-aromatic chain, so both are downstream of the same cracker benzene as the ABS.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.name: Nylon 6 from caprolactam
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.description: Caprolactam is opened with water at 250-270 C in a hydrolysis-polymerisation reactor under 1-15 bar, giving a nylon 6 with a very narrow molecular weight distribution because the chemistry is a step growth from a single monomer. Nylon 6 is the form used where a low melt viscosity matters, and it was the standard for the textile filament and the carpet fibre trade.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.name: Caprolactam from phenol
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.description: Phenol hydrogenated to cyclohexanol, then dehydrogenated to cyclohexanone; cyclohexanone oximation to cyclohexanone oxime; the oxime rearranged with oleum (the Beckmann rearrangement, which expands the ring from six to seven members) to caprolactam, and the ammonium sulphate byproduct stripped and recycled. This is a five-step route from phenol and it is one of the longest petrochemical chains in the C64's ancestry.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.oleum.name: Oleum and the Beckmann rearrangement
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.oleum.description: The rearrangement needs concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum, and it produces ammonium sulphate - typically 1.1-1.3 tonnes of ammonium sulphate per tonne of caprolactam, which has to be sold as fertiliser. It is the same sulphuric acid and the same fertiliser market that the Claus sulphur plant feeds. In 1983 the industry was moving to oleum-free rearrangements over solid acid or over a zeolite, precisely to lose that waste.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.pheno.name: Phenol to cyclohexanone
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.pheno.description: Phenol hydrogenated over a nickel or palladium catalyst at 120-180 C and 10-30 bar to cyclohexanol, which is dehydrogenated over copper at 250-300 C to cyclohexanone. The phenol comes from cumene, and cumene's propylene comes from the cracker, so nylon 6 is a third-generation descendant of the naphtha cracker.

chem.polyamide.nylon-66.adiponitrile.name: Adiponitrile from butadiene
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.adiponitrile.description: The 1980s route to nylon 6,6 feedstock: hydrocyanation of butadiene with hydrogen cyanide over a nickel catalyst, then hydrogenation of both nitriles. It made a cracker-based nylon 6,6 possible for the first time, and it is the reason hydrogen cyanide - the toxic gas of the acrylonitrile and methyl methacrylate chemistry - was on the books of a plastics company.

chem.polyamide.nylon-66.name: Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and HMDA
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.description: Adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine condense to nylon salt at 250-270 C and 10-20 bar in a batch or continuous process, then polymerise at 270-280 C under a small nitrogen pressure. Adipic acid in 1983 came mostly from the oxidation of cyclohexane or of a C4 route with nitric acid; hexamethylenediamine came from adiponitrile hydrogenation or from adipic acid plus ammonia.

chem.polycarbonate.name: Polycarbonate
chem.polycarbonate.description: Bisphenol A polycarbonate, made by the interfacial phosgene route from BPA and phosgene in dichloromethane, then melt polycondensed at 250-290 C. It is the transparent, tough, dimensionally stable engineering plastic of the 1980s, and in electronics it went into connector housings, terminal blocks, relay covers and the housings of the switchgear it replaced metal in. The C64 itself was not made of polycarbonate - the case was ABS - but the material surrounds the machine in the peripherals and in Commodore's later machines, and it shares the bisphenol A and the cumene chain with the epoxy and the polyester.

chem.polycarbonate.properties.name: Why it was chosen
chem.polycarbonate.properties.description: Amorphous at 100-150% linear retention, glass transition near 145 C, tensile strength 60-70 MPa, and a notched Izod of 8-15 kJ/m2. It is the transparent tough polymer of the 1980s: sunglasses lenses, camera and instrument housings, the disc of a compact disc from 1982, and the dome of the keyboard on some machines. It was also the first engineering polymer to be explicitly targeted at the electronics market as a metal replacement.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.name: Phosgene
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.description: Carbonyl chloride, COCl2, made by oxidising carbon monoxide with chlorine over activated carbon at 100-150 C. It is acutely toxic, and it is one of the reasons the polycarbonate industry of the 1980s was moving toward the non-phosgene route based on bisphenol A carbonate and on the methylene chloride and pyridine route. The bisphenol A it consumes is the same bisphenol A as the epoxy, and the chlorine is the same chlorine.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.name: Chlorine and carbon monoxide
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.description: Chlorine from brine electrolysis plus carbon monoxide from a reformer or from coke. This is the point at which the chlor-alkali industry - which needs hydrogen to sell its chlorine, and therefore needs natural gas - touches the plastics industry through a molecule with two chlorine atoms and one oxygen.
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.note: Chlorine electrolysis belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrochloric-acid.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene-route.name: Interfacial phosgene route
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene-route.description: Bisphenol A dissolved in aqueous caustic soda is reacted with phosgene in dichloromethane at 20-40 C with a tertiary amine catalyst. The product is a chloroformate-terminated oligomer that is then washed, and the oligomer is polymerised by melt condensation at 250-290 C under 0.1-1 mbar until the molecular weight is high enough. The plant has two halves - a wet interfacial reactor with a rotary film contactor and a dry finishing extruder - and the balance between them is the whole economics.

chem.epoxy.name: Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin
chem.epoxy.description: DGEBA epoxy is made by hydrolyzing bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinating to close the epoxide ring. About 800,000-1,000,000 tonnes of epoxy resin were made in 1983, of which the largest single use was the glass-reinforced laminate for printed circuit boards. A C64 has epoxy in its board, in the transformer and coil potting of its power supply, in the die-attach of its chips, and in the adhesive that holds the SID's heatsink tab.

chem.epoxy.uses-c64.name: Epoxy in a C64
chem.epoxy.uses-c64.description: Four places. The board's laminate resin. The power supply's transformer bobbin and coil potting, and the mains filter capacitor's encapsulation. The die attach inside the VIC-II, the SID and the CPU packages, where the chip was bonded to a small ceramic or epoxy header with an epoxy that had to survive 180-260 C without delaminating. And the heatsink adhesive in the SID's tab, which in some designs was a two-part filled epoxy.
chem.epoxy.uses-c64.note: The mass figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical laminate and encapsulation weights.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.name: Curing agents
chem.epoxy.hardeners.description: An epoxy is useless until something cross-links it, and the curing agent decides the properties. Amines (aliphatic triethylenetetramine, cycloaliphatic diamines) give fast cures at room temperature and good mechanical properties; anhydrides give high-temperature cures and excellent electrical insulation, which is why the power supply's transformer potting and the chips' die attach were epoxy; and the phenols and novolacs give the flame-retardant laminates.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.name: Anhydride cure
chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.description: A cyclic anhydride (a methyl substituted tetrahydrophthalic or nadic anhydride) catalysed by an amine or a tertiary amine. The cure is slower and needs 150-200 C, but the network is very tight and the dielectric properties are excellent - which is why anhydride epoxy was the potting and the chip-attach system of the 1980s, where a chip sitting on a cured epoxy die attach with a controlled coefficient of thermal expansion was worth the cure temperature.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM/MDA)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.description: Made by condensing aniline with formaldehyde, it is the first-generation hardener: cheap, and it is the amine that showed up in the early carcinogenicity work on epoxies in the 1970s, which pushed the industry toward DDM's less toxic relatives. It is still in laminates and in the rubber industry as a vulcanisation accelerator.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.note: The 4,4'-methylenedianiline classification work dates from the 1970s-early 1980s and was a driver of substitution in both epoxy and elastomer applications.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.description: The high-temperature laminate hardener: about 80 parts per 100 of DGEBA, cured at 180-200 C. DDS is made by sulphonating diphenyl sulphone, nitrating it to the dinitro compound and reducing the nitro groups - an aniline and chlorobenzene route for the aniline part. It is the hardener in the aerospace laminates and in the higher-temperature grades of FR-4, and it costs several times what the amine does.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.amine-cure.name: Amine cure and its problem
chem.epoxy.hardeners.amine-cure.description: A primary or secondary amine adds to the strained epoxide ring, which is what starts the cure. The classic complaint of amine-cured epoxy is amine blush - a sticky, hygroscopic surface film from an atmospheric amine-carbon dioxide reaction with surface epoxy - and the reason the die-attach and potting processes of the 1980s used a controlled-amine epoxy with a controlled cure cycle rather than a general-purpose one.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.name: Bisphenol A from cumene
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.description: Two phenol molecules plus acetone, condensed over a strong acid to give 4,4'-isopropylidenediphenol, with the water stripped. In 1983 most BPA was made this way from the cumene process's phenol, and the rest from the older two-step route using bis(4-chlorophenyl) ketone. The 1980s were the period when BPA's endocrine activity was being investigated by accident, and when the epoxy industry began to substitute boron oxides and novolac epoxies to remove it from can linings and bottle resins.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.name: Acetone as the BPA co-reactant
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.description: The BPA reaction is where the case polymer meets the laminate resin: the phenol for BPA comes out of the cumene oxidation that also yields the acetone for the reaction, so the two halves of bisphenol A come from one reactor 20 km apart. The same bisphenol A went into the polycarbonate and the unsaturated polyester of the era.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.name: Epichlorohydrin
chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.description: 1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane: the C3 building block. In 1983 most of the world's epichlorohydrin was made by the chlorohydrin route - propylene chlorohydrin from propylene plus hypochlorous acid, dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry - which is the same chlorohydrin chemistry that makes propylene oxide. It is a sensitiser and a carcinogen, and it is the reason the epoxy industry carried the same respiratory-protection regime as the propylene oxide plants.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.name: DGEBA (diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A)
chem.epoxy.dgeba.description: The workhorse epoxy: bisphenol A condensed with two moles of epichlorohydrin, giving a resin with an epoxide group at each end of the molecule and epoxide number 172-190 equivalents per 100 g. It is a solid at room temperature (melting 4-12 C for the liquid grades) and it cures into a cross-linked network with anything that has active hydrogen or amino groups.

facts.label: Typical formulation
facts.value: DGEBA 100 parts, amine or anhydride hardener 20-60 parts

chem.pvc.name: PVC: vinyl chloride and suspension polymerisation
chem.pvc.description: About 3.5 million tonnes of PVC in 1983, of which maybe 5-8% was flexible and the rest rigid. Two-thirds of the monomer came from the oxychlorination of ethylene and the rest from acetylene and HCl. The C64 used it in the power cord's jacket and insulation, in the moulded cable accessories, and in the odd keycap or knob; the stability system matters because unstabilised PVC decomposes at 140 C.

chem.pvc.uses-c64.name: PVC in a C64
chem.pvc.uses-c64.description: The power cord: a two-core or three-core flexible PVC jacket, typically 1.5-3 mm of wall, with PVC insulation on the conductors and a PVC or PVC/rubber strain relief at the moulded connector. A C64 power cord is a couple of hundred grams of PVC. The keyboard keys and the side vents of the earlier cases were also often PVC or a PVC blend. A C64 whose power supply was the internal one had less of it, because the mains cable went to the brick.
chem.pvc.uses-c64.note: Cable constructions varied by market and by supplier; the jacket material was almost always flexible PVC.

chem.pvc.plasticiser.name: Plasticisers
chem.pvc.plasticiser.description: A flexible PVC is PVC with 30-60 parts per 100 of a liquid plasticiser, and the plasticiser is where most of the toxicology lived. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP, DOP) was the standard from the 1950s into the 1990s, made by esterifying phthalic anhydride with 2-ethylhexanol - itself from butyraldehyde or oxo synthesis of propylene and a C6 or C8 fraction. In 1983 there was no accepted evidence of harm at the levels in use, and the reappraisal came later.

chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.name: Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.description: C8H17OOC-C6H4-COOC8H17, 391 g/mol, a colourless liquid with a very slight odour. About 200,000-250,000 tonnes of DEHP a year were made in 1983, most of it for PVC. The C8 alcohol comes from propylene and from ethylene via butyraldehyde, so a PVC cable jacket is a direct consumer of the cracker.
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.note: DEHP production volumes in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude estimates.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.name: Heat stabilisation, and the lead problem
chem.pvc.stabilisation.description: PVC is unstable above about 140 C: the dehydrochlorination produces HCl, which catalyses more dehydrochlorination, which is why unstabilised PVC cannot be processed at all. The 1980s stabiliser systems were lead salts - dibasic lead phosphite, tribasic lead sulphate, lead stearate - which are excellent scavengers and which put lead into millions of tonnes of consumer product. Calcium-zinc systems based on stearates and organic co-stabilisers were the 1980s technology that began to displace them, and the reason is health regulation rather than performance.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.name: Calcium-zinc stabilisers
chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.description: Calcium and zinc carboxylates (stearate, hydrostearate) with an organic co-stabiliser such as a beta-diketone or a polyol. Zinc carboxylates are the primary stabilisers and calcium carboxylates are the co-stabilisers that exchange zinc for calcium at the right moment. The 1980s engineering problem was matching the zinc-to-calcium ratio and the lubricant balance so the compound did not plate out on the extruder die, which is a real and stubborn processing problem rather than a trivial substitution.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.name: Tribasic lead sulphate and lead phosphite
chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.description: The lead salts are cheap, opaque, and superb at scavenging HCl and chelating chlorine. The cost is that lead is a cumulative neurotoxin and PVC was, until recently, a major route of human lead exposure through pipes, and in 1983 the limits on lead in consumer products were tightening. The chemistry is basic: the metal salt of sulphuric or phosphorous acid, made by precipitating the oxide or sulphate onto a lead base.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.name: Initiator and chain transfer
chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.description: Acyl peroxide or a persulphate at 0.05-0.5%, with a chain transfer agent (often chloroform, tetrachloromethane or an ester) to control molecular weight. The transfer agents are chlorinated for a reason: they also terminate the radicals that would otherwise go on to make chlorinated by-products, and the PVC industry has always been able to sell them.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.name: PVA suspending agent
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.description: Partially hydrolysed polyvinyl alcohol at 0.5-2% of the water phase, with a second colloid stabilizer if needed. It is the same PVA chemistry as the suspension polystyrene suspending agent - one more appearance of a polymer from the vinyl acetate chain doing structural work in a different polymer's reactor.
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.note: PVA suspending agents came from the same vinyl acetate hydrolysis used for the emulsion polymerisation of PVAc; the two uses share the chemistry.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.name: PVC polymerisation
chem.pvc.polymerisation.description: Suspension polymerisation in water with a suspending agent is about 65-70% of world PVC production: VCM is dispersed as 0.1-1 mm beads in water at 50-70 C and 6-12 bar for 5-10 hours to 70-85% conversion. Mass polymerisation gives a cleaner bead and no water to evaporate, and emulsion (paste) polymerisation is used for flexible and calendared products. The suspension process is essentially a stirred autoclave and the whole design problem is keeping the beads spherical and of a narrow size.

chem.pvc.vcm.storage.name: VCM storage and inhibition
chem.pvc.vcm.storage.description: Bulk VCM in a refrigerated atmospheric tank at 10-15 C with a nitrogen blanket, or in a pressure vessel. It is inhibited against polymerisation with a phenolic or an organic peroxide, and it is kept below 50 C because vinyl chloride is a powerful inhibitor of its own polymerisation - a fact the industry discovered painfully, and which turned out to be a safety feature once understood.

chem.pvc.vcm.oxychlorination.name: Oxychlorination of ethylene
chem.pvc.vcm.oxychlorination.description: Ethylene, chlorine and hydrogen chloride over a copper(II) chloride catalyst at 150-250 C and 4-10 bar, giving VCM with 85-95% selectivity. The ratio of chlorine to HCl controls the dichlorethane versus vinyl chloride, so the plant can swing between making EDC for the chlorinated-solvent business and making VCM. By 1983 this was about two thirds of world VCM.

chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.name: Acetylene plus HCl (the mercury route)
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.description: Acetylene and anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute, at 15-25% conversion per pass with 90-95% selectivity. This is the route that ties PVC to natural gas, because acetylene is made from methane. It survives where there is no cracker - in Western Europe, in India, in China and in the Soviet Union - and where there is one, the oxychlorination route is cheaper.
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.note: The acetylene end of this route is chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.name: Acetylene to vinyl chloride
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.description: The reason the whole acetylene industry existed. Acetylene plus anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a 0.3-0.5% mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute gives vinyl chloride at 15-25% conversion per pass and 90-95% selectivity, the low conversion forced by the HCl ratio and by the fact that vinyl chloride is a vinylogous acrylate that polymerises readily.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.name: Mercuric chloride catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.description: Anhydrous HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and ethyne adds across it. The catalyst is a genuine environmental liability: mercury lost from a large acetylene plant was tens of kilograms a year, and by the 1980s both West Germany and the Netherlands were restricting mercury emission from chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride plants.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.note: Mercury restriction dates vary by country; German and Dutch controls on mercury from chlor-alkali and acetylene plants began in the 1970s and tightened through the 1980s-90s.

chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.name: Mercury in the PVC plant
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.description: The mercury chloride catalyst is a genuine environmental liability. A 1980s European PVC plant was a mercury emitter at tens of kilograms a year, and by the mid-1980s both the German and the Dutch authorities were requiring either catalyst recovery or a switch to the oxychlorination route. The engineering answer, delivered in the 1980s, was a mercury recovery system on the reactor effluent that stripped the mercury into the hydrochloric acid stream and concentrated it to about 20%.
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.note: The specific national dates and legal instruments for mercury limits in the PVC industry are jurisdiction-specific; the general direction and the mercury-recovery technology are well established.

chem.pvc.vcm.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
chem.pvc.vcm.description: C2H3Cl, boiling at -13.4 C, so it is a liquid only under pressure. It is a proven human carcinogen (angiosarcoma of the liver), it is flammable from 4-33% in air, and it is the reason the PVC industry of the 1980s had an unusual public health profile. In 1983 world VCM capacity was of the order of 9-10 million tonnes a year.

chem.abs.c64-case.name: The Commodore 64 case, in ABS
chem.abs.c64-case.description: About 350-400 g of ABS: a two-shot moulding, the beige or brown textured skin over the structural frame, with the moulding texture itself - a fine leather grain applied by the tool's EDM process - as the only decoration. Behind the front bezel there is a metal RF shield and a plastic shield can, and the vents are moulded through the wall. Everything visible on the outside of a C64, apart from the keycaps and the badge, is this one polymer.
chem.abs.c64-case.note: The C64 case material is described as ABS in the plastics trade of the period; the precise grade is not on the record.

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: two-shot / multi-cavity injection moulding with EDM texture

chem.abs.grade.name: The ABS grade the C64 case used
chem.abs.grade.description: A high-impact, general purpose injection moulding grade in the family of the low-cis, medium-graft commercial ABS sold as Cycolac 2800 or equivalent, with a notched Izod impact strength of 150-250 J/m and a moulding shrinkage of 0.4-0.7%. The UL 94 flammability rating would be HB or 2A: a home computer in a living room could not be in a 0.4 mm wall V-0 plastic, so the case had to be thicker than the V-0 rating allowed.
chem.abs.grade.note: The specific commercial grade used for the C64 case is not documented in the sources used here; the description above is the class of material its mechanical and cosmetic requirements imply.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB or 2A at typical wall thickness

chem.abs.regrind.name: Regrind
chem.abs.regrind.description: Runner, sprue and rejected mouldings are chopped and fed back. A 1980s injection moulder typically ran 5-10% regrind in the case and up to 20% in less critical parts, on the grounds that a second heat history costs some molecular weight and some impact strength. Commodore's own case moulding ran regrind; the amount is not documented and the C64's impact strength specification is a good indication of how much.
chem.abs.regrind.note: Regrind fractions are practice rather than specification; a moulding plant's own rules governed this.

chem.abs.additives.name: Compounding additives
chem.abs.additives.description: Colour and processing aids, dosed into the twin screw before the vacuum vent so that anything volatile is stripped there: 1-3% of a pigment masterbatch, 0.1-0.5% of an external lubricant (a metal stearate, usually zinc or calcium stearate or an EBS wax), and a UV stabiliser. The beige of the C64's case is a pigment on top of the natural colour of the polymer; the grey of a later model is a carbon black or a titanium dioxide blend.

chem.abs.additives.stearate.name: Metal stearate release agent
chem.abs.additives.stearate.description: Calcium stearate or zinc stearate, 0.1-0.5%, dosed to stop the ABS sticking to the screw and the die, and to help the mould release. The stearates come from stearic acid (from tallow or from a C18 fraction) neutralised with lime; the metal itself is the only heavy metal routinely added to a consumer plastic.

chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.name: Pigment masterbatch
chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.description: A pre-dispersed concentrate - typically titanium dioxide (rutile, for weather resistance), carbon black, ultramarine blue, phthalocyanine green, or an iron oxide - at 20-60% loading in an ABS or LDPE carrier, dosed at 1-3% into the compounding line. A masterbatch exists because a pigment dropped into a twin screw as a powder will not disperse, and undispersed pigment is visible as specks in the moulding.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.name: Molecular sieve desiccant
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.description: A 3A or 4A zeolite in a heated bed at 200-350 C that adsorbs water to below 0.1% of its own weight, with a purge cycle on a hot air or nitrogen sweep. The same zeolite family as the cracker drier and the FCC catalyst, and in the 1980s this was the standard way every plastic was dried before moulding.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.name: The 3A molecular sieve itself
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.description: The desiccant in the dryer is a synthetic zeolite with a 3 angstrom pore opening, which admits the water molecule (kinetic diameter about 2.65 angstrom) and excludes anything bigger. That single geometric fact is why a molecular sieve can dry a plastic to 200 ppm: it is a molecular filter, not an absorber. The zeolite is made by hydrothermal synthesis from an alumina gel, a silica source and an organic template at 150-200 C and autogenous pressure in an autoclave - and then the template is burned out of the pore at 500-550 C, which is what opens the pores.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.name: Binder and the shaped pellet
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.description: A zeolite powder cannot go in a dryer bed: it will dust and it will fluidise. So the powder is formed into 2-4 mm extruded pellets with a clay and silica binder, and the binder is the part that stops the pellet from taking up water itself - a 4% clay binder will hold several weight percent of water and the bed's capacity is only about 20-22% of its own weight. The circle closes here: the drying equipment for the plastic is itself dried in a dryer.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.name: Zeolite hydrothermal synthesis
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.description: Alumina, sodium silicate and sodium hydroxide are gelled together, seeded with a few crystals of the product zeolite as nuclei, and heated in an autoclave at 150-200 C for 24-96 hours. The nucleation and growth control is the whole art: it is why the crystal size distribution of a zeolite is a commercial specification, and why a 2-micron zeolite for a cracker drier costs more than a 50-micron one for a different job.

chem.abs.drying.name: Drying
chem.abs.drying.description: ABS is hygroscopic: its equilibrium moisture content is about 0.3-0.4% by weight, and a wet pellet in a mould produces a part with silver streaks on the surface, voids, and a lower impact strength than the design assumed. The moulding shop therefore dried the pellets at 80-90 C for 2-4 hours in a dehumidifying dryer before every moulding run. This is the step that separates a plastics engineer from a chemist and it is done with the pellets in a hopper with a 3A molecular sieve bed.
chem.abs.drying.note: The 200 ppm specification is a common engineering target; typical material arrives at 0.05-0.15%.

chem.abs.pelletising.name: Compounding and pelletising
chem.abs.pelletising.description: The dry blend is melted in a twin-screw extruder at 230-260 C, the volatile xylene and the residual styrene are pulled out under vacuum, and the melt is cut into pellets. This is the operation that turns a powder into a product a moulding machine can eat, and it is where the ABS gets its second heat history - which is why the regrind content matters.

chem.abs.pelletising.static-mixer.name: Static mixer in the melt line
chem.abs.pelletising.static-mixer.description: A motionless packed element in the transfer pipe or the die adapter that blends the pigment and the regrind into the melt without shear. It matters because the impact property depends on the particle size distribution surviving, and every unnecessary shear element costs you 0.5-1 micron of particle size.

chem.abs.pelletising.cutter.name: Die plate, water bath and rotary cutter
chem.abs.pelletising.cutter.description: The melt is extruded through a die plate as a number of strands into a circulating water bath at 20-40 C, solidifies, is pulled by a first calender and chopped by a rotary knife mounted on the extruder die. The alternative is underwater pelletising, where the die is submerged and the pellets are cut in the water - fewer steps, no strands, and it was becoming the 1980s preference for a new line. Pellet size is 2-4 mm in both cases.

chem.abs.pelletising.vacuum-vent.name: Vacuum venting
chem.abs.pelletising.vacuum-vent.description: A vent at 10-100 mbar with a steam ejector or a liquid ring pump, sized to remove the residual monomer and solvent. The residual styrene specification matters: a high-styrene ABS smells, and the monomer content of a 1980s pellet was typically under 500 ppm.

chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.name: Twin-screw extruder
chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.description: Two intermeshing screws 50-90 mm in diameter at 10-30 rpm, length to diameter ratio 30-40:1, with an L/D feed zone, a melting zone, a vacuum vent and a second vent for the devolatilisation. In 1983 the counter-rotating or co-rotating twin screw was the standard compounding machine for ABS because it handles the powder blend, the pigment and the regrind in one pass; a 70 mm machine ran 500-2,000 kg/h.
chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.note: Machine sizes and throughputs are typical of the era's compounding lines.

chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.devolati.name: Devolatilisation in the compounding line
chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.devolati.description: The xylene in the graft has to come out, and it comes out in the compounding extruder rather than in the reactor, because the reactor's melt is too viscous to devolatilise in a small unit. A falling-film or wiped-film vent at 240-260 C and 5-50 mbar with a steam ejector, or with a liquid ring pump for the high-boiling tail, is what turns a sticky powder blend into a pellet that does not smell of solvent. It is the single most expensive operation in the ABS plant per kilogram of resin.

facts.label: Vapour load
facts.value: 1-2 t xylene per t of polymer

chem.abs.blending.name: Blending the graft into the matrix
chem.abs.blending.description: The graft is mixed into the SAN at 25-50 parts graft per 100 parts SAN for a general purpose grade and up to 50-70 parts for a high-impact grade. That ratio - not the chemistry - is what a plastics buyer specifies: rubber content sets the impact strength, the heat distortion temperature and the price per kilogram.

chem.abs.san-matrix.name: The SAN matrix
chem.abs.san-matrix.description: The continuous phase: styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made separately by bulk, emulsion or suspension polymerisation. It has to be made separately because it has to be a continuous phase, not a grafted one. In 1983 a large ABS plant bought its SAN in, or made it on site in a bulk reactor and then devolatilised - the two-route choice is a plant's economics, not a chemistry question.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.name: SOVERE ammoxidation process
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.description: A mixture of propylene, ammonia, oxygen and steam is passed at 400-460 C and 15-25 bar (1.5-2.5 MPa) over a bismuth molybdate or antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst in a fixed-bed or fluidised-bed reactor. The reaction is a partial oxidation plus an ammonia substitution in one step: propylene + 1.5 NH3 + 0.75 O2 -> acrylonitrile + 2 H2O. Per tonne of acrylonitrile the plant consumes about 1.0-1.1 t of propylene, 0.22-0.30 t of ammonia (most of which is lost to N2 and to acetonitrile) and 1.0-1.3 t of air, and it makes 0.04-0.08 t of acetonitrile as the main by-product.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.name: Recovery and purification train
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.description: The reactor effluent is cooled and partly condensed, the unreacted propylene and ammonia are stripped and recycled, the acrylonitrile and acetonitrile are separated by distillation (acrylonitrile boiling 77 C, acetonitrile 81.6 C, which is a genuinely difficult separation and was the reason for the extractive or entrainer-assisted designs), and the acrylonitrile is finished to 99.9% with a stabiliser. In a plant where acrylonitrile boils at 77 C and is flammable from 3% in air, the distillation column was also the largest single gas hazard.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.name: Acrylonitrile stabiliser
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.description: A phenolic or amine stabiliser (a small percentage of a phenol such as hydroquinone, or a hindered amine) is added to prevent anionic polymerisation of the monomer in storage. Acrylonitrile has a third-order rate constant for anionic polymerisation that is high enough that a drum of uninhibited monomer left in a warm warehouse can polymerise from the bottom up, and this was a real and recurring accident.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.hydrogen-oxyge.name: The hydrogen and oxygen side of the loop
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.hydrogen-oxyge.description: A side reaction makes hydrogen: propylene plus ammonia plus oxygen makes propene imine, which cracks to acetonitrile and hydrogen, and the hydrogen is then burned to water with the oxygen. The 1980s development was to recover that hydrogen - it is a high-value gas and the plant bought hydrogen for the reactor - by separating the purge gas and feeding it to a hydrogen recovery unit. It is also why the net oxygen demand of the process is lower than the stoichiometry suggests.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.name: By-products: acetonitrile, hydrogen cyanide, acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.description: Acetonitrile is the biggest by-product at 3-8% of the acrylonitrile and it had a real market - it went into solvent and into acrylonitrile copolymer fibres. Hydrogen cyanide was a small but lethal by-product, and its formation was the reason for the halide promoter. Acrylic acid came from the hydrolysis of a little of the acrylonitrile, and it was a nuisance in 1980s practice because it fouled the distillation train.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.name: Ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.description: Three families existed. Bismuth molybdate on silica (Bi2Mo3O12 or Bi2(MoO4)3 on silica) was the original and still the industry standard for selectivity in fixed beds. Antimony oxide with phosphorus and boron oxides on a silica support (Sb2O3/P2O5/B2O3) was the workhorse of the fluidised-bed designs, cheaper and more active but a little less selective. Bismuth molybdate with vanadium and tungsten additives, and nickel or cobalt catalysts, were the newer directions.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Making the ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a shaped, robust porous solid, and making it is a small ceramics industry. A bismuth molybdate catalyst is prepared by impregnating precipitated bismuth molybdate or by sol-gel methods onto a silica support, then shaping it into 3-5 mm extrudates or spray-dried microspheres and calcining at 500-700 C. The support is silica gel, and silica gel is made from sand. That is the whole chain from a dune to a transistor's acrylonitrile in three steps.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Soda silica from sand
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: Quartz sand is fused with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, which is dissolved in hot water to make the silicate solution, which is acidified to gel. This is the same soda-silica chain that gives the silica sol for the polysilicon ingot's crucibles and the quartz for the fused silica, and it is the industrial descendant of a two-thousand-year-old glassmaking reaction. It is the last dig-it-out node in this branch: sand.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: The soda-silica route is the classical one for both glass and silica sol; its scale-up is the industrial glassmaking reaction.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Silica gel support
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: A porous amorphous silica of 300-700 m2/g surface area and a 6-20 nm pore diameter. The pore diameter matters twice over in this file: in the ammoxidation catalyst a small pore keeps the diene from cracking, and in the FCC catalyst a large pore lets the bulky alkylated intermediates in. The silica gel is made by hydrolysing a silicate solution and gelling it, and the silicate solution is made from silica sand.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Shaping and calcination
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: The powder is extruded into trilobe or quadrilobe shapes - the lobes exist because a lobed extrudate has more external surface per unit volume than a cylinder, and more external surface means less diffusion limitation - then dried and calcined at 500-700 C. The calcination is what converts the oxide precursor into the active bismuth molybdate phase; too hot and the surface area collapses and the selectivity falls.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: Lobed extrudates and the calcination temperature range are standard catalyst-manufacturing practice.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.deact.name: Catalyst deactivation and promoters
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.deact.description: Coking from the organic by-products and the loss of phosphorus are the two deactivation routes. A trace of a halide promoter (a few hundred ppm of hydrogen chloride or an alkyl chloride) was the standard answer: it suppressed the side reactions that made hydrogen cyanide, and its use is the reason the plant needed a chlorine supply of its own.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.deact.note: Halide promoter levels of a few hundred ppm are the range quoted in reviews; the exact figure varies by licensor.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.name: Antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.description: The fluidised-bed catalyst: a silica support promoted with phosphorus and boron oxides so that the phosphorus does not volatilise away at 450 C. It was less selective but far more active and far more mechanically robust than the bismuth catalyst, which matters in a fluidised bed.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.name: Bismuth molybdate on silica
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.description: The standard catalyst, chosen for its selectivity to acrylonitrile and its resistance to reduction by ammonia. The 1980s development targets were the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions and, later in the decade, the bismuth-molybdenum-phosphorus systems aimed at raising the acrylonitrile yield above 90%.

facts.label: Catalyst family
facts.value: Bi2Mo3O12 / bismuth molybdate on silica, with V or W promoters

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.name: Fixed-bed or fluidised-bed ammoxidation reactor
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.description: The original SOVERE design was a series of fixed beds with salt bath or oil bath cooling, giving 90-93% conversion and 85-92% selectivity. The 1980s industry had largely moved to fluidised-bed or moving-bed designs, which were easier to heat and to strip of coke, at the cost of a lower selectivity (about 80-90%). A 1980s plant was a 100,000-250,000 tonne a year unit with a salt bath or a hot water reactor jacket and a lot of downstream distillation.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.note: Selectivity figures vary with catalyst age and design; the ranges are the standard ones quoted in reviews.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: Heat removal from the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: The ammoxidation gives out roughly 1,000 kJ per kilogram of acrylonitrile, and the reactor has to be taken out at a rate the metallurgy can live with. That is the single hardest engineering problem in the process, and it is why the original SOVERE design was a salt-bath reactor and why the later fluidised beds were better: the fluidised catalyst carries its own heat around, so the temperature is uniform and there is no hot spot to crack the catalyst.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: Molten salt bath reactor
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: A tubular reactor immersed in a bath of a molten nitrate-nitrite salt (the working point is around 300-330 C), with the bed of catalyst on an inert support inside the tube. It is a beautiful heat-transfer arrangement and a nasty maintenance one: the salt is oxidising, the reactor is at 400-450 C inside, and a tube failure means salt into the process. By 1983 it was being replaced by the fluidised bed for exactly this reason.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Salt bath temperatures are quoted in the 250-330 C range depending on the salt mix; the precise working point varies between licensors.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: The molten salt itself
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: A mixture of potassium nitrate, sodium nitrite and sometimes calcium nitrate, chosen for a melting point a little below the operating temperature and for a decomposition temperature a good deal above it. It is a beautiful heat-transfer medium and an oxidising one, and a small leak from the reactor puts hot nitrate into a hydrocarbon process - which is why the original SOVERE design was eventually superseded. The nitrate salts came from the same nitric acid that a fab's wet bench bought.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Salt compositions vary by licensor; the nitrate-nitrite family is the standard choice.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.san.name: Styrene-acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN)
chem.styrene.polymerisation.san.description: Styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made in bulk at 130-180 C or in emulsion or suspension. The acrylonitrile raises the heat distortion temperature from about 100 C to about 110-120 C and cuts the solubility in aromatic solvents, which is what turns a commodity polystyrene into the structural plastic the SAN matrix of ABS is made of. SAN production in 1983 was of the order of 0.4-0.5 million tonnes a year.
