chem.styrene.polymerisation.san.note: SAN capacity in the early 1980s is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

chem.abs.san-matrix.acrylonitrile-raw.name: Acrylonitrile monomer
chem.abs.san-matrix.acrylonitrile-raw.description: 99.5%+ acrylonitrile with less than 45 ppm of the stabiliser, from a SOVERE ammoxidation plant. Because acrylonitrile is acutely lethal through the skin, it arrived in the ABS plant in tankers and was handled in a closed system with an outside storage tank; the 1980s industry norm was glove boxes and an emergency shower at every sampling point.

chem.abs.san-matrix.styrene-raw.name: Styrene monomer
chem.abs.san-matrix.styrene-raw.description: 99.5%+ styrene with less than 100 ppm inhibitor, from a dehydrogenation unit. The inhibitor has to be removed or it stops the graft reaction dead, which is why the plant distils its own styrene or buys uninhibited grade.

chem.abs.grafting.reaction-medium.name: Reaction medium: xylene and water
chem.abs.grafting.reaction-medium.description: The rubber is dissolved in xylene (or toluene) and the monomer is emulsified in an aqueous phase containing the initiator, chelant and transfer agent. At the end the polymer is devolatilised at 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar to strip the xylene, which is the single biggest energy item in the plant - the solvent has a heat capacity of about 2 MJ/kg/K and there is one to two tonnes of it per tonne of polymer.

chem.abs.grafting.graft-level.name: Graft level and particle morphology
chem.abs.grafting.graft-level.description: How many SAN chains are grafted onto each rubber molecule, and what shape the particle ends up. High-graft material (more than about 70% grafted) gives a small, uniform particle and the best impact strength; low-graft gives larger particles and lower impact. The morphology is either salt-like (a grafted particle with an elastomeric core and a rigid SAN shell) or sandwich-like (SAN core with a grafted skin), and the choice is set by how fast the graft shell precipitates.
chem.abs.grafting.graft-level.note: Particle morphology terminology (salt-like, sandwich) and graft-level thresholds vary by producer; these are the standard descriptions.

chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.name: Chain transfer agent (modifier)
chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.description: A mercaptan - typically a tertiary dodecyl mercaptan, or thioglycolic acid in some processes - at 0.2-1.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical, capping each SAN branch and setting the graft chain length. Too little transfer and the graft crosslinks into a gel that is insoluble and unprocessable; too much and the graft has too few grafts per rubber particle and the impact strength collapses.

chem.abs.grafting.chelant.name: Chelating agent
chem.abs.grafting.chelant.description: A polycarboxylic acid or its salt - trisodium citrate, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt, or a polyacrylate - at 0.05-0.3 parts. It chelates the trace transition metals that would otherwise decompose the persulphate catalytically and produce a wild, uncontrolled radical rate. In the 1980s this was a standard part of the recipe and one of the few places where a detergent chemistry shows up inside a structural plastic.

chem.abs.grafting.initiator.name: Potassium persulphate initiator
chem.abs.grafting.initiator.description: K2S2O8 at 0.1-0.5 parts per 100 monomer, thermally decomposed in the aqueous-organic system at 60-80 C. The persulphate is deliberately an aqueous-phase initiator: it generates radicals in the aqueous phase, which is where the monomer droplets are, so grafting starts on the surface of the rubber particle rather than deep in the hydrocarbon phase.
chem.abs.grafting.initiator.note: Exact initiator levels vary with the licensor's process; the persulphate-in-aqueous-phase rationale is standard.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.name: The polybutadiene rubber phase
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.description: A low-cis (40-60% cis, therefore glassy rather than rubbery on its own) butyllithium-polymerised polybutadiene at 0.5-2% residual oil, with the whole chain ending in a couple of reactive sites. The low cis content is deliberate: a high-cis rubber dissolves in its own polymer at reactor temperature and the particle boundaries blur, whereas a low-cis rubber keeps a sharp core-shell particle that survives compounding.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.name: How butadiene is polymerised
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.description: Three chemistries, chosen for what you were making. Emulsion polymerisation gives cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and vinyl-1,2 structures mixed - a rubber but not a specific one. Anionic polymerisation with lithium butyllithium gives cis-1,4 selectively and controls chain ends. Coordination polymerisation with neodymium or titanium gives cis-1,4 with an extremely high cis content. The 4-vinyl group left on a cis-1,4 chain is the reactive site that grafting later exploits.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Neodymium-catalysed cis-polybutadiene
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: The high-cis technology of the 1980s: a neodymium (or lanthanide) compound with an alkylaluminium in a hydrocarbon diluent gives 97-99% cis-1,4, and because the cis content is so high the rubber does not need to be plasticised with oil. Linear low-cis polybutadiene was the growth product of the decade; the older lithium-process cis-PB at 90-95% was still the volume product in 1983.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Neodymium from bastnasite
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: The high-cis polybutadiene catalyst needs a rare earth metal, and the rare earths come from bastnasite, a light-brown carbonatite ore mined in Mountain Pass, California, in Bayan Obo in China, and in Australia and India, concentrated and then separated by a long solvent-extraction cascade. The separation is the interesting part: fifteen chemically similar elements have to be separated one at a time by a solvent-extraction train, and the neodymium is the one that came into industrial demand in the 1980s for reasons nobody had predicted - a rubber catalyst.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Bastnasite ore
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: A light rare earth carbonate fluorosilicate, about 6-9% rare earth oxides, discovered in 1878 at Bastnas in Sweden and mined in quantity from 1949. It is the last dig-it-out node of the ABS branch's rubber phase: a C64's rubber comes from butadiene from a cracker, but the catalyst that gives that butadiene its cis content begins in a carbonatite dyke in California or in Inner Mongolia.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.note: The rare earth chain is a metals subsystem; this node marks where a 1980s rubber catalyst entered it.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.name: Lithium butyllithium polymerisation
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.description: The living anionic process: butyllithium in a hydrocarbon diluent (diesel oil or hexane) at 0-60 C, with the cis content set by solvent and temperature. Living means the chain end stays active, so the polymer can be chain-stopped with an electrophile - water, carbon dioxide, epoxide - and the whole molecule is a single block. This is the chemistry that makes the ABS graft rubber phase possible.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.name: Butyllithium
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.description: A pyrophoric organolithium, always supplied as a 10-20% solution in hexane and never in bulk. In 1980s practice it was the initiator for the solution polymerisation of polybutadiene and for the SBR made by anionic polymerisation, and its manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane was a speciality chemical operation with a lot of solvent handling.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.name: The four polybutadiene microstructures
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.description: cis-1,4 (the elastomer; the chain is flexible below its glass transition), trans-1,4 (the chain is regular and crystalline, so it is a plastic not a rubber), 1,2-vinyl (a pendant vinyl group, also rubbery but with a high glass transition because of the pendant group), and 3,4-vinyl (rare). The rubbery ones are cis-1,4 and 1,2; the ratio between them is set by temperature, catalyst and solvent, and it is why polybutadiene rubber has a glass transition near -100 C and is the most flexible of the common rubbers.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.note: Glass transition values for elastomers vary a few degrees with grade and measurement.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.name: Controlling cis, trans and vinyl
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.description: The ratio of the four microstructures is not an accident; it is the dial the polymer chemist turns. Coordination catalysts with a rare earth or a titanium give cis-1,4 because the metal holds the growing chain in a specific geometry. Lithium butyllithium in a polar solvent gives more 1,2-vinyl; in a hydrocarbon it gives more cis-1,4. Temperature moves it again. And each structure has a different transition: cis-1,4 is the rubber, trans-1,4 crystallises into a hard plastic, and 1,2-vinyl is rubbery but with a pendant group that lifts its glass transition by about 20 C.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.note: Glass transition and melting points for polybutadiene microstructures vary with tacticity and crystallinity; the ranges here are the standard textbook figures.

facts.label: trans-1,4
facts.value: crystalline, Tg about -80 C but Tm about +100 C

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Butadiene monomer for the rubber phase
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: 99.0-99.7% butadiene from a cracker C4 extraction unit. The chain is why the C64's rubber phase is a petrochemical and not a natural rubber: the natural rubber alternative is cis-1,4-polyisoprene from latex, and the graft chemistry that works on polybutadiene's pendant vinyl group does not work on isoprene's chain.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Getting 99.7% butadiene out of the cracker's C4
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: An ABS plant in 1983 did not make its own butadiene. It bought polymerisation-grade monomer, which meant the plant upstream had to extract butadiene from a C4 stream where it is one component among six, with a relative volatility from the alpha-olefins of about 1.01. That extraction unit is one of the largest distillation towers in the chemical industry, and its solvent is a forestry chemical or a pyrrolidone - so the rubber phase of a C64's case starts in a pine forest or a cracker, and the choice between them is thirty years old.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: The extraction unit
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: Two columns, each 40-70 m tall: the first extracts butadiene and the butenes into the solvent, the second strips pure butadiene overhead and recycles the solvent. Capacity on a single unit in 1983 was 100,000-400,000 tonnes a year of C4, and the column's diameter was the throughput. It was also, incidentally, the largest single user of furfural or NMP in the world.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: NMP from butanone
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: The petrochemical route to N-methylpyrrolidone: butanone and ethylenediamine condensed to a cyclic amide, then methylated. Both reactants are cheap petrochemicals - butanone from acetone or from butanol, ethylenediamine from ethylene oxide or from 1,2-dichloroethane - so the same solvent molecule could be made from a cracker or bought from a forestry route. By the 1980s the chemical route had won, and NMP then went on to displace the chlorinated degreasers.
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.note: NMP manufacture from butanone and ethylenediamine followed by methylation is the standard industrial route.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: The methanol in the NMP
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: The last step of the NMP route is a methylation, and the methylating agent is methanol, which in 1983 was made from synthesis gas - from natural gas by steam reforming, or from coal, whichever the country had. So the degreaser that replaced the chlorinated solvents in the electronics plant was, three steps back, natural gas; and the plastic it was replacing in the very same plant was naphtha. Two feedstocks, one plant.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Methanol from synthesis gas
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: CO plus hydrogen at 200-300 C and 50-100 bar over a copper-zinc-aluminium catalyst gives methanol. The hydrogen comes from a reformer - so from natural gas - and the carbon monoxide from the reformed methane, from coal gasification, or from coke oven gas depending on the country. By 1983 more than half the world's methanol was made from natural gas, which makes methanol a gas product that behaves like a liquid fuel, and is the reason the world's gas and coal markets met inside a single molecule.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Furfural from pentosan (the forestry route)
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: Furfural is made by treating a pentosan - hemicellulose, which is a fifth of the dry weight of a hardwood - with acid and steam. The classic sources are rice hulls, corn cobs and bagasse, the fibrous residue of sugar cane after the juice has been squeezed out. A C64's rubber phase, if the extractor ran on furfural, traces back through a cracker and an extractor to a sugarcane field. That is the least obviously petroleum thing in the machine.
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.note: Furfural from agricultural residues is a well-established industrial route; the specific feedstock used by any one extractor is not known here.

chem.abs.grafting.name: Graft copolymerisation: growing SAN on the rubber
chem.abs.grafting.description: The heart of the process. 20-40 parts of a low-cis polybutadiene rubber dissolved in xylene or toluene is charged to a reactor, and styrene plus acrylonitrile is added at 60-80 C in the presence of a persulphate initiator, a chelating agent and a mercaptan chain transfer agent. The radicals abstract a hydrogen from the polybutadiene's 1,2-vinyl unit, creating a radical site on the rubber; styrene and acrylonitrile then copolymerise from that site, and SAN chains grow out of the rubber particle. Each particle therefore becomes a rubber core with a SAN shell.

chem.styrene.name: Styrene: benzene plus ethylene, and the plastics of it
chem.styrene.description: Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, and the ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene. About 12-14 million tonnes of styrene were made in 1983, of which roughly two thirds went to polystyrene and the rest to SAN, ABS and SBR. Styrene is a C64 material in a way that is easy to miss: the SAN matrix of the case, the styrene in the graft phase, and the polystyrene that was in the packaging and in some of the mouldings.

chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.name: Divinylbenzene
chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.description: A 40/60 to 80/20 mixture of the two divinylbenzene isomers made by the same ethylbenzene route with a second vinyl group. About 1-2% of the styrene monomer, and essentially all of it goes into ion exchange resins and into the crosslinking monomer of unsaturated polyester. The cation exchange resin in the water treatment plant of a plastics factory is a styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer, so this molecule sits quietly in the supply chain of almost everything else in this file.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.name: Styrene polymerisation
chem.styrene.polymerisation.description: Styrene polymerises readily by free-radical mechanisms because the benzyl radical it makes is resonance stabilised. Almost all commercial polystyrene is made by free-radical polymerisation; the ionic routes that give syndiotactic and isotactic polystyrene existed in the 1980s but were curiosities.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.eps.name: Expanded polystyrene
chem.styrene.polymerisation.eps.description: Styrene with 5-6% pentane or butane as a blowing agent, polymerised at 90-150 C and 1-5 bar with the beads expanding 10-30 times. It was the standard packing material for electronics and for the C64's carton inserts, and it is the one polymer in the C64's own packaging whose feedstock chain is styrene rather than the case's ABS.
chem.styrene.polymerisation.eps.note: Halon blowing agents (CFC-11, CFC-113) were the dominant technology for EPS until the 1980s; their phase-out under the Montreal Protocol is the reason pentane took over, and it is the clearest consumer-packaging link to that treaty.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.sbs.name: Styrene-butadiene-styrene block copolymer
chem.styrene.polymerisation.sbs.description: Made by sequential addition to a living anionic chain: butadiene to a 60-80% cis polybutadiene block, then styrene to a polystyrene block on each end. The hard polystyrene end blocks are the physical crosslinks and the middle block is the rubber, so the material is a thermoplastic elastomer that flows hot and returns. It is the same butadiene and styrene as SBR and ABS but in a completely different architecture.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.name: General purpose polystyrene, bulk and suspension
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.description: Bulk polymerisation at 140-200 C and 20-40 bar in a stirred or plug-flow reactor with a benzoyl peroxide or a hindered phenol initiator, the classic route for general purpose and crystal grade. Suspension polymerisation, in which styrene is dispersed as 0.1-2 mm beads in water with a suspending agent, is preferred for foam grades because the beads can be expanded. General purpose polystyrene production in the 1980s was of the order of 5-6 million tonnes a year.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: Finishing: devolatilisation and pelletising
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: Polystyrene has to be devolatilised after the bulk polymerisation, because the monomer left in the melt is both a smell and a peroxide risk. A 1980s finishing line was a twin-screw extruder at 200-240 C and 5-50 mbar with two vacuum vents, then a strand die into a water bath, then a rotary cutter - the same machine geometry as the ABS line, and for the same reason: somebody in the plastics industry decided once that devolatilisation and pelletising should be one operation and never went back.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: Strand die, water bath and cutter
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: Extruded through a die with 10-30 holes of 2-3 mm, quenched in a water bath at 20-30 C, drawn by a first calender and cut by a rotary knife. The alternative - underwater pelletising - cuts the strands in the water and was becoming the 1980s choice for polystyrene as it had been for ABS, for the same reason: fewer handling steps and no strand breakage.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: The devolatiliser
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: A falling-film or wiped-film evaporator with two stages of vacuum, taking the residual styrene from a few per cent down to a few hundred parts per million. The polymer is deliberately kept above its own melting point but below its decomposition point, which for polystyrene is a window of about 40 C - the whole of the finishing engineering is about staying in that window while the pressure falls and the viscosity rises.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.name: Suspending agent for suspension polystyrene
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.description: Gelatin, methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, at 0.1-1% of the water phase. It has to hold the bead together without letting the bead coalesce, and the whole engineering of suspension polystyrene is the engineering of that balance: too little and the beads fuse, too much and the bead has a hard skin that traps monomer and leaves styrene odour in the bead.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.name: Benzoyl peroxide initiator
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.description: Dibenzoyl peroxide, dosed at 0.05-0.5 wt%, thermally decomposed at 60-90 C to give a benzoyloxy radical and then a phenyl radical. It leaves a benzoic acid residue in the polymer and a trace of styrene in the reactor bottoms, which is why polystyrene made with it has a characteristic faint smell and a yellowing tendency that the 1980s stabiliser industry existed to fix.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.name: Dehydrogenation to styrene
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.description: Ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene at 600-700 C and 1-3 bar over an iron oxide catalyst (the classic Feeders-Rudd, now UOP ST-110, a shell-and-tube bed of promoted magnetite with potassium and copper promoters). Single-pass conversion is 40-50% and the selectivity to styrene 90-93%. The conversion is deliberately held below completion because styrene polymerises over the same catalyst, and because the dehydrogenation is strongly endothermic and needs a large fired furnace.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.name: The dehydrogenation furnace
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.description: The dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is strongly endothermic - about 0.22 GJ of heat per tonne of ethylbenzene - and it is carried out in a bank of shell-and-tube reactors with the heat applied from the outside. A 1980s styrene plant's furnaces were its largest energy consumers and its largest single source of stack emissions, which is why the industry spent the 1980s on better coil metallurgy, on vacuum insulation of the reactor, and on a staged feed arrangement that fed the preheated reactor's effluent straight back into the next reactor's inlet.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.name: Furnace fuel
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.description: Refinery fuel gas or natural gas. It is worth noting what this means for the tree: the styrene that goes into the C64's case was made with heat from a refinery or a gas field, and the same refinery that made the ethylbenzene also made the fuel. A substantial part of the carbon in a plastic is therefore not in the polymer at all but was burned to make it.
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.note: The heat of dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is about 0.22 GJ/t; the figure here is rounded.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.name: Inhibitor and diluent feed
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.description: Steam diluent to keep the partial pressure low, and a polymerisation inhibitor - sulfolane, a chlorinated hydrocarbon, or a proprietary organic - dosed at tens of parts per million to hold the styrene down. The inhibitor is a recurring cost and a recurring loss: it ends up in the styrene product and has to be removed, and it is one of the reasons styrene plants have a product purification section that looks like a fourth distillation tower.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.reactor.name: ST-110 dehydrogenation reactor
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.reactor.description: A bank of shell-and-tube reactors, 20-50 tubes 4-6 inch in diameter by 20-30 m long, at 1-3 bar, fired on the outside. A 1980s styrene plant had 8-20 such reactors per train and several trains. The furnace is the plant's energy hog, which is why the styrene industry was the largest single consumer of heat-integration improvements in this part of the chemical industry.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.name: Promoted iron oxide catalyst
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.description: Magnetite or hematite promoted with potassium oxide, copper oxide and sometimes molybdenum or chromium, formed as extruded rings or as a granular bed. Steam is used as a diluent to keep the partial pressure low and to suppress coking, and a trace of a polymerisation inhibitor (sulfolane or a chlorinated hydrocarbon) is fed to hold the polymer down.

chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.name: Ethylbenzene from benzene and ethylene
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.description: Benzene plus ethylene in a large molar excess of benzene (3-6 to 1) over a zeolite or a phosphoric acid catalyst at 250-400 C and 10-30 bar. The 1980s breakthrough was the Mobil process using a shape-selective zeolite (the ZSM-5 family) at about 350 C, which gives over 97% selectivity to ethylbenzene and almost no diethylbenzene. The old process, phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar, had a diethylbenzene problem that ate benzene and made the distillation columns enormous.

chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.name: Shape-selective alkylation catalyst
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.description: A zeolite whose pore geometry lets a benzene molecule in, lets ethylbenzene out and does not let diethylbenzene in - the same shape selectivity that let ZSM-5 crack gasoline to high-octane and propylene, and that later let MFI zeolites make para-xylene. One catalyst family, three jobs, all in this file.

chem.styrene.benzene.name: Benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.description: The feedstock. In 1983 world benzene production was of the order of 15-17 million tonnes a year, and it came from three sources: catalytic reforming (about half), hydrodealkylation of toluene (roughly a quarter to a third, and the growth share of the 1980s), and coal tar from coke ovens (10-20%, and a bigger share outside North America and Western Europe).

chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.name: Coke oven benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.description: Byproduct benzene from the coking of coal in an integral coke plant: the coke oven gas is cooled and the aromatics stripped out, giving a crude benzole with toluene and xylenes. In 1983 coal tar benzene was still a major share of world benzene - more so in Europe and Asia than in the United States - and it is the one benzene of that era that is not a petrochemical at all.

chem.styrene.benzene.hda.name: Toluene hydrodealkylation
chem.styrene.benzene.hda.description: Toluene plus hydrogen gives benzene and methane at 500-600 C and 30-60 bar over a cobalt-molybdenum or alumina catalyst. This was the route that grew fastest through the 1980s because toluene was abundant (from the C7+ cracker fraction and from the reformer) and benzene was tight; it also makes the methane by-product that a reformer makes as hydrogen, so the two operations fit together.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.name: Aromatics recovery from reformer naphtha
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.description: The C6 to C8 aromatics have to be extracted from a naphtha stream where they are only a few percent by weight. The 1960s and 1980s workhorse was the UOP EdCo process: extractive distillation with sulfolane (a four-plus-four ring sulfone, 218 C boiling point) followed by azeotropic distillation with isooctane. Sulfolane replaced sulfuric acid extraction because it did not invert the alkylbenzenes and did not make a waste acid stream - and sulfuric acid hydrodealkylation was the older, waste-generating route.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: Tetrahydrothiophene-1,1-dioxide, a polar aprotic solvent that dissolves aromatics preferentially to paraffins and is thermally stable and non-corrosive. It is also the inhibitor chemistry's solvent cousin: sulfolane is used as a polymerisation inhibitor in the styrene dehydrogenation reactors, and it belongs to a small family of molecules - NMP, sulfolane, dimethylformamide - that turns up in three different jobs in this file.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane from butadiene
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: The solvent that extracts benzene out of a naphtha stream is itself made out of the cracker's C4. Butadiene is reacted with sulfur dioxide and water to give tetrahydrothiophene 1,1-dioxide. So the styrene chain - benzene, ethylbenzene, styrene - is fed by butadiene twice over: once as the rubber in the ABS, and once as the solvent that separated the benzene. It is the clearest example in this file of a chemical park's flows being a web rather than a line.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfonation and ring closure
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: CH2=CH-CH=CH2 plus SO2 at 100-140 C gives the sulfolene, a five-membered ring with one double bond left; a second equivalent of water at 100-140 C with a base opens a second ring, giving sulfolane. The sulfur dioxide comes from burning sulfur - usually the same recovered elemental sulphur that the Claus plant in a nearby refinery produced from the same sour gas that fed the cracker.
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..note: Sulfolane is industrially made by the butadiene/SO2/hydrolysis route; the conditions quoted are representative.

chem.butadiene.name: Butadiene and the elastomers of it
chem.butadiene.description: Butadiene is the C4 diene that makes synthetic rubber, and in 1983 about 5-6 million tonnes a year of it was made, roughly 60% from cracker C4 by extractive distillation and the rest by dehydrogenation of butane. It is the molecule behind the rubber in the C64's case feet, the plinths, and the elasticity of the power cord's jacket - and behind the graft phase of the ABS case.

chem.butadiene.butadiene-adiponitrile.name: Butadiene to adiponitrile
chem.butadiene.butadiene-adiponitrile.description: Two molecules of butadiene plus two of hydrogen cyanide give adiponitrile by hydrocyanation, catalysed by nickel(0) with a triphenylphosphine ligand. It was an academic curiosity until the 1970s and became commercial in the 1980s (BASF and the DuPont/ICI route), and it is the reason a nylon 6,6 plant of the late 1980s could be fed from a cracker rather than from adipic acid. The reaction needs hydrogen cyanide, which is the toxic gas of the older acrylonitrile and MMA chemistry.
chem.butadiene.butadiene-adiponitrile.note: Industrial adoption dates vary; commercial processes were announced in the early-mid 1980s.

chem.butadiene.nitrile-rubber.name: Nitrile rubber
chem.butadiene.nitrile-rubber.description: Butadiene with 25-40% acrylonitrile, emulsion-polymerised the same way as SBR. The acrylonitrile makes the oil and fuel resistance good and costs the low-temperature flexibility. It is the material for oil seals and for the elastomer pads of many electrolytic capacitors; in 1980s electronics it also appeared in the conformal-coating and adhesive chemistries of the power supply.
chem.butadiene.nitrile-rubber.note: The acrylonitrile comes from chem.acrylonitrile; the butadiene from chem.butadiene.sources.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber.name: Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR)
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber.description: The largest synthetic rubber by a wide margin: of the order of 6-7 million tonnes a year in 1983, in a handful of grades. It is not a C64 material, but it is the material whose emulsion polymerisation recipe - cold, water, persulphate, rosin acid soap, chain transfer agent - is the same recipe the ABS graft phase uses, and the rosin in it is the same pine rosin as the solder flux.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Chain transfer agent
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: A mercaptan - diethyl dithiocarbamate, tetraethyl thiuram disulphide, or a dodecyl mercaptan - at 0.1-0.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical to the sulphur and caps the chain, which limits molecular weight and prevents the gelation that would otherwise turn a linear rubber into a useless network. Every emulsion polymerisation has one; in ABS it is called a modifier and it is the same chemistry.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Potassium persulphate initiator
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: K2S2O8 or the cheaper sodium persulphate, thermally decomposed to sulphate radical, generating the first polymer radicals at the aqueous droplet surface. Persulphate initiators leave a residue of sulphate groups on the chain ends, which is why an emulsion SBR cannot be re-polymerised as a living polymer and has to be made in one shot.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Rosin acid soap emulsifier
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Sodium or potassium salts of pine rosins (about 60% abietic acid) and of tall oil fatty acids, mixed 50/50. Two jobs: the rosin part stabilises the polymer against oxidation, and the fatty acid part controls the particle size and the rate. Rosin emulsifiers also give the rubber a slightly tacky surface, which is why tread compounds still add tackifying resin.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The rosin itself is chem.rosin, which also supplies the solder flux.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Fatty acid emulsifier and tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: About half of a cold SBR or ABS emulsifier system is a fatty acid salt, and the fatty acid came from tallow - the rendered fat of cattle and sheep - split into oleic and stearic acid and neutralised with sodium or potassium hydroxide. So part of the emulsifier that keeps the rubber particles apart in the graft reactor was, in 1983, a byproduct of the meat industry, which is a genuinely surprising provenance for a molecule that ends up inside a computer case.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Rendered animal fat, roughly 50% palmitic, stearic and oleic acid. Historically a by-product of the meat industry and increasingly, through the 1980s, a rendering industry of its own. Its oleic acid was the emulsifier and its stearic acid was the release agent, and both ended up in the polymer. The C64's case therefore contains a trace of a livestock product through the soap that helped the rubber particles form.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The tallow provenance of fatty-acid emulsifiers is well established; synthetic fatty acids were substituting for it through the 1980s.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Cold emulsion polymerisation (5 C)
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Styrene at 23-25 parts and butadiene at 75-77 parts in water, with a rosin or oleate soap emulsifier at 2-5 parts and a persulphate initiator at 0.05-0.2 parts, polymerised at 5 C for 8-12 hours to 60-70% conversion. The cold polymerisation, invented in 1947, gives a far more regular chain than the hot 50 C version because the slower initiation lets the chain length control the structure. The resulting latex is coagulated with salt or acid, and the crumb washed and dried.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The ABS graft reaction uses the same chemistry at 50-80 C; see chem.abs.grafting.

chem.butadiene.sources.name: Butadiene sources
chem.butadiene.sources.description: Two industrial routes and a third that was still just about alive in 1983: extractive distillation of the steam cracker's C4 stream, dehydrogenation of n-butane, and thermal dimerisation of acetylene (the old Reppe route, dead by 1960). The choice between them is a function of whether a cracker was nearby and whether butane was cheap.

chem.butadiene.sources.acetylene-dimeris.name: Acetylene dimerisation (Reppe, obsolete)
chem.butadiene.sources.acetylene-dimeris.description: Two acetylene molecules make butadiene over a copper catalyst, and before 1960 that is how the world made it. It is a beautiful route - butadiene from a C1 feed with perfect atom economy - and it died because acetylene was expensive relative to the C4 it was displacing. It is the third example in this file of the same lesson: the elegant route from natural gas lost to the abundant route from naphtha.

chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.name: Houdry butane dehydrogenation
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.description: n-Butane dehydrogenated endothermically at 480-550 C over platinum on alumina or chromia at 1-5 bar to butenes, which are then extracted and the butadiene purified separately. It was the on-purpose route, it made isobutylene for MTBE as a co-product, and it suffered from the thermodynamics of an endothermic reaction: every 1% of conversion costs a lot of fuel, and 1980s furnace designs pushed single-pass conversion to 40-50% with recirculation.

chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.name: The butane dehydrogenation furnace
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.description: Dehydrogenation of butane to butenes is endothermic, so the reactor is a bank of fired tubes - cast iron or cast alloy, several hundred tubes, with the furnace gas at 500-700 C. The catalyst inside is platinum on alumina or chromia, and the giveaway of a fouled furnace is the pressure drop across the tubes: the butene polymerises on the catalyst, makes green coke, and the coke blocks the tube. This unit is the reason the butadiene plant in a 1980s complex was often the noisiest building on the site.
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.note: The description of furnace-tube coking in butane dehydrogenation is standard; specific designs vary.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.name: Sounsby extractive distillation
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.description: The standard butadiene recovery unit from 1962 onward: an extractive distillation with a selective polar solvent that dissolves butadiene and the butenes but not the saturated C4s, followed by a second stripper to recover the pure diene. A 1980s unit processing 100,000-400,000 tonnes a year of C4 stood about 60-100 m tall and was one of the tallest distillation towers in the world, because alpha-olefins and butadiene have a relative volatility of about 1.01 - the hardest separation in the whole C4 business. The process works because butadiene is the only diene and the only component that will add a second solvent molecule.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.name: 99%+ butadiene
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.description: The polymerisation-grade monomer has to be 99.0-99.7% with less than 100 ppm of inhibitor residue, less than 100 ppm water and less than 50 ppm carbonyls. The spec is enforced because the polymerisation catalysts of the era - both the persulfate emulsion ones and the lithium butyllithium ones - were exquisitely sensitive to all three.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.name: How the monomer was actually specified
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.description: The four numbers on the certificate were purity by gas chromatography, inhibitor as the number of minutes before a calibrated sample polymerised, water by Karl Fischer, and carbonyls by a colorimetric test. All four existed because of what each one does to a polymerisation: water kills the lithium catalyst, the inhibitor sets the shelf life, the carbonyls kill the persulphate graft, and the purity sets the branching. In 1983 this certificate was a 30 kPa cylinder delivered in a hazardous-materials truck, and a plant that had used the drum too long found out by making bad rubber.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.note: The analytical methods are period-correct and standard; the specific limits are those quoted elsewhere in this file.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.name: N-methylpyrrolidone as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.description: NMP (a strongly polar, high-boiling amide, 202 C) replaced furfural because it does not polymerise and needs less make-up. NMP was the 1980s solvent of choice and it is the same molecule that later arrived in the electronics plant as the chlorinated-solvent replacement for 1,1,1-trichloroethane.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.note: The solvent substitution history is under chem.solvents.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.name: Furfural as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.description: Furfural (furan-2-carbaldehyde) made from furfural-bark or from pentoses in bagasse hemihydrate pulping, with a boiling point of 161 C and a high selectivity for diene over alpha-olefin. It was the original Sounsby solvent and its dominant drawback is that it polymerises in the presence of acid, so the unit had to be kept dry and inhibited and it consumed make-up solvent continuously.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.note: Furfural is a biomass-derived chemical rather than a petrochemical one, and it is the one clear biomass input in the C4 chain.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.name: Cracker C4 stream
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.description: A NGL stream of 1-butene (15-25%), cis-2-butene (10-15%), trans-2-butene (30-35%), isobutylene (15-25%) and isobutane/isopentane, with butadiene at 20-30% of the C4 - which is 4-6% of the cracker's total hydrocarbon output. The butadiene has to be taken out by a separate, very large unit.
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.note: C4 compositions depend heavily on cracker severity and feedstock; the ranges given are typical naphtha-cracker figures.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: C4 recovery and the depentaniser
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: Before the butadiene extractor there is the C4 recovery section: a depentaniser that takes the C5+ out of the whole cracker liquid so the C4 unit does not have to handle pentanes and heavier, and then a C3/C4 splitter that separates propane from the butanes. Both columns are ordinary fractionations, but the depentaniser runs at 30-40 bar and is where a lot of the plant's fouling comes from, because the C5+ fraction carries the naphthalene and the heavier aromatics that the C4 extractor does not want.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: The C3/C4 splitter
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: A 60-80 tray column separating propane overhead from the butanes. It is a good example of a column that has nothing to do with the product of interest: the butadiene extractor's feed comes off the bottom of this splitter, and the splitter's job is only to keep the propane out of the extractor so the extractor's solvent does not have to separate propane from butadiene as well.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: The depentaniser
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: A 40-60 tray column operating at 25-40 bar, taking the C5 cut point at about 50-60 C. Its overhead is the C4 stream that goes to the extractor; its bottoms are the C5+ gasoline fraction that goes to the aromatics recovery or to the gasoline pool. It is the least glamorous column in the plant and the one that most often needs its furnace cleaned.

chem.acrylonitrile.name: Acrylonitrile and the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.description: The SOVERE process - SOx-free reductive ammoxidation - oxidises propylene with ammonia and air in one step to acrylonitrile. It was invented at Standard Oil of Ohio and licensed worldwide from 1960-1965, and by 1983 essentially all the world's roughly 1.2-1.5 million tonnes a year of acrylonitrile was made by it. Acrylonitrile is the most dangerous liquid in a polymer plant: it is acutely lethal by skin absorption, flammable at 3-20% in air, and boils at 77 C.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.name: Downstream acrylonitrile
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.description: What the acrylonitrile was for in 1983: acrylic fibre (Orlon, Dralon, and in Japan the acrylics), nitrile rubber (butadiene copolymer), SAN and ABS copolymer, and the polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.name: Methyl methacrylate (acetone cyanohydrin route)
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.description: A separate molecule with the same nitrile: acetone plus hydrogen chloride gives acetone cyanohydrin, which is esterified with methanol and then dehydrated with sulphuric acid to methyl methacrylate. The acetone cyanohydrin route was introduced from 1938 and became dominant in the 1950s-60s. The hydrogen cyanide for it came either from the acrylonitrile plant's by-product or from its own Andrussow process, and the methanol came from synthesis gas.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.name: Acetone cyanohydrin
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.description: A compound that made the C64 possible twice over: it is the intermediate for methyl methacrylate, and the HCN it carries is the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the older butadiene-adiponitrile route to nylon 6,6. It is acutely toxic and it has killed people by being absorbed through the skin, which is the reason the ACH plants had such aggressive containment.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: Made by hydrolysis of acrylonitrile in an 85-93% sulphuric acid solution at 90-120 C in a batch or continuous reactor in the 1980s (the later propane-oxidation route came later and took over). The acrylonitrile had to be purified first because the hydrolysis is irreversible and the by-product ammonium sulphate ends up in the polymer. Superabsorbent diapers drove the growth of this route from the late 1970s.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Ammonium sulphate by-product
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: One tonne of acrylic acid from acrylonitrile hydrolysis throws out about one tonne of ammonium sulphate, which is a low-grade fertiliser that is expensive to dry and transport. It is the classic penalty of the hydrolysis route and the reason the later oxidation route won.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.pan-precur.name: PAN as a carbon fibre precursor
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.pan-precur.description: More than half of all the acrylonitrile made in the world in the early 1980s went into acrylic fibre, and a growing slice of the fibre-grade acrylonitrile went into polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre. PAN had to be made from a very pure comonomer - methyl acrylate at 0.5-3% - because any ionic impurity in the precursor ends up as a carbon defect in the fibre, and carbon fibre's entire value is in the defect count.
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.pan-precur.note: Carbon fibre for aerospace became a real commercial product in the late 1970s-early 1980s but had essentially no place in a 1982 home computer; the link here is the shared acrylonitrile supply.

chem.acrylonitrile.hno3-route.name: The older nitric acid route
chem.acrylonitrile.hno3-route.description: Propylene nitrated with 15-20% nitric acid at 30-60 C and 2-5 bar to a mixture of 1- and 2-nitropropane, the 1-nitropropane converted with a dialkyl amine to a propylhydroxylamine, then dehydrated to acrylonitrile. It was a 30-50% route with a heavy nitrate waste stream and a very large plant, and by 1983 it existed only in a few older Soviet and Eastern European plants. It is the standard example of how completely a single-step oxidation can displace a three-step one.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.safety.name: Acrylonitrile hazard
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.safety.description: Acrylonitrile inhibits cytochrome oxidase and causes methemoglobinemia; it is absorbed through intact skin, which is why a 1980s acrylonitrile plant used gloves, face shields and shower-and-eyewash stations at every sampling point, and why the recommended limits fell through the 1980s. The 1980s occupational limits in force were around 10 ppm as an 8-hour time-weighted average in the United States, with much lower values adopted by later committees. There is no safe long-term exposure and the whole industry of the period treated it as an acute poison.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.safety.note: Occupational limits for acrylonitrile were being revised downward through the 1980s and the figures above are the era's order of magnitude rather than a single legal value.

chem.propylene.name: Propylene and its derivatives
chem.propylene.description: Propylene is the C3 that the cracker makes whether you wanted it or not, and for two decades the propylene splitter process existed purely to turn that unwanted C3 into more of it. By 1983 most propylene came from the cracker and from FCC, and it went into polypropylene, propylene oxide, cumene for phenol and bisphenol A, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

chem.propylene.cumene.name: Cumene route to phenol and acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.description: Benzene plus propylene gives cumene; cumene plus oxygen gives cumene hydroperoxide; the hydroperoxide is cleaved with acid to give phenol and acetone. About a million tonnes a year of phenol in 1983 came out of this route, and phenol went to bisphenol A (and therefore to the C64's epoxy laminate resin), to phenol-formaldehyde plastics, and to caprolactam. Acetone came out of the other end of the same reaction, which is why acetone supply in the 1980s was really cumene capacity in disguise.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.name: Acid cleavage to phenol and acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.description: The cumene hydroperoxide is cleaved with sulphuric acid (or with a zeolite in later plants) at 50-80 C, giving phenol and acetone with 85-95% selectivity. The 1980s safety concern was the rearrangement of the cumene hydroperoxide to the phenol and acetone, which is violently exothermic: a small holdup upstream of the cleavage reactor would flash-boil, and the famous 1979 and 1985 phenol plant incidents are what the modern design rules are written around.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.description: The co-product of the cumene process and, from 1960s, a major product in its own right from the acetone cyanohydrin process. Acetone was the electronics plant's solvent of choice for degreasing and photoresist stripping in 1980s practice, and it is also the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the bisphenol A plus chloroform route to epoxy.
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.note: The solvent uses are under chem.solvents.acetone.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.name: Phenol
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.description: The molecule that goes into bisphenol A for epoxy, into phenol-formaldehyde for the phenolic plastics of switches and sockets, and into caprolactam for nylon 6. 1983 world phenol production was of the order of 3.5-4 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it from cumene.

chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation.name: Cumene oxidation to the hydroperoxide
chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation.description: Cumene with air at 120-140 C, either with a hydroperoxide initiator or with a cobalt or manganese catalyst, gives cumene hydroperoxide at 20-40 wt%. This is a liquid-phase autoxidation, and it has the classic autoxidation hazard: the reaction is exothermic, it runs away above 150 C, and the product is a shock-sensitive organic peroxide.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 120-140 C, air, initiator or Co/Mn catalyst

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.name: Cumene alkylation
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.description: Benzene with excess benzene over phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar in an adiabatic bed, or over a solid acid. The large excess of benzene (3-5 mol per mol of propylene) is deliberate: it suppresses the diethylbenzene and triisopropylbenzene by-products and stops the reactor polymerising the propylbenzene.

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Phosphoric acid on silica
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: The classic cumene alkylation catalyst is orthophosphoric acid on a silica carrier: the acid is absorbed into the silica's pore structure and the pore structure holds it there, and the catalyst's whole life is the slow loss of that acid to the reactor walls. The 1980s industry answer was a solid acid and a moving-bed or slurry reactor; the answer that arrived later was a zeolite. Three catalysts for one reaction in fifty years, and the C64's epoxy resin is downstream of all three.

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Silica carrier (the same silica as the cracker drier)
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: A silica gel of 200-400 m2/g surface area, and a strong family resemblance to the 3A molecular sieve's carrier and to the FCC catalyst's matrix and to the ammoxidation catalyst's support. One amorphous silica, made from sand by the soda-silica route, appears in this file as a support four different times, and it is the petrochemical branch's quietest link to a mineral.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.name: Chlorinated flame retardants from propylene
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.description: Polymers and elastomers for electronics and furniture were made to burn slowly by chlorinating a paraffinic or a phosphate ester. Chlorinated paraffins, and the phosphorus esters derived from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride, went into the flame-retardant grades of ABS, polypropylene and polyurethane foam that a consumer electronics company would specify for enclosures but not for a home computer.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.name: Tris(2,3-dichloropropyl) phosphate
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.description: The organophosphate flame retardant made from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride. It is an effective flame retardant for ABS, rigid polyurethane foam and polyester resins, and its precursor, tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate, is the classic story of a flame retardant that was banned in the United States in the 1970s after it caused animal tumours. That ban is the single clearest link between a 1960s consumer polymer and a 1990s regulation.
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.note: The US ban on tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate under the Consumer Product Safety Act dates from 1977; the chlorinated phosphate was its less-toxic replacement.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.name: Chlorinated paraffin
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.description: Paraffins chlorinated to 40-70% chlorine, used as a secondary flame retardant and, in the 1970s, as a plasticiser for PVC. It is a cheap and effective flame retardant and a persistent environmental contaminant, which is why the 1980s trend in electronics housings was towards phosphorus systems and towards thin walls that did not need as much of it.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.name: Propylene oxide
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.description: Propylene epoxidised, then made into propylene glycol, polyether polyols for polyurethane foam, and propylene chlorohydrin. World production was of the order of 0.7-0.9 million tonnes in 1983. Because the epoxidation of propylene was historically done with hypochlorous acid, a chlorinated by-product stream came with it, and that is why 1,2-dichloropropane and the flame retardants derived from it were part of the same business.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.name: Hydrogen peroxide epoxidation
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.description: Propylene plus hydrogen peroxide over a titanium-on-silica catalyst at 40-80 C and 1-10 bar, with the propylene chlorohydrin recycled as the phase-transfer catalyst. It makes no chloride, it is nearly quantitative, and it depends on a cheap supply of hydrogen peroxide - which in 1983 was the reason the anthraquinone peroxide plant and the propylene oxide plant sat next to each other in a few integrated sites.
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.note: The chlorohydrin-recycling hydrogen peroxide route was the commercially important one in the 1980s; the halide-free TSCA process came later.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: Chlorohydrin route
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: Propylene plus hypochlorous acid gives 1-chloro-2-propanol (about 90%) and 2-chloro-1-propanol (about 10%); the mixture is dehydrochlorinated with a lime or caustic slurry to propylene oxide and the chlorides are recycled as chlorine. The 10% isomer is the problem: it goes on to make propylene chlorohydrin and then the toxic 1,2-dichloropropane, so the plant had a dedicated caustic hydrolysis section for it.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1,2-dichloropropane
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The unwanted isomer stream, made when propylene chlorohydrin is treated with excess caustic. It is a solvent and a flame-retardant intermediate, and it is toxic to the liver and kidney. In the 1980s the industry reduced its production by selling propylene oxide as a propylene glycol monomethyl ether ether or by shifting to the hydrogen peroxide route, both of which avoid the chloride.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1-chloro-2-propanol
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The intermediate whose dehydrochlorination is propylene oxide. It is mildly toxic, it is the reason propylene oxide workers were exposed to a chlorinated alcohol, and it is the direct chemical relative of propylene chlorohydrin, the skin sensitiser that caused occupational dermatitis in the plastics industry before closed systems became normal.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.name: Polypropylene
chem.propylene.polymerisation.description: About 7 million tonnes of polypropylene in 1983, the fastest-growing major plastic. It needs a stereospecific catalyst to be anything but glue: isotactic polypropylene is crystalline and rigid, atactic is a sticky amorphous gum, syndiotactic is a curiosity in the 1980s. The 1980s advances were the high-yield supported catalyst and, on the way in, gas-phase and slurry-loop reactors.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.name: Slurry loop, gas phase and slurry reactor
chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.description: The 1980s reactor competition: the slurry loop (heptane diluent, polymer as a slurry, then solvent recovery and devolatilising), the loop slurry with 30-50% solids, and the gas-phase fluidised bed with no solvent at all. The gas-phase process was the 1980s newcomer and its whole commercial case was the elimination of the solvent recovery section.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.name: Stereospecific titanium catalyst
chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.description: Titanium trichloride or titanium tetrachloride on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl, refined in the 1970s and 1980s to give activities high enough that no catalyst removal was needed. The MgCl2-supported catalyst with an internal donor (a phthalate or a diether) was the technical development that made modern polypropylene economics work, and the diether donors were commercialised around 1980-83.
chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.note: The activity figures for late-1980s catalysts are order-of-magnitude and were rising quickly year to year.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 or TiCl3 on MgCl2 with AlEt3/AlEt2Cl, internal donor

chem.propylene.separation.name: Propylene purification
chem.propylene.separation.description: The propylene has to be at 99.5-99.9% with less than 10-20 ppm of carbonyl compounds, because propanal and acetone stop an ionic polymerisation dead. In 1980s practice the purified propylene was made by distillation plus an alkaline wash, and by the later 1980s by hydrazine or hydrazone treatment which converts the carbonyls into something removable.

chem.propylene.sources.name: Where propylene comes from
chem.propylene.sources.description: Three sources, in order of size in 1983: the steam cracker (roughly 40-45% of world propylene supply), catalytic cracking (roughly 30-35%), and dedicated processes. A naphtha cracker makes propylene at about 15% of its hydrocarbon product, so a cracker and a propylene splitter were bolted together in the 1960s to turn the whole C3 stream into pure propylene; by the 1980s the splitter had mostly been bypassed because the C3 could just be purified.

chem.propylene.sources.c5-isoprene.name: Isoprene from C5
chem.propylene.sources.c5-isoprene.description: The other half of the cracker C5 problem. Isoprene was isolated from the FCC C5 stream or synthesised from isobutylene and formaldehyde until synthetic isoprene replaced it in the 1980s. Natural rubber was never seriously displaced - isoprene's polymerisation gives cis-1,4-polyisoprene only with a stereospecific catalyst, and cis-1,4-polyisoprene is a poor substitute for the natural article.
chem.propylene.sources.c5-isoprene.note: Isoprene is not a C64 material; it is here because it shares the C5 stream and the same cracking chemistry.

chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.name: Depolymerisation of polypropylene
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.description: Reheated polypropylene was fed back to a reactor to recover the propylene it was made from. This was developed as a recycling route in the early 1970s when the word recycle meant something and it survived as a niche process for decades, mostly because the chemical plant could not discharge a plastic waste stream.
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.note: Reactor operation temperatures and the commercial fate of the process in the 1980s are not well documented; treat as a minor route.

chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.name: Propylene splitter (the older dedicated unit)
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.description: A dedicated thermal cracker that re-cracked propane and the cracker's propylene-rich C3 stream at 500-600 C to make more propylene, at 15-25% selectivity, with a big furnace and a bad energy balance. It was the standard propylene route of the 1960s, it was still running in 1983 in a few places, and it was generally obsolete by the mid-1980s because the selectivity was hopeless and the cracker had become the cheaper source.
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.note: Splitter conditions and selectivity vary; the key point is the low selectivity relative to modern routes.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.name: Cracker C3 stream
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.description: The propylene and propane that distil out of the cracker's quench separator. Naphtha crackers make roughly 0.15 t of propylene per tonne of feed, which on a 500,000 t/yr cracker is about 75,000 t/yr of propylene - more than a small polypropylene plant needs.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: C3 recovery and the propylene column
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: How the propylene actually leaves the cracker. The C3 and C4 streams are separated in a deethaniser, then the propane and propylene go to a propylene splitter column where the propylene is taken overhead. Before that column, the stream is caustic washed to remove the carbonyls and the oxygenates; in the 1980s this was an option rather than an obligation, and the plants that skipped it were the plants whose polymerisation catalyst was drinking acetone.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: The propylene splitter column
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A 50-70 tray column 50-70 m tall that separates the propylene overhead from the propane that has to be recycled back to the furnace. Propylene and propane have a relative volatility of about 1.1, so this is a distillation with a reflux ratio of 15-25 and a lot of energy; the 1980s development was a packed or tray hybrid with a side stripper and a low-pressure-drop design, because the column's cost is its energy consumption.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Chlor-alkali (brine electrolysis)
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: Salt water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 60-90 C and 3-4 V DC to give chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. It is the source of every chlorine molecule in this file - the PVC monomer, the epichlorohydrin, the chlorinated solvents, the hypochlorous acid of the propylene chlorohydrin, the phosgene of the polycarbonate, and the trichlorosilane precursor chain of the silicones - and the source of the caustic and the acid that made the phenol-formaldehyde and the ester plasticisers. It is the largest single tonnage of chemistry that a 1983 computer sits on top of, indirectly.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Brine (salt)
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A saturated sodium chloride solution, made from a salt mine or a solar evaporation pond, purified to remove calcium and magnesium because they foul the membrane and foul the diaphragm. Salt is the one raw material in this branch that is dug out of the ground rather than taken from a refinery, and it is the true end of the chlorine chain.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Membrane cell
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: The cell type that replaced the mercury cell through the 1980s: a perfluorosulfonate membrane separating the anode and cathode, giving chlorine at 99.5%+ without the mercury the older cell had to manage. The conversion of the world's chlor-alkali from mercury to membrane was one of the largest and fastest industrial changeovers of the decade, and it was driven by mercury emissions - the same environmental logic that removed mercury from the PVC acetylene process.
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.note: The membrane cell commercialised from the late 1970s and displaced mercury cells through the 1980s-90s; the timetable varied by region.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Caustic wash
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A 10-20% sodium hydroxide wash column that neutralises the acidic oxygenates - propanal, acetone, propionic acid, and the phenol and cresols from the C9+ - that the cracker makes. The spent caustic is a refinery effluent problem: it is a phenolic wastewater with a high chemical oxygen demand, and in the 1980s it was often incinerated on the site.

chem.ethylene.name: Ethylene: steam cracking and the polymers of it
chem.ethylene.description: Steam cracking naphtha at 800-900 C over cast alloy coils is the largest single chemical reaction in the world by tonnage. World ethylene capacity in 1983 was about 27-30 million tonnes a year, and roughly half of it went into polyethylene and the rest into ethylene oxide, styrene and solvents. Every polyethylene cable sheath, every styrene monomer and every polyester fibre in a C64 starts in a coiled coil furnace.

chem.ethylene.uses-c64.name: Where the C64's ethylene ends up
chem.ethylene.uses-c64.description: Concretely: the styrene monomer for the ABS case and the SAN matrix, the ethylene oxide route to ethylene glycol for anything polyester in the power supply, the polyethylene in the power cord's insulation and in the moulded cable accessories, and the C2 in the vinyl chloride monomer for the PVC jacket and for the keyboard's keycaps in the less common grades. A C64's ethylene demand is a few tens of grams.
chem.ethylene.uses-c64.note: This figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical material masses and is not a measured value.

facts.label: Ethylene per C64
facts.value: tens of grams of ethylene monomer

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.name: Polyethylene
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.description: The largest use of ethylene: about 12-14 million tonnes of polyethylene were made in 1983, split roughly between low-density (free radical, high pressure) and high-density (coordination catalysis, low pressure). The C64-scale uses are the power cord's insulation and jacket, the moulded cable accessories, and the keyboard membrane's insulation.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.name: Polyethylene additives
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.description: Antioxidants (hindered phenols such as BHT, and phosphites), stabilisers, and pigment. The antioxidant is the reason a polyethylene cable in a C64's power supply does not go brittle: a radical from the mains or from a metal ion attacks the chain and causes scission or cross-linking, and a phenol traps it.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.name: BHT (2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol)
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.description: The workhorse antioxidant, dosed at 0.05-0.2 wt%. It is made by alkylating para-cresol with isobutylene over a solid acid or an aluminium chloride catalyst, and it was also in the C64's power supply as a capacitor-filling fluid (as the antioxidant of the impregnant).

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.name: HDPE: coordination catalysis at low pressure
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.description: Ethylene at 20-60 bar and 150-260 C over a transition-metal catalyst gives linear polyethylene with almost no long-chain branching, so it crystallises tightly and has a density of 0.94-0.97. Because the polymer comes out of the reactor as a powder or a slurry rather than a melt, HDPE in 1983 was made in a slurry loop or a gas-phase fluidised bed and then converted by extrusion.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.metallocene.name: Metallocene catalysis (emerging)
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.metallocene.description: A single-site catalyst: one sandwich compound with a zirconium atom between two cyclopentadienyl rings, activated with methylaluminoxane. Discovered in the early 1980s (Kaminsky and Sinn, 1980), it was not yet an industrial process in 1983, but it was the obvious next step because it gives a narrow molecular weight distribution and predictable comonomer placement. The full industrial arrival of metallocene polyethylene was in the 1990s.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.name: Linear low density polyethylene
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.description: Copolymers of ethylene with a small amount of alpha-olefin - 1-butene or 1-octene - which gives a linear chain with short branches: low density with high stiffness. LLDPE was the fastest-growing polyethylene family of the 1980s (about 10-15% of PE production by 1983 and climbing), and the switch from 1-butene to 1-octene was a change in the crackers' product slate rather than in the polymer plant.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.note: The exact LLDPE share of 1983 is an estimate; growth in this period was rapid.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.gas-phas.name: Gas-phase polymerisation
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.gas-phas.description: Union Carbide's Unipoly process: ethylene polymerised as a gas in a fluidised bed at 20-30 bar and 70-100 C with the catalyst dispersed on a support. No diluent to recover, no slurry to centrifuge, and by the early 1980s it was the technology for new large plants - it is exactly the same fluidised-bed machinery the ethylene and polyethylene industries shared with the catalyst makers.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Ziegler-Natta polymerisation
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: Titanium tetrachloride or titanium dichloride with an aluminium alkyl (triethylaluminium or diethylaluminium chloride) at 50-100 bar and 50-80 C in a hydrocarbon diluent. Ziegler was the 1953 discovery that started the whole low-pressure polyethylene industry; by the 1960s it had become Ziegler-Natta by supporting the titanium on magnesium chloride, which gave the multiplicity of active sites and therefore the control of molecular weight distribution that made high-density pipe grades possible.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Triethylaluminium
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The cocatalyst. It alkylates the titanium and reduces Ti(IV) to Ti(III), and it scavenges the water and oxygen that would kill the catalyst. It is pyrophoric, and the 1980s industry response to that fact was the standard practice of diluting it to 5-10% in a hydrocarbon before it ever left the cylinder.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium-magnesium chloride catalyst
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: TiCl4 supported on finely divided MgCl2, activated with an aluminium alkyl. The MgCl2 support is the whole trick: it generates about a hundred active titanium sites per gram of catalyst with a range of stereospecificity, and that is what turned HDPE from a family of blends into a graded set of grades.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 on MgCl2, AlEt3 or AlEt2Cl cocatalyst

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium tetrachloride and the sponge route
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The titanium tetrachloride of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is made from titanium ore - rutile or ilmenite - by chlorinating it with coke and chlorine at 900-1,000 C, then distilling the TiCl4 out at 136 C. Titanium metal comes back by reducing the tetrachloride with magnesium (the Hunter process, which is the Kroll process in reverse) and distilling the magnesium chloride off. So the most important catalyst in the low-pressure polyethylene business is made in a plant that looks exactly like the zirconium and hafnium plants of the nuclear industry, because they all make volatile tetrachlorides.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Magnesium reduction to titanium sponge
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: TiCl4 plus magnesium at 800-900 C under argon in a sealed can, then vacuum distillation of the magnesium chloride at 1,000 C leaves a porous titanium sponge. The titanium sponge is then argon-melted and turned into the mill product. It is an expensive route to an element used in a catalyst at one per cent, which is why the catalyst industry never made the titanium - it bought the tetrachloride.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Carbochlorination of rutile
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: Rutile or ilmenite plus coke plus chlorine at 900-1,000 C gives TiCl4 with iron chloride and vanadium chloride impurities that have to be removed by distillation. The metallurgy is the reason a titanium-bearing sand exists at all: it is an oxide in a rock, and making a volatile chloride is the cheapest way to get a pure element out of an oxide. It is the same trick the silicon business uses in reverse, with methyl chloride instead of chlorine.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.phillips.name: Phillips chromium oxide process
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.phillips.description: Chromium oxide on silica at 20-40 bar and 150-200 C in a slurry (diluent) loop reactor. The Phillips process dates from 1952 and is the reason the 1980s plastics plant looked the way it did: the diluent recovery section was the biggest energy consumer on the site, and the catalyst was a supported chromium oxide whose active site nobody fully understood.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.name: LDPE: free-radical high-pressure process
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.description: Ethylene is polymerised at 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar in a jacketed or tubular reactor with a peroxide initiator, in the liquid phase (below about 280 C) or the gas phase (above it). The density of 0.91-0.93 comes entirely from chain branching: the very high pressure creates radicals on the growing chain, the chain folds, and the branches that stop it crystallising. In 1983 the process was mature to the point of being a cost exercise, and it still made most of the world polyethylene.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.autoclav.name: Autoclave versus tubular reactor
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.autoclav.description: The autoclave process (Union Carbide, 1930s) stirred the gas-phase reaction; the tubular process (Sons, 1950s) had plug flow with injection quills and much better temperature control. By the 1980s the tubular reactor was the standard large unit because it gave a narrower molecular weight distribution and better ethylene conversion, and because the autoclave's bulk polymer needed devolatilising.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.name: Peroxide initiator
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.description: Di-tert-butyl peroxide, or in the autoclave process a mixture of di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate. The initiator decomposes at temperature to give the two tert-butoxy radicals that start the chain, and the choice of half-life at operating temperature sets the run length.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.name: Ethylene glycol and the glycols
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.description: Monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and triethylene glycol, made by hydration of ethylene oxide in a 1:1 to 1:20 mole ratio of oxide to water, with the ratio chosen to steer the product distribution towards the wanted glycol. In 1980s practice monoethylene glycol was about half the output and went into polyester, antifreeze and diester coolant, and diethylene glycol went into antifreeze and into the unsaturated polyester resins of the same family as the C64's case resin.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-dis.name: Glycol finishing by vacuum distillation
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-dis.description: Water is removed in a multi-column vacuum system because the glycols boil at 197, 245 and 285 C and water outranks them everywhere; a set of vacuum columns at 30-100 mbar separates mono-, di- and triethylene glycol and recovers the unreacted oxide. This is one of the clearest cases in the whole tree where the separation, not the chemistry, is the expensive part.

facts.label: Boiling points
facts.value: MEG 197 C, DEG 245 C, TEG 285 C (1 atm)

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.direct-oxi.name: Direct oxidation-hydratation
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.direct-oxi.description: The Shell process, commercialised in 1965: ethylene, oxygen and water are converted in one step over a supported silver-phosphorus-tungsten catalyst, avoiding the separate oxide intermediate. It gives a higher MEG yield and less waste water but needs very pure oxygen and is harder to control; both routes were still running side by side in 1983.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.catalytic-.name: Catalytic hydration (the older process)
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.catalytic-.description: Ethylene oxide over phosphoric acid on silica at 200-220 C and 60-70 bar, with about 20% ethylene glycol recycled as diluent to suppress the ether side products. Selectivity to monoethylene glycol is 85-90%, and the whole plant's economics depend on keeping that selectivity, because the diethylene glycol and the dioxane by-product have to be sold at a discount.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.name: Ethylene oxide
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.description: The oxidation of ethylene over silver at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar, in which every eighth or tenth ethylene molecule is burned to carbon dioxide and water instead of being oxidised. It was about 1.5-2.5 million tonnes a year in 1983, most of it going to ethylene glycol for polyester and to surfactants, and it is one of the most hazardous large-scale chemical processes in existence.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.to-glycol.name: Ethylene oxide to ethylene glycol
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.to-glycol.description: One tonne of ethylene glycol needs about 3.5 tonnes of ethylene oxide at 100% selectivity. The world ethylene glycol capacity was around 4-5 million tonnes a year in 1983, and the big consumers were polyester fibre and film and polyethylene terephthalate.

facts.label: Ethylene oxide per tonne of glycol

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.name: Ethylene oxide safety
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.description: Ethylene oxide boils at 10.7 C, so it is a liquid only just below ambient and a gas in a warm tank; its flammable range in air is 3-80% by volume and its ignition energy is about 0.06 millijoule. It is acutely toxic, it polymerises without catalyst into a runaway, and it is kept in equilibrium by a trace of tertiary butyl alcohol or hydrochlorinated hydrocarbon inhibitor. In 1980s practice the industry standard was a fixed tank or a pressure vessel with an inert blanket, nitrogen purging and a quench section that could handle a deflagration.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.note: Flammability limits for ethylene oxide are commonly quoted as roughly 3-80% by volume; the flash point is about -20 C.
