chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Air-oxidation process (the industrial one)
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: Ethylene and air over silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina in a multi-tubular reactor at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar. Per-pass conversion is only 10-15% and the selectivity to ethylene oxide is 80-90%, so the unreacted ethylene is recycled with the inert diluent. The alternative process - the chlorohydrin route, ethylene plus hypochlorous acid to chloroethanol to oxide - was still running in the United States in the early 1980s but had been almost entirely displaced by air oxidation elsewhere.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Chlorohydrin route (superseded)
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: Ethylene chlorinated in water to ethylene chlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry to ethylene oxide. It was the original process and it made a chlorinated calcium salt waste for every tonne of product, which is why it did not survive outside the United States. It is the classic example of a process displaced not by yield but by waste.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.note: Chlorohydrin EO production was already minor by the early 1980s and was essentially gone by the mid-1980s in Europe and Japan.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Silver on alpha-alumina catalyst
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: 10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, promoted by chlorine. Silver is the only catalyst that works: it is the only metal that both activates oxygen and lets ethylene through, and the geometry matters as much as the chemistry, because the low surface area keeps the pore diameter small enough to suppress the combustion pathway. Catalyst life is 2-5 years and the silver is recovered at the end of it.

chem.ethylene.purification.name: Ethylene purification
chem.ethylene.purification.description: Before the ethylene can be polymerised it has to be dry and essentially free of oxygen and carbon dioxide, because both water and oxygen poison a radical or coordination polymerisation catalyst irreversibly. A cracker therefore had a molecular sieve drier taking water to under 1 ppm and a CO2/CO removal stage.

chem.ethylene.purification.oxygen-remova.name: Oxygen and CO2 removal
chem.ethylene.purification.oxygen-remova.description: Oxygen under 1 ppm and CO2 under 5 ppm, by an amine or a solid bed. CO2 is the dangerous one: it poisons the coordination catalysts and it reacts with the organoaluminium cocatalyst of a Ziegler-Natta polymerisation to give carbon dioxide polymers and aluminium alkoxides.

chem.ethylene.purification.drying.name: Molecular sieve drying
chem.ethylene.purification.drying.description: A 3A or 4A zeolite molecular sieve in beds switched in parallel, taking the water to below 1 ppmv. The zeolite is the same material family as the FCC catalyst and the styrene alkylation catalyst - a good illustration that one piece of chemistry (a synthetic zeolite) runs through the whole tree.

chem.ethylene.quench.name: Quenching and acetylene control
chem.ethylene.quench.description: The cracked gas leaves the coil at 800-900 C and has to come down to under 40 C in a second or two before anything can be separated, or the reactor metallurgy melts. The choice of quench is a real fork in the road: a gas quench to 350-400 C followed by selective hydrogenation, or a direct spray quench to under 40 C.

chem.ethylene.quench.decanter.name: Decanter and quench oil circuit
chem.ethylene.quench.decanter.description: The condensed liquid is settled and decanted, separating the heavy C9+ tar from the gasoline and C4 streams. The heavy fraction - about 5-10% of the cracker feed - was the benzene, toluene and xylenes rich C9+ cut in the 1980s, and it was the aromatics feed for the styrene plants and the solvent plants.

chem.ethylene.quench.spray-quench.name: Spray quench to under 40 C
chem.ethylene.quench.spray-quench.description: Liquid hydrocarbon or quench oil is sprayed straight into the cracked gas. It is simple and it is cheap and it puts the gas into the quench oil circuit immediately, but it cannot be combined with selective hydrogenation because the acetylene has already polymerised in the cooler. In 1980s practice a naphtha cracker could run either way; the gas quench became standard on the big units where acetylene had to be controlled.

chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.name: Gas quench to 350-400 C
chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.description: The cracked gas is quenched with recycled process gas rather than directly with liquid, stopping at 350-400 C. This keeps the gas hot enough that the acetylene survives, so the acetylene can be destroyed deliberately afterwards in a selective hydrogenation reactor (palladium on alumina at 130-180 C, 10-30 bar hydrogen) rather than being allowed to polymerise into gums in the cooler. Ethylene purity of 99.9%+ with acetylene under 5 ppm is the target.

chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.selectiv.name: Acetylene selective hydrogenation
chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.selectiv.description: Pd on alumina at 130-180 C and 10-30 bar of hydrogen converts acetylene to ethylene (and some to ethane) with high selectivity. It is the standard ethylene finishing step of the 1980s and it is why palladium was one of the few precious metals in a cracker: the catalyst was typically a few tonnes of 0.5-2% Pd, and the hydrogen partial pressure had to be controlled tightly because too much hydrogen makes ethane and costs ethylene yield.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.name: Steam cracking
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.description: A hydrocarbon feed mixed with steam is brought to 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second in a serpentine coil inside a radiant furnace, at 1-3 bar. The chemistry is brutal free-radical chain cracking: the large molecules fall apart into smaller ones and a large hydrogen-rich tail gas. What decides the plant is how fast the coil can be taken to temperature without coking it, and how fast it can be cooled again.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.expander.name: Cracked-gas expander turbine
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.expander.description: The cracked gas at 800-900 C is not simply cooled; in the 1980s it was let down through a turboexpander that recovered most of the sensible heat as work, doing the job of the quench exchanger. The expander recovered 10-20% of the cracking energy and was one of the reasons the energy crisis of the 1970s produced a generation of much more efficient crackers.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.name: Coke and decoking
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.description: Coke builds up on the coil, which insulates it, raises the skin temperature and finally blocks the tube. 1980s practice was to shut the furnace and decoke in place by burning the coke out with steam and air (off-line decoking), taking several hours and costing several thousand dollars a cycle; a shift to shorter, more frequent on-line decokes came later with the high-performance coils. The coke itself is a fine, hard, low-metal material that has to be disposed of.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.name: Cracker coke
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.description: A granular, high-carbon, low-hydrogen solid with vanadium and nickel that came out of the feed. It is a nuisance rather than a product in the 1980s - the FCC coke market was far bigger and the cracker coke was dirty - and a large cracker made a few hundred to a few thousand tonnes a year of it.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.steam-dilut.name: Steam dilution and coke suppression
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.steam-dilut.description: Steam does two jobs: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so radical recombination makes smaller molecules rather than carbon, and it is the heat carrier. Naphtha crackers of the 1980s ran 200-400 mol% steam per mole of hydrocarbon, and the hydrocarbon partial pressure at the coil outlet was 0.3-0.8 bar. The trade is explicit: more steam means less coke and less ethylene, less steam means more coking and a shorter cycle.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.name: Ceramic (CHA) coil coating
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.description: Cracking alumina or silicon carbide coated onto the coil inside the furnace. The industry spent the 1970s and early 1980s trying to reduce coil metal temperature by 50-100 C; silicon carbide coatings (the CHA process, from Combustion Heat Exchanger) were the commercially successful route and let a furnace run hotter for the same metal temperature, which is worth several percent of ethylene yield.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.note: Coating technologies and their names vary by licensor; the general point - coatings lower the metal skin temperature - is solid.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.name: Cracker coil metallurgy
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.description: The coil is cast alloy, not steel: 25Cr-35Ni (Incoloy 800, 800H, 802) or the HP-modified 35Cr-45Ni alloys of the 1980s. The radiant fire gas is oxidising and its metal skin runs 30-50 C above the process temperature, so at 850 C process the skin is 880-900 C; a carbon steel coil crept and failed. Incoloy 800 became the industry standard, and its nickel content is one reason a cracker is so expensive.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.note: Coil alloy compositions vary between licensors (Sons, Lummus, Mitsubishi, Linde) and the alloy detail is a metals-chain item; what matters here is that it is a cast high-nickel alloy bought in tonnes.

facts.label: Tube size
facts.value: 4 in (100-114 mm) OD, 4-6 mm wall, cast

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.name: Cracker furnace and radiant section
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.description: A refractory-lined box 20-40 m long with 40-80 coiled coils hung side by side, each coil 30-80 m of 4 in (100 mm) cast tube in ten passes of 10-20 m. The fire is gas- or oil-fired at 30-50 MW per furnace, and the radiant duty is the whole point: roughly 70% of the process heat has to arrive by radiation because convection through the gas is too slow to get the coil to 850 C in half a second.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.name: Cracker feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.description: Naphtha was 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983, ethane and propane 20-30%. The choice is regional and historical: US Gulf crackers run on ethane piped from the Gulf's gas fields because the ethane price under a gas contract made it unbeatable; European and Japanese crackers run on naphtha because they had no ethane to hand. A naphtha cracker is the one that makes propylene and butadiene as well as ethylene, which is why the older chemical industry grew up on it.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.name: Gas oil feedstock (the third choice)
chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.description: The heavier option, chosen when naphtha and gas oil were both dear: a 300-700 F cut cracked harder to get ethylene, coking heavily, and yielding the most propylene of the three. Gas oil cracking existed in the Middle East and in Japan through the 1970s and mostly disappeared in the 1980s because its cost per tonne of ethylene was the worst of the three.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.name: Ethane feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.description: Ethane cracks cleanly with little coke and needs almost no steam dilution, so an ethane cracker is cheaper to run and its ethylene yield (50-55%) is much higher. But it makes almost no propylene and no butadiene, so a pure ethane cracker has to buy its co-products. The 1980s US Gulf argument about ethane versus naphtha was really an argument about whether propylene and butadiene were worth more than the extra ethylene.

chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.name: Ethane and propane (LPG)
chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.description: The C2 and C3 that make natural gas liquids, recovered as LPG at 1.5-8 bar in the field and as a debottlenecking liquid at the gas plant, then split for heating or fed to a cracker. LPG was the preferred cracker feedstock precisely because it is already light and needs no naphtha handling.

chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.name: Propane as cracker feed
chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.description: A dedicated propane cracker needs far less steam dilution (20-40 mol% versus 200-400 mol% for naphtha) and so makes far less process gas per tonne of ethylene, but it makes relatively little co-product: the propylene and butenes streams shrink and the C4 stream effectively disappears. That single trade-off has moved cracker economics for forty years.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.name: Naphtha feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.description: A C5 to 200-220 F hydrocarbon cut, hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% sulphur and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen. Beyond its hydrocarbon content what matters is the coniocarbon and the asphaltene content: those are what coke the coil. The naphtha from an Arabian light crude is comparatively clean, which is one reason Gulf crackers could run at a lower steam dilution than a naphtha cracker fed with heavy California naphtha.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.note: The refinery side of this handover is chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha-to-ethylene.

chem.ethylene.scale.name: The ethylene industry in 1983
chem.ethylene.scale.description: About 27-30 Mt/yr of world ethylene capacity in 1983, of which the United States held roughly 19 Mt (about two thirds) and Western Europe about 8 Mt, with the Gulf Coast of the US, the Rhine-Ruhr, Antwerp, the Suez Gulf and the Japanese and Korean coasts as the clusters. A 1980s cracker cost $150-400 million and took three to five years to build.
chem.ethylene.scale.note: Capacity and cost figures for this period are approximate; cracker capital costs roughly doubled between 1978 and 1981.

chem.refining.name: Refining: turning crude into fuels and feedstocks
chem.refining.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation to cut crude into fractions, then conversion and upgrading processes to make the specific products industry wants. For the C64 the interesting products are not the fuels but the naphtha that gets steam-cracked to ethylene, the benzene for styrene, the LPG for crackers, and the elemental sulphur recovered from hydrogen sulphide. In 1983 world refining capacity was roughly 65-70 million barrels a day, about 30% above demand, and the industry was running at 65-75% utilisation.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.name: Refinery to polymer: the handover
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.description: Three handovers matter. Naphtha plus steam into a cracker gives ethylene and propylene. C4 from the same cracker gives butadiene and isobutylene. Reformer naphtha into the aromatics complex gives benzene, which with ethylene gives styrene. This node is the place where the fuel industry stops and the polymer industry starts, and it is the join that makes a C64 physically possible.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.benzene.name: Benzene to styrene
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.benzene.description: Benzene from the aromatics complex is alkylated with ethylene in the presence of excess benzene (to suppress diethylbenzene) to give ethylbenzene, which is dehydrogenated. Both steps are the styrene branch.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.c4-to-b.name: C4 to butadiene
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.c4-to-b.description: The cracker produces a C4 stream of 1-butene, cis- and trans-2-butene and isobutylene; extracting the butadiene out of it is a second plant (see chem.butadiene.sounsby). The isobutylene left behind goes to MTBE or alkylate; the 1- and 2-butenes left behind go to butene hydroformylation for plasticisers, or are put back into the cracker.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.name: Naphtha to ethylene
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.description: The handover. Naphtha plus steam at 800-900 C over a cast alloy coil, giving 25-35% ethylene by weight with propylene, butenes and a benzene-rich C9+ residue. Roughly 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983 was naphtha-based, with the rest ethane and propane; the Gulf Coast and the Far East were naphtha and the Texas Gulf was liquid-fuelled ethane.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.name: Steam dilution and coke suppression
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.description: Steam does two jobs in the cracker: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so the cracking goes towards smaller molecules and away from carbon, and it carries heat into the coil. Naphtha crackers of the 1980s ran 200-400 mol% steam per mole of hydrocarbon, and the coil deposited coke at 0.05-0.2 wt% of the feed before it had to be decoked.
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.note: Steam dilution ratios in the literature range from about 100:1 molar for some designs to several hundred; ethane crackers used much less.

chem.refining.products.name: Refinery products and by-products
chem.refining.products.description: Fuels, lubricants, waxes, coke and sulphur. For this tree the interesting list is short: naphtha to the crackers, benzene to styrene, LPG to crackers, propylene and butylene to the older chemical plants, and sulphur to rubber and to sulphuric acid.

chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.name: Fuel oil
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.description: The bottom of the barrel: a 1-3% sulphur residue sold to power stations and ships. After 1973, and especially after the 1980s tanker accidents, the political life of fuel oil in Europe and the US got hard, and the refinery's answer was more conversion. In 1983 fuel oil still took about 25-30% of world refinery production.
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.note: The fuel-oil share of 1983 refinery output and the regulatory context are order-of-magnitude figures; exact shares varied widely by region.

chem.refining.products.waxes.name: Petroleum waxes and slack wax
chem.refining.products.waxes.description: Waxy distillate from solvent deasphalting, deoiled on a centrifuge train to give hard, medium and soft paraffin wax and microcrystalline wax. Slack wax goes into paper, board and packaging film; the microcrystalline waxes are the petroleum fraction that was blended into the first generation of hot-melt adhesives.

chem.refining.products.lubricants.name: Lubricant base oils
chem.refining.products.lubricants.description: Distillate fractions solvent-extracted (2,700-5,000 Ns at 100 C) and hydrofinished, or in the 1980s increasingly hydroisomerised. The C64 link is not the lubricant in the gearbox but the fact that the same hydrofinishing catalysts and the same additive chemistry (zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, made from phosphorus pentasulphide) appear in the machine's grease and in the rubber and plastic stabilisers.
chem.refining.products.lubricants.note: The C64-scale claims here are inferential; the base-oil processes described are standard but the specific link to a 1983 consumer machine's lubricants is not documented in the sources used here.

chem.refining.octane.name: Lead phase-down and the unleaded problem
chem.refining.octane.description: Tetraethyl lead was phased out of most industrialised markets between 1978 and 1985 as catalytic converters spread. The lead phase-down is the single most consequential fuel specification change of the decade and it is the reason MTBE, alkylate, isomerate and the ZSM-5 additive were all developed on that timescale.

chem.refining.octane.unleaded-blending.name: Unleaded blending and the octane shortfall
chem.refining.octane.unleaded-blending.description: Without lead the refiner needed 3-8 octane numbers from somewhere. In 1983 the US was short and the industry solved it with MTBE, ZSM-5 and alkylate; Europe, with the smaller and cleaner European car fleet, was much less short, which is why MTBE uptake was overwhelmingly American.

chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.name: Tetraethyl lead
chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.description: Pb(C2H5)4 blended at a few grams per litre, discovered in 1921 and the cheapest octane technology for fifty years. It was the cheapest route to octane and the most expensive in externalities: it destroyed the lead and phosphorus catalysts that were the whole point of the catalytic converter. Teledyne and DuPont stopped adding it to road fuel in most markets by 1985.

chem.refining.isomerisation.name: Isomerisation and octane boosting
chem.refining.isomerisation.description: The C5 and C6 straight-chain paraffins in naphtha have terrible octane numbers; isomerising them to the branched isomers does something about that with almost no yield loss. This is the cheap half of the unleaded-gasoline story; MTBE and alkylate were the expensive half.

chem.refining.isomerisation.alkylate.name: Alkylate (isooctane by HF alkylation)
chem.refining.isomerisation.alkylate.description: Isobutane plus isobutylene or propylene over anhydrous HF at 20-40 C, or over solid acid, giving the premium aviation and premium gasoline blending component. HF alkylation was a large and dangerous business in 1980s practice: a cloud of HF is dense, water-soluble and causes deep burns, so alkylation units had their own HF storage and a dedicated water curtain.

chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.name: MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether)
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.description: Methanol plus isobutylene over an acidic ion-exchange resin (Amberlyst, sulphonic acid polystyrene, about 100 C, 5-10 bar), giving a 100+ octane component. MTBE was the big gasoline technology story of the late 1970s and early 1980s in the United States, and its feedstock - isobutylene - came from the crackers and the FCC, which is the direct petrochemical link: the same C4 that becomes butadiene rubber becomes the octane booster in American petrol.

chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.name: Ion-exchange resin catalyst
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.description: A macroporous or gel-type sulphonic-acid polystyrene resin, the same chemistry as the ion exchange resins used in water treatment. MTBE resins had to be replaced every 10,000-20,000 hours in the 1980s as they aged.

chem.refining.isomerisation.c5-c6.name: C5/C6 isomerisation
chem.refining.isomerisation.c5-c6.description: 300-180 C over platinum on chlorided alumina (a 1960s process) or, from 1980s, a zeolite (molecular sieve) isomerisation unit running at 250-350 C with an aromatics-rich recycle. Yield was 98-99% and the octane gain about 8-12 numbers, which sounds trivial until it is multiplied by a million barrels a day.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.name: Catalytic reforming and the aromatics complex
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.description: Reforming naphtha over platinum at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar converts paraffins and naphthenes into aromatics, releasing about 0.2-0.3 tonnes of hydrogen per tonne of feed and upgrading the octane number. It is where the world's benzene comes from, and therefore where the styrene in the C64's ABS comes from.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.name: Spent catalyst and platinum recovery
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.description: Deactivated catalyst is shipped out and the platinum, rhenium and gallium recovered by chlorination, aqua regia dissolution and solvent extraction. This closed loop was one of the better examples of industrial metal recycling in the 1980s and it is also where the refinery's radioactive coke (from the feed's radium) had to be disposed of.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.aromat.name: Aromatics complex (benzene, toluene, xylene)
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.aromat.description: The benzene plant: extract the C6 aromatics from the reformer effluent, separate benzene, toluene and the C8 isomers, and hydrogenate the xylenes back to benzene because a tonne of xylene is worth less than a tonne of benzene. Around 1983 the benzene yield from a reformer run for octane was only 2-5% of the feed, so a refinery that wanted aromatics ran a dedicated naphtha aromatics complex in parallel with its octane unit.

facts.label: Benzene in reformer feed
facts.value: 2-5% of naphtha when run for octane, up to ~50% when run for aromatics

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.name: Platinum-rhenium on chlorided alumina
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.description: Platinum crystallites of about 1 nm on gamma-alumina promoted with chlorine to keep the metal and the acid function in balance. Platinum is one of the most expensive catalysts in the plant, so catalyst regeneration and platinum recovery are real economics: the platinum in a 1980s reformer was worth tens of thousands of dollars, and the catalyst was shipped off site for reclamation.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platfo.name: Platforming (UOP, 1943)
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platfo.description: The process that made the aromatised gasoline era possible: naphtha (C5 to about 220 C) over 0.3-0.4 wt% platinum and rhenium on chlorided alumina, at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 5-6. Rhenium was the key 1970s development: it let the platinum loading drop and the operating severity rise, so a unit could make 100-120 octane unleaded without coke trouble.

chem.refining.claus.name: Claus process: recovering elemental sulphur
chem.refining.claus.description: Three-quarters of a mole of oxygen is used to burn a third of the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur dioxide, then the two react over an alumina catalyst to make sulphur and water: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. The Claus unit turns the refinery's or gas plant's worst stream into a saleable commodity, and its output is the elemental sulphur that the whole 1980s chemical industry - rubber vulcanisation, fungicides, sulphuric acid - depended on. The Canadian oil sands' sulphur problem and the Arabian gas sweetening builds both exist because of this unit.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.name: Claus catalyst (activated alumina)
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.description: High-surface-area alumina, sometimes promoted with titanium, in two or three fixed beds at 200-350 C with interstage reheating. Because the reaction is exothermic and reversible, a multi-bed converter with controlled quench keeps the equilibrium favourable; a single-bed converter cannot get above about 80% overall recovery.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.name: Claus alumina catalyst and its support
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.description: The catalyst is not a mystery material: it is activated alumina, and the alumina is refined from bauxite. A Claus unit's catalyst life is measured in years and its loss rate is what sets the unit's sulphur recovery, so a good 1980s unit used a promoted, high-surface-area alumina with a shape (extrudate or cylindrical) chosen to hold surface area at 300-400 C.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.name: Bayer process
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.description: Bauxite digested in hot caustic soda at 150-250 C and 3-5 MPa, the alumina dissolved as sodium aluminate, the iron and silicon left behind as a red mud, and the alumina precipitated as aluminium hydroxide and calcined at 1,000-1,200 C to give the alumina. The caustic is recovered, the water is recycled, and the red mud is a waste stream of 1-2 tonnes per tonne of alumina - the well-known environmental problem of the alumina industry. The Claus unit's catalyst is the last stage of this process, run by a completely different industry.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.name: Bauxite
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.description: An aluminium oxide hydroxide rock, 30-60% Al2O3, which is the only ore worth mining for aluminium. The Claus catalyst is therefore a dig-it-out node too, just a different one from the oil and the sand: a bauxite mine in Guinea or Australia, or a later low-grade Australian deposit, feeds a refinery's sulphur recovery.

chem.refining.claus.furnace.name: Claus furnace
chem.refining.claus.furnace.description: A refractory-lined furnace at 250-400 C where a third of the H2S is burned with oxygen or air. The burn has to be kept on the rich side: too much oxygen and the H2S is oxidised all the way to SO2, which wastes the sulphur; too little and soot forms and plugs the catalyst.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.name: Hydrotreating and desulphurisation
chem.refining.hydrotreating.description: The refinery's chemistry of taking things out: sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals, plus saturation. It is the answer to sour crude, and it is the process that made Arab Light and Mexican crudes usable in 1980s refineries. It also produces the acid gas from which elemental sulphur is recovered.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.name: Acid gas to the Claus unit
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.description: Every hydrotreater and every amine unit makes an acid gas of mostly H2S with some CO2. In 1983 that stream was worth real money: recovering its sulphur turns a disposal liability into a product, and about 80-90% of world sulphur production was elemental sulphur recovered this way.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.ami.name: Amine scrubbing of the acid gas
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.ami.description: A 20-35 wt% MEA or DEA absorber removes H2S and CO2 from the hydrogen recycle gas, and the rich amine is stripped in a 120-130 C reboiler. The amine itself is degraded by the oxygen in the gas and by hydrocarbons, and the resulting amine/oil/water effluent was one of the refinery's worst waste streams in 1980s practice.
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.ami.note: Same amine chemistry as the gas sweetening plant: chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.sweetening.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.kero-hdt.name: Jet kero hydrotreating
chem.refining.hydrotreating.kero-hdt.description: Aviation turbine fuel must be under 3 wt% sulphur (later 0.3-0.5 wt%), free of water, and made to a smoke point and a thermal stability specification, because the fuel goes through a turbine at 800-1,000 C with water condensing in the fuel-oil nozzles. The kero hydrotreater is a 300-400 C, 30-50 bar hydrogen unit with a naphthenic acid problem of its own.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.diesel-hdt.name: Diesel hydrodesulphurisation
chem.refining.hydrotreating.diesel-hdt.description: 300-400 C and 30-80 bar hydrogen over Co-Mo/Ni-Mo to take the sulphur in the gas oil down to 0.1-0.3 wt%, with a 0.05 wt% deep-desulphurisation variant developed in the late 1970s for the emerging 1990s fuel specifications. In 1983 the pressure on refineries to build these units was rising because of the US 1990 diesel sulphur rules and Europe's equivalent, and because every barrel desulphurised is a barrel of fuel oil turned into saleable middle distillate.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.naphtha-hdt.name: Naphtha hydrodesulphurisation
chem.refining.hydrotreating.naphtha-hdt.description: 300-400 C, 20-50 bar hydrogen, cobalt-molybdenum on alumina, to 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur. This is the pretreatment that makes a crude usable in a cracker; see the naphtha node under the fractionating tower.

chem.refining.vacuum-residue-processing.name: Converting the vacuum residue
chem.refining.vacuum-residue-processing.description: The 2-5% of crude that will not distil is the hardest material in the refinery. It must be converted - into coke, into gasoline, or into distillate - or it is sold as fuel oil. This is where the refinery's biggest single units and its biggest capital decisions sit.

chem.refining.hydrocracking.name: Hydrocracking
chem.refining.hydrocracking.description: A fixed or trickle-bed catalytic process at 350-450 C and 80-200 bar of hydrogen that cracks heavy oils and hydrogenates the fragments in one step, giving 70-90% diesel yield with almost no sulphur. By the early 1980s hydrocracking had been converted from coal-liquefaction-derived catalysts to the cobalt-molybdenum and nickel-molybdenum on alumina and silica-alumina form, and it was the process that allowed a refinery to make diesel rather than fuel oil.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.name: Fluid catalytic cracking
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.description: Vacuum gas oil is contacted with a zeolite catalyst at 500-530 C and 1-3 bar in a riser, cracked into gasoline, light ends and coke, and the catalyst is continuously regenerated in a fluidised-bed regenerator at 650-750 C. FCC was the largest refinery process by capacity in the early 1980s - a large unit processing 40,000-100,000 bbl/d - and the source of most of the world's leaded-free gasoline blending components and of the propylene that fed the older chemical crackers.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.name: Cracked gasoline and the propylene route
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.description: FCC gasoline is high in olefins, aromatics and isoparaffins, with an octane number well above the reformer's, and it is the blending component that let the industry drop lead. Its propylene stream - 2-4% of FCC feed - fed the old chemical industry: by 1983 propylene from FCC and from crackers together supplied roughly half the world's propylene, and the older propylene splitter process existed precisely to make more of it.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: FCC zeolite catalyst
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite (USY, made by dealuminating Y zeolite) dispersed in a silica-alumina or silica matrix, rare-earth exchanged by lanthanum and neodymium. The zeolite gives shape-selective acid sites; the matrix gives attrition resistance and heat capacity. This is the same family of materials as the zeolites that would crack naphtha for styrene a decade later.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Making the FCC zeolite
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite is not mined; it is crystallised. The reagents are an alumina source, a silica source, an alkali and a template, and the product is a 3-5 micron crystal of a lattice so regular that it was named after the mineral zeolite. The FCC catalyst's lattice is what makes it a shape-selective acid, and the same recipe with a different template and a different silica-to-alumina ratio gives the MFI zeolite of the styrene alkylation and the 3A sieve of the cracker drier. One family of chemistry, four jobs, and about a tenth of a tonne of catalyst per year for every 10,000 bbl/d of FCC capacity.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Hydrothermal crystallisation and the dealuminated Y
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: The Y zeolite is grown from an aluminosilicate gel at 100-200 C with a seed, and then dealuminated to raise its silica-to-alumina ratio - by acid leaching, by chlorination with HCl or ammonium persulphate, or thermally with steam. Dealumination is what turns the dealer's USY into the ultrastable Y that became the standard cracking component, and it is also the step that makes the zeolite's acid site density lower and its selectivity higher. The dealumination agents are, note, the same mineral and base chemistry as the wet bench: hydrochloric acid and ammonium hydroxide.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Dealumination silica-to-alumina ratios vary by process and product; the values are representative of the era's USY.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Catalyst additives and contaminant tolerance
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: Vanadium and nickel in the feed deposit as mobile vanadates and nickels that destroy zeolite acid sites and accelerate dehydrogenation, so passivation additives (aluminium monohydride slurry, antimony compounds) were standard by the 1980s. Gasoline desulphurisation additives appeared later, at the end of the decade.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: ZSM-5 octane additive
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A small-pore zeolite (mordenite framework, 10-membered rings) blended at 3-15% into the USY catalyst to crack the C7-C10 straight chains that were killing octane after the lead phase-down. This is the direct ancestor of the propylene and isobutylene it also made: ZSM-5 selectively shapes the products towards C3 and C4 olefins.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Silica-alumina matrix
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: Amorphous silica-alumina, precipitated from sodium silicate and aluminium sulphate and caustic-gelled, then spray dried as 40-90 micron microspheres. The matrix is what gives the catalyst its attrition resistance and its heat capacity; it also carries a good part of the cracking, because the matrix surface area is large and the zeolite is expensive.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.r.name: Riser and regenerator
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.r.description: The riser reactor is a vertical pipe 10-20 m long with the catalyst and feed entering at the bottom; the cyclone separators strip entrained catalyst back; the regenerator burns the coke off the catalyst with air. A 1980s unit's two-stage regeneration was the standard answer to how to get more heat into the reactor while cutting carbon monoxide from the stack.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.name: Delayed coking
chem.refining.delayed-coking.description: Vacuum residue is heated to 350-400 C and held in large coke drums for 12-24 hours, during which it cracks to 15-25% petroleum coke while the vapours are continuously drawn off and fractionated. Delayed coking was the dominant residue conversion process of the 1960s and remained so through the 1980s, handling maybe 40-50% of vacuum residue in a complex refinery, largely because it makes the anode-grade coke the aluminium industry needs.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.name: Green coke
chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.description: The unreformed coke straight out of the drum: 85-92 wt% carbon, 8-15% volatiles, with all the feed's sulphur and metals still in it. Green coke is the intermediate between the coker drum and the calciner, and it is also what the plastics industry noticed in the 1980s: green coke is a needle-coke precursor, and it is the reason carbon fibre of aerospace grade became possible after the large-scale-carbon-fibre work of the late 1960s.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.name: Calcined petroleum coke
chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.description: Green coke is calcined at 1,250-1,350 C in a rotary kiln or a fluid-bed calciner to make calcined coke for carbon anodes. Needle coke, with low sulphur, low metals and low volatile matter, is the anode grade; sponge coke is the fuel grade. The aluminium smelting industry consumes a few million tonnes a year of anode coke, which is the economic reason delayed coking survived the fuel-oil era.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.name: The anode plant that consumes the coke
chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.description: The reason a refinery bothered with delayed coking at all: an aluminium smelter's carbon anode is made from calcined petroleum coke, petroleum coke pitch and a petroleum coke binder, and the anode plant is a 200,000 tonne a year market for a product that is otherwise a waste. Green coke is crushed, blended with calcined coke and pitch, extruded at 100-140 C, and baked at 1,000-1,100 C for hours in a ring furnace. The whole coking complex - the delayed coker, the calciner, the coke handling and the anode plant - is one market chain with one customer.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.name: Green anode and the ring furnace
chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.description: Anodes are baked at 1,000-1,100 C for up to 30 hours in a ring or shaft furnace on a car of green anode, under a forced hydrocarbon flame. The carbon comes out as calcined coke; the volatiles come out as a burner gas that heats the calciner. It is a carbon plant, not an aluminium plant, until the anode is dropped into the pot.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.name: Coke sulphur and metals specification
chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-co.description: Anode coke must be under about 1.5-2 wt% sulphur, because sulphur burns off during electrolysis and eats the carbon lining and the anode plant. Vanadium, at over 200-300 ppm, is worse still because vanadium carbide is abrasive on the anode. A sour crude therefore yields fuel-grade coke while a light sweet crude yields anode coke - which is why the biggest cokers stand next to the biggest sweet crude streams.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.coke-drum.name: Coke drum
chem.refining.delayed-coking.coke-drum.description: A 6-11 m diameter vessel 20-35 m tall holding 100-400 tonnes of coke per cycle, switched in parallel with a fractionator overhead. Switching a drum is the highest-risk operation in a refinery: the drum is water-quenched and de-coked with a full-diameter drill and coke cutter while the neighbouring drum runs at temperature.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.name: Atmospheric distillation
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.description: Fractional distillation of crude at atmospheric pressure in a 35-50 m fractionating tower, separating a barrel of crude into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, and a 700 F residue. It is the first process every molecule of the polymer industry passes through, and it is where the difference between a 30 and a 40 degree API crude turns into a 200 versus 260 dollar a tonne cracker feedstock.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.name: Vacuum distillation
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.description: A second column at 25-50 mmHg absolute (740-760 mmHg vacuum) that distils the 700 F plus residue down to a vacuum gas oil and a vacuum residue of 2-5% of the crude, without cracking it. Lowering the pressure raises the boiling points' relative spacing so heavy molecules can be distilled instead of decomposed, and the vacuum is made by steam ejectors or by a barometric leg.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.name: Flash zone and thermal cracking side reactions
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.description: Below about 350 C the residue starts to crack rather than distil, so the vacuum column flash zone runs at 340-370 C and the vacuum gas oil contains some cracked material. Side reactions make coke and acids, which is why vacuum columns need wash sections, anti-fouling coatings and a coke limit in the feed.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.name: Steam ejectors and vacuum
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.description: Three-stage steam ejectors holding 25-50 mmHg, using 10-25 t of steam per hour for a mid-size unit. Ejectors are simple but they cost a lot of steam; by the 1980s mechanical vacuum pumps (rotary or liquid-ring, with a surface condenser) were being installed to save that steam, and most plants still had ejectors as backup.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Overhead corrosion control
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: The naphtha overhead is where refinery corrosion happens: water condenses out of the vapour, dissolves HCl from the brine that came with the crude, and dissolves H2S to make very aggressive sulphuric acid. By 1980s practice this was attacked with an overhead neutraliser - ammonia or an amine - injected to the overhead condenser plus a wash-water draw, and with alloy upgrade in the worst services. The naphthenic acids in Arabian crudes added a second, hot-side corrosion problem in the vacuum column.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.note: Total acid number values are crude-specific and the threshold for accelerated attack is generally quoted as above about 2 mg KOH/g at the column temperature.

facts.label: Typical naphthenic acid index
facts.value: 1-3 mg KOH/g for Arabian heavy crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Fractionating tower
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: A 35-50 m column with 40-50 trays, at about 1.1-1.5 bar overhead and 2.5-3 bar at the bottom, condensing a vapour-liquid staircase in which each tray separates hydrocarbons by boiling range. A large atmospheric tower is a pressure vessel of 100-200 tonnes, and it is still the cheapest separation device ever built per tonne of product.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Naphtha hydrotreating before the cracker
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The cracker feedstock was almost never straight-run naphtha. It was hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% total sulphur (often 0.05-0.3 wt%) and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen, because sulphur poisons the reforming and cracking catalysts and nitrogen poisons the polymerisation catalysts downstream. Naphtha hydrotreating is the first place refinery chemistry meets polymer chemistry.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Sour water stripper
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The hydrogenating reactors make water and ammonia, and the separator water carries dissolved H2S and NH3. A stripper removes them, otherwise the recycled hydrogen carries ammonia into the cracker, where ammonia poisons the polymerisation catalysts and shows up as a colour defect in the polymer.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cobalt-molybdenum / nickel-molybdenum catalyst
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: Sulphided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo on alumina in a fixed bed at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar hydrogen, with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 200-1,000. Lumping several reactors in series gave 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur naphtha; a naphtha cracker in 1980s practice wanted 0.5 wt% S or less.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cut points and the product slate
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The fractions a refinery aims for, by boiling range: naphtha (C5 to about 200 F end point, roughly 30-40% of crude), kerosene/jet (200-300 F, 8-15%), gas oil (300-700 F, 20-30%), and the atmospheric residue (700 F plus, 25-40%). Naphtha is the fraction that matters to this tree: it is the steam-cracker feedstock, and its exact end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker will run at 800 or 850 C.

facts.label: Naphtha
facts.value: C5 / 33 C to 200-220 F end point; 30-40 vol% of crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Overhead condenser and gas recovery
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The naphtha overhead is condensed in a shell-and-tube condenser with a reflux drum, and the non-condensable gas (methane, ethane, hydrogen, H2S) goes off to the fuel gas header. In 1980s practice the gas was usually simply burned, although the recovery unit for ethane and propane (an absorber) was standard in complex refineries because it paid for itself.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Off-gas recovery unit
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: An absorber (propane) or a deethaniser-absorber column recovers 60-90% of the ethane and propane from the fuel gas before it is burnt. The recovered propane and butane become LPG, the same stream that feeds the crackers in the ethylene branch.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Reboilers and side strippers
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: A fired or steam reboiler supplies the vapour to the bottom of the tower, and side strippers remove the light ends from the kerosene and gas-oil draws so the side columns are not loaded with vapour. Kerosene is stripped with a few hundred kPa of steam; diesel often went straight to the bottom because the vacuum column handled its light ends.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Tray efficiency and reflux
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: A modern valve tray is 70-90% efficient against an ideal stage, and the tower needs enough reflux (a few percent of the feed, recirculated as a liquid stream) to wet the trays. Cutting reflux to save furnace duty is the classic operating trade, and it costs separation; the 1970s energy crisis pushed the industry toward heat integration and then toward better internals instead of more energy.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Distillation trays
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: Valve, sieve, bubble-cap or proprietary proprietary-type trays at 0.4-0.6 m spacing. In 1980s practice a new refinery would install valve or sieve trays, and an old one would often be kept and given a new tray-packing section on the vacuum side.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: Tray packing on the atmospheric side was rare in the 1980s; structured packing arrived mainly on vacuum columns and on hydrotreaters.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Crude preheat train
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: A train of shell-and-tube exchangers that takes crude from ambient to 220-300 C by recovering heat from every hot stream in the refinery, then the fired heater takes it the rest of the way to 350-370 C. Preheating was the classic refinery heat-integration project: a crude preheat train alone recovers tens of megawatts and pays for itself in fuel.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Fouling and how the preheat train was kept clean
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: A crude preheat train is a hundred shell-and-tube exchangers in series, and everything in the refinery that is hotter than crude is a source of fouling for one of them: coker bottoms gas, FCC slurry oil, diesel bottoms, hot water. Fouling costs pressure drop and fuel, and the 1980s counter-measures were crude preheat exchangers designed with a deliberately large shell-side velocity, online cleaning with a pigging system, and - in a few cases - a fouling monitor using a differential pressure transmitter on one exchanger as a leading indicator.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.note: Fouling monitoring practice varies; the mechanisms described are standard.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Fired crude heater
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: A radiant box furnace with 150-400 coils of cast alloy or wrought-alloy tube (Cr-Mo, 5 in outside diameter, 0.3 m apart), firing gas at 30-80 MW. Tube metallurgy matters: the coil sees a 30-40 C metal temperature above the oil temperature, and the 1980s move to coiled tubing and to higher radiant efficiency cut fuel use several percent.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.note: Coil counts and duty vary widely by refinery; these are typical 1980s figures.

chem.refining.scale.name: The refining industry in 1983
chem.refining.scale.description: Around 750-850 refineries existed worldwide, of which more than 300 were in the United States alone (US capacity about 19 million bbl/d). The largest refining regions in 1983 were the US Gulf Coast, the US Midwest, Western Europe (Rotterdam, Antwerp, Fos-sur-Mer), the Caribbean (USVI, Curaçao), Japan and Singapore, and the Middle East (Ras Tanura, Ruwais, Kuwait). About 3-5% of the crude throughput was burned as refinery fuel gas.
chem.refining.scale.note: Refinery counts and capacities are approximate; the 1983 figures bracket a decade-long plateau in OECD capacity.

chem.natural-gas.name: Natural gas: the gas field
chem.natural-gas.description: Methane, mostly: either the gas cap sitting on an oil reservoir or a gas-only field. In 1983 world gas production was roughly 2.9-3.0 trillion cubic metres a year, of which about 70% was still associated with oil and much of it was flared or burned at the wellhead. Gas matters to a C64 three ways: as acetylene for PVC and chlorinated solvents, as hydrogen for ammonia and hydrochloric acid, and as the fuel that moved the plastics.

chem.natural-gas.uses.name: What the gas is for
chem.natural-gas.uses.description: Three jobs in 1983: burn it, crack it, or reform it. Burning dominated volume; the petrochemical jobs - acetylene, hydrogen, ammonia - were small in tonnage but disproportionate in value, and they are the reason the polymer industry existed at all.

chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.name: Fertiliser ammonia
chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.description: About 80% of ammonia goes to fertiliser, a demand that sets the size of the hydrogen industry and therefore, indirectly, the amount of ammonia available for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The link to the C64 is indirect but real: the same ammonia plants that fertilised the fields also supplied the nitrogen that went into the case polymer.

chem.natural-gas.uses.fuel.name: Gas as fuel
chem.natural-gas.uses.fuel.description: The largest single use of gas: heat, boilers, industrial furnaces and gas turbines. A 1980s gas turbine power station of 40-100 MW fired natural gas at 15-25 bar through a dual-fuel combustor; a plastics plant's furnace was gas-fired with 10-30% excess oxygen so its stack oxygen stayed high. Because gas burns cleanly, a gas-fired furnace could run a polyethylene line without the sulphur constraint of a fuel-oil furnace - one reason gas-based polymer plants grew up in the Gulf and in Western Europe.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen by steam methane reforming
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.description: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2 over nickel at 750-850 C and 20-30 bar, followed by the water-gas shift (iron oxide/chromia, 350-450 C) to raise the hydrogen fraction, then CO2 removal and cryogenic or PSA purification. A world-scale 1980s plant made 50-100 million m3 of hydrogen a day. Almost all of it went to ammonia; the rest to hydrotreating and to hydrochloric acid.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrot.name: Hydrogen for hydrotreating
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrot.description: The refinery's hydrogen - desulphurisation, hydrocracking, reforming - came from naphtha reformers and, as sour crudes grew, from dedicated gas reformers or hydrogen manufacturing units fed with refinery off-gas. In 1983 hydrogen was roughly 3-5% of refinery energy consumption and a genuine bottleneck.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Hydrogen to ammonia (Haber-Bosch)
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 over promoted iron or ruthenium at 400-500 C and 150-250 bar, in a 1,000-2,500 tonne a day synthesis loop fed from a purge cascade. Ammonia is the single largest use of hydrogen, and it matters to the C64 in two places: the nitrogen for the polybutadiene and SAN polymerisations, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Ammonia synthesis catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is promoted iron: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with potassium oxide and with alumina or calcium oxide. Ruthenium is better by an order of magnitude but was, in 1983, still a research curiosity as far as ammonia plants were concerned. The catalyst is made by melting magnetite with the promoters, granulating, and reducing it in situ with hydrogen, and a 1980s ammonia plant had a few hundred tonnes of it.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Magnetite from iron ore
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: Fe3O4, the reduction product of hematite, and the raw material for the ammonia catalyst. It is also the mineral in the Claus catalyst's neighbourhood and in the polishing lapidary industry. A tonne of ammonia carries about 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron in its catalyst, and the catalyst is replaced every few years, so the ammonia business has a real, if modest, appetite for iron ore.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.note: The iron ore chain itself belongs to the metals subsystem; this node marks where it enters the ammonia catalyst.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: Aqueous ammonia at 20-29 wt% for semiconductor processing, made by sparging anhydrous ammonia into ultrapure water under a scrubbed laminar-flow hood. One of the handful of wet chemicals delivered to a fab in a fluoropolymer or electro-polished bottle rather than a tank.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.description: Nickel on alumina, or the older nickel-chromium used in the pre-1957 Topsoe SMR-180. By the 1980s the modern multi-bed reformer ran 25-40 tubes of 10-16 inch diameter at 30-50 bar, with an inlet temperature near 550 C and an outlet at 850-870 C, burning gas in a process furnace alongside the tubes.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.name: Acetylene from natural gas
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.description: The Reppe process, commercialised from 1959-1965: a mixture of roughly 6-8% methane with 30-38% air and 55-60% hydrogen is fired through a water-cooled burner at 1,200-1,800 C and quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds. The acetylene yield per pass is only 2-3% of the feed, so the process has to recycle a large stream, and the furnace consumes several GWh of electricity per tonne of acetylene. It survived because it made a C2 unit out of a C1 feed - the only route that can make vinyl chloride, and hence PVC, without cracking a barrel of naphtha.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.chlorome.name: Chloromethanes and the semiconductor chain
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.chlorome.description: Acetylene plus chlorine gives tetrachloroethane and from it trichloroethylene and chloroform, while the same high-temperature HCl chemistry gives methyl chloride from methane - the starting material for the chlorosilane and semiconductor-grade silicon chain. Natural gas therefore reaches the C64's chips as well as its case, by a very indirect route.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.chlorome.note: The semiconductor chain itself belongs to the silicon subsystem; the chloromethane source is gas-derived and belongs here.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.carbon-b.name: Acetylene black
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.carbon-b.description: Cracking acetylene at 1,200-1,400 C in a water-cooled steel retort and quenching in nitrogen gives a fine, high-surface-area carbon black, historically the standard channel black for rubber reinforcement and printing inks. Furnace black made from natural gas (CATB, from 1950) largely displaced it in tyres during the 1960s.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-trich.name: Acetylene to chlorinated solvents
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-trich.description: Chlorination of acetylene to tetrachloroethane followed by dehydrochlorination to trichloroethylene (1,1,2-TCE) was the original industrial route to the electronics degreaser and was still the route in much of the world in 1980. The acetylene-HCl chemistry is the same as the vinyl chloride chemistry; only the degree of chlorination differs.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-trich.note: The solvent and its regulation are under chem.solvents.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.name: Quench and acetylene recovery
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.description: The hot gas is quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds, then acetylene is absorbed selectively from the acetylene-hydrogen-methane-hydrogen-sulphide mixture by acetone at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar (about 2.2 volumes of acetylene per volume of solvent), stripped and the solvent recirculated. Recovered acetylene is 99.5-99.8% pure once hydrogen sulphide and water are removed.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: The absorption and recovery train
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The acetylene is absorbed out of the cracked mixture in a solvent and taken off the top of the tower at high purity, which is the whole reason for doing the separation this way. Acetone's job is to hold acetylene - which at 20 C and 12 bar will dissolve to about 2.2 volumes of solvent per volume of acetylene - while letting the hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide straight through. The dark, dangerous part of this plant is not the chemistry but the acetylene itself: above 2 bar in the presence of a metal, acetylene will detonate into its own decomposition products, and the whole extraction plant is designed around never letting that happen.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Drying and finishing the acetylene
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The last step before the acetylene goes to the vinyl chloride plant is a drying and finishing train: a molecular sieve or a chilled water wash to get the water under 10 ppm, a caustic or amine wash to take the last of the hydrogen sulphide, and a final distillation if the grade has to be 99.8%. Vinyl chloride does not tolerate water - it hydrolyses - so the last drying step before the HCl addition is not optional.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Absorber and stripper
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: A 20-40 tray absorber at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar with the acetone circulated, and a stripper that takes the pure acetylene overhead at 3-5 bar and the solvent off the bottom for recycle. The solvent must be regenerated at intervals because it accumulates the hydrogen sulphide and the water from the feed gas, and because the acetylene polymerises in it if it is left standing - the plant has a permanent low-temperature nitrogen blanketing problem.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Acetone as the selective solvent
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The choice of solvent is a compromise. Acetone has a high acetylene solubility and a low methane solubility and a manageable vapour pressure, and it is made from cumene on the same site, which is the practical reason it was chosen. It is also flammable and it is a reproductive toxin, which is a modern objection to a molecule the industry has used since 1945.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.partial-.name: Partial oxidation burner
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.partial-.description: Methane is partially oxidised to CO and H2, which then combine to acetylene at flame temperature. The furnace runs at atmospheric to 2 bar with the flame held above the acetylene decomposition point; the burner is water-cooled because copper and steel both survive the flame while the mixture would otherwise decompose to soot. The process is violently sensitive to soot: any carbon in the gas feed poisons the burner.

facts.label: Furnace temperature
facts.value: 1,200-1,800 C depending on variant and measurement point

chem.natural-gas.processing.name: Gas processing and transport
chem.natural-gas.processing.description: The plants that turn a wet, sour wellstream into a pipeline gas, a liquefied gas or a natural-gas-liquids fraction. A large 1980s gas plant handled 5-30 billion standard cubic feet a day; the North Sea, Gulf and Middle Eastern plants of that decade were among the largest chemical plants ever built.

chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.name: Gas pipeline
chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.description: Line pipe 0.6-1.4 m in diameter, API 5L grade X52-X70, laid by a lay barge or a trenching spread and internally coated with epoxy and polyethylene powder. Transmission lines run at 60-100 bar with compressors every 100-200 km. The 1980s were the years of the great gas transmission builds: the Central Asia-Centre system, the Norwegian and North Sea systems and the Trans-Med pipelines all date from this decade.

chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.sub.name: Subsea pipeline and riser
chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.sub.description: Concrete weight-coated line with a hot-water or electrical trace heater for hydrate prevention, and a wet-insulated riser with a buoyancy module for the first 100-300 m of water. Deepwater gas tiebacks of the 1980s established the standard development: subsea wellhead manifold, a dedicated line to a central platform, gas gathered ashore.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG liquefaction
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: Chilling gas to -162 C so it becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure, cutting volume about 600-fold for the same energy. In 1983 world LNG trade was roughly 55-70 billion m3 a year, about 2-3% of world gas production, on a network of roughly 60-70 liquefaction trains. The dominant cycles were the propane-precooled mixed refrigerant (9 stages, about 7-8% specific power) and the nitrogen expander cycle.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG carrier
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: A 70,000-125,000 m3 membrane or independent-tank ship with a re-liquefaction plant, because LNG boils off at 0.1-0.3% a day and the load has to be reliquefied in transit. The world LNG fleet in 1983 was of the order of 90-130 ships at $40-90 million each.
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.note: LNG carrier prices and fleet size in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude figures.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG storage and regasification terminal
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: A vacuum-insulated cylindrical tank of 20,000-160,000 m3 with a nickel-alloy inner tank over perlite insulation, plus a jetty for a 125,000-165,000 m3 carrier. Regasification burns about 0.3 tonnes of fuel gas per tonne of LNG, which is where the C64-scale fact becomes visible: the fuel burned to regasify enough LNG to make one machine's plastics is tens of grams.
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.note: The regasification fuel figure of about 0.3 t/t LNG is the standard design value; the C64 extrapolation is order-of-magnitude.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: Mixed refrigerant cycle
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: Propane pre-cooling to -30 to -40 C, then an ethylene/ethane/propane mixture expanded through a series of exchangers to -120 C, then a nitrogen expander to -162 C. The hydrocarbons in the refrigerant are the same ones the petrochemical industry buys; the nitrogen expander cycle burns almost nothing but needs a lot of power and very large exchangers, which suited a plant with cheap power and no other outlet for its fuel gas.

chem.natural-gas.processing.ngl-recovery.name: Natural gas liquids recovery
chem.natural-gas.processing.ngl-recovery.description: Ethane, propane, butane and pentane are stripped out of the gas and sold as NGL: ethane for crackers, propane and butane for LPG, C5+ for gasoline. A cryogenic plant recovers 90-99% of the methane but less of the heavy end, so the design trade is expander versus absorption. The NGL stream is the LPG that feeds the crackers in the ethylene branch.

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Cryogenic separation (expander plant)
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: The JT-expander process that became the industry standard for large gas plants in the 1980s: the gas is chilled by expansion through a turbine to -30 to -80 C and the resulting cold box distils methane from ethane and heavier. The plant cost is dominated by the aluminium cold boxes, which remain one of the largest single uses of aluminium in the world per tonne produced.

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Aluminium cold box
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: A brazed plate-and-fin aluminium exchanger 10-30 m long, cryogenic to -80 C, containing dozens of channels. Aluminium-brazed cold boxes replaced copper wound exchangers in the 1970s and are one reason the gas plant business grew so fast in that decade.

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Cryogenic turboexpander
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: A radial or axial turbine in the cold box, handling 10,000-40,000 kW on a big plant, recovering 5-15% of the gas enthalpy and reaching -30 to -80 C. The expander train was the mechanical heart of the 1980s gas plant and its efficiency set the plant cost.

chem.natural-gas.sources.name: Where the gas comes from
chem.natural-gas.sources.description: Associated gas from the gas cap of an oil reservoir, and non-associated (gas-only) gas. The distinction matters industrially: associated gas was a by-product that had to be flared or reinjected until the late 1970s made it commercial, while gas-only fields carry the pipelines and the LNG trains.

chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.name: Gas hydrate (a hazard, not yet a resource)
chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.description: Methane trapped as a clathrate of water, stable below about 20 C at surface pressure. Known since the 1930s and already recognised in the deep ocean and permafrost as a potentially enormous resource, but in the early 1980s it was a hazard - it plugged subsea pipelines and was one reason offshore gas lines carried inhibitors and heated risers - not a supply.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Non-associated (gas-only) field
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A gas reservoir with no oil at the contact. The North Sea fields of the late 1970s - Frigg (1977), Heimdal, Sleipner, Troll (discovered 1979) - turned Europe from an import market into a gas market, and the Norwegian and British gas grids of the early 1980s were built around them. In the US the equivalent discovery was the tight and geopressured gas of the Anadarko and Rocky Mountain basins.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Unconventional gas (tight and coalbed)
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: The gas fields that had to be stimulated rather than merely completed: tight low-permeability sandstone and coalbed methane. The techniques are the oil branch's - massive hydraulic fracturing, and dewatering for coal seams - applied to rock that is not a reservoir in the classical sense. In 1983 tight gas was a real but small share of US supply and coalbed methane was still essentially an experiment in the Black Warrior basin.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas reservoir
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fills a porous sandstone or a fractured carbonate just as oil does, but with a lower density and a higher compressibility, so gas in place is quoted in trillions of standard cubic feet rather than billions of barrels. The largest gas fields in the world in the early 1980s were the giant Permian Basin fields (US), Urengoy and Yamburg in West Siberia, and Groningen (Netherlands, discovered 1959).

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas in place
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Trillions of standard cubic metres of gas in the pore space. The C64-scale fact: all the natural gas used worldwide in 1983 was of the order of 3,000 billion cubic metres a year, so one machine's plastics and energy are far below a thousandth of a cubic metre.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Discovering and drilling a gas field
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fields are found by the same seismic and drilled with the same rig as oil fields, but the completion differs: the log response that proves a gas column is high resistivity with low neutron density, and the well must be tested for absolute gas flow rather than liquid rate. Gas viscosity is about a hundred times lower than oil but its compressibility ten times higher, so the well responds to drawdown very differently.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Dehydration to pipeline dew point
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas must arrive at the pipeline dew point or the higher-pressure steps downstream condense water out and the line fills with liquid. By 1980s practice that meant a glycol unit (triethylene glycol at 80-95 wt% purity, contactor at 20-50 C and 40-70 bar, reboiler 120-140 C) and increasingly a 3A or 4A molecular sieve adsorption unit for the last kilogram of water per million standard cubic metres.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Triethylene glycol
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A heavy glycol made by reacting ethylene oxide with diethylene glycol; the standard dehydration absorbent because of its low vapour pressure at the contactor temperature. The 1980s trend was towards 95 wt% TEG purity, because glycol vapour carried upstream into a gas turbine or a carburettor was a real emission problem.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Glycol synthesis is the ethylene oxide branch: chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Sweetening to pipeline specification
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: H2S and CO2 are removed with a 20-35 wt% alkanolamine in an absorber at 30-45 C and 20-70 bar, with the rich amine regenerated at 120-130 C and 1.5-2 bar in a reboiler. By the early 1980s the trend was to diethanolamine for economy and MDEA for lower heat duty and no carbamate degradation.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Alkanolamine
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Monoethanolamine (MEA, primary), diethanolamine (DEA, secondary), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA, tertiary). MDEA was the growth amine of the 1980s because it does not form carbamate with CO2, so its degradation and reboiler duty are lower; the penalty is a slower absorption rate and a lower equilibrium loading.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Wellhead separation of gas
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A wellhead separator and a test separator drop the liquid out of the gas at 30-70 bar, then the gas goes to a knockout drum and to the gathering system. The liquid is the same crude or condensate as in the oil case; the gas is dried and sweetened at the plant, not at the wellhead.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Casing and perforation for a gas well
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Identical hardware to an oil well, different discipline: a gas well has to be tested to destruction of the casing and tubing if it is perforated below the point of no return, because the gas column is light and there is no fluid level to swallow a leak. High-strength casing and a cemented, pressure-tested completion were the rule.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Drilling fluid for a gas well
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas wells were drilled with the same bentonite mud as oil wells, with two differences: a low filter loss was mandatory because filtrate invasion had to be reversed before logging, and a gas-cut mud had to be controlled because entrained gas reduced hydrostatic pressure and made the well hard to control. The standard 1980s control was a mechanical gas trap plus defoamer.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Bentonite mud
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota, the same clay as the oilfield mud. In a gas well the requirement is a low solids count so the log response is not screened by a thick filter cake.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The mineral chain is under chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite; this node exists because gas wells consumed the same clay.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Seismic over a gas prospect
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas sands are often visible before they are drilled: gas lowers the acoustic impedance of the rock, so the reflector dims and sometimes inverts (a bright spot). The amplitude anomaly is a well-known risk - it is also produced by a shale lens or by a tuning effect - which is why a 1980s exploration manager still had to drill to find out.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The seismic acquisition chain is shared with the oil branch: chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.

chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.name: Associated (oil-associated) gas
chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.description: Gas from the gas cap of an oil field, produced at roughly 50-150 m3 of gas per barrel of oil. Around 70% of world gas production was associated gas in 1983, and a large share was still flared: world flaring ran at the order of 100-130 billion m3 a year in the early 1980s, several million tonnes of hydrocarbons a year simply burned at the wellhead.

chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas..name: Flare and gas reinjection
chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas..description: A flare tip burns whatever the oil plant cannot handle; in 1980s practice it was sized for peak oil rate, so routine gas-cap growth had to be reinjected into the reservoir or sold. Recovering associated gas was one of the clearest economic arguments for the gas-processing plants built in the Middle East and Nigeria in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

chem.natural-gas.composition.name: What natural gas is
chem.natural-gas.composition.description: A mixture, not a compound. A sour gas well may deliver methane with 2-10% ethane and propane, 1-8% C4, 1-20% hydrogen sulphide, 0.5-5% carbon dioxide and up to 15% nitrogen. Everything downstream - the pipelines, the dew point specification, the hydrogen plant - is set by those five impurities.

chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.name: Hydrogen sulphide (sour gas)
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.description: A lethal, corrosive, smelly component that must be taken to a few ppmv before the gas enters a steel pipeline, because H2S embrittles steel and attacks copper alloys. Sweetening it produces a concentrated acid gas stream whose H2S is the feedstock for the Claus sulphur plant in the refining branch.
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.note: The amine plant and the Claus plant are under chem.natural-gas.sources and chem.refining.claus.

chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen in natural gas
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.description: 1-15% N2 in many fields. It is the impurity that most affects heating value, that forces the Wobbe index (a measure of interchangeability between gas supplies) onto a pipeline tariff, and that makes a gas which is 90% N2 unsaleable as town gas.
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.note: Nitrogen content is highly field-specific; the Wobbe index framing is standard.

chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.name: Methane
chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.description: CH4, 80-98% of a dry gas, 39.8 MJ/m3 gross calorific value, -161.5 C boiling point. The single molecule most of this branch is about: because methane is hard to polymerise and hard to functionalise, the industry of the 1980s broke it into acetylene at extreme temperature or into hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, and those two products underwrote most of the polymer industry.

chem.crude.name: Crude oil: finding it, drilling it, lifting it
chem.crude.description: The upstream end of the chain. Seismic surveys pick a structure, a rig drills a 5-7 km hole through rock, casing and cement line the hole, the well is completed and perforated into the reservoir, then often artificially stimulated. An 8 kg C64 case corresponds to only 1-3 litres of crude oil, but that crude was found under 5-10 km of overburden using a drilling rig that cost tens of millions of dollars.

chem.crude.c64-fraction.name: One Commodore 64's share of the wellhead
chem.crude.c64-fraction.description: The plastic mass of a C64 is about 350-400 g of ABS in the case plus 100-200 g in the keys, and ABS comes from roughly 2 kg of crude oil per kilogram of polymer. Add the energy to make it, the fuel to ship it and the polymer's own energy in the burning, and one machine corresponds to roughly 1-3 litres of crude oil - about one minute of production on a small Arabian field, and undetectable in the world oil balance. This node is the reminder that the whole upstream industry exists to supply a mass flow, not a concept.
