chem.crude.c64-fraction.note: The 2 kg crude per kg of olefin-derived polymer figure is a widely used mass-balance rule of thumb; the 1983 world production number is approximately 57-60 Mb/d for liquids.

facts.label: Crude per kg of ABS
facts.value: about 2 kg crude (mass balance across cracker to polymer)

chem.crude.assay.name: Crude assay
chem.crude.assay.description: The certificate that turns crude into a priced commodity: density and API gravity, sulphur, metals, pour point, carbon residue, and a simulated distillation curve. Assay decided which refinery gets which crude and, ultimately, which chemicals are made from it.

chem.crude.assay.properties.name: Pour point, cloud point and viscosity
chem.crude.assay.properties.description: The cold-flow properties of the residue and the crude. A Middle East crude at 4 deg C in the North Sea was, in 1980s practice, handled by heating the tanks or by blending with a pour-point depressant copolymer; that is a real recurring cost on North Sea production.

chem.crude.assay.conradson.name: Conradson carbon residue and metals
chem.crude.assay.conradson.description: Coking value and the vanadium/nickel/iron trace metals that poison catalytic cracking catalysts. Nickel and vanadium at 1-20 ppm are a hard constraint on FCC feed; sour crudes with high metals were thus discounted for refinery use relative to their heating value.

chem.crude.assay.simulated-distillation.name: Simulated distillation (ASTM D2887)
chem.crude.assay.simulated-distillation.description: A GC method that fakes a slow fractionation, giving a boiling curve from the C7 fraction to the 538 C end point. The naphtha cut, the gas-oil cut and the vacuum residue are all defined by this curve, so this assay is the direct ancestor of the distillation scheme in the refining branch.

chem.crude.assay.sulfur.name: Sulphur content (ASTM D1266)
chem.crude.assay.sulfur.description: Total sulphur by bomb combustion with an oxyhydrogen burner and infrared detection. 0.5% S is a rough dividing line between sweet and sour crude. The 1980s pattern of increasing sourness (Arabian and Mexican crudes) was the single most important driver of the rise in demand for desulphurisation and for recovered Claus sulphur.

chem.crude.assay.api-gravity.name: Density and API gravity (ASTM D1298/D287)
chem.crude.assay.api-gravity.description: Specific gravity at 60/60 F measured in a pycnometer, converted to API gravity by 141.5/SG - 131.5. Light crude means a low API number. This single number set the transport economics: a tanker mile costs the same whether it carries 35 or 40 API crude.

facts.label: Light sweet reference
facts.value: West Texas Light 40 deg API, 0.3% S

chem.crude.separation.name: Wellhead and terminal separation
chem.crude.separation.description: The wellstream arrives at 15-100 bar and 60-100 C as an oil/gas/water froth. It is separated in stages: test separator, stock tanks, heaters and desalters, gas-oil separator, and finally a train of electrostatic and coalescing vessels that make a storable crude. Field separation is where the crude assay is determined and where the oil is counted.

chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.name: Oil-water coalescer
chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.description: A packed or membrane device that lets separated water droplets out of the crude without carrying oil. Produced-water disposal in 1983 was to a pit or a treatment plant; the offshore discharge limit under the 1983 amendments to the US Clean Water Act required 42 ppm oil and no visible sheen, which is why coalescers and hydrocyclones appeared on offshore platforms.
chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.note: The 42 ppm / 30 ppm benchmark figures for produced-water oil content are the long-standing offshore standard; the 1983 date for that particular rule reference is a common citation but the precise effective date varies by jurisdiction.

chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.name: Electrostatic coalescer (electrogravitational)
chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.description: Charged droplets are attracted into the water phase, collapsing the emulsion in seconds instead of hours. Small pipeline electrocoalescers were introduced in the mid-1980s for crude pretreatment, cutting the demulsifier dose; they were used in 1980s practice wherever the crude conductivity allowed (hence electrogravitational not electrocoalescing for most crudes).
chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.note: High-conductivity crudes could not be electrocoalesced in the 1980s; that limitation is why electrogravitational units (large DACC-type vessels) were preferred for crude.

chem.crude.separation.heater-treater.name: Heater-treater and desalter
chem.crude.separation.heater-treater.description: A crude preheater to 150-200 C followed by a settler and then a desalter, where the crude is washed with recycled water to strip salts. Needed because sour Middle East crudes carry 1-3 wt% dissolved salts, and because naphthenic acids plus water at 200 C will corrode the hot exchanger on the way to the refinery. A crude desalter separates maybe 90-95% of the salt in one stage.

chem.crude.separation.three-phase.name: Three-phase separator and stock tanks
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.description: A horizontal or vertical vessel at 2-10 bar with a mechanical or electrostatic coalescing section that separates oil, gas and water, then atmospheric storage tanks that settle the remaining water and sediment. Stock tank bottoms and the settled water carry the production's salt and heavy ends, and their disposal was the field's environmental problem in the 1980s.

chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.name: Demulsifier chemistry
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.description: Nonylphenol- or alcohol-based surfactants dosed at 5-50 ppm to break the oil-water emulsion; in the 1980s a growing share of demulsifiers were polyalkoxyamine and polyglycol ethers. A stable water-in-oil emulsion (chocolate mousse) could hold 20-50% water into the crude and was the single largest quality loss on a wet field.

chem.crude.separation.test-separator.name: Test separator
chem.crude.separation.test-separator.description: The first vessel, sized 1-5% of the field's liquid capacity, where the wellstream is bled at 25-70 bar to a stable pressure and temperature. Its records are the raw data for reservoir performance, gas-oil ratio and oil assay. A field with 100,000 bbl/d of oil needed a test separator of a few hundred bbl.

chem.crude.stimulation.name: Well stimulation: fracturing and acidising
chem.crude.stimulation.description: Almost no reservoir delivers its whole potential through a millimetre perforation. Stimulation makes the rock permeable by fracture or by dissolving the rock; it is one of the biggest single levers on oil and gas supply and it consumes enormous volumes of water, sand and, for acidising, corrosive acid.

chem.crude.stimulation.thermal-stimulati.name: Steam stimulation
chem.crude.stimulation.thermal-stimulati.description: On heavy oil and tar sands, steam at 250-350 C injected into the formation to lower viscosity, followed by soak and production. In 1983 this was a Cold Lake and Athabasca-scale proposition; the C64-scale point is the water and fuel: a single steam cycle consumed several tonnes of water and roughly 0.5-1 barrel of 60% FO-2 fuel oil per tonne of steam.
chem.crude.stimulation.thermal-stimulati.note: Heavy-oil thermal work existed but was marginal to light-sour supply; the numbers are order-of-magnitude.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.name: Matrix acidising and fracture acidising
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.description: Hydrochloric or hydrofluoric acid injected to dissolve or acid-fracture the rock, typically 15-28% HCl in sandstone and HF-containing mud acid in carbonate. Sandstone acidising only reached the late 1970s as a standard service; carbonate mud-acid fracturing with a 12% HCl-3% HF system had become the standard carbonate treatment by the mid-1980s.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.acid-pu.name: Acid pumping and coiled tubing
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.acid-pu.description: Acid was bullheaded down casing or, by the mid-1980s, coiled-tubed into the perforation tunnels; continuous coiled tubing for acid and sand work was itself a growth industry in the 1980s. Placement mattered more than chemistry: because HF precipitates calcium fluoride, a 1.2-1.5 m of HCl preflush was always pumped first to keep Ca out of the rock.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Mud acid (HCl + HF)
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrochloric acid to dissolve carbonate, with 1-3 wt% HF to attack the clay in sandstone and 2-5 wt% HF in carbonate muds. The reason for mud acid was a reserve shift: by the early 1980s mudstone was around 80% of world oil reserves, and mudstone cannot be treated with pure HCl because of its clay reactivity. Acid is pumped downhole in steel or titanium coils, with corrosion inhibitors (amines, thiourea) and a surfactant.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: HF and HCl chemistry is the same as chem.fab-chemicals in this file; HF from fluorspar, HCl from chlorine.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid corrosion inhibitor
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrofluoric acid at 12% and hydrochloric acid at 12%, pumped down a steel coil, will remove a hundredth of an inch of steel a day. The inhibitors - a long-chain amine, thiourea, an acetylenic alcohol - adsorb on the steel and cut the corrosion rate by several orders of magnitude without touching the rock. It is a thin grey film of chemistry doing the work, and it is the reason mud-acid jobs of the 1980s could be pumped downhole at all.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid-resistant tubing
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Coiled tubing and the acid lines were, by the mid-1980s, routinely nickel alloy - a nickel-molybdenum alloy such as Alloy C-276 or a titanium grade - rather than carbon steel, because the inhibitor was never perfect and the steel was never quite good enough. Nickel alloys and titanium both come out of a metallurgical chain that this file does not own; the reason they are here is that the acid chemistry forced them there.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: Alloy selection for acid service is metallurgy rather than petrochemistry; this node marks the boundary of the subsystem.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Hydraulic fracturing
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A water-based or gel fluid pumped down the casing into the pay, then into the perforations at 40-100 bbl/min and up to 6,000-10,000 psi surface pressure to part the rock; a proppant is carried in to hold the fracture open when pressure is released. Born in 1947 (experiments) and industrialised in the late 1950s (Massive Hydraulic Fracturing, 1961-1965), by the 1980s it was routine on low-permeability gas reservoirs and increasingly common on oil wells. A big 1980s job used 10,000-100,000 bbl of fluid and 500-2,000 tonnes of sand.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracture geometry and conductivity
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A propped fracture's job is conductivity x length. The first fractures were vertical and planar (d = 2h for radial, reservoir height-limited), so 1980s design moved toward multiple parallel fractures per zone; conductive fracture area had to be raised by resin-coated proppant (1980s) or by larger grains, because proppant embedment in soft rock closed fractures within months.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing pumping equipment
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Blender trucks, sand trucks and a high-pressure pump unit (one pumping unit at 25,000 psi), laid out in a yard over the rig. A 1980s job mobilised 10-40 trucks and 100-200 people, and it was the largest single water consumer in the oilfield outside steam flooding.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Proppant sand
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Sized, round, silica sand or resin-coated sand, typically 20/40 or 30/50 mesh (0.4-0.6 mm), graded to carry a hundred thousand tonnes a year in a region. Ottawa River and Illinois Basin sands were the standard, with regional sources in Texas and Arkansas. It was a heavy, low-value, high-bulk freight commodity.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Sand proppant is the same silica route as the glass fibre and fused silica branches.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing sand and its plant
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: The proppant is a silica sand that has been sieved, washed, resin-coated and graded, and the plant that does it is a small mineral processing operation that exists in the Permian basin because the proppant has to be nearby. The oilfield sands of the Permian have a problem that glass sands do not: a weak grain crushes under the closure stress of a hydraulic fracture, so the 1980s industry coated a fraction of the proppant with a phenolic resin to make it stronger.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Frac sand mine
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A sand quarry that happens to contain almost pure silica in a dune, worked at 1,000-10,000 tonnes a day. The last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's stimulation chain, and a reminder that a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral supply chain: the water, the sand and the chemicals are all mining and manufacturing, and only the pressure is petroleum engineering.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Resin-coated proppant
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A fraction (5-30% in the late 1980s) of the sand is coated with a cured phenolic or furfural resin so that it does not embed into the formation when the fracture closes. The consequence for the industry was a new solid waste: sand that cannot be reused, because it has been used once and coated once. That is the same shift - from a mineral commodity to a consumable - that the chlorinated solvents made in the electronics plant.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Coating fractions and the date of commercial introduction vary by basin and supplier.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing fluid and gel
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Water plus a viscosity builder (hydroxyethyl cellulose in water, or a hydrocarbon gel), often crosslinked with borate or an organometallic zirconium/titanium chelate to hold the proppant in suspension at high temperature. Waterfracs (no crosslinker, friction-reducer only) took a large share of the market by the mid-1980s because they were cheaper and left less residue.

chem.crude.well-completion.name: Well completion
chem.crude.well-completion.description: Turning a drilled hole into a producing well: set production casing, cement to the pay, run and perforate the tubing, pack the annulus, and install a tree. This is where the reservoir is deliberately connected to the borehole for the first time.

chem.crude.well-completion.production-lo.name: Production logging and well testing
chem.crude.well-completion.production-lo.description: Spinner and turbine flowmeters, noise logs, temperature logs and a well test with a multi-hour rate and pressure buildup. The 1980s production log also included an EST (emission spectral tool) for tracer detection in injection wells.

chem.crude.well-completion.christmas-tre.name: Christmas tree (wellhead assembly)
chem.crude.well-completion.christmas-tre.description: The valve stack on top of the casing: casing spool, tubing spool, master valve, wing valves with gauges, and the flowline tee off the wing. Every stream the well ever produces has to pass through this steel gatework, which is why it is the most pressure-rated cluster of parts in the business.

facts.label: Parts count
facts.value: 80-200 components, several hundred kg of forged steel

chem.crude.well-completion.packer.name: Packer and completion hardware
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.description: An elastomer-sealed packer run and set in the casing to isolate zones and provide a seat for the tubing hanger. In 1980s completions this was single- or dual-packer tubing with sliding sleeves or selective stimulation, increasingly mechanical rather than hydraulic.

chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.name: Packer elastomer (nitrile / HNBR)
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.description: A nitrile (acrylonitrile-butadiene) or HNBR element that swells or mechanically expands to grip the casing. Nitrile is the same chemistry as chem.nitrile-rubber in the polymer branch: acrylonitrile copolymerised with butadiene.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.name: Perforation
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.description: Shaped charges fired down the casing to punch 1-3 cm holes through steel, cement and formation in one shot, linking pay zone to borehole. A 1980s completion might be 4-6 perforations per metre of pay; perforation is done in stages so only the best footage is shot.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.e.name: Entry hole into the pay zone
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.e.description: The first connection to the reservoir is itself a jet-perforated hole in cement, and it is the smallest diameter in the whole production system: a few millimetres through which the entire well's flow must pass. That single fact justifies the next node in the tree.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.name: Shaped-charge perforator
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.description: A copper or steel cone lined with a high explosive (RDX/HMX or HMX-wax, 5-30 g per shot in the 1980s) with a steel or ceramic liner; the detonated cone forms a copper or tungsten-alloy jet at 8-10 km/s which drills the hole. Charges were fired on a wireline in a gun barrel or in a TCP (tubing conveyed perforator).
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.note: Charge weight and composition varied widely with depth and rock toughness; the jet mechanism is well established.

chem.crude.rig.name: The drilling rig
chem.crude.rig.description: Rotary drilling: the drill string is rotated from the surface, the bit mills a hole, mud circulates to carry cuttings out and to control formation pressure. Offshore this is a jack-up, a semisubmersible or a drillship; onshore it is a land rig with a derrick. 1980s rigs reached 6,000-7,500 m total depth on routine programs.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.name: Core drilling and coring
chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.description: Diamond core barrels cut 1-4 in core in a special drilling string, giving the reservoir rock, its porosity, its saturation and its capillary properties undamaged. A cored well is the most expensive way to get reservoir data, so it was used on 1-3 wells out of 20 and almost always on the discovery well.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.core-barrel.name: Diamond core barrel
chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.core-barrel.description: A steel or aluminium tube with a diamond-set reaming shell and a core lifter, run on the bottom hole assembly at low RPM (20-100) and low weight. Carbit tungsten-carbide bits dominated abrasive sandstone, PCD for softer beds, and set diamond for carbonate.

chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.name: Well control: BOP, diverter and kill
chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.description: The blowout preventer stack (annular preventer plus 3-5 ram preventers) and the choke manifold above the wellhead, rated 5,000-15,000 psi. Before the 1970s and 1980s safety emphasis, the classic profile was a vertical string, overbalanced mud and a diverter; 1980s practice added the above-the-bit diverter packoff for kick tolerance.

chem.crude.rig.rig-types.name: Rig types and their 1980s cost
chem.crude.rig.rig-types.description: Jack-up rigs (4-6 legs, 60-90 m water-depth limit) and fixed derricks onshore; semisubmersibles (700-1,000 m, self-propelled, expensive); drillships (ice-strengthened, for deep water and harsh climates). Costs in the early 1980s: onshore rig $1-3 million, jack-up $20-45 million, drillship $30-70 million, semisubmersible $60-120 million. Offshore dayrates in 1983 ran $25,000-60,000 a day.
chem.crude.rig.rig-types.note: Rig newbuild prices moved violently through 1981-83 (a deepwater rig that cost $60m in 1980 was quoted above $100m in 1983); treat these as order-of-magnitude figures.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.name: Casing and cementing
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.description: Steel casing is run to isolate the hole and to carry the pressure; cement is pumped between casing and formation (and sometimes inside the casing) to seal the annulus. Without a good cement job the whole completion leaks and stimulation injects into the wrong zone. Cementing is one of the few oilfield jobs that is nearly a repeatability disaster: 10-30% of wells take a cement squeeze.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.casing-stri.name: Casing string and cement sheath
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.casing-stri.description: Conductor, surface, intermediate and production casing, each cemented across its shoe. The C64-scale point: even a modest producing well consumes tens to hundreds of tonnes of cement and hundreds of metres of steel, dwarfing the machine it ultimately supplies.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.name: Cement dispersants and additives
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.description: Sulfonated naphthalene formaldehyde condensates (BNS) or sulfonated formaldehyde melamine (SFM) to keep the slurry workable at low water; and bentonite as an extender. Early 1980s practice was to optimise with laboratory thickening-time tests before the job, because a primary cement job cost $0.2-1 million.
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.note: Exact additive ranges vary widely by job; the chemical identities are standard.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.name: API Class G oilwell cement
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.description: Portland-type cement with 40-60 wt% Class G sulphate-resisting blend, gypsum for set control, silica flour as a retarder for the thickening time, and additives for fluid-loss control. Mixed on location with water and spacers at 1.7-2.0 g/cm3 and pumped at 30-90 bbl/min.

chem.crude.rig.bit.name: Drill bits
chem.crude.rig.bit.description: The cutting tool at the bottom of the string. In 1980s practice a soft-formation bit was a sealed journal bearing with a cone of natural diamond, a medium bit a sealed or unsealed mud turbine with tungsten-carbide nose buttons, and a hard rock bit a milled-steel body with tungsten-carbide inserts on the three cones.

chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.name: PDC (polycrystalline diamond compact) bit
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.description: The emerging bit of the early 1980s: sintered diamond compact cutters brazed to a steel body with no cones and no bearings, turning rather than grinding. PDC began as a hard-rock bit, spread into soft rock in the mid-1980s and largely replaced roller cones in soft formations by the early 1990s. In 1983 it was perhaps 10-20% of the market.

chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.name: Polycrystalline diamond compact cutter
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.description: Diamond powder sintered at 5,000-6,000 bar and 1,400-1,600 C with a cobalt metal catalyst from the diamond-graphite phase boundary. Over a 1980s field life a soft-formation PDC cutter could cut tens of kilometres of sandstone; hard-rock PDC arrived later with tungsten-carbide substrates and domed cutters.

chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.name: Natural diamond (soft-formation bit)
chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.description: Gem-quality or bort diamond in a matrix of tungsten and cobalt sintered into a cone. Natural diamond bits dominate soft sandstone and were the standard drag-bit insert in 1980s drilling; synthetic (polycrystalline) diamond began to displace them in abrasive sandstone late in the decade.

chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.name: Tungsten carbide cutters and buttons
chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.description: WC-Co cemented carbide: 6-12% cobalt binder, 900-1,600 HV, pressed and sintered in a vacuum furnace then brazed onto the cone or into a milled-steel body. Cemented-carbide rock-bit consumption was the largest single use of tungsten carbide in the world in the 1980s, comparable to carbide tooling.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.name: Rotary drilling
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.description: A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit. Weight-on-bit and torque are the two variables the driller steers with; the drilling engineer watches torque and bit exponent while the driller watches penetration rate.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.name: Drilling mud (drilling fluid)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.description: A thixotropic clay-water or oil-water emulsion that removes cuttings, lubricates and cools the bit, carries hydraulic pressure to the formation, and crucially gels to hold formation pressure when the pumps stop. In practice it was a chemically engineered suspension with four control jobs: viscosity at the bit, gel strength in the hole, filtrate control to stop the formation claying off, and compatibility with the formation.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.name: Chelants, biocides and defoamers
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.description: The 1980s mud chemist's standard additive cabinet: phosphate and polyphosphate sequestrants for calcium, lignosulphonate and polyacrylamide viscosifiers, benzyl alcohol defoamer, and glutaraldehyde or formaldehyde-based biocides against sulphate-reducing bacteria, which produce hydrogen sulphide and sour the cuttings.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.rheology-con.name: Mud rheology and filtration control
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.rheology-con.description: Funnel viscosity, plastic viscosity, yield point and the PV/YP ratio (a rule of thumb required PV/YP <= 3 for good hole cleaning at the pump), plus low-pressure filtration rate (Baroid/API filtration test) to limit the mud filtrate that causes formation damage and differential sticking.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.rheology-con.note: The exact 1980s API target numbers vary by formation and by whether a water or oil mud is in use; the PV/YP guidance is the well-established part.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.name: Mixed-weight additive (iron ore + barite)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.description: Where barite was unavailable or too expensive, ground iron ore was blended in as a second weighting agent. It attacks steel components by corrosion and needs a passivation layer of lime or sulphide film, but it saved cost in a tight barite market.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.name: Oil-based (diesel) mud
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.description: Diesel or mineral oil as the continuous phase with water as the dispersed phase, organophilic clay (amine-treated montmorillonite) for viscosity. Chosen for high-temperature deep wells and for formations where water filtrate would swell clay. Its environmental reputation in the Gulf in the 1980s was poor, and it had to be stabilised with organophilic bentonite and lime.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.note: Petroleum diesel is the same distillate stream as the refining branch: chem.refining.distillation.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.name: Chrome/lime mud (invert emulsion)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.description: The classic high-temperature mud: a water-in-oil (invert) emulsion with oil as the continuous phase, bentonite in the aqueous phase, and calcium carbonate and a lime (Ca(OH)2) emulsion. Chrome/lime muds were standard to about 120-150 C but they fail in a cement job because the calcium in cement breaks the emulsion, so a salt-water mud or a chrome-free lime mud had to be switched in first.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.note: The name comes from the use of sodium chromate as a corrosion inhibitor on the ferrous cutting and drilling hardware, which had to be neutralised before disposal.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite.name: Barite (barium sulphate) weighting agent
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite.description: Almost all the weight in a mud: API-grade barite at 4.28 g/cm3 (42.8 ppg) added to a base mud of about 1.03-1.2. Barite is also the standard drilling weighting because it is nearly insoluble in water. The same mineral appears as filler in the plastics and cable branches of this file, via chem.barium-sulfate.

facts.label: Density
facts.value: 4.20-4.30 g/cm3; mud density at 1,700 m can reach 2.1-2.3 g/cm3

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.name: Bentonite (montmorillonite clay)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.description: Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota; the single most important mud component. It gives the thixotropy: at rest a high gel strength to suspend cuttings, under shear it drops to low viscosity so the bit can cut. Drilling-grade bentonite is API 13/14 with a viscosity of 30+ s/qt and a low montmorillonite ratio.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.note: Montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite; Wyoming sodium bentonite is the reference grade because of its high cation-exchange capacity and layer charge.

facts.label: Typical mud loading
facts.value: 20-60 kg/m3 of bentonite in a water mud

facts.label: Yield stress target
facts.value: 3-20 Pa for hole cleaning; gel 10-30 Pa on the low-yield muds

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Montmorillonite and the bentonite bed
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: Sodium montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite: two tetrahedral silica sheets sandwiching an octahedral aluminium sheet, with the negative layer charge balanced by exchangeable sodium. Between the layers is water, and that water is why the clay swells, gels and gives the mud its thixotropy. The drilling grade comes from the Cretaceous Bentonite bed of Wyoming and South Dakota, a marine sediment about 65-72 million years old that is a calcium montmorillonite until it is mined and soda-ashed to the sodium form.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: The clay pit
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: A 10-20 m thick bentonite bed, opened up and worked as an open pit or a shallow underground mine, in a landscape that looks like a lunar plain because the clay is grey-white when fresh and weathers to a pale crust. It is the last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's drilling chain, and it is the point at which a machine that will one day hold a C64's case first touches something that came out of the ground with no hydrocarbons in it at all.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Soda ash conversion to sodium bentonite
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: The pit clay is a calcium montmorillonite and has to be converted. The clay is blunged with water, treated with sodium carbonate so that the exchangeable calcium is replaced by sodium, and then dried and milled. That step is what turns a geological curiosity into an industrial material, and it is also the step that makes the drilling specification possible, because the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-syste.name: Mud circulation system
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-syste.description: Active and reserve pits, the pump, the surface mixing hopper (mud pit) and the flowline over the shaker. 1980s volumes for a single rig were 400-1,500 m3 of active mud with 150-400 m3 of reserve, and the pit room needed chemical dosing, dilution and waste disposal for one well's worth of chemically treated clay.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.name: Drill string
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.description: Drill pipe, drill collars and a bit, threaded or coupled API 5-1/2 in and 6-5/8 in in the 1980s, with 3-1/2 in drill collar subs. Length is a queue of 5,000-7,000 m of 5 in pipe plus 200-400 m of collars; the string must be strong enough for tensile load at the maximum string weight yet remain within the derrick.
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.note: Drill pipe steel is a metals chain, not a petrochemical one; the petroleum-derived material here is the mud, the cement and the bit matrix.

chem.crude.reservoir.name: The reservoir: where the oil sits
chem.crude.reservoir.description: Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water. This is the physical thing that the whole upstream industry is trying to reach.

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.name: Oil column in the pore space
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.description: An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume. That gap, plus the reservoir rock and the seal, is why recovery factors are 15-35% and why hydraulic fracturing and acidising exist.

chem.petroleum.asphaltene.name: Asphaltenes and resins
chem.petroleum.asphaltene.description: The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude. Roughly 2-20% of crude, soluble in the light ends and precipitated by heptane in the standard n-heptane asphaltene test. Asphaltenes are the coke precursors in every thermal cracker, coker and reformer, and their content is what decides whether a crude makes a good or bad feedstock.

facts.label: n-C7 asphaltene content
facts.value: 2-10 wt% for a light sour crude

chem.petroleum.name: Petroleum: light sour crude oil
chem.petroleum.description: The dig-it-out endpoint of the whole petrochemical chain. Crude is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons from methane to asphaltenes, plus sulphur compounds, nitrogen compounds, resins, asphaltenes and trace metals. The grades that feed the 1980s steam crackers are light, low-sulphur: Arab Light at 35-36 degrees API and Brent Blend at 38-39 were the benchmarks of the era.
chem.petroleum.note: Saudi Light at 38-39 API is the classic light sour grade; Arab Light (35-36 API) is the heavier sour crude that historically dominated Saudi exports. Assay figures vary by stream and year.
inputs: organic matter buried in marine shale

facts.label: Arab Light (Saudi), 1983 assay
facts.value: 35.0-36.0 deg API, 0.9-1.5 wt% S, ~2.2 wt% S (typical)

facts.label: Mass of C64 case in crude
facts.value: about 1-3 litres of crude oil per machine (plastic + energy)

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.name: Oil in place
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.description: The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor. Multiply it by the C64 scale: the entire world shipped about 200,000 Commodore 64s in 1983, so the machine is a rounding error on a single wellhead's hourly output.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.name: Reservoir rock: sandstone and carbonate
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.description: Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone; carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity. Around 60% of world oil reserves and 80% of world gas reserves were in carbonate rock, most of it fractured Arab-type in the Middle East.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.name: Marine carbonate (Arab-type) reservoir
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.description: Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline and high water cut. Saudi production was essentially all of this rock type in 1983.

chem.crude.reservoir.trap.name: Geological trap
chem.crude.reservoir.trap.description: Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap. The Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia, discovered in 1948, remained the largest oil field on earth for decades, holding some 100+ billion stock-tank barrels in a stacked series of Arabian carbonate reservoirs.

facts.label: Ghawar field
facts.value: >100 billion stock-tank barrels recoverable (Arabian Suwayb member carbonates)

chem.crude.reservoir.migration.name: Migration up the carrier bed
chem.crude.reservoir.migration.description: Oil squeezed out of the source rock moves updip along a permeable sandstone or through a fault until it is trapped. Buoyancy of about 0.2-0.4 API gravity per 1,000 ft drives it; the seal is an impermeable shale or an evaporite whose capillary entry pressure sets the column height.

chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.name: Source rock and kerogen
chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.description: Organic-rich marine shale. Type I and type II kerogen give oil; type III, humic and mainly terrestrial, gives gas. Maturation is measured by vitrinite reflectance, with the oil window at roughly 0.6-1.3% Ro and the gas window above about 1.3%.

chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.kerogen.name: Thermal cracking of kerogen in the source rock
chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.kerogen.description: At 60-160 C kerogen breaks down into oil, and at higher rank into wet gas and dry gas; the same thermal-cracking chemistry, far slower and without a catalyst, that a steam cracker performs in seconds. Laboratory kinetics (Messelbrock-type compilation) were fitted to these systems from the 1960s.

chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin.name: Sedimentary basin
chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin.description: A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed; the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it takes 1-100 million years of that history. By 1983 the world's producing basins were a few hundred in number, with the Middle East and the Gulf of Mexico dominating reserves.

chem.crude.exploration.name: Petroleum exploration
chem.crude.exploration.description: Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well. In 1980s practice this was reflection seismology over regional grids, closed by wildcat drilling. Cost per barrel discovered had fallen from tens of dollars to roughly $2-8 by the early 1980s.

chem.crude.exploration.mud-logging.name: Mud logging and cuttings examination
chem.crude.exploration.mud-logging.description: A mud-logging unit beside the rig sampled cuttings and gas continuously, with a hot-wire or infrared hydrocarbon detector on the gas line. It found the shows that decided whether to run a full log suite, and in 1980s practice a mud-logging unit was manned for 24 hours a day on a producing-field well.

chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.name: Reserve estimation
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.description: Volumetric and material-balance estimates, presented to a board and to governments as proved, probable and possible reserves. Rules of thumb: recovery factor 15-35% of oil-in-place for a sandstone reservoir, higher (35-60%) for a fractured carbonate. Reserve booking was and remains a commercial and legal judgement, not a measurement.

chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..name: Reserve uncertainty and contingency
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..description: Undiscovered reserves behind existing fields were treated as of similar magnitude to proved reserves. The industry view of world ultimately-recoverable oil in 1983 was around 1,500-2,000 billion stock-tank barrels, versus about 700 billion produced or proved.

chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..name: Oil-in-place calculation
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..description: H = pore volume x saturation x (1 - water saturation) x formation volume factor B_o. B_o for a light crude at reservoir temperature can be 1.1-1.3, so reservoir barrels convert to stock-tank barrels at a meaningful ratio; the calculation is sensitive to saturation, which is the least measurable input.

chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.name: Exploration (wildcat) well
chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.description: The first hole into a prospect. Cheap success-failure logging with mud logging and core, drilled to the deepest prognosis rather than the shallowest pay. Exploration wells in the early 1980s averaged about 3,000-5,000 m of hole and took 30-90 days offshore.

chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well..name: Wildcat cost and success statistics
chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well..description: A North Sea or Gulf of Mexico wildcat cost $3-20 million in the early 1980s; the historical industry success rate was about 1 in 10 wells dry, 1 in 15 total wildcats a commercial discovery, and about 1 in 8 wildcats found non-commercial hydrocarbons. Exploration cost per barrel discovered was roughly $2-8.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.name: Reflection seismic survey
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.description: A surface source sends a pressure wave down through the rock section; reflectors return it to hydrophones and the travel times are stacked into a two-dimensional depth section. Seismic is a time-domain method: it maps reflectivity contrasts (sandstone/shale, gas-sand amplitude dimming) and gives no direct information about fluid type.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.di.name: Discovery test and hydrocarbon indication
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.di.description: A log response indicating oil or gas in a sandstone (high resistivity, low neutron density, gas effect on the seismic) is a test, not a discovery. A discovery required a producing well; industry experience was that one test in eight to one in thirty was commercial.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.da.name: Seismic data processing (CDP stack)
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.da.description: Common-midpoint stacking, normal-moveout correction via velocity analysis, deconvolution, migration and depth conversion, run on a mainframe or minicomputer. 1980s emphasis was on multiple suppression and on 2-D and early 3-D (a 3-D survey over one field cost $1-3 million per acre-foot).

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.re.name: Seismic recording system
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.re.description: Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-compatible cartridges. The whole array recorded simultaneously; it was common for the record to be demultiplexed and copied to a computer tape for onshore stacking.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Seismic geophone array
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried. In 1980s 2-D the fold of coverage (usually 6-fold to 24-fold) was chosen by geophone group interval and source spacing, not by 3-D binning.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Geophone takeout cable and junction box
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: Polythene-insulated multi-pair takeout cable to a junction box, then a line-trap and telemetry radio link to the recording truck. Cable insulation here is polyethylene from the same steam-cracking chain as the C64's power cord jacket.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Moving-coil geophone
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across; coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity. A second coil acts as a position feedback for the servo. Cost per channel in the early 1980s was several hundred to a few thousand dollars.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.name: Marine seismic streamer and hydrophone cable
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.description: A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups; it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry line whose integrity was the limiting factor on data quality. Hydrophone elements used piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-5) discs coupled to silicone oil in a pressure-compensated housing.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.name: PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.description: Lead zirconate titanate ceramic discs, typically 25-50 mm diameter, epoxied onto a diaphragm and back-electrode in a silicone-oil-filled housing; sensitivity about -190 dB re 1 V/uPa in the 10-60 Hz band. Silicone oil here is one of the petrochemical elastomers/fluids, unrelated to the case material.
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.note: The silicone and epoxy cross-links are chem.silicone and chem.epoxy in this file.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.name: Dynamite shothole source
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.description: Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot. Cheap per shot but slow, noisy and it polluted a producing field's drill cuttings.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.name: Seismic shot-hole explosive ammunition
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.description: Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation. This is a one-off consumable of a survey, not part of any C64 material.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ai.name: Airgun and marine seismic source
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ai.description: Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel. Compressed air from compressor trucks on deck; a single 1980s 3-D crew vessel carried up to four sources.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vi.name: Seismic vibrator truck
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vi.description: A truck-mounted hydraulic vibrator sweeps 10-80 Hz into the ground under hold-and-hold conditions; on land it replaced explosive shot holes because it gave repeatable, higher-energy sources with no shothole cleanup. Regionally a 1,000-2,000 m shotpoint spacing was normal in 1980s 2-D work.

metal.name: Metals, ores and industrial minerals
metal.description: Every mineral stream behind a 1982 Commodore 64: the quartzite that becomes silicon, the bauxite and cryolite that becomes aluminium foil, the porphyry copper that becomes PCB track and transformer magnet wire, the tin and lead that become 63/37 solder, the iron ore and coke that become the steel chassis and the transformer laminations, and the specialty metals - gold, silver, nickel, tantalum, zinc, chromium, manganese, cobalt - that end up plating contacts, filling ceramic capacitors and setting the sinter point of every solder joint. Each branch runs from the finished metal down to the quarry, the open pit, the evaporite bed or the seabed.

metal.barium.name: Barium titanate: the ceramic capacitor dielectric
metal.barium.description: The disk and multilayer ceramic capacitors on a 1982 C64 mainboard are barium titanate - BaTiO3 - and barium titanate is an industrial material made from barite, the same heavy white mineral that makes the drilling mud. The chain is barite to barium sulphide to barium carbonate to barium titanate, and then a 1000-1400 C calcination and a ceramic pressing. It is the most complete oxide-mineral chain in this file: a sulphate ore, a carbothermal reduction, a carbonate, a perovskite, and a dielectric constant of several thousand.

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~1000-5000 for X7R barium titanate; ~10,000 for the pure material near its Curie point

facts.label: China's share
facts.value: China supplied the majority of world barite in 1982

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the glass frit of the ferrite coating, the ferrite body itself, and the barium ferrite magnet

metal.barium.titanate.name: Barium titanate BaTiO3, calcined at 1100-1350 C
metal.barium.titanate.description: The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: perovskite, ABO3, a cubic cell with Ti in an octahedron of O6 and Ba in the 12-fold site

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ball-milled to 0.1-1 um for the dielectric; coarse powder for the low-end grades

facts.label: Reducing atmosphere
facts.value: must be avoided: Ti4+ reduced to Ti3+ turns the material semiconducting and lossy

metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.name: The ceramic capacitor and its dielectric classes
metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.description: The finished use. A 1982 C64 mainboard carries perhaps 30-60 ceramic capacitors, mostly small discs and a few multilayer blocks. The disc is a pressed or cast barium titanate body, sintered at 1250-1350 C, silver-coated on both faces and fired to make the electrodes, and dipped in an epoxy or phenolic encapsulant. The multilayer capacitor stacks hundreds of microns-thick dielectric layers with internal nickel or palladium electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired - a technology that was genuinely new in 1982 and was the reason a 10 nF 50 V part started to fit in a 1.6 mm-tall package. The dielectric classes are named by their temperature coefficient: X7R and Z5U for the general-purpose 1980s parts, Y5V for the high-capacitance low-stability ones.
metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.note: The class nomenclature and the sintering temperatures are standard; the count of ceramic capacitors on a C64 mainboard is an estimate and belongs to the passives agent.

facts.label: Multilayer
facts.value: 1-10 um dielectric layers, Ni or Pd internal electrodes, co-fired at 1200-1350 C in a reducing atmosphere, then re-oxidised

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: silver for discs (fired at 700-900 C); base-metal nickel for multilayer

metal.dielectric-grading.name: Grading barium titanate into the dielectric classes
metal.dielectric-grading.description: The same powder cannot make a Y5V capacitor and an X7R one. Y5V is made from a fine, uniform, high-surface-area powder near the Curie point, where the dielectric constant is enormous and wildly temperature-dependent - a huge capacitance that changes by a factor of five over the working range. X7R is made from a coarser powder with barium zirconate or barium strontium titanate added, which flattens the temperature curve at the cost of the peak. So the capacitor 'class' is really a powder specification, and the class marking on the part is a statement about the ball mill that ground it.
metal.dielectric-grading.note: Medium confidence; the class-to-chemistry mapping is standard and the recipes are proprietary.

facts.label: Y5V
facts.value: fine powder near the Curie point, K of several thousand, very high temperature coefficient

facts.label: X7R
facts.value: coarser powder with solid solution, K of 1000-4000, +/-15% over -55 to +125 C

facts.label: Additives
facts.value: Ba(Zr,Ti)O3, Ba(Sr,Ti)O3, and rare-earth dopants for the high-capacitance grades

metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.name: The internal electrode metal and the reducing atmosphere
metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.description: A multilayer capacitor's internal electrode is nickel or palladium, printed as a paste and co-fired with the ceramic. That will not work in air - the ceramic would reduce and become a lossy semiconductor - so the whole stack is fired in a low-oxygen atmosphere at 1200-1350 C in hydrogen or in a nitrogen-hydrogen mix, and then re-oxidised afterwards so the barium titanate goes back to being an insulator. The oxygen partial pressure is controlled to a few millibars. It is the most metallurgically demanding step in the whole electronics supply chain that nobody ever sees, and it is a barium carbonate problem.
metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.note: Medium confidence; the co-firing atmosphere is standard practice but the exact pO2 is proprietary.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2, a few millibars, in H2 or N2/H2

facts.label: Reoxidation
facts.value: a separate anneal afterwards to restore the insulator

metal.titanium-dioxide.name: Titanium dioxide from rutile sand
metal.titanium-dioxide.description: The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: ilmenite at 42-60% TiO2, and rutile at 90-95% TiO2, both from beach placer sands

facts.label: Chloride process
facts.value: ilmenite + coke + Cl2 at 900-1000 C -> TiCl4, then flame oxidation at 1200-1400 C -> TiO2 + Cl2

facts.label: Sulfate process
facts.value: ilmenite + concentrated H2SO4 -> titanyl sulphate, then hydrolysis and calcination

facts.label: Ceramic grade
facts.value: needs high purity and low iron; much of the pigment grade is too impure for a dielectric

metal.ilmenite-sand.name: Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge
metal.ilmenite-sand.description: The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

facts.label: Sand grade
facts.value: 1-10% heavy minerals in a quartz sand

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredging of a beach or an offshore bar, with a gravity and electrostatic concentrator onshore

facts.label: Products
facts.value: ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite (and in Kerala, the monazite for thorium and rare earths)

metal.barite.reduction.name: Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate
metal.barite.reduction.description: The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: rotary, 2-3 m diameter, 30-50 m long, 0.5-1 rpm

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: the cake is leached with water, hot, and the BaS solution is clarified

facts.label: Carbonation
facts.value: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S, at room temperature

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~90% on the reduction, 95%+ on the carbonation

facts.label: Barium carbonate purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% for ceramic grade; iron is the impurity to watch

metal.hydrogen-sulfide.name: Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation
metal.hydrogen-sulfide.description: The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.
metal.hydrogen-sulfide.note: Medium confidence on the H2S yield; the hazard mechanism is textbook.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.15-0.3 t of H2S per tonne of BaCO3

facts.label: Control
facts.value: flared or sent to a Claus plant, with continuous monitoring

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: H2S paralyzes the sense of smell at high concentration

metal.barium-carbonate.name: Ceramic-grade barium carbonate
metal.barium-carbonate.description: A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: BaTiO3, glass frit, ferrite, barium ferrite magnets

metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.name: Calcining barium carbonate to a reactive powder
metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.description: The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.
metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.note: Medium confidence; the calcination step is standard but the specific practice varies.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: to raise the reactivity of the carbonate for the solid-state reaction with TiO2

metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.name: Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade
metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.description: The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.
metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.note: Medium confidence; the impurity mechanisms in barium titanate ceramics are standard in the ceramics literature.

facts.label: Iron
facts.value: below a few hundred ppm; an acceptor dopant that degrades the dielectric

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: must be removed by the carbonation and the calcine; it degrades the breakdown voltage

metal.barite.name: Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98%
metal.barite.description: Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 90-98% BaSO4 for drilling grade; chemical grade requires Fe2O3 <0.5% and SiO2 <1-2%

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground or surface; sometimes a byproduct of lead-zinc and of fluorspar

metal.barite.drilling-mud.name: Drilling grade barite and its mud
metal.barite.drilling-mud.description: The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.
metal.barite.drilling-mud.note: Medium confidence; the mud consumption figure is representative rather than a specific well.

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: specific gravity above 4.2, 90% below 45 um, low soluble salts

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 100-300 t of barite per km of hole in a deep well

metal.barite.mine.name: Barite vein and replacement mine
metal.barite.mine.description: Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.
metal.barite.mine.note: Medium confidence on the chemical-grade processing route; it varies a lot by deposit.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: crush to 25 mm, log wash, deslime, size to 200 mesh for drilling grade

facts.label: Chemical grade
facts.value: flotation plus an acid leach to bring Fe2O3 below 0.5%

metal.barite.mud-system.name: Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system
metal.barite.mud-system.description: A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.
metal.barite.mud-system.note: Medium confidence; the mud chemistry is standard drilling engineering.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: barite takes the mud to 1.5-2.0 specific gravity

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: bentonite, swollen to several times its dry volume

facts.label: Calcium control
facts.value: lime and inhibitors, because calcium flocculates the clay

metal.lime.name: Lime (CaO) and calcium
metal.lime.description: Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone; limestone is quarried rock.

facts.label: Kiln temperature
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in a vertical or horizontal lime kiln

facts.label: Loss on ignition
facts.value: ~44% by weight; a 100 t kiln yields roughly 56 t of CaO

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke, coal fines or anthracite depending on local availability

facts.label: Slaking
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 is exothermic and adds about 65% to the mass

metal.lime.kiln.name: Shaft and rotary lime kilns
metal.lime.kiln.description: Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln - a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom - makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product; the rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

facts.label: Shaft kiln
facts.value: 20-40 m tall, 2.5-4 m diameter, 250 kg limestone per 40 kg coke

facts.label: Rotary kiln
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, inclined, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~110-130 kg coke or coal per tonne of CaO, or ~80 kg in a rotary kiln with a preheater

metal.lime.rotary-kiln.name: The rotary kiln and the preheater
metal.lime.rotary-kiln.description: A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln - the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt - but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.
metal.lime.rotary-kiln.note: Medium confidence; the fuel figure assumes a preheater, which is where most of the saving is.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: pulverised coal, coke, anthracite or gas, at about 80 kg per tonne of CaO with a preheater

metal.lime.kiln-clinker.name: Overburnt lime and the clinker problem
metal.lime.kiln-clinker.description: If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.
metal.lime.kiln-clinker.note: Medium confidence; the mechanism is standard.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: overburning: local temperature above about 1200 C for too long

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: the grains sinter; the lime slakes slowly and lumps in the mixer

metal.lime.kiln-gas.name: The lime kiln gas and its CO2
metal.lime.kiln-gas.description: A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and - much later - the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.
metal.lime.kiln-gas.note: Medium confidence; the stoichiometric yield is certain, the 1982 disposition is a generalisation.

facts.label: CO2 yield
facts.value: ~0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, plus the fuel

facts.label: 1982 fate
facts.value: burnt for heat, or vented; the sequestration era had not arrived

metal.lime.slaking.name: Slaking: quicklime to hydrated lime
metal.lime.slaking.description: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, +64% by mass, strongly exothermic

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: about 1.7 g/L at 20 C - enough to be caustic, not enough to be a base

metal.lime.cement.name: Lime in Portland cement
metal.lime.cement.description: By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch - limestone, kiln, CaO - and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

facts.label: Clinker
facts.value: 75-80% limestone, 20-25% clay, fired at 1450 C in a rotary kiln

facts.label: Gypsum
facts.value: 3-5% added at the cement mill to control the set

metal.limestone.name: Limestone (CaCO3) quarry
metal.limestone.description: High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.

facts.label: Use rate
facts.value: order 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal in the blast furnace

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: surface quarry, 5-15 m benches, crushed to 10-50 mm

metal.limestone.quarry.name: Limestone quarry and crushing plant
metal.limestone.quarry.description: A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.

facts.label: Product sizes
facts.value: 0.5-5 cm sinter feed, 5-40 mm furnace and kiln feed, plus fines

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 0.2-5 Mt/year for a chemical-grade supplier

metal.limestone.bed.name: Carbonate platform limestone
metal.limestone.bed.description: The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: fossiliferous limestone, commonly a carbonate platform deposit

metal.lime.shaft-kiln.name: The counter-current shaft kiln
metal.lime.shaft-kiln.description: Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.
metal.lime.shaft-kiln.note: Zone layout is standard practice; medium confidence on the yield range.

facts.label: Burn zone
facts.value: the upper third of the shaft

metal.lime.scavenger.name: Lime as a metallurgical slag flux
metal.lime.scavenger.description: Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.
metal.lime.scavenger.note: Snelter lime practice is very smelter-specific; medium confidence.

facts.label: Lead sinter
facts.value: order 15-25% limestone in the sinter mix

metal.lime.pcb-etch.name: Lime as etch regeneration and neutralisation
metal.lime.pcb-etch.description: At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride, CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath - which is where a lot of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed. Lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; this node exists only because the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Regeneration
facts.value: FeCl2 + air/Cl2 -> FeCl3; then CuCl2 + Ca(OH)2 -> Cu(OH)2 + CaCl2

metal.lime.blast-flux.name: Limestone and lime as blast furnace flux
metal.lime.blast-flux.description: The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.
metal.lime.blast-flux.note: Typical burden practice; specific works ran tighter ratios.

facts.label: Burden rate
facts.value: order 0.25-0.35 t limestone per t hot metal

metal.lime.bayer-uses.name: Lime in the Bayer circuit
metal.lime.bayer-uses.description: Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently - the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.
metal.lime.bayer-uses.note: Dosage range varies with ore; medium confidence.

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite

facts.label: Desilication reaction
facts.value: kaolinite + lime -> calcium silicate hydrate, permanently wasted

metal.lime.pre-desilication.name: Pre-desilication by attrition washing
metal.lime.pre-desilication.description: By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings - and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.
metal.lime.pre-desilication.note: Medium confidence; the adoption rate was highly ore-dependent.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: attrition scrub followed by desliming at about 40-60 um

facts.label: Removes
facts.value: typically 1-4% of the mass as clay, which was 10-40% of the reactive silica

facts.label: Trade
facts.value: less lime and less caustic consumed, more water and more tailings

metal.lime.causticisation.name: Causticisation: the lime goes round the loop
metal.lime.causticisation.description: The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.
metal.lime.causticisation.note: Medium confidence; the reversibility of the causticisation is the textbook caveat.

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: a stirred causticiser with a settler and a filter

facts.label: Caveat
facts.value: this reaction is reversible; it only goes far enough because the carbonate is continuously removed and the liquor stays dilute

metal.bentonite.name: Bentonite binder from a clay pit
metal.bentonite.description: A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.
metal.bentonite.note: Pellet binder levels are standard; the specific source geology is medium confidence.

metal.barite.rock.name: Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue
metal.barite.rock.description: The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: hydrothermal vein or replacement body in carbonate rock

metal.ferrite.name: Ferrite: transformer and choke cores
