Every one of those is a different regulatory jurisdiction and none of them was solved in 1982.
metal.solder.lead-hazard.note: Lead-free alternatives existed as patents and laboratory melts in the 1980s-90s; nothing displaced 63/37 in commercial manufacture until the 2000s. High confidence.

facts.label: Fume mechanism
facts.value: PbO aerosol from the reaction of lead oxide in the flux with rosin acids

facts.label: Exposure limit
facts.value: an airborne lead limit existed in the US under the OSHA lead standard from the 1970s

facts.label: Later developments
facts.value: lead-free solder (Sn-Ag-Cu SAC305, Sn-Ag-Bi) only took commercial share after about 2000-2010, driven by RoHS

metal.solder.silver-solder-paste.name: Silver-bearing solder and silver paste
metal.solder.silver-solder-paste.description: A distinct and important thing in the 1980s electronics industry, which is easy to confuse with the lead-tin eutectic: high-temperature silver solder - 62Ag/38Cu, 50Ag/50Cd, 70Ag/30Sn - melts at 600-750 C and is brazed, not soldered. Silver-tin solder melts at 217-220 C and is used where lead-free behaviour is wanted. Silver brazing is how the heat sinks and the chassis joints were made. And separately there is the silver-filled epoxy and silver-filled ink of the electronics industry: real silver powder at 60-80% by weight in an epoxy or an organic vehicle, screen-printed or stencil-printed and fired, used for die attach and for the conductive ink of the keyboard membrane. That is a genuine and separate use of silver in a C64, and it is a chemistry, not a metallurgy.
metal.solder.silver-solder-paste.note: The keyboard membrane of a 1982 C64 is a triple-layer flex circuit with printed conductive ink - whether that ink was silver-filled or carbon/graphite is the keyboard agent's call. Silver-filled epoxy die attach was a specialised 1980s technology used mostly in power devices and in some hybrid ICs.

facts.label: Silver brazing
facts.value: Ag-Cu or Ag-Cd, 600-750 C, with a flux

facts.label: Silver epoxy
facts.value: 60-80% Ag powder in epoxy, cured at 150-250 C

facts.label: Silver ink
facts.value: a fine silver flake powder in an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the flexible membrane

metal.solder.paste.name: Solder paste: powder in flux
metal.solder.paste.description: Solder paste is a mixture of atomised alloy powder at 60-90% by weight in a flux vehicle, and in 1982 it was the technology for surface-mount parts, which Commodore did not really use on the mainboard but which every other electronics maker in the world was. The powder particle size is controlled by the printing stencil: a 0.5 mm gap needs 20-45 um powder so the powder does not bridge the gap with two particles. Alloy powder is not made by atomising finished solder; it is made by atomising the melt and then the 63/37 particles are aged so they develop an oxide shell of a controlled thickness, so that paste sits on a pad for minutes without the paste shrinking or the surface going dull.
metal.solder.paste.note: Paste is mostly a surface-mount story rather than a through-hole story; included because it is the other half of the solder industry in 1982 and because Commodore's own subsidiaries used it.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: type 2 (25-45 um) to type 4 (15-25 um) in 1982 practice

facts.label: Paste consistency
facts.value: classified by viscosity, e.g. solder paste Type 1 through 6

metal.solder.wave-solder.name: Wave soldering with the alloy pot
metal.solder.wave-solder.description: The board assembly method for a 1982 C64. The bottom of the board is swept across a standing wave of molten 63/37 at 250-280 C, the excess drains through a hot-air knife, and the whole board lives in a hood full of the vapour of flux decomposition products. A few kilograms of solder in the pot are held at a temperature just above the 183 C liquidus, and the pot is kept clean with a rotating skimmer. Wave soldering is why solder consumption in electronics manufacturing was measured in kilograms per day per line rather than grams per board, and why the flux vapour was a genuine occupational exposure that the electronics industry was only beginning to quantify in the late 1980s.
metal.solder.wave-solder.note: The 1982 wave-solder process for a large through-hole board is well documented; wave time and pot temperature ranges are typical rather than from a specific manual.

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: pre-fluxed board via a foam or spray fluxer, then preheated at 100-150 C

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 3-8 s per board; a 1982 line ran a few hundred boards an hour

metal.solder.wave-solder.knife.name: The hot-air knife and the solder wave
metal.solder.wave-solder.knife.description: A pump throws molten solder up a nozzle to form a standing wave 3-8 mm high, and the board is dragged across it on a conveyor with fingers. As the board leaves, a 'hot-air knife' - a duct blowing 200-300 C air across the solder line - blows the excess solder off the pads and off the solder side of the board, and what runs off goes back into the pot through a trough. The whole operation is a temperature profile in space: preheat, flux activation, wave, drain, and the knife. Getting the four temperatures right - preheat, pot, board and cleaning - is the entire craft.
metal.solder.wave-solder.knife.note: The temperature windows are standard; medium confidence on the conveyor speed range.

facts.label: Conveyor
facts.value: 1.5-3 m/min for a large through-hole board

metal.solder.preheater.name: Preheater, fluxer and the thermal profile
metal.solder.preheater.description: Before the wave, the board goes through a preheater - infrared lamps, a hot plate or hot air - to 100-150 C, and through a fluxer that lays a foam or sprayed layer of flux on the solder side. The reason for preheating is thermal expansion: a FR-4 board with a big hole pattern expands by a different amount in different directions, and if the solder side heats faster than the component side the board warps and the joints crack. A C64's mainboard is a large single-sided board with a lot of heat-generating parts on one side, so warp was a real yield problem. The preheater is the cheapest fix and it is a temperature-control problem.
metal.solder.preheater.note: Medium confidence; the temperatures are standard, the warp mechanism is well established.

facts.label: Fluxer
facts.value: foam or spray, 10-30 g of flux per board

facts.label: Why
facts.value: to control the through-thickness thermal gradient and stop the board warping

metal.solder.board-warp.name: Board warp, thermal stress and the epoxy
metal.solder.board-warp.description: Why preheat exists at all. A single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 board with a large hole pattern expands and contracts with a coefficient of about 14-18 x 10^-6 per K, and it is not isotropic - the copper layer and the epoxy cloth have different coefficients, and the weave gives the board different stiffness in the warp and weft directions. Warm the solder side faster than the component side and the board bows; cycle it and the board stays bowed; and on a double-sided board it can delaminate the copper from the epoxy. So the preheater is really an epoxy-handling device, and the epoxy is the resin agent's problem while the solder pot is the metals one, and they meet at the warp.
metal.solder.board-warp.note: Medium confidence on the coefficient ranges; the mechanism is textbook.

facts.label: CTE of FR-4
facts.value: 14-18 x 10^-6 per K in-plane; anisotropic between warp and weft

facts.label: Copper
facts.value: 17 x 10^-6 per K; epoxy cloth 50-70 x 10^-6

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: bow if the solder side heats faster; delamination if the gradient is severe

metal.solder.joint-microscopy.name: The solder joint itself and lead leaching
metal.solder.joint-microscopy.description: A good 1982 through-hole joint is a shallow concave meniscus filling the pad hole about 70-90%, with a fillet at the lead. The metallurgical reason it works is the intermetallic: copper and tin react to form Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn, and the joint is a composite of unreacted solder and intermetallic compound. On the PCB side the pad is tin-plated and forms a Cu-Sn intermetallic too. What nobody in 1982 was measuring was how much lead leached out of a solder joint into the copper land when the joint was at 200 C for an hour - and it is a lot, which is the mechanism behind the later 'solder fatigue' literature.
metal.solder.joint-microscopy.note: The microstructural description is standard; the specific metallurgy of a Commodore board in 1982 would need the actual board. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Intermetallics
facts.value: Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn form at the interface

facts.label: Phases
facts.value: Sn-rich matrix plus brittle intermetallic skeleton

metal.solder.wire.name: 63/37 solder wire with a rosin core
metal.solder.wire.description: The wire that went through a C64 assembly line: a solid 63/37 core inside a flux core inside a tin-lead sheath, made by the cored-wire method and drawn on the same kind of multiwire machine the copper industry uses, in a smaller and more delicate setup. This is a deliberate convergence node: the solder alloy branch, the rosin branch and the wave-solder branch all meet here, and it is the single most identifiable material in the whole tree - it is why the C64 is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: 0.5-0.8 mm for through-hole boards; 0.3 mm for fine work

facts.label: Spool
facts.value: 100 g to 2 kg retail, 5-10 kg industrial spools for wave solder

facts.label: Consumption in a C64
facts.value: roughly 3500 through-hole joints at about 30 mg each, so order 100 g per machine

metal.solder.alloy-making.name: Casting the 63/37 bar
metal.solder.alloy-making.description: The alloy is made in a handful of ways, all of them embarrassingly simple. The best is the cored wire method: rods of high-purity tin are cast inside a steel tube pre-filled with molten lead at exactly 37%, so the tube's own wall meters the lead; the tube and the core are then rolled and drawn out to wire in one operation, and the core forms down the middle as the flux. This is how most electronics solder wire is still made. The alternative, and what the solder manufacturer would do for its own bar stock, is simply to melt the two ingots together in a grease pot with a little antimony or phosphorus and pour into ingot moulds.

facts.label: Composition control
facts.value: to +/-0.5%; the liquidus is steep enough that 2% off composition moves the melting point by 10-20 C

facts.label: Antimony
facts.value: 0.1-0.5% Sb added to raise fluidity and prevent the solder sticking to the pot

facts.label: Oxide control
facts.value: a covering flux of resin or glycerine prevents tin oxide dross

metal.solder.cored-wire.name: The cored-wire manufacturing method
metal.solder.cored-wire.description: The standard way to make electronics solder wire, and the reason the alloy composition is so consistent. A steel tube with a wall thickness calculated for 37% lead by volume is filled with molten high-purity tin - actually with the exact alloy, but the wall does the metering - and the tube is cold-drawn and then drawn to wire in the same multiwire machine the copper industry uses. The core forms down the middle as the tube collapses. The result is a wire in which the flux core is in the middle of the metal rather than smeared along it, which is what stops the flux from being wiped off during handling. The alternative - extruding a bar of flux and then jacketing it in molten alloy - gives a worse wire and was being displaced by the cored method through the 1980s.
metal.solder.cored-wire.note: Medium confidence; the cored-wire method is well established in the solder industry literature.

facts.label: Metering
facts.value: a steel tube wall of controlled thickness meters the lead, or the melt ratio is set in the fill

metal.solder.flux-core-fill.name: How the flux core is filled
metal.solder.flux-core-fill.description: The flux core is a paste, not a powder: rosin dissolved in a solvent - turpentine, or in the 1980s increasingly a mild-rosin paste - with the zinc chloride activator, made viscous enough to hold a column. It is injected into the tube with a hydraulic filler in a batch, and the tube's ends are crimped and drawn closed. The viscosity and the shrinkage matter, because the core has to survive being drawn to 0.5 mm without either splitting out of the wire or shrinking away from the axis. So the flux chemistry in a C64's solder wire is a colloid and a rheology problem as much as it is a chemical one.
metal.solder.flux-core-fill.note: Low confidence; the cored-wire fill process is proprietary and I am describing the general shape of it, not a specific machine.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: rosin dissolved in a terpene solvent, or a mild rosin paste

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: hydraulic injection, batch, into a drawn steel tube

metal.solder.antimony.name: Antimony addition to stiffen the alloy
metal.solder.antimony.description: Pure Sn-Pb solder creeps. A 1982 instrument or a through-hole joint under a hot component would push itself out of the joint over a few years, and the classic failure was a capacitor that walked out of its pads. Two tenths of a percent of antimony, as an Sb-Sn hardener or as a lead-antimony master alloy, makes the alloy's creep resistance about an order of magnitude better with only a small rise in melting point. So the solder in the C64 very probably contained 0.1-0.5% antimony, and none of it is on the bill of materials.
metal.solder.antimony.note: Antimony level is a supplier specification, not something visible on a C64; 0.1-0.5% is the normal commercial range for electronics-grade Sn-Pb.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: much better creep resistance; melting point up a few degrees

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: below the fluid point, so 60/40 and 63/37 differed more by creep than by melt

metal.lead.name: Lead: the other half of the solder
metal.lead.description: Lead is the soft, low-melting, cheap half of the solder alloy, and it is the reason soldering works at all: pure tin wets copper badly and has no strength, and pure lead does not wet anything. Lead also has its own huge pre-electronics industrial life - storage batteries, cable sheath, pigment - and its 1982 smelting industry is the oldest continuous industrial process in the book. The C64 carries a couple of hundred grams of it, which is why the machine is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.99% (4N); 'corroding lead' at 99.99% was the standard for 1980s solder manufacture

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 5% Pb ore -> ~15 t of 60% Pb concentrate -> ~5 t of crude lead -> ~4.7 t of refined lead

metal.lead.sintering.name: Roasting/sintering of galena to PbO
metal.lead.sintering.description: The concentrate is roasted in a sinter plant: a travelling grate on which a 1-2 m bed of concentrate is ignited and slowly drawn through with the gas being pulled after the fire. The sulphide oxidises to lead(II) oxide: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. The point of sintering rather than fluidised-bed roasting is that the heat can be high and localised enough to sinter the fine particles into a coherent porous cake, which is exactly what the blast furnace needs to breathe. The sinter is 50-60% Pb and the SO2 - at 10-14% - goes to the acid plant, the same one the copper smelter uses.
metal.lead.sintering.note: The sinter plant is where lead's energy cost sits; it is a genuinely old process and the dominant sinter machine type in 1982 was the Dwight-Lloyd.

facts.label: Sinter machine
facts.value: Dwight-Lloyd travelling grate, ~60-90 m2 of grate area, 1-2 m bed

metal.lead.self-fluxing.name: Self-fluxing sinter mix
metal.lead.self-fluxing.description: Sinter is not simply roasted concentrate. The mix is designed so the sintered cake is its own flux: the silica that comes with the concentrate is balanced with limestone so the blast furnace slag has a basicity near 1.5-2.0. Anything between about 1.0 and 2.0 works; outside that range the slag either freezes in the furnace or dissolves too much lead. The smelter's metallurgist is balancing silica, iron, calcium and lead every shift.
metal.lead.self-fluxing.note: Slag basicity range varies with the ore; medium confidence.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 of 1.5-2.0 in the blast furnace

metal.lead.sinter-plant.name: Dwight-Lloyd sinter strand
metal.lead.sinter-plant.description: A continuous chain of cast-iron pallets on an endless track about 1.2-1.5 m wide, with the ignition hood at the discharge end. Feed is a mix of concentrate, sinter returns, flux and coke spread to exactly 1-2 m - there is nothing clever about it and it works. The strand advances 1-2 m/min, the fire burns through the bed in about 20 minutes, and the hot sinter is broken off by a set of crusher jaws at the end and tipped into the blast furnace. One machine makes 200-400 t of sinter an hour and runs continuously for years.

facts.label: Grate width
facts.value: 1.2-1.5 m for a single-width strand; multi-width for large smelters

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 200-400 t of sinter per hour per strand

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 8-12% - the bed has to hold together

metal.galena.name: Galena (PbS) concentrate
metal.galena.description: Galena is cubic, bright grey when fresh and dull grey when oxidised, extremely heavy at 7.6 g/cm3, and it is one of the few common ores that a prospector could identify by eye. The great mining districts in 1982 were the Tri-State district of Missouri, Oklahoma and Kansas (which supplied most of the United States' lead and is a fossil limestone-hosted deposit), the Broken Hill and Mount Isa districts of Australia, Cerro de Pasco and Huancavelica in Peru, and the Iberian and Atlas belts. Concentrates assay 40-75% Pb and are always accompanied by enough silver and zinc to make a good deal of the mine's revenue.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: carbonate-hosted replacement bodies (Tri-State) and metamorphosed massive sulphide (Broken Hill)

metal.galena.mine.name: Underground lead-zinc mine
metal.galena.mine.description: The Tri-State district's galena bodies sit as veins and bedding replacements in Mississippian limestone only a few metres thick, and they were worked by room-and-pillar mining - essentially taking the limestone out and leaving the lead in place, because the ore grade at 3-6% Pb did not pay for selective mining. The mineral was hand-picked off the back of the working face and off the cars. This is a soft-rock, shallow, cheap mining operation, and its day had largely gone by 1982 as the deeper and lower-grade Missouri deposits took over.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar in limestone, ore bodies 3-15 m thick

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 3-6% Pb, and a lot of hand sorting

metal.galena.sorting.name: Hand picking and gravity sorting
metal.galena.sorting.description: The Tri-State district's ore was a 3-6% lead limestone that could not be selectively mined and could not be concentrated, so the technique was brute force: the rock was shot down, the lead-bearing rock was picked out of the face by hand by a face worker, and then the cars were run over a sorting table or a picking table where a sorter took out the visibly lead-coloured lumps from the limestone. In 1930 the Tri-State had about 15,000 sorters - a third of them children - and that is what made the district the largest lead producer on Earth. It is a labour technique rather than a machine, and it is a genuine leaf of the tree.
metal.galena.sorting.note: Medium confidence; the Tri-State hand-sorting era is well documented in the labour history literature.

facts.label: Recovery by sorting
facts.value: a face worker and a car sorter could double the mill feed grade

facts.label: Sorters
facts.value: order 15,000 sorters at the peak of the Tri-State, a third of them children

facts.label: Why it stopped
facts.value: the ore got deeper and thinner, and the labour became uneconomic; the district closed in the 1960s-70s

metal.galena.sorting-table.name: The sorting table
metal.galena.sorting-table.description: A sloping table with a light on it and a raised lip, worked by two or three people, one on each side. Galena is bright and heavy and galena-bearing limestone is dark and light, so the visual contrast is real, and the sorter's job is to lift out the dark lumps at perhaps 2-4 tonnes per shift. It is the lowest-skill, lowest-pay, highest-volume job in the lead industry, and it is where a great many Missouri families started.
metal.galena.sorting-table.note: Medium confidence; sorting rates are anecdotal and vary enormously with the ore.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: order 2-4 t of rock sorted per person per shift

metal.galena.rock.name: Galenite replacement in carbonate rock
metal.galena.rock.description: The leaf: galena crystals and veins in a fossiliferous limestone - literally the remains of a Carboniferous sea floor. The Tri-State district is one of the great fossil-mineral coincidences of industrial history: a lead-bearing limestone under a farm field.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: replacement bodies and veins along bedding and fractures

metal.tin.name: Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts
metal.tin.description: Tin is the metal that made electronics solderable. On a 1982 C64 board there are roughly 3,500 through-hole joints and most of them are joined with a lead-tin alloy, so there is a couple of hundred grams of tin per machine. Tin also does two other jobs in the machine: it is the coating on tin-plated steel (tinplate, though a home computer case is not canned food) and it is the facing on tin-plated copper-alloy switch and connector contacts, where it stops the copper from tarnishing and gives a low and stable contact resistance.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: cassiterite, SnO2, at 0.2-1.5% Sn in alluvial and lode deposits

metal.tin.refining.name: Tin refining: liquation or electrolysis to 99.9%
metal.tin.refining.description: Crude tin at 99.5-99.8% still carries iron, copper and arsenic, and the difference between 99.5% and 99.9% matters enormously for solder because iron is a solder poison and raises the liquidus. Two routes. Liquation, the old one, melts the crude tin at about 400 C: tin melts at 232 C, so the iron and copper stay solid and bottom out, and the clean tin is drawn off. Electrolysis, the modern one, uses a stannic chloride or a fluorostannate bath and gives 99.97-99.99%. Malaysia ran electrolysis; Bolivia's low-grade concentrate still used liquation.

facts.label: Liquation
facts.value: melt at 380-400 C; iron and copper stay solid

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: iron above ~0.1% wets badly and raises the melting range of solder

metal.tin.plating.name: Tin plating of steel and of copper alloys
metal.tin.plating.description: Tinplate - a 1.1-11.2 g/m2 tin coating on 0.15-0.3 mm of steel - is made by electrolytic tinning of a continuous steel strip on a horizontal passivating line: the strip is degreased, pickled in acid, tinned in a sulphate or fluoroborate bath, rinsed, and then either passivated in chromic acid (food can) or - through the 1980s - given an electrolytic chromate or tin-oxide passivation to stop the tin growing dendrites during storage. Food can was the dominant market by mass. A C64 uses tinplate only incidentally, in a switch body or a shield; tin plating of copper-alloy contacts uses a different chemistry altogether and is the node that matters for the machine.

facts.label: Coating mass
facts.value: 1.1-11.2 g/m2 (2.8-28.2 g per 100 cm2); 5-6 g/m2 typical for electronics sheet

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: chromic acid for food can, or an electrolytic chromate or oxide passivation in the 1980s

facts.label: Tinplate market
facts.value: food can was about 90% of production

metal.tin.contact-plating.name: Tin plating of copper-alloy contacts
metal.tin.contact-plating.description: Not tinplate on steel, but tin on brass or phosphor bronze - the plating on the contacts of a C64 switch or a keyboard connector. The 1980s chemistry was an acid stannate or an alkaline stannate bath: SnSO4 with sulfuric acid, or sodium stannate with caustic soda and a puller such as sodium gluconate. Tin is on a connector contact because it forms a soft, low-resistance, non-tarnishing intermetallic with the copper. The reason it fails is the tin whisker - a single-crystal filament of tin that grows out of the plating under compressive stress in humid storage and can bridge a 0.1 mm gap. Tin whiskers were the reliability nemesis of exactly this kind of contact.
metal.tin.contact-plating.note: The specific plating system used on Commodore's connectors is not something I can confirm; both chemistries were in use in 1982. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 2-5 um of tin on a Cu-Sn alloy or brass

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: tin whisker growth, and on tin-plated copper under high stress, copper-tin intermetallic embrittlement

metal.tin.ingot.name: Refined tin ingot or tin powder, 99.9-99.97%
metal.tin.ingot.description: Shipped as a 25-50 kg or 250 kg ingot at 99.9-99.97%, or - for the electronics industry - atomised into a fine powder. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tin smelting branch and the solder branch: the solder manufacturer needs the ingot, and the solder-paste manufacturer needs the powder. Iron is the impurity that matters, because iron is a solder poison that wets badly and raises the liquidus.

facts.label: Powder
facts.value: atomised, 10-25 um, for solder paste and for making solder alloy powder

facts.label: 1982 context
facts.value: most electronics soldering was still a hand or wave-solder pot of solid-core wire; paste was a minority

metal.tin.atomisation.name: Air atomisation of tin to powder
metal.tin.atomisation.description: Molten tin at about 1150 C is poured into a launder and a high-pressure air jet at the bottom of a vertical stack sprays it into a fog of droplets that solidify on the way down. It is cheap, it works for metals that do not oxidise much, and it gives a bimodal powder. Under nitrogen it gives the fine, oxide-free powder that solder paste needs. Every particle in the can came out of a slot in a nozzle.
metal.tin.atomisation.note: The 1980s powder market was real but small relative to solid wire; medium confidence on relative volumes.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: air, or nitrogen for the low-oxide grade

metal.tin.smelting.name: Tin smelting: reduction of SnO2 with carbon
metal.tin.smelting.description: Cassiterite is one of the easiest oxide ores to reduce: SnO2 + C -> Sn + CO2 goes at only 1200-1400 C, far below copper or iron, because tin's oxides are unstable. The Malaysian and Indonesian smelters in 1982 were reverberatory or electric furnaces on 5-20 t capacity, fired with coke, charged with concentrate and about 15% limestone as a flux, and tapped a crude tin at 99.5-99.8% in maybe eight hours. The furnace is a long, narrow, brick-lined box with a step grate at the firebox end, so the charge moves gradually forward and meets rising temperatures - a reverberatory used for a purely solid-solid reaction, which is why tin smelting smells of SO2 only when the concentrate is sulphide.
metal.tin.smelting.note: Tin smelting is one of the few pyro-metallurgical processes that did not move to electric furnaces until well after 1982.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: SnO2 + 2C -> Sn + 2CO; below 1200 C the reduction is too slow

facts.label: Reagent
facts.value: coke or anthracite, 15-25% of concentrate mass

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 15% limestone, to take silica into the slag

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron and silica with some tin left in it - the usual tin smelter loss is 1-3%

metal.tin.slag.name: The tin smelter's slag and its tin loss
metal.tin.slag.description: A tin smelter loses 1-3% of its tin into the slag, and the slag is a silicate of iron and silica with tin locked up in it. Recovering that tin is a separate business: the slag is crushed and re-smelted, or in Malaysia and Brazil it was re-smelted in a small furnace to recover the tin. A tin smelter therefore has a second, smaller smelter, and the discipline of a tin plant is judged by its recovery, which is why the industry published recovery figures with a seriousness that most primary metals do not.
metal.tin.slag.note: Medium confidence on the loss figure; it varies with the slag basicity and the furnace.

facts.label: Loss to slag
facts.value: 1-3% of the tin in the charge

metal.tin.charge-prep.name: Charge preparation: drying, sieving, mixing
metal.tin.charge-prep.description: Cassiterite concentrates are roasted if they carry fluorine or arsenic, dried to remove the 8-12% moisture, and sieved - because a reverberatory furnace with fine charge in it just makes dust. The charge is then mixed with the limestone flux and the coke, in the ratio that gives 15-20% flux and 15-25% reductant. Nothing about this is clever and everything about it is critical: an Indonesian smelter that got the coke ratio wrong lost a few percent of its tin into the slag, which at 3% is a third of its margin.
metal.tin.charge-prep.note: Medium confidence; the ratios are typical of Southeast Asian practice.

metal.tin.bolivian-roast.name: Roasting of fluorine-bearing Bolivian concentrate
metal.tin.bolivian-roast.description: Bolivian concentrates carry fluorine, which would carry through into the tin as a stubborn impurity. So they are roasted at 600-800 C before smelting to drive off the fluorine as HF and the arsenic as arsenic oxide, and the hot gas is scrubbed with lime to make calcium fluoride before release. That lime scrub is a genuine environmental control fitted in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is one of the reasons the smelters are the only tin plants with a scrubber.
metal.tin.bolivian-roast.note: Applied mainly to Bolivian and Brazilian concentrates; medium confidence on the exact scrub chemistry.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 600-800 C in a rotary or fluidised-bed roaster

facts.label: Offgas scrub
facts.value: limestone slurry neutralises the HF, giving calcium fluoride

metal.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) and hydrofluoric acid
metal.fluorspar.description: Fluorine chemistry is unavoidable in aluminium and unavoidable in the tin smelter's gas scrub and in the tantalum digest. Fluorspar, the commonest natural fluoride, was mined mainly from Mexico's San Luis Potosi and Chihuahua districts and from South Africa's Transvaal, and about 90% of all fluorite went into aluminium electrolysis - as cryolite feed, as calcium fluoride in the bath, and as flux. Hydrofluoric acid is made from it, and HF is the reagent that turns silicon into trichlorosilane in the silicon branch, tantalum into K2TaF7 in the tantalum branch, and glass into etch gas in the plastics-and-glass branch - so this is one of the genuine convergence points of the whole tree. Note that the 1980s ozone worry about fluorocarbons does NOT apply here: this is the calcium salt, not a CFC.

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~90% to aluminium smelting for cryolite and bath flux; the rest to HF and to steelmaking

metal.fluorspar.mine.name: Fluorite open-pit and underground mine
metal.fluorspar.mine.description: Fluorite fills the cavities and fracture zones of limestone, so it is mined either as a replacement body in a working limestone quarry or as a vein. Mexican fluorite was underground at Naica - where it grows the famous 12 m transparent crystals in a cave - and in open pits in Chihuahua. The South African deposits are in the carbonate sequences of the Transvaal Group, and the Chinese and Mongolian ones, which became dominant in the late 1980s, are in greisen and vein systems related to granite.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: epigenetic fill in limestone cavities, and veins in greisen

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit and underground, with flotation to 60-95% CaF2

metal.fluorspar.vein.name: Fluorite vein in limestone
metal.fluorspar.vein.description: The leaf: a purple, green or white vein of CaF2 a few centimetres to a few metres thick in a fractured carbonate host, in a limestone hill.

metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.name: Fluid-bed reduction of fine cassiterite (later invention)
metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.description: Worth noting as the direction the industry went in rather than as 1982 practice: the fine concentrates that a gravity circuit now produces reduce easily in a fluidised bed at 850-1000 C, which is a temperature no reverberatory furnace can hold at its hearth. This process is why the modern tin industry uses much less coke and produces much less CO. In 1982 essentially none of this existed.
metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.note: Post-1982 process; marked era=modern so the tree does not imply it existed in the C64 window.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: lower carbon and lower reductant per tonne; adopted after 1985

metal.cassiterite.name: Cassiterite concentrate (SnO2)
metal.cassiterite.description: Cassiterite is a very heavy, very hard, brown-to-black mineral - the specific gravity of 7 makes gravity separation unusually effective on it, which is why tin mining has always had a placer tradition. The concentrates bought by an smelter in 1982 came from four very different operations: alluvial and offshore dredging in Malaysia and Indonesia, hard-rock lodes in the Bolivian and Brazilian Precambrian shields, hard-rock in Cornwall and the Pan, and shallow residual deposits in Thailand and Nigeria. Concentrates assayed 40-80% Sn with arsenic, iron, tungsten and fluorine as the problem impurities - fluorine in particular is the reason the Bolivian smelter needed a roast.

facts.label: Smelting route
facts.value: 70% of world tin was smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Bolivia; China emerged in the 1990s

facts.label: Problem impurities
facts.value: As, Fe, W, and F (fluorine in Bolivian concentrates)

metal.cassiterite.alluvial.name: Alluvial cassiterite gravel: dredging and panning
metal.cassiterite.alluvial.description: Tin gravel is a beach or stream deposit: pebbles and clay with a few grams of cassiterite per tonne. The classical recovery is the sluice and the jig, where a stream of water over an inclined riffled box stratifies by density and the heavy mineral stays behind. The Kinta Valley in Perak, Malaysia, was dredged on an enormous scale from the 1900s through the 1980s by suction dredges working a 100 m wide alluvial fan at 30-100 m depth, pumping gravel through a 3-6 inch suction pipe to a floating washing plant and a jig. Off Thailand and Indonesia it was offshore and shallow-sea dredging. Gravel is essentially quarried from a sea floor.

facts.label: Recovery route
facts.value: sluice box, jig, then a shaking table and a magnetic separator

facts.label: 1982s shift
facts.value: the Kinta dredging era was ending and hard-rock and residual mining was taking over as the Malaysian industry

metal.cassiterite.gravel.name: Stanniferous alluvium and laterite
metal.cassiterite.gravel.description: The leaf: unconsolidated stony clay and gravel of a valley floor or a coastal plain, with cassiterite grains scattered through it and concentrated at the base of gravel layers where the wave or the stream action is right. In Malaysia it is a young alluvial fan over limestone; in Bolivia it is not alluvial at all but a hard-rock lode in Ordovician slates and granites, which is why Bolivia's process chain is longer.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: alluvial gravel over limestone (Perak) or residual laterite over a lode (Bolivia, Cornwall)

metal.cassiterite.lode.name: Cassiterite lode in the Bolivian and Cornwall tin belt
metal.cassiterite.lode.description: For contrast: the tin lodes of the Cordillera Real in Bolivia and of the Cambrian granite cupolas in Cornwall are hydrothermal cassiterite in quartz veins and greisens, and they have to be blasted and milled. Bolivia's Oruro and La Paz districts still supply a fraction of world tin from ore averaging 0.3-1% Sn, with the famous manioc mill and the hydraulic concentrator. Cornwall's industry was by 1982 essentially finished - the last deep mine closed in 1984 - a hundred years after the smelter industry had been moved to the East.

facts.label: Cornwall's end
facts.value: Grezmerry closed in 1984, ending Cornish tin mining after 2,500 years

metal.cassiterite.greisen.name: Greisen and quartz vein
metal.cassiterite.greisen.description: The leaf for the hard-rock route: a pneumatolytic alteration halo of topaz-bearing greisen and milky quartz with cassiterite disseminated through it, around a granite cupola. It is a rock, it is in a hillside, and it is drilled.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: greisen and quartz vein in a granite cupploa

metal.cassiterite.topaz.name: Topaz and the greisen alteration
metal.cassiterite.topaz.description: The leaf, geologically: a pneumatolytic alteration halo around the granite cupola in which the feldspars are replaced by topaz (Al2SiO4F2) and quartz, and in the interstices sit the crystals of cassiterite, wolframite and native bismuth. The fluorine in the topaz is the whole reason the alteration happened - it is a fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluid - which is a satisfying way for the tin branch to close, because the same fluorine chemistry that greened the rocks is the fluorine chemistry that made the cryolite in the aluminium pot and the hydrofluoric acid for the silicon plant.
metal.cassiterite.topaz.note: Medium confidence; the greisen mineralogy is standard, the specific Cornwall detail is a generalisation.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: greisen around a granite cupola, with quartz and cassiterite in the interstices

metal.copper.name: Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts
metal.copper.description: The most-used metal after iron, and in a C64 it is everywhere the electricity goes and everywhere the heat has to leave. The PCB tracks are 35 um copper foil on 1.6 mm FR-4; the switch-mode transformer is wound with 0.2-0.4 mm enamelled magnet wire; the rectifiers and the regulator leadframes are copper; the edge connector fingers and the heatsink mounts are copper alloy. All of it starts as porphyry ore at 0.4-1% Cu, which is why copper smelters are, in the 1980s, as much sulfuric acid plants as they are metal plants.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu in porphyry; US average fell to ~0.55% by 1980

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 0.6% ore -> 1 t of concentrate at 28% Cu -> ~0.3 t of Cu metal in the concentrate

metal.copper.crushing.name: Crushing, the copper-in-sulphide test and the mine call
metal.copper.crushing.description: Ore that has been crushed and assayed is worth what its copper is worth, and the assay is the contract between the mine and the mill. A fire assay of a 100 g charge gives the total copper, and a leach assay of the fines gives the recoverable copper, and the difference between them - the oxide and locked-up copper - is what makes a mill's flowsheet design difficult. The crush is a gyratory at 1500 t/h followed by a screen, and nothing about a porphyry ore is subtle except this.
metal.copper.crushing.note: Medium confidence; the assays are standard but the plant flowsheet detail is site-specific.

facts.label: Crusher
facts.value: 1500-4000 t/h gyratory, with a screen at 25-50 mm

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: fire assay for total copper, leach assay for the oxide fraction

metal.copper.foil.name: Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil
metal.copper.foil.description: Two completely different foils with the same name, and this is a deliberate convergence node. The PCB foil is 35 um copper (70 um on very old boards) electrolytically deposited or rolled; the C64's board is single-sided, so it is one sheet of foil laminated to 1.6 mm FR-4. The capacitor foil is electro-deposited drum foil, deposited 6-18 um onto a rotating stainless or titanium drum from a copper sulphate bath, stripped and wound, then roughened again for etching just like aluminium foil.

facts.label: PCB foil
facts.value: 35 um (2 oz/sq ft) standard, 70 um on very early boards

facts.label: Capacitor foil
facts.value: 6-18 um electro-deposited, with base copper under the etched layer

metal.copper.foil.ra.name: Rolled annealed copper foil
metal.copper.foil.ra.description: The traditional foil: heavy copper strip rolled on a Sendimir mill to 35-105 um and slit. It has a rolled, fibrous grain that is anisotropic, so it is easy to form and easy to drill, and it was the foil of record for anything that needs to be bent rather than etched. By 1982 electronic-grade rolled foil had been mostly displaced by electro-deposited foil for PCBs because deposition was cheaper and the bonding treatment was more reliable, but rolled foil remained the foil of choice for fine pitch and for capacitor cathodes.
metal.copper.foil.ra.note: Copper foil mills are Sendimir-type 20-high machines, the same family as the aluminium foil mill; medium confidence on which mill type made which foil in 1982.

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: rolled and elongated along the rolling direction

facts.label: 1982 position
facts.value: electro-deposited foil had taken most of the PCB market; rolled foil kept the high end and the cathode business

metal.copper.foil.ed-drum.name: Electro-deposited drum foil
metal.copper.foil.ed-drum.description: A rotating drum cathode, 1-2 m diameter and 1-1.5 m wide, dips into an acid copper sulphate bath and turns; copper plates onto it at 20-100 A/dm2. A scraper peels the foil off at the top of the drum as a continuous 6-18 um web, which is then slit and wound. The deposit is not bulk metal: it is a columnar, sometimes dendritic growth, which is exactly why it etches into foil capacitors so well and why, for PCBs, it needs a bonding treatment before the laminate resin will stick to it.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: CuSO4/H2SO4 with a brightener and a suppressant; the additive package is proprietary

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: columnar and favourably oriented, unlike rolled foil's rolled structure

metal.copper.foil.bonding.name: Nodular treatment for PCB foil adhesion
metal.copper.foil.bonding.description: Bare copper foil will not bond to epoxy; it delaminates. So the foil is treated in a warm sulfuric acid bath with a silicofluoride or a silane - historically sodium silicofluoride, later silanes - which grows a forest of microscopic oxide nodules on the surface. The resin flows into the forest and locks in, and the peel strength goes from a few N/cm to about 20 N/cm. This etching of the foil surface is the single most important step in making a copper-clad laminate, and the silicofluoride comes from the same fluorochemical industry as the hydrofluoric acid in the aluminium and tantalum branches.
metal.copper.foil.bonding.note: The exact chemistry shifted through the 1980s and the chromate-era process was being abandoned for toxicological reasons; medium confidence.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: 0.5-2.5% silicofluoride in 15-30% sulfuric acid at 40-70 C

facts.label: Peel strength
facts.value: order 20 N/cm after treatment, versus a few N/cm untreated

facts.label: 1982 practice
facts.value: sodium silicofluoride in sulfuric acid; the chromic-acid treatment was being phased out

metal.copper.wire.name: Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings
metal.copper.wire.description: The switch-mode transformer in a C64's power supply - and any small mains-frequency transformer - is a coil of enamelled copper wire. The wire starts as 6-8 mm rod, is patented (heated to 200-350 C so the work-hardening from drawing anneals out), then drawn through a series of diamond dies to 0.15-0.5 mm, then enamelled and baked. 1982's magnet wire was overwhelmingly polyurethane enamel, sometimes with a nylon or polyester overcoat; polyurethane is the classic because it strips cleanly from the copper and does not need a flame to remove. This is a deliberate convergence node: the transformer winding, the ferrite core and the soldered joint all come off it.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: AWG 24-34 (0.5 down to 0.2 mm) for a small transformer; AWG 38-42 for fine coils

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyurethane, thermal class 130-155, sometimes with a polyester or nylon overcoat

facts.label: Film build
facts.value: 15-40 um total for a class 155 wire

metal.copper.enamelling.name: Enamelling and cure of magnet wire
metal.copper.enamelling.description: The drawn wire is passed through a die and coated with liquid polyurethane enamel in a continuous length of 10-20 coats, each flash-dried, then cured in a vertical oven at 150-220 C for up to an hour. The result is a wire whose insulation survives a 155 C winding temperature and whose dielectric strength is 5-10 kV between turns. Enamelling is a chemical coating line rather than a metallurgy process, but the wire underneath it is this branch's problem.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 10-20 flash-dried coats for a 15-40 um build

metal.copper.enamelling.furnace.name: The enamelling line and the cure oven
metal.copper.enamelling.furnace.description: A magnet-wire enamelling line is a 20-40 m long machine: a pay-off, a bunch of dies applying 10-20 coats with flash-off between them, a vertical cure oven 8-15 m tall, a capstan, a take-up. The cure oven is gas or electric at 150-220 C with the wire passing through it in a helix, and it is the cure schedule and not the coating that decides the wire's class. A class 155 wire needs a full hour at temperature; a class 130 wire can get away with less. In 1982 the whole world's magnet wire was made on lines of exactly this design, whether the wire came from Japan, France or the United States.
metal.copper.enamelling.furnace.note: Medium confidence on the speed range; it is strongly gauge-dependent.

facts.label: Speed
facts.value: 60-300 m/min depending on the wire gauge

metal.copper.enamel-resin.name: Polyurethane enamel from a di-isocyanate
metal.copper.enamel-resin.description: The wire enamel is a thermosetting urethane, made from a diol and a di-isocyanate such as toluene di-isocyanate, with a blocked-isocyanate cure so the coating is stable in the coating bath and only reacts in the cure oven. Its advantage over phenolic (vinyl formal, the pre-war standard) and polyester is that it strips cleanly and bonds without a heat gun. So a C64 transformer's insulation is a chemical product of the polyurethane industry, not a distillation product.
metal.copper.enamel-resin.note: The chemistry of commercial wire enamels is proprietary; medium confidence on the general description.

facts.label: Former standard
facts.value: vinyl formal (phenolic) enamel, still used for thermal class 180

metal.copper.multiwire-drawing.name: Multiwire drawing through diamond dies
metal.copper.multiwire-drawing.description: Since the 1960s the industry stopped drawing one wire at a time and started drawing 7-19 wires simultaneously through a cone of dies, so the die size needed for a 0.2 mm wire is much larger and lasts much longer. The dies are natural diamond - or, as synthetic diamond tooling matured through the 1980s, polycrystalline diamond compact - set in a steel holder with a hardened steel casing. Drawing to 0.15 mm means the copper has been elongated by a factor of order 1600, which is why magnet wire is made only from low-oxygen, low-sulphur electrolytic cathode and never from cast copper.

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: 7-19 wires per pass through coned dies

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: natural diamond or synthetic PCD in a steel holder

facts.label: Total reduction to 0.2 mm
facts.value: from 8 mm, a total elongation of order 1.6 x 10^3

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: needed above about 1-2 mm drawn diameter

metal.copper.patenting.name: Patenting: annealing the rod before drawing
metal.copper.patenting.description: Copper work-hardens fast: a few percent of reduction raises the tensile strength enormously and the wire simply snaps in the die. So the rod is heated - in steam, in air, or in a fluidised bed - to about 200-350 C, which recrystallises the elongated drawing structure back to equiaxed grains, and then quenched. The black oxide that air patenting leaves is actually helpful, because it stops the wire rusting in the draw bin. Patenting is the cheapest trick in the whole wire business.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 200-350 C in steam, or a fluidised bed at up to about 400 C

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: recrystallisation: copper goes from about 60-70 kg/mm2 work-hardened to 35-45 kg/mm2 annealed

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: steam or air - air leaves a useful black oxide; inert gas only for fine wire

metal.copper.wire-lubricant.name: Drawing lubricant: copper sulfonate or oil emulsion
metal.copper.wire-lubricant.description: The die must be lubricated or the copper galls and the die wears out. In the 1980s the standard was a water-based emulsion or a copper-sulfonate-and-fatty-acid concentrate, applied in a die box or as a once-through bath. Lubricant chemistry is also the friction and galling story in the die, which is why the drawing lubricant industry is a small speciality chemical business rather than an oil business.
metal.copper.wire-lubricant.note: Formulations are proprietary; medium confidence on the general chemistry.

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: copper sulfonate or ammonium sulfonate in a fatty-acid base, or an oil-in-water emulsion

metal.copper.tankhouse.name: Electrolytic refining of copper to 99.99%
metal.copper.tankhouse.description: The refinery's tankhouse is a building a couple of hundred metres long containing rows of concrete or rubber-lined steel cells. Each cell holds a 150-250 g/L copper, 200-250 g/L free sulfuric acid solution at 55-65 C, with one or two anodes and one cathode per cell. Current at 20,000-40,000 A per cell is passed through; copper dissolves off the anode and plates onto the cathode at 98-99% efficiency, and gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and the platinum group fall out as a sludge on the bottom of the cell - the anode slime - which is worth more per tonne than the copper. A refinery producing 100,000 t a year has 300-500 cells and about 100,000 MWh of DC power.
metal.copper.tankhouse.note: Tankhouse technology has changed very little since 1982; the later innovation was more automation and the move to higher current density with ion-exchange purification.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 0.15-0.35 V; power about 200-250 kWh per tonne of copper

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, LME Grade A 99.9935%, one cathodic plate ~1 m x 1 m, 50-125 kg

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: anode 4-28 days, cathode 4-14 days, by plate weight

metal.copper.tankhouse.starters.name: Starter sheets, seeding and the tankhouse floor
metal.copper.tankhouse.starters.description: Everything in a tankhouse depends on nucleation. The cathodes start on stainless steel or titanium starter sheets, or on copper seed plates that have been roughened. If too many nuclei start, the deposit is dull and soft and hard to strip; if too few, it is bright and hard and needs a big shear force. The whole art is seeding the right number. The electrolyte is also circulated at 200-400 mm/s across the cell face, because the anode slime would otherwise build up and short.
metal.copper.tankhouse.starters.note: Medium confidence; the seeding practice is proprietary.

facts.label: Starters
facts.value: stainless steel or titanium, or roughened copper seed plates

facts.label: Slime removal
facts.value: a travelling scraper on the cell floor

metal.anode-slime.name: Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper
metal.anode-slime.description: The sludge on the tankhouse cell floor, 5-20 kg per tonne of copper refined, containing gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium. It is dried and shipped to precious-metals refineries, where the gold is separated by cupellation, the selenium by roasting to SeO2 and volatilising, and the platinum group metals by solvent extraction and precipitation. By 1982 the anode slime was typically worth more per tonne than the copper in the anode, and a copper mine with good gold credits could be a gold mine that happened to have copper in it. This is a deliberate convergence node: the copper, gold and silver branches all meet in it.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 5-20 kg of dry slime per tonne of copper

facts.label: Value in 1982
facts.value: typically 30-100% of the value of the contained copper

metal.anode-slime.cupellation.name: Cupellation of the gold-silver dross
metal.anode-slime.cupellation.description: The slime is smelted with lead and flux into a litharge, then the litharge is blown with air in a cupellation furnace. The lead and everything else oxidises and is absorbed by a bone-ash or magnesite cupel, and what is left on the cupel is gold and silver together. This is the oldest refinery process in the book and it was still standard in 1982, because it is simple and it works.

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 6-24 h per charge depending on the mass

metal.cupellation.cupel.name: Bone ash cupel from animal bone
metal.cupellation.cupel.description: Traditional cupels are made of calcined bone - tricalcium phosphate - ground and pressed into a shallow cup with a porous, low-density surface that absorbs the molten litharge. Bone ash is the reason cupellation is called what it is, and by the 1982 industry the major refineries had largely moved to magnesia and alumina cupels for the big furnaces, though bone ash was still in use. So a refinery furnace foot was, historically, a rendering-house product.
metal.cupellation.cupel.note: By 1982 the major refineries were largely on magnesia or alumina cupels; medium confidence that bone ash remained in use anywhere significant.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: calcined bone ash Ca3(PO4)2, or magnesia or alumina for larger units

metal.palladium.name: Platinum-group metals from the anode slime
metal.palladium.description: The anode slime also carries platinum, palladium, ruthenium, iridium, rhodium and osmium, at grams per tonne of copper rather than kilograms, so the volumes are tiny and the values are astronomical. In 1982 most of the world's refined palladium came from the nickel-copper ores of the Sudbury and Norilsk basins and from the Bushveld's platinum mines rather than from the copper anode slimes, but the slimes were a real secondary source for platinum and rhodium. The refining route is a solvent extraction and precipitation circuit followed by a final electrolytic or thermal refining, and by 1982 the platinum-group market was dominated by South Africa and the Soviet Union, whose platinum was the ore of choice for autocatalyst converters in the 1970s - which is a genuine and slightly absurd piece of industrial history, since the autocatalyst is a device for cleaning up the exhaust of a car and the platinum came out of the same layered intrusion as the chrome in the ignition plugs.
metal.palladium.note: Medium confidence on the slime assays; the primary sources and the autocatalyst history are well documented.

facts.label: PGM in anode slime
facts.value: grams per tonne of copper; order 0.5-5 g/t of each metal

facts.label: Primary sources 1982
facts.value: the Bushveld Complex in South Africa and the Norilsk nickel-copper ores in the USSR

facts.label: 1970s driver
facts.value: autocatalyst demand set the platinum-group market

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: solvent extraction and precipitation, then electrolytic or thermal refining

metal.copper.cathode.name: Electrolytic copper cathode, 99.99%
metal.copper.cathode.description: The end product of the mine-to-metal chain and the shape in which essentially all world copper trades. A flat plate grown on a stainless steel or copper starter sheet, with a characteristic slightly rough surface because too many nucleation sites make a soft, dull deposit. Cathode mass is 45-125 kg depending on the refinery. Weighed, sampled, stamped and shipped. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tankhouse branch, the foil branch and the wire branch.

facts.label: Typical impurities
facts.value: Fe 3-8 ppm, S 1-10 ppm, Pb 1-10 ppm, O 10-50 ppm

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

metal.copper.anode.casting.name: Anode casting and the anode scrap stream
metal.copper.anode.casting.description: About 10-20% of the anode never makes it into a cell - it is broken in handling, or the bars are too thin, or the busbar is corroded away - and it goes back to be remelted and recast. Every tankhouse therefore has a stub and an anode scrap yard and a melt, and the plant's anode book is a mass balance between the smelter's output and the tankhouse's demand. At the end of its life an anode is a thin, perforated, gold-bearing skeleton of iron and lead oxide that goes back to the smelter, so the gold in the anode is in a closed loop with the refinery and the melt is where the loop is closed.
metal.copper.anode.casting.note: Medium confidence on the stub and scrap rate; it varies by tankhouse practice.

facts.label: Anode stub and scrap
facts.value: 10-20% of the anode mass returns to remelting

facts.label: Busbar
facts.value: a cast copper bar, and the contact point where the anode is electrically connected

metal.copper.ingot-casting.name: Copper ingot and rod casting
metal.copper.ingot-casting.description: The cathode is melted in an induction furnace or a reverberatory with a controlled sulphur addition, then cast - either continuously into wire rod by the Properzi upcast method or into 250-450 kg ingots for further processing. The 1980s standard route to rod was continuous casting; the alternative, longer route was a DC casting machine feeding a wire rod mill. Melting loses almost nothing because copper does not oxidise appreciably; the real problem is gas absorption.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 1150-1250 C, induction or gas-fired reverberatory, under a cover

facts.label: Rod diameters
facts.value: 6.0-8.0 mm for drawing, cast as wire rod

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: phosphorus added as a copper-phosphorus master alloy, 0.01-0.05% residual

metal.copper.upcasting.name: Upcast wire rod line
metal.copper.upcasting.description: In the Properzi upcaster the melt runs out of a horizontal holding furnace into a vertical casting trough behind a steel die that is being drawn upward by a rotating carousel; the trough is water-cooled and the copper solidifies against the moving die face, giving a controlled solidification structure. It makes 6-9 mm rod very cheaply and was standard in the 1980s, though the resulting cast structure needs patenting before drawing.
metal.copper.upcasting.note: Upcasting was still widely used in the 1980s but continuous casting replaced it from the 1990s; medium confidence on the 1982 split.

metal.copper.anode.name: Blister copper anode, 99.9%+
metal.copper.anode.description: Blister is poured into a horizontal straight-mould casting machine - a ladle of molten copper that pours into a row of cast-iron moulds on a moving chain, giving a rectangular anode of 200-500 kg, roughly 700-1000 mm long, 400-800 mm wide and 30-50 mm thick, with a hanging loop cast on top. In 1982 the standard anode assay was 99.5-99.9% copper, and the gold and silver in it - typically 5-30 g/t gold equivalent - is why anodes are not made to 99.99%: that would be throwing away money.

facts.label: Casting method
facts.value: horizontal straight-mould casting machine with a water-cooled chain

metal.copper.converting.name: Peirce-Smith converter to blister copper
metal.copper.converting.description: The matte from the flash furnace is charged into a horizontal cylindrical steel converter with refractory lining and is blown with air through tuyeres along the side. The iron in the matte oxidises preferentially and goes into a slag that is skimmed off the top every few hours; once the iron is gone the copper sulphide itself oxidises to copper metal and gives off SO2. The blow takes 4-8 hours and takes 1 t of 60% matte to roughly 0.85 t of blister copper at 98-99% purity, still containing iron, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. The converter is a batch process and by the 1980s it was the target of the new continuous technologies (Noranda, Inductokemco) that were not yet commercial.
metal.copper.converting.note: The Peirce-Smith converter remained the dominant technology into the 2020s, accounting for roughly 90% of world matte refining.

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron silicate, skimmed through the converter mouth

metal.copper.converter.name: The Peirce-Smith converter and its tuyeres
metal.copper.converter.description: The converter is a cylindrical steel shell, 3.5-4.8 m inside diameter and 8-10 m long, on trunnions so it can be tilted, lined with magnesite brick, with 20-40 tuyeres along one side at the trunnion line. Air at 30-50% oxygen is blown in at 5-10 bar through water-cooled tuyeres that must be cleared and re-cleared by hand every few hours as the lining erodes - and a tuyeres that is not cleared becomes a plug and the whole heat is lost. The operator tilts the converter so the slag runs out of the mouth, then charges back, and there is no continuous process anywhere else in smelting with quite that much manual involvement. It is the machine that has been unchanged since 1865, and it is still the standard.
metal.copper.converter.note: Medium confidence; the Peirce-Smith converter geometry is very well documented.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 3.5-4.8 m diameter, 8-10 m long, on trunnions

facts.label: Tuyeres
facts.value: 20-40, water-cooled, hand-cleaned of lining several times a heat

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesite brick, eroded by the oxidising slag

facts.label: Slag removal
facts.value: the converter is tilted so the slag pours out of the mouth

metal.copper.fire-refining.name: Fire refining and the anodic slimes of arsenic
metal.copper.fire-refining.description: Blister copper still carries arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and every one of them is a nightmare for the electrolytic tankhouse because they float to the cathode and destroy the deposit. So the blister is ladle-refined: an oxidising slag of sodium carbonate with the impurities skims off, and then the copper is under-oxidised by dropping in green charcoal to reduce the whole mass back to copper, with the arsenic floatationised out. Where the arsenic is high, the refinery buys a second, smaller furnace.
metal.copper.fire-refining.note: There was real variation in refinery strategy between operators in this era; medium confidence on specifics.

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: As, Sb and Bi down to 0.02-0.1% before anode casting

facts.label: 1982s practice
facts.value: outright refining in the converter or in a tilting launder furnace; anode casting with a low-As anode became the later route

metal.copper.smelting.name: Flash smelting of concentrate to copper matte
metal.copper.smelting.description: Concentrate, silica flux and limestone are dropped into a vertical reverberatory shaft where a hot gas blast, 40-60% oxygen-enriched, burns the concentrate as it falls. Three reactions happen simultaneously: the sulphides oxidise to copper oxide and iron oxide, the oxides react with each other to form a copper-iron matte, and the iron oxide reacts with the silica flux to make a slag. The furnace runs at 1250-1400 C and the products settle into three layers - matte at the bottom, slag above it, and offgas above that - which are tapped separately. By 1982 the flash furnace had largely displaced the reverberatory furnace: it is smaller, faster and needs less fuel, and it works on concentrate straight from the flotation circuit with only a small amount of dried concentrate added as fuel.
metal.copper.smelting.note: Copper smelting has barely changed since the 1980s; the industry still runs flash furnaces and Peirce-Smith converters today. The changes since are in slag cleaning and in higher oxygen enrichment.

facts.label: Dried concentrate as fuel
facts.value: order 0.15-0.35 t per tonne of charge

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 held around 1.0-1.5 so the slag stays fluid

facts.label: SO2 strength
facts.value: 10-14% SO2 in the flash furnace offgas, which the acid plant takes

metal.copper.flash-furnace.name: The flash furnace, its tuyeres and the concentrate burn
metal.copper.flash-furnace.description: The furnace is a 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter vertical shaft with a refractory lining, fed by a few hundred tonnes an hour of dried concentrate through a hopper, and blown at the bottom by 30-60% oxygen-enriched air through tuyeres. The concentrate burns as it falls - it is the fuel as well as the charge - so the furnace needs almost no external heat. The reaction happens in the first metre above the tuyeres, the particles are spent, and the matte and slag settle into the two-deep bath at the bottom. The shaft above is used to preheat the charge with the rising offgas, and a flash furnace treats more tonnage in less volume than anything else in smelting.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter, refractory lined

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: two layers: matte at the bottom, slag above

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: the concentrate is both the charge and the fuel, so the furnace is close to thermoneutral

metal.sulphuric-acid.name: Sulphuric acid, 93-99%, from smelter SO2
metal.sulphuric-acid.description: The most-produced inorganic chemical in the world, and about half to three fifths of it was made not from burning sulphur but from the offgas of the copper, zinc and lead smelters in this file. The plants are the same: gas cleaning, drying, 10-14% SO2, 400-450 C over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, absorption in 98-99% acid in the first absorber, and then a second absorber with fresher acid - the double contact, double absorption process that was the industry standard by 1982. This node is the deliberate convergence point: the copper flash furnace, the zinc sinter plant, the lead sinter plant, the copper tankhouse and the zinc leach all feed or draw from the same acid plant.

facts.label: Inlet SO2
facts.value: 8-14% from a flash furnace, roaster or sinter plant

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: double contact / double absorption, the 1980s standard

facts.label: Acid per tonne
facts.value: roughly 3-6 t of 100% acid per tonne of copper

metal.sulphuric-acid.uses.name: Where the smelter acid goes
metal.sulphuric-acid.uses.description: Roughly half of world sulfuric acid production is made from smelter offgas. In 1982 the biggest single use was fertiliser: phosphoric acid from Florida apatite, then superphosphate. The second was metal refining - the copper tankhouse electrolyte, the zinc plant leach circuit and the iron and steel pickling line, all of which are in this tree. The third was hydrofluoric acid. So a great deal of the world's phosphate rock was fertilised with acid made from the sulphur in somebody else's copper ore.

facts.label: Global split
facts.value: ~50-60% of sulfuric acid capacity was smelter-based in the early 1980s

facts.label: End uses
facts.value: phosphoric acid and fertiliser, metal pickling, hydrofluoric acid, oil refining

metal.phosphate-ore.name: Apatite ore for phosphoric acid
metal.phosphate-ore.description: The Florida pebble phosphate - a marine sedimentary phosphorite of fossil bones and excreta - is the classic source, and it is the end consumer of most of the sulfuric acid made in the copper and zinc branches of this file. It is mined by dragline or bucket-wheel stripping of 5-15 m of overburden over a 3-6 m ore layer, then crushed and slurry-piped to a beneficiation plant. Almost no phosphate rock in 1982 came from a chemical process: the whole fertiliser industry downstream of the copper and zinc smelters is a sedimentary rock mined out of a swampy coastal plain.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: strip mining with a dragline or bucket-wheel, 3-6 m of ore under 5-15 m of overburden

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: crushing to 2-3 cm, washing in a sluice, and gravity or flotation upgrading

metal.phosphate.rock.name: Marine phosphorite bed
metal.phosphate.rock.description: The leaf: a 1-10 m bed of unconsolidated, often glauconitic phosphatic sand and clay in a marine or coastal plain sequence, sitting directly on limestone. It is dug, washed in a slurry pipeline, and floated or gravity-separated.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: marine shelf and coastal plain phosphorite, commonly over limestone

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: carbonate-fluorapatite with clays and quartz sand

metal.silica-flux.name: Silica flux from a sand quarry
metal.silica-flux.description: The smelter adds sand or quartzite so that the iron in the concentrate can be thrown off as a slag instead of entering the matte. The quartz is often a cheap nearby dune sand - which is exactly the same material the glass industry buys, and the reason a copper smelter in the 1980s had a sand dryer and a small silica prep plant. The flux is dosed so the slag's silica content matches what the concentrate brings.

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: quartz sand or quartzite, sized 0.1-1 mm

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: order 5-15% of the dry concentrate weight

metal.silica-sand.name: Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand)
metal.silica-sand.description: Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: wash, screen, dry, magnetite separation; <150 um for foundry and smelter use

facts.label: Vitrified silica
facts.value: used in foundry moulds and in fused silica, at 99.9%+

places: map of the Mississippi valley dune sands

metal.silica-sand.dune.name: Aeolian dune sand and beach placer
metal.silica-sand.dune.description: The leaf: quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges - a sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: surface dune and beach sand, over bedrock or older sediment

metal.copper.concentrate.name: Copper flotation concentrate (~25-30% Cu)
metal.copper.concentrate.description: A damp, fine, almost black powder shipped by rail or truck to the smelter. What the smelter really wants is not the copper but the sulphur, because that is what makes the smelter a sulfuric acid plant. A 25% Cu concentrate is roughly 50% sulphur and 10% iron, and the smelter's job is to burn out the iron, keep a copper-iron matte, and send every tonne of SO2 to an acid plant.

metal.copper.concentrate-handling.name: Thickening, filtration and the concentrate shipment
metal.copper.concentrate-handling.description: The flotation concentrate at 25-30% Cu arrives as a pulp at 10-20% solids and has to be dewatered to 8-12% moisture to be shipped, because shipping water is shipping money. A 30,000 t/day concentrator produces 1,000-3,000 t of concentrate a day, and it is thickened in a 30-50 m diameter tank, filtered on a vacuum belt or a plate-and-frame press, and often dried to 8% on a steam belt dryer so it does not cake in a railcar. Copper concentrate that arrives wet is worth less per tonne and smelters charge for the water.
metal.copper.concentrate-handling.note: Medium confidence on the specific flowsheet; the practice is standard.

facts.label: Moisture in
facts.value: 10-20% solids by weight from the flotation circuit

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: thickener, then vacuum filter or filter press, then a belt dryer

metal.copper.ore.name: Porphyry copper ore (0.4-1% Cu)
metal.copper.ore.description: A porphyritic intrusion - a granite-textured quartz monzonite that has been split by its own crystallisation and had its cracks filled with hot copper-bearing fluids. The copper minerals are chalcopyrite CuFeS2, bornite and chalcocite Cu2S, covellite and enargite Cu3AsS4. The ore body is graded by porphyry systems but the grade is low and getting lower, which is the whole problem with the industry. In 1982 the great producers were Chuquicamata and El Teniente in Chile, Bingham Canyon in Utah, Butte, the Arizona porphyry belt, Oyu Tolgoi and the Escondida development, and the copper belt of northern Zambia.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu, 0.3-5% S, 1-5 g/t Au and Ag as by-product credits

facts.label: Main minerals
facts.value: chalcopyrite CuFeS2, chalcocite Cu2S, bornite, covellite, enargite

facts.label: Overburden
facts.value: 50-200 m of barren porphyry and oxidized capping above the sulphide

facts.label: Decline
facts.value: average US head grade fell from ~0.9% in 1960 to ~0.55% by 1980

metal.copper.flotation.name: Froth flotation of chalcopyrite
metal.copper.flotation.description: The slurry is conditioned with lime to a pH of 8-9.5 and with a xanthate collector, then aerated in a bank of 20-50 cubic metre rectangular cells. Air bubbles pick up the particles of chalcopyrite that the collector has made water-repellent and float them into a froth; the gangue stays in the water. Each cell in a bank is stage-controlled, with a froth of 100-300 mm. In 1982 the workhorse collector was sodium or potassium ethyl xanthate, made from carbon disulphide, caustic soda and ethanol, and the frother was pine oil or a synthetic such as methyl isobutyl carbinol.

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 8.0-9.5, set with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Concentrate grade
facts.value: 20-30% Cu; about 0.3 t of concentrate per tonne of Cu metal

metal.xanthate.name: Ethyl xanthate collector from carbon disulphide
metal.xanthate.description: Xanthate is the workhorse flotation reagent, and it is a petrochemical in disguise: carbon disulphide (from natural gas or from coke-oven gas and methane) reacts with ethanol and caustic soda. Potassium and sodium ethyl xanthates were the standard 1980s collectors for sulphide copper, with a frother on top. So the flotation chemistry that recovers copper in 1982 depends on a sulphur-and-alcohol chain that ends in a gasworks, not a mine.
metal.xanthate.note: Dosage varies with mineralogy and water chemistry; medium confidence on the range.

metal.cs2-synthesis.name: Carbon disulphide from natural gas
metal.cs2-synthesis.description: Carbon disulphide, the feedstock for every xanthate collector and for the rayon and cellophane industries, was made in 1982 almost entirely from natural gas or from methane recovered from coke-oven gas: the gas and a fraction of hydrocarbon oil are passed over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C, and the carbon disulphide is condensed out. So the flotation collector that separated copper from a porphyry in Nevada was made from gas, and the same molecule went into the rayon that was in the 1980s' idea of a flame-retardant textile. It is a leaf of the copper branch that is unambiguously a chemical plant rather than a mine.
metal.cs2-synthesis.note: Medium confidence; the CS2-from-methane route is well documented.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: methane plus naphtha over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: carbon disulphide, condensed out of the gas stream

natural-gas.name: Natural gas: the atmosphere-derived feedstock
natural-gas.description: The leaf of this branch and of several others in this file. Natural gas is not mined, it is the accumulated hydrocarbon gas of ancient life that was trapped under an impermeable rock, and where it reaches the surface unburned it is burned off as a safety flare. In 1982 it fed the Haber-Bosch ammonia for the gold cyanide, the CS2 for the copper xanthate, the hydrogen for the ferrosilicon, the reforming for the direct reduction of iron ore, and the methanol for the phenol-formaldehyde and the epoxy. So the deepest shared leaf of the metals tree is not a rock at all: it is a gas that came out of the ground.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: thermogenic gas generated from buried organic matter and trapped under an impermeable caprock

facts.label: 1982 uses in this tree
facts.value: ammonia for cyanide, CS2 for xanthate, hydrogen for ferrosilicon and for direct reduction

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: most of the world's ammonia and methanol was gas-based by 1982

metal.pine-oil-frother.name: Pine oil and MIBC frothers
metal.pine-oil-frother.description: Frothers are oily surfactants that stabilise the air-water interface. Until the 1970s the standard was pine oil distilled from pine stumps and mill residues - a forestry residue, not a mineral. Pine oil was being displaced by methyl isobutyl carbinol, a petrochemical, precisely because the natural supply was limited and the synthetic one gave a more stable froth.
metal.pine-oil-frother.note: The pine oil to MIBC transition is well documented in mineral processing literature; medium confidence on exact 1982 split.

facts.label: Pine oil
facts.value: alpha-terpineol-rich fraction, from kraft and sulphite pulp-mill residues

facts.label: Synthetic
facts.value: MIBC (methyl isobutyl carbinol), fully synthetic by the 1980s

metal.caustic-lime-flotation.name: Lime and soda ash as pH regulators
metal.caustic-lime-flotation.description: Flotation needs the ore surfaces clean of slime and the water at a controlled alkaline pH, or the xanthate decomposes to xanthic acid and carbon disulphide and evaporates. Lime from a limestone kiln is the cheapest and most common regulator; soda ash where lime is unavailable; and in the deep concentrators of Chile and Arizona the process water has to be lime-treated hard before use because the Andean water is very soft and very acid.

facts.label: Water treatment
facts.value: lime softening to remove carbonate hardness where process water is soft

metal.copper.grinding.name: Crushing and grinding to 100-150 um
metal.copper.grinding.description: The ore arrives at 1 m. It goes through a gyratory crusher, then a semiautogenous mill (which uses the ore itself as the grinding medium, so no steel balls to pay for at that stage), then one or two ball mills in a closed circuit with a spiral classifier and then a cyclone. Autogenous grinding came in during the 1970s and was fully established by 1982 because it both saved the grinding media cost and produced a much cleaner surface - less steel contamination matters when you are about to float it. The grind has to be fine enough to liberate chalcopyrite but not so fine that the froth washes out.

facts.label: Product size
facts.value: P80 of 100-150 um for a porphyry flotation feed

facts.label: Typical circuit
facts.value: one 1.2-1.8 m semiautogenous mill plus two 1-1.2 m ball mills, or SAG plus ball in series

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 35-55 kWh per tonne of ore ground

facts.label: Steel contamination
facts.value: why autogenous was adopted: iron in the concentrate poisons the smelter
