metal.copper.steel-grinding-media.name: Forged steel grinding balls
metal.copper.steel-grinding-media.description: Even in an autogenous circuit the ball mills need some steel, and the balls themselves are a ferroalloy product: rail steel or scrap forged and quenched. Hardness matters more than anything - a 1982 ball mill ran 100-150 mm balls in the harder grind, and the wear rate was the plant's second-biggest cost after power. Nickel and chromium in the steel were deliberately kept low here, unlike in a crusher liner.
metal.copper.steel-grinding-media.note: Consumption depends heavily on the abrasive index of the ore; medium confidence.

facts.label: Ball size
facts.value: 100-150 mm for a coarse grind in 1980s practice

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.05-0.2 kg of balls per tonne of ore ground

metal.copper.mine.name: Open-pit copper mine
metal.copper.mine.description: An enormous terraced pit. Ore is drilled and blasted on 15 m benches, loaded into haul trucks by 3-6 cubic metre shovels or loaded onto a conveyor, and hauled in 100-150 tonne trucks out of the pit on ramps. The waste:ore ratio at a mature porphyry pit is often 2-5:1, which is why the waste dumps are larger than the pit. As the pit deepens into the ore, block caving takes over: a fracture zone is undercut and the ore caves into a series of drawpoints, and the mining cost per tonne collapses - El Teniente in Chile was the world's largest block-cave operation from 1958 onwards.

facts.label: Waste:ore
facts.value: 2-5:1 in the mature part of a large porphyry pit

facts.label: Truck capacity
facts.value: 80-150 t; the haul road is often ~1 km round trip per lift

facts.label: Block caving
facts.value: ore broken by a cave above drawpoints, recovered by gravity; production 20,000-100,000 t/day at the largest operations

facts.label: Alternate method
facts.value: long-hole stoping with delayed blasting, used underground when the orebody is steep and deep

metal.copper.haulage.name: The haul road, the ramp and the truck cycle
metal.copper.haulage.description: The economics of an open pit are a haulage problem. A 130-tonne truck on a 2 km round trip from the loading point to the crusher, at about 25 km/h loaded and 40 km/h empty, takes 3-5 minutes per cycle including spotting and loading, so a shovel with a 4-second loading cycle needs about 6-8 trucks to keep it fed. The ramp grade matters enormously - every 1% of extra grade costs roughly 1-2% of the truck's payload - and so does where the crusher is put. A large porphyry pit moves 100,000-400,000 tonnes a day, and the fleet is 100-400 trucks.
metal.copper.haulage.note: Medium confidence on the cycle times and the grade penalty; both are well documented in mining engineering but vary by operation.

facts.label: Fleet
facts.value: 100-400 haul trucks at a large porphyry pit

metal.copper.dust-suppression.name: Dust suppression and the environmental limit
metal.copper.dust-suppression.description: A 100,000 t/day pit with unsuppressed haul roads produces a very large tonnage of airborne dust, and by the 1970s that had become a legal problem: the Clean Air Act of 1970 and the 1974 federal mine-safety inspection regime both applied to metal mines, and the pit had to water its roads, restrict the speed on unpaved haulage, and in the worst cases stop blasting in a high wind. So the environment is a genuine node in the middle of the ore chain, not a decoration at the end of it, and it is the same regulation that produced the sinter-plant dust precipitator in the steel branch.
metal.copper.dust-suppression.note: Medium confidence on the specific US regulatory application to metal mines; the controls themselves are standard.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: road watering, speed limits on unpaved haulage, blast restrictions in wind

facts.label: Regime
facts.value: Clean Air Act 1970 and the federal mine-safety inspection regime of 1977

metal.copper.block-cave.name: Block cave drawpoints and ore pass
metal.copper.block-cave.description: The block cave is the deepest and most sophisticated piece of 1980s mining engineering anywhere near a C64: a slot is cut along the base of the ore block, the slot is blasted, the overlying ore fractures and subsides into the void, and a finger stoper trains stop releasing ore once the cave front has moved past a drawpoint, to stop surface subsidence from outrunning the cave. Ore falls 100-1000 m to a conveyor at the bottom. Throughput per drawpoint is low - a few hundred tonnes a day - so a big block cave has hundreds of them.
metal.copper.block-cave.note: Drawpoint rates are mine-specific; medium confidence on the range.

facts.label: Controls
facts.value: finger stopers, or chutes with flow-control doors in modern installations

metal.copper.intrusion.name: Tertiary porphyry intrusion
metal.copper.intrusion.description: The leaf: a granodiorite or quartz monzonite stock, once liquid and now frozen, with the copper-bearing sulphide veins filling fractures and disseminated grains through it. Under a 100 m of leached, iron-stained capping lies the transition ore and then the primary sulphides, so the pit's first 50-150 m of material is nearly worthless and has to be hauled anyway.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granodiorite / quartz monzonite porphyry with hydrothermal alteration

facts.label: Oxidation profile
facts.value: leached zone, then mixed sulphide-secondary enrichment, then primary sulphide

metal.aluminum.name: Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion
metal.aluminum.description: Where the C64's aluminium comes from. Bauxite is dug, digested in caustic soda to alumina, and electrolysed in molten cryolite to 99.7% metal - about 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne, the largest single industrial electricity draw anywhere in this tree. The ingot is then DC-cast to a rolling ingot and rolled down to 6-25 um foil for the electrolytic capacitors in the power supply, to sheet for the case and shield cans, and extruded for the heat sinks. Note that the capacitor foil and the plain foil are different jobs for the same rolling mill.

facts.label: Typical chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

metal.aluminum.extrusion.name: Aluminium extrusion: the case and the heat sinks
metal.aluminum.extrusion.description: A hot billet is forced through a steel die by a ram at 420-500 C, at 20-100 MN of pressure, at several metres a second, and the profile that comes out is straight and, if the die is good, dimensionally within a fraction of a millimetre. The Commodore case is a complicated extrusion: the cooling fins, the rail and the case walls are all one profile, and the visible finish is a consequence of the die geometry. The rectifier and regulator heat sinks are separate small extrusions or machined blocks.

facts.label: Extrusion pressure
facts.value: 20-100 MN, of order 500-1500 t of force

facts.label: Extrusion speed
facts.value: up to about 100 m/min for a light 6063 section

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: hot-work tool steel; 600-1000 roughing holes and 1000-1500 h of die life in order

facts.label: Case profile
facts.value: 6063 with a 0.2-0.4 mm wall and integral cooling fins

metal.aluminum.extrusion.die.name: Steel extrusion die and its forging
metal.aluminum.extrusion.die.description: The die is a disc of hot-work tool steel with a cavity machined into it, and it has to be made before it can be used: drilled, rough-machined, heat-treated, then finish-machined and nitrided. A case profile takes a lot of steel and a lot of hours, which is why the extrusion industry is full of small specialist shops rather than a few giants. The same die steel family, SKD61 and H13, is the tooling steel of the plastics agent's injection-moulding branch.
metal.aluminum.extrusion.die.note: Die lives vary enormously with profile complexity and alloy; medium confidence.

metal.aluminum.extrusion.press.name: Hydraulic extrusion press, 500-2500 t
metal.aluminum.extrusion.press.description: The industry standard was the 2300-2500 t class press with a 200-500 mm container, driven by a hydraulic intensifier that gave a hard step change in speed at the start of the stroke. A heated soak furnace beside the press holds the billets, a shear cuts them to length, and the runout bench stretches the profile while it is still hot. A C64 case would have been pressed at a Taiwanese or Hong Kong extrusion shop on a machine of exactly this size.

facts.label: Press size
facts.value: 2300-2500 t in the largest class, 500-1500 t for smaller sections

facts.label: Straightening
facts.value: in-line stretcher on the runout bench

metal.aluminum.soak-furnace.name: The soak furnace and the billet's temperature history
metal.aluminum.soak-furnace.description: Billet quality is set before the press ever sees it. The billets are heated in a gas- or oil-fired pit furnace to 420-500 C and held for 3-24 hours so that the temperature is uniform through the section, because a billet with a hot core and a cold skin extrudes with a surface tear and a soft interior. The furnace is a 3-5 m long box with a hot zone and a transition zone, and the entire extrusion industry's reputation for inconsistent profiles is mostly the reputation of its furnaces. A C64's case extrusion depended on the profile being within a fraction of a millimetre, because it had to fit a plastic moulding and a painted finish.
metal.aluminum.soak-furnace.note: Medium confidence; the soak practice is standard but the times depend entirely on the section size.

facts.label: Why so long
facts.value: a 25 t billet needs hours for the core to reach temperature

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: gas or oil fired pit furnace with hot and transition zones

metal.aluminum.sheet.name: Aluminium sheet: the case and the shields
metal.aluminum.sheet.description: Two uses in a C64: the heat-sink and shield material, and the case itself. The Commodore breadbin case is an aluminium extrusion with a stove-enamel finish, and the internal shields and the modulator compartment are plain sheet. Cold-rolled 1050A or 3003 sheet at 0.3-1.5 mm goes into drawing and stamping; the anodising or powder coating is the plastics-and-paint agent's business, but the substrate starts here. Also the convergence point for the die-casting branch: a 1982 C64 has several kilograms of aluminium foundry alloy in its key plungers and the joystick and case-bracket castings.

facts.label: Alloys
facts.value: 1050A (pure, for foil and case), 3003 (Al-Mn, general sheet), 6063 (extrusion), A13 (Al-Si casting alloy, for die castings)

facts.label: Typical gauge
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 mm for a case or shield

metal.aluminum.blending.name: Alloying to 3003, 6063 or A13
metal.aluminum.blending.description: The rolling mill is not a refinery. It melts primary ingot, remelted can scrap and dross recovery in a reverberatory or an induction furnace, adds the alloying elements as lumps of master alloy, degasses with a rotating argon lance to strip hydrogen, and skims the dross. Manganese for 3003, magnesium and silicon for 6063, silicon for the A13 casting alloy. So the C64's case metal is partly recycled metal, and its chemistry is set in a small furnace rather than a pot.
metal.aluminum.blending.note: The specific alloy used for the Commodore case is not something I can confirm; 6063 and 1050 are the plausible candidates. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: oil- or gas-fired reverberatory melting furnace of 100-300 t, or an induction furnace

facts.label: Degassing
facts.value: rotating argon or nitrogen lance, or a chlorine-salt flux

metal.aluminum.foil.name: Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors
metal.aluminum.foil.description: The C64's power supply is full of electrolytic capacitors, and every one of them is an aluminium foil sandwich: a thin cathode foil wound with a thicker anode foil and a paper separator soaked in electrolyte. Making 6 um foil is a genuinely hard rolling problem - at that gauge the metal is thinner than the oxide skin that forms on it, so the rolls and the housekeeping are the whole technology. This is a deliberate convergence node: the foil branch, the anode-foil etch branch and the rolling-mill branch all hang off it.

facts.label: Gauges
facts.value: 6-9 um cathode foil, 8-16 um anode foil

facts.label: Roll gauge count
facts.value: of the order of 20-30 um rolled per pass to reach foil

metal.aluminum.anode-foil.name: Etched anode foil for electrolytic capacitors
metal.aluminum.anode-foil.description: The trick that made a decent electrolytic fit into an 8 mm diameter can. Plain anode foil etched in a hot acid bath grows an aluminium oxide/hydroxide layer over essentially the whole surface - up to about a hundred times the geometric area, and therefore a hundred times the capacitance per unit of volume. The 1980s etching chemistry was a chloride bath or, in the Japanese-dominated high-end market, a chlorate bath with acetic acid; the etch pits are then hardened with a phosphate or chromate formation treatment and the surface is impregnated with the electrolyte. This is a deliberate convergence node: the etch chemistry, the foil branch and the chromate chemistry of the plating branch all meet here.
metal.aluminum.anode-foil.note: The 1980s high-capacitance anode foil industry was concentrated in Japan and the exact etch chemistry was proprietary, split between the chloride and the chlorate camps. Medium confidence on the bath detail. Some formation treatments used chromate for stability, and hexavalent chromium was already being restricted in the workplace by 1982.

facts.label: Surface area gain
facts.value: ~50-100x the geometric area after etching and formation

facts.label: Oxide layer
facts.value: order 0.1-1 um of Al2O3, grown by a DC formation voltage

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chloride, or chlorate plus acetic acid, at about 60-80 C

facts.label: Formation voltage
facts.value: raised in steps to the working voltage of the finished capacitor, typically 6-25 V for a computer supply rail

metal.aluminum.foil-pore.name: The etch pit and the dielectric
metal.aluminum.foil-pore.description: The chloride ion eats its way into the foil along grain boundaries and leaves a field of round tunnels a few microns across. Oxidation inside those tunnels is what multiplies the area. The tunnels are then forced into a fixed geometry by a formation step that grows oxide in a controlled taper - the oxide at the mouth of the pit is the weakest point and it fails first if you get it wrong, which is why a 1982 capacitor that failed early usually failed as a short circuit and not as a leak.
metal.aluminum.foil-pore.note: Low confidence on the exact pit geometry; the mechanism itself is well established.

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: oxide breakdown at the pit mouth, then thermal runaway and venting

metal.aluminum.foil-slitting.name: Foil slitting and rewinding
metal.aluminum.foil-slitting.description: The 1-2 tonne coil of foil, 400-1300 mm wide, is slit into narrower coils for the capacitor maker and re-spooled. Slitter knives are tungsten-carbide or ceramic coated; a 6 um foil cut by a blunt knife simply tears. Slitting is also where a lot of the roll-to-roll handling difficulty lives, because a 6 um foil has almost no stiffness.
metal.aluminum.foil-slitting.note: Actual widths are customer-specific; the range is representative.

facts.label: Foil coil mass
facts.value: order 1-2 t for a wide coil

metal.aluminum.cold-rolling.name: Cold rolling on a Sendimir high-roll mill
metal.aluminum.cold-rolling.description: The 2-6 mm hot strip goes to a multi-high cold mill - a Sendimir 20-high or 24-high arrangement where a small work roll is backed by many intermediate rolls, giving the enormous rolling force needed at a small gap without a mill body the size of a building. The work rolls are hardened tool steel, 100-300 mm diameter, with a chasing finish that the operator keeps polished with emery and a lint-free cloth while the mill runs; at 6 um a single fingerprint is a visible defect. From 1980 onwards the Sendimir Z-High mill, which adds separate work-roll bending and flattening control, was the state of the art for aluminium foil width.

facts.label: Mill configuration
facts.value: 20-high or 24-high Sendimir; the Sendimir Z-High from 1980

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: about 40-70% per pass, 15-30 um per pass to foil

facts.label: Gauge control
facts.value: hydraulic or electromechanical gap and bending control to about 1-2% thickness tolerance

metal.aluminum.foil-annealing.name: Interstage and final annealing
metal.aluminum.foil-annealing.description: Cold work leaves aluminium hard and full of stored energy, and a foil mill's rolls are too small to take that much reduction in one pass, so the strip is annealed between passes. A gas-fired or electric annealing furnace holds it at 200-400 C until the residual stress relaxes and the grains recrystallise. This is also where the rolling-direction texture that gives foil its foldability is reset, and where the elongated grain structure that capacitor foil later needs is created.
metal.aluminum.foil-annealing.note: Exact temperatures vary with alloy and end use; medium confidence.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: air for impervious foil, controlled atmosphere for coated foil

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.name: Aluminium rolling oil and the degreaser
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.description: Cold rolling of aluminium would tear without a lubricant: a water-in-oil emulsion or a neat mineral oil with fatty-acid esters, applied by nozzles at order 0.1-1 g/m2. The oil is what lets the gauge get down without the surface tearing, and it has to be removed afterwards - a few grams of oil left on capacitor foil ruin the capacitor, because the electrolyte chemistry and the oxide interface are that sensitive. Foil mills ran a dedicated degreasing line with naphtha or trichloroethane and a 200-300 C bake.
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.note: Solvent choice varied with local regulation; perchloroethylene was being phased out in Europe and North America through the 1980s. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Oil application
facts.value: order 0.1-1.0 g per m2 of strip

facts.label: Residual after degrease
facts.value: below about 50 mg/m2, lower for capacitor foil

facts.label: Degrease solvent
facts.value: naphtha, perchloroethylene or trichloroethane, plus a 200-300 C bake

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.name: Fatty-acid esters from tallow and palm fat
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.description: The ester lubricants are made from animal or vegetable fats - tallow, palm, rapeseed - hydrolysed to fatty acids and re-esterified, on a paraffinic mineral base or a synthetic ester. This is the one place in the aluminium chain where biomass chemistry is genuinely load-bearing: an aluminium rolling lubricant is a soap-and-fatty-acid chemistry, not a petrochemical one. In 1982 tallow was still the dominant base; vegetable ester formulations grew through the 1990s.
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.note: Medium confidence on the 1982 split between tallow, vegetable and petroleum-based grades.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: rendered animal fat, pressed palm oil, rapeseed oil

facts.label: Note
facts.value: crude petroleum was still a common base in the cheaper grades

metal.aluminum.hot-rolling.name: Hot rolling to 2-6 mm
metal.aluminum.hot-rolling.description: The ingot is preheated to 300-400 C for wide slab or 450-550 C for narrower, thicker slab, and a reversing hot mill takes it down to 2-6 mm in one or two passes. Aluminium's rolling window is famously narrow - too cold and it tears at the edges, too hot and the ingot surface oxidises and scales - so a 1980s reversing hot mill had two or three stands and quite tight control. Scale is removed with hot descaling rolls, which presses a rolled-in oxide pattern into the surface that later helps the lubricant out of the pores.

facts.label: Reheat temperature
facts.value: 300-400 C for wide slab, up to 450-550 C

facts.label: Reduction per pass
facts.value: order 3-8 mm per pass, about a 30% reduction limit

facts.label: Descaling
facts.value: hot descaler rolls force water under the oxide scale and knock it off

metal.aluminum.mill-scale.name: Mill scale (iron-bearing aluminium oxide)
metal.aluminum.mill-scale.description: Hot rolling oxidises the surface and the scale is knocked off by the descaling rolls. The chips that fall are a mix of alumina and iron oxides pulled in from the ingot surface, and they are the same material the ferroalloy and cement industries fought over - and, ground and magnetically separated, the raw iron oxide for soft ferrites. In 1982 most was dumped.
metal.aluminum.mill-scale.note: Iron content varies with ingot surface condition; medium confidence on the range.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 30-60 kg of scale per tonne of hot-rolled strip

metal.aluminum.dc-casting.name: DC casting to a rolling ingot
metal.aluminum.dc-casting.description: Molten aluminium at 700-750 C is poured into a steel mould that is being withdrawn by a hydraulic jack at a controlled few millimetres per second, so the metal freezes progressively behind a solidification front instead of all at once. The front is water-cooled and the emerging surface is squirted with a water mist to control its shape. This produces a big flat rectangular billet - typically 500-1000 mm wide, 600 mm thick, 5-25 t - with a fine equiaxed chill zone at the surface. Because it is a continuous process, a 1980s smelter and a modern one produce ingots of essentially identical shape.

facts.label: Section
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 m wide by 0.5-0.8 m thick, 1-6 m long

facts.label: Chill zone
facts.value: 10-25 mm of fine equiaxed surface grains, which helps the ingot survive rolling without cracking

facts.label: Homogenisation
facts.value: a follow-up soak of 6-24 h at 450-600 C to dissolve Al-Zn-Mg clusters

metal.aluminum.homogenising.name: Homogenising soak
metal.aluminum.homogenising.description: A long hold in a gas- or electrically-heated pit furnace, typically 12-24 h at 450-600 C, whose only job is to let the alloying elements diffuse evenly. Without it a slab rolled on one edge behaves differently from the same slab rolled on the other and the foil tears. It also rounds the dendritic structure into equiaxed grains, which is what makes the achievable surface quality possible.
metal.aluminum.homogenising.note: Typical range; specific alloy timetables vary by producer.

metal.aluminum.ingot.name: Primary aluminium ingot, 99.7%
metal.aluminum.ingot.description: The metal itself, and the deliberate convergence point of the electrolysis branch and the rolling branch. Tapped from the pot every 24-48 hours, brought up to about 720 C, filtered to remove the entrained alumina and metal droplets, alloyed if the customer wants it, and cast. In 1982 the standard product was the 20-25 kg P1020 ingot, or the 500 kg or 1.5 t minimum-content ingot that newer smelters preferred, 99.70% minimum aluminium with iron and silicon the main impurities. Rolling ingots for the foil mills were a different shape entirely - see the foil branch.

facts.label: Impurities
facts.value: Fe 0.1-0.25%, Si 0.05-0.2%, plus Ga, Ti and Zn traces

facts.label: Ingot forms
facts.value: 20-25 kg stackable ingot, 500 kg minimum-content ingot, or 1.5 t

metal.hall-heroult.name: Hall-Heroult electrolysis of alumina in cryolite
metal.hall-heroult.description: The cell is a steel shell the size of a bathtub lined with carbon, containing 300-500 t of molten cryolite at 950-970 C. Alumina dissolves in the melt and is reduced at a carbon cathode; current passes through the anodes, where the oxygen from the alumina burns the carbon away and makes carbon dioxide. The metal pools on the floor and is tapped every day or two. A pot takes 3-6 V at 100-200 kA, which is why a 200,000 t/year smelter is also a 2-3 GW power station.
metal.hall-heroult.note: The ~2.1 V theoretical minimum cell voltage and the ~90% ceiling on current efficiency are why the energy number has barely moved since 1950.

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: 950-970 C; cryolite alone melts at 1012 C

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.5-4.5 V against a theoretical minimum of about 2.1 V

facts.label: Current
facts.value: 100-200 kA per pot; one pot makes 1-3 t of aluminium a day

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium; 1982-era plants were commonly 15,000-17,000

facts.label: 1980s technology
facts.value: the point feeder and prebaked anode design of 1980, which raised current density to 0.7-0.8 A/cm2, is still the state of the art; no fundamental change since

metal.hall-heroult.dross.name: Aluminium dross and the skimmings
metal.hall-heroult.dross.description: Two or three tonnes of dross and sludge per pot per year: oxide, carbon, and aluminium that never reached the cathode. Because aluminium dross burns spectacularly it must be handled under cover, and the smelter had a dross furnace to burn out the aluminium and get it back. The recovered metal is dirty and low grade, and in 1982 it went straight back into the pot - a small but real recycling loop, since remelted aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy of primary metal.
metal.hall-heroult.dross.note: The roughly 5% remelt saving is the widely quoted fraction of primary energy; medium confidence on precision.

facts.label: Yield loss
facts.value: roughly 2-4% of metal production leaves as dross

metal.hall-heroult.alumina-dredge.name: Alumina dredges and the alumina crust
metal.hall-heroult.alumina-dredge.description: Alumina fed into the pot floats and solidifies into a chilled crust on the bath surface, which is far more stable than loose powder. Machines called dredges or skimmers break holes in this crust and feed alumina down them at a controlled rate; the classic 1980 design was the dual-feed with pneumatic runners. The holes are also where carbon dust from the anode is skimmed off. A floating crust is good for the pot but insulates the bath, so the balance between a thick stable crust and a cool cell is the operator's whole job.
metal.hall-heroult.alumina-dredge.note: The feed rate is a rule of thumb that varies with cell design; medium confidence.

facts.label: Feed rate
facts.value: order 1-1.5 kg of alumina per kA-hour

metal.hall-heroult.pot-lining.name: Carbon pot lining and the cathodic block
metal.hall-heroult.pot-lining.description: The steel shell is lined first with refractory brick, then with a monolithic carbon lining about 400-600 mm thick made of calcined coke, graphite and hot pitch, rammed in place. A block lining of graphitised carbon blocks is better and was common in newer cells. The lining is deliberately cathodic: the aluminium that seeps into the pores becomes a cathode of itself, and when the cell is finally relined after 3-8 years the spent lining is leached for the metal it swallowed.

facts.label: Lining thickness
facts.value: 400-600 mm monolithic, plus 200-300 mm of brick

facts.label: Metal locked up in a spent lining
facts.value: order 5-15 t of aluminium per pot

metal.alumina.name: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5% Al2O3
metal.alumina.description: A white, sandy, hygroscopic powder delivered to the smelter in railcars or 1-2 t bags. The contract is brutal: 99.5% Al2O3 minimum, loss on ignition below about 1%, total iron below 0.02%, because every gram of iron that reaches the cell ends up in the metal and the ingot stops being 99.7%. In 1982 this was a global commodity with about a dozen producers - Alcoa, Alcan, Kaiser, Norsk Hydro, Sumitomo, and the Australian and Jamaican national producers. This is the deliberate convergence point for the bauxite and the pot branch: both hang off it.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: free-flowing sandy powder, 0.05-0.5 mm, bulk density ~1 t/m3

facts.label: Physical
facts.value: hygroscopic - shipped and stored sealed, and preheated to avoid steam spalling in the pot feed

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

metal.bayer.name: Bayer process
metal.bayer.description: A 110-year-old caustic-leach purification that every tonne of aluminium still goes through. Five steps: crush and wash, digest in caustic at pressure, clarify and throw away the red mud, cool and precipitate pure aluminium hydroxide, calcine to alumina. It works because the alumina in bauxite is amphoteric - it dissolves in hot caustic as sodium aluminate - while the iron and titanium oxides are not, and silica is neutralised by lime into a harmless calcium silicate.

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: preparation, digestion, dilution and red-mud separation, precipitation, calcination

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 150-200 C for low-temperature gibbsitic ore; 240-280 C for high-temperature diasporic

facts.label: Lime
facts.value: added during digestion as a desilication reagent

metal.bayer.calcination.name: Calcination of alumina trihydrate at 1000-1100 C
metal.bayer.calcination.description: The hydrate goes into a rotary kiln or, more often by 1982, a fluidised-bed calciner, and at 1000-1100 C it gives off its water of crystallisation and recrystallises from gamma through theta to alpha alumina. Alpha alumina is the hard, insoluble, spark-resistant form that will dissolve in cryolite. The rotary kiln burns 400-600 kg of fuel oil or gas equivalent per tonne of alumina and emits a lot of carbon dioxide; the fluidised bed is more efficient and was being adopted through the 1980s.

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: alpha-Al2O3, 99.5%+, with under 1% loss on ignition

facts.label: Water removed
facts.value: 3 H2O per Al2O3, i.e. 34% of the hydrate's mass

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~300-600 kg of oil equivalent per tonne of alumina

facts.label: Steam recovery
facts.value: the kiln flue gas is used to generate process steam, standard since the 1970s

metal.bayer.calciner.name: Fluidised-bed calciner
metal.bayer.calciner.description: Hot gas from a multi-flash evaporator is blown through a bed of alumina hydrate on a distributor of alloy nozzles, holding the bed fluid at 1000-1100 C by balancing gas throughput against feed rate. The bed fluidises like a boiling liquid and every grain sees the same temperature, which is exactly why the alpha alumina comes out with a tight particle-size distribution. The 1980s smelter-grade alumina market effectively standardised on this machine.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: uniform residence time, so alpha conversion completes in one pass

metal.bayer.precipitation.name: Precipitation of Al(OH)3 from cooled liquor
metal.bayer.precipitation.description: The clear caustic aluminate solution is cooled from 100-110 C to 60-80 C and seeded with a few grams per litre of finely ground aluminium hydroxide already in the plant. The seed grows into the supersaturated solution as a hexagonal-plate alumina trihydrate over 24-48 hours, and the mud is filtered and washed. Washing matters twice over: to remove the caustic that would otherwise attack the kiln, and to recover the soda. The mother liquor goes back to digestion, and this recycle loop is what makes the caustic consumption manageable at all.

metal.bayer.filter.name: Rotary vacuum filtration and counter-current washing
metal.bayer.filter.description: The hydrate is filtered on a rotating vacuum drum with cloth- or paper-covered segments, then washed on a multi-stage counter-current filter. By the time the wash water reaches the pregnant liquor the caustic is essentially recovered, so the caustic circuit closes to better than 95%. This single piece of equipment is why alumina refining has the caustic efficiency it does.
metal.bayer.filter.note: Filtration rates vary with product particle size; medium confidence on the range.

facts.label: Filtration rate
facts.value: order 0.3-1.5 kg of hydrate per m2 of filter area per minute

metal.bayer.clarification.name: Clarification and the red mud dam
metal.bayer.clarification.description: The digested slurry is diluted with process water, cooled, and settled in a bank of gravity settlers with mechanical rakes; the red mud bottoms out and is pumped to the mud dam. A large plant produces 100-150 tonnes of red mud per tonne of alumina, which is why every alumina refinery has a mud dam engineered like a tailings facility.

facts.label: Red mud ratio
facts.value: 100-150 t per t of Al2O3 produced

facts.label: Settling time
facts.value: 1-4 hours in a deep cone settler

facts.label: Sodium loss
facts.value: order 5-15 kg Na2O per tonne of alumina goes out with the mud

metal.red-mud.name: Red mud (bauxite residue)
metal.red-mud.description: A caustic, red, kaolin-rich sludge, typically 2.5-6 mol/L free NaOH, containing essentially all the iron, titanium and silica from the ore. A large refinery produces 100-150 tonnes of it per tonne of alumina. In 1982 the industry standard for handling it was to build a dam and pump it in; the search for a use was real academic work with no commercial outcome. Successful commercial red-mud use at scale did not arrive until the 2000s and later, so nothing in a 1982 C64 contains it.

facts.label: 1980s handling
facts.value: thickened to a dry-stack dam; clay-dry-lining of the dam floor became common in the 1990s-2000s

metal.bayer.digestion.name: Caustic digestion in autoclaves
metal.bayer.digestion.description: Bauxite slurry and 150-300 g/L free caustic (as Na2O) are charged into stirred autoclaves and held at temperature for 30-90 minutes. The alumina dissolves as NaAl(OH)4; the iron oxide stays as a red slurry. Older low-temperature plants used a bank of horizontal autoclaves with indirect steam heating; high-temperature plants used vertical autoclaves. The pressure was only 5-15 bar because the vessel was not a modern high-pressure autoclave but a horizontal drum with a vapour space.
metal.bayer.digestion.note: The pressure figure follows from the temperature; 1980s Bayer autoclaves were not pressure vessels in the modern sense.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: order 5-15 bar gauge, set by the boiling point of the liquor

metal.bayer.desilication.name: Reactive silica and the lime reaction
metal.bayer.desilication.description: The killer impurity in bauxite is reactive silica - kaolinite clay and opal - which dissolves in the caustic and then reacts with aluminate to form a non-redissolving kaolinite-nepheline hydrate that permanently traps alumina. Two defences. In low-temperature digestion the clay is left undissolved by keeping the caustic concentration high. In high-temperature digestion the reactive silica dissolves, so lime is added and the silica is converted to hydrogrossite; the liquor is then given a short holding period during which the silica precipitates harmlessly. Every tonne of bauxite eats some caustic and some tens of kilos of lime that never come back.
metal.bayer.desilication.note: The penalty range depends strongly on how the silica is mineralogically bound; medium confidence.

facts.label: Reactive silica penalty
facts.value: order 3-6 kg Na2O and 1-2 kg Al2O3 lost per 1% reactive silica

facts.label: Pre-desilication step
facts.value: removing clay by attrition washing before digestion, standard for high-silica ore

metal.bauxite.name: Bauxite (hydrated alumina ore)
metal.bauxite.description: A soft, red-brown, pisolitic or clayey laterite, 45-60% Al2O3, still essentially the ore it was before anybody wanted it. Ore below about 180 C of gibbsite digest easily at low temperature and is called low-temperature bauxite; ore with diaspore and boehmite needs 240-280 C and is called high-temperature bauxite, which costs much more in steam. The three great districts in 1982 were Boke and Kindia in Guinea, the Weipa and Gove platforms in northern Australia, and the Clarendon and Saint Ann parishes in Jamaica.

facts.label: Mineralogy split
facts.value: low-temperature gibbsitic (<180 C) versus high-temperature diasporic (>180 C)

facts.label: Silica penalty
facts.value: each 1% reactive silica costs roughly 3-6 kg Na2O and diverts alumina into red mud

metal.bauxite.mine.name: Open-cast bauxite mine with dragline
metal.bauxite.mine.description: Strip mining on a 10-20 m bench height, with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline stripping 10-50 m of overburden and then a bench of bauxite perhaps only 3-6 m thick. The dragline is the point: it digs the bauxite, swings and dumps it onto a ramp, and strips the next strip of cover, all in one machine. Loading is by conveyor, almost never by truck. The Weipa and Gove operations were built this way.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open cast, drill and blast where hard, dragline stripping, conveyor loading

facts.label: Bench height
facts.value: 10-20 m of overburden, 3-6 m of ore

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 1-10 Mt/year for the largest operations

facts.label: Sizing
facts.value: primary jaw or gyratory crusher to about 25-50 mm, then direct to the digestor

metal.bauxite.beneficiation.name: Bauxite crushing, washing and drying
metal.bauxite.beneficiation.description: The Bayer plant does not want a 300 mm boulder and it certainly does not want the clay. The run-of-mine ore is crushed in a gyratory or a jaw crusher to 25-50 mm, and then - in the wet-grinding route that became standard for high-temperature bauxite - it is ground in a ball mill in a rod or a wet scrubber to a slurry, and that slurry is screened and washed to remove the clay, which is called 'desilication by attrition washing'. The under-0.5 mm clay is discarded as tailings, and it is often 15-30% of the mass. What goes into the digestor is a 40-50% solids slurry of 25-50 mm lumps with the reactive silica taken out, and the moisture matters because every kilo of water into the autoclave is a kilo of steam wasted.
metal.bauxite.beneficiation.note: Medium confidence on the mass fractions removed by washing; they are strongly ore-dependent.

facts.label: Crushing
facts.value: to 25-50 mm in a gyratory or jaw crusher

facts.label: Desilication by washing
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is removed, often 15-30% of the mass

facts.label: Direct-feed route
facts.value: the older route, in which crushed ore went to the digestor unwashed, is still used on low-silica ore

metal.bauxite.laterite.name: Lateritic bauxite profile
metal.bauxite.laterite.description: The leaf: a 3-12 m pisolitic blanket of iron-stained bauxite nodules sitting on a Cretaceous or Tertiary lateritic surface above a kaolinitic clay. Guinea's deposits are the classic tropical pisolite; the Australian Weipa and Gove ores are flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments. Either way the rock outcrops at the surface and is dug, not tunnelled.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 3-12 m of economic bauxite over kaolinite

metal.bauxite.kaolinite.name: The kaolinite and gibbsite beneath the bauxite
metal.bauxite.kaolinite.description: The leaf of the aluminium branch, and the reason the alumina process exists in the form it does. The economic bauxite is a 3-12 m blanket of iron-stained nodules sitting directly on kaolinite clay, and the kaolinite is the reactive silica that has to be neutralised by lime or washed out. Below that is the saprolite, the partly-weathered parent rock. So the aluminium in a C64 case began as an oxide that precipitated in a tropical weathering profile above a clay, on top of Cretaceous or Tertiary sediment, and the silica problem is a mineralogical fact about the same profile rather than an impurity someone failed to remove.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite blanket over kaolinite over saprolite over parent rock

facts.label: Clay mineral
facts.value: kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, is the reactive silica

facts.label: Gibbsite
facts.value: Al(OH)3, the low-temperature alumina mineral that digests at 150 C

metal.bauxite.creek-wash.name: The creek and the pisolite
metal.bauxite.creek-wash.description: The last leaf of the aluminium branch. In the Weipa and Gove deposits on the Cretaceous laterite surface, bauxite is dug in the wet season and the clay is washed out of it in a creek: a 200 m long, 30 m wide sluice excavated along the edge of the terrace, into which the bauxite is tipped and a stream of water is run, and the light clay washes away over a long distance while the pisolitic bauxite nodules, 5-50 mm and iron-stained, stay behind and are recovered by hand or by a mechanical rake. It is a 1980s technology on a Cretaceous rock surface in tropical Queensland, and it is the reason those deposits look the way they do.
metal.bauxite.creek-wash.note: Medium confidence; the Weipa creek-washing practice is well described in Queensland mining history.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: a sluice or creek 200-300 m long, washing the clay out of the nodules

facts.label: Season
facts.value: worked in the wet season, when there is water to run the sluice

metal.laterite-terrace.name: The Cretaceous laterite surface
metal.laterite-terrace.description: The leaf, geologically: a flat, deeply weathered surface on Cretaceous sandstone where a tropical lateritic profile has developed over tens of millions of years, with a bauxite horizon at the top, kaolinite below it, and the saprolite and fresh rock beneath. The flatness is the point - it is why the pits are cheap and the ore is shallow - and it is a direct consequence of the rock type and of the extraordinarily long, warm, wet chemical weathering that made it.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite, kaolinite, saprolite, fresh Cretaceous sandstone

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: a few metres over tens of kilometres, which is what makes surface mining cheap

metal.potassium.name: Potassium chloride (KCl) for tantalum reduction
metal.potassium.description: Not a C64 component - potassium never appears in the machine - but it is a mandatory reagent in the tantalum branch, because the metal is won as a fluoride salt and reduced with metal, not from an oxide. Potassium also divides tantalum from niobium in the fluoride chemistry. It is included so the tantalum branch reaches a real, mined leaf instead of stopping at an implied reagent.

facts.label: Consumers
facts.value: potash fertiliser dominated; tantalum metallurgy a small but non-negotiable share

metal.potassium.flux.name: KCl as the tantalum and fluoride flux
metal.potassium.flux.description: The only reason potassium is in this tree. Potassium chloride is added to the tantalum fluoride solution to precipitate K2TaF7, and potassium fluoride is used as a flux in some silicon and aluminium processes. Both are bought from the potash industry as a commodity, in tonnes. So a handful of grams of tantalum in a C64's capacitors required a few grams of potassium chloride, which required a shaft in Saskatchewan or a pond on the Dead Sea, which required a bed of evaporite. It is the shortest branch in this file and the funniest, because it starts with an ocean drying up.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: precipitating K2TaF7 from the fluoride solution

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the potash industry, as a 60-95% KCl commodity

metal.sylvinite.name: Sylvinite (KCl + NaCl)
metal.sylvinite.description: The ore of the Devonian Prairie Evaporite in Saskatchewan, mined underground at 800-1100 m by potash shafts where the ground is artificially frozen so the salt stays put, or by solution mining in Ontario. Run of mine is about 8-14% K2O; it is beneficiated by flotation or hot leaching and sold as muriate of potash.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: shaft mining with freeze-assisted ground support, or solution mining

metal.sylvinite.solution-mining.name: Solution mining of potash
metal.sylvinite.solution-mining.description: Where the potash seam is deeply buried and thin - as at Thames, Ontario - the shaft is not worth sinking. Instead two horizontal wells are drilled into the seam, one to inject hot water and one to draw the resulting brine, and the potash is recovered from the brine by evaporation. Two wells can produce a million tonnes a year. It is a solution-mining technique borrowed from the salt industry and it works because sylvinite dissolves in hot water while the clay it sits in does not.
metal.sylvinite.solution-mining.note: Medium confidence; the Thames operation is well documented.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: two horizontal wells, hot water injection and brine recovery

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 1 Mt/year from a single pair of wells

facts.label: Suitable where
facts.value: deep, thin, uniform seams with impermeable roof

metal.solution-mining.well.name: The injection and recovery well pair
metal.solution-mining.well.description: Solution mining is two wells and a plant. A cemented well is drilled horizontally into the potash seam and a casing is set with a perforated liner; hot water at 80-90 C is injected at a pressure of a few hundred psi, the seam is about 1-3 m thick and dissolves over a 30-200 m horizontal section, and a second well 500 m away draws the brine back. The well field is fracked between the wells to connect the fracture, and the plant evaporates the brine in a multiple-effect evaporator. It is a genuine engineering oddity - a mine with no mine - and it works because potash dissolves in hot brine and clay does not.
metal.solution-mining.well.note: Medium confidence; solution mining of potash at Thames and Belle Plaine is well described in the mining literature.

facts.label: Injection
facts.value: hot water at 80-90 C, a few hundred psi, along a 30-200 m horizontal well

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: a second well about 500 m away

metal.sylvinite.beneficiation.name: Potash flotation and hot leaching
metal.sylvinite.beneficiation.description: Run-of-mine sylvinite is about 12% K2O with a lot of NaCl and clay. Beneficiation is by flotation of the sylvinite in a saturated KCl-brine solution (because sylvinite is barely soluble while halite is much more so, so the brine selectively wets the sylvinite), or by hot leaching at 85-100 C which dissolves the potassium chloride and leaves the salt. For the tantalum industry the relevant product is not potash at all - it is the KCl that goes into the K2TaF7 precipitation.
metal.sylvinite.beneficiation.note: Both routes are standard; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between them in Saskatchewan (hot leaching is more common in the USSR and Canada east of Saskatchewan).

facts.label: Flotation
facts.value: in a saturated KCl or NaCl brine, with amines or fatty-acid collectors

facts.label: Hot leach
facts.value: 85-100 C, dissolves KCl and leaves halite

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 60-95% KCl, sold as muriate of potash

metal.potash-product.name: Muriate of potash and the tailings
metal.potash-product.description: The product is 60-95% KCl, bagged or bulk, and the waste is a slurry of NaCl and clay that goes into a tailings pond impoundment. Two points of interest for this tree: the potassium chloride that ends up in a potassium fluoride bath for the tantalum reduction is bought from this industry, and the tailings pond is a genuinely large hole in the ground - the Belle Plaine potash mine near Esterhazy had a tailings pile that became, by the 1980s, a place people went to watch birds. So a fertilizer industry byproduct is where the tantalum industry gets its potassium.
metal.potash-product.note: Medium confidence on the specific Belle Plaine details; the waste-impoundment issue is well documented.

facts.label: Tailings
facts.value: NaCl and clay slurry, pumped to a lined impoundment

metal.potash.stockyard.name: The potash rail link
metal.potash.stockyard.description: Saskatchewan potash moved to world markets by unit train - a dedicated train of a hundred or more hopper wagons - to Vancouver, Prince Albert or Minneapolis, and then by ship from Vancouver or by barge and lake freighter to Chicago. So the potassium in a 1982 tantalum capacitor travelled down a potash shaft, through a washer and a flotation plant, into a bulk railcar, onto a ship, and into a plastics extruder. It is the most ordinary logistics chain in the tree and it is the shortest path from a geological process to a metal part.
metal.potash.stockyard.note: Medium confidence on the specific rail and port routes; the Saskatchewan potash logistics are well documented.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: unit trains of hopper wagons to Vancouver or Prince Albert, then ship or lake freighter

metal.sylvinite.freezing.name: Artificial ground freezing in the potash shaft
metal.sylvinite.freezing.description: The Saskatchewan potash ore is 800-1100 m down in a bed that is 30-40 C and gassy, and it is a weak, water-bearing shale-like rock that would flow into the shaft. The solution since 1967 has been to freeze it: brine is circul through freeze pipes in the shaft and the decline for two to three years before sinking, turning the ground into a self-supporting frozen plug of ice and salt. It works, and it is one of the more unusual pieces of mining engineering anywhere - and it is the reason the Saskatchewan potash industry looks the way it does.

facts.label: Rock temperature in the seam
facts.value: 30-40 C, which is what makes freezing necessary

metal.potash.evaporite.name: Potash evaporite bed
metal.potash.evaporite.description: The leaf: a buried evaporite sea - sylvinite interbedded with halite, carnallite and mudstone, formed by the same evaporation of a restricted sea that made the salt used in chlor-alkali. The Colville and Hatchet lakes area of Saskatchewan sits over one of the largest.

metal.sodium.name: Sodium compounds: caustic soda and soda ash
metal.sodium.description: Sodium is not in the machine as a metal, but the C64 could not exist without it: caustic soda dissolves bauxite to make alumina, and the same chlor-alkali industry that makes the caustic soda also makes the chlorine and hydrogen that become the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Behind both sits a bed of rock salt or a bucket of evaporite from a solar salt pan.

metal.soda-ash.name: Soda ash (Na2CO3) by the Solvay process
metal.soda-ash.description: Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

facts.label: Solvay tower
facts.value: ~10 m diameter, 20-30 m tall, cooled to about -10 C at the top

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, then 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: order 1 t of CaCl2 brine per t of soda ash

metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.name: Recovery of the salt from the brine
metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.description: The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.
metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.note: Medium confidence on the salt consumption figure; the chemistry is standard.

facts.label: Re-saturation
facts.value: brine is re-saturated with mined salt and returned

metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.name: The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower
metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.description: The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: shaft kiln, 1000-1100 C, beside the tower

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: the lime itself, sold to steel and to agriculture

metal.soda-ash.ammonia.name: Ammonia-soda carbonation tower
metal.soda-ash.ammonia.description: A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.
metal.soda-ash.ammonia.note: Tower internals varied; the conical settler is universal.

facts.label: Tower temperature
facts.value: near 40 C at the precipitation zone

facts.label: NH3 loss
facts.value: order 0.1-0.3 t ammonia per t of soda ash, mostly vented

metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.name: Coal/coke ammonia from the gasworks
metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.description: In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: iron promoted with K2O, or activated coke

metal.caustic-soda.name: Caustic soda (NaOH), 50% solution
metal.caustic-soda.description: Two entirely different consumers in this tree. The Bayer process digestion liquor, where a caustic grade tanker holds roughly 300-400 t of 50% solution and a refinery's caustic and steam costs dominate its operating cost. And the chlor-alkali industry, where the same product comes out of the same cell as the chlorine and hydrogen that make the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Cost accounting in aluminium is dominated by caustic and steam; every tonne of caustic lost to red mud is recovered by lime in the causticisation circuit or bought.

facts.label: Bayer consumption
facts.value: order 100-200 kg of Na2O-equivalent per tonne of alumina, plus process losses

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, done with lime

metal.salt-brine.name: Rock salt and solar salt brine
metal.salt-brine.description: Salt for a chlor-alkali plant arrives either as mined halite from a salt operation or as brine evaporated from seawater. Solar evaporation was the cheap route for a plant on a hot, dry coast - Israel's Dead Sea and Atlantic coast, California's San Francisco Bay, the Gulf of Mexico - while inland plants in the saltbelt of Michigan, Ohio, New York and Ontario bought mined rock salt from underground, which is also where the bromine came from.

metal.salt-solar-pan.name: Solar salt evaporation pond
metal.salt-solar-pan.description: A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.
metal.salt-solar-pan.note: Yields are strongly climate-dependent; medium confidence on the per-hectare figure.

facts.label: Depth steps
facts.value: 2-5 m intake, 0.3 m evaporator, 0.2 m crystalliser

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 100-200 kg per m2 of pond per year

metal.salt-rock.name: Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt
metal.salt-rock.description: Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.

facts.label: Typical assay
facts.value: NaCl 95-99%, with calcium and magnesium salts as the impurity

metal.salt-evaporite.name: Halite evaporite: the rock
metal.salt-evaporite.description: The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: massive to bedded halite with gypsum, anhydrite and clay partings

metal.chlor-alkali.name: Chlor-alkali electrolytic cell
metal.chlor-alkali.description: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. In 1982 almost all of it was a diaphragm cell or a mercury cell. The diaphragm cell - an asbestos-cloth cathode separator - gave low-purity caustic loaded with salt and was steadily displaced through the late 1970s and 1980s by the membrane cell, which delivers 50% NaOH essentially free of salt. Mercury cell caustic went to a short finishing step, causticisation with sodium carbonate, to strip the last mercury; the Hooker Chemical conversion of its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984 is the emblematic date.

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.0-4.5 V diaphragm, 4-5 V membrane, 4.5-5 V mercury

facts.label: 1982 technology split
facts.value: diaphragm dominant, membrane a fast-growing minority, mercury still common

metal.chlor-alkali.dechlorination.name: Dechlorination and the brine circuit
metal.chlor-alkali.dechlorination.description: The brine leaving a cell still has hypochlorite in it, because chlorine dissolves in the caustic. It is treated with sodium sulphite and then acidified, the brine is re-saturated with salt and re-purified on a soda ash and barium carbonate cycle, and it goes back to the cell. So a chlor-alkali plant also consumes sodium carbonate and barium carbonate - the latter being, note, the barium carbonate from the barium branch of this file. The barium carbonate is there to remove the sulphate from the brine as barium sulphate, which is filtered off and, until the 1980s, dumped.
metal.chlor-alkali.dechlorination.note: Medium confidence on the consumption figures; the barium carbonate sulphate removal is standard practice.

facts.label: Dechlorination
facts.value: sodium sulphite, then hydrochloric acid to pH 2-3

facts.label: Sulphate removal
facts.value: barium carbonate -> barium sulphate sludge, filtered and discarded

facts.label: Brine consumption
facts.value: order 0.3-0.6 t of salt per tonne of chlorine

metal.chlor-alkali.digram-cell.name: The diaphragm cell and the asbestos problem
metal.chlor-alkali.digram-cell.description: The 1980s chlor-alkali cell was a rectangular steel box, 2-3 m long, with an anode compartment of brine and a cathode compartment of water separated by an asbestos cloth diaphragm deposited on a wire gauze. The diaphragm was cheap, durable and effective, and it was the reason the world's chlor-alkali industry had a mesothelioma problem. The cell voltage was low, 3.0-3.5 V, and the caustic carried 10-15 g/L of salt because the diaphragm let chloride through. The Hooker Chemical conversion at Niagara Falls in 1984 to a membrane cell was the moment the asbestos diaphragm began to disappear from the industry.
metal.chlor-alkali.digram-cell.note: The Hooker conversion year is a well-documented landmark in the chlor-alkali industry.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 2-3 m long rectangular steel box, brine anode compartment, water cathode compartment

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth on a steel gauze

facts.label: Transition date
facts.value: Hooker Chemical converted its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984

metal.hydrogen.name: Electrolysis hydrogen from the chlor-alkali cathode
metal.hydrogen.description: The wet hydrogen off the cathode goes to acid synthesis, and in a silicon plant it also goes to the Siemens reactor as the carrier that carries trichlorosilane to the rod and strips the chlorine off. The purification train is a caustic scrubber, then a drying tower, and the carbon monoxide has to be taken below a few ppm or the polysilicon comes out with carbon in it. The same hydrogen, purified a stage further, is what a stainless bright-annealing line uses.
metal.hydrogen.note: The CO limit is my recollection of silicon-grade hydrogen specifications; medium confidence.

facts.label: Purishment
facts.value: caustic scrub, molecular-sieve dry, CO below 5-10 ppm

metal.chlorine.name: Chlorine gas (Cl2)
metal.chlorine.description: A pale yellow-green gas denser than air, made in the chlor-alkali plant and piped or tanker-shipped to the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit. Around 1982 much of it went to solvent makers and to water treatment as chlorinated organics; only a fraction ever reached a silicon plant, and silicon-grade chlorine must be bone dry, because water plus trichlorosilane gives hydrochloric acid and hexasiloxane gel that plugs the fluidised bed.
metal.chlorine.note: The water specification varies by plant; stated as a typical order.

facts.label: Water content spec
facts.value: <40 ppm H2O for electronic-grade silicon plants

facts.label: Liquefaction
facts.value: shipped as liquid at about -34 C, or as dry gas in tube trailers

metal.silica.name: High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)
metal.silica.description: The refined element every chip in the machine is cut from. A 1982 Commodore 64 mainboard carried a handful of silicon dies and one 2 MHz quartz crystal, both traceable to this chain: quartzite or silica reduced to 98-99% metallurgical silicon, chlorinated to trichlorosilane, distilled to 9-nines, deposited as polysilicon, then pulled as a single Czochralski crystal. Note that the 6510 is NMOS, so the 1982 die uses ALUMINIUM gate metal and thermally grown field oxide, not a polysilicon gate; the polysilicon branch below is the industry feedstock route, which is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Feedstock purity
facts.value: 9N-11N (99.9999999%) for modern polysilicon; 6N-7N typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Boron budget
facts.value: B must be held near 1 ppb; boron is the contaminant that made metallurgical silicon unusable directly

metal.silica.quartz-crystal.name: 2.048 MHz quartz clock crystal
metal.silica.quartz-crystal.description: The C64's timing reference: an AT-cut quartz plate about 7.6 x 2.5 mm brazed between metal caps, resonating at 2.048 MHz. Quartz is the only material with a usable temperature-stable mechanical resonance that cheap. The plate itself is usually not natural rock - it is hydrothermally grown synthetic quartz in an autoclave of sodium hydroxide solution at about 400 C and 1.5 kbar.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: order 10-50 ppm across 0-70 C for a consumer part

metal.silica.quartz-crystal.synthetic.name: Hydrothermal synthetic quartz
metal.silica.quartz-crystal.synthetic.description: A seed of natural quartz hangs in aqueous NaOH in a steel autoclave at 380-450 C and 100-200 bar, and quartz grows on the seed at a few mm/day. The advantage over mined Brazilian rock is that the growth conditions are repeatable, so the Q and defect density of every boule match. Brazilian vein quartz was still used where natural material beat synthetic on Q.
metal.silica.quartz-crystal.synthetic.note: Medium confidence on the exact window; autoclave conditions vary by producer.

metal.silica.czochralski.name: Czochralski monocrystalline ingot
metal.silica.czochralski.description: Where the polysilicon chain ends and the semiconductor business begins. A 2 kg chunk is melted at 1420 C in a silica crucible over a seed crystal, and a slow pull at 0.5-2 mm/min with rotation grows a 75-150 mm boule. Every defect the 6510 die had in it - dislocations, oxygen precipitates, the dopant gradient along the length - was frozen in during this pull. Gas-phase-grown poly was cheaper and lower-defect than Czochralski poly in 1982, so the route below was standard.

facts.label: Boule diameter
facts.value: 75-150 mm, yielding 6510 dies of roughly 3-6 mm

metal.silica.field-oxide.name: Thermally grown silicon dioxide
metal.silica.field-oxide.description: Gate oxide, field oxide and the photoresist mask oxides are not bought - they are grown. The wafer goes into a 1000-1150 C steam or dry-O2 furnace for an hour and a half and roughly a thousand angstroms of SiO2 comes off the silicon itself. So the machine's insulation is, chemically speaking, the same element as the chip, oxidised in place.

facts.label: Wet vs dry
facts.value: dry O2 for the thin gate oxide, wet steam for the thicker field oxide

metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.name: Fused quartz growth crucible
metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.description: The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.
metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.note: Crucible life varied enormously with melt temperature discipline; treat as order of magnitude.

facts.label: Fusing temperature
facts.value: ~2000 C in vacuum or wet H2

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: a few hundred growth runs in 1980s practice

metal.silica.polysilicon.name: Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N
metal.silica.polysilicon.description: Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. IMPORTANT: the 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate. This branch is the industry feedstock route, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: sawn rod segments, 5-30 kg per chunk in 1980s practice

metal.silica.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N
metal.silica.tcs.description: Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.name: Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C
metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.description: Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> HSiCl3 + H2, with Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2 as the side reaction

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: historically copper or copper chloride; most modern plants run catalyst-free

metal.hydrochloric-acid.name: Hydrochloric acid (32-37%)
metal.hydrochloric-acid.description: The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.

facts.label: Typical silicon-plant demand
facts.value: order 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output

metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.name: HCl synthesis and absorption
metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.description: Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

facts.label: Flame temperature
facts.value: >2000 C, quenched below 400 C within milliseconds

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: water scrubber, adiabatic, controlled by a weak-acid bleed

metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.name: Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling
metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.description: Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.
metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.note: The fraction and its fate vary strongly between plants and years; high confidence in the chemistry, medium on the 1982 commercial split.

facts.label: 1980s practice
facts.value: a large fraction of by-product SiCl4 was sold as a solvent or to fumed-silica makers; full recycle came later

metal.silica.mgsi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
metal.silica.mgsi.description: The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

facts.label: Why not steel coke
facts.value: coke ash carries boron and phosphorus above the electronics budget

metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.name: Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C
metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.description: A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.
metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.note: The off-gas silicon monoxide chemistry was well understood by the 1980s and was the basis of several recovery processes that were still being commercialised then.

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite or UHP carbon, consumed at ~1-1.5 t per t of silicon

facts.label: Off-gas
facts.value: SiO-rich gas leaving at 400-1000 C, cleaned in cyclones and baghouses

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 11,000-13,000 kWh per tonne of silicon from the arc furnace alone

metal.silica.reducer.name: Carbothermic carbon: petroleum coke and woodchips
metal.silica.reducer.description: The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.
metal.silica.reducer.note: The consumption ratio varies with furnace design and recovery; treat as order of magnitude.

facts.label: Ash target
facts.value: <1% for the reducer, versus the 10-12% typical of foundry coke

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.9-1.1 t of carbon per t of silicon

metal.silica.petcoke.name: Calcined petroleum coke for silicon
metal.silica.petcoke.description: Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.

metal.silica.tcs.distillation.name: Fractional distillation of HSiCl3
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.description: Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.note: The boron cuts are the hard part: BCl3 boils close to trichlorosilane and boron has a low distribution coefficient, so 1980s plants used tall columns and many theoretical plates.

metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.name: Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods
metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.description: Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon across the whole chlorosilane route

facts.label: Deposition rate
facts.value: single-digit micrometres per hour per rod in 1980s reactors

metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.name: Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod
metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.description: The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.
metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.note: The etch chemistry varied plant to plant and was rarely published; described here from general practice.

metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.name: Doped vs undoped polysilicon
metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.description: Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.
metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.note: I could not confirm which dopant gas a given 1982 Taiwanese polysilicon plant used; the specific pairing is medium confidence.

facts.label: Target resistivity
facts.value: 0.005-0.02 ohm-cm for a doped polysilicon film; subcollector 0.1 ohm-cm

facts.label: Dopant sources
facts.value: PH3 for both polarities in older practice; AsH3 for n-type

c64.extras.name: Finishing and bundled extras
c64.extras.description: Branches that hang off the machine rather than being part of it: how legends and colours were printed onto plastic, how one keyboard key becomes a bit, and the joystick that shipped in the box in some markets.

c64.joystick.name: Joystick controller
c64.joystick.description: The self-centring 4-way joystick Commodore bundled with the C64 and sold with most of its software: a moulded gate plate held neutral by four springs, four miniature microswitches underneath it, a steel shaft with a ball top, a plastic knob, and a coiled cable to one of the DE-9 control ports. Five moving electrical contacts and one mechanical centring mechanism, in a shell of black ABS.
c64.joystick.note: The C64's bundled joystick is a plain 2-button 4-way unit; the 3-button version came later and was supplied separately or with the C64C. Commodore also sold a version with a fire button on the shaft and a third button on the knob top ('Commodore 4611' and successors are cited for these in the retro literature, but I could not verify a Commodore part number for the specific 1982 bundle and have not asserted one).

facts.label: Centring
facts.value: 4 torsion/coil springs, not a positional detent

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: coiled, terminating in a DE-9 male plug

c64.joystick.cable.name: Coiled cable and DE-9 plug
c64.joystick.cable.description: A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.
c64.joystick.cable.note: The coiled cable was traditionally PVC-insulated stranded copper; some units shipped with a straight lead. The number of conductors varies between joystick models and I have not verified the C64 bundle's exactly.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.name: DE-9 male plug contacts
c64.joystick.cable.plug.description: Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.note: The stamping, forming and plating route is described at c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.name: Stranded conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.description: Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.name: Tinning of the conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.description: The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.name: Cable assembly and strain relief
c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.description: The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.

c64.joystick.knob.name: ABS knob and top button
c64.joystick.knob.description: The moulded handle on the top of the shaft.
