On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.
c64.joystick.knob.note: A soft overmould on the grip was a quality feature on some 1980s sticks and absent on the cheap bundled ones; I cannot say which the C64 bundle shipped with.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, sometimes with a soft TPE or rubber overmould

c64.joystick.knob.abs.name: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
c64.joystick.knob.abs.description: The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.note: The styrene and butadiene chains are expanded at c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs; referenced rather than duplicated.

facts.label: Melt flow
facts.value: chosen grade ~5-15 g/10 min for housings

c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.name: Fire button on shaft and knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.description: On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.description: The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.name: Knob mould tool
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.description: A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.iron.name: Iron ore
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.iron.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.name: Glass or mineral filler and the TiO2 whitener
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.description: The knob's black colour is a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS. Where a lighter colour was wanted the pigment was titanium dioxide, a white pigment made from ilmenite, and it is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.note: The titanium dioxide route is shared with the MLCC powder tree at mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.titanium-dioxide; referenced rather than duplicated.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Pigment dispersion in the ABS
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Titanium dioxide whitener
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Alumina from bauxite
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Bauxite profile
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

c64.joystick.shaft.name: Steel shaft and ball top
c64.joystick.shaft.description: A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: ~6 mm square steel section, pressed into the gate

facts.label: Top
facts.value: moulded ball or ball-and-paddle, ~20 mm diameter

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.name: Cold-drawn steel bar
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.description: Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed.
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.note: The frozen-shaft failure is well documented across the vintage joystick genre; the steel chain itself belongs to the metals file.

facts.label: Corrosion
facts.value: the shaft rimes in place in the bushing, freezing the stick

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.name: Iron ore (limonite / hematite)
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.description: The steel shaft begins as iron ore. The bulk of world steel in 1982 was made in a blast furnace from sintered hematite-magnetite pellets/coke, refined to steel in a basic oxygen furnace. Rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.note: The blast-furnace coke chain belongs to the power file; referenced here.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: blast furnace -> basic oxygen furnace -> continuous cast bar

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet.name: Pelletising and blast furnace
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet.description: Concentrate is pelletised and fired with limestone and coke, charged with the coke burden, and reduced to pig iron. The coke is what makes it economically possible, and it is where the energy density that lets a steel part cost less than a plastic one comes from.

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet.name: Metallurgical coke
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet.description: Coking coal heated in coke ovens to drive off the volatile matter, leaving a porous carbon fuel that is also the reducing agent. Mined coal, and the reason a 1982 steel plant sits next to a coking battery.

c64.joystick.microswitches.name: Four miniature microswitches
c64.joystick.microswitches.description: Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold-plated on brass or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Case
facts.value: moulded thermoset or thermoplastic body, sealed or dust-covered

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.name: Switch case polymer
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.description: A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Through-hole mounting and solder lugs
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Joystick switch board
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: A small printed board inside the joystick carries the four microswitches and drops the switch pins to the cable. It is a two-layer FR-4 board with the same glass-epoxy laminate and copper foil as the keyboard board.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Glass-filled nylon case
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Nylon-6-6 resin
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: Caprolactam polymerisation - the same chain as the switch body and the keycap legend. A single C64 contains nylon in its switch housings, its joystick bushings and its microswitch cases.

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.name: Sprung leaf and contact-plating detail
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.description: Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.note: Gold-plated microswitch contacts are correct for the era; many cost-built equivalents were silver- or nickel-plated instead.

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.name: Gold plating of the microswitch leaf
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.description: The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.name: Brass leaf metal
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.description: Phosphor bronze or brass strip, stamped and formed into a bowed leaf. Copper alloy from mined ore, as everywhere else in this file.

c64.joystick.gate.name: 4-way direction gate
c64.joystick.gate.description: A cross-shaped sliding gate that physically interlocks so only one of the four directions can be closed at a time - the same gating trick as a keyboard's 3-key rollover prevention. The gate rides on four ribs and is held centred by four springs, so it is self-centring and has no detented 'gate 2' half-way position.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded glass-filled nylon or PBT gate on an ABS chassis

facts.label: Gating
facts.value: one direction at a time; diagonals blocked

facts.label: Return
facts.value: four coil or torsion springs on the gate ribs

c64.joystick.gate.friction.name: Bushing and friction washer
c64.joystick.gate.friction.description: The shaft is supported by a plastic bushing or a nylon washer in the chassis, and a felt or fibre friction pad under the gate sets the feel. Friction pads compress and shed debris with age, which is the second classic cause of a stiff or drifting stick.
c64.joystick.gate.friction.note: Friction pads are standard in this class of joystick; I have not measured the C64's.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.name: Friction pad
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.description: A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.name: Wool felt
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.description: Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Nylon bushing in the chassis
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: A moulded nylon bushing in the ABS chassis that the steel shaft runs in. Nylon is used because it is self-lubricating and will not gall the shaft; a metal bushing would seize onto the shaft as it rimes.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Nylon resin for the bushing
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. Nylon-6-6 from caprolactam, the same polymer as the microswitch case.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Caprolactam
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: The caprolactam-to-nylon-6-6 chain. The joystick contains nylon in its bushing, its microswitch cases and its knob overmould.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

c64.joystick.gate.spring.name: Centring springs
c64.joystick.gate.spring.description: Four small compression or torsion springs push the gate back to neutral from every direction. They are the part that wears out: once the springs weaken, the stick stays pushed, which is the most common repair on a vintage joystick and the reason 'joystick centering' appears in every retro repair guide.

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: the limiting part; springs lose tension and occasionally snap

c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement.name: Why springs are the failure point
c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement.description: Gate springs carry the whole centring duty and are cycled by every direction press. Once one is weakened the stick sits off-centre and the machine reads a direction the user is not pressing - the most common single joystick fault of the era.

c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.name: Spring wire for the centring springs
c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.description: Drawn music-wire or stainless spring wire, coiled and closed. Centring springs are the cheapest consumable in the whole joystick and the one that is always replaced rather than repaired.

c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.iron-ore.name: Iron ore for the spring wire
c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.iron-ore.description: The same ore-to-bar-to-wire chain as every other steel spring on the machine.

c64.keyboard-switches.name: Keyboard matrix switches and domes
c64.keyboard-switches.description: How one keystroke on a C64 becomes a 1 in memory: 63 rubber domes on a rigid printed circuit board, scanned by CIA #1 as an 8 x 8 matrix. The domes are carbon-loaded rubber pills that short two plated pads when a keycap's plunger drives them closed, and the scanned result is simply a pair of row and column lines being connected.
c64.keyboard-switches.note: CORRECTION to the brief in one respect: the C64 keyboard is NOT a flexible membrane with silver-ink traces. It is a rubber-dome keyboard on a RIGID printed circuit board with plated conductive pads, and the domes themselves are the conductive element. Earlier VIC-20-generation Commodore keyboards also used rigid boards with bare (unplated) copper pads, which oxidise - the reason some early C64 keyboards need cleaning while later ones do not. Commodore did use silver-filled ink pads on some other keyboards and peripherals of the period, so that branch is included, but it is not the breadbin C64.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 63 (including 5 cursor keys); matrix directly covers 64 of 66 positions

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: 8 columns driven on CIA #1 port A, 8 rows read on port B

facts.label: Domed keys
facts.value: 61 of the 63; SHIFT LOCK is wired on the same line as LSHIFT

facts.label: Out-of-matrix
facts.value: RESTORE (wired to NMI) and SHIFT LOCK

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.name: Flat ribbon cable to the mainboard
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.description: A flat multi-conductor ribbon leaves the keyboard board, loops through the case, and terminates at the pin header on the front-left edge of the mainboard. The ribbon is crimped into an insulation-displacement connector on the keyboard end in later designs, and soldered directly to the header on the mainboard end.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.note: Fatigue fracture where the ribbon flexes at the header is by far the most-reported C64 keyboard fault of the period and later; it produces keys that work only when the cable is bent a certain way.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: flat flexible cable, PVC-jacketed, 0.5-1.27 mm pitch

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: conductor fatigue fracture at the header - the single most common C64 keyboard fault

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.name: PET/PVC flat flexible cable
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.description: Parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film layers with a PVC jacket. The jacket and the film are all hydrocarbon polymers, so this cable is chemically the same family as the switch housings and the case.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.note: Insulation-displacement contacts on the keyboard end were common from the late 1970s; some Commodore designs used soldered connections at both ends.

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.name: PVC jacket
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.description: The ribbon's outer jacket is extruded PVC, the cheapest flexible insulation available. Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from salt - rock salt mined or solution-mined - while the ethylene comes from a steam cracker. So the ribbon cable ends at both rock salt and crude oil.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.note: The salt-to-chlorine step is expanded in the fluids file.

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vi.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vi.description: Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine over a promoted catalyst. The ethylene comes from a steam cracker and the chlorine from brine electrolysis - so the ribbon jacket touches both an oil field and a salt field.

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vi.name: Naphtha
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vi.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.name: SHIFT LOCK and RESTORE, the two off-matrix keys
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.description: Two of the 63 keys are not in the scanned matrix. SHIFT LOCK is wired to the same line as LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot distinguish it and simply sees a latched shift. RESTORE is wired directly to the 6510's NMI line, so pressing it halts the CPU without any firmware involvement at all - a hardware reset, not a key.
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.note: Documented on the C64 wiki keyboard page. SHIFT LOCK is a latching dome arrangement (the dome is deformed or a second contact is added) rather than a scanner-visible key.

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: wired to the same wire as LSHIFT

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: wired to NMI, outside the matrix entirely

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.wiring.name: Wiring to the LSHIFT line
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.wiring.description: SHIFT LOCK is simply wired in parallel with LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot tell the two apart: pressing SHIFT LOCK just holds the shift bit down. Restore is on a completely different wire, straight to the 6510 NMI pin.

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.name: Latching dome for SHIFT LOCK
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.description: A dome that latches: pressing it collapses it and it stays collapsed, requiring a second, firmer press (or a press on a neighbouring key) to release. Mechanically it is a deformation of the rubber dome itself rather than a separate switch, which is why no space in the matrix is spent on it.

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.name: Bistable dome geometry
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.description: The latching dome works because the rubber is shaped so that under a light press it collapses past the rubber's own elastic limit and stays collapsed. It is a mechanical latch, not an electrical one, which is why the firmware has no idea a separate key exists.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.name: Keycap and plunger mechanism
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.description: A double-shot moulded keycap on a cross-shaped plastic stem. The stem sits in a plunger barrel and carries either a coil spring back up (the common later C64 keycap) or, on the earliest VIC-20-derived keyboards, nothing at all - those rely purely on the rubber dome for their return and feel markedly sluggish.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: double-shot moulded ABS or ABS/PC, legend printed or moulded

facts.label: Plunger
facts.value: moulded plastic cross stem in a barrel

facts.label: Return
facts.value: coil spring in later keycaps; absent on the earliest keyboards

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.name: Coil return spring
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.description: A small stainless or music-wire spring inside the plunger barrel returning the key to its rest position and setting the initial (pre-dome) force. Without it the user bottoms out on the dome itself, which is why the earliest keyboards feel hard and inconsistent.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.note: Music wire (high-carbon steel) or stainless; the spring wire is wound on a small coil-winder in the millions.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Spring coiling machine
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: A cam-controlled coiler winds a coil spring from wire, sets its free length and closes the ends, tens of thousands per hour. Every keycap plunger spring on the keyboard was made on a machine of this type.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Tool steel cam and dies
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: The coiler tool is hardened tool steel, and the coiler is a Camweld or similar automatic machine. Ferrous tooling, so iron ore again.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Iron ore
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.name: Music wire (patented steel)
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.description: A high-carbon steel wire, patented and drawn to a fine diameter, with a very high tensile strength - which is what lets a millimetre-thick coil inside a keycap return thousands of times without taking a set.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.name: Iron ore for spring steel
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.description: The same hematite/magnetite chain as the joystick shaft. Almost all ferrous stock in 1982 was basic-oxygen-furnace steel from imported ore.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Double-shot moulding of the legend
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The keycap is injection-moulded twice: once in the base colour, then a second shot of a second colour is injected into a slightly larger cavity, covering everything except the legend characters, which were left as uncoated islands of the first shot. This gives a legend that cannot wear off - the reason a forty-year-old C64 keycap still reads.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: Double-shot keycaps were standard on quality keyboards of the period; whether every C64 keycap of 1982 was double-shot rather than pad-printed varies by supplier and I have not verified it for the whole set.

facts.label: Shots
facts.value: two injection mouldings, co-moulded in the same tool cycle

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: island of the base-colour shot, not a printed decal

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Co-moulding cycle
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: Both shots are moulded in one press cycle using a hot-runner or a runnerless hot manifold so the second colour is injected onto the first while the first is still hot enough to bond. That is what makes the legend wear-proof rather than a coat of paint.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Second-shot colour
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The outer shot is pigmented with an organic or inorganic colourant at high loading. Brown, red, orange and grey legends - the four C64 keycap colours - are all achievable with pigmented ABS; the moulding must be run at a high enough pressure that the two shots fuse rather than delaminate.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Colourant in the second shot
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The second-shot colour is a pigment dispersed in the ABS matrix at high loading. Organic pigments give brighter colours and are more expensive; inorganic iron oxides give the earthier browns and reds.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Iron oxide pigments
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: Synthetic iron oxides, made by oxidising iron scrap, were the standard browns, reds and blacks of the period and are still used. They begin at iron ore and end up in the keycap.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Iron ore
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.name: ABS keycap polymer
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix rubberised with polybutadiene. It is tough, dimensionally stable, chemically scratch-resistant and - crucially for legends - it takes paint and plating well. Almost every C64 keycap is ABS or ABS/PC.

facts.label: Why ABS
facts.value: impact strength plus the ability to hold a printed legend

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Acrylonitrile monomer
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The acrylonitrile monomer is made by the Sohlo process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen are passed over a bismuth-antimony or bismuth-molybdenum catalyst to give acrylonitrile selectively. Propylene itself comes from steam cracking of naphtha, so the keycap of a C64 is roughly one and a half hydrocarbon molecules away from crude oil.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Bismuth-antimony catalyst
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a bismuth molybdate or bismuth-antimony promoted silica. Bismuth came from bismuthinite, a comparatively rare ore worked chiefly in Bolivia and China, and it was a real bottleneck for acrylonitrile capacity in the 1980s.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.note: Bismuth supply was genuinely tight in the early 1980s and the ammoxidation catalyst industry was a significant consumer; flagged medium because I have not quantified it.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.name: Styrene monomer
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene, itself made by alkylating benzene with ethylene from steam cracking. Styrene is the rigid phase of the copolymer; benzene is ultimately a refinery product of crude oil or of pyrolitic gasoline from steam crackers.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.note: Chain expanded in the plastics file.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.name: Ethylbenzene to styrene
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.description: Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, then dehydrogenated to styrene over a promoted iron oxide catalyst.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.name: Naphtha
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.name: Polybutadiene rubber phase
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.description: The elastic phase that makes ABS impact-resistant, made by polymerising butadiene derived from refinery butadiene, which itself comes from steam cracking propylene. This is the hydrocarbon tree: propylene to butadiene to the rubber in the keycap's grip surface.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.note: The steam-cracking-to-polymer chain is expanded in the plastics file.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.name: Butadiene monomer
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.description: The rubber phase of ABS is made from butadiene, produced by steam cracking of refinery butane or by dehydrogenating butenes. It is the same butadiene the synthetic-rubber industry used.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.name: Crude oil
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.description: The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.name: Carbon-loaded rubber domes
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.description: Each key position has a small moulded rubber pill, domed upwards, whose underside carries a conductive carbon-loaded contact that bridges two pads when the dome is crushed. Because carbon is loaded into the rubber as a filler rather than plated on, the dome is its own contact - it wears slightly with use and it is the consumable part of the switch.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: carbon black or graphite powder in a silicone or neoprene elastomer

facts.label: Activation force
facts.value: ~150-250 g on the dome alone, plus the keycap spring

facts.label: Life
facts.value: ~millions of actuations, but the conductive face tarnishes with skin oil and dust

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.name: Compression moulding of the dome sheet
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.description: The domes are moulded as a continuous sheet on a heated platen press: uncured compound is placed in a multi-cavity tool, pressed, cured, and the sheet released as one piece with every key's dome attached. Domes therefore arrive as a single printed-circuit-sized rubber sheet that has to be aligned to the pads by hand.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.note: Compression-moulded dome sheets were standard; whether the C64's came as a sheet or pre-applied to a carrier film I could not determine.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: ~150-180 C, minutes, for silicone; ~100-140 C for neoprene

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Steel dome tool
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: A machined or spark-eroded steel tool with one hemispherical cavity per key. It has to be replaced as the dome geometry is re-specified, and its surface finish is what the dome's mating face is polished against.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Spark-erosion machining of the dome cavity
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: A fine copper electrode is brought within micrometres of the workpiece in a dielectric bath and pulses of a few microseconds melt a microscopic crater per pulse. Spark erosion is how a one-micron hemispherical cavity gets cut in hardened tool steel without any mechanical stress on the surface.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Graphite tool electrode
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: Graphite is the standard spark-erosion electrode: it is conductive, machinable to a fine tip, and wears slowly by re-graphitising. Machined graphite is made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.pla.name: Heated platen press
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.pla.description: A hydraulic flat-bed press with heated platens holds a multi-cavity dome tool against the compound long enough to cure the elastomer. Small presses of this type did the whole dome sheet for a keyboard in one shot.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.name: Carbon-filled elastomer compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.description: Carbon black is compounded into the elastomer at a few tens of per cent by weight. The particles form a percolation network so the dome conducts along its own bulk, and the higher the loading the lower the resistance - but too much loading makes the dome brittle. This is the same black powder that goes into resistor films and pot tracks.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.note: The dome resistance being in the tens-to-hundreds of ohms range is why a dirty dome still 'works' for a 6526 input but why cleaning it matters; the characteristic failure is drift upward into the CMOS threshold region.

facts.label: Contact resistance
facts.value: typically tens to hundreds of ohms - enough to trip a CMOS input, far too much for a logic 'low'

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Carbon black filler (petroleum-derived)
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The same furnace-black feedstock used in the resistors, compounded into the elastomer. The dome's conductivity and its wear rate are both set by the grade and loading of this powder.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: The full carbon-black tree is at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.powder.carbon-black; referenced rather than duplicated.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Grade selection for the dome
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: A high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, so a dome can be made conductive with less filler and stay soft. The grade choice is the difference between a responsive key and a stiff one.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone or neoprene elastomer
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The dome body. Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) was favoured for its high compression set and wide temperature range; neoprene (polychloroprene) for oil and abrasion resistance. Both are thermoset elastomers, vulcanised in the mould rather than injection-moulded as thermoplastics, which is why they are compression-moulded sheet.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Which elastomer the C64's dome sheet used is not something I could determine; both were standard.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone dome compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: Silicone rubber is built on a silicon-oxygen backbone and is filled with reinforcing silica. It stays elastic over a wide temperature range and does not take up much oil, which is why a silicone dome does not swell and seize.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silica sand
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.name: 8 x 8 keyboard matrix
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.description: Eight column lines snake around the board and eight row lines snake around the other way, each pair of crossing traces forming one key. Pressing a key connects its column to its row; the firmware walks the matrix by writing a pattern to CIA #1's port A and reading port B. Because one row line can touch eight different columns, a single conducting bridge is the entire 'switch'.

facts.label: Scan
facts.value: write column pattern to $DC00, read rows from $DC01

facts.label: Latency
facts.value: one scan per ~1/60 s frame unless idle

facts.label: Ghosting
facts.value: 3-key combinations can produce an extra false key - the classic matrix ghosting problem

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.name: Glass-epoxy laminate (FR-4)
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.description: Woven glass-fibre cloth impregnated with epoxy and pressed into a sheet. The standard printed-circuit laminate since the 1960s, replacing the older phenolic paper board. The keyboard board is a trivial two-layer FR-4 part, but it goes through the same copper foil lamination and hole-drilling lines as a mainboard.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.note: The glass fabric is drawn from molten glass (silica); the chemistry chain is expanded in the board file.

c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.name: Epoxy resin of the laminate
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.description: The epoxy that binds the glass cloth is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both of which are petrochemical. A two-layer keyboard PCB is thus a woven silica sheet glued with a fossil-derived resin and clad in copper.

c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlor.name: Epichlorohydrin
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlor.description: One of the two building blocks of epoxy resin, made by chlorinating propylene with hypochlorous acid. Epoxy is used on the keyboard laminate, on the capacitor bungs, on the tantalum seals and on the connector overmoulds - one of the most widespread materials on the whole machine.

c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlor.name: Crude oil
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlor.description: The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.name: Woven E-glass cloth
c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.description: Silica glass is melted and drawn into fine filaments a few microns across, woven into a cloth and woven again into a fine gauze. This cloth is the reinforcement in every FR-4 board in the world.

c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.name: Silica batch from silica sand
c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.description: The glass batch is made from silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes. The sand is dredged or quarried, and it is the same quartz sand that fed the hydrothermal quartz reactors.
c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.note: The quartz sand node is shared with mb.crystal; referenced rather than duplicated.

c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.name: Glass batch formulation
c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-clo.description: Silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes, and a little salt as a catalyst, melted at ~1400-1600 C. The same batch chemistry as container glass, only drawn rather than floated.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.name: Rigid keyboard PCB with plated pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.description: A glass-epoxy laminate board, drilled and plated through in the usual way, carrying the matrix traces as copper and terminating each key position in a pair of plated pads. On the breadbin keyboard the pads are plated metal; on the earlier VIC-20-derived boards they were bare copper, and bare copper oxidises into a high-resistance film - the reason those keyboards need periodic cleaning and later ones generally do not.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.note: The bare-copper-pad claim comes from a restoration account of an early (VIC-20-derived) C64 keyboard which notes its activation pads are not protected from oxidation the way later keyboards' are. The PCB materials and fabrication are expanded in the board file.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: rigid FR-4, not a flex membrane

facts.label: Pads
facts.value: plated through-hole pads on breadbin boards; bare copper on earliest

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: standoffs and screws into the case, not clips

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Plating of the key pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: The exposed pads are plated - gold over nickel on later keyboards - so the carbon contact of the rubber dome has a low-resistance, non-oxidising surface to bridge onto. Where the plating is absent or has worn through, the bare copper oxidises and the key needs cleaning.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Gold for the pad flash
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: A thin gold flash over nickel on the key pads. Gold does not oxidise, so the dome keeps making contact for decades; where the flash is thin or gone, the key stops working until cleaned.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.name: Electrodeposited copper foil
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.description: The matrix traces are copper, deposited on the laminate by an electroplating line using acid copper sulphate solution and an insoluble anode. The same copper foil process as the mainboard, at a much thinner gauge.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.name: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2)
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.description: The dominant copper ore, mined underground in porphyry and skarn deposits and in open pits. Copper was electrorefined to cathode and rolled into foil long before it was ever plated onto a board; the board industry simply bought the foil that the copper industry already made.

c64.decor.name: Decoration: legends, logos and metallised inks on plastic
c64.decor.description: Getting colour and type onto moulded plastic in 1982 meant printing it, not moulding colour into it. Commodore used two-colour pad printing for the keycap legends and the rainbow badge, screen printing where a flat surface allowed it, metallised flake ink for the shiny logo bars, and - in later production - two-shot moulding and painted or lacquered surfaces. Each process has its own pad, ink, screen and cure chemistry.
c64.decor.note: The dominant decorating process on a 1982 C64 is pad printing, because the parts are curved, crowned, textured and one-shot moulded - none of which suit screen printing. Two-shot moulding and in-mould labelling existed but were expensive and not used on the breadbin case.

c64.decor.prepress.name: Prepress: artwork to printing film and plate
c64.decor.prepress.description: Every legend and every logo started as artwork, which in 1982 was mechanically or photographically composed, then copied onto film by a process camera, and the film was used to expose a plate. Text was set in hot metal or phototype, and the Commodore rainbow artwork was assembled from painted separations by hand.
c64.decor.prepress.note: The C64 rainbow is one of the most reproduced pieces of 1980s graphic design, and it was made the slow way: separations drawn and painted, then screened. There was no desktop publishing until the late 1980s.

facts.label: Text setting
facts.value: hot metal or phototypesetting (later CRT phototype)

c64.decor.prepress.film.name: Ortho photographic film (negative)
c64.decor.prepress.film.description: The black-and-white film that carries the image to the plate. It is a cellulose or polyester film coated with a silver-halide emulsion; exposed in a process camera or a contact frame, then developed and fixed in a chemical line.

c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.name: Silver halide emulsion
c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.description: Silver bromide or silver iodide crystals suspended in gelatin. The silver comes from silver ore, and most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.

c64.decor.prepress.silver.name: Silver (recovered from ore and refinery residue)
c64.decor.prepress.silver.description: Silver metal recovered from argentite and galena ores, and from the anode slimes of electrolytic copper refining. It is refined to photographic purity by cupellation and electrolytic refining.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: mostly a byproduct of lead/copper refining

c64.decor.prepress.lead-ore.name: Galena (lead sulfide ore) and silver-bearing concentrates
c64.decor.prepress.lead-ore.description: Galena is the dominant lead ore and almost always carries silver as argentite or as silver dissolved in the galena lattice. It is mined, concentrated by flotation, and reduced in a blast furnace or sinter plant.

c64.decor.prepress.cupellation.name: Cupellation of lead bullion
c64.decor.prepress.cupellation.description: Lead bullion is oxidised in a cupellation furnace; the litharge formed is absorbed back into the bath and the noble metal - silver and gold - floats as dross on top. The silver is then refined electrolytically to photographic purity.
c64.decor.prepress.cupellation.note: So the legend on a keycap is, several steps down, partly silver that came out of a lead ore in a cupellation furnace.

c64.decor.prepress.silver-electrolysis.name: Electrolytic refining of silver
c64.decor.prepress.silver-electrolysis.description: Crude silver from the cupellation hearth is dissolved in nitric acid and electrolytically refined: silver anodes, silver-nitrate electrolyte, pure silver cathodes. The result is 99.99% silver - the purity photographic chemistry needs for its emulsion.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: silver nitrate in aqueous nitric acid

c64.decor.prepress.nitric-acid.name: Nitric acid (Ostwald process)
c64.decor.prepress.nitric-acid.description: Ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-950 C, to nitrogen dioxide, and absorbed in water to give nitric acid. The ammonia comes from natural gas via steam reforming and Haber-Bosch synthesis.
c64.decor.prepress.nitric-acid.note: The same nitric acid that dissolves the silver also oxidises cyclohexanol to adipic acid for the nylon latches in the connectors. One chemical, several very different products.

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: NO2 absorbed in water in a packed column

c64.decor.prepress.silver-nitrate.name: Silver nitrate
c64.decor.prepress.silver-nitrate.description: Made by dissolving silver in hot nitric acid. Silver nitrate is the classic photographic salt: reacting it with halide in gelatin is what makes the silver-halide grains in a film or paper negative.

c64.decor.prepress.film-base.name: Film base (cellulose triacetate or polyester)
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.description: A flexible transparent film on which the emulsion is cast. Cellulose triacetate was the standard photographic film base, made from acetic anhydride and cellulose; polyester (PET) film base became common later for its dimensional stability.
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.note: The cellulose comes from wood pulp (a dissolved pulp paper route) and the acetic acid from methanol oxidation - so a printing negative is partly wood and partly natural gas.

c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.name: Cellulose (for triacetate)
c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.description: Dissolved from wood pulp and regenerated into fibre. The film route is a small, high-purity use of cellulose compared with paper, but it is the same feedstock: a tree.

c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.name: Acetic acid / acetic anhydride for film base
c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.description: Made by catalytic oxidation of ethanol, or by the carbonylation of methanol. Methanol comes from synthesis gas, which comes from natural-gas reforming.

facts.label: Carbonylation
facts.value: methanol + CO -> acetic acid, rhodium catalyst, 150-200 C

c64.decor.inspection.name: Decoration inspection (100% look)
c64.decor.inspection.description: Printed parts are checked for legibility, registration and offset before they go into the machine. On a two-colour legend, a shift by half a character width is a reject, so this is a genuinely tight tolerance - and one of the reasons legends look so consistent on surviving machines.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: registration to a fraction of a character width

c64.decor.overlay.name: Keycap legend overlays and printed inserts
c64.decor.overlay.description: An alternative to printing the cap is to bond a printed film or a moulded insert onto or into the cap. Commodore keycaps are printed, not overlaid, but the technique was in use on contemporary keyboards and appears on some Commodore accessories and on the memory-expansion modules. Recorded here for completeness with low confidence for the C64 specifically.
c64.decor.overlay.note: Unverified for the 1982 breadbin C64 keycaps. What is verified is that the caps are moulded ABS with printed legends, with the font weight, legend position and printed faces varying between production runs - which is itself a good way to date a keyboard.

facts.label: Technique
facts.value: screen-printed polyester film bonded into a recess, or a two-shot printed insert

c64.decor.paint.name: Spray lacquer and paint (used on accessories, not the case)
c64.decor.paint.description: Spray-applied lacquer over plastic - used on joystick housings, on some panels and on plastic accessory parts - was an acrylic or nitrocellulose lacquer, sprayed in a ventilated booth and stoved at 60-80 C. It is how a plastic part gets a uniform, slightly textured finish that hides mould flow marks.
c64.decor.paint.note: I could not confirm that the C64 case itself was sprayed, and the beige ABS is normally unpainted; spray lacquering is included because it was routine on the plastic accessories and on some case variants, and because the haze it gives is what is sometimes mistaken for 'moulded-in colour'.

c64.decor.paint.cure-oven.name: Cure oven (batch, gas-fired)
c64.decor.paint.cure-oven.description: A batch oven with gas burners and forced circulation, holding 60-80 C for 20-30 minutes to flash off the solvent and crosslink the lacquer. The gas burners are the only fossil fuel on the decorating line.

c64.decor.paint.lacquer.name: Spray lacquer (acrylic or nitrocellulose)
c64.decor.paint.lacquer.description: A solvent-borne film former with pigment, sprayed and baked. Nitrocellulose was standard for consumer plastic coatings in 1982; 2K polyurethane and water-borne acrylic were the better performers but more expensive and better suited to metal.

c64.decor.two-shot.name: Two-shot / in-mould decoration
c64.decor.two-shot.description: Deciding not to print at all and moulding the colour or the decoration in: a second shot in a second colour, or an in-mould printed film or transfer placed in the tool before the shot. Both existed in 1982 but were expensive, and neither is used on the breadbin case - the colour there is pigment in the resin.
c64.decor.two-shot.note: In-mould decoration is scratch-proof and cycle-fast, which is why it became the norm for later consumer plastics; for a 1982 breadbin case the cost was not justified. The idea that the legend is part of the plastic rather than on it did not become common until the 1990s.

facts.label: In-mould printing
facts.value: a pre-printed film or decal placed in the tool, flooded with resin

facts.label: In-mould labelling
facts.value: a printed label applied to the core of the tool before moulding

c64.decor.metallised.name: Metallised and pearlescent ink
c64.decor.metallised.description: The shiny bars in the Commodore rainbow logo and the metallic trim on some panels are metallised ink: pigment-grade aluminium flake, or vacuum-metallised polyester film, suspended in a binder and printed, then optionally burnished to align the flakes flat so they reflect.
c64.decor.metallised.note: Flake ink is genuinely a compromise: randomly oriented flakes only reflect a fraction of the light, so metallised ink looks duller than metal - unless it is burnished, which is why a good logo feels smoother than the plastic around it.

facts.label: Flake
facts.value: atomised aluminium, ~5-15 um, or vacuum-metallised polyester film

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: a flat mirror-like metallic that changes with viewing angle

c64.decor.hot-stamping.name: Hot foil stamping (alternative to flake ink)
c64.decor.hot-stamping.description: A heated metal foil is pressed onto the plastic with a type plate and the image transfers. On rigid ABS this needs a rougher surface or a soft stamping die, which is why flake ink beat foil stamping on a textured case - but foil stamping was used on smooth panels and on some packaging.
c64.decor.hot-stamping.note: Included because it is the era's standard metallic-decoration alternative and because the 'mirror' finish on some Commodore trim is hot-stamped film rather than ink.

c64.decor.metallised.burnish.name: Burnishing (or calendering) the flake
c64.decor.metallised.burnish.description: Passing the printed part between heated polished rollers flattens the flakes into the surface so they mirror rather than scatter. Burnished metallic ink on a moulded part looks like a metal panel - which is precisely the intent of a rainbow badge.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: heated roller calender between nylon or paper rolls

c64.decor.metallised.binders.name: Binder for metallised ink (acrylic or alkyd)
c64.decor.metallised.binders.description: A drying ink binder that holds the flakes flat and lets them reflect. Formulated so the flake lies parallel to the surface; this is what produces the flat metallic look rather than a sparkly one.

c64.decor.metallised.flake.name: Atomised aluminium flake
c64.decor.metallised.flake.description: Molten aluminium is atomised with air into 5-15 um flakes, which are then washed, sifted by size and coated with an oxidation-inhibiting lacquer so they do not go grey. The same basic process makes the aluminium in the EMI shield, only at a different scale.
c64.decor.metallised.flake.note: Aluminium flake pigment for inks is a genuinely old chemistry - used in water-based paints and print metallic inks since the nineteenth century.

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: lacquer or chromate wash to stop further oxidation

c64.decor.screen-printing.name: Screen printing
c64.decor.screen-printing.description: Silk screening through a mesh, used on Commodore parts where the surface is flat enough: printed panels, keycap sets on flat-topped caps, cartridge labels and some case markings. It cannot print the grain-textured bezel reliably, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: nylon monofilament or stainless steel wire, 100-200 mesh

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: one-part epoxy or solvent ink, cured by UV or heat

c64.decor.screen-print.ink.name: Screen-printing ink (one-part epoxy)
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.description: A one-component epoxy or polyester ink with a latent hardener, screen-printed through the stencil and then heat-cured. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels and keycap overlays used.
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.note: One-part epoxy inks cure at 120-150 C for 5-20 minutes, or flash to UV if the formulation is UV-curable. The epoxy supply chain (bisphenol A + epichlorohydrin) is documented under c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy.

c64.decor.screen-print.squeegee.name: Squeegee blade
c64.decor.screen-print.squeegee.description: A rubber or neoprene blade in a wooden or aluminium holder that forces ink through the stencil and wipes the surface. The durometer of the blade is the operator's variable: hard for fine detail, soft for heavy coverage.

c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.name: Neoprene squeegee rubber
c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.description: Polychloroprene, chosen because it resists the solvents in screen ink and wears well. It is the same chloroprene rubber used for cable jackets and gaskets, again pointing back to the C4 cracker cut.

c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.name: Screen emulsion (PVA or diazo)
c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.description: The photosensitive coating that becomes the stencil. Diazo emulsions, standard in 1982, are washed out with water after exposure; PVA emulsion requires a separate exposure through the base and is more solvent-resistant. The stencil is exposed through a film positive and then washed.

c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.name: Screen mesh (nylon monofilament or stainless wire)
c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.description: A woven mesh stretched and glued to an aluminium frame. Nylon is used where solvent or epoxy inks would attack a wire screen; stainless wire is used where long life under abrasive inks matters. Both are woven from a drawn filament or wire on a loom.
c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.note: The nylon is hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid again - the same PA6,6 that goes into connector latches, drawn down to 50-80 um for the mesh.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: ~100-200 mesh for fine legends, coarser for solid areas

c64.decor.pad-printing.name: Pad printing (tampo printing)
c64.decor.pad-printing.description: The workhorse process. A soft silicone rubber pad is pressed onto a flat metal cliche carrying the image in wet ink, picks the ink up on its raised relief, then deforms against the curved or crowned plastic part and transfers the image. One pad, one colour, one station; two stations give the two-colour keycap legends.

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of impressions per hour

facts.label: Surface tolerance
facts.value: curved, crowned and textured parts, unlike screen printing

c64.decor.pad-print.ink.name: Pad-printing ink (solvent or UV)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink.description: A free-flowing, low-viscosity ink that will transfer off a soft pad and then dry on a plastic part. In 1982 most pad inks were solvent-based (glycol ether / xylene / ester solvent with an alkyd or acrylic resin and a pigment); UV-curing pad inks existed and were gaining ground, and were faster but needed a lamp.

c64.decor.uv-curing.name: UV curing of ink
c64.decor.uv-curing.description: A mercury or metal-halide lamp floods the printed part in under a second and the photo-initiator in the ink polymerises it in place. It was the big printing-technology change of the late 1970s and early 1980s: instant cure, no solvent, no oven, and a harder, more abrasion-resistant print.
c64.decor.uv-curing.note: By 1982 UV curing was established in screen printing and pad printing on plastics but not yet universal; solvent drying was still the volume route. Its big advantage for a decoration shop is that you can print a keycap and immediately stack it with no drying time.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.name: Ink solvent (glycol ether / ester blend)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.description: The volatile carrier that gives pad ink its low viscosity. Common 1980s pad-ink solvents were propylene glycol ethers, dibutyl phthalate or xylene blends. It flashes off the pad quickly enough to give a sharp print and slowly enough that the impression can be placed.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.note: Solvent-based pad ink is largely gone from consumer goods today because of VOC regulation; UV-curing pad ink, which needs no solvent at all, is the modern replacement and was already available in 1982.

c64.decor.propyloxide.name: Propylene oxide (for the glycol ether solvent)
c64.decor.propyloxide.description: Made by the chlorohydrin route (propylene + chlorine + water, then caustic dehydrochlorination) or the older hydroperoxide route (propylene + hydroperoxide, then a base-catalysed rearrangement). It is what turns propylene into propylene glycol ethers and acetates, the commonest 1980s pad-ink and screen-ink solvent.
c64.decor.propyloxide.note: A pad-printing ink is therefore not a purely cosmetic chemical: its main solvent begins at the same propylene that feeds the acrylonitrile in the ABS case.

facts.label: Chlorohydrin route
facts.value: additive chlorination then dehydrochlorination with Ca(OH)2

facts.label: Glycol ether
facts.value: propylene oxide + alcohol (e.g. n-propyl) at base, then distillation

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.name: Legend and logo pigments
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.description: The legend white is almost always titanium dioxide in an alkyd binder; the rainbow logo uses a set of saturated organic pigments - phthalocyanine blue, quinacridone magenta, azo yellow - and sometimes a metallised flake for the bright bars.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.note: The same pigment supply chain as the case masterbatch and the box ink: a set of convergences that all end at the same handful of chemical plants.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.name: Ink binder resin (alkyd or acrylic)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.description: The film-forming part of the ink: an alkyd built from drying-oil fatty acids and a polyacid (the same chemistry as the printing ink vehicle on the box), or an acrylic copolymer. It is chosen for adhesion to ABS, which is notoriously hard to print on without a surface treatment.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.note: ABS has a low surface energy and low surface tension (~38-39 dynes/cm, against ~72 for water), which is why printing ink on it needs a good wetting binder or a plasma/corona treatment - and why the legends on a forty-year-old cap can be abraded off but not easily peeled.

c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.name: Cliche (the printing plate) and its electrotype
c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.description: The image is held in a flat copper or nickel electrotype, or a photopolymer plate, sunk into a plate table and flooded with ink. The traditional route is a photograph on a copper plate, which is electroplated up to 0.5-1 mm and then hand- or machine-polished back to leave only the image proud - the electrotype.
c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.note: A flat pad-print cliche is a simpler object than a litho plate because there is no water damping - it is essentially a stencil on a copper block, which is why pad printing was chosen for short runs as well as long ones.

c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.name: Copper electrotyping of the plate
c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.description: The sensitised copper plate is electroplated in an acid copper bath to build a thick deposit on the image, then the surface is ground and polished back so only the image stands proud. It is an old, slow process, but it gives an image hard enough to print millions of impressions.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acidified copper sulphate with an additive

c64.decor.pad-print.photopolymer.name: Photopolymer plate
c64.decor.pad-print.photopolymer.description: A photosensitive polymer film laminated to a steel backing, exposed through a film negative, washed out to leave the image in relief, and cured. It replaced the electrotype for short runs because it needs no electroplating step.
c64.decor.pad-print.photopolymer.note: This is the prepress step the whole packaging and decoration industry shared with offset lithography in 1982: artwork went to a camera or a phototypesetter, and plates were contact-printed from film.

facts.label: Negative
facts.value: film or glass, from the artwork

c64.decor.pad-print.pad.name: Silicone rubber printing pad
c64.decor.pad-print.pad.description: A soft, solvent-resistant, low-surface-energy pad - almost always silicone rubber - cut or cast with the relief to pick up and transfer the image. It is the consumable that has to be replaced every few thousand impressions, and pad choice (hardness, hardness-to-image ratio) is the operator's main variable.

facts.label: Life
facts.value: thousands to tens of thousands of impressions

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: two-part cast pad with a hardened steel or aluminium backing

c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.name: Two-part silicone pad compound
c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.description: A polydimethylsiloxane casting system cured at room temperature with a tin catalyst or an addition-cure platinum system. Pads are cast in a mould against the plate image so the relief matches exactly.
c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.note: The same PDMS chemistry as the switch contact pad; a 1982 pad-printing shop and a keyboard switch factory were buying essentially the same silicone.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: room temperature, ~24 h; or heat-accelerated addition cure

c64.decor.pad-print.machine.name: Two-colour pad printing press
c64.decor.pad-print.machine.description: A small cast frame with a plate table, an ink cup or doctor blade, a silicone pad on a shuttle head, and part fixtures on a rotating or indexing table. Each colour station is one table position with its own pad.
c64.decor.pad-print.machine.note: Registration on a two-colour legend is the skill of the job: the second impression has to land exactly on top of the first, shifted symbols and all.

facts.label: Registration
facts.value: micro-adjustable pad alignment; the hard part on a keycap

c64.peripherals.name: Also required to use it
c64.peripherals.description: A C64 shipped as a box with no screen, no way to save a program, and no way to enter one. In 1983 the machine was useless without a television set, a cassette recorder, and a joystick — arguably all three were part of 'a computer' in the way the question was meant.

peripheral.name: What you plug into it
peripheral.description: A C64 shipped with no screen. It drove a television set through an RF modulator, saved to a cassette deck through the 1541 drive, and took input from a joystick. These three are arguably part of 'a full computer' in 1983.

peripheral.plug.name: The connectors that carry the signal
peripheral.plug.description: Three connectors that made a C64 usable rather than just powered: the aerial socket the RF modulator hijacked, the nine-pin link to the 1541, and the 34-conductor ribbon on the back that opened the machine up. This branch is deliberately short. The mains plug and the C64's own power inlet belong to another agent's branch.

peripheral.plug.cassette-port.name: The six-pin cassette port
peripheral.plug.cassette-port.description: The connector that carries both the audio to a tape recorder and the power to a 1541. It is a 6-pin connector, carrying read, write, sense, motor, 5 V and the 9-12 V motor rail. Commodore's own cable turned it into a DIN-style socket that plugged into a consumer cassette recorder, so a C64 could save to a music deck. The same port carried the power for the 1541, which is why a 1541 has no power socket of its own.
peripheral.plug.cassette-port.note: The sense pin was how the C64 knew a motorised deck was present, and the motor pin was how it started a consumer recorder. I am not certain of the exact pinout ordering and do not want to state one that is wrong; the functional set of connections is the reliable part.

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: serial read, serial write, motor on/off, sense, and 5 V plus the 9-12 V rail

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a moulded 6-pin plug to a 6-pin DIN socket or a cassette-REC-style plug

peripheral.plug.userport.name: The 34-conductor user port ribbon
peripheral.plug.userport.description: On the back of the C64, a 34-conductor edge connector on a card, which brought out the 6510's eight data lines, twelve address lines, the read and write strobes, the IRQ and NMI lines, the serial and parallel ports, and the 5 V and ground. It was the machine's expansion door, and it was how a disk interface, a printer interface, a sampler or an EPROM programmer reached the CPU. The cable was a flat ribbon with a mylar or tinned-copper conductor, a foil shield and a PVC or polyester jacket.
peripheral.plug.userport.note: A ribbon cable of this type is a laminated structure: parallel copper conductors, 0.03-0.05 mm thick, separated by a polyester film, laminated between films, wrapped in a mylar or aluminium-foil shield and a PVC jacket. The foil and the polyester are petroleum and silica products respectively. Whether the 1982 C64 user port card edge was gold-plated or plain nickel I am not certain of; many were simply tin-plated board edge.

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: about 20 cm to 30 cm of ribbon, foil-shielded with a drain wire

facts.label: Card edge
facts.value: a gold-plated or nickel-plated PCB edge that plugged into the C64's rear connector

peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.name: Card-edge and D-sub connectors
peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.description: The connectors were gold-plated or nickel-plated brass and copper contacts in a thermoplastic (usually glass-filled nylon or a phenolic) insulator, crimped or soldered to the ribbon. A D-sub has a metal shell (often tinned steel or nickel-plated brass) that both shields the connection and provides the mechanical polarisation that stops anyone plugging it in backwards.
peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.note: The gold on a connector contact is the same anode-slime gold as the bond wire on the 6502. Gold plating on a connector is thin gold over a nickel underplate so the gold does not diffuse into the copper and leave a brittle intermetallic.

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 microns of hard gold on the contacts, over nickel, from anode slimes

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: brass or steel, nickel-plated, with a ground latch

peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.name: PVC jacket and polyester film from crude oil
peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.description: The ribbon's jacket is PVC (from ethylene and salt-derived chlorine) and its insulation between conductors is polyester film (from the same PET chain as the cassette tape base). Both are grandchildren of crude oil, and both are the same two chemistries already traced elsewhere in this tree.

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: suspension-polymerised, 57 degrees C, plasticised with a phthalate ester

facts.label: Plasticiser
facts.value: DOP or DINP, itself from an oxo process on butanol, which is from propylene

peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.salt.name: Converges on the salt for chlorine
peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.salt.description: The chlorine in the PVC came from the electrolysis of brine or rock salt, the same sodium-chloride electrolysis that fed the chlorinated solvents used to clean printed circuit boards. The chain is documented under peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.salt.

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.s.name: Rock salt, NaCl, for the chlorine
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.s.description: Salt was either mined from bedded evaporite (rock salt) or pumped as brine and evaporated in the sun (the Gulf Coast and the Cheshire salt towns). Electrolysis of the brine or of a saturated salt solution gives chlorine and sodium hydroxide, and the chlorine went into PVC jackets, into the chlorinated solvents used to clean printed circuit boards, and into the chloromethane blowing agent for cable foam.

facts.label: Electrolysis
facts.value: membrane cell, 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2 at 3-4 V

facts.label: Chlorine use
facts.value: PVC, chlorinated solvents (TCA, perchloroethylene for PCB cleaning), flame retardants

places: Gulf Coast (salt domes and solar evaporation)

peripheral.plug.serial-link.name: Nine-pin serial link to the drive
peripheral.plug.serial-link.description: The 1541 was not daisy-chained through the cassette port; it plugged into the C64's second serial port through a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable. That separate port is how the computer knew a disk drive was present at all: there was no other way for the 1541 to announce itself except by talking on this line, and the drive type was auto-detected from what it said.
peripheral.plug.serial-link.note: It was a 9-pin high-density D-sub on the drive side. On the C64 itself the drive port was a 9-pin D-sub, the same physical connector, and the signals were Commodore serial, not RS-232. Note the parallel with the user port below: the C64's expansion port was a 34-conductor card edge.

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a flat or twisted pair cable, about 1 m

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a serial bus, logic levels at 5 V, not RS-232

peripheral.plug.rf.name: The aerial socket, hijacked
peripheral.plug.rf.description: The 75 ohm coaxial socket on the back of the television. The C64's modulator lead was a short 75 ohm coax with an F-type plug that went into it in parallel with the set's aerial. Because the modulator was a weak source, the lead had to be a good 75 ohm match and the set's aerial input had to be isolated or the local signal would back-feed.

facts.label: Lead
facts.value: about 1.5 m of RG-59, supplied with the C64

peripheral.plug.rf.cable.name: Converges on the coaxial antenna lead
peripheral.plug.rf.cable.description: The copper braid, the copper centre conductor, the polyethylene dielectric and the PVC jacket are all documented under peripheral.tv.aerial.coax. The F-type connector's brass and nickel plating are under peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.

peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.name: F-type coaxial connector
peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.description: A threaded, quarter-turn connector for 75 ohm coax, usually brass with a nickel or cadmium plate and a dielectric insert of PTFE or polyethylene. Brass is copper-zinc, so this little part pulls from both the copper and the zinc industry; the zinc can also be the zinc plated steel shell.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: brass (60% Cu, 40% Zn) with a nickel or cadmium plate

facts.label: Center contact
facts.value: brass or copper with a silver or nickel plating

peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.brass.name: Brass from copper and zinc
peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.brass.description: Brass is melted from cathode copper and zinc ingot, roughly 60/40 for free-cutting brass, and cast or extruded into fittings. The zinc came from sphalerite and the copper from chalcopyrite, both already in this branch.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 60% Cu, 40% Zn for a free-cutting brass; cartridge brass is 70/30

facts.label: Zinc source
facts.value: the same sphalerite concentrate and electrolysis as the CRT phosphor zinc sulphide

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.name: Coaxial or twin-lead antenna lead
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.description: RG-59 or RG-6 coax: a copper or tinned copper braid, a polyethylene or PTFE dielectric, and a solid copper centre conductor. RG-59 is 52 ohm and was what an indoor or a bench lead of the era was. The alternative was 300 ohm flat twin-lead, which matched indoor dipoles and did not need coax. The polyethylene in the coax came from ethylene, which came from the cracker, which came from naphtha and from crude.

facts.label: PE dielectric
facts.value: chemical blowing makes a foam, or solid PE

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.name: Polyethylene from ethylene, and the salt that made the chlorine
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.description: Polyethylene is polymerised from ethylene, which comes from a steam cracker on naphtha. Where the chlorination route was used (for PVC or for the chloromethane that goes into the foam blowing), the chlorine came from salt electrolysis. Both the polymer and the chlorine are therefore descendants of crude oil and of halite, and both branches meet in the cable jacket.

facts.label: LDPE
facts.value: high-pressure polymerisation, 1000-3000 bar, 200 degrees C, for cable

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: salt electrolysis, 2NaCl -> Cl2 + 2Na, at about 3 V and 30-40 degrees C

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: vinyl chloride from ethylene plus chlorine, then polymerised

peripheral.cassette.name: Datasette and cassette
peripheral.cassette.description: A C64 with no drive could not save. Commodore's answer was a 1530 or 1541 disk-shaped drive that took ordinary compact cassettes and wrote them with a magnetic head at 9,600 baud, plus a spool of tape that was mostly polyester film and mostly iron oxide. Saving a 1541 program to tape was a two minute operation of real-time winding, and the alignment problems of a 1541 were a running joke precisely because a cassette had no feedback.
peripheral.cassette.note: The 1541 had no mains supply of its own. It drew 5 V (through a fuse and reverse-polarity diode) and about 12 V from pins 4-7 of the C64's cassette port. The 1530 datasette was the same idea in a different box, with the tape slot on top and a position sensor; the 1541 is the one people remember because it had no position sensor at all.

facts.label: Tape
facts.value: standard compact cassette, C-60 or C-90, 1/8 inch wide

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 5 V and about 12 V DC, both from the C64's own supply via the cassette port

peripheral.cassette.tape.name: The cassette tape itself
peripheral.cassette.tape.description: A compact cassette is a 3.81 mm wide strip of polyester film 12 microns thick, coated on one side with about one to two microns of acicular iron oxide pigment in a binder, and wound onto hubs inside a plastic shell. The C64 wrote 9,600 baud onto it, which at 4.76 cm/s works out to a flux transition every 200 to 300 microseconds, near the limit of what a standard-bias cassette could resolve. Almost everything in it is either crude oil or iron ore.
peripheral.cassette.tape.note: A C64 could use a standard C-60, a C-90, and in principle any compact cassette. Commodore recommended particular brands because the format was sensitive to tape formulation: a high-bias C-120 tape was on the wrong bias wavelength for the 1541, and a Type II chrome tape had a different coercivity and a different noise floor.

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: about 1-2 microns of gamma-Fe2O3 (or CrO2 for Type II)

facts.label: Areal density
facts.value: roughly 4-9 g/m2 of magnetite, so a whole 90 m C-60 carries only 1-3 g of iron oxide

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: about 25-30 kA/m standard bias; 45-55 kA/m for CrO2

facts.label: C60 length
facts.value: 90 m total, 45 m per side at 4.76 cm/s

facts.label: Oxide
facts.value: iron(III) oxide or, for Type II, chromium dioxide

peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.name: Slitting to 1/8 inch
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.description: The coating line made a web a metre or more wide; it was then slit into 3.81 mm strips with rotary knives, tens of kilovolts of static keeping the thin film from clinging to the rollers. The slit tape was wound onto master reels, then onto cassette reels by a winding line that also cut it to length (45 m per side for a C-60), formed the leader, and inserted the hub.
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.note: A C-60 and a C-90 differ in length and gauge. A C-60 at 12 microns and a C-90 at 9 microns hold about the same total oxide per side, so the C-90 has to be made of a higher-output oxide (often cobalt-modified) to hold as much.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: 45 m per side for a C-60, 135 m total; a C-90 is 45 m per side at a thinner gauge

peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.film.name: The polyester film that is slit
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.film.description: The web being slit is 9-12 micron biaxially oriented PET, made from dimethyl terephthalate condensed with ethylene glycol. The whole chain from crude oil to a 90 metre C-60 is the same petrochemical chain that made a television cabinet and a ribbon cable.

facts.label: Stretch
facts.value: biaxially oriented, roughly 3x in each axis

peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene.name: Para-xylene from naphtha reforming
peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene.description: Para-xylene is the key intermediate to PET. It is produced by catalytic reforming of naphtha, then by selective adsorption (UOP Parex, a molecular sieve that picks out the para isomer from the mixed xylenes) because only the para isomer is useful and it is a minority of the xylene mixture. It is then oxidised to terephthalic acid or esterified to DMT.

facts.label: Reforming
facts.value: 450-520 degrees C, Pt, gives mixed xylenes

facts.label: Para-selectivity
facts.value: about 90-95% via a molecular-sieve adsorption process (Parex)

facts.label: To DMT
facts.value: esterified with methanol, or oxidised to TPA and reacted with methanol

peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene.name: Converges on the naphtha fraction
peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene.description: The same naphtha fraction of crude oil that feeds the styrene and the ethylene in the television cabinet branch. One barrel of crude is the ultimate ancestor of both the plastics cabinet and the polyester tape base.

peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzen.name: Naphtha fraction from crude oil
