facts.value: pressed and sintered at 1200-1250 degrees C

peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.name: Pressed steel basket
peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.description: The cone is glued to a stamped steel basket that holds the magnet and the voice coil in register. It came off the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, with the same iron ore behind it.

peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.steel.name: Cold-reduced low-carbon steel for the basket
peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.steel.description: The basket was stamped or drawn from the same low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, because it needed stiffness at low cost. The whole speaker weighed less than a kilogram and used perhaps 200 g of steel.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 150-250 g of steel in a 3.5 inch basket

facts.label: Joining
facts.value: spot welded or riveted to the magnet

peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.name: Paper pulp cone
peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.description: The cone is a paper pulp: refined wood fibre pressed wet into a shaped blank and dried, giving a light, stiff, cheap diaphragm. It is essentially the same material as a paper bag, which is why it creases if you poke it. A small set used a paper cone; a later or better one a woven or moulded polypropylene cone.
peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.note: The sound cone is one of the few parts of a television that starts as a tree. Pulp is wood reduced to fibre, and the fibre is from softwood, which is a renewable, not a geological, raw material. It is the one leaf in this branch that is not dug out of the ground.

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: slurry of kraft pulp pressed in a hot press and dried in a kiln or on a belt

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: a few grams for a 3.5 inch cone

peripheral.tv.chassis.name: The chassis: video, sync, line output, audio
peripheral.tv.chassis.description: The electronics of the set. By 1982 this was a single-sided or double-sided printed circuit board carrying a mix of discrete transistors, a handful of silicon integrated circuits (the video amplifier, the chroma, the vertical, the audio), a rotary switch bank and about forty electrolytic and film capacitors. The board sat in a zinc-plated steel chassis with a perforated steel cover, and the flyback sat beside it throwing both heat and electromagnetic noise.

facts.label: Board
facts.value: FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate, single-sided in a cheap set

facts.label: Power input
facts.value: B+ rail about 115-120 V from a linear supply, or a small switcher

facts.label: Colour decoder
facts.value: NTSC quadrature demodulator with a phase-locked multiply

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.name: Power supply: mains transformer and reservoir
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.description: Most 1982 sets were linear: a hot-chassis or a cold-chassis series/parallel mains transformer stepping 117 V down to about 110 V AC, a diode bridge rectifier, and a big electrolytic reservoir at 120 V feeding the line output. The main electrolytic was the largest, hottest component on the board and usually the first thing to dry out. A minority used a small switchmode supply for the logic rails with a flyback of its own.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.note: A cold-chassis set had the mains referenced to the line output and the whole board was at mains potential; a hot-chassis set had an isolated secondary and a common return. Repairing a 1982 TV meant first determining which, which is why it was dangerous and why sets were sold with the chassis not user-serviceable.

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 200-400 microfarad at 160 V, an aluminium can electrolytic

facts.label: Mains transformer
facts.value: E-I laminated silicon steel, 40-60 VA, potted or taped

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge.name: Mains rectifier bridge
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge.description: Four silicon diodes in a moulded bridge package, rated at a few amps and 100-200 V. Cheap sets rectified with two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer instead. The bridge was usually on the chassis edge with the heatsink tab or in free air.

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.name: Mains transformer, E-I silicon steel
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.description: A laminated core of thin silicon steel (about 0.35 mm) stamped into E and I shapes and stacked, with copper windings on bobbins, potted in epoxy or wrapped in tape and varnished. The laminations were needed because mains hum would otherwise magnetostrict the core; the 1982 design was exactly the design from the 1930s.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.note: The silicon steel is a different alloy from the low-carbon steel of the shadow mask: it is deliberately alloyed with silicon to raise resistivity and suppress eddy currents, and it is a thin, carefully annealed strip. Both, though, came off a blast furnace.

facts.label: Lamination
facts.value: 0.30-0.35 mm silicon steel, C5 or C21 grade

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.name: Audio: 4.5 MHz intercarrier to a speaker
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.description: The sound carrier is taken off the same IF strip at 54.75 MHz, recovered at 4.5 MHz above the video, limited and FM-demodulated, then amplified. The 4.5 MHz intercarrier was chosen so the sound did not interfere with the video and to let the sound survive a picture cut-off (the 'intercarrier' idea). Amplified to a few watts into an 8 ohm speaker, or about 2 W per speaker into two 8 ohm speakers in parallel. The C64's audio came out of this amplifier, which is why it was loud, thin and slightly buzzy.
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.note: The 75 kHz deviation and 15 kHz maximum audio are the NTSC TV audio figures. PAL/SECAM used 50 kHz deviation and a 6.5 MHz intercarrier for stereo, which is why PAL sets used a sound trap filter and NTSC sets used a notch.

facts.label: Sound carrier
facts.value: 54.75 MHz IF, 4.5 MHz intercarrier, 75 kHz deviation, 15 kHz max audio

facts.label: Detector
facts.value: quadrature FM or a Foster-Seeley / ratio detector, sometimes with a limiter

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 2-5 W into 8 ohm; stereo sets about 2 W per side

facts.label: Audio bandwidth
facts.value: about 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz on a small set

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot.name: Volume potentiometer, carbon track
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot.description: A rotary carbon track pot, typically 10 kohm or 100 kohm logarithmic (audio taper), spliced into the audio line. The track is a carbon film printed or sprayed on a phenolic or ceramic substrate; the wiper is a sprung brass or copper blade. This is the same technology as the volume control in a pocket radio, and the carbon comes from petroleum coke exactly as the CRT blackening does.

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot.c.name: Carbon track from petroleum coke
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot.c.description: A mix of graphite and carbon black in a resin or ceramic binder, screen-printed onto the substrate and fired. Carbon track pots were cheap, noisy and prone to wear, and a 'crackle' as the volume control was turned was a common household complaint. Cermet (metal oxide) track came in for better pots, and the two technologies coexisted for decades.

facts.label: Application
facts.value: sprayed or screen-printed onto an alumina or phenolic substrate, then fired at 700-900 degrees C

facts.label: V2O5 for cermet pots
facts.value: a few percent vanadium pentoxide in a glass binder

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.name: Audio output amplifier
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.description: An integrated amplifier (a few watts, a single 8-14 pin IC) or a discrete predriver plus two complementary power transistors pushing 5-20 W peak into 8 ohms from a 115 V rail. The output stage ran in class B or class AB, and the bias and the idle current were the main design problem.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 2-5 W rms at 8 ohm from about 15-25 V DC

facts.label: Devices
facts.value: complementary NPN/PNP silicon pair, TO-3 or a plastic power package

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.power-de.name: The output power transistor
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.power-de.description: The device that actually pushed the current into the speaker: an NPN/PNP complementary pair on a thick die in a TO-3 or plastic power package, bolted to the chassis as its own heatsink. From 1990s multisilicon dice replaced the single-crystal die, but a 1982 set had one transistor per output channel.
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.power-de.note: Beryllium oxide isolators were common in power audio of the era; beryllium came from bertrandite and beryl ores and is toxic, which is why it was later replaced by bonded aluminium nitride and alumina.
inputs: TO-3 can with a beryllium oxide or mica isolator

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 5-20 W peak from a 20-40 V rail

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-3 with a mica or beryllium oxide washer, screwed to the chassis

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.name: Silicon wafer, P-type, 99.99%
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.description: The same trichlorosilane and Siemens process as the EHT rectifier gave the wafer, then it was doped p-type with boron to build a pn substrate and n-epitaxy grown on top for the bipolar transistors. A 4-micron process of 1982 was a 100 or 125 mm wafer. Note the silicon itself came from the same quartz-to-metal-to-trichlorosilane chain documented under the EHT rectifier; the difference here is the epitaxy and the oxide.
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die.note: This node deliberately converges on the same polysilicon chain as peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.silicon rather than repeating it. The trunk line to quartz sand is shared; that is the whole point of a manufacturing tree.
inputs: oxygen and steam for the oxides

facts.label: Wafer
facts.value: 100 or 125 mm; 150 mm wafers were arriving in 1983

peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.traps.name: Sound traps and SAW
peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.traps.description: The 4.5 MHz intercarrier has to be lifted out of the video baseband without disturbing the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier, so a trap or SAW filter at 4.5 MHz ran between the video detector and the audio detector. A ceramic or SAW trap on 4.5 MHz was a very visible part in a 1982 set.

peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.name: Vertical output stage, 60 Hz
peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.description: The vertical sweep at 60 Hz. The oscillator ran at twice the line rate and a count-down circuit divided by two, a design that keeps the vertical locked to the horizontal. The output stage amplified a small ramp and drove the vertical yoke, with a small electrolytic capacitor across the coil to correct the crosstalk that coupling into the horizontal yoke produced. A IC did most of this, with one or two power transistors at the output.

peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.ic.name: Vertical IC
peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.ic.description: A single IC contained the oscillator, the count-down divider, the ramp generator and the driver, needing only two or three external transistors. It was one of the first large consumer uses of a mixed-analogue IC that made a television much easier to build, and it is the reason a 1982 TV was a single-board affair.
peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.ic.note: By the mid-1980s these verticals had integrated the whole deflection drive on to one chip including the line output; that trend began here.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: oscillator, divider, ramp, driver in one 16-20 pin package

peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.name: Horizontal line output stage, 15,734 Hz
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.description: The heart of the set's power and geometry. The line oscillator runs at 15,734 Hz; the driver and the output transistor switch the flyback primary, so the collector current rises linearly during scan and then collapses in the flyback retrace. The flyback uses that collapse to develop a high-voltage pulse, rectified to the EHT. The same transformer runs back through the damper to create a 200-250 V pump rail for the video output stage. In 1982 this was usually a discrete silicon EFT (a triple-diffused or a high-voltage epitaxial transistor) because a single silicon transistor could not safely switch a 900 V collector at 15.7 kHz.
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.note: The brief's '12 kHz' figure is PAL. NTSC is 15,734 Hz, and a 13 inch US set of 1982 is a 15.7 kHz machine. The '1 kV across the yoke' figure is a large-set number; see the flyback note.

facts.label: Output transistor
facts.value: silicon EFT, 600-1000 V Vce, 5-15 A peak, 400-1000 W peak pulse

facts.label: Flyback pulse
facts.value: 150-350 V above B+, for 5-15 microseconds, every line

facts.label: Pump rail
facts.value: 200-250 V DC from the damper and a rectifier

peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hv-caps.name: High-voltage film capacitor
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hv-caps.description: A metallised polypropylene or polystyrene film capacitor rated at kilovolts. The film is stretched polypropylene, metallised with a thin aluminium or zinc layer, wound, and the whole thing impregnated and potted. Zinc metallising was cheap and equivalent to aluminium for small values; aluminium became standard for reliability.

peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hvt.name: EHT rectifier and capacitor
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hvt.description: After the flyback, a single silicon rectifier at 25 kV. On larger sets a doubler or tripler with plastic film capacitors at 2-5 kV each was used. The current was tiny (1-2 mA) so the capacitors were small in value but enormous in voltage rating, and their failure mode was spectacular and occasionally violent.

facts.label: Capacitors
facts.value: 0.1-1 microfarad film at 2-5 kV each, in a doubler or tripler

facts.label: Failure
facts.value: a shorted film cap can throw the rectifier and the flyback

peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.choke.name: Line choke or choke-and-flyback combination
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.choke.description: Some sets had a separate choke, some combined the choke with the flyback into one transformer. The choke carries the DC component of the line current and presents a high impedance to the 15.7 kHz pulse. It was an iron-powder or ferrite part with a thousand volts across it and was a common failure.
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.choke.note: The 13 inch sets of the early 1980s more often used a separate flyback with a discrete line choke; the integrated choke-and-flyback became common in the mid 1980s.

facts.label: Inductance
facts.value: a few hundred microhenries at 15.7 kHz

peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.oscillato.name: Line oscillator and AFC
peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.oscillato.description: A free-running LC oscillator locked to the incoming video by a sync separator and an automatic frequency control loop. When the set was fed a C64 signal it was free-running off the internal oscillator and being pulled by the modulator's sync; it could not lock to a broadcast, so it did not drift. Most of the visible misbehaviour of a C64 on a TV (rolling, tearing, drifting) came from this loop or from the modulator's own sync, not from the computer.

facts.label: Hold range
facts.value: several kHz either side of 15,734 Hz

facts.label: V-hold
facts.value: a control that shifts the vertical frequency to stop the picture rolling

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.name: Video chain: IF, detector, video amp, colour
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.description: The 45 MHz IF is amplified, limited, then detected: the video signal rides on the picture carrier at 45.75 MHz, the colour subcarrier sits 3.58 MHz below it as a sideband, and the sound carrier sits 9 MHz above at 54.75 MHz. The synchronous detector recovers the baseband video; a PLL multiplies the recovered 3.58 MHz subcarrier up and phase-shifts it 90 degrees to drive the two demodulators; the result is U and V, added back to luminance to give R, G and B, which drive the gun cathodes.
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.note: The video bandwidth of 4.5 MHz is why a C64's 320x200 pixels, drawn as a very narrow TV line, showed colour fringes and lost horizontal resolution on a set with no notch filter. A set with a notch filter and a comb filter, common on 1980s sets, recovered much of it. The 'quality' switch on a late-70s set simply inserted a notch at the colour subcarrier.

facts.label: Detectors
facts.value: synchronous (PLL multiplier) in a good set, envelope plus a Reinschmidt envelope detector in a cheap one

facts.label: Video bandwidth
facts.value: 4.5 MHz (-3 dB), so the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier is attenuated at the picture edges

facts.label: Colour demodulation
facts.value: quadrature, 90 degrees apart, PLL recovered subcarrier

facts.label: IF gain
facts.value: 60-70 dB total across three to five stages

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.agc.name: Automatic gain control
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.agc.description: The AGC samples the DC level off the video detector and feeds a reverse bias back to the first two IF stages, holding the picture bright whether the aerial is good or the C64 modulator is a milliwatt away from nothing. This was the one part of a TV that genuinely cared about the C64 signal, because a C64 was a much weaker source than a broadcast station and the AGC had to find a way to open up. A key-operated AGC defeat, or a 'manual gain' switch, was a modification for fringe-area reception.
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.agc.note: The AGC on a set being fed from a C64 modulator was a genuine issue: the wanted signal was tiny and the AGC would clamp down. Some hobbyists inserted an attenuator or a bias into the AGC line.

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors.name: Discrete IF, driver and video transistors
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors.description: Most transistors in a 1982 set were discrete: a high-gain IF transistor, the video driver, the video output transistors, the horizontal oscillator and driver, the vertical output, the audio output, and the horizontal output. Each is a tiny die, 10-40 transistors, wire-bonded to a plastic or metal can. Metal-can transistors (TO-18) were still common in the IF and video stages where heat and shielding mattered.

facts.label: Packages
facts.value: TO-92 plastic, TO-18 metal can, TO-3 or a plastic power package for the audio and line output

facts.label: Bipolar
facts.value: mostly NPN small-signal, gain-bandwidth product 100 MHz to a few GHz

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors..name: The transistor die and its package
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors..description: A small-signal NPN transistor is a few hundred square microns of silicon, aluminium metallised, mounted on a header and sealed in epoxy or metal. The die itself is a slice of the same 99.99% wafer as the video IC, cut with a diamond-impregnated wheel and diced on a saw.

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: a few hundred square microns to about 1 mm square

facts.label: Beta
facts.value: 100-400 for a small-signal IF or video transistor

peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.name: Silicon integrated circuit, 4-micron NMOS
peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.description: The video, chroma and audio functions in a 1982 set were often one or two chips of 40 to 80 pins, made on a 4-5 micron NMOS or bipolar process. The die is a slice of 99.99% silicon, oxidised, photolithographically patterned through eight to ten mask steps, and packaged in epoxy or ceramic. Purity, oxide quality and aluminium interconnect over a polysilicon gate is the whole story of the 4-micron generation.

peripheral.tv.tuner.name: RF tuner, VHF and UHF
peripheral.tv.tuner.description: The front end. In 1982 the US TV band was VHF channels 2-13 (55-220 MHz) and UHF 14-83 (470-890 MHz), and most sets had either a combined tuner or two side-by-side ones behind a single dial. A high-quality set used a rotary switch with a chain of interlocking contacts; a cheap one used a varactor diode and a small motor, or a continuous mechanical tuning with a motor and a rotor. Whatever the mechanism, the output was always the same: a fixed 45 MHz intermediate frequency.
peripheral.tv.tuner.note: The prompt describes a 4-gang or varactor tuner with a UHF/VHF split. A 4-gang was the older high-quality approach (separate RF and mixer coils for both bands in one switch); by 1982 varactor tuning with a motor and AFC was increasingly common, and a mechanical rotary tuner with a 4-gang arrangement was still on plenty of sets.

facts.label: IF carriers
facts.value: picture 45.75 MHz, colour 42.47 MHz, sound 54.75 MHz

peripheral.tv.tuner.dial-cord.name: Dial cord and pulley gear train
peripheral.tv.tuner.dial-cord.description: The channel knob turned a pulley that wound a braided cord onto another pulley geared to the tuner rotor. It was a real mechanical system that stretched, slipped and broke, and it is the reason every vintage-TV owner has a drawer of spare dial cords. The cord was a braided polyester or nylon sheath over a cotton core.
peripheral.tv.tuner.dial-cord.note: The polyester dial cord is the same base polymer as the tape leader and the oven bag: PET again.

peripheral.tv.tuner.can.name: Die-cast zinc or stamped steel RF can
peripheral.tv.tuner.can.description: The tuner and front end were a sealed metal can soldered to the main board. On a cheap set it was a stamped zinc-plated steel can; on a good one a die-cast zinc or aluminium can with a machined seam. Zinc plating comes from zinc electroplating baths, so it is the same zinc industry as the galvanised chassis.
peripheral.tv.tuner.can.note: Zinc die-casting was one of the biggest single uses of zinc in 1982, far larger than the CRT frit. A zinc-plated steel can is also a small, forgotten consumer of zinc alongside the chassis and the screws.
inputs: zinc-plated sheet steel or die-cast zinc

peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc.name: Zinc electroplate on the RF can
peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc.description: The stamped steel RF can was plated in a zinc sulphate or zinc chloride bath with an aluminium or steel anode, then often given a chromate passivation. Zinc plating is cheap corrosion protection and it is the same zinc industry as the CRT phosphor and the die-cast tuner body.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acid sulphate or cyanide; sulphate was dominant by 1982 for non-electroplate

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.name: RF amplifier and mixer
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.description: A low-noise bipolar or MOSFET amplifier at the antenna frequency, then a mixer down to 45 MHz. In 1982 the RF device was often a silicon planar MOSFET (dual-gate, for the UHF) or a wideband bipolar. The whole RF section lived in a die-cast or stamped zinc-plated steel can to keep it away from the switching supply and the line output.

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.name: SAW filter at 45 MHz
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.description: By the early 1980s a SAW (surface acoustic wave) filter had largely replaced the LC or ceramic filter in the IF path. Two interdigital transducers on a piezoelectric crystal launch and pick up an acoustic wave along the surface; the finger pattern is designed to pass the wanted band and reject the adjacent channel, sound and colour carriers. It gave a picture with no intermodulation and no cross modulation between the picture, colour and sound carriers.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 40-cut Y-cut lithium niobate, or lithium tantalate

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.name: Lithium niobate wafer from spodumene
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.description: The acoustic medium. Spodumene (LiAlSi2O6) ore is beneficiated and converted to lithium carbonate by sulphuric acid roasting; the carbonate is reacted with niobium pentoxide from pyrochlore (columbite-tantalite) tantalum residue in a lithium hydroxide or carbonate flux at 1000-1200 degrees C to grow Czochralski crystals of LiNbO3, which are sliced and polished to a 0.25-1 mm wafer. In 1982 much of the world's LiNbO3 came from Japanese and Chinese plants, with the tantalum industry as the source of the columbite residue.

facts.label: Czochralski growth
facts.value: about 1100-1200 degrees C, from a charge of carbonate flux, pulled at 2-20 mm/h

facts.label: Piezoelectric coefficient
facts.value: large, about 6-30 C/m2 per N depending on cut

places: Bikita, Zimbabwe and Tanco, Manitoba for spodumene

peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.name: Spodumene pegmatite ore
peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithiu.description: A lithium aluminium silicate, 6.0-7.0% Li2O, that occurs in granitic pegmatites and is mined in enormous tonnages because a lithium battery plant in 1982 needed thousands of tonnes a year. Roasting with sulphuric acid turns it into lithium sulphate, and the impurity that everyone fights is iron.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 1050-1100 degrees C with H2SO4 to Li2SO4

facts.label: Iron problem
facts.value: iron from the pegmatite contaminates the carbonate and is removed by precipitation or a calcine

peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.name: UHF tuner with varactor diode
peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.description: At 500-800 MHz a lumped LC circuit is hopeless, so the UHF tuner used a coaxial cavity or a stripline distributed resonator made of folded sheet metal, with a silicon varactor diode as the tuning element. Reverse-biasing the diode changed its junction capacitance from tens to a few picofarads, which moved the resonance across the band. A small DC motor rotated the cavity to track, or a servo pushed a varactor.

facts.label: Varactor capacitance
facts.value: about 3-20 pF at the bias range, changing with reverse voltage

facts.label: Cavity
facts.value: folded-sheet transmission line, about 10-20 mm across

facts.label: Tuning motor
facts.value: a small DC gearmotor with a plastic cam, 12-24 V

peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.cavity.name: Cavity resonator, brass or nickel-plated steel
peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.cavity.description: The UHF resonant circuit is a piece of metal: folded sheet or machined brass forming a half-wavelength line, with the shunt capacitance of the varactor at the open end and a tap for the transistor. This is one of the few places in a television where the RF circuit is metal rather than a PCB, because at 800 MHz a printed board would radiate. Brass came from zinc and copper ores.
inputs: silver plating on the contact fingers

peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.varactor.name: Varactor diode, silicon planar junction
peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.varactor.description: A reverse-biased silicon pn junction used as a voltage-variable capacitor. At zero bias the depletion layer is thin and the capacitance is at its maximum; raising the reverse voltage widens the depletion layer and drops the capacitance. The diode is a small pill or a leaded axial part soldered into the cavity wall, and the DC bias arrives through a high-value resistor from the tuner supply.
peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.varactor.note: Silicon varactors, and later the whole family of PIN diodes used for AGC and trap switching, were the reason TV tuners had a whole discrete semiconductor family of their own in the 1980s.

peripheral.tv.tuner.vhf.name: VHF gangs: RF amplifier and mixer coils
peripheral.tv.tuner.vhf.description: Two tuned circuits on ferrite cores: an RF amplifier and a mixer, both switched through a gang so they track. The coils are a few turns of enamelled copper on ferrite slug cores; the switch has a rotor with printed or wound inductors that tap through the band, and an AFC or motor to pull it into lock.

facts.label: Band
facts.value: 54-216 MHz, four switched ranges in older sets

facts.label: Core
facts.value: nickel-zinc ferrite, tunable with a ferrite slug

peripheral.tv.crt.name: The picture tube (CRT)
peripheral.tv.crt.description: A vacuum envelope of two pieces of glass welded together: a flat-ish panel carrying the phosphor screen inside its face, and a flanged funnel tapering to a cylindrical neck that carries the electron gun. The panel-to-funnel joint is sealed with a lead-oxide frit fired in a belt kiln. Inside the tube, electrons leave a hot cathode, are focused and accelerated to about 25 kV, steered magnetically across the panel, and slam into phosphor grains through a steel mask.

facts.label: Envelope volume
facts.value: roughly 5-8 litres, evacuated to better than 1e-6 mbar

facts.label: Envelope weight
facts.value: about 6-9 kg of glass for a 13 inch tube, roughly half of it the neck-adjacent cone

peripheral.tv.crt.implosion.name: Implosion protection and the safety faceplate
peripheral.tv.crt.implosion.description: A colour TV tube holds about 0.5-1.5 tonnes per square metre of glass at a quarter atmosphere, and shatters into shards that will cut. Three defences: a laminate or thicker-than-necessary faceplate whose edges are the thickest part, a mask retaining ring that holds the faceplate to the frame rather than letting it come out, and a wraparound rim so the panel cannot pop forward. Cheap sets used less glass; expensive and safe sets used a tempered or laminated panel and, from the late 1970s, an implosion protection plate bonded to the front.
peripheral.tv.crt.implosion.note: The pressure figure needs care. A TV tube is evacuated to high vacuum, but the internal volume is large and the glass is thick enough that the tube is deliberately designed so that a manufacturing flaw (a large void or a heavy impurity in the glass) is a slow leak, not a bomb. Post-deflection the tube may be brought back to a small positive pressure by letting in a little inert gas; the net differential is around a fifth of an atmosphere, not one atmosphere. That is a large fraction of the energy a naive reader would assume, and it is the reason the safety story is not simply 'it is a vacuum bomb'.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: about 0.2-0.3 bar differential (a partial vacuum, not a hard vacuum, by design)

facts.label: Front glass
facts.value: 3-6 mm, often laminated or bonded to an implosion plate

facts.label: Rim
facts.value: wraparound steel or plastic retaining ring

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.name: Aluminium coating on the funnel wall
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.description: A separate aluminium mirror, vapour-deposited on the inside of the funnel behind the gun, intended to bounce stray light back towards the phosphor and raise light output. It is distinct from the phosphor back layer, which is where the black level comes from. Modern practice replaced it with a black internal coating on the neck to absorb stray light instead, and moved efficiency to the phosphor and to tinted faceplate glass.
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.note: Both the aluminium funnel coating and the phosphor aluminium layer are real and were often both present. The prompt's 'aluminium-backed faceplate' is a reasonable description of the phosphor back layer, and the funnel coating is the separate, less discussed item.

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.foil.name: The aluminium foil that goes in the evaporator
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.foil.description: The same 0.1-0.15 mm four-nines aluminium foil used for the phosphor black layer, pinched to a wire in the evaporator and flashed off in the same pump run. One roll of 4N foil fed both the mirror behind the phosphor and the mirror behind the gun.

facts.label: Evaporation
facts.value: resistive or e-beam heated to about 1500 degrees C in a vacuum

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.name: Evacuation, getter flash and exhaust tip
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.description: The tube is evacuated on a manifold to better than 1e-6 mbar with a backing line of mechanical and diffusion pumps, tested with a spark-gap or ion gauge. Then the exhaust tip, a small tubulation drawn on the end of the funnel with a tantalum or aluminium-alloy cap welded over it, is opened with a glass break or an RF induction heater. The get, a flash of barium-titanium-palladium inside the neck, absorbs any remaining gas and then fixes a mirror-like barium film on the tube wall. The tip is then crushed flat and sealed.
inputs: high-voltage feedthrough for the anode button

facts.label: Getter
facts.value: Ba-Ti-Pd flake, flashed by RF induction

facts.label: Exhaust tip cap
facts.value: tantalum, or an aluminium-magnesium alloy, welded on

facts.label: Pump combination
facts.value: rotary or water-ring roughing plus an oil diffusion or BHK mercury pin pump

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.tantalum.name: Tantalum exhaust tip, from coltan
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.tantalum.description: The exhaust tip cap has to be sealed by welding without oxidising and has to be gas-tight at 10^-7 mbar. Tantalum was chosen because it is refractory and forms its own oxide. It is also the material behind every solid-state tantalum capacitor, which is why a small 1980s television contributed a gram of coltan to a supply chain that later became a political problem.

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: HF digestion to H2TaF7 and KF2TaF7, then solvent extraction of the tantalum fluoride

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: electrochemical or Kroll-type reduction to tantalum powder, sintered and drawn

places: Kigali and the North Kivu coltan belt

peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium.name: Barium getter, from barite ore
peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium.description: The getter is a thin foil strip of barium, titanium and palladium powder bonded with a glass frit in a nickel tube. When RF-heated it explodes in a burst of vacuum, sprays barium across the neck, and the barium burns and sticks to the glass as a mirror film. That film is the biggest vapour getter in the tube and turns residual gas into metal. Barium metal was made by reducing barite (BaSO4) with carbon or aluminium.

facts.label: Barite
facts.value: BaSO4, 4.5+ tonnes per m3, mined open pit and underground

facts.label: Barium metal
facts.value: Al reduction at 1100-1200 degrees C, then vacuum distillation

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.name: EHT / line output transformer (flyback)
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.description: The flyback does three jobs at once: it steps the 120 V B+ up to 20-25 kV for the anode, it develops the high flyback pulse that the line output transistor uses to make its collector current fall fast, and it carries auxiliary windings that supply the 12-25 V the gun heater, the tuner motor, the oscillator and the horizontal oscillator circuits need. In 1982 it was an open-frame transformer on a laminated or ferrite core, wrapped in epoxy and varnished, mounted on the chassis next to the tube neck with several hundred volts between it and everything else.
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.note: The brief said the line output swung about 1 kV across the yoke. That is the figure for a large 25 inch set with a 110 degree tube and a high line current. On a 13 inch set with a 90 degree deflection the yoke current is of the order of 1-2 A peak to peak into a few tens of ohms, so the voltage across the yoke is tens to a couple of hundred volts, and the flyback still steps it to 20-25 kV. The 1 kV figure is also sometimes quoted as the voltage on the yoke during retrace once the damper is included.

facts.label: Primary voltage
facts.value: about 120 V B+, switched at 15,734 Hz

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: epoxy and mylar, rated for a 1 kV test

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.name: Anode terminal: the lead burned through the funnel wall
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.description: The EHT gets into the tube through a metal button, usually a nickel or Kovar cup, sealed into the funnel wall with a glass frit and then fired. Above that terminal sits a silicone-rubber-covered anode cap that had to survive being touched with a screwdriver in a live set. A rubber anode cap failing was a genuine fire and electrocution hazard, and the safety information people remember about 1970s-80s TVs comes from exactly this part.
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.note: The internal portion of the anode button was itself the visible example of a glass-to-metal seal, and was where most early implosion-protection advertising pointed.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: nickel or Kovar button frit-sealed into the funnel wall at 430-460 degrees C

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.sea.name: The glass-to-metal seal materials
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.sea.description: The anode button was a nickel or Kovar cup frit-sealed into the funnel wall, and the external cap was moulded silicone rubber. The seal frit was the same lead borosilicate as the panel seal, which is why the button had to be fired at the same 430-460 degrees C in the same continuous kiln as the tube.

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: frit printed and fired at 430-460 degrees C

facts.label: External cap
facts.value: silicone rubber, rated for the full EHT

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.name: Kovar, the Fe-Ni-Co lead-in glass match
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.description: A 29% Ni, 17% Co, 53% Fe alloy whose expansion matches a lead borosilicate glass. It is how the anode lead and the stem get sealed into the glass funnel without cracking the tube wall, and it is the same idea as the frit seal but metal instead of glass.
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.note: Category corrected to metals. Kovar was standard in every CRT factory and its own supply chain came from nickel and iron rather than anything exotic.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 53% Fe, 29% Ni, 17% Co, expansion about 5 x 10^-6 / K

facts.label: Use
facts.value: frit-sealing the anode stem and the heater stem

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.inputs.name: The iron and nickel behind Kovar
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.inputs.description: Kovar is 53% iron, 29% nickel and 17% cobalt, so it draws on the iron ore of the blast furnace, the nickel of the electrolytic refinery and the cobalt of the laterite or the Congo copper belt. Cobalt was a genuinely scarce metal in 1982 and set the price of the alloy.

facts.label: Iron
facts.value: 53% Fe, blast-furnace pig or direct-reduced iron

facts.label: Cobalt
facts.value: 17%, from Congolese or Ugandan laterite or copper-belt electrorefining

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.nickel.name: Nickel sheet for the grid foil
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.nickel.description: 99%+ nickel, rolled to 0.02-0.1 mm, chosen because it has no gas to give up in vacuum and it does not sputter. Electroformed nickel was the higher-grade route. Nickel itself is refined from sulphide ore concentrate, usually laterite-derived or from pentlandite in Sudbury-type nickel iron sulphide.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.name: Lead borosilicate frit seal (about 24% PbO)
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.description: The seal that makes a television tube possible. A paste of lead oxide, silica, boric oxide and alkali is screen-printed as a thick band onto the panel rim and the funnel rim, fired to devitrify, and then the two parts are brought together in a continuous belt kiln where the frit softens and fuses. Lead does three jobs: it drops the sealing temperature far below the point where the base glass would slump, it can be tuned to match the expansion of either glass, and its high atomic number soaks up the bremsstrahlung X-rays that 25 kV of beam current unavoidably produces inside the tube.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.note: Because the frit is a lead glass, a 1982 television tube is one of the largest deliberate lead-containing objects in the house. Modern sets moved to glass-to-glass bonding with lead out of the frit entirely.

facts.label: PbO content
facts.value: roughly 24 wt% in the standard lead frit

facts.label: Screen-print thickness
facts.value: 1-2 mm wet, shrinking to about 0.8-1.5 mm fired

facts.label: Seal temperature
facts.value: 430-460 degrees C in a continuous tunnel or belt kiln

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.ink.name: Frit paste and screen-printing of the seal
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.ink.description: Frit is mixed into a paste with a water-soluble or organic vehicle, printed through a fine mesh screen onto the rim of the panel and the flange of the funnel, then dried and fired to devitrify. The printed band has to be dimensionally exact: too narrow and it will not seal, too wide and it costs lead.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.ink.note: Modern seal bands use a photo-patterned photopaste so the frit only fires where it is needed, but the 1982 process was plain screen printing.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: about 60-100 mesh for the seal band

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 600-700 degrees C to remove the vehicle and devitrify

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.name: Lead oxide, PbO, from galena concentrate
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.description: The lead in the frit started as galena, PbS, roasted in air to a PbO litharge cake, then smelted. Nothing about this is exotic: it is the same 1900s Parkesine process that made lead-acid battery plates, refined to the point where the oxide is pure white and free of the bismuth and antimony that would grey it.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 600-750 degrees C in a fluid-bed or reverberatory furnace, PbS + O2 -> PbO + SO2

facts.label: Smelt
facts.value: sinter plus coke and limestone in a blast furnace to crude lead at 1100-1250 degrees C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: drossing, then electrolytic refining to 99.99% Pb for litharge

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.name: Roasting, sintering, blast furnace and cast refining
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.description: The whole lead chain in one furnace hall. Concentrate is roasted in a fluid-bed roaster to litharge, PbO, with the SO2 sent to a contact plant for sulphuric acid; the litharge is mixed with sinter, coke and limestone and charged to a blast furnace that produces crude lead at about 1250 degrees C and 1100-1250 degrees C of shaft temperature. The crude is drossed and electrolytically refined to 99.99% Pb, then converted back to pure white PbO for the frit. The economics were dominated by the acid plant and by how much silver the Parkesine dross carried.

facts.label: Roaster
facts.value: fluid bed, 600-750 degrees C, PbS + 3/2 O2 -> PbO + SO2

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: roasted concentrate sintered on a Dwight-Lloyd grate, 1200-1400 degrees C

facts.label: Blast furnace
facts.value: shaft at 1100-1250 degrees C, crude lead at about 1250 degrees C, 3-5% by mass in the metal

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: anode slime carries the silver; electrolytic tankhouse to 99.99% Pb

facts.label: To litharge
facts.value: the refined Pb is oxidised back to PbO in a reverberatory or fluid-bed converter

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.name: Galena (PbS) concentrate, 60-80% Pb
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.description: Galena is cubic and dense at 7.6 g/cm3, which is why it separates from gangue so cleanly in froth flotation or a heavy-media washer. A lead-zinc mine's flotation plant produces three products: lead concentrate, zinc concentrate and a copper concentrate, and the economics of a 1982 lead plant stood or fell on the price of the sulphuric acid made from the roast's SO2.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.name: Underground lead-zinc mine and concentrator
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.description: Sulphide ores are heavy and low-grade, so they are mined underground and milled rather than scraped off a hillside. The rock is broken, ground to a few tens of microns in a ball mill and floated; the concentrate is trucked or rail-loaded a thousand kilometres to a smelter. In 1982 the American lead belt along the Mississippi and the Mexican states of Chihuahua and Sonora were the sources for the North American television trade.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 2-6% lead and 4-12% zinc as sphalerite-galena ore

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: xanthate or fatty-acid collectors in a froth flotation cell

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.name: Lead-zinc sulphide ore in the ground
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-s.description: Galena and sphalerite intergrown in limestone and dolomite, deposited from hydrothermal fluids in Palaeozoic sediments. The whole industry of this branch's lead and zinc hangs off a few stratabound orebodies in Missouri, Broken Hill, Sullivan, the Upper Mississippi valley and northern Mexico.

facts.label: Geometry
facts.value: replacement bodies along bedding and cross-cutting veins

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.name: Silicon EHT rectifier diode
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.description: A single high-voltage silicon diode, or a small stack of them, rated 3-10 kV reverse and 1-5 mA forward, potted in silicone rubber or epoxy so the 25 kV does not arc. The cathode end of the HV winding goes to the rectifier and the anode to the tube's anode terminal. A set with a failing EHT rectifier was a common and unpleasant repair.

facts.label: Reverse rating
facts.value: 3-10 kV silicon, or a 2-3 diode stack

facts.label: Potting
facts.value: silicone rubber or epoxy, rated for the full EHT

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.name: High-purity silicon from quartz
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.description: The EHT rectifier needed silicon of 200-1000 ohm cm with very low oxygen, because the junction had to hold 25 kV without leakage or breakdown. High-purity silicon is made by reducing trichlorosilane or silane, in the trichlorosilane route, from metallurgical silicon, which itself is made in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and coke.

facts.label: Metallurgical silicon
facts.value: submerged arc furnace, 1800-2000 degrees C, 98-99% Si

facts.label: SiC deposition
facts.value: 1100-1200 degrees C, Siemens process, trichlorosilane plus H2

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.name: Quartz (high-purity SiO2) for the arc furnace
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.s.description: Metal-grade quartz, not glass sand. The furnace needs the silicon dioxide to be chemically clean enough that the reduction goes to 98-99% silicon in one pass. Quarried rock is crushed and purified by acid leaching to quartz, then reduced with coke in a submerged arc furnace where the arc itself is the furnace's only heat source.

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: 99.99%+ semiconductor grade via trichlorosilane and the Siemens process

peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core.name: Ferrite E-I or C core
peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core.description: An open-frame core of MnZn ferrite or powdered iron with a gapped section. The gap is deliberate: the flyback has to store a lot of field energy and be reset every line. The core is wound on a bobbin, then potted in epoxy so the 15 kHz and 25 kV windings cannot move.

facts.label: Core size
facts.value: roughly 40-60 mm across for a 13 inch set

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 mm, often a paper or epoxy gap

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.name: Deflection yoke and deflection coils
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.description: A bell-shaped ferrite or powdered-iron core clamped on the tube neck carrying two orthogonal saddle windings. The horizontal winding is driven by the line output stage and sits in series with the flyback, so the scan current is the same current that steps up to 25 kV. The vertical winding is in the collector of the vertical output stage and carries a sawtooth at 60 Hz.

facts.label: Deflection angle
facts.value: 90 degrees typical, 100 degrees on the higher-power sets

facts.label: Deflection
facts.value: about 8-9 mm peak in the horizontal direction on a 13 inch tube

facts.label: Pincushion correction
facts.value: pins and a C-core on the yoke, or electronic linearity in the line stage

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.name: Conicity and geometry correction magnets
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.description: A 13 inch set with a 90 degree deflection had visible pincushion and barrel distortion. Correction was partly mechanical: a pair of small magnets on the neck that tilted the field to change the deflection centre, a static C-core for pincushion, and inside the flyback a 'geometry' winding that shapes the scan current. The customer-facing result was a V-hold, H-hold, width, height, linearity and convergence control on the back of the chassis, and on a cheap set a bright-line adjustment they could get wrong.
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.note: Electronic pincushion correction using a diode and capacitor in the line stage was common from the mid 1970s; the amount varies by set.

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets.name: Alnico and samarium-cobalt correction magnets
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets.description: The small magnets that set the deflection centre and the geometry of a 1982 set were usually Alnico, an iron-aluminium-nickel alloy, or a small ferrite. Samarium-cobalt was the high-performance alternative but was too expensive and too new for a domestic set; it became standard in the small deflection magnets of the 1990s. Samarium is a rare earth, and the rare earths came from bastnasite.
inputs: iron, aluminium and nickel for Alnico
samarium oxide from bastnasite for SmCo

facts.label: Alnico
facts.value: about 8-12% Al, 15-26% Ni, the rest Fe; cast and magnetised

facts.label: Samarium-cobalt
facts.value: a rare earth, expensive and barely used in 1982 sets

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.name: Europium (or calcium sulphide) for the red
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.description: The 1980s red was the least settled of the three. CaS:Eu and Eu-doped ZnS were both in service; CaS:Eu has the better red chromaticity but is hygroscopic and needs protection from moisture. The europium came from bastnasite, a light rare-earth carbonate, cracked with acid and solvent-extracted to 99.9% europium oxide.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium.note: The specific red formulation for any given 1982 tube is proprietary and I cannot verify which manufacturer used CaS:Eu versus Eu-doped ZnS. Flagging as uncertain.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: rare earths are roughly 0.1% of the ore, so bastnasite was mined in large tonnages

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.name: Enamelled copper winding, single harness
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.description: Copper wire, 0.2-0.4 mm, enamel-insulated and wound onto a bobbin with the horizontal coils outside and the vertical coils inside, then immersed in epoxy or polyurethane varnish to lock the winding rigidly. The hum-cancelling trick on the read head of a cassette deck has an ancestor here: the horizontal coils are arranged so their fields oppose.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.2-0.4 mm, and the hum-bucking deflection coils use bifilar or twisted pairs

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.name: Glass-filled nylon bobbin
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.description: Yoke bobbins and coil formers were glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF30) because the winding runs hot and phenolic would crack. Nylon 6,6 comes from adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine, both from petroleum.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: PA66, glass filled to 30% for stiffness above 150 degrees C

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.name: MnZn ferrite or powdered iron core
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.description: The yoke has to carry a 15 kHz sawtooth of several amps and not heat up, so the core is a high-permeability ferrite or a bonded powdered iron (ferrite dust in a phenolic or rubber binder), pressed and sintered. Ferrite is MnO with ZnO added to raise the saturation flux; powdered iron (Ferralium-type alloys) was used where saturation beat loss mattered.

facts.label: MnZn ferrite
facts.value: used up to about 100-200 kHz, saturation about 0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: Powdered iron
facts.value: sintered alloy, saturation about 0.6-0.8 T, higher loss

peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.manganese.name: Manganese oxide and manganese ore
peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.manganese.description: Most manganese ore went to steelmaking, but a small fraction of high-purity electrolytic manganese dioxide went into ferrite. The ore is a sedimentary or lateritic material and the metallurgical chain runs ore to manganous sulphate to electrowinning.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.name: Electron gun, three guns
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.description: Three parallel electron guns in one pinch, one per phosphor, each with a hot cathode, a control grid, a screen grid, a focus grid and an anode. In a 13 inch set of 1982 they were usually separate but adjacent, converging at the screen; the convergence magnets on the neck bent them into line and the electrostatic or magnetic focus brought the three spot sizes down to about 0.5-1.0 mm at the panel.

facts.label: Heater voltage
facts.value: 6.3 V per gun at about 0.6-0.9 A each, all three in parallel off a flyback auxiliary winding

facts.label: Spot size at panel
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 mm at the centre of screen

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.focus-coil.name: Static focus coil on the neck
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.focus-coil.description: On the cheaper sets the three guns were focused by one small coil slipped over the neck outside the vacuum envelope, adjustable from the back of the set. Sets without static focus simply ran the focus grid at a fixed voltage and adjusted focus only for the corners with a convergence adjustment in the yoke.
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.focus-coil.note: Static focus coils were common in small sets of the early 80s and largely disappeared as focus went entirely electrostatic.

facts.label: Field
facts.value: a few hundred gauss in a short air-core solenoid

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.name: Carbon blacking of the anode
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.description: The anode block and the inside of the funnel near the neck are flame-blacked with a sooty acetylene flame so that any stray electrons are absorbed rather than bouncing around the tube. Carbon black, the same pigment as in the cabinet and in a car's tyres, does the job here.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.name: Focus and screen grids, nickel sheet
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.description: The grid stack is a set of thin nickel foils laser-welded or spot-welded into a unit: G1 the Wehnelt and video modulator, G2 the screen grid at a few hundred volts, G3 the focus grid at 5-20% of the anode voltage, and the anode block itself in graphite or aluminium with a ceramic or mica spacer stack. Every surface is blackened.

facts.label: G1
facts.value: Wehnelt and video, a few volts negative to cathode

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.name: Tungsten heater filament
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.description: A hair-fine tungsten wire folded into a flat zig-zag under the cathode cup and buried in its oxides. Typical wire 0.04-0.08 mm diameter, 60-150 mm long, running at 6.3 V. It is the only hot tungsten in the gun and by far the largest source of tube failure.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.name: Scheelite (CaWO4) ore
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.description: The calcium tungstate ore, usually from scheelite skarn or from the Climax and Pine Creek molybdenum-tungsten porphyries. It decomposes in sodium carbonate or caustic, and its tungsten content is often a fraction of a percent of the rock, so the mill has to be big and the recovery obsessive.

facts.label: WO3 content
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% in porphyry ores, far higher in some skarns

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.d.name: Soda decomposition to sodium tungstate
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.d.description: Scheelite has to be opened chemically because it is calcium tungstate and calcium is hard to leach. The ore is crushed and cooked with soda ash or caustic soda at about 900-1000 degrees C, converting it to sodium tungstate in solution; the calcium stays behind as calcium carbonate and the liquor is filtered. From sodium tungstate the APT intermediate is precipitated with ammonium chloride.

facts.label: Decomposition
facts.value: about 900-1000 degrees C with Na2CO3 or NaOH

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: APT crystallised out with NH4Cl from the tungstate liquor

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.d.name: Soda ash from trona or salt
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.d.description: The caustic in the scheelite and wolframite decompositions. In the 1980s most of the world's soda ash was made from trona (a sodium carbonate-bicarbonate double salt) in Wyoming by roasting and leaching, with the Solvay process from salt and limestone filling the rest. Both are diggings.
inputs: trona ore or salt and limestone

facts.label: Solvay
facts.value: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3, then calcined at 200 degrees C

facts.label: Trona route
facts.value: Green River, Wyoming, about 30% of 1980s US soda ash

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite.name: Tungsten wire from wolframite concentrate
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite.description: Tungsten does not exist as a pure ore anywhere. Wolframite (Fe,Mn)WO4 and scheelite CaWO4 are decomposed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate to sodium tungstate, then to APT (ammonium paratungstate), then to tungsten trioxide reduced with hydrogen at 800-1000 degrees C to a fine powder, which is doped with potassium and drawn.
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite.note: Korea and China were becoming dominant in tungsten supply by the early 1980s.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: 800-1000 degrees C, H2, to W powder

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: doped powder, hydrogen-annealed, swaged and drawn to 0.04 mm

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9-99.95%, and the potassium content is controlled to control the grain

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite..name: Tungsten mine and concentrator
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite..description: Wolframite is dense and refractory, so the ore is mined, crushed and gravity-concentrated or floated to a 60-70% WO3 concentrate. Because the ore is often a by-product of a tin or molybdenum mine, tungsten supply followed the fortunes of tin mining, and the price spiked hard whenever the tin market wobbled.
inputs: greasey and xanthate collectors for flotation

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground stoping and hand sorting, plus alluvial allutan placers on the Malay Archipelago tin belt

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.name: Oxide-coated cathode, Ba-Sr-Ca on nickel-chromium
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.description: A cup-shaped nickel-chromium alloy base, sprayed with barium, strontium and calcium carbonates fired to oxides, with a caesium or platinum-tantalum dispenser. The oxides are a thermionic emitter: work function about 2 eV against 4.5 eV for tungsten, which is why a cathode runs at 750-850 degrees C while a tungsten filament runs at 2500.
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.note: The cathode is one of the few parts of a television that is a genuine consumable with a finite life, and its end-of-life symptom was a dim, discoloured picture that a serviceman could fix with a 'gun rejuvenator' that momentarily pushed the heater voltage far above rating.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.name: Nickel-chromium cathode base, and the barium source
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.description: The base metal is a nickel-chromium alloy because it does not react with the oxide and does not outgas badly in vacuum; the barium, strontium and calcium came from barium carbonate and strontium carbonate, both alkaline-earth salts. This is the same barium and strontium as the ferrite magnet in a loudspeaker and the barium getter in the neck, so one barite and strontinite mining chain served three parts of the same set.

facts.label: Base alloy
facts.value: Ni-Cr, about 82% Ni with 18% Cr, spun or deep drawn

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: BaO, SrO and CaO fired onto the surface at about 800-950 degrees C

facts.label: Dispenser
facts.value: a caesium or a Pt-Ta dispenser welded to the cup

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.nic.name: Converges on the nickel chain
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.nic.description: The same electrorefined 99.0-99.2% nickel cathode that went into the CRT grid foils and the permalloy head cores went into the cathode cup, where it had to be free of hydrogen because the cathode is heated in vacuum for thousands of hours.

peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.bar.name: Barite ore for the barium carbonate
peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.bar.description: Barium carbonate is made from barite (BaSO4), the same ore that is reduced to barium metal for the CRT getter and sintered into a speaker magnet. Barite is mined both as a vein fill (underground) and as a residual beach placer (open pit).

facts.label: To carbonate
facts.value: reduction to BaS with coke, then carbonated, or a soda ash roast

facts.label: Use split
facts.value: drilling fluid (most), barium metal for the getter, magnet ferrite, and the cathode oxide

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.name: Shadow mask and aperture grille
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.description: Without something to stop every beam landing on every phosphor, a CRT would be a monochrome tube with three faint colour washes. The shadow mask is a curved steel foil perforated with about 25,000 slots; the electron beam is steered so each of the three guns aims through the correct hole. The alternative is the aperture grille, two combs of tensioned vertical wires with no foil at all.
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.note: The brief's '0.6 mm slot pitch etched from 0.05 mm low-carbon steel' is directionally right on pitch but the sheet gauge in practice was thicker than 0.05 mm. A mask at 0.05 mm would deflect itself into a catenary under its own weight during the 600 degree C stress relief; the industry used 0.1-0.2 mm cold-reduced low-carbon (1008) steel, and Sony's aperture-grille wires are about 0.12-0.15 mm diameter plated with nickel and chrome. 0.6 mm pitch is right for a 1982 set.

facts.label: Shadow mask pitch
facts.value: 0.63-0.8 mm slot pitch (0.63 mm typical, 0.8 mm on the wider-pitch sets of the early 80s)

facts.label: Vertical wires
facts.value: about 350-450 for a 13 inch tube at 0.63-0.8 mm pitch

facts.label: Mask material
facts.value: cold-reduced low-carbon steel strip, about 0.1-0.2 mm

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.grille.name: Aperture grille (Trinitron-type)
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.grille.description: The alternative to a foil: two combs of vertical wires under tension, typically nickel-chrome plated steel wire, at a 0.5-0.6 mm pitch. Because the mask is vertical wires only, the beam can strike them from any horizontal position, which gives the Trinitron its famous vertically sharp picture and lets the two outer guns share a defocus. Two thin damper wires keep the combs from ringing.
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.grille.note: Sony's Trinitron was licensed to a handful of Japanese and European makers through the 1980s, so Trinitron-type tubes appeared in non-Sony sets too.

facts.label: Tension
facts.value: a few newtons, the combs are stressed by the frame

peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.name: Photoetch of the slots
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.description: The flat sheet is cleaned, coated with photoresist, exposed through a master plate that defines every slot, developed, and etched. Ferric chloride is the etchant of the period for steel. After etching the sheet is washed, stress-relieved by heating, then pressed into a spherical section on a matched former, and the round holes open into slots as it bends.
peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch.note: Electroformed nickel masks and bimetallic masks came later and solved the thermal expansion mismatch between steel mask and panel; a 1982 tube used a single low-carbon steel mask whose expansion roughly matched the panel glass.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: ferric chloride, or nitric plus sulphuric acid

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed to a radius about 1.5x the panel face radius

facts.label: Stress relief
facts.value: annealed after etching so the foil does not spring

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.name: P22 phosphor screen, blue/green/red
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.description: The inside face of the panel carries a printed tri-colour phosphor: blue zinc sulphide doped with silver, green zinc sulphide doped with gold, and a red phosphor around 610 nm, arranged as a dot triad maybe 0.6-0.8 mm pitch behind the shadow mask. The whole layer is only about 25-40 microns thick wet and shrinks to 15-25 microns fired, then gets a mirror of aluminium vapour on top so the electron beam that misses the phosphor is absorbed instead of lighting the room.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.note: The exact activator recipe for the red was proprietary and differed between manufacturers; the blue and green ZnS:Ag and ZnS:Au pair is the solid part of the P22 story. Blue ZnS:Ag is bandgap-limited emission from the ZnS host itself, the Ag is a co-activator that traps the electron, and Au in the green sits at a discrete level that emits 525 nm. A modern LCD has no phosphor at all.

facts.label: Green
facts.value: ZnS:Au (often with Cu or Sb), peak about 525 nm

facts.label: Red
facts.value: about 610 nm; formulations varied between CaS:Eu and Eu-doped ZnS

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.name: Zinc sulphide from sphalerite concentrate
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.description: Zinc sulphide is the host crystal for all three P22 phosphors. It came from sphalerite, the zinc-iron sulphide ore, roasted in air to ZnO with the sulphur captured as SO2 for sulphuric acid. The ZnO was then converted back to high-purity ZnS, either by reacting with H2S or by reducing with hydrogen and re-sulphurising, because phosphor-grade sulphide has to be free of the iron and manganese that quench the emission.
inputs: hydrogen sulphide or hydrogen and sulphur

facts.label: Phosphor calcine
facts.value: 900-1100 degrees C in a sealed quartz or alumina crucible under N2 with the activator

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: Fe and Mn kept below a few hundred ppm

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper.name: Copper activator, from chalcopyrite
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper.description: Copper, usually added as copper oxide, deepens the green and creates the donor level that the blue's co-activator needs. It came from copper concentrate, smelted and electrorefined to 99.99% copper and converted to CuO.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.name: Gold activator, from gold ore
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.description: The green ZnS:Au needs a discrete gold level about 0.1% down. The gold came from cyanide leaching of refractory ore and from the anode slimes of copper refining, refined by the Wohlwill process to 99.99% and dissolved in aqua regia.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold.note: A television green phosphor contains a genuinely tiny amount of gold. Several tens of thousands of colour tubes a year is a real, if small, consumer of the metal.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.name: Sulphur dioxide to sulphuric acid
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.description: The roaster's off-gas is cleaned, converted to SO3 on a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at about 450 degrees C and absorbed in 98% acid in a double-contact plant. It is the reason a 1982 zinc smelter had an acid plant as large as the roaster.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfu.name: Sulphur feed, from sour natural gas
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfu.description: Where a smelter did not have its own roast gas, elemental sulphur was produced from hydrogen sulphide in sour crude oil or sour natural gas, or by the Claus process. The sulphur then burned to make the SO2 the contact plant needed.

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfu.name: The Claus process for elemental sulphur
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfu.description: Where a zinc smelter had more roast gas than its contact plant could take, hydrogen sulphide was burned to make elemental sulphur in a Claus unit: two thermal reactors at 250-450 degrees C and a catalytic reactor over alumina at about 350 degrees C. The sulphur then went to a new roaster, which is why sour gas fields and zinc smelters were economically linked.
inputs: hydrogen sulphide from sour gas or sour crude

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: about 99% sulphur recovery with a hydrogenation step

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.name: Vapour-deposited aluminium black layer
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.description: The single most important trick in a CRT. Without it, ambient light reflecting off the phosphor coating would lift the black level and the picture would look grey in a lit room. Aluminium is evaporated at better than 1e-4 mbar onto the phosphor; it is a mirror that passes 25 kV electrons but reflects visible light, so emitted light passes through while room light is bounced back out through the glass. Afterwards a thin dust-protection layer of a silicate or organosilicon compound is vapour-deposited on top of the aluminium, because bare aluminium under 25 kV slowly forms aluminium oxide.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.note: The brief conflated two things: the vacuum-deposited aluminium behind the phosphor (the black level) and the separate aluminium coating on the funnel wall behind the gun, which is a rear-facing mirror to recover light that would otherwise bounce around inside the tube. Both exist; they are different parts.

facts.label: Foil
facts.value: 99.99% aluminium, 0.1-0.15 mm, pinched to a wire

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.fire.name: Firing at 430-450 degrees C
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.fire.description: The printed panel goes into a conveyor oven. The organic vehicle decomposes and burns off completely, which is why the tunnel has to be exhausted, and the glass frit flows and wets the phosphor grains. Under-400 degrees leaves carbon in the layer; over 460 starts to attack the phosphor and shift the colour.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: air, exhausted; some lines ran N2 to protect the blue

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.name: Internal screen print through a nylon mesh
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.description: Three slurries are laid down in turn: red, then green, then blue, each through a fine nylon mesh onto the inside of the panel, each registered to the last to a few tens of microns. The mesh, not a photo-emulsion, defines the dots. A photographic stencil fixes the screen area and the black border.

facts.label: Registration
facts.value: better than 25 microns between colour prints

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: PVA plus a plasticiser, burnt out in the firing

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.frit.name: Glass frit binder in the phosphor slurry
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.frit.description: Without a glassy binder the phosphor dust would wipe off the panel at the first wipe. A low-melting glass frit, finely ground, is mixed into the slurry at 10-30% by weight and melts during the firing step to fuse the phosphor grains into a solid, adherent, moisture-resistant layer.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.frit.note: Screen frits of this era could contain lead or barium; formulations were proprietary.
inputs: lead-free or lead-bearing frit depending on cost

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.mill.name: Three-roll mill
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.mill.description: The phosphor slurry is refined on a three-roll (three-mill) gap mill: the rollers set a gap of a few microns and shear the agglomerates down so that the particle size distribution is tight. Screen printing needs a narrow size distribution or the dots print with a rough edge and the resolution falls off.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: a few microns, set by feel across the roll

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.name: Faceplate panel and funnel, borosilicate glass
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.description: The tube is made of two glass parts that must expand at the same rate or the tube shatters at the seal. The funnel is a leaded or unlead borosilicate; the panel is a flatter, alkali-free glass with a much lower thermal expansion coefficient. Their junction is a strip of lead borosilicate frit, printed onto both parts and fired, which melts at a temperature low enough that the base glass does not slump.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.note: The 24% PbO figure in the brief is the number quoted for the standard X-ray absorbing lead frit of the era; real formulations ran from about a quarter to two thirds PbO depending on whether the set was sold as a colour tube with a separate shadow mask or a lower-cost monochrome-style lead frit. Treat 24% as representative, not universal.

facts.label: Funnel glass
facts.value: about 1.5-2.5 mm through the cone, flaring to 3-4 mm at the panel edge

facts.label: Frit border
facts.value: roughly 8-12 mm wide, 1-2 mm thick, all round the panel perimeter

facts.label: Frit firing
facts.value: devitrified at 600-700 degrees C, then belt-sealed to the funnel at 430-460 degrees C

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.name: Panel glass, alkali-free
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.description: The panel is not the same glass as the funnel. It is alkali-free borosilicate with an expansion coefficient about a third lower than the funnel, so that when the panel is pressed against a mould during cooling it develops exactly the curvature the shadow mask geometry needs and stays there. Alkali is kept out because sodium and potassium diffuse and react with the phosphor layer on the inside face.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.note: The curved 13 inch panel of the period was not spherical. It used a spherical base plus a cylindrical or sphericon section, because a purely spherical screen needed too much mask curvature and too much deflection for its size.

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: about 3.0-3.5 x 10^-6 / K for the panel

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed against a ribbed refractory block during annealing

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.name: Alkali-free batch: silica, alumina, boron
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.description: Where the funnel batch leaned on lead and alkali for its expansion match, the panel batch deliberately excluded sodium and potassium and got its properties from silica, alumina and boric oxide plus a small amount of barium to suppress solarisation under the phosphor firing. It is the same silica sand as the funnel, but a batch designed to be unfriendly to sodium.
inputs: antimony or arsenic as a fining agent

facts.label: Na2O + K2O
facts.value: held below about 1% for an alkali-free panel glass

facts.label: Melt
facts.value: same 1380-1500 degrees C tank furnace as the funnel

facts.label: Solarisation
facts.value: the phosphor firing at 430-450 degrees C can darken a glass with too much alkali; barium and antimony suppressed it

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.name: Alumina for the panel batch
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.description: Refractory-grade alumina from bauxite, the same Bayer-process alumina chain as the CRT's aluminium foil. It raises the panel glass's viscosity and its thermal shock resistance, which matters because a tube has to survive being handled and shipped while cold.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.name: Belt kiln and vacuum leak test
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.description: Panel and funnel enter a continuous refractory belt kiln, aligned by a jig, and travel through the firing zone where the frit melts. The seal is judged by how far the heated frit bulges past its own edge. The tube is then helium leak tested before it ever goes near the vacuum pumps.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.note: Ion-pump/penning-gauge helium leak testing at that sensitivity was standard practice; the exact acceptance spec varies by plant.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.name: Funnel glass batch, melted at 1400 degrees C
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.description: Funnel glass is a borosilicate with low alkali, formulated so that its thermal expansion matches the panel. The batch is silica sand, boric acid, soda ash, limestone and a little red lead or litharge as a fining agent, melted for tens of hours in a regenerative gas-fired tank furnace and then drawn into tubing.

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: lehr cooling 450 down to 20 degrees C over 10-20 hours

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.name: Boric acid, from colemanite ore
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.description: Borates lower the glass's expansion coefficient and its melting point, which is exactly what a funnel that must survive a 25 kV implosion needs. Most borax for the western hemisphere came from borate ores in southern California and from Turkey.

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.name: Colemanite and borate ore
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.description: A calcium borate mineral, often in veins with gypsum and limestone, crushed and digested in acid to give boric acid which is then crystallised out as sodium tetraborate.

peripheral.why-rf.name: Why a television set was mandatory
peripheral.why-rf.description: The VIC-II chip outputs a 1 MHz-ish analogue composite signal on its own pin: luma, blanking and a colour subcarrier, but no RF. In 1982 there was no agreed analogue video standard between a computer and a monitor, no DE-15 or VGA, and no DVI. Commodore's answer was a small RF modulator, a printed board with one video modulator oscillator and a VHF converter, whose output was injected into the aerial socket of an ordinary television. The TV then had to be tuned to channel 3 (61.75 MHz in the US) or channel 4, and the picture was in colour only if the TV had a colour decoder for that subcarrier frequency.
peripheral.why-rf.note: The modulator board is usually treated as part of the C64, not as a peripheral, so it lives here as the hinge of this branch. Output power figures vary between sources; treat them as order-of-magnitude. A TV modulator injected at the aerial socket needs a floating (isolated) aerial input or the local TV signal will back-feed and wash out the computer picture, which is why sets with an isolated aerial socket were prized.
inputs: composite video from the VIC-II pin

facts.label: Output power
facts.value: roughly 0.5-1 mW (a few hundred microwatts to 1 milliwatt)

peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.name: What replaced it
peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.description: Commodore's own 1702 monitor took a composite luma-and-blank input over a 5-pin DIN, and in 1985-86 Commodore adopted the DE-9 connector used by the C128's RGBI monitors, which carried separate red, green and blue analogue signals on pins 5, 6, 7 with no modulation at all. There was still no standard, which is why the C128 ended up with a proprietary DIN-8 video connector rather than a DE-15.

peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.name: The -60 dB that nobody mentions
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.description: A broadcast TV station transmitted tens of kilowatts; a C64 modulator put out about a milliwatt. The set had to be tuned by hand, and reception quality was a function of the modulator's output impedance matching the aerial input. Anyone who ever moved the TV or unplugged the aerial lead knows how marginal this was.
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.note: Quantitative comparison of received signal levels is reconstructed from general receiver-sensitivity reasoning rather than from a measurement of a specific 1.1902-type modulator.

c64.packaging.name: Retail packaging: printed box, foam, polybag, manual
c64.packaging.description: A breadbin C64 shipped in a corrugated board box printed lithographically with Commodore's rainbow graphics, with the machine cradled in two moulded polystyrene end blocks and wrapped in a polyethylene bag, plus the user's manual and a warranty card. Boxes went to a corrugated master carton on a timber skid for shipping to warehouses.
c64.packaging.note: Internal packaging varied by region, by production run and by whether the machine was sold boxed or shipped in bulk to a distributor, so 'the C64 box' is really several packages: an early plain brown box with a rainbow stripe, later 'rainbow' graphics, and machined-in plain boxes. The user's manual is documented as Commodore part 320974 in the service-manual parts list. I could not verify the exact internal foam arrangement for every region.

facts.label: Box
facts.value: corrugated board, lithographically printed, rainbow graphics

facts.label: Bag
