facts.value: plain polyethylene sleeve over the machine

facts.label: Paperwork
facts.value: user's manual (Commodore part 320974) and a warranty/registration card

c64.packaging.packaging-line.name: Final pack-out and pack-out line
c64.packaging.packaging-line.description: At the end of the case-moulding and assembly plant, machines are bagged, placed in the foam blocks, dropped into the printed box with the manual and card, and the box is closed and labelled. This was semi-automatic and was the labour-heavy step that determined where a home computer was finally assembled.
c64.packaging.packaging-line.note: Pack-out in Hong Kong and Taiwan in the early 1980s was where the cost advantage of shipping a nearly-finished machine - rather than a finished one - to be finished and packed in Asia was actually realised.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: bag, foam, box, insert paper, close, label, case-pack

facts.label: Labour
facts.value: a few operators per line; the constraint on Commodore's throughput

c64.packaging.master-carton.name: Shipping master carton and skid
c64.packaging.master-carton.description: Retail boxes were packed into corrugated master cartons, several to a carton, and banded on a timber skid for palletised shipping from the Hong Kong or Taiwan assembly plant to a regional warehouse. Skids - not euro-pallets - were the norm for export shipping of this period.

facts.label: Master carton
facts.value: double-wall corrugated, usually printed stencilled with contents and count

facts.label: Skid
facts.value: sawn timber skid with a bearers, no deckboards

facts.label: Strapping
facts.value: steel or polypropylene band around the carton

c64.packaging.carton-board.name: Master-carton board
c64.packaging.carton-board.description: Heavier double-wall corrugated, usually a recycled medium and recycled liners, with the shipping marks stencilled or flexo-printed rather than litho-printed.

c64.packaging.strapping.name: Strapping (steel or polypropylene)
c64.packaging.strapping.description: Steel band with a stamped seal, or the polypropylene strapping that had largely displaced it by the 1980s because it does not rust, does not cut the carton and is lighter to ship back as waste.

c64.packaging.skids.name: Timber skid
c64.packaging.skids.description: A wooden skid: three or more bearers with a top deck, or a bare skid with the cartons loaded straight onto it. Skids are made from rough-sawn softwood offcuts, which is why they are the cheapest way to make a heavy load forkable.

c64.packaging.timber.name: Rough-sawn softwood
c64.packaging.timber.description: Kiln-dried or green softwood, band-sawn to bearers and deckboards. The sawmill waste that cannot be pulped into paper - knots, ends, slabs - is exactly what a skid is made of, which is a neat closure of the wood chain.

facts.label: Moisture
facts.value: green or kiln-dried, depending on the shipping leg

c64.packaging.warranty-card.name: Warranty and registration card
c64.packaging.warranty-card.description: A small printed card with the warranty terms and a serial-number registration slip. It is the same litho process as the manual on a heavier board stock, and it is the only part of the package with a legal function.
c64.packaging.warranty-card.note: Warranty terms and the presence of a registration card varied by market; this node records the printed card as a class of object rather than claiming specific wording.

c64.packaging.manual.name: User's manual (fold-in-fold booklet)
c64.packaging.manual.description: The Commodore 64 user's manual - part 320974 in the service-manual parts list - is a cheap but well-made fold-in-fold booklet: a single sheet of coated wood-pulp paper printed in colour on both sides, folded twice with a 16-page section glued in the middle. It is the same construction as a road atlas, which is how a large amount of operating documentation was printed in 1982.
c64.packaging.manual.note: The C64 manual is well known for its fold-in-fold format and its colour printing on cheap stock - a deliberate cost decision on a product that was being sold through discount and supermarket channels. Some regional printings differ.

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: coated wood-pulp paper, ~60-100 gsm, colour both sides

facts.label: Binding
facts.value: 16-page fold-in-fold, glued on the centre spread

c64.packaging.manual.letterpress.name: Letterpress covers (regional variants)
c64.packaging.manual.letterpress.description: Some Commodore manuals and the box artwork of this period were printed letterpress from metal type on a platen or cylinder press rather than litho, and some C64 documentation was printed that way. Where a manual was letterpressed, the type impression is visible on the reverse and the cover has that slightly embossed, absorbent-paper look.
c64.packaging.manual.letterpress.note: Recorded because letterpress was still in use for 1980s Commodore collateral, but I could not verify that any particular C64 manual printing was letterpress rather than litho. Type metal would be lead-antimony, and the ink an oil-based printing ink of the same family as the box ink.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: relief printing from cast metal type or polymer plates

facts.label: Giveaway
facts.value: a slight debossed impression you can feel

c64.packaging.manual.bindery.name: Fold-in-fold bindery
c64.packaging.manual.bindery.description: A long sheet is printed with the page imposition for a 16-page booklet, folded twice with a plate, and a 16-page section is glued into the middle crease. The result is a bound booklet that opens flat and costs almost nothing to assemble - it is pure paper engineering.
c64.packaging.manual.bindery.note: The fold-in-fold is the dominant cheap-booklet construction of the era and is why so many 1980s computer manuals fall open to the same two centre pages.

facts.label: Imposition
facts.value: 16 pages on one sheet, fold twice

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: PVA or hot-melt for the centre section

c64.packaging.manual.printing.name: Colour offset printing of the manual
c64.packaging.manual.printing.description: Sheet-fed offset litho in four colours (CMYK), plus spot colours for the Commodore rainbow and the red 'RESTORE' key highlights. The manual's diagrams and BASIC listings were set in hot-metal or phototypeset, then printed from plates.
c64.packaging.manual.printing.note: Some C64 manuals have colour photography composited from transparencies, which is typical of pre-digital prepress in 1982: a mechanical or phototypeset page with a separately shot colour plate.

facts.label: Prepress
facts.value: phototypesetting and photographic copy for the diagrams

c64.packaging.manual.paper.name: Coated printing paper
c64.packaging.manual.paper.description: Wood-pulp paper filled and coated with clay (kaolin) and a binder, then calendered, so the ink sits on the surface and the colours are bright and sharp. It is the same stock as a supermarket leaflet.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: mostly softwood mechanical and kraft pulp

c64.packaging.polybag.name: Polyethylene sleeve over the machine
c64.packaging.polybag.description: A plain polyethylene bag over the boxed machine, to stop the moulded case and the printed manual from rubbing and to keep dust out during transit. It is a low-cost LDPE sleeve, blown as a tube on the same film-blowing line used for all commodity packaging film.
c64.packaging.polybag.note: Antistatic bags with an added conductive agent existed by the early 1980s but were not standard for a consumer computer at this price point; I could not verify an antistatic bag in the C64 box, so the bag is recorded as a plain polyethylene sleeve.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: dust and abrasion protection during distribution

c64.packaging.film-blowing.name: Film blowing and bag making
c64.packaging.film-blowing.description: LDPE pellets are blown as a thin tube through a die and a bubble, cooled in an air ring, collapsed and wound; the tube is then cut and heat-sealed into a bag. Film blowing is high-volume and very cheap - the bag is cents, not dollars.

c64.packaging.foam-caps.name: Moulded polystyrene end blocks
c64.packaging.foam-caps.description: Two white expanded-polystyrene blocks that cradle the ends of the machine so the case cannot be crushed in the box and cannot slide. They are moulded to the machine's outline in a steam-heated block mould, then cut down to size.
c64.packaging.foam-caps.note: EPS blocks were the standard protection for beige consumer electronics through the 1980s. Their disadvantage - they cannot be recycled with paper and they shatter into Styrofoam - is exactly why they vanished from Commodore's later packaging in favour of pulp and cardboard trays.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: chlorinated hydrocarbon (CFC-11 / dichloromethane), ~5-7% into the bead

c64.packaging.eps.name: Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
c64.packaging.eps.description: Small beads of polystyrene, each already blown up with a chlorinated blowing agent, are heated and expanded again in a mould so the beads fuse into a solid block shaped to the part. The polymer is the same styrene copolymer chemistry as the ABS and the SAN; only the physical form is different.

c64.packaging.eps-moulding.name: Block moulding in a steam-heated mould
c64.packaging.eps-moulding.description: Beads are blown into a heated aluminium mould and the steam expands them to fill it; the mould is then cooled and the block ejected. A block mould makes a slab that is later cut on a band saw or hot wire into the end blocks. The mould is a heat exchanger - the steam lines run through it.
c64.packaging.eps-moulding.note: Hot-wire cutting with a nichrome wire uses the same principle as a foam cup: a heated wire through a block. It is how the complex end-cap profiles were cut.

facts.label: Cutting
facts.value: band saw or hot wire for complex profiles

c64.packaging.eps-expansion.name: Bead expansion (bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-expansion.description: Beads are fed into a steam-heated expander where they expand, are held at temperature to sinter them into a cake, and are then cooled and dried in a silo. The expander is the machine that sets the final foam density.

c64.packaging.eps-beads.name: EPS beads (expanded in a bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-beads.description: Styrene is suspension-polymerised in water to small beads, then a chlorinated blowing agent is dissolved into them under pressure; on heating the agent flashes and expands each bead from ~0.5-1 mm to 2-6 mm, and the beads are chilled and sieved by size.
c64.packaging.eps-beads.note: In 1982 the blowing agent was still a chlorinated hydrocarbon. Pentane is what you find in EPS today, but it only arrived after the 1987 Montreal Protocol drove CFC-11 out — so a period C64 is packed in ozone-depleting foam, which is why expanding or reprocessing thirty-year-old packaging is a regulated activity rather than a chore.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) or dichloromethane, ~5-7 wt% in the bead

c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.name: Chlorinated blowing agent (CFC-11 / dichloromethane)
c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.description: Trichlorofluoromethane, or methylene chloride in the European trade. Both are excellent blowing agents: low boiling point, no flammability risk in the bead, and chemically inert enough to survive the polymerisation. They are also chlorinated, which is the whole problem — they destroy stratospheric ozone, so they were phased out of packaging foam through the 1990s and replaced by pentane and by butane.
c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.note: The fluorine came from fluorspar and the chlorine from the chlor-alkali cell — the same two mineral chains that make the etchant and the trichlorosilane elsewhere in this tree.

facts.label: Why not then
facts.value: non-flammable, cheap, and already produced in bulk as a refrigerant

c64.packaging.retail-box.name: Retail corrugated box
c64.packaging.retail-box.description: A regular slotted container or a tuck-end box in B-flute corrugated board, printed on a sheet-fed or web offset press in up to four or six colours plus a rainbow gradient, then creased, cut and glued. It is a commodity: the board is a mill product and the printing is a printshop product, not a Commodore product.

c64.packaging.parts-tray.name: Parts tray for the loose items
c64.packaging.parts-tray.description: Inside the box, below or beside the machine, the power cord, the A/V lead and the paperwork were either tied together in the foam or held in a separate moulded tray. Where a tray was used it was expanded polystyrene or, on later runs, a folded pulp tray.
c64.packaging.parts-tray.note: I could not verify the exact internal arrangement of the C64 box by region and run. This node records that a tray or folded pulp cradle for the loose items existed as a class of 1980s arrangement, and flags the uncertainty rather than claiming a specific one.

facts.label: Materials used
facts.value: expanded polystyrene block, or moulded pulp

facts.label: Contents
facts.value: mains cord, A/V lead, manual, warranty card

c64.packaging.box-converting.name: Slotting, creasing, folding and gluing
c64.packaging.box-converting.description: The printed board goes through a slotter-creater which cuts the slots, scores the creases and trims the blanks; the blanks are then folded on a folder-gluer, which applies a hot starch or PVA glue to the tab and forms the box. It is a fast, near-fully-automated process.

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: PVA or hot-melt; starch for heavy board

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of boxes per hour

c64.packaging.box-printing.name: Box printing (offset litho) and the rainbow graphics
c64.packaging.box-printing.description: The printed sheet is run on an offset litho press - sheet-fed for short runs, web-fed for long runs - in a small number of process colours, with the Commodore rainbow reproduced as a multi-stop gradient. The board is then cut, creased and glued.
c64.packaging.box-printing.note: Flexographic printing on corrugate with rubber or photopolymer plates became the normal route for high-run corrugated print during this period and later; for a mid-run consumer box in the early 1980s, sheet-fed offset on a liner was still common.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed offset or rotary web offset

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: typically 3-6 process colours; the rainbow needs extra separations or a duotone gradient

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: uncoated kraft board; often a thin aqueous varnish for scuff resistance

c64.packaging.varnishing.name: Varnish / water-based coating
c64.packaging.varnishing.description: A thin scuff-resistant coating over the printed board, applied on the press or in-line. It stops the rainbow rubbing off in the warehouse. Modern converters would use a water-based or UV-cure acrylic; 1982 used a solvent or water-based acryl.

c64.packaging.rainbow-gradient.name: Rainbow gradient (duotone / multi-stop blend)
c64.packaging.rainbow-gradient.description: Commodore's rainbow on the box and the case logo is a set of graded colour bands. On a flexo or litho box it is made either with a multi-colour duotone (the two separations overprinted at varying screen densities) or, on later short runs, printed with a spray/airbrush unit. This is where a printing shop makes one-off artwork effects cheaply.
c64.packaging.rainbow-gradient.note: The exact number of colours and whether the box used duotone or spray varies by printing run and region; the visual effect (a rainbow gradient band) is consistent across the packaging.

c64.packaging.offset-litho.name: Offset lithographic printing
c64.packaging.offset-litho.description: The image is on a flat plate, wetted with dampening solution so the image areas reject ink, and printed by a rubber blanket onto paper. Litho gives fine detail and consistent colour on uncoated board, at the cost of a plate-making step per colour.

c64.packaging.litho-press.name: Offset press (sheet-fed or web)
c64.packaging.litho-press.description: A printing press: plate cylinders, blanket cylinders, inking units, and either a sheet feed with a delivery stacker or a web unwind and rewind with a folder. For a corrugated box liner, the press is the capital equipment a converter owns.

facts.label: Units
facts.value: 2-6 inking units for up to 6 colours

c64.packaging.litho-ink.name: Offset printing ink
c64.packaging.litho-ink.description: A pigment dispersed in a drying-oil-based vehicle (linseed/soy alkyd) with resin, wax and a drier. Water-based offset inks became the norm for corrugated in the 1990s; oil-based inks were standard in 1982.

facts.label: Pigments
facts.value: titanium dioxide white, phthalocyanine blues, phthalochromate yellows

c64.packaging.ink-pigment.name: Ink pigments (organic and inorganic)
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.description: In 1982 most packaging colourants were still inorganic: iron oxides, chrome yellow, ultramarine. The bright synthetic organic pigments (phthalocyanines, azo yellows) were used for the saturated rainbow, and the titanium dioxide white for the light areas.
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.note: The 1970s-80s shift from lead chromate and cadmium pigments toward these organic and titanium whites in packaging inks was driven by toxicity regulation, and is one of the reasons a 1982 box does not smell like a 1972 one.

c64.packaging.soy-oil.name: Soy or linseed oil (ink vehicle base)
c64.packaging.soy-oil.description: A vegetable oil pressed from a crop. It oxidises (dries) on the printed sheet, which is what 'drying ink' means. In 1982 soybean oil was becoming the preferred ink vehicle because of the 1970s linseed-oil shortages.

c64.packaging.ink-resin.name: Alkyd / drying-oil ink vehicle
c64.packaging.ink-resin.description: Built from vegetable oil (linseed or soybean) fatty acids condensed with a polyol and a phthalic or maleic anhydride, then crosslinked by oxidative polymerisation on the press. So the ink vehicle on the box traces back to a phthalic anhydride plant, the same chemistry as the pigment in the case.

c64.packaging.litho-plate.name: Lithographic printing plate
c64.packaging.litho-plate.description: A thin aluminium or copper plate, grained and treated, with a photopolymer or metal-image layer carrying the separations. The classic long-run offset plate is an aluminium sheet electro-grained and anodised; short runs use photopolymer plates directly.

c64.packaging.box-board.name: Corrugated board (liner + medium)
c64.packaging.box-board.description: Two kraft liners glued to a fluted medium. In 1982 a consumer-electronics box was usually C-flute or B-flute single wall, made from semichemical or recycled kraft; the flute is what gives the box its edge crush strength for a couple of Newtons of stacking force.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: liner / fluted medium / liner, single wall

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: starch or dextrin, hot-water resistant grade

c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.name: Starch corrugating adhesive
c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.description: The glue holding the flutes and the liners is a corn- or tapioca-starch dextrin, cooked on the corrugator and applied hot. It is the standard adhesive in corrugated board and the reason the board is not a fire hazard in the way solvent glues would be.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: starch / dextrin, hot-water resistant grade for the liners

c64.packaging.corn-starch.name: Corn (maize) starch
c64.packaging.corn-starch.description: Starch is wet-milled from maize: the kernels are steeped in warm water to soften the germ, ground, and the starch is separated by gravity or centrifugally and dried. Every corrugated box is glued with a plant, not a petrochemical.

c64.packaging.maize.name: Maize crop
c64.packaging.maize.description: A cereal grain grown in enormous tonnages in the US corn belt and in Europe, China and Brazil; the harvested cobs are shelled and the kernels go to wet milling. This is the agricultural end of the adhesive chain.

c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.name: Fluted medium (recycled)
c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.description: The wavy centre of the board is usually made from 100% recycled paper, because the flute does not need virgin-fibre strength. Old corrugated boxes are collected, pulped (the recycled / OCF route), and run onto a corrugating machine.

c64.packaging.corrugating.name: Corrugating and sheet making
c64.packaging.corrugating.description: Medium paper is corrugated between two rotating fluted rolls with heat and starch glue, then glued to liners; the sheet is cut and creased. The board then goes to the box plant for slotting, folding and gluing.
c64.packaging.corrugating.note: The reason a pizza box folds and a used sheet does not: the flute is a beam. C64 boxes are usually single-wall B or C flute.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: reuse office paper makes poor medium; box fibre is preferred

c64.packaging.wastepaper.name: Recovered paper (OCC / mixed waste)
c64.packaging.wastepaper.description: Collected corrugated and box board, baled, repulped in a hydrapulper and screened. The deinking stage is needed for printed waste; unprinted OCC is repulped as it is. The fibre in a C64 box's fluted medium is therefore almost certainly several previous boxes.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: OCC (old corrugated container) or mixed waste paper

c64.packaging.deinking.name: Repulping and deinking
c64.packaging.deinking.description: Bales are dropped into a hydrapulper, torn up into fibre, screened, and deinked with a flotation cell and surfactant to remove printing inks. A high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered in exactly this way.

c64.packaging.kraft-liner.name: Kraft liner (topside and underside)
c64.packaging.kraft-liner.description: Unbleached paper made from long-fibre softwood pulp, typically 120-200 gsm. Its brown colour is the kraft process itself: the pulp is brown before it reaches the paper machine, because the kraft cook keeps the lignin.

c64.packaging.paper-machine.name: Fourdrinier paper machine
c64.packaging.paper-machine.description: The pulp is diluted to a few tenths of a percent solids and laid as a continuous web on a moving wire mesh, squeezed, dried over felt-covered heated cylinders, calendered, and wound onto reels. This machine is where a tree becomes a sheet.

facts.label: Web speed
facts.value: 300-600 m/min on a modern machine; slower in 1982

c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.name: Kraft pulp
c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.description: Wood chips are steamed, cooked in a kraft digester with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide, washed, and bleached only lightly. The brown colour is retained kraft lignin, which is why kraft paper is brown and recycling it is easy.

c64.packaging.kraft-process.name: Brown (kraft) grade versus bleached
c64.packaging.kraft-process.description: Unbleached kraft keeps its brown colour and is the cheapest strong liner. A bleached or semi-bleached top liner costs more and is used where the print needs a white background. Commodore's boxes are brown board with printing on top, so the brown liner is exactly right.
c64.packaging.kraft-process.note: Chlorine bleaching of pulp was standard in 1982 and has since been largely displaced by chlorine-free processes for environmental reasons - a clear 1980s-vs-modern difference in the same plant.

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine, chlorine dioxide or oxygen/peroxide delignification

c64.packaging.digestion.name: Kraft cooking (digestion)
c64.packaging.digestion.description: Chips are cooked in a spherical or continuous digester with white liquor (sodium hydroxide + sodium sulfide + sodium carbonate) at 160-180 C. The alkali dissolves the lignin; the sulfide keeps the dissolved lignin in solution so the fibres do not darken.

facts.label: Chemical recovery
facts.value: black liquor is evaporated and burnt to regenerate the chemicals

c64.packaging.sodium-hydroxide.name: Caustic soda for the digester
c64.packaging.sodium-hydroxide.description: The same chlor-alkali caustic that makes VCM and soaps comes to the paper mill, typically as a 50% solution in tank cars.

c64.packaging.wood-chips.name: Wood chips from sawmill waste
c64.packaging.wood-chips.description: Roundwood is debarked and chipped into 20-30 mm chips in a disc chipper, ready for the digester. The chips are the whole reason the paper mill sits next to a forest: you cannot make paper without wood fibre.

c64.packaging.forest-stand.name: Planted softwood stand
c64.packaging.forest-stand.description: Managed conifer plantations (spruce, pine, or southern pine) felled on a rotation and replanted. This is where the fibre chain ends: a box is wood, and the wood is a tree that was grown, cut and chipped.

c64.packaging.log.name: Roundwood logs
c64.packaging.log.description: Trunk sections felled and delimbed, usually conifer in northern Europe and North America. Softwood is preferred for kraft because its long fibres give paper strength; hardwoods go into hardwood kraft or into mechanical pulp.

c64.cables.name: Supplied cables: RF lead, A/V lead, mains cord
c64.cables.description: Three cables shipped with or sold alongside a breadbin C64. The RF cable carries the modulator's VHF output from the machine's phono socket to a television's aerial input, so it is a 75-ohm coaxial. The A/V lead carries luma, chroma, composite and audio to a monitor through an 8-pin DIN. The mains cord is a two- or three-core PVC-jacketed cord with a moulded plug that feeds the external power supply.
c64.cables.note: The breadbin's RF modulator sits on the motherboard (Astec or Mitsumi depending on production run) and its output leaves through the machine's own phono socket. The supplied RF cable is therefore a coax lead with a phono plug at the C64 end and a television-plug at the TV end. Early boards used a 5-pin video socket; later ones an 8-pin DIN, which changes the A/V cable but not the RF cable.

facts.label: A/V socket
facts.value: 8-pin DIN, CN5 on the motherboard, on early sets a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Switch box
facts.value: Commodore part 904778-01, an RF splitter/box accessory

c64.cables.switch-box.name: TV switch box (optional accessory)
c64.cables.switch-box.description: Commodore part 904778-01, an external box that let the C64's RF output share a television aerial socket with an actual antenna, switching between them. It is an accessory rather than a cable, but it is in the same moulded-plastic-and-coax family and shares the cable supply chain.
c64.cables.switch-box.note: The service-manual parts list gives this number; its exact internals are not documented in the sources I found.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: switch between computer RF and TV aerial

c64.cables.power-cord.name: Mains power cord
c64.cables.power-cord.description: A detachable mains lead for the external power supply: two or three PVC-insulated copper conductors in a moulded outer jacket, with a moulded mains plug at one end and a moulded figure-8 or IEC connector at the other. In Europe it is a two-pin contour plug; in North America a three-pin NEMA plug, often polarised.

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: PVC per conductor; outer jacket PVC or rubber

facts.label: Current
facts.value: 2.5 A or 10 A rated, well over the C64's ~15 W draw

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: figure-8 (C7) or IEC C8 inlet on the power supply

c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug.name: Moulded mains plug
c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug.description: A plug with a thermoplastic cord body wrapped around the cable entry to take the bending strain, and two or three brass prongs riveted or crimped in. The cord body is the part that actually fails: the plug is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.

facts.label: Prongs
facts.value: brass, plated, on the North American 3-pin plug also nickel-plated

c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.name: Cord body / strain-relief grip
c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.description: Moulded in PVC or polypropylene and over-moulded onto the jacket. It is deliberately flexible so the cable can swivel, which is also why a moulded cord body eventually tears at its root after years of being yanked out of a wall socket by the wire.

c64.cables.power-cord.brass-prongs.name: Brass prongs
c64.cables.power-cord.brass-prongs.description: Blanked, formed and plated brass strip. Brass is used rather than steel because it must not spark and must not corrode; the plating gives the dull, non-tarnishing surface a moulded plug has.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: brass strip, often leaded free-cutting grade

c64.cables.power-cord.jacket.name: Outer jacket
c64.cables.power-cord.jacket.description: A second extrusion over the assembled, twisted conductors. The conductors are first twisted together on a planetary twister so the cord resists unwinding, then jacketed.

facts.label: Cord twist
facts.value: planetary or bunch twisting, tens of twists per metre

c64.cables.power-cord.insulation.name: PVC insulation extruded onto the conductors
c64.cables.power-cord.insulation.description: Each conductor is passed through a die in an extrusion line and coated with a rigid or semi-rigid PVC at a few hundred volts' worth of insulation. Extrusion is continuous and the colour is added by pigment masterbatch.

c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.name: Stranded copper conductors
c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.description: Fine-strand flexible copper, made by bunching many small wires in a roving machine and twisting them. Flexible stranding is what lets a mains lead bend without breaking the strands.

c64.cables.av-cable.name: A/V cable to a 1701/1702 monitor
c64.cables.av-cable.description: A monitor lead carrying luma, chroma, composite video, audio in and out, and +5V/ground, in an 8-pin DIN connector at each end. It was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 8-pin DIN (CN5); early machines used a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: luma, chroma, composite, audio out, audio in, +5 V, ground

c64.cables.av-cable.wires.name: Cable conductors and insulation
c64.cables.av-cable.wires.description: Stranded tinned copper conductors with PVC insulation, colour-coded to the DIN pinout. Shielded or twisted pairs for the audio lines to keep the 1 MHz clock out of the speaker.

c64.cables.av-cable.din.name: DIN connector and cable
c64.cables.av-cable.din.description: A moulded DIN plug with a metal shell and a screw-on or clip-on backshell that clamps the cable and provides strain relief. The shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, and the interior is filled with a phenolic or thermoplastic insert holding the female contacts.
c64.cables.av-cable.din.note: The DIN plug is a European standard (DIN 41512) and is one of the few connectors where the C64's whole monitor ecosystem was deliberately European.

facts.label: Insert
facts.value: phenolic or thermoplastic, holding the contacts

c64.cables.rf-cable.name: RF cable (phono plug to TV plug)
c64.cables.rf-cable.description: A 75-ohm coaxial lead. Its job is to get a 1 MHz video signal, sitting on a VHF carrier, into a television's analogue aerial input without picking up half the room on the way. Impedance matching and a decent screen are what keep the picture from ghosting.

facts.label: TV end
facts.value: coaxial television plug (the old round type)

c64.cables.rf-cable.assembly.name: Cable assembly and test
c64.cables.rf-cable.assembly.description: Cables are made by cutting, stripping, crimping or soldering the conductor into the plug, moulding or snapping the plug body on, and testing. A continuity and insulation-resistance check, often on an automatic line tester, catches the faults before the lead reaches the box.
c64.cables.rf-cable.assembly.note: Cable assembly is one of the lowest-marginal-cost steps in consumer electronics, which is why Commodore and its contract manufacturers made leads in enormous volume in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

facts.label: Tests
facts.value: continuity, insulation resistance, and for coax a capacitance or impedance check

facts.label: Typical labour
facts.value: a minute or two per lead on a semi-automatic line

c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief.name: Strain-relief boot
c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief.description: A moulded rubber or PVC boot at each cable end where it enters the plug body, taking the bending load so the conductor does not fatigue at the termination. Cheap to add, and the difference between a lead that survives ten years and one that breaks at the root.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: moulded-in taper or a slid-on sleeve

c64.cables.rf-cable.plug.name: Moulded phono plug and TV plug
c64.cables.rf-cable.plug.description: Both ends are moulded: a phono (RCA) plug with a nickel-plated centre pin in a moulded barrel at the C64 end, and a television coaxial plug at the other. The pin is plated rather than bare so it survives being shoved in and out of the TV a thousand times.

facts.label: Barrel
facts.value: knurled, presses onto or screws onto the cable jacket

c64.cables.rf-cable.brass.name: Brass pin stock
c64.cables.rf-cable.brass.description: Free-cutting brass (typically leaded brass) machined or cold-formed into the pin and barrel. Brass is the standard connector material because it machines well, springs enough to take a wipe, and does not rust.

c64.cables.rf-cable.plating.name: Nickel plating of the pin
c64.cables.rf-cable.plating.description: Electrolytic nickel plating on a brass pin, giving a hard, corrosion-resistant, non-tarnishing surface. Nickel is the classic choice for connector contacts because its contact resistance stays low and it does not corrode in a socket.
c64.cables.rf-cable.plating.note: Nickel comes as ferronickel (from laterite ore or from matte), not as a pure metal. It is one of the few metals whose demand in the 1980s was genuinely driven by consumer plating rather than by steel.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sulfate or sulfamate nickel, with a brightening additive

c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.name: 75-ohm coaxial cable
c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.description: Centre conductor, dielectric, braid screen, PVC jacket. The braid is what does the shielding; the jacket is only there to survive being dragged under a TV cabinet for twenty years.
c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.note: A consumer RF lead of this type was often a thin-wall 75-ohm coax rather than a strict RG designation; the important properties are 75 ohm and a full-coverage screen.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: solid or stranded centre conductor, PE or PTFE dielectric, braided tinned-copper screen, PVC jacket

c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.name: Outer jacket (PVC)
c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.description: A lead-compounded PVC jacket, usually flexible grade with a plasticiser so the cable stays bendable. The jacket has nothing to do with the signal; its job is abrasion and handling.

c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.name: Plasticiser in flexible PVC
c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.description: Cable PVC is not rigid: it is compounded with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate (DOP) or trimellitates, dropped into an extruder at 5-10% and mixed before extrusion. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle.
c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.note: DOP is made from phthalic anhydride (via phthalate esterification with 2-ethylhexanol), and the 2-ethylhexanol comes from hydroformylation of propylene - so a cable jacket shares its whole feedstock chain with the pigment in the case.

c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.name: Dielectric (polyethylene or PTFE)
c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.description: The insulating foam between conductor and braid. Polyethylene is the volume material for consumer coax, often gas-injected or foam-injected to lower the dielectric constant and hold 75 ohm with a bigger centre conductor. PTFE (Teflon) is the low-loss, low-noise alternative used where a very clean signal or a tight bend radius matters.
c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.note: Foamed polyethylene is worth noting because it is the same polymer as the plastic bags in the packaging: chain-grafted or chemical-blowing-agent foam, blown in the extrusion line.

facts.label: Premium choice
facts.value: PTFE for low loss and low dielectric constant

facts.label: Extrusion
facts.value: pre-extruded dielectric tube, then conductor drawn in

c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.name: Low-density polyethylene (the volume dielectric)
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.description: The bulk of consumer coax dielectric is LDPE made by high-pressure or low-pressure polymerisation of ethylene. LDPE is branched and low-density, which is exactly what you want here: the branching lowers the dielectric constant so the coaxial geometry lands on 75 ohm with a reasonable centre-conductor size.

c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe-polymerisation.name: LDPE polymerisation of ethylene
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe-polymerisation.description: Ethylene is polymerised either at high pressure (1000-3000 bar, 200-300 C, initiated by peroxides) or at low pressure with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (20-40 bar, 70-110 C). Cable plants typically run high-pressure LDPE because it extrudes cleanly and fast; low-pressure LLDPE is the modern preference for some uses.
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe-polymerisation.note: High-pressure LDPE is still made the same way today; the difference between 1982 and now is mainly catalyst control and polymer-grade consistency, not the process.

c64.cables.rf-cable.purity-ethylene.name: Polymerisation-grade ethylene purity
c64.cables.rf-cable.purity-ethylene.description: Cable-grade polyethylene needs a very clean monomer: oxygen, water, sulphur and acetylene all poison or degrade the polymer. Ethylene from the cracker is therefore purified to 99.9%+ by distillation, molecular sieves and catalyst scrubbing before it reaches a reactor.
c64.cables.rf-cable.purity-ethylene.note: This is a good example of why the same chemical sold as 'ethylene' has a ladder of grades, and why the price of a cable-grade polymer is set by the polymer, not by the monomer.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9%+, with O2 and H2O at ppb

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: multi-column distillation, molecular sieve drying, guard beds

c64.cables.rf-cable.zn-catalyst.name: Ziegler-Natta catalyst (TiCl4 + alkylaluminium)
c64.cables.rf-cable.zn-catalyst.description: The low-pressure catalyst: titanium tetrachloride supported on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl co-catalyst. It polymerises ethylene in a stereoregular way and gives the higher-density grades.

c64.cables.rf-cable.aluminium-alkyl.name: Aluminium alkyl co-catalyst
c64.cables.rf-cable.aluminium-alkyl.description: Aluminium triethyl or aluminium diethyl, made by reacting aluminium with the corresponding alkyl chloride. It is what activates the titanium and controls the polymer's branching.
c64.cables.rf-cable.aluminium-alkyl.note: Ethyl chloride comes from hydrochlorination of ethylene, so this catalyst reaches back into the same ethylene/chlorine pool as the PVC.

c64.cables.rf-cable.titanium-tetrachlori.name: Titanium tetrachloride
c64.cables.rf-cable.titanium-tetrachlori.description: Made by chlorinating titanium metal or a titanium-bearing slag at 400-900 C in carbon or fluidised bed. The metal itself is made by the Kroll process: rutile or ilmenite is chlorinated to TiCl4, which is reduced with magnesium metal.

facts.label: Chlorination
facts.value: 400-900 C, with coke or in a fluidised bed

facts.label: Kroll reduction
facts.value: TiCl4 + 2 Mg -> Ti + 2 MgCl2, 800-900 C under argon

c64.cables.rf-cable.rutile-feedstock.name: Rutile / ilmenite feedstock for titanium metal
c64.cables.rf-cable.rutile-feedstock.description: The same titanium ores that make the white pigment in the case, here reduced to sponge titanium and then chlorinated for the polymerisation catalyst. One ore, two very different products.

c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.name: Braided screen (tinned copper)
c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.description: A flat bundle of tinned copper wires woven over the dielectric by a braiding machine, usually with a second pass to push coverage from ~70% toward 90%. Tinning reduces oxidation and makes the braid easier to terminate.
c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.note: Coverage is the number that matters: a 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture.

c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.name: Cable extrusion line
c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.description: A vertical or horizontal line where conductor is drawn through a die, dielectric tube is extruded or foamed around it, braid is laid on from a rotating carrier, and the jacket is extruded and cooled in a trough. Cable extrusion is one of the few polymer processes that is genuinely continuous and high-speed.

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: conductor -> dielectric -> braid -> jacket, often on separate lines

facts.label: Spark testing
facts.value: each length passes a high-voltage spark tester

c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.name: Centre conductor (copper, or copper-clad steel)
c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.description: The signal-carrying core. Consumer coax uses solid bare copper or, to save money, copper-clad steel. At RF frequencies a CCS core is perfectly adequate for a metre of cable.

c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.name: Copper wire rod and drawing
c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.description: Copper cathodes are melted, cast into wire rod, then drawn through a series of dies to the finished diameter. A cable plant buys rod and draws it in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.
c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.note: The copper supply chain (chalcopyrite ore -> flotation -> flash smelting -> converting -> tankhouse electrolysis) is documented once under c64.case.abs-resin.chalcopyrite; the same cathode feeds every copper conductor in the machine.

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: wet or dry, through carbide or diamond dies

c64.mains.name: C64 mains side: cord, plug, switch, fuse
c64.mains.description: Everything between the wall socket and the transformer primary: the three-conductor line cord and its moulded plug, the rocker switch, the line fuse, the X-rated suppression capacitor and the protective-earth bonding. The brick's case is entirely plastic, so the earth conductor never bonds to an enclosure - it terminates on the interwinding screen inside the transformer, and that is the whole of the earthing arrangement.
c64.mains.note: The reported 120 mA / 200 mA primary fuse ratings are consistent with a 15-30 W supply and the recommendation of a fuse at about 125% of the calculated input current, so they are plausible rather than confirmed from the factory documentation.

facts.label: Cord
facts.value: three conductors in the North American build (line, neutral, protective earth); two conductors in some markets

facts.label: Primary fuse
facts.value: reported as 120 mA or 200 mA depending on the mains voltage and build

facts.label: Thermal protection
facts.value: a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary winding, documented on the 251053-02

facts.label: Switch
facts.value: rocker or slider, in-line with the line conductor

c64.mains.approvals.name: Safety approvals and standards
c64.mains.approvals.description: The brick is certified as a component rather than as an appliance. In the United States that is UL 478, Power Supply Units, with the file number moulded into the case - 13J5 with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER' on the 3-83 build. In Canada it is CSA, in Singapore the NLS scheme, and in West Germany VDE. Each is a recognised component mark; the finished C64 was then certified separately under whichever national scheme applied to the appliance.
c64.mains.approvals.note: UL 478 was the correct US standard in 1982-84 and has since been withdrawn in favour of UL 62368-1, which replaced the shock-hazard model with a hazard-based energy model; the test voltages and limits quoted in this tree are the 1980s values and will not appear in the current standard.

facts.label: Europe
facts.value: VDE; the appliance-level standard was IEC 65 / BS 415 / EN 41003

c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.name: Routine production tests
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.description: Beyond the type tests, every unit gets a dielectric withstand test between the primary and the secondaries, an earth-continuity test, and a functional test with a load on both outputs. The dielectric withstand is the test that actually keeps people alive, because the failure it detects - a foil short, a pinched wire, a solder splash across the bobbin - is the fault that puts mains on a 5 V rail.

facts.label: Dielectric withstand
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for about 1 s, leakage current monitored

facts.label: Functional
facts.value: both outputs loaded and measured, case temperature observed

c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.name: Lot sampling and the critical-component control plan
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.description: Listing does not mean every unit is tested at every test. Instead the manufacturer submits a control plan: the dielectric withstand and earth continuity are 100% tests because they are the safety-critical ones, while the routine functional and leakage-current checks are sampled at an agreed quality level - typically one in three to one in thirty, with any failure escalating the lot to 100%. Critical components (the transformer, the switch, the fuse, the line capacitor, the cord set) come only from named manufacturers and are subject to incoming inspection.
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.note: This division of labour is why a cheap 1980s appliance could be certified at all: the safety-relevant parameters were checked on every unit and everything else was sampled.

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: from a named-vendor list only, with certificate-of-conformance required

c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.sam.name: Lot definition and rejection
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.sam.description: A lot is normally one shift's or one day's production from one set of tools. When a sampled test fails, the whole lot is quarantined, 100% tested, and the failing unit traced back to a component lot; if the failure rate exceeds the reject number the lot is rejected and the process capability reviewed. This is the mechanism that turns a bad batch of glass into a recall rather than a field failure.

facts.label: Lot size
facts.value: typically one shift, one line, one component lot

facts.label: Reject number
facts.value: from the original sample plan, not re-derived

c64.psu.assembly.hipot.name: Hi-pot dielectric withstand test
c64.psu.assembly.hipot.description: 1-1.5 kV AC is applied between the primary and the joined secondaries for about one second, with the leakage current monitored and the test set tripping on either a flashover or an excess leakage current. It finds a pinhole in the enamel, a missing layer of insulation paper, or a solder splash bridging the bobbin.

facts.label: Trip current
facts.value: typically 5 mA for a basic-insulation product

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 50/60 Hz, or 0.1-0.5 Hz on modern electronic test sets

c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.name: The safety file
c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.description: Listing is not just a test. The applicant submits a design file: schematic, printed-board artwork, bill of materials, critical-components list, the transformer's winding instruction and insulation system drawing, the enclosure material specifications, and the test report. The follow-up inspection checks that production still matches the file, and it is the reason a safe transformer cannot simply be substituted with a cheaper one after manufacture.
c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.note: Every listed appliance of the era had a manual, a technical file and a quality plan, and the follow-up inspection was where most of the safety effort actually happened - the type test is the easy part.

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: the transformer, the line capacitor, the switch, the fuse holder, the cord set and the enclosure flammability

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: periodic factory inspection of the listed factory

c64.psu.assembly.approval.name: UL 478 / IEC 65 listing
c64.psu.assembly.approval.description: The brick is certified as a component, not as a consumer appliance: UL 478 'Power Supply Units' in the United States, the equivalent IEC/EN 41003 and IEC 65 (BS 415 in the UK, VDE in West Germany) in Europe, plus CSA in Canada and Singapore's NLS scheme. Getting on the list required submitting the transformer winding instruction and the critical parts list, because those are the two things that cannot be verified by testing a finished unit.
c64.psu.assembly.approval.note: UL 478 was the correct standard in 1982-84; it has since been withdrawn and replaced by UL 62368-1, which moved from a shock-hazard model to a hazard-based energy model. That change is why the old test voltages and limits quoted here no longer appear in current standards.

facts.label: File number seen
facts.value: 13J5, moulded into the case, with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: Other marks seen
facts.value: CSA, NLS (Singapore), and on European units VDE

c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.name: Isolation, creepage and clearance
c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.description: The physical rules that make the layout safe: a primary-to-secondary creepage of about 6.4 mm and clearance of 3.2 mm for a 250 V basic insulation, the earthed foil between the windings, and the bobbin and terminal block designed so that a wire cannot fall across the isolation barrier. Every one of those dimensions is on the drawing and is checked at the follow-up inspection.
c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.note: Exact creepage and clearance figures depend on the pollution degree, the insulation type and the applicable standard edition; the values above are the order of magnitude for basic insulation at these voltages, not a substitute for the standard's tables.

facts.label: Pinhole test
facts.value: a 0.5-1.0 mm hole in the earth screen is allowed to be probed without breakdown

c64.mains.earthing.name: Protective earth bonding
c64.mains.earthing.description: The brick is entirely moulded ABS with no metal chassis, so there is nothing external to bond earth to. The earth conductor runs from the plug, into the epoxy-filled case, and terminates on the aluminium or copper screen buried between the transformer's primary and secondary windings. The earthing path therefore closes and opens entirely inside one potted block, and the C64 itself has an unconnected earth: the supply behaves like a Class II appliance even though it carries an earth conductor.
c64.mains.earthing.note: A two-conductor cord with no earth at all would have been perfectly acceptable for a doubly-insulated Class II appliance of this size, and some Commodore builds do use a two-wire cord. Carrying an earth into an all-plastic supply is belt-and-braces: it protects against the earth pin being energised by a primary-secondary fault inside the transformer, which is precisely what the interwinding screen does.

facts.label: Bond point
facts.value: the interwinding screen inside the transformer

facts.label: Continuity test
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded screen

c64.mains.earthing.screen-foil.name: Interwinding screen foil
c64.mains.earthing.screen-foil.description: A thin aluminium or copper foil wrapped between the primary and the secondary windings, with the earth conductor crimped to a tab on it. Its purpose is to intercept capacitive current that would otherwise couple the hazardous primary voltage onto the secondary; the foil is deliberately not bonded to either winding, so it must be insulated from both and must survive a probe voltage without puncturing.
c64.mains.earthing.screen-foil.note: In an all-plastic supply the screen is the only thing the earth conductor is bonded to, so this crimp is a single point of failure for the earth path and a named inspection point in the safety audit.

facts.label: Bonding
facts.value: a crimp ring to the earth conductor, not soldered to either winding

c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.name: Interwinding earth screen
c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.description: The protective-earth conductor is bonded to an aluminium or copper foil laid between the primary and the secondary windings - or sometimes to the transformer frame bolt. It does not leave the transformer: the earthing path is closed inside the potted block and never reaches the plastic case or the computer.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.note: Observed on the 902503-02: the protective-earth pin 'somehow connects to the transformer, looks like it goes in the layer between the primary and secondary winding', and does not extend to the output. The brick is all-plastic, so there is nothing to bond earth to on the outside.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: aluminium or copper foil, 0.02-0.05 mm, lapped to a tab

facts.label: Termination
facts.value: crimp ring or soldered to the earth conductor of the line cord

c64.mains.line-capacitor.name: X-rated line filter capacitor
c64.mains.line-capacitor.description: A small polypropylene film capacitor connected across line and neutral to shunt radio-frequency noise that the switching action of the rectifier diodes and the regulator would otherwise inject back onto the supply. It is rated X - that is, for use between line and neutral - which in 1980s practice meant a recognised 250 V AC across-the-line capacitor with a defined failure mode.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.note: I could not confirm from a teardown photograph that a specific Commodore brick contains an X2 capacitor, although they are a standard fit in any listed appliance of this era and enthusiasts repairing original bricks commonly replace an RIFA suppression capacitor. The node is here because the brief asks for it and because the physics of the circuit requires it, but its presence in this specific assembly is inferred rather than documented.

facts.label: Safety approval
facts.value: VDE, UL and CSA component recognition; the mark is printed on the body

c64.mains.line-capacitor.rifa.name: RIFA suppression capacitors
c64.mains.line-capacitor.rifa.description: RIFA, a Swedish manufacturer of interference-suppression components, became in the 1980s the dominant supplier of X-rated capacitors across Europe, and its part numbers are still legible in equipment of that vintage. Decades later their products became notorious: the electrolyte in the metallised film absorbed moisture, the capacitor began to draw a leakage current, heat up, and in the worst cases short and catch fire in equipment that had been sitting unused for years. The whole class of parts is now treated as a safety hazard and is routinely replaced on sight.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.rifa.note: The failure was a design weakness rather than a manufacturing defect: the parts used a metallised film and a construction that did not resist humidity ingress, and decades-old parts can now be unsafe even without having been used hard. This is one of the few places where a component from 1984 is a present-day fire risk.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: metallised polypropylene, X2 rated, typically 0.01-0.68 uF

facts.label: Supply chain
facts.value: dominant European supplier of X capacitors in the 1980s

c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.name: Electrolytic electrolyte
c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.description: An aqueous solution of an ammonium or amine salt - ammonium pentaborate was the classic low-voltage recipe - that forms the counter-electrode ion layer against the oxide. In an aluminium electrolytic the cathode reaction deposits a hydrated aluminium oxide or tin layer from the metal ion, and the leakage current is exactly that reaction rate.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.note: Modern practice for long-life parts is a higher-boiling organic solvent (propylene glycol, GBL esters) with a benzotriazole inhibitor instead of ammonium salts - ammonium systems dry out faster and leak more once the solvent is gone.

facts.label: Typical system
facts.value: ammonium pentaborate / ammonium chloride, or an amine salt

facts.label: Leakage current
facts.value: I = kC V, roughly 2x the CV product rated current at 25 C

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Metallised polypropylene film capacitor
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: A 6-12 um polypropylene film is metallised with vapour-deposited aluminium to form the electrodes, then wound with a polypropylene or paper separator. Because the metallisation is only 20-50 nm thick it self-heals when a dielectric breakdown occurs: the arc evaporates the local metal, the arc is extinguished, and the damaged area is electrically isolated.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: Self-healing metallised film is why these capacitors are chosen for snubber and suppression duty: a transient across the line does not destroy the part.

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: clears a dielectric fault by evaporating the electrode around it

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Polypropylene film
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Made by polymerising propylene from a steam cracker in a slurry or gas-phase process; the resulting isotactic polypropylene is extruded into a thin film, biaxially oriented for tear strength, and wound onto a core. It is the normal dielectric for a suppression capacitor because it does not soften or shrink with temperature the way polyester does.

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Propylene from natural gas liquids
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Propane is separated from natural gas liquids or from a crude fraction, mixed with butane, and steam cracked at 800-900 C in coils of 304H stainless steel with a residence time under a second. The cracked gas is quenched, compressed, hydrogenated to remove acetylenes, and the propylene is separated by distillation. This is the same propylene that goes into the C64's plastics.

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Naphtha fraction
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: A refinery streams a barrel of crude into fractions by boiling point; naphtha is everything from roughly 30 to 200 C - light naphtha, heavy naphtha and kerosine - and it is the feed for the steam cracker. In 1982 a large integrated cracker was built next to the refinery so the hot naphtha could be piped straight across.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: The cracker does not need a specific molecule: anything in the naphtha range at sufficient severity will crack. That is why the plastics industry sits downstream of the refinery in a way the electronics industry does not.

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Crude distillation tower
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: A fractionating tower 30-50 m tall, internally a stack of trays, separates a barrel of crude continuously by boiling point: residue at the bottom, then gas oil, diesel, kerosine, naphtha, and finally overhead gases. It runs at essentially atmospheric pressure with steam stripping at the top.

facts.label: Trays
facts.value: 20-40 bell or valve trays in a 1980s unit

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 GJ of fuel per barrel of crude distilled

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Crude oil
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: The raw petroleum lifted from a wellhead and separated from its associated gas and water. A barrel is 42 US gallons of a hydrocarbon mixture whose composition depends entirely on where it came from - the same crude ranges from light paraffinic to heavy asphaltic. This is the leaf of the petroleum branch and, for the C64, the origin of nearly every polymer and every solvent in the machine.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: The case's ABS, the capacitor's polypropylene and polyester films, the epoxy's phenolic and amine hardeners, the cord's PVC and the switch's thermoset all trace back to barrels of this.

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Film winding and vacuum metallisation
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: The film web is wound on a rotating vacuum-chamber drum while a wire feed head traverses it, laying down an aluminium layer 20-50 nm thick by resistive evaporation. At the same time a nucleation solution is dosed in to promote columnar crystal growth, so the metal grains follow the drum direction and the resulting capacitor has a low-loss, self-healing electrode. The web is slit to width and the capacitor is wound from slits onto a core.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: The un-metallised capacitor film is made on a separate line by a similar drum winder with a die and a chill roll; the metallising line normally sits downstream of the film line in the same plant.

facts.label: Evaporation rate
facts.value: ~1-3 nm per second, drum 300-800 mm diameter

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Cast film production
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Polypropylene is extruded through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll, then stretched and heat-set so it is strong in both directions, then slit into webs 20-60 um wide. A plain film is wound on the same type of machine as the metallised film, so the two steps are usually separate plants.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: machine-direction orientation is typical for capacitor film

c64.mains.fuses.name: Primary fuse and thermal fuse
c64.mains.fuses.description: Two serial protections on the mains side. The primary fuse is a small cartridge type rated at roughly 120 mA (115 V) or 200 mA (230 V), sized at about 125% of the running input current so the transformer draws its inrush without nuisance failure. The second, documented in the 251053-02, is a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary: a fusible alloy element that opens irreversibly if the transformer overheats.
c64.mains.fuses.note: The 3 A fuse in the 9 V AC conductor exists so a short on the output cable cannot damage the transformer before the brick is ever plugged into a C64; the 5 A slow fuse in the rectifier conductor is sized for the charging surge of the 4700 uF reservoir capacitor.

facts.label: Primary fuse rating
facts.value: reported 120 mA / 200 mA, depending on build and mains voltage

facts.label: Secondary fuses
facts.value: 3 A in the 9 V AC conductor, 5 A slow-blow in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

facts.label: Thermal fuse
facts.value: in series with one end of the primary winding on the 251053-02

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.name: Thermal fuse
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.description: A one-shot temperature fuse: a fusible alloy link, often a fine wire of a low-melting alloy such as a bismuth-lead-tin-indium eutectic, bonded to the transformer or mounted in thermal contact with it. At its trip temperature - typically 100-130 C - the link melts and opens the circuit permanently. It cannot be reset, which is intentional: the fault that overheated the transformer is not allowed to be repeated.
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.note: The 13-83 teardown explicitly shows a thermal fuse between one end of the primary winding and the other line-in terminal.

facts.label: Fusible alloy
facts.value: a low-melting eutectic, melting at a controlled temperature

facts.label: Fuse alloy
facts.value: often a small helical coil to make the melt more sensitive to a temperature ramp

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.name: Low-melting fusible alloy
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.description: An eutectic or near-eutectic mixture chosen so that it melts sharply at one temperature. A common mains fuse alloy is 50% tin, 50% lead melting at 180 C; a common thermal-fuse alloy is a bismuth-lead-tin-indium low-melting eutectic below 100 C. The alloy is cast or extruded into a strip or wire in air, then plated to keep it from oxidising.

facts.label: Example
facts.value: 50Sn/50Pb melts at 183 C; Bi-Pb-Sn-In systems melt at 70-120 C

facts.label: Sensitivity
facts.value: a thin section melts at a lower power because its surface-to-volume ratio is high

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.name: Bismuth and its ore
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.description: Bismuth is recovered commercially as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from anode slimes and from the residues of the Wohlwill process, and as a minor component of some tin and tungsten ores. Native bismuth and bismuthinite occur too, but refinery by-product is the industrial source.

c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.name: Ceramic wirewound fuse
c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.description: A slow-acting fuse for the high inrush of the reservoir capacitor: a length of resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin, shunted by a strip of fusible alloy that runs beside it. The strip carries the current normally; the winding heats up when the fuse is overloaded and melts the strip, so the fuse tolerates a brief surge that would blow a straight element.
c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.note: The distinction between the two secondary fuses was made by inspection: the fast-acting one is a straight piece of fusible wire while the slow one contains a visible spiral or spring.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: resistance wire in parallel with a fusible alloy strip

facts.label: Characteristic
facts.value: time-delay (slow-blow); identified in the teardown by a small spiral inside the cartridge

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 A 250 V in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.name: Glass cartridge fuse
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.description: A fuse element of pure tin or a tin alloy, historically a lead-antimony or tin-lead alloy, held between two metal end caps inside a glass tube. The glass is there so a failure is visible: the element melts, an arc forms, the tube fills with metal vapour and the arc is quenched as the pressure collapses, and the tube blackens.

facts.label: Voltage rating
facts.value: 250 V for the sizes used here

facts.label: Breaking capacity
facts.value: ~35-100 A for a small cartridge fuse

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Soda-lime tube glass
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The fuse tube is a drawn borosilicate or soda-lime glass tube, chosen because it is dimensionally stable, easy to seal and does not outgas. Glass tubing is made by melting the batch and drawing the softened gather between rollers, so the wall thickness and diameter stay within a few microns along the length.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 70-74% SiO2, ~13% Na2O, ~10% CaO, with alumina and magnesia

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Glass batch and silica sand
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The batch is a few hundred kilograms of silica sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C. The silica sand, dug from high-silica deposits, is the leaf of the glass chain.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: ~70% silica sand, ~15% soda ash, ~10% limestone, ~5% cullet

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Regenerative furnace and cowper
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: A glass furnace cannot simply burn gas, because glassmelting needs far more heat than combustion can deliver at that temperature. The answer is regeneration: a Cowper regenerator beside the furnace stores the heat of the exhaust in a refractory mass, then blows the air through it on the next firing. The two 1980s designs were the regenerative box furnace and the unit-regenerator furnace.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: natural gas or oil, preheated to 600-1000 C by the regenerator

facts.label: Waste-heat recovery
facts.value: ~20-40% of the fuel energy returned to the air blast

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Refractory lining and checker plates
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The furnace and regenerator are lined with refractory brick, and the regenerator's internal mass is a stack of checker plates of silica or chrome-magnesite. Refractory brick is made by pressing or hand-moulding a graded mineral aggregate with a clay binder and firing it in a tunnel or car kiln; the grading, not the chemistry, is what gives a lining its thermal-shock resistance.
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.note: Beryllium oxide had even higher conductivity but was withdrawn from general use in the 1980s because of its toxicity.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1400-1500 C for silica brick; 1600-1750 C for magnesia

facts.label: Silica brick
facts.value: ~94-98% SiO2, use limited to about 1500 C

c64.mains.switch.name: Rocker switch
c64.mains.switch.description: A mains switch in the line conductor, mounted in the case wall so the rocker is the only part exposed. It is a snap-action mechanism: a spring-loaded plunger forces a moving contact against a fixed one with a definite wiping motion as it passes through centre, which both makes the circuit and scrapes oxide off the contact faces.
c64.mains.switch.note: The C64's own rear-panel power switch interrupts both supplies; the brick's switch interrupts only the line conductor of its own input, and the computer's switch on the 5 V and 9 V rails does the rest.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 V AC for a small rocker

facts.label: Contact alloy
facts.value: silver or a silver-nickel brazed contact on a brass carrier

c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.name: Glass-reinforced switch body
c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.description: Glass fibre is added to the switch body at 20-30% by weight and the compound is compression moulded. The glass reduces creepage and raises the distortion temperature, which is what keeps the moulding from softening near a hot transformer.
c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.note: Glass reinforcement also makes the material abrasive, so a switch mechanism with glass-filled tracks must be designed so the moving contacts never ride on a glass-filled surface.

c64.mains.switch.actuator.name: Rocker actuator and case
c64.mains.switch.actuator.description: The external rocker is moulded in a glass-filled thermoset or a self-extinguishing thermoplastic and clips over a phenolic or nylon body carrying the fixed contacts. The case must be rated for the insulation class and have the flammability rating appropriate to an appliance, and the actuator must not be able to be jammed in the on position.

facts.label: Creepage
facts.value: ~4 mm between line and neutral terminals, set by the moulding

c64.mains.switch.contacts.name: Silver-alloy contacts and arc erosion
c64.mains.switch.contacts.description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any metal and, unlike copper, its oxide is still conductive, so a silver contact keeps working even when it blackens. Contacts are riveted or welded to brass carriers so the spring force is set by the carrier rather than by the contact material. Every make operation evaporates a microscopic amount of metal as an arc; the contact is sized so that tens of thousands of makes erode it only slightly, and so that a failed contact fails open rather than welded shut.
c64.mains.switch.contacts.note: Modern low-voltage switches often use silver-tin-oxide rather than pure silver because it does not weld; for a 250 V AC mains switch the plain silver contact remained standard well into the 1990s.

facts.label: Contact material
facts.value: Ag, Ag-SnO2 or Ag-Ni, on a brass or phosphor-bronze carrier

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: ~1-3 N, giving a low and stable contact resistance

facts.label: Erosion rate
facts.value: ~0.01-0.1 mm per 10,000 operations in the worst case

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.name: Copper and silver ores
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.description: The moving and fixed blades are brass or phosphor bronze (copper with tin), and the contact faces are silver. Copper comes from sulphide concentrate and silver from argentiferous lead ores or from cyanide leaching of low-grade residues.

facts.label: Phosphor bronze
facts.value: ~90% Cu with 4-10% Sn, the standard spring carrier alloy

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..name: Silver refining from lead residues
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..description: Argentiferous lead concentrates are roasted and smelted, and the silver reports to the lead bullion, from which it is recovered by Parkes' process: the bullion is cooled so copper crystallises out and is skimmed, then zinc is added, which scavenges the silver and gold into a zinc crust that is skimmed off and distilled. The crude silver is cupelled and electrolytically refined to 99.9% or better.
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..note: Silver for electrical contacts has always been by-product metal, so its price is set by the lead and zinc smelters rather than by silver mines; most of the 1982 supply came from Mexico, Peru and the Soviet bloc.

facts.label: Parkes process
facts.value: zinc added at 1-2% of the bullion mass, crust skimmed at 600-700 C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: Moebius or Balbach-Thum electrolysis, silver nitrate electrolyte

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..name: Cupellation
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..description: An ancient refining step that survives into the 1980s for precious metals: the metal is melted with a lead oxide flux and blown with air, which oxidises the lead and the base metals to litharge that floats off, while the silver and gold stay as metal. Agricola described it in the 16th century and it is still the standard way to remove base metal from silver dross.

facts.label: Litharge
facts.value: PbO, the oxidised lead, absorbed into the bone ash cupel

c64.mains.plug.name: Moulded mains plug
c64.mains.plug.description: A two- or three-pole moulded plug permanently attached to the cord: in the North American build a polarised NEMA 1-15P with one blade rotated 180 degrees so it can only be inserted one way round; in most of Europe a CEE 7/16 Europlug with two round 4.0 mm pins. The body is a thermosetting or thermoplastic moulding with the cord entering through a separate bushing so the strain is not carried by the conductors.

c64.mains.plug.nickel-plated-brass.name: Nickel-plated brass contacts
c64.mains.plug.nickel-plated-brass.description: The blades are stamped from cartridge brass sheet and plated. Nickel under-plate plus a flash of nickel is the 1980s default for mains contacts because brass alone tarnishes and corrodes; silver plating was used where the contact had to carry more current or where the plug was screwed down, and silver-plated contacts remain the modern choice for high-current switchgear.
c64.mains.plug.nickel-plated-brass.note: The C64's expansion and user ports use similar nickel-plated brass contacts, and the DIN power connector on the brick uses plated brass pins.

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: brass with a 2-5 um nickel or nickel strike under a 0.1-0.5 um nickel plate

c64.mains.line-cord.name: Three-conductor line cord
c64.mains.line-cord.description: A flexible cord with one heavier line conductor, one neutral and a green or green-and-yellow earth conductor, exiting the case through a clamp or grommet. The sheath is PVC in the 1980s rather than the older rubber; PVC is tougher, thinner and better suited to being moulded into the case.
c64.mains.line-cord.note: The teardown photographs show the three conductors separated inside the case and browning of the PVC right at the transformer pin, which is the classic signature of a loose or arcing mains connection.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: stranded annealed copper in a PVC or rubber sheath

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 2.5 A / 250 V for a light-duty appliance cord

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: black or white sheath; green or green/yellow earth in the North American build

c64.mains.line-cord.strain-relief.name: Strain relief clamp and grommet
c64.mains.line-cord.strain-relief.description: A nylon or rubber bushing, or a two-screw clamp on a moulded boss, that stops the conductors being pulled out of their terminals. In a safety audit this is a named inspection point: the conductors must not be able to move more than a couple of millimetres, and no strand may be able to reach a terminal screw under tension.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: a defined pull force applied to the cord, applied to all conductors together

c64.mains.line-cord.stranded-copper.name: Stranded copper conductors
c64.mains.line-cord.stranded-copper.description: Stranded rather than solid, because a cord is flexed at the strain relief and a solid conductor cracks there within a few years. Each strand is 0.15-0.20 mm bare copper wire; a 1.0 mm2 cord has roughly 30 strands.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.name: Wire drawing
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.description: A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.name: PVC sheath compound
c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.description: The sheath is not raw PVC resin but a plasticised compound: PVC resin mixed with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate or, from the mid-1970s onwards, with a polyester plasticiser as the industry moved away from phthalates. The resin itself is made by addition polymerisation of vinyl chloride.

facts.label: Plasticiser load
facts.value: 30-50 parts per hundred resin for a flexible cord sheath

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB, and a flame-retardant grade for the mains lead

c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.description: Made by the oxychlorination of ethylene with oxygen and chlorine over a fluidised bed of copper(II) chloride at 180-220 C, or by the chlorination of acetylene. Vinyl chloride monomer is acutely toxic and carcinogenic, and its manufacture was one of the worst occupational hazards in the chemical industry until the 1970s-80s control campaigns.
c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.note: The oxychlorination route invented in the late 1960s is what makes PVC cheap; the acetylene route was used where carbide acetylene was cheap.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: C2H4 + Cl2 + 1/2 O2 -> C2H3Cl + HCl, CuCl2 catalyst, 200 C

c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.name: Chlorine for oxychlorination
c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.description: Chlorine is made by electrolysing a brine of sodium chloride in a membrane, mercury or diaphragm cell. The membrane cell, introduced commercially in the 1970s, has no mercury and gives much purer caustic soda as a co-product; in 1982 the older diaphragm and mercury cells were still very widely used.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~1.35 t Cl2 per tonne of caustic soda

c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.name: Brine, from halite
c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chl.description: Saturated sodium chloride solution, made by dissolving mined rock salt in filtered water and purging the carbonate with hydrochloric acid.
