c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Stove and furnace linings are fired silica brick or aluminous firebrick, made from carefully graded silica sand or bauxite blended with a clay binder and fired in a tunnel kiln. Getting the grain size distribution right matters more than the chemistry: a graded pack gives a lining that survives thermal shock without spalling.

facts.label: Refractoriness
facts.value: SiO2 94-98% for silica brick; Al2O3 40-50% for firebrick

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Iron ore concentrate, ~62-66% Fe
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Run-of-mine hematite and magnetite is crushed and either shipped as lump ore to a blast furnace or upgraded to sinter/pellet. Commodore's steel chain in 1982 was almost entirely sinter-based: the ore was blended with coke and limestone, sintered on a Dwight-Stewart travelling grate into 5-6 cm porous sinter, and charged hot.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Metallurgical coke
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Metallurgical coke is made in 1980s batteries or coke ovens by carbonising coking coal at 1000-1100 C in the absence of air; later plants added petroleum coke to the blend. It is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Limestone flux
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Calcite crushed to 3-6 mm and used both as sinter flux and as the blast-furnace flux that combines with silica to form a fluid slag. It is mined quarried and used essentially as dug.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Limestone quarrying and calcination
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: High-grade calcite is extracted by drilling and blasting, then crushed in two stages to 3-6 mm for the sinter mix and to 25-75 mm for the furnace burden. Only a small fraction is calcined; the bulk goes to the sinter mix as a flux, and the remainder goes down the furnace to become the fluid lime slag. Calcination itself, CaCO3 to CaO plus CO2, happens in the sinter mix and in the coke ovens.

facts.label: CaCO3 content
facts.value: >=52 wt% CaO equivalent for metallurgical limestone

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: ~0.4-0.6 t limestone per tonne of hot metal

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Magnetic anneal in hydrogen
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Coils of 0.35 mm strip are annealed for 20-40 hours at 1100-1200 C in a stream of high-purity hydrogen at dew points below -60 C. Hydrogen both removes oxygen that would pin grain boundaries and, on cooling through the Curie point at about 770 C in the field-free furnace, lets the austenite transform into oversized aligned grains.
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.note: Strictly the two variants are 'grain-oriented' (field-free hydrogen anneal, the dominant 1980s process) and 'orientation by magnetic field' (applied field during the Curie-point cooling). The field-free hydrogen anneal is what Hi-B and most 1980s GOES plants ran.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: dry hydrogen, dew point below -60 C

facts.label: Field during cooling
facts.value: field-free (magnetic field anneal requires a field; the high-volume process is the field-free variant)

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: High-purity hydrogen
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: Made in the 1980s by steam methane reforming of natural gas followed by pressure-swing adsorption and a cryogenic final purification to 99.999%. It was the standard controlled-atmosphere gas for grain-oriented electrical steel because it neither oxidises nor carburises the surface.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.name: Cold rolling to 0.35 mm
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.description: A reversing four-high cold mill takes hot strip down through several annealing and rolling passes to 0.35 mm, with the rolling direction being the future flux direction. Reduction ratios above 20:1 in the final pass are what set the grain elongation.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.name: High-speed stamping press
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.description: A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.name: Hardened tool-steel stamping die
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.description: Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.

c64.mainboard.name: Mainboard ASSY 250407
c64.mainboard.description: A single two-layer FR-4 board carrying the whole computer. Eight 4164 DRAMs make the 64 KB of main RAM; a 1 KB static RAM holds screen colour; the 6510 processor, the VIC-II, the SID, two CIAs, the PPI, a mask-programmed PLA and three mask ROMs do the rest, wired together with a dozen 74-series parts, three CMOS parts and a handful of small-signal transistors. Everything is through-hole DIP. About 320 components and 20 integrated circuits.
c64.mainboard.note: Board ASSY 250407 is the long 'breadbin' layout, schematic 251138. Earlier revisions differ mainly in having no plated-through holes at all — where later boards have a via, the early ones carry a short single-core jumper wire soldered across the same pads. The U-numbers quoted throughout this tree are the canonical 250407 set and do not line up with the 250425, 250466 or short boards. A validated copy of the 250407 layout has zero vias and exactly two wire jumpers, E1 and E2.

mb.photo.name: Phototooling: how C64 copper artwork became an etched board
mb.photo.description: The chain that turns a board database into a resist image. The 250407 artwork is number 251137. It was drawn on a design workstation, reduced to aperture-table plot files, plotted onto photographic film at a jobbing house, developed, checked on a test coupon, and used as the mask that prints the board's dry-film resist before etching.
mb.photo.note: Modern practice is direct imaging from the CAM data with no film at all. The film phototooling described here is how the board in the machine was actually made.

facts.label: Layers plotted
facts.value: 2 copper, plus solder mask and legend

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: vacuum-frame contact exposure of the artwork film onto dry film

mb.photo.panel.name: Panelising the order
mb.photo.panel.description: The board is one part out of a panel of identical boards nested in a sheet large enough for the process equipment. The panel gets tooling holes for registration and for the drill, and the boards are separated later. This is where the layout cost of an order is amortised, and why a two-layer panel in 1983 could hold a surprising number of boards.

mb.photo.panel.mousebites.name: Tooling and mouse-bite tabs
mb.photo.panel.mousebites.description: The nested boards are held by small perforated tabs, broken out by hand or by a router after the panel is finished. The tabs leave a characteristic rough edge on the board outline, which is visible on a 1983 board if you look at it.

mb.photo.mask.name: Printing the artwork onto the resist
mb.photo.mask.description: The artwork film is laid against the exposed dry-film resist on the board and exposed in the vacuum frame. Where the film is clear, the resist hardens and resists the etch; where it is opaque, the resist stays soft and the copper beneath is etched away. This is the moment the phototooling chain finally touches the board, and every solder joint on the finished machine is located by this exposure.

mb.photo.mask.registration.name: Two-sided registration
mb.photo.mask.registration.description: The hard part of a two-sided board. The second side's artwork has to land on the copper to within a fraction of a millimetre, using alignment pins and a register mark. On this board it matters mainly for the mounting holes and the connector slots; on a via-heavy board it is what decides whether every barrel lands on its own pad.
mb.photo.mask.registration.note: Having no vias makes two-sided registration a far less critical operation than on a modern via-heavy board, one of the quieter payoffs of the layer-change-by-component-lead strategy.

mb.photo.rephoto.name: Rephotography, the master, and the coupon
mb.photo.rephoto.description: The plotted working film is rephotographed onto a higher-quality film to get a sharper, dimensionally stable master. Before a whole panel is committed, a test coupon is exposed and etched with every line width the panel uses, and the widths are measured. This is how a shop proves its process still holds tolerance.
mb.photo.rephoto.note: The coupon is the quiet heart of 1980s board making: a cheap, fast way to prove that the narrowest trace the designer asked for is still coming out, before a hundred boards are committed to it.

facts.label: Coupon
facts.value: a small test board carrying every line width and pad size on the panel

facts.label: Check
facts.value: measure the narrowest trace on the panel under a measuring microscope

mb.photo.rephoto.master.name: The artwork master
mb.photo.rephoto.master.description: The film treated as the authoritative copy of the design, stored flat and handled by the edges. It is the board's master record, and losing it means paying for the panel again.

mb.photo.develop.name: Developing and fixing the film
mb.photo.develop.description: The exposed film is developed, fixed, washed and dried before it can serve as a mask. The chemistry is ordinary silver-halide photographic processing, run as a short line of tanks.

mb.photo.develop.fixer.name: Fixer (ammonium thiosulfate)
mb.photo.develop.fixer.description: The unexposed silver halide is dissolved away and the image made light-stable, so the film can be handled, stored and re-exposed without latent-image changes.
mb.photo.develop.fixer.note: Thiosulfate chemistry is a sulfur chain, ultimately from sulfur or from sulphur dioxide off sulfide roasting, so it is a different mineral chain from the aromatic one.

mb.photo.develop.developer.name: Photographic developer (hydroquinone)
mb.photo.develop.developer.description: The film emulsion is silver halide; hydroquinone reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, giving the opaque image that will block the resist. The reducing agent is itself an aromatic chemical made from benzene, so the mask chemistry is a petroleum chain like everything else in this branch.

mb.photo.develop.developer.aromatic.name: Benzene-derived intermediates
mb.photo.develop.developer.aromatic.description: Hydroquinone is made by dihydroxylating benzene. Benzene comes from the heavy naphtha fraction of crude oil, so the developer that draws the copper pattern is two refinery steps from crude.

mb.photo.develop.developer.naphtha.name: Heavy naphtha
mb.photo.develop.developer.naphtha.description: A mid-boiling petroleum fraction, solvent-extracted for benzene.

mb.photo.develop.developer.crude.name: Crude oil
mb.photo.develop.developer.crude.description: The unrefined petroleum the naphtha is cut from.

mb.photo.develop.developer.reservoir.name: Petroleum reservoir
mb.photo.develop.developer.reservoir.description: The sedimentary rock that holds it.

mb.photo.plotter.name: Photoplotting the artwork film
mb.photo.plotter.description: The plot files drive a photoplotter that draws the copper artwork onto a transparent film. In 1983 these machines lived at the fabricator, not the design office, and were the company's most valuable single asset.

mb.photo.plotter.laser.name: Laser plotter (arriving)
mb.photo.plotter.laser.description: An argon-ion or, later, a diode laser writes the film or the photoresist directly. Sharper than corona discharge and faster, but in 1983 it was still being adopted and the electrostatic plotter was not yet history.
mb.photo.plotter.laser.note: The last piece of 1980s phototooling equipment before direct imaging replaced film entirely in the 1990s.

mb.photo.plotter.pen.name: Pen plotter (older, slower)
mb.photo.plotter.pen.description: A carriage carrying a light-sensitive pen draws the artwork directly on film or mylar. Simple and reliable, but slow, with real line-width variation, so it was being displaced by the electrostatic plotter through the early 1980s and by the laser plotter later.
mb.photo.plotter.pen.note: Still used for check plots and for prototype single-layer boards well into the 1980s.

mb.photo.plotter.film.name: Artwork film stock
mb.photo.plotter.film.description: A high-contrast, dimensionally stable photographic film that the plotter exposes and the shop develops into a finished mask. It must hold its geometry over a store door and be opaque where there is copper. The polymer base is the same class of polyester as the dry-film photoresist carrier.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.name: Polyester film base (PET)
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.description: The dimensionally stable base the emulsion is coated on, made from polyethylene terephthalate. It is the reason a 1983 plotter film does not stretch and shift during handling, and it is the same polymer family as the photoresist carrier used on the board itself.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg.name: Ethylene glycol
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg.description: One of the two feedstocks of PET, made by oxidising ethylene derived from ethylene. Ethylene comes from steam cracking of naphtha.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg.ethylene.name: Ethylene
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg.ethylene.description: The two-carbon olefin from a steam cracker, parent of polyethylene and, with glycol, of polyester film.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.naphtha.name: Naphtha
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.naphtha.description: The liquid petroleum fraction that is steam-cracked to make ethylene.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.crude.name: Crude oil
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.crude.description: The hydrocarbon mixture from a reservoir, fractionated and cracked into the aromatics and olefins that make the film, the resist, the ink and the machine tools of this entire tree.

mb.photo.plotter.film.base.reservoir.name: Petroleum reservoir
mb.photo.plotter.film.base.reservoir.description: Porous rock holding crude under pressure, produced through steel casing into a gathering system. This is the bottom of the whole tree: everything on this branch that is not mineral is a refined version of this.

mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.name: Electrostatic plotter
mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.description: The dominant plotting technology of the era. A fine wire or shaped electrode is stepped across the film under computer control and a corona discharge exposes the emulsion wherever copper is wanted. Flatbed machines laid a film flat and exposed quickly, which is why they became the standard for two-sided work.
mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.note: This is the technology lineage behind the Gerber format: Gerber Scientific commercialised these plotters and the aperture-table format that drove them, which is the format the industry still uses. Modern shops use laser plotters or direct imaging, but the format and its film are a direct inheritance.

mb.photo.cam.name: Data reduction and CAM
mb.photo.cam.description: The database is converted into per-layer plot files. This is where a net becomes copper, a component pin becomes a pad, and the drill hits are separated out. Errors here are replicated across a whole panel, which is why the step is done once, carefully, for hundreds of boards.

mb.photo.cam.checks.name: Design rule checks
mb.photo.cam.checks.description: Automated checks for minimum track width, minimum spacing, pad-to-pad clearance and annular ring. On a board with no vias the annular-ring check has almost nothing to check, but spacing between fine pads on the IC footprints still matters.
mb.photo.cam.checks.note: A later twist on the C64 itself: owners of later board revisions found the layouts so tight that home repair needed bodge wires across the copper. That is a board designed to the limit.

mb.photo.cam.drill.name: Drill file separation
mb.photo.cam.drill.description: The drill programme is split out from the copper data. On this board that is easy and low-risk because there are no vias, so the drill file is only component holes, mounting holes and the connector slots. A via-heavy board of the same era is where plot data and drill data were most often confused, and the result was a hole in the wrong place.
mb.photo.cam.drill.note: The no-via strategy simplifies CAM, not just drilling. It is one of the quieter efficiencies of the design.

mb.photo.cam.apertures.name: Aperture table
mb.photo.cam.apertures.description: Every distinct pad shape and track width is assigned an aperture in a table the plotter reads, so a 1.0 mm round pad and a 0.3 mm track are drawn as repeated simple shapes rather than as free curves. This aperture-table idea is the direct ancestor of the Gerber format, still the universal interchange format for board artwork today.
mb.photo.cam.apertures.note: Gerber format was invented at this time to carry exactly this table, which is why it is still about apertures and flashes rather than geometry.

mb.photo.cam.netlist.name: Netlist to routed copper
mb.photo.cam.netlist.description: Connectivity becomes tracks per layer. On this two-layer board the routing problem is comparatively simple because there is no plane layer, but the ground return still has to be poured around the routing, and it is that pour which carries most of the finished board's signal integrity.
mb.photo.cam.netlist.note: Autorouters handled most of the bulk in 1983 and a human cleaned up the critical nets. Hand pour plus hand cleanup is why the copper on a 1983 board looks the way it does.

mb.photo.design.name: The board database on the design system
mb.photo.design.description: In 1983 the layout lived on the CAD vendor's own workstation, not in a modern repository. Traces, pads, components and drill data were edited on the machine and periodically written out as plot files on tape or floppy. Copying it to the jobbing house was a physical act of transporting magnetic media.

mb.photo.design.backannotation.name: Backannotation from a drawn overlay
mb.photo.design.backannotation.description: The designer taped mylar over the plotted printout, drew routing changes with a special pen, and passed the overlay through a digitizer that read the new lines and apertures back into the database. Slow, physical, and fiddly, and the reason routing history on boards of this era reads the way it does.
mb.photo.design.backannotation.note: Some of the most awkward-looking copper on a 1983 board is the residue of this workflow: a routing decision made on a sheet of plastic and converted by an encoder.

mb.photo.design.workstation.name: CAD workstation
mb.photo.design.workstation.description: A dedicated 16-bit microcomputer or small minicomputer with its own storage, a high-resolution monochrome display, and often a pen plotter and a digitizer on the desk. The digitizer mattered as much as the plotter: designers drew and revised artwork on mylar overlays and digitised the changes back into the database.
mb.photo.design.workstation.note: Interactive PCB CAD in the 1980s was a commercial market dominated by a handful of vendors. The C64 layout predates every open format and tool used today.

mb.photo.design.workstation.storage.name: Plot-file storage media
mb.photo.design.workstation.storage.description: Plot files and library data were written to nine-track tape, then to 8-inch floppy disks. The magnetic oxide on a thin polymer backing is the physical carrier the jobbing house receives, and a lost tape meant the whole panel waited.
mb.photo.design.workstation.storage.note: This is the handover point between design and fabrication.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.name: Monochrome CRT display
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.description: A high-resolution green or white phosphor CRT on which the layout was examined trace by trace. The glass envelope, the phosphor coating and the shadow mask are all thin-film processes on a drawn glass bulb.
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.note: This is a designer's tooling CRT, not the machine's own video output, which is a separate branch of this tree.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.name: CRT envelope glass
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.description: The bulb is soda-lime glass formed on a glass lathe from the same kind of batch as the reinforcing cloth: silica sand plus limestone plus alkali. A design workstation's screen is a small consumer item, but it is the terminal through which every copper trace of the board was examined.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.name: Silica sand in the display glass
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.description: The main glass former in the CRT envelope, from the same washed and purified sand used for glass fibre. The glass chain of this tree has two exits to the same rock: reinforcing cloth and display glass.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.name: Quartz sand deposit
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.description: Unconsolidated or friable sandstone worked for its sand. A dug mineral, and one of the few things in the whole phototooling chain that is not a petroleum product.

mb.test.name: Factory test of the C64 mainboard and machine
mb.test.description: How a populated C64 board was proved working before it left the factory. Electrical test on the bare board, then a functional test that boots the machine from a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port and checks it against a monitor and a test cradle, then burn-in, then final test and packing. The practice was mostly manual, and Commodore's own engineers admitted it was thinner than it should have been.
mb.test.note: There are documented examples of new C64 machines shipping with cut traces, and a software developer's account of opening brand-new machines and finding them. That is the honest backdrop to this branch: it describes what was actually done, not what a modern line would do.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: bare-board electrical test, functional test, burn-in, final test

facts.label: Test ROM
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM run from the cartridge port

facts.label: Display check
facts.value: the machine's own video output viewed on a test monitor

mb.test.final.name: Final test and packing
mb.test.final.description: A last pass over the complete machine in its case: keyboard, control ports, serial port and a final power-on. Surviving machines are packed with the cord and the manual for shipment.

mb.test.final.pack.name: Packing for shipment
mb.test.final.pack.description: The machine, cord and manual go into a carton, typically corrugated board with a printed outer. The packaging branch has its own industrial chemistry; this node marks only where the tested board leaves the factory.

mb.test.final.ports.name: Control and serial port check
mb.test.final.ports.description: The two control ports and the serial port are exercised with known-good peripherals or loopback plugs. These are the connectors most often left untested on a line that was under pressure, and it is where the documented field failures of this era cluster.

mb.test.burnin.name: Burn-in
mb.test.burnin.description: Finished machines are powered up under load, often at elevated temperature, for an extended period. This was originally to weed out infant-mortality failures in the custom chips, which is exactly where the C64's problems were, and it is why there had to be a diagnostic ROM that could run unattended.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: catch early-life failures, especially in the custom chips

facts.label: Method
facts.value: machines run in racks, often warm, sometimes cycling

mb.test.burnin.attended.name: Unattended running
mb.test.burnin.attended.description: The diagnostic ROM is left to run so a machine that fails on its own gives a visible failure, freeing the line from one operator per machine. This is why the dead-test ROM's pattern output mattered as much as its pass or fail verdict.

mb.test.burnin.oven.name: Burn-in oven or rack
mb.test.burnin.oven.description: A room or cabinet holding powered machines on racks, warmed to speed up failure. Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is, which is why burn-in exists at all.

mb.test.burnin.oven.rack.name: Burn-in rack
mb.test.burnin.oven.rack.description: A steel frame carrying a shelf of machines, with ventilation so the heat is actually reaching them. Racks were moved in and out of the oven on a schedule, which is a large amount of manual handling for what looks like a passive wait.

mb.test.burnin.oven.element.name: Heating element (nichrome)
mb.test.burnin.oven.element.description: The resistance wire in the oven heater, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists oxidation at red heat.

mb.test.burnin.oven.chrome.name: Chromium
mb.test.burnin.oven.chrome.description: The second constituent of nichrome, from chromite ore. It is also the wear-resist plating on cutting tools and a constituent of the stainless steel used all over this factory.

mb.test.burnin.oven.chromite.name: Chromite ore
mb.test.burnin.oven.chromite.description: Iron chromium oxide, smelted to ferrochrome. Diggable rock.

mb.test.burnin.oven.nickel.name: Nickel
mb.test.burnin.oven.nickel.description: The main constituent of the heating alloy, and also the underplate under the gold on the board's edge contacts. Nickel comes from sulphide ore, and later heavily from laterite.

mb.test.burnin.oven.ore.name: Nickel ore (sulphide or laterite)
mb.test.burnin.oven.ore.description: Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite. Smelted, refined and electrolytically won to metal. Diggable rock.

mb.test.burnin.oven.mine.name: Laterite or sulphide ore body
mb.test.burnin.oven.mine.description: A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined by open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter.

mb.test.video.name: CRT display test
mb.test.video.description: The machine's own composite video output is fed to a test monitor and the inspector reads the picture. Nothing instruments this: the pass criterion is that the picture is correct, which means the human being in the loop is doing the measuring.
mb.test.video.note: The engineering team said outright that testing colour quality automatically was effectively impossible, and that line workers were told to adjust a colour control until they saw colour. Several thousand machines shipped with garish colours as a result, and the instruction itself was the cause.

facts.label: What is checked
facts.value: a correct picture and sound: colours, borders, sprites, cursor

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: the human eye, plus a monitor

mb.test.video.monitor.name: Test monitor
mb.test.video.monitor.description: A small composite monochrome monitor, or a colour television, used as the reference picture. Each is a cathode-ray tube: drawn glass envelope, phosphor coating, deflection yoke and a high-voltage supply.

mb.test.video.monitor.mask.name: Shadow mask
mb.test.video.monitor.mask.description: A perforated steel sheet just behind the phosphor screen that makes each phosphor dot land on its own gun. It is made from Invar, a nickel-iron alloy whose thermal expansion is almost zero, so the mask does not move as the tube warms up.

mb.test.video.monitor.mask.invar.name: Invar (nickel-iron)
mb.test.video.monitor.mask.invar.description: About 36 % nickel in iron, notable for expanding almost not at all between 0 and 200 deg C. Nickel comes from sulphide ore or laterite, iron from iron ore.
mb.test.video.monitor.mask.invar.note: Invar is the classic example of an alloy whose whole point is a property, not a strength.

mb.test.functional.name: Functional test with a test ROM
mb.test.functional.description: The populated board is mounted in a test cradle with a power supply and a monitor, and the machine proves itself by running a diagnostic program from the cartridge port. This exercises the real boot path: CPU, ROM, RAM, character ROM, VIC, SID and the I/O chips, all in the configuration they will ship in.
mb.test.functional.note: Using the cartridge port as the test-vector delivery mechanism is an elegant piece of period engineering: no extra fixture hardware, and it tests the bus the machine actually uses.

facts.label: Test medium
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port

facts.label: What it proves
facts.value: the machine can reach its own boot ROM and produce a correct picture and sound

mb.test.functional.keyboard.name: Keyboard and ribbon test
mb.test.functional.keyboard.description: Because the keyboard connects to the mainboard through a soldered ribbon on this design, the functional test has to cover that joint: every key is checked, which is a simultaneous test of the connector, the ribbon, the keyboard matrix and the CPU's scanning routine.

mb.test.functional.cradle.name: Test cradle
mb.test.functional.cradle.description: A jig that holds the board, presents a regulated 5 V and 12 V, routes the video and audio outputs to a monitor and speaker, and presents the cartridge and edge connectors. Several cradles were usually in line so inspectors could work in parallel.

mb.test.functional.cradle.psu.name: Test power supply
mb.test.functional.cradle.psu.description: A regulated supply with a current limit so a shorted board does not destroy it. The C64's 5 V and 12 V came from its external supply, so the factory had to prove both the board and that supply; testing the PSU itself belongs to the power branch of this tree.

mb.test.functional.cradle.frame.name: Cradle body and fixture plate
mb.test.functional.cradle.frame.description: A machined plate with locating pins that hold the board in exactly one position, mounted on a steel frame with the electronics below. Every fixture on the line has this same problem: the board has to land in the same place every time, and the pins are what guarantee it.

mb.test.functional.cradle.steel.name: Fixture steel
mb.test.functional.cradle.steel.description: Mild steel plate, machined and hardened at the locating pins so they do not wear out of tolerance. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

mb.test.functional.cradle.ore.name: Iron ore and coke
mb.test.functional.cradle.ore.description: Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal, the two materials that make every steel jig on the line.

mb.test.functional.cradle.coalseam.name: Coal seam
mb.test.functional.cradle.coalseam.description: Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. A dug rock.

mb.test.functional.rom.name: Diagnostic and dead-test ROM
mb.test.functional.rom.description: A small EPROM in a cartridge shell which, on power-up, prints a screenful of named tests and runs each one, reporting RAM, ROM and video faults by pattern rather than by instrument. The operator's job is to look at the picture and read the verdict.
mb.test.functional.rom.note: These test ROMs were so successful that Commodore later sold the same idea to the public as the Dead Test cartridge, which is why they are so well documented today.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: no instruments needed; the machine tests itself and says so

mb.test.ict.name: In-circuit electrical test
mb.test.ict.description: A bare populated board is checked electrically before it is ever plugged into a machine. The point is to catch a missing component, a shorted pad or a broken trace while it is still trivially fixable.

mb.test.ict.tester.name: The tester itself
mb.test.ict.tester.description: A rack of switching electronics driving the fixture, with a go or no-go readout and a reject bin. It is ordinary 1980s digital test equipment: a small computer, a relay matrix and a display, all built from the same logic families the C64 itself uses.

mb.test.ict.presence.name: Component-presence and seating check
mb.test.ict.presence.description: Checking that the right part is in the right place is a distinct and important test on a board with thirty sockets and a hundred passive parts. A missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the single most common fault on any 1980s logic board.
mb.test.ict.presence.note: Verifiers that push each socket to confirm its pins are actually in the hole were in use in this era, alongside visual and continuity checks.

mb.test.ict.measure.name: Continuity, resistance and short detection
mb.test.ict.measure.description: The tester looks for opens in the artwork and for shorts between nets that should be isolated, and on some fixtures measures absolute values. On a simple two-layer board with no vias, continuity checking is very nearly the whole job.
mb.test.ict.measure.note: A modern flying-probe or X-ray system would do this without a custom fixture; in 1983 the bed of nails was the economical choice at volume.

mb.test.ict.nails.name: Bed-of-nails fixture
mb.test.ict.nails.description: The board is pressed down onto a fixture whose probes touch every node of interest, so the tester can measure each net without a probe being placed by hand. On a board with no vias and only DIP footprints, the fixture is comparatively simple to design and to wire.

mb.test.ict.nails.spring.name: Spring probe pins
mb.test.ict.nails.spring.description: Small hardened probes on a sprung wire that survive repeated thousands of insertions. The fixture pinout has to be cut specifically for the board artwork, which is why fixtures were an expensive per-part-number investment.

mb.test.ict.nails.spring.wire.name: Probe wire
mb.test.ict.nails.spring.wire.description: Fine gold-plated or beryllium-copper wire drawn to a small diameter and formed into a sprung pin. Beryllium copper is used because it takes a permanent set and keeps its spring force after millions of cycles.

mb.test.ict.nails.spring.copper.name: Copper (and beryllium) in the probe
mb.test.ict.nails.spring.copper.description: The probe wire is copper alloy, drawing on the same copper supply as the board foil itself and the wave-solder pot. Copper is traced from cathode to concentrate by the metals subsystem.

mb.assembly.name: Populating, cleaning and finishing the C64 mainboard
mb.assembly.description: What happens between the bare board and the tested machine. Components are inserted, a few hand-fitted wires and jumpers are added, the board is soldered, cleaned, shielded and screwed into the case. On this board the whole operation is through-hole and hand-and-machine insertion: there is no surface-mount reflow anywhere in the C64 mainboard assembly.
mb.assembly.note: Commodore specifically laid this board out for automated insertion, which cost them their Japanese assembly line and forced production into Hong Kong. The design decision to use DIP sockets rather than soldering the chips directly is a serviceability choice: it made field replacement possible, and it roughly doubled the number of joints on the board.

mb.assembly.volume.name: Volume and yield reality of the line
mb.assembly.volume.description: Commodore sold on the order of two million C64s a year at the 1983-84 peak, on a production cost that started near 130 dollars and fell as volume rose. Every board here was one of millions per year through the same line. Boards were made in Hong Kong, and in the first year of production at Kentron in Japan, which is where the 1982-83 units came from.
mb.assembly.volume.note: The 1982-83 units were built at Kentron in Ina, Japan under Commodore Japan Limited, and the boards were made in Hong Kong. Whether Commodore ever had its own in-house PCB etching line is not established; the engineering account says the boards were made in Hong Kong, which implies an outside fabricator rather than a Commodore plant.

facts.label: Peak annual output
facts.value: roughly 2-2.5 million units a year around 1984

facts.label: Board yield
facts.value: high; a two-layer no-via board has few failure modes

mb.assembly.repair.name: Board-level rework and repair
mb.assembly.repair.description: Bad joints are reworked on the line: the joint is reflowed with an iron, the part is replaced, and a full set of consumable tips is kept to do it. Commodore's own engineering position was famously to ship rather than to hold back, which shows up here as rework being a normal, high-volume operation rather than an exception.
mb.assembly.repair.note: The engineering team's stated culture was that if a product worked it shipped, and that quality control was not coming close enough to where it should have been. That is visible in this subsystem as rework rather than scrap.

mb.assembly.shield.name: EMI shield bonding
mb.assembly.shield.description: The metal shield around the video and audio circuitry is bonded to the board's ground so that the enclosure is actually part of the ground return. Without a real bond the shield picks up the very signals it is there to contain.

mb.assembly.shield.tab.name: The VIC-II heat-sink tab
mb.assembly.shield.tab.description: A metal tab welded inside the shield lid pressed against the top of the video chip package, so the shield doubled as a heat sink for the chip that dissipated about 1.5 W. This was a deliberate design fix for a real heat problem, not a later addition.
mb.assembly.shield.tab.note: The design history explicitly describes this tab being welded to the shield lid so the enclosure became a heat sink. It is a nice example of the enclosure, the ground return and the thermal path being one part.

mb.assembly.shield.lug.name: Shield lug and solder bond
mb.assembly.shield.lug.description: A small tab on the shield is soldered to a ground pad or held by a screw into a plated hole, giving the enclosure a low-impedance path to the board's ground pour.
mb.assembly.shield.lug.note: A through-hole into which a shield screw goes, or a soldered tab; the C64 used a combination, and the shield-to-board bond is one of the joints most often disturbed by owners.

mb.assembly.conformal.name: Conformal coating
mb.assembly.conformal.description: A thin insulating coating over the assembled board to keep moisture and contaminants off the copper. The C64 mainboard was not conformally coated.
mb.assembly.conformal.note: Conformal coating existed in 1983 for military and automotive work and was increasingly common in commercial electronics, but not for a home computer in a dry indoor case. If the tree you are building has conformal coating on the C64 mainboard, it is over-modelled.

mb.assembly.cleaning.name: Cleaning after soldering
mb.assembly.cleaning.description: Rosin flux leaves a sticky, slightly conductive film. The board is washed, historically in a solvent or detergent wash, sometimes with a little ultrasonic, then dried. The film matters: rosin is hygroscopic and mildly acidic, and in humid climates it slowly corrodes the board.
mb.assembly.cleaning.note: Cleaning was the step Commodore was known to skip or rush, which is a large part of why so many forty-year-old C64 boards show corrosion and leakage damage. Modern production uses deionised water and a resinous no-clean flux instead.

facts.label: Consequence if skipped
facts.value: surface leakage and, over years, corrosion

mb.assembly.reflow.name: Reflow and surface-mount: not on this board
mb.assembly.reflow.description: It is worth being explicit that the C64 mainboard has no surface-mount parts and no reflow step. Everything is through-hole, everything is either waved or hand-soldered. Reflow ovens were already known in 1983 but were used for flat-pack IC packages and for the small daughterboards, not for the main logic board.
mb.assembly.reflow.note: A tree that claims reflow of the C64 mainboard is wrong. Modern boards are dominated by reflow; this one is not.

mb.assembly.reflow.note.name: The RF modulator as a separate daughterboard
mb.assembly.reflow.note.description: The C64's analogue RF modulator is a small separate board, not part of the main logic board, and in early machines it sits on the mainboard. Its construction and any SMT content belong to that module, not to this through-hole assembly.
mb.assembly.reflow.note.note: Its SMT content, if any, has not been verified here.

mb.assembly.connector.name: Connector and ribbon soldering
mb.assembly.connector.description: The edge-connector slots, the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips and the keyboard ribbon interface are all fitted and soldered by hand, because a conveyorised wave cannot hold them. This is a long bench task and a common source of rejects.
mb.assembly.connector.note: The keyboard connection on this board uses a flat ribbon; it is a delicate soldered joint and a classic failure point on surviving machines.

mb.assembly.jumpers.name: Wire jumpers and configuration links
mb.assembly.jumpers.description: Because the board has no vias, the few places where a connection must cross between the two copper layers with no component to do it are bridged with a short tinned copper wire, hand-fitted into two holes and hand-soldered. These are the E1 and E2 links on the 250407 layout.
mb.assembly.jumpers.note: These are visible on the bottom of the finished board and are now a small collector's item in their own right. A modern board would put a via or a 0-ohm resistor there instead.

facts.label: Fitted
facts.value: by hand, after the wave soldering

mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.name: Tinned single-core jumper wire
mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.description: A short length of fine tinned copper wire, cut and formed to the two holes, fitted and soldered by hand. It is the mechanical ancestor of the jumper link on every later board.
mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.note: Modern equivalents are 0-ohm resistors, jumper pins, or just a via. None of those were on this board.

mb.assembly.resistors.name: Resistors and the resistor networks
mb.assembly.resistors.description: The board is full of small carbon-film resistors, some laid down as axial parts and some consolidated into resistor networks to save board area. The C64 is a good example of the 1980s trend toward integrating discrete resistors into single packages.

mb.assembly.resistors.film.name: Carbon-film resistor element
mb.assembly.resistors.film.description: A thin ceramic substrate coated with a semiconducting carbon film, trimmed to value. The resistor is the most numerous single part on the whole board.
mb.assembly.resistors.film.note: Manufactured from petroleum-derived organics on a ceramic substrate; the materials detail is owned by the passives subsystem.

mb.assembly.resistors.networks.name: Resistor networks and hybrid packs
mb.assembly.resistors.networks.description: Several resistors in one small package with a common connection, replacing a handful of separate parts and their board area. The C64's data-line resistors are a good example of the era's move toward integration.
mb.assembly.resistors.networks.note: The exact part numbers and manufacturers of the C64's resistor networks vary by revision and have not been verified here; the practice itself is well attested for this period.

mb.assembly.sockets.name: DIP sockets as the C64's serviceability choice
mb.assembly.sockets.description: This is the single most underappreciated decision on the board. The C64 sockets its integrated circuits rather than soldering them directly. It means any chip can be swapped in the field, and it means the number of joints roughly doubles, because each socket has two contacts per pin on each side.
mb.assembly.sockets.note: The cost of a socketed chip is not just the socket money: it is four joints per pin where the original designer wanted one, and it is the reason C64 boards need so much rosin flux and so much cleaning. Commodore chose sockets because a home computer with unfield-serviceable ROMs or SID chips would generate warranty returns.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: roughly doubles the joint count and adds a failure mode of its own

mb.assembly.leadforming.name: Axial and radial lead forming
mb.assembly.leadforming.description: Axial parts are cut to length and formed to a right angle or left-right offsets so they drop into a fixed hole pitch. Radial parts are spread to the lead spacing of the board. The forms are set in the machine and are a real cost: a wrong form is a board that will not insert.
mb.assembly.leadforming.note: Modern practice forms nothing and mounts surface-mount parts; lead-formed axial parts are essentially gone from new consumer hardware.

facts.label: Formed at
facts.value: the component maker or the insertion machine, not by hand on the line

facts.label: Radial pitch
facts.value: matched to the board hole pitch, often 0.1 in or 0.2 in

mb.assembly.insertion.name: Component insertion
mb.assembly.insertion.description: Every part goes into the board from the top. Because there are no vias and no bottom-side components, the whole machine is one-sided: one operator can see every joint from the solder side and there is no second-side insertion operation at all.

mb.assembly.insertion.manual.name: Manual insertion and bench work
mb.assembly.insertion.manual.description: Everything the machine could not do: the fuse clips, the connectors, the small-signal parts in awkward places, the wire jumpers. Operators sat at the line with a board in a fixture and worked down a traveler's list of parts.
mb.assembly.insertion.manual.note: Mixed human-and-machine insertion on one board is a recipe for a component inserted twice or missed entirely, so the line had a checking station: a verifier that confirms every part is present and seated before the board goes into the wave.

mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.name: Insertion fixture and board handling
mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.description: The board is held in a jig with locating pins while components go in, and the same family of jig carries the board through the wave and into test. Every fixture on the line solves the same problem: the board has to land in exactly one position, every time.

mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.steel.name: Fixture steel plate
mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.steel.description: Machined mild steel with hardened locating pins. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.name: Insertion engine and its cycle time
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.description: A machine with a magazine per part type picks a part, leads it to the right hole and pushes it in, typically in 0.3-0.6 s per component. On a board of about 90 parts that is roughly half a minute of machine time, which is why insertion engines paid for themselves on volume this high.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: the machine cannot compensate for a bent lead, so lead forming matters

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.name: Part magazines and vibratory feed
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.description: Radial magazines shake components down a track to a pick head. Cut, formed axial leads are the hardest part to feed; resistors and capacitors with wide leads feed easily.
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.note: Failure of vibratory feeding, not of the machine itself, was the usual reason a line stopped on a board full of axial parts.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.frame.name: Machine frame and bedplate
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.frame.description: A cast-iron or welded steel bed with a linear axis and a vertical insertion head. The bedplate's flatness is the limit on how accurately a lead can be placed in a hole.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.iron.name: Cast iron machine base
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.iron.description: Grey cast iron, machined flat. The same material and the same blast-furnace iron ore as the laminate press platen; machine tool bases have been cast iron for a century for the same reason.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.ironore.name: Blast-furnace iron ore
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.ironore.description: Hematite or magnetite reduced with coke in a blast furnace. The industrial floor under this whole subsystem is iron ore and metallurgical coke.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coke.name: Metallurgical coke
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coke.description: Baked coal, the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace and the source of its carbon monoxide.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coalseam.name: Coal seam
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coalseam.description: Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. Diggable rock.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.orebody.name: Iron ore body
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.orebody.description: A concentration of iron oxides, mined open pit or underground, crushed, concentrated and sintered before the furnace.

mb.assembly.insertion.layout.name: Insertion pitch set for the machine
mb.assembly.insertion.layout.description: Component spacing on this board was dictated by the insertion machine rather than by the circuit designer, which is exactly the argument Commodore had with its Japanese plant and lost. The same board could not be hand-inserted efficiently and machine-inserted efficiently at once.
mb.assembly.insertion.layout.note: The IEEE Spectrum account of the C64's design case history states the board was laid out for automated insertion and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools.

mb.solder.name: Lead-tin solder and every joint it makes on the board
mb.solder.description: The metallurgical spine of the whole machine. Every joint on the C64 mainboard is made with 63/37 tin-lead alloy activated by rosin flux: about 600 in one pass through a wave-soldering machine, the rest by hand afterwards on the connectors, fuse clips and wire jumpers.
mb.solder.note: The eutectic was the right choice, and the reason is worth stating: at 63/37 the alloy melts and solidifies at one temperature instead of a mushy range, so a joint leaves the wave already set. 60/40, common for hand work, freezes over a range and gives duller, greyer joints.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 183 deg C, a sharp single transition

mb.solder.selective.name: Connectors, fuse clips and heavy joints
mb.solder.selective.description: The parts that cannot simply be taken through the wave in the usual way: the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers and the large electrolytics. These were soldered by hand, sometimes with a second iron used as a heat sink, and sometimes with a small solder pot.

mb.solder.selective.heat.name: Two-iron technique for heavy joints
mb.solder.selective.heat.description: One iron on the joint and one on the lead keeps the lead at temperature while the solder melts, so the solder actually wets the lead instead of freezing a cold slug around it. Slower per joint, but the only way to get a sound joint onto a big thermal-mass part.

mb.solder.selective.bridge.name: Bridging between connector pins
mb.solder.selective.bridge.description: A D-sub or DIN connector has pins close enough that molten solder wicks along a pin and jumps the gap to the next pad, and inside a shell the bridge cannot be seen happening. The countermeasures in 1983 were flux plus a steady iron, then a probe and rework iron to break the bridge.
mb.solder.selective.bridge.note: Modern lead-free practice would drag a solder bead along the pins to wick off the excess and, failing that, use a solder pot.

mb.solder.selective.tack.name: Soldering with the connector already fitted
mb.solder.selective.tack.description: The board-mount connectors on the C64 mainboard are right-angle types with solder tails projecting out of the back of the shell. They were soldered from the underside with the shell already in place, which means a short working time and a hot iron in a cramped space.
mb.solder.selective.tack.note: The prevalence of resoldered connector joints on surviving C64 boards, decades later, is decent evidence that these joints were marginal from the start.

mb.solder.hand.name: Hand soldering on the line
mb.solder.hand.description: Soldering iron, solder wire and pliers on a bench under a smoke extraction arm. Used for the connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers, the big electrolytics and every joint the inspector rejected. A small minority of joints, but where the line rejects come from too.
mb.solder.hand.note: A small hand-held solder pot or a solder fountain was used for the fuse clips and heavy connector leads where a wave cannot reach.

facts.label: Tip material
facts.value: copper, often plated so it does not dissolve away

mb.solder.hand.extraction.name: Fume extraction
mb.solder.hand.extraction.description: An arm or hood over the bench draws off the flux smoke. The smoke is resin vapour, not tin vapour, but it is unpleasant and it is the reason every solder bench in 1983 had a hood over it.

mb.solder.hand.tip.name: Copper tip material
mb.solder.hand.tip.description: Oxygen-free copper for heat transfer, sometimes plated. Copper dissolves into molten tin if left sitting in the pot, so tips were changed once they had thinned noticeably.

mb.solder.hand.iron.name: Soldering iron and tip
mb.solder.hand.iron.description: A nichrome or cartridge heater in a barrel with a replaceable copper tip. The tip has to be kept tinned; a dry tip oxidises and then stops transferring heat at all, which is the real reason beginners conclude solder will not melt on a joint.

mb.solder.reliability.name: What the joint is actually made of
mb.solder.reliability.description: Solder does not merely sit on a pad, it reacts with it. Within seconds of contact, tin and copper fuse at the surface into a hard intermetallic, which grows over time and eventually turns brittle and cracks. That is the origin of solder fatigue, and it explains why a leaded joint is forgiving and a lead-free one is not.

mb.solder.reliability.defects.name: Named defects and what causes them
mb.solder.reliability.defects.description: Dull grainy joints mean a dirty pad or too little preheat. Dry joints and unfilled holes mean a hole too tight for the lead or a wave too slow. Solder balls and spatter mean moisture in the board. Bridging between fine pads means too much flux, a pot too hot, or a wave too shallow. Blowholes in the joint mean damp.
mb.solder.reliability.defects.note: This is the diagnostic vocabulary a line supervisor used in 1983, and it has barely changed since.

mb.solder.reliability.intermetallic.name: Copper-tin intermetallic growth
mb.solder.reliability.intermetallic.description: Cu6Sn5 forms at the pad surface and is the actual metallurgical bond holding the joint. It is hard and brittle, and its growth is limited by diffusion through itself, which is why higher-temperature solders containing silver or gold exist: to slow the reaction at the pad.

mb.solder.profile.name: The wave-soldering profile
mb.solder.profile.description: The machine is set by five numbers together: pot temperature, conveyor speed, preheat temperature, preheat time, and flux concentration. Get them wrong in a specific way and you get a specific, diagnosable defect.

mb.solder.profile.thermalmass.name: Heavy leads set the slowest joint
mb.solder.profile.thermalmass.description: Large thermal-mass leads, such as the big axial electrolytic or the tabbed regulator, heat far more slowly than the solder around them. The line compensates by running the conveyor slowly enough that the solder stays molten until the lead is hot, which in turn slows every board on the machine.
mb.solder.profile.thermalmass.note: This is why the big electrolytics are among the joints most often hand-touched after the wave, and why the instruction to check them existed at all.

mb.solder.profile.thermal.name: Why preheat sets joint quality
mb.solder.profile.thermal.description: A joint cools from 250 deg C to 183 deg C in about a second. If the board and the lead start cold, the joint solidifies from the outside inward and you get the dull, grainy, poorly wetted fillet a line inspector rejects. Starting at 120 deg C lets the alloy flow properly before it freezes, which is the entire point of the preheat tunnel.

mb.solder.wave.name: Wave-soldering machine
mb.solder.wave.description: A conveyorised machine that drags the underside of the board through a standing wave of molten solder. Components are all inserted from the top so they point the same way, and the wave only ever touches leads and pads. It is why a 1983 line could put hundreds of sound joints on a board for the price of the solder.

facts.label: Preheat
facts.value: approx. 110-150 deg C in a tunnel before the wave

facts.label: Wave contact
facts.value: a few seconds, the length of the wave's contact length

mb.solder.wave.spares.name: Spares pot and solder return
mb.solder.wave.spares.description: A small pot under the wave catches solder running off the ends, which is then returned to the main pot. Recycling saves tin and, more importantly, stops the pot chemistry from drifting toward copper contamination.

mb.solder.wave.cooling.name: Cooling zone
mb.solder.wave.cooling.description: After the wave, boards sit in moving hot air before leaving the machine. Hot air rather than cold, because chilling a freshly soldered joint around a large thermal-mass lead is how you get a cracked solder fillet.

mb.solder.wave.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen blanket over the pot
mb.solder.wave.nitrogen.description: Many machines piped nitrogen over the solder surface to keep the oxide skin thin and stop dross forming. It also stops the skin from insulating the pot from the wave, which makes the wave itself erratic.
mb.solder.wave.nitrogen.note: Cheaper machines ran open to air and simply lived with the dross.

mb.solder.wave.conveyor.name: Conveyor chain and fixtures
mb.solder.wave.conveyor.description: A stainless or phenolic chain carries boards through the machine, held by their edge in fixtures spaced along the chain. Chain pitch and fixture design, not the pump, set the real throughput. The fixtures were often the board's own edge, which is one reason board edge quality was a production concern.

mb.solder.wave.foam.name: Flux foamer
mb.solder.wave.foam.description: Just before the wave, a bank of porous stone immersed in rosin flux bubbles air through it and lays a thin, even, pre-activated film on the board's underside. Foaming gives uniform coverage a spray or brush never does, and it is where the smell of boiling pine on a board line comes from.

mb.solder.wave.foam.stone.name: Sintered porous stone
mb.solder.wave.foam.stone.description: A sintered polyethylene or polyurethane stone whose pore size is chosen to bubble air finely through the flux. It clogs with crystallised flux and has to be soaked out on a schedule.

mb.solder.wave.preheat.name: Preheat tunnel
mb.solder.wave.preheat.description: An oven before the wave that brings the whole board to roughly 120 deg C so the thermal shock of hitting 250 deg C solder is spread out. It also drives off moisture, which would otherwise spit solder out of the holes as the board hits the wave.

mb.solder.wave.preheat.air.name: Recirculating hot-air preheat
mb.solder.wave.preheat.air.description: Preheating is by moving air or radiant tubes, with the zone held below the solder melting point so nothing melts early. Too little preheat gives thermally shocked joints; too much dries the resin and lifts pads off the laminate.
mb.solder.wave.preheat.air.note: A board full of large electrolytics takes a long time to come through, and preheater capacity is usually what sets the conveyor speed for the whole line.

mb.solder.wave.dragfree.name: Drag-free twin-wave design
mb.solder.wave.dragfree.description: A single long wave exerts a strong forward drag on the board, which tears fine-pitch parts sideways and is the mechanical reason wave soldering lost to through-hole reflow. A twin-wave machine uses a main wave plus a smaller, faster secondary wave, or a double-peak former, that cuts the drag while still filling holes. Any serious 1983 machine had some version of this.
mb.solder.wave.dragfree.note: The same problem, later made worse by lead-free's higher melting point, is what pushed through-hole assembly off wave soldering onto selective solder.

mb.solder.wave.pot.name: Solder pot and wave former
mb.solder.wave.pot.description: A stainless or cast-iron pot holding tens to hundreds of kg of molten solder at roughly 250 deg C. Inside, a pump or a tilted paddle throws solder up against a forming dam, which spills over as a smooth standing wave. The pot is lined or plated because molten tin attacks iron.

facts.label: Pot metal
facts.value: cast iron with solder-resistant plating, or solid stainless

facts.label: Wave height
facts.value: a few millimetres above the pot lip, set by pump rate

mb.solder.wave.pot.lining.name: Pot lining and dross skimmer
mb.solder.wave.pot.lining.description: Dross collects as a floating raft that is dragged off the surface by a skimmer bar. Skipping this is the classic way to put oxide particles into every joint on the line, and it is why the skimmer is on the machine and not optional.

mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.name: Stainless steel pot wall
mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.description: The pot is stainless or plated cast iron, chosen because molten tin dissolves iron at 250 deg C. A bare iron pot would be eaten away in weeks, taking the wave geometry with it. This is the material decision that makes a wave machine a five-year purchase instead of a consumable.

mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.name: Nickel in the stainless steel
mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.description: Nickel is the component that makes stainless steel stainless: it forms a self-repairing chromium-oxide surface film that survives molten tin and most acids. The same nickel is the underplate beneath the gold on the board's edge contacts and the element in the burn-in oven's heating alloy.

mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.ore.name: Nickel ore
mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.ore.description: Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite, smelted and refined to metal.

mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.body.name: Laterite or sulphide ore body
mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.body.description: A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter. The last rock in a chain that began as the lining of a solder pot.

mb.solder.wave.frame.name: Welded machine frame and shell
mb.solder.wave.frame.description: The pot, tunnel and conveyor sit in a welded steel frame that also carries the fume hood and the flux plumbing. It is a heavy, deliberately boring object: the machine is bought for its repeatability, not its elegance.

mb.solder.wave.frame.steel.name: Structural steel sections
mb.solder.wave.frame.steel.description: Mild steel angle and section from the arc or induction furnace. The mass of the frame is what keeps the wave flat while the pot runs.

mb.solder.wave.frame.iron.name: Steel from iron ore and coke
mb.solder.wave.frame.iron.description: Pig iron made in a blast furnace, refined in a basic oxygen furnace. The same ore, coke and limestone as the laminate press platen and the insertion machine bedplate.

mb.solder.wave.frame.iron.ore.name: Iron ore and metallurgical coke
mb.solder.wave.frame.iron.ore.description: Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal. The two materials that make every steel machine on this floor, from the wave machine to the drill press.

mb.solder.wire.name: Solder wire with a rosin core
mb.solder.wire.description: For joints the wave cannot reach, the line uses 0.5-0.8 mm wire with a rosin flux core extruded down the middle. About a quarter of the wire by weight is flux; as the solder melts the flux boils off ahead of it, cleaning the joint just before the tin arrives.

facts.label: Wire gauge
facts.value: approx. 0.5-0.8 mm at this lead pitch

facts.label: Flux core
facts.value: roughly 25 % of wire weight, rosin based

mb.solder.wire.core.name: Rosin flux core
mb.solder.wire.core.description: Sticky pine resin dissolved in alcohol with a mild organic-acid activator. Rosin is not corrosive, and at wave temperature it burns off cleanly, but what is left behind is a sticky, mildly acidic film that has to be cleaned off the board. Its whole job is to displace the oxide film on the copper in the few milliseconds before the solder touches it.
mb.solder.wire.core.note: Rosin flux was still the default in 1983. Low-solids 'no-clean' fluxes that skip the cleaning step existed but were not standard here; the goal was halide-free, not no-clean.

mb.solder.wire.core.activator.name: Flux activator (halide-free)
mb.solder.wire.core.activator.description: A small addition of organic acid, chosen to be aggressive against copper oxide but free of ionic halides. An ionic chloride in a flux does a better job of the chemistry and then quietly destroys the board with corrosion under the mask years later, so the halide-free requirement is a deliberate long-term trade.
mb.solder.wire.core.activator.note: Periodic practice was to specify a halide-free (non-ionic) flux and test for it; ionic contamination testing only became routine later.

mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.name: Colophony (rosin) from pine
mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.description: The sticky amber resin tapped from living pine and, in modern supply, distilled from pine stumps. Dissolved in alcohol it is the flux; it is non-corrosive and, crucially, only slightly conductive, which is what keeps a rosin-fluxed board from slowly corroding itself.

mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.acid.name: Abietic acid in the rosin
mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.acid.description: The organic acid that gives rosin its mild acidity and its ability to dissolve metal oxides. It is also what makes the residue on an uncleaned board slowly corrosive, which is the whole argument for cleaning after soldering.

mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.stumps.name: Pine stumps and resin
mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.stumps.description: Stumps left by logging are chipped and steam-distilled to recover the resin, which is why pine-resin supply for electronics solder is a forestry business and not an agriculture one.

mb.solder.wire.draw.name: Drawing the wire from the bar
mb.solder.wire.draw.description: Cast bar is hot-worked and cold-drawn through a series of dies to a fine round or rectangular section, with the flux core fed into the tube just before the final pass. The dies are carbide, because tin-lead is abrasive and destroys steel tooling quickly.

mb.solder.wire.draw.die.name: Carbide drawing die
mb.solder.wire.draw.die.description: A tungsten-carbide insert in a steel holder. Carbide is used throughout the solder shop and the board shop, from wire drawing dies to the wave pot's skimmer blade, because nothing softer survives contact with molten tin.

mb.solder.wire.draw.tungsten.name: Tungsten and cobalt in the carbide
mb.solder.wire.draw.tungsten.description: Tungsten comes from wolframite and scheelite concentrates, cobalt from cobalt ore. Both are mined metals, and both are chosen here for one reason only: they do not wear away in molten tin.

mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.name: Tungsten ore (wolframite)
mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.description: Heavy, dark ore worked for its tungsten content, usually concentrated from alluvial and vein deposits before conversion to ammonium paratungstate and then to the metal.
mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.note: In 1980s carbide tooling was increasingly using the far cheaper cemented carbide rather than the older hardened steel; the ore behind it is a genuine dependency of the fabrication process.

mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.body.name: Wolframite ore body
mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.body.description: A vein or alluvial concentration of iron-manganese tungstate, mined by stope or by hydraulic gravel washing and concentrated before the conversion plant. Diggable rock, at the very bottom of a chain that exists only because a die must survive molten tin.

mb.solder.bar.name: Cast solder bar and the dross it makes
mb.solder.bar.description: Solder arrives at the plant as roughly 0.5-1 kg bars and is dropped into the wave machine's pot. As tin dissolves copper from every pad that passes through the wave, the pot chemistry drifts and a grey oxide sludge called dross accumulates on the surface, which has to be skimmed off or the wave itself is contaminated.

facts.label: Pot capacity
facts.value: tens to hundreds of kg in a production machine

facts.label: Dross
facts.value: tin oxide plus dissolved copper, skimmed off the surface

mb.solder.alloy.name: 63/37 tin-lead eutectic
mb.solder.alloy.description: A true eutectic: solid below 183 deg C, liquid above it, no pasty region in between. That sharpness is what lets a drag-soldered joint finish setting the instant it leaves the wave, and it is why the wave pot and the pad finish are the same alloy.

facts.label: Main weakness
facts.value: creeps under load, especially at elevated temperature

mb.solder.alloy.additives.name: Antimony and silver additions
mb.solder.alloy.additives.description: A little antimony hardens the alloy and slows the tin pest; silver is used in higher-temperature solders to slow pad dissolution. General-purpose wave bar in 1983 was usually plain 63/37.
mb.solder.alloy.additives.note: Whether Commodore specified antimony-bearing bar is not established.

mb.solder.alloy.lead.name: Lead, 37 % of the alloy
mb.solder.alloy.lead.description: Lead lowers the melting point, widens the working window and suppresses tin whisker growth. It is also soft, creeps, and is a cumulative poison that nobody in a 1983 electronics factory thought about.
mb.solder.alloy.lead.note: Lead's chain from galena through the sinter and blast furnace to refined bullion is traced by the metals subsystem under metal.lead.

mb.solder.alloy.tin.name: Tin, 63 % of the alloy
mb.solder.alloy.tin.description: Tin does the actual joining: it reacts with the copper in the pad to form the intermetallic that holds the joint, and it flows first and wets the joint, which is why a good joint is shiny where the tin pooled.
mb.solder.alloy.tin.note: Tin's own supply chain, from cassiterite concentrate to refined tin, is traced by the metals subsystem under metal.tin.

c64.connector-jacks.name: Front and rear I/O connectors
c64.connector-jacks.description: Every plug-in interface on a C64: the 24-pin user port, the 2x6 cassette port, the 44-pin cartridge socket, the 8-pin DIN video/audio and 6-pin DIN serial connectors, the two DE-9 control ports, the 7-pin PSU inlet and the keyboard ribbon header. They share one manufacturing sequence: stamped-and-formed brass contacts, nickel underplate, gold flash, and an injection-moulded thermoplastic or glass-filled phenolic insulator.
c64.connector-jacks.note: CORRECTION to the brief: the breadbin C64 has NO RCA jacks. Composite video, luma, chroma, audio and the RF modulator output all leave through a single round 8-pin DIN connector on the rear panel (an earlier 1982 revision used a 5-pin one); RCA sockets appear on the C64C and on Commodore's own 1701/1702 monitors. The 'DIN-5 cassette port' is also not quite right - the datasette port is a 2x6 card-edge socket on the motherboard, and the DIN plug lives on the datasette cable. The PSU inlet is 7-pin, not 6.

facts.label: User port
facts.value: 24-pin card edge, 3.96 mm pitch, gold over nickel

facts.label: Control ports
facts.value: 2 x DE-9 subminiature D, plastic shell, gold-flashed

facts.label: Keyboard
facts.value: soldered board header at the front-left edge carrying a flat ribbon

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.name: Keyboard ribbon header
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.description: A soldered pin header at the front-left edge of the mainboard carrying the keyboard's flat ribbon cable. The keyboard's matrix lines and the shift-lock return run out of the machine this way; it is the one connector on the board that is not an industry-standard part but a plain 2.54 mm row of pins.
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.note: I could not establish the exact position count of the C64 keyboard header from a primary source. C64 repair references consistently describe a 2.54 mm-pitch male header along the front-left board edge, and replacement parts are sold as 2.54 mm rows of varying length; I have therefore described it generically rather than committing to a pin count. The matrix needs at most 8 column lines plus 8 row lines plus shift-lock and the 6510 I/O port lines, so a 2 x 12 (24-way) header is plausible but unverified.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: soldered straight male header on the PCB

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Wave-soldered pin header
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: The header's pins were pushed into the board and wave-soldered in one pass with the rest of the components, in 63/37 lead-tin solder. That is why the pin material is brass with a tin plate rather than nickel: it wets tin-lead, and it does not need the corrosion resistance a gold-plated control-port contact does.
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.note: The leaded-solder claim matches the era; the interconnect file carries the solder chemistry.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Wave-soldering machine
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: A pumped solder pot with a travelling wave, a heated conveyor and pre- and post-heating tunnels. The whole C64 board went through one wave in about ten seconds; that is why the pins were tinned and the leads formed for a flat joint.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Flux and its origin
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: Rosin flux, dissolved in alcohol, cleaned the board in the wave-solder bath. Rosin is the sticky residue of pine trees, and the cleaning step after soldering removes it because ionic residue is what makes a board drift or corrode.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Pine rosin
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: Rosin is the fossilised sticky resin of conifers, dissolved in alcohol as the soldering flux and then washed off because ionic residue causes drift and corrosion.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Softwood resin
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: Collected from pine and conifer stands; the tree that keeps the board clean.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: 63/37 lead-tin solder
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: The alloy that joined every part on the board. Snelled with a small amount of lead to make it flow better at a low temperature, it has a eutectic at 183 C. The lead came from galena, the ore of lead, and the tin from cassiterite - two of the oldest traded metals, both still mined rather than synthesised in 1982.
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.note: Commodore did not use lead-free solder on the breadbin mainboard; the lead-free transition in consumer electronics did not begin until the 1990s and was driven by RoHS in 2006.

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Galena (lead ore)
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: Lead came from galena, PbS, a dense cubic mineral mined underground often as a by-product of silver and zinc. It is roasted and sintered to litharge and reduced in a blast furnace - the same cupellation metallurgy that has produced lead for three thousand years.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.name: Power inlet, 7-pin round DIN
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.description: The rear-panel socket the external PSU brick plugs into. A 7-pin round connector in a large 'type C' shell, following the DIN 45329 / IEC 10 form: pins 1 and 5 carry the regulated +5 V DC and pins 6 and 7 the 9 V AC from the transformer, with the switched side feeding the board through L5, C97, C100 and SW1.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.note: CORRECTION to the brief: the C64 power connector is 7-pin, not 6. Sources agree on 7 pins; some 1982 supplies shipped a lead with only four populated contacts, which is a different and well-documented issue (the 'pin 5 damage' fault).

facts.label: Standard
facts.value: DIN 45329 / IEC 10 style, large type C shell

facts.label: Pin 1 and 5
facts.value: +5 V DC from the regulator, filtered by L5, C97 and C100

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.switchin.name: SW1 switching of the 5 V rail
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.switchin.description: The socket feeds straight into the board's main filter (L5, C97, C100) and then through switch SW1, so SW1 breaks the load current rather than the supply - which is why the switch's contact rating looks absurdly high for the job. The external brick's own rocker does the real mains isolation; SW1 only breaks DC at a few amps.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.switchin.note: The L5/C97/C100/SW1 ordering is from Commodore's own service manual text on the power supply.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Friction-lock and pull-proof contacts
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: A mains-adjacent DC supply connector needs its contacts to survive being tugged by the cable. The mating pins are a friction type with a deliberately stiff crimp barrel so a pull is taken by the metal, not the solder fillet; some Commodore supplies additionally used a friction-lock retention ring on the plug body.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.note: The brief's 'friction-lock contacts' description matches the pull-proof crimp on this connector; I have not found a C64-specific retention-ring part number.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.name: The pin 5 damage fault
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.description: One of the best-known Commodore power faults: a partially populated or incorrectly wired supply lead damages the 5 V pin in the machine's socket, so the machine will not power up even with a known-good supply. It is a wear-and-misalignment problem on a friction contact carrying a DC load that the connector was not designed to be unplugged under.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.note: Widely reported in Commodore service literature; I have not verified a primary factory bulletin on it.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Crimp barrel construction
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: The pin is a hollow brass tube with an interference crimp onto the conductor rather than a solder joint. That is the actual meaning of a friction-lock contact: the metal grips the metal, so a tug on the cable is carried by a mechanical interference fit and not by the solder fillet.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Brass pin stock
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: Cartridge brass drawn wire, the standard material for crimp contacts because it is springy enough to hold an interference fit yet soft enough to take the crimp without cracking.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Copper ore to brass
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: Brass is a copper-zinc alloy, so it begins at a copper ore and a zinc ore. Both are ancient mined materials and both were still being mined rather than synthesised in 1982.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.name: Control ports, 2 x DE-9 subminiature D
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.description: The two nine-pin D-sub sockets on the rear panel for joystick or paddle controllers, a light pen or a mouse. Each is a DE-9 female in a plastic D-shaped shell with gold-flashed brass contacts dimpled for reliable mating - the connector everyone remembers from Atari, Commodore and Amiga alike.

facts.label: Type
