mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.note: The brief's chemistry is the standard industrial route and I am reasonably confident in it, but I have compressed several genuinely distinct flows into one node rather than over-claim which variant a given capacitor maker used.

facts.label: Digestion
facts.value: HF in an autoclave at ~100-200 C

facts.label: Reduction routes
facts.value: Na reduction, Al or Cu reduction, or KCl/KF salt melt

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..name: Columbite-tantalite ore
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..description: The tantalum-bearing ore, a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, mined both as placer gravels and as lode pegmatites. Concentrating it requires ore dressing by gravity and magnetic separation, because only a few per cent of the rock is Ta2O5. Historically the ore was concentrated from the Congo and Rwanda-Burundi, which is precisely why Western capacitor supply chains were politically and economically exposed in this period.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..note: The DRC ore became a headline conflict-mineral story only from the late 1990s; in 1983-84 the problem was ordinary market tightness and price escalation.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..name: Dressing and concentration
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..description: Columbite-tantalite is run through gravity, magnetic and electrostatic separation and then an acid-leach circuit to recover a concentrate of perhaps a few per cent Ta2O5. Because the ore is bulk low-grade rock, the mining and concentration stage - not the chemistry - is where most of the cost of a tantalum capacitor lives.

facts.label: Concentration methods
facts.value: gravity shaking tables, magnetic separation, electrostatic separation

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..name: Alluvial and pegmatite placer workings
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..description: Tantalum-bearing minerals are dense, so they concentrate naturally in stream and beach placers below any pegmatite outcrop. Much of the 1980s supply was won by artisanal and semi-industrial alluvial mining in the Kivu highlands, which is exactly why ore supply could be disrupted by regional politics rather than by mine closure.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.name: Early-1980s tantalum supply squeeze
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.description: Capacitor tantalum depends on columbite-tantalite ore, essentially all of it from the Kivu region of Zaire and neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi. A collapse in the electronics market in 1982-83 drained the supply chain's stocks, then demand spiked again in 1984 on the PC and automotive booms. The USGS records a significant spike in tantalum demand in 1984, with US factory sales of tantalum capacitors at an all-time high and escalating prices pushing consumers to substitute aluminium parts and to design tantalum out where they could. It was a real, documented shortage in exactly the C64's production window.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.note: The 1984 demand spike and the all-time-high factory sales figure are verified against USGS Circular OF01-349. I have deliberately not stated a peak capacitor-grade powder price for 1983-84 because I could not source a reliable figure for that specific grade and year.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..name: Engineering response to the squeeze
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..description: The documented response was to reduce tantalum content where possible, substitute aluminium electrolytics, and lengthen qualified lead times. It is a good example of how a metals shortage propagates into board design decisions within eighteen months.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..name: Capacitor-grade recycling loop
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..description: Because tantalum metal is expensive, tantalum-bearing scrap - rejected capacitors, anode dust, trimmed pellet scrap - was recovered and returned to the powder supply. This is why a 1983-84 shortage hit prices so hard: recycled powder could not be substituted for virgin powder in a dielectric that had to be defect-free.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.name: Tantalum lead, braze and epoxy seal
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.description: The anode lead is drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, then the assembly is sealed by an epoxy dip. On wet-slug types the hermetic case is glass or a welded metal can with a Teflon ring seal. The part is then marked with its value, rating and the manufacturer.

facts.label: Anode lead
facts.value: drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the pellet

facts.label: Braze
facts.value: silver or silver-graphite drop for the lead joint; Ta-Au braze on some types

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: epoxy dip for solid types; welded metal can for wet-slug types

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.mark.name: Value and rating marking
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.mark.description: The dipped part was marked along its length with the capacitance, rated voltage, tolerance, manufacturer and date code, usually by ink printing on the epoxy.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Epoxy dip seal
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: Solid tantalum parts were sealed by dipping in epoxy and curing, which protects the brittle MnO2/dielectric stack against handling and moisture. Wet-slug parts instead used a welded metal can with a glass or Teflon seal.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Epoxy resin and bisphenol A
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: The standard epoxy of the period: bisphenol A condensed with epichlorohydrin, cured with an amine. Both halves are petrochemical, and bisphenol A was the dominant resin for adhesive, coating, printed-board and capacitor sealants alike.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.name: Anodic Ta2O5 formation and MnO2 solid electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.description: The sintered anode is anodised to grow the Ta2O5 dielectric, then coated with manganese dioxide by pyrolytically decomposing manganese chloride vapour on the surface - the classic 1980s solid tantalum part. A sintered silver-paste counter-electrode existed as an alternative construction. Today's conductive-polymer tantalum is a late-1990s development.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.note: The brief lists silver paste as the solid counter-electrode; the standard 1980s solid tantalum counter-electrode was MnO2. Both constructions existed, so this is a correction of emphasis rather than of substance.

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from MnCl2 pyrolysis (standard); sintered Ag paste (alternative)

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: ~50-200 V DC sets the working voltage

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.name: Forming voltage and working rating
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.description: The anode is anodised at a voltage above its rated working voltage, usually by a factor of 1.5-2, to build a defect-free oxide. The rated voltage of the part is set by that formation step and is not adjustable afterwards.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.name: The counter-electrode body
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.description: Below the manganese dioxide sits the original tantalum anode body and its second termination. The layer stack is metal, dielectric, counter-electrode, then a conductive path to the case - all inside an epoxy dip.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.name: Manganese chloride for pyrolysis
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.description: MnCl2 is vapour-decomposed on the hot tantalum surface in a furnace at several hundred degrees, leaving a conformal MnO2 layer that acts as the solid counter-electrode. The chloride is shipped as a hydrate and is hygroscopic, so it had to be kept dry.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.name: Manganese ore (pyrolusite)
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.description: Manganese came from pyrolusite and other oxide ores, and mostly as a by-product of the iron and steel industry, since most manganese ore is mined to be alloyed into steel rather than for its own sake.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.name: Sintered tantalum anode
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.description: Capacitor-grade tantalum powder is pressed around a tantalum wire anode lead and sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, producing a porous body with an enormous internal surface area. The Ta2O5 dielectric then grows on that surface, which is why a gram of powder stores far more capacitance than a gram of film.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.name: Anode pressing and sintering
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.description: Powder is blended with a binder and pressed around the wire, then debound and sintered in vacuum or flowing hydrogen at 1200-1400 C. The pressed pellet is deliberately porous - roughly half its volume is void - because that void is where the dielectric forms.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.name: Drawn tantalum wire
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.description: The anode lead is fine drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet. Tantalum wire was drawn by the same machinery as refractory metals for furnace leads, from the same powder-to-wire routes.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.red.name: Capacitor-grade tantalum metal and oxide
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.red.description: Whether the anode is built from reduced metallic powder or from sintered oxide powder, the specification is the same: extremely high purity, sub-micron, high surface area. Impurities here are the defect mechanism that causes tantalum dielectric failures.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.red.name: Columbite-tantalite concentrate
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.red.description: The concentrate that becomes capacitor-grade powder. Every stage from ore to powder discards most of the feed, which is why tantalum capacitors had a high metal cost per cubic centimetre even in 1982.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.name: Aluminium electrolytic capacitor
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.description: The polarised bulk capacitors: about fifteen 10 uF/25 V radial parts decoupling the SID and video analogue rails, plus larger axial 100-2200 uF parts on the rectified supply rails. Value comes from a nanometres-thick anodic oxide on etched aluminium foil soaked in electrolyte - cheap, large capacitance, and the bulk of the board's supply-rail filtering.

facts.label: Radial parts
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V, 5 x 5 mm can

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.name: Ageing and burn-in
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.description: Finished parts are held at an elevated temperature under DC bias so the oxide re-thickens and the leakage current settles. A 1980s capacitor arrives already partly formed, which is why an electrolytic recovered from a two-year-old Commodore machine often measures better than a brand-new one straight from a 2020s reel.

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: ~1-2x rated voltage at 85-125 C, hours to days

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: reduces initial leakage and stabilises capacitance

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..name: Capacitance and leakage test
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..description: Parts are tested for capacitance, dissipation factor and leakage at rated temperature. Rejection rates in a commodity 10 uF 25 V part were small but non-zero, and every rejected part was a loss of scrap aluminium.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..name: Capacitance and dissipation-factor measurement
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..description: A bridge or LCR meter at rated frequency and temperature gives capacitance and dissipation factor; a DC bias step gives leakage. Rejection on leakage is what catches a pinhole in the oxide, the classic failure mode of a fresh electrolytic.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..name: Burn-in chamber
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..description: A temperature-controlled rack of trays in which finished parts are held at temperature and bias. A good capacitor plant in 1982 might burn in for hours or days, which is why vintage electrolytics so often arrive already formed.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Crimping, sleeving and end-fill bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Aluminium or tinned-copper alloy terminal tabs are crimped onto the anode and cathode edges of the wound pack. The pack is then sleeved - PVC heat-shrink or a printed cardboard outer - and sealed at the end with a rubber or PVC bung that retains the electrolyte against its expansion over temperature. The paper and foil layers you see when you cut one open are the winding itself.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: crimped Al or Cu alloy tab; anode polarity marked on the sleeve

facts.label: Sleeve
facts.value: PVC heat-shrink or printed cardboard outer

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Aluminium terminal tab
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: A soft aluminium or aluminium-alloy tab, crimped onto the foil edge. Pure aluminium is used because it is the only metal that will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil it must touch.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Aluminium purity of the tab
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Capacitor tabs and foils are made from very high-purity aluminium; iron and silicon above a few tenths of a per cent make the alloy hard and prone to sludge in the electrolyte, so capacitor-grade purity is stricter than structural grade.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: End-fill bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: A rubber or PVC disc that fills the end of the sleeve and retains the electrolyte against thermal expansion and the internal pressure generated during burn-in. It is the visible rubber disc at the base of a radial electrolytic.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Silicone rubber bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Heat-cured silicone rubber, chosen because it stays soft and chemically inert in contact with the acid electrolyte for decades. Silicone is a siloxane polymer built on a quartz-derived silicon-oxygen backbone.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Silica sand
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding on a mandrel and impregnation
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: Anode foil, separator and cathode foil are wound together on a rotating mandrel into a compact roll. Electrolyte is then vacuum- or pressure-impregnated into the wound roll, filling every pore and pushing out air, which is what finally gives the part its capacitance.

facts.label: Impregnation
facts.value: vacuum impregnation, repeated 2-4 times to drive out trapped air

facts.label: Slitting
facts.value: cathode foil is slit into two or three ribbons for a multi-section winding

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding pitch and section count
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: The number of anode/cathode sections and their winding pitch set the ripple current behaviour and the ESR of the finished part, which is why a low-ESR part is physically bigger than a same-value general-grade one.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding mandrel
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: A polished steel mandrel, often Teflon-coated, on which the foil sandwich is wound. Mandrel diameter and surface finish are set by the smallest foil thickness so the finished pack can be released without creasing.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Iron ore
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Separator (paper or polyolefin)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A porous, electrolyte-wicking separator keeping the foils apart while letting current through. Bleached kraft paper was still the standard for most 1980s aluminium electrolytics; low-porosity oriented polypropylene or polyethylene sleeves were the premium, longer-life alternative.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.note: Correcting the brief: paper was still the volume material in 1982. Polypropylene separators had been commercial for years but were not yet dominant.

facts.label: 1982 default
facts.value: bleached kraft paper; PE/PP sleeves for higher-reliability parts

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: the separator is the main leakage path and electrolyte reservoir

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Bleached kraft paper separator
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A very thin, very porous cellulose tissue wound between the foils. It must be wetted completely by the electrolyte but must not contain ions that would raise the leakage current, so it is washed and bleached before use. Kraft paper separators are why the electrolyte is held in place at all.

facts.label: Why paper
facts.value: absorbent, cheap, dimensionally stable when wetted

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Wood pulp
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: Kraft paper is made from softwood (long-fibre) pulped in the kraft process. Because the separator is a fraction of a gram of tissue it uses a negligible mass of wood, but it is one of the very few places where a C64 is literally made of a tree.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Working electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: The conducting liquid that soaks the separator and carries current between the oxide and the cathode: boric or phosphoric acid dissolved in ethylene glycol, dimethylformamide or dimethyl sulfoxide. The solvent must wet the porous separator without dissolving or attacking the oxide, and the acid concentration sets the oxide's equilibrium thickness.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Glycol-ether solvent from petrochemistry
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Ethylene glycol and the glycol ethers used as high-voltage capacitor solvents were derived from ethylene oxide, itself made by oxidising ethylene from a steam cracker. They replaced the glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s because they dissolve the anode oxide without attacking it.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: The refining chain itself is expanded in the plastics and chemicals files.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: crude -> steam cracking -> ethylene -> ethylene oxide -> glycol ether

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Ethylene glycol ethers from ethylene oxide
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Ethylene oxide is made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, then reacts with an alcohol to give the glycol ether. The solvent chemistry of an aluminium electrolytic is therefore set two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Naphtha
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Boric acid in the electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Boric acid sets the oxide chemistry of the anode and, with phosphoric acid, is the reason an aluminium electrolytic has a usable voltage range at all. Commercially it was made from borax, which is mined from evaporite deposits.

facts.label: Key deposits
facts.value: California (US), Turkey, Chile - the US borates led world supply in 1982

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Borax (tincalconite) evaporite
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Sodium tetraborate decahydrate occurs in the playas and evaporite deposits of closed desert basins, where boron-bearing volcanic hot springs have fed an evaporating lake for millions of years. It is mined, not synthesised, in the borate districts.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Cathode foil
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: Aluminium foil, usually a cheaper alloy and often unetched, serving as the return electrode. It carries no dielectric of its own; its job is simply to collect the return current through the electrolyte.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Cathode foil rolling
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: High-purity aluminium rolled to a few tens of microns, often lightly etched, slit into ribbons for the winding. It uses the same aluminium as the anode but a looser specification, because no dielectric quality depends on it.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Alumina from bauxite
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Bauxite profile
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: High-purity anode foil, rolled and etched
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: 99.5 %+ aluminium foil, chemically etched in a hot hydrochloric/nitric acid or chlorate bath to grow microscopic pits on the surface. Effective cathode area rises by a factor of fifty to a hundred, which is how a hundred microfarads fits into a 5 mm can.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: hot HCl/HNO3, or a sodium chlorate bath

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anode foil from re-melted foil-mill scrap
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: Rolled foil offcuts, edge trim and rejected capacitor-grade foil were re-smelted in a holding furnace and re-rolled into fresh anode foil rather than being returned to the general scrap stream. That closed loop is why capacitor makers were, in effect, recycling their own aluminium, and why an aluminium price move showed up in 1982 capacitor prices with a lag.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Closed-loop recycling of capacitor foil scrap was standard practice, but prime foil from the primary smelter was still used for the tightest-tolerance parts; I cannot say which proportion applied to Commodore's 1982 supply.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Primary aluminium from bauxite
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The other half of the loop: alumina from bauxite, smelted in a Hall-Héroult cell by dissolving it in molten cryolite and electrolytising at ~950-970 C. The cathode metal is 99.7 % pure and it is this, or re-melted scrap of it, that rolls into capacitor anode foil.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Cryolite (Na3AlF6) from fluorspar
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The bath solvent that lets aluminium be smelted below its own melting point. Cryolite is made synthetically from hydrofluoric acid and alumina, and the hydrofluoric acid historically came from fluorspar - a calcium fluoride mineral mined in Mexico, South Africa and China.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anodic formation (the real dielectric)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The etched foil is made the anode in a phosphoric or boric acid bath at 90-200 V DC, growing a barrier-type aluminium oxide layer tens of nanometres thick. The rated working voltage of the finished capacitor is just the voltage the oxide can hold, so higher ratings need a thicker oxide and hence less capacitance for the same area.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~90-200 V DC for parts rated 6-50 V

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Phosphoric acid from phosphate rock
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The phosphate acid in the forming bath fixes the oxide growth characteristics. It is made by burning rock phosphate - calcium phosphate from sedimentary apatite deposits - in a furnace and absorbing the fumes in water.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.name: Monolithic ceramic capacitor (MLCC)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.description: The 0.1 uF bypass and small timing capacitors. Dozens of layers of barium-titanate ceramic with screen-printed metal electrodes buried between them, then fired and terminated. Monolithic construction gives huge capacitance in a tiny body because the electrode area is the whole face of every layer.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.note: The 250407 parts list as transcribed by the replica-board project specifies 0.1 uF 50 V X7R, 0.22 uF Z5U and small C0G parts; Commodore's exact mix of ceramic disc versus monolithic changed between board revisions, and the X7R/Z5U designations are modern restatements of what were then simply 'ceramic'.

facts.label: Dielectric classes
facts.value: X7R / Z5U for the big values, C0G for the small timing caps

facts.label: Size (1982)
facts.value: ~2.5 x 3.2 mm radial blocks and discs

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.name: End terminations (nickel + solderable outer)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.description: After firing, the two exposed end faces are terminated with a conducting band that collects current from the hundreds of buried electrodes. In 1982 this was a fired-on or sputtered nickel layer with a solderable silver or tin outer layer, or a simple dipped solder band. The C64 boards were wave-soldered in tin-lead, so the termination had to wet 63/37 solder.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.note: I am confident about the nickel barrier plus solderable outer layer; I am less sure which of the outer-layer options Commodore's capacitor supplier used in 1982.

facts.label: 1982 termination
facts.value: Ni barrier with Ag or Ni-Sn outer layer, or dipped tin-lead solder

facts.label: Modern difference
facts.value: pure sintered Ni-Sn terminations with no precious metal are today's standard

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.tin.name: Tin for the solderable termination
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.tin.description: The outer termination layer has to wet 63/37 lead-tin solder in a wave bath, so it is tin or tin-silver. Tin came from cassiterite, and the whole world electronics industry in 1982 was competing for the same tin that solder and bronze also needed.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.tin.note: The cassiterite chain is at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-composition.end-cap.tin; referenced rather than duplicated.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.name: Firing in a continuous belt kiln
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.description: The blanks go through a continuous belt or pusher kiln under a controlled low oxygen partial pressure, so the ceramic sinters dense and hermetic while the nickel internal electrodes are not oxidised away. Density matters enormously: a porous body lets moisture attack the electrode stack and destroys the insulation resistance.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.note: Two kiln temperatures in the brief refer to two different operations: 1150-1250 C is the BaTiO3 powder calcination, ~1300 C is the finished body's sinter. Both are right for their step.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2 / forming gas or N2

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.atmosphe.name: Low-oxygen atmosphere
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.atmosphe.description: A forming-gas or nitrogen atmosphere with a controlled oxygen partial pressure, just low enough that nickel does not oxidise but high enough that the organic binder burns off cleanly. Getting this window right is the hardest part of base-metal MLCC manufacture.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.elements.name: Kiln heating elements
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.elements.description: Silicon-carbide or nichrome elements in a continuous belt kiln held at ~1300 C for hours. Long soaks at high temperature are what drive the ceramic to theoretical density.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.name: Dicing into blanks
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.description: The laminated bar is cut with a resin-bonded diamond saw into hundreds or thousands of identical blanks, each one capacitor body. This is why MLCC manufacture is a barrel process: one sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors, and the economics only work at that scale.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.yield.name: Barrel economics
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.yield.description: One sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors and one furnace run yields many bars. The economics only work at that scale, which is why MLCC production consolidated into a handful of very large Japanese, European and later Taiwanese plants by the early 1980s.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.name: Resin-bonded diamond blade
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.description: A thin, flat, run-of-the-mill diamond wheel; the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder but applied to a sintered ceramic bar.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.synth.name: Synthetic diamond abrasive
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.synth.description: Industrial diamond in 1982 was made almost entirely by shock-wave synthesis from graphite, and its price set the cost of grinding, drilling and sawing across the whole ceramics and glass industry.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.name: Stacking, lamination and debinding
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.description: The printed green sheets are stacked offset so every sheet's electrode lands alternately on the two opposed faces, then compressed in a hydraulic laminator and the organic binder burned out slowly. The result is a monolithic bar of hundreds of ceramic layers with the electrodes sealed inside.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: ~10-60 active layers for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part

facts.label: Debinding
facts.value: slow ramp 200-400 C to avoid cracking the stack

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.off.name: Layer registration
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.off.description: Each successive sheet is offset by exactly the margin width so that the printed electrodes line up alternately with the two opposed faces. Nothing in a modern capacitor is more precise than this stack-up.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.lam.name: Hydraulic laminator
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.lam.description: A heated hydraulic press that stacks and consolidates hundreds of sheets at once, aligned by registration pins. This is the step that turns a pile of loose printed film into one solid bar.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.name: Screen-printing internal electrodes
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.description: A metal paste is printed onto the green sheets to define the buried internal electrodes. In 1982 the commodity MLCC used a base-metal nickel paste fired in a low-pO2 atmosphere, because silver would diffuse down the grain boundaries of the BaTiO3 and wreck its insulation resistance. The older, more expensive palladium-silver internal electrodes the brief mentions were by 1982 largely a legacy technology kept for a few high-reliability parts.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.note: This is the one place where the brief's chemistry needed correcting: PdAg was the 1960s-70s internal electrode, not the 1980s one. Nickel-Pd-Ag composite pastes (Ni with a Pd-Ag core) only became the standard after about 1985.

facts.label: Legacy alternative
facts.value: PdAg, mostly phased out by the early 1980s

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen through a photoemulsion mask, offset on high-volume lines

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.name: Base-metal nickel paste
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.description: The internal electrode paste: finely divided nickel in a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the green sheet and co-fired with the ceramic. Nickel was chosen over silver for cost and over palladium for cost, and it is what let a 0.1 uF 50 V bypass capacitor be sold for a fraction of a cent.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.name: Nickel from its ore, in the plating and paste supply chain
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.description: The nickel in a nickel internal electrode came ultimately from laterite ore or from nickel matte imported as an intermediate. By 1982 the intermediate trade in ferronickel and matte was a well-developed global market, which is why a capacitor cost in Hong Kong was sensitive to South African chrome and New Caledonian nickel.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.note: This is an economic description of the supply chain rather than a specific process step; flagged medium deliberately.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.name: Tape casting to green sheets
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.description: The slip is doctor-bladed onto a moving polyester carrier film to a controlled dry thickness. This single step sets the eventual capacitance density, because capacitance is dielectric thickness divided by the number of electrode layers stacked.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.note: Correcting the brief slightly: the 1-10 um figure is modern; 1982 parts cast thicker, coarser sheets to keep the layer count and the cost of handling down.

facts.label: Green sheet thickness
facts.value: ~1-10 um; early-1980s parts often cast 5-20 um

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.doctor-b.name: Doctor blade
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.doctor-b.description: A precisely-ground steel or ceramic blade with a controlled edge angle, set to micrometres over the belt. The single most important tool in MLCC making: it sets layer thickness and therefore capacitance density.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.belt.name: Moving carrier belt
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.belt.description: The green sheet is carried on a continuous polyester belt and dried in a short oven as the doctor blade lays it down, so the green thickness is set by blade clearance against a moving web rather than by a single-shot cast.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.name: Tape-casting slurry (powder + frit + binder)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.description: The BaTiO3 powder is blended with a glass frit - an aid to sintering and to dielectric strength at the electrode interface - and an organic binder into a homogeneous, flowable slip. In 1982 this was an acrylic or PVA binder in water, or a cellulose ester in an organic solvent; fully water-based PVA systems became dominant later.

facts.label: Glass frit
facts.value: ~5 % by weight of the ceramic body

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit.name: Glass frit in the slurry
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit.description: A few per cent of low-melting glass, added so that on sintering it wets the barium titanate grains, closes the porosity and gives the internal electrode a hermetic interface. Without it the MLCC is not gas-tight and its insulation resistance collapses.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit..name: Silica sand
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit..description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.name: Barium titanate dielectric powder
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.description: The heart of the MLCC: sub-micron BaTiO3 crystallites, the only powder that has a very high dielectric constant AND survives the high-temperature processing. Chemistry is shifted from pure BaTiO3 by dopants to move the Curie point below room temperature, giving a Class II (X7R/Z5U) part with high capacitance that still decays with temperature.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.note: Y5V, also a Class II code, is real but was not the dominant 1982 designation; the breadbin C64 parts are best described as X7R/Z5U-era ceramics.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ~0.2-1 um; coarse-grain BaTiO3 was typical of early-1980s X7R

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.name: Donor / acceptor doping
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.description: Trivalent donor dopants (La2O3, Dy2O3, Y2O3) or pentavalent acceptors (Nb2O5, Ta2O5, Sb2O5) are added during calcination. Donors leave the ceramic 'depleted' so the grains sit uniformly in the paraelectric phase at room temperature, which gives the stable, moderate-loss X7R curve. Acceptor dopants raise the Curie point so the material stays ferroelectric and gives a much higher, more temperature-sensitive Z5U.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.note: The physics is standard ceramics; the specific dopant-to-Class assignments are my summary and are flagged medium.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.name: Rare-earth dopant oxides
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.description: Lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium oxides, ground and sieved to sub-micron, are the donor dopants that set the temperature coefficient of an X7R dielectric. They are rare-earth minerals mined and separated in small tonnages, and their price was a visible line item in MLCC costing.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.name: Bastnaesite (monazite and bastnaesite concentrates)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.description: Rare-earth minerals are worked chiefly from carbonatite and monazite/bastnaesite concentrates, with the world supply dominated by one mining complex and its associated separation plants. The oxides are then produced by acid leach and solvent extraction.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.note: The rare-earth separation chain is complex; flagged medium because I have deliberately compressed it.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.name: Solid-state BaTiO3 synthesis
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.description: Barium carbonate and titanium dioxide are ball-milled with the dopants in water to a homogeneous slurry, then calcined in a kiln at about 1050-1200 C. The carbonate decomposes and the perovskite BaTiO3 crystallises. The mass is reground and wet-milled with a dispersant down to the target particle size.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.note: The brief's '1150-1250 C' is the right order of magnitude for the calcination fire; I have narrowed it slightly.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.name: Titanium dioxide (TiO2) feed
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.description: Ceramic-grade TiO2, made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidising, or by sulphuric acid digestion. Low-iron pigment-grade material is used so the fired ceramic has good insulation resistance.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.name: Ilmenite (FeTiO3) sand
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.description: A black, heavy placer sand mined from beach and dune deposits. The principal titanium ore, either smelted to high-titanium slag or chlorinated directly to pigment.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.note: Australia was the dominant ilmenite supplier to the ceramic-grade pigment chain in 1982.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.b.name: Barium carbonate (BaCO3) feed
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.b.description: Made by carbonating barium sulfide solution, or by precipitation from soluble barium salts. Barite is the natural source: it is beneficiated, reduced to BaS and carbonated back to the carbonate.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.b.name: Barite (BaSO4), mined
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.b.description: Heavy-spar ore, usually a vein or cavity filler in limestone and evaporite, mined underground. It is the world source of essentially all barium and therefore of the barium in every BaTiO3 MLCC.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.b.note: Morocco, China, Mexico and India were the leading barite producers of the early 1980s.

mb.passives.resistors.name: Resistors
mb.passives.resistors.description: Fixed resistors on the 250407: about seventy 1/4 W axial parts in values from 100 ohm to 1 megohm, plus four thick-film SIP resistor networks and one 500 ohm trimmer. Almost all were 5 percent carbon film; the handful of 1 percent metal film parts sat in the VIC-II colour and timing network.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: axial, 6.3 x 2.3 mm, 0.63 mm lead pitch

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.name: Trim and adjustable resistors
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.description: The single adjustable part on the 250407 is R27, a 500 ohm cermet trimmer potentiometer that biases U31's crystal oscillator so the 14.31818 MHz colour subcarrier lands exactly on NTSC's subcarrier frequency. It is the reason a C64 needs no colour adjustment in normal use but will show colour shimmer when the crystal ages.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.note: On later C64 boards (the '8710' revision and Commodore's own C64C), this variable resistor was replaced with a trimmer capacitor in the crystal's load network. Both do the same job: pulling the oscillator to exactly the right frequency.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-10 % body; the ADJUSTMENT is what matters

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster.name: Adjuster screw and slider
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster.description: A knurled brass or stainless screw drives a moulded slider that rides the wiper along the track. Backing-off epoxy locks the setting once the board is aligned.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Epoxy lock
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: After alignment a drop of epoxy is flowed over the adjuster so the setting cannot drift in service. On a machine with no calibration facility this trimmer is effectively a one-time factory adjustment for forty years.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Locking epoxy
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: A drop of epoxy flowed over the adjuster and allowed to cure hard. It is a destructive, deliberate lock: once the trim is set on the factory line, that trimmer is not adjustable again.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Adjuster screw
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: A brass or stainless screw, knurled or slotted, driving the slider. Brass is the usual choice because it machines cleanly at small diameters and does not gall against the moulded slider.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Copper ore to brass
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: Cartridge brass from copper and zinc ore; the same alloy as the connector contact strip.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Cermet resistive element and track
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: A thick-film RuO2 resistive track deposited on the top face of an alumina substrate, with a metal-foil wiper that slides along it. Because the element is a printed film rather than a carbon blob, the tracking is smooth and the part does not develop a scratchy potentiometer feel the way a carbon composition pot does.

facts.label: Wiper
facts.value: Ni alloy or precious metal, fork or blade

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Electrical travel and resolution
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: The usable travel is a fraction of the physical length because the track is designed to have most of its resistance in the middle of the sweep. That is how a 500 ohm trimmer gets a usable 0-500 ohm range from a single turn of an adjuster screw.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Wiper alloy
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: A nickel-alloy or precious-metal spring contact rubbing on the RuO2 film. Because the cermet element is hard, the wiper is deliberately the sacrificial element and is made of a soft, wear-resistant alloy.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Nickel ore
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: Laterite ore, the origin of the wiper alloy as well as the plating and the MLCC internal electrode.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.name: Thick-film cermet SIP resistor networks
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.description: The four resistor arrays on the 250407: two 8-way isolated 33 ohm packs (series terminators on the DRAM data bus), one 8-way 3k3 bussed pack and one 10-way 3k3 bussed pack. Each is one alumina substrate with several ruthenium-oxide resistive tracks screen-printed and fired together.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.note: The parent brief mentioned a RIFA 481 resistor pack. RIFA (British Insulated Callender's Cables, Boxhill, UK) did supply SIP resistor networks to the European electronics trade in the 1980s, but I found no direct evidence that a RIFA 481 is fitted to a C64 mainboard - treat that specific part number as unverified. A Bourns 4308R-series or equivalent Vishay pack is the functionally correct part.

facts.label: Arrays on board
facts.value: 4 (RP1, RP2 = 33 ohm isolated 8-way; RP3 = 3k3 bussed 8-way; RP4 = 3k3 bussed 10-way)

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Epoxy potting and marking
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The trimmed network is coated in a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish that also carries the colour code - here a small white dot or body colour denoting the resistance. Glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Lead frame
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The array's leads are formed from a copper-alloy lead frame, plated in tin or solder, so the package can be inserted on a 2.54 mm pitch and wave-soldered.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Lead-frame plating
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The copper-alloy leads are plated in tin or tin-lead so the array wavesolders cleanly. The frame is stamped from a coil in the same high-speed presses as the connector contacts.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Glass-filled epoxy coat
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The whole array is coated in an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica, which both seals the tracks and gives the package its mechanical rigidity. The colour body is the colourant in that coat.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Silica sand
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser trimming of the network
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: An excimer or Nd:YAG laser ablates slots in each printed resistor until a closed-loop bridge calls out the right value. Bulk trimming can be 'slug' or 'v-cut' (pushing a wedge of resistive material aside) rather than ablating material away.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.note: In 1982 a good fraction of commodity SIP networks were still trimmed by abrasive nozzle jet rather than laser.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser source (Nd:YAG)
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: Neodymium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet was the standard solid-state laser for resistor trimming: a garnet crystal doped with neodymium, pumped optically and emitting at 1.06 microns. The yttrium-aluminium-garnet host is grown from alumina and yttrium oxide.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Alumina from bauxite
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Bauxite profile
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser trimming system
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: A pulsed laser head over a moving substrate with an in-line ohmmeter, cutting and re-measuring thousands of times per second. Excimer lasers were used for fine-resolution cuts on thick films.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Screen printing through a photoemulsion
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: A stainless-steel mesh stretched over a frame, coated in photosensitive emulsion, contact-exposed through a film or direct-imaged artwork, developed, and then the paste squeegeed through the open areas onto the substrate. Line width is the resistance knob.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Paste rheology
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: A thixotropic paste is essential: it must flow under the squeegee and then stand without slumping, or the printed line will blur and the resistance will drift off value. Thixotropy comes from the shape of the glass frit particles.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Stainless steel mesh
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: The printing screen is a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged. Stainless was standard because it must survive repeated abrasion by the abrasive paste in the paste.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Iron ore
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: RuO2 cermet resistive paste
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: The resistive phase is sub-micron ruthenium dioxide powder blended with a lead-borosilicate glass frit and an organic vehicle (butyl acetate / terpineol) into a thixotropic paste. Its sheet resistance is a known function of powder loading, so a given RuO2 fraction sets a given ohms-per-square.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal, recovered as a by-product of platinum ores; it was the most expensive thing in a 1980s thick-film resistor and a genuine cost driver. The ore-to-powder chain is not traced here.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Platinum-group ore bearing ruthenium
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium occurs almost only as a minor by-product in platinum and nickel ores (Merensky Reef, Sudbury, Norilsk) rather than in a ruthenium ore of its own. It reaches the resistor paste as ammonium ruthenium chloride after a complex refining sequence.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Coarse chain only; the ammonium ruthenium chloride route is my summary of standard refining practice, not a C64-specific fact.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Merensky Reef and nickel-copper sulphide ores
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium and the other platinum-group metals have no ore of their own. They occur at a few parts per million in the Merensky Reef of the Bushveld Complex and in the Sudbury and Norilsk nickel-copper sulphide ores, so the resistor industry bought ruthenium as a refinery by-product at platinum-group prices.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Chromitite layer
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: The Bushveld Reef sequence is layered, with a chromitite band, and ruthenium concentrates in that band. Its concentration is why South Africa, not Russia or Canada, supplied the ruthenium.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Ruthenium dioxide powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Anhydrous RuO2 is the only resistor phase that survives to 900 C without oxidising away; the surrounding glass is what actually carries the current. Its scarcity set the price of every cermet resistor made in the 1980s.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Refining to capacitor-grade powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: The refinery dissolves platinum-group metal concentrate, precipitates the individual metals as ammonium or chloride salts, and reduces them to fine powder. Every step is a controlled chemical precipitation, and particle size is a sale specification in its own right.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Alumina substrate with printed elements
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A 0.6 mm thick 96 percent alumina bar, pre-fired and metallised. Conductive paste is printed through a photo-plated stainless screen onto the top face only, then the whole bar is fired to fuse the glass frit and mature the resistor.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Tunnel-kiln firing of the printed bar
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A continuous belt or pusher kiln takes the printed substrate through a controlled temperature ramp so the resistors are 'aged' in the firing. Thick-film resistors are typically driven 50 percent above their rating for 15-25 minutes to burn in the grain boundaries and stabilise the value.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Refractory kiln furniture
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: Alumina setters and shelves carrying the fired substrates through the kiln, themselves made from tabular alumina. Furnace furniture consumption is a real cost line in ceramics, and it comes from the same alumina as the substrate.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Alumina from bauxite
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Bauxite profile
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Continuous kiln
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A belt or pusher kiln with profiled hot zones, carrying the printed bar through drying, burnout, peak and controlled cooling. The cooling rate matters as much as the peak, because too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Thick-film conductor metallisation
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A base-metal paste of finely divided silver or copper in a glass frit, screen-printed and fired at ~850 C to form the end lands, jumpers and common bus the resistive tracks connect to. Silver-palladium pastes were common in this era; copper pastes needed a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid oxidising.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: Lead-free base metals such as Ni were not yet standard in 1982; the Ni-bearing pastes the prompt alludes to became common later.

facts.label: Base metal
facts.value: Ag or Ag-Pd (Ni-Pd-Ag common from the late 1980s)

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Silver ore (argentite)
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: Silver came from argentite and other primary veins, but by 1982 a large and growing share of the world supply was a by-product of lead-zinc and copper refining - the metal recovered from anode slimes and residues rather than from its own mine. Mined silver is essentially a by-product metal.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: The Mexico, Peru, US and Canadian mining districts were still significant, but lead-silver ore grades were so low by the 1980s that silver was economically a by-product of base-metal mining.

facts.label: Common ore
facts.value: argentite Ag2S; also pyrargyrite and stephanite

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Silver powder for the conductor paste
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: The conductor paste is fine silver flake or powder, not a bulk metal: it has to print as a paste and then fuse into a continuous conductor at 850 C without melting. Domestically mined silver was almost entirely gone by 1982; the metal was bought on the London spot market.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: atomised or electrolytic silver powder / flake, typically 99.9 %

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.name: Discrete axial resistor families
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.description: Three manufacturing routes to a 1/4 W axial resistor coexisted in 1982. The 250407 used overwhelmingly carbon film; carbon composition was still common in cheaper consumer goods; metal film was reserved for precision.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal-foil precision resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: An ultra-precise resistor built from rolled, etched metal foil - nickel, a nickel-chromium-iron alloy, or copper - clamped between a rigid steel/ceramic case and a polished die. Changing the roll geometry stretches the foil, so the resistance can be set with a screw to one part in a million.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Included to explain the 'foil' end of the precision-resistor family. No metal-foil parts appear in a Commodore 64; these were calibration standards in the lab and appeared in later high-precision analogue equipment.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Case, die and tension screw
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The foil roll is sandwiched between a hardened case and a polished die with a slight bow. Turning the adjustment screw changes the roll's circumference, stretching the foil and raising the resistance by a controlled fraction of a part per million.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The polished die was lapped on cast iron with progressively finer abrasive; a diamond paste finish gives sub-micron flatness.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Lapped die surface
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The die is lapped on cast iron with successively finer abrasive and finished with a sub-micron diamond polish. A die flat to a fraction of a micron is what lets the tension be controlled to a fraction of a part per million.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Etched metal foil roll
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A strip of pure or alloy foil is rolled to a very tight radius on a mandrel and acid-etched to remove most of it, leaving fine islands of metal in series across the roll. The number of islands, not the sheet resistivity, sets the resistance.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Foil metal
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Pure nickel or a nickel-iron-chromium alloy, chosen for a low temperature coefficient of resistivity and for its mechanical stability under tension.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Selective acid etch
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The rolled foil is immersed in a ferric-nitrate or nitric-acid etch that removes most of it, leaving a fine grid of metal islands. Resistance is then set by the number of islands in the path, which is why foil resistors have their characteristic very high, very stable resistance values.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Nitric acid
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A standard mineral acid made by the Ostwald process from ammonia oxidised over a platinum-rhodium gauze. Included here only to keep the chain honest.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Wirewound power resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin and vitreously enamelled. Used for the few watts-and-above duties - notably the 7805 regulator's dropping resistor and the video level network. Accurate, stable, but large and inductive.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Wound resistors do not appear in the 250407 BOM I checked; included because they were the standard answer for the same problems in the C64's power supply and peripherals of the same era.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Resistance alloy wire (NiCr / FeCr / CuNi)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Nichrome has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys and so minimises the wire length needed; constantan (CuNi) is used where a lower temperature coefficient matters more.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Constantan is 60/40 copper-nickel. Neither alloy is traced to ore here.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Vitreous enamel coating
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: The wound wire is coated in a glassy enamel and baked, which is why wirewounds are glassy-bodied. Continuous operation above about 200 C needs cement or silicone instead.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Vitreous enamel
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: A glassy coating on the wound wire, applied as a slurry and baked. The enamel is what makes a wirewound part look like a glass-bodied component and is what lets it run hot without the wire oxidising.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Silica sand
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Ceramic bobbin
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: A grooved steatite or alumina former on which a length of enamelled resistance alloy wire is wound. Steatite (magnesium silicate) was the classic low-cost bobbin material.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Steatite bobbin material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite, a compacted and fired magnesium silicate, was the classic low-cost bobbin and ceramic insulator material: it machines green, fires to a hard white body and is cheap.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Talc and soapstone
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite is a mixture of talc with clay. Talc is mined from metamorphosed dolomitic rock and is one of the few minerals still worked in a form close to its natural state.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Dolomitic host rock
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Talc forms where magnesium-rich carbonate rock is metamorphosed; the talc is quarried from that host.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal film resistor (1 % precision)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A NiCr or FeCr film vacuum-deposited onto an alumina substrate, then laser-trimmed to a tight tolerance. Where the VIC-II colour burst and the composite video level had to be set to a few parts in a thousand, a 1 percent metal film part was used instead of a 5 percent carbon film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The 250407's parts list is dominated by 5 percent parts; I have not been able to confirm which individual reference designators were 1 percent metal film.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Termination cap and lead
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A crimped steel or aluminium cap grips the lead and makes contact with the film, then the whole assembly is plated in nickel. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads, never bare tin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Termination cap material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A nickel-plated steel or aluminium cap, crimped onto the lead and forming the low-resistance joint to the film. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads: the plating has to be uniform for the part to be consistent.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Laser scribing of the spiral
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A pulsed ruby or Nd:YAG laser ablates a thin groove across the film, lengthening the resistive path. A closed-loop measuring bridge runs thousands of cuts per second until the value converges. This - not a mechanical wheel - is what buys the 0.1-1 percent tolerance.

facts.label: Achievable tolerance
facts.value: 0.1-1 %, vs +/-5 % for a cut carbon film

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Vacuum deposition bell
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Parts are racked in a bell jar under vacuum; NiCr is evaporated at high current and condenses as a sub-micron film over the resistive area only, defined by an evaporated aluminium mask. Vacuum deposited - not sputtered - was standard for axial resistors in 1982.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: NiCr resistance alloy
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: 80/20 nickel-chromium, or 75/25 iron-chromium, evaporated or sputtered from a heated wire or boat in a vacuum bell. NiCr is chosen for its bulk resistivity (~1.1 uohm-m) and, critically, for having a near-zero temperature coefficient of resistivity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The chromium master alloy is itself a metallurgical product; I have not traced it to ore in this tree.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Chromium source (chromite)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The chromium in NiCr comes overwhelmingly from chromite, FeCr2O4, a hard black spinel mined from the Bushveld Complex and the Stillwater Complex in South Africa - then, as now, essentially the whole world supply. Ferrochrome is made in submerged-arc furnaces and shipped to the resistor alloy makers as 60-70 % Cr alloy.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: South Africa supplied the majority of the world chrome ore consumed by the Western electronics industry in 1982.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Flat ceramic substrate (not a tube)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or a flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, because the uniform flat substrate is what makes laser scribing produce a stable, precise spiral.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal-film substrate material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Metal film resistors need a very flat and very uniform substrate because the film resistance is set by the length of the deposited track, not by the substrate geometry. Alumina ceramic bar or a flat ceramic tube is used for that flatness.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Alumina from bauxite
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Bauxite profile
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon composition resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A rod of carbon and clay, compression-moulded into a small cylinder with metal end caps. Very cheap and very noisy, with a wide temperature coefficient and drift. Still used in 1982 in low-cost consumer goods and audio gear, but on the C64 itself it was already being displaced by carbon film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Some very early Commodore boards (VIC-20, early PET) did use composition resistors; the 250407 does not appear to.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Swaged metal end caps and wire leads
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Soft tin or brass caps are pressed over the moulded slug, then a tinned copper wire lead is swaged inside the cap, giving the familiar bulbous ends of a composition resistor.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Lead wire is tin-plated copper drawn from rod, not tinned after the fact.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tin for the end caps (cassiterite)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Tin is smelted from cassiterite, SnO2, the ore of tin. Because cassiterite is heavy and chemically inert it concentrates in placers and in alluvial tin streaming, and because cassiterite is dense it also accumulates in some alluvial gold deposits, where it was a nuisance.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Compression moulding
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The mix is pressed in a matched-metal die at tens of tonnes to fill a slug shaped like a small pill, then baked. End caps of tin or brass are pressed on after cure.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Matched metal die
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A matched-metal compression die with a cavity shaped like the finished slug. The cavity is chrome plated to survive the abrasive mix and the pressure.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Iron ore
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Composition mix (graphite + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A stiffer, higher-carbon paste than the film slurry. Because it is bulk rather than surface-conductive, the resistance is set by the geometry of the moulded rod itself, not by a pattern on its skin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Diluent clay in the composition mix
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A much higher clay fraction than in the film slurry, because a composition resistor has to be a weak conductor in bulk. Kaolin was the traditional diluent, the same mineral as in the film mix.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Feldspar weathering front
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Kaolin forms where granite decomposition leaves an acid-leached clay blanket; the parent rock is mined as dimension stone or washed as sand.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Kaolinite
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, formed by intense feldspar weathering and worked from kaolin pits.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon film resistor (1/4 W axial)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The bulk of the board's resistors. A thin, discontinuous film of carbon and clay laid on a hollow alumina ceramic tube; carbon loading sets the resistance. Cheap, 5 percent, and tolerant of being bent during manual insertion.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 1 ohm to 10 Mohm, here 100 ohm to 1 Mohm

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Offset-printed colour-code bands
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The value and tolerance rings are printed on the epoxy body by an offset (rotogravure / dry-offset) coater using inks fired onto the surface. Three bands give significant figures, one multiplier, one tolerance. A 5 percent part gets a gold band; 1 percent gets brown.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Bands are printed AFTER the part is trimmed and moulded - the trim determines the value, the print only reports it.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white; gold, silver

facts.label: Method
facts.value: offset printing, ink cured onto epoxy

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Ink cure
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The printed body is cured in a conveyor oven, not flame-fused. This is why the epoxy body has to be a thermoset: it has to survive the band-printing cure without flowing.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Band ink
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Offset printing inks cured onto the epoxy body. The ink is a pigment in an oil and resin vehicle fired at a few hundred degrees so it will not rub off or solvent-attack during board cleaning.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Moulded epoxy body
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The trimmed resistor is transfer-moulded in epoxy, or coated in a phenolic shell, sealing the film from humidity. Moulding compound is a phenolic or epoxy resin filled with silica flour.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Epoxy moulding of the resistor body
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The resistor is placed in a transfer tool and encapsulated in epoxy resin cured at ~150-175 C for several minutes. Epoxy is chosen because it shrinks little and does not stress the film on cooling.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Value trimming (abrasive wheel)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A diamond wheel cuts a narrow slot through the film from the end of the tube, lengthening the resistive path a few micrometres at a time until the measured resistance hits the middle of the tolerance band. This is why carbon film resistors are called 'film' and why their tolerance is fixed after firing rather than before.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Modern carbon film is still trimmed this way; laser trimming only ever made sense for thin film.

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: abrasive slot, NOT a laser scribing cut

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Abrasive cut-off wheel
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A thin abrasive wheel, run at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, cuts a slot through the film. Each pass lengthens the resistive path slightly; a few passes reach value.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Aluminium oxide abrasive
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The standard grinding abrasive of the era, made by calcining alumina. Synthetic diamond was used only where the cut had to be finer.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Alumina from bauxite
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Bauxite profile
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Axial lead termination (electroplate)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A lead is pushed down each end of the tube through the carbon film, and the assembly is barrel-plated in an electroless or electrolytic nickel bath so the film and lead make a low-resistance, solderable joint. In 1982 this was almost always nickel, sometimes with a thin silver flash.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tinned copper lead wire
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The axial lead is drawn copper wire, cut to length, tinned in a molten tin or tin-lead pot so the resistor dips cleanly in the wave-solder bath. Tinning is what stops the bare copper wire from oxidising between the barrel plating step and the board.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: ~0.6 mm diameter, tinned in a 230-250 C pot

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Electrolytic nickel plating bath
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The lead and film are plated in a sulfamate or a Watts-type nickel bath. A sulfonamide-derived depolarising agent suppresses hydrogen evolution, so the deposit is ductile and the lead does not become brittle - which matters because a brittle lead snaps inside the resistor.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Nickel ore (laterite)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Garnierite, an hydrated nickel-magnesium silicate, is the classic ore. New Caledonia in the South Pacific and Cuba dominated world laterite supply in 1982, and the laterite is smelted to ferronickel rather than refined to pure nickel - the ferronickel then goes to a converter for the plating grade.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The nickel chain is carried in the metals file; this node exists so the plating bath has an origin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Electroplating line (sulfamate / alkaline nickel)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Racks of resistors are plated in a barrel or belt line, then rinsed and dried. Plate thickness is the mechanical anchor that stops the lead being pulled out.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Film deposition on the tube
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The carbon-clay slurry is sprayed or dipped onto the rotating tube in a controlled spiral so the film lands only over the intended resistance length. Patterning the film length, not its thickness, is the primary way the value is dialled in.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Cure fire and carbonisation
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A conveyor tunnel oven takes the coated tube to about 260 C, curing the phenolic and converting the carbonaceous binder to a stable conductive carbon film.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Ceramic tube substrate
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A thin-wall extruded alumina tube, 0.5 mm outside diameter, whose wall carries the film. Hollow construction halves the ceramic mass per resistor, and the tube's inner bore is what the trimmer's abrasive cut reaches.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tube extrusion and firing
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Plasticised alumina is extruded through a die to a tube, cut to length on a flying saw, and fired in a tunnel kiln. Density is controlled so the film sees a reproducible surface.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Alumina (Al2O3) powder
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: 99 percent or better calcined alumina, the standard substrate for both resistor tubes and ceramic capacitor bodies. Strong, cheap, dimensionally stable, and electrically insulating.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Bayer alumina refinery
