mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Bauxite is crushed, digested in hot caustic soda to dissolve the alumina as sodium aluminate, the liquor is seeded with fine alumina to precipitate pure hydroxide, and the hydroxide is calcined at 1000-1300 C to finished 99.7 % alumina. Everything that does not dissolve - the red mud - is pumped to a tailings dam.

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: red mud, tens of tonnes per tonne of alumina

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Caustic soda digestion
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The Bayer process step that actually dissolves the ore: concentrated sodium hydroxide at pressure converts gibbsite to soluble sodium aluminate. NaOH was the dominant digestant because soda ash was cheaper; the potassium-hydroxide variant appeared in later residue-reduction schemes and is not the 1982 mainstream.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Bauxite (aluminium ore)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The only ore that is predominantly aluminium. A soft, earthy, red-brown laterite of hydrated aluminium oxides (gibbsite, boehmite, diaspore) with iron and silica in the clay fraction. Roughly half of all aluminium ever smelted has come from bauxite.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The Weipa (Australia) and Boké (Guinea) deposits were the dominant bauxite sources in 1982.

facts.label: Al2O3 content
facts.value: 45-60 % typical, Guinea and Weipa ores the richest

facts.label: Formed by
facts.value: intense tropical chemical weathering of aluminous bedrock

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Laterite and its parent rock
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Bauxite is the end product of one of the most intense weathering processes on Earth: hot, wet, tropical conditions strip silica and alkalis out of clay and shale and leave the nearly insoluble aluminium hydroxides behind. The parent rock is often a clay or a weathered basalt, and the whole profile is metres thick.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Laterite hardens on exposure, which is why bauxite outcrops are quarried rather than dug, and why the term covers a family of tropical residual soils and ferricretes.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Resistor slurry (carbon + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Carbon black mixed with china clay as a diluent and a phenolic binder in alcohol to a printable paste. Clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance; binder keeps the film from flaking off the tube.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Clay here is kaolin, not the ball clay used in porcelain.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Phenolic binder resin in the slurry
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Phenol-formaldehyde, dissolved in alcohol, holds carbon and clay to the tube and survives the 260 C cure. Cured phenolic also serves as the resistor's opaque body coating, which protects the film from humidity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Some 1980s resistor makers switched the body coating to epoxy; the C64's were visually indistinguishable without a microscope.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Kaolin (china clay) diluent
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, crushed and classified to a fine particle size. It is inert and non-conducting, so raising its share raises the sheet resistance of the dried film.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Feldspar weathering front
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Kaolin forms where granite and pegmatite decomposition leaves an acid-leached clay blanket. The parent rock is potassium-sodium aluminosilicate, typically mined as dimension stone or as a sand wash.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The dioctahedral 1:1 clay mineral that gives kaolin its name. Formed by intense feldspar weathering and redeposition in kaolin pits.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black (channel/process black)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Furnace black made by feeding heavy residual oil (or natural gas) into a hot air-cooled furnace so that it impinges and soots on water-cooled steel. Furnace black from petroleum feedstock was the standard conductive phase in resistors by the 1980s.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Petroleum residuum (heavy oil feed)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The heaviest fraction of an atmospheric or vacuum refinery distillation, a viscous bituminous residue rich in aromatics. Historically the feedstock for furnace black; later, natural gas.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Crude oil (refinery feed)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The whole hydrocarbon chain of the board terminates here: the carbon in the resistors, the epoxy and phenolic mouldings, the plastic film capacitors and the connector housings all began as crude.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black furnace (soot reactor)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A refractory-lined combustion chamber with a ~1500 C flame and water-cooled steel scraper blades. Feed oil is sprayed across the flame; the resulting soot is scraped off as a mat and pelletised.

mb.rf-modulator.name: Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV)
mb.rf-modulator.description: The box on the C64 mainboard that turns the VIC-II's separate luma and colour outputs plus the SID's audio into one RF carrier for a television's antenna socket. Commodore published it as schematic 251025 and 251696: a handful of Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, one trimmer capacitor and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack and a ten-way terminal strip on the edge of the board.
mb.rf-modulator.note: Three corrections to the brief. First, 55.25 and 62.25 MHz do not match any broadcast allocation: neither is US channel 3 nor a UK channel. US VHF channel 3 has its picture carrier at 61.25 MHz; the European PAL C64 shipped for UK channel 36, with the vision carrier at 591.25 MHz. Second, the part numbers 474040 and 474041 could not be corroborated in any Commodore document I could reach; the documented modulator identifiers are the schematic numbers 251025 and 251696 and the part numbers 250469, 326130-01, 51A1-10 and the Mitsumi MD6 series. Third, the standard Commodore modules are discrete through-hole boards with Japanese transistors, not thin-film hybrids - the hybrid subtree is included as illustrative.

facts.label: US channel 3 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 61.25 MHz, chroma 64.25 MHz, sound 67.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: US channel 4 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 67.25 MHz, chroma 70.25 MHz, sound 73.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: UK channel 36 (PAL-I, UHF)
facts.value: vision carrier 591.25 MHz, chroma 585.75 MHz, sound 585.25 MHz, intercarrier 5.5 MHz

facts.label: Channel switching
facts.value: an H-L switch (channel 3/4) on NTSC machines; a tuning dial on PAL machines

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the C64's ~9 V unregulated rail, stabilised internally by a zener

facts.label: Terminals
facts.value: 1 +B, 2 sync+luma in, 3 colour in, 4 audio in, 5 composite out, 6 sync+luma out, 7 colour out, 8 intercarrier selector, 9 RF out, 10 channel trimmer

facts.label: Size
facts.value: ~63.6 x 62.6 x 24 mm for the 251025 module

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.name: Modulator manufacture, alignment and test
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.description: A 1980s RF module was assembled by hand through a small number of components, soldered, then aligned: the channel trimmer is set against a television signal generator or a spectrum analyser, the intercarrier selector link is fitted for the market, the level network is checked on a video monitor, and the unit is burn-in tested with a television running.
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.note: The 1980s practice was to align each module against a television set rather than a calibrated instrument, which explains why modules from different batches did not all land on exactly the same channel and why the rear-panel trimmer dial existed.

facts.label: Soldering
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, wave or hand, flux residue cleaned

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: trim the channel capacitor to the exact vision carrier for the market

facts.label: Test
facts.value: modulate a known composite pattern and check picture, sound and intercarrier beat

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.name: Tin-lead solder and flux
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.description: A 60/40 tin-lead alloy melts at around 190-215 C depending on composition, which is why it was the universal electronics solder of the era; the lead keeps the melting point low and wets the copper lead frames and the nickel-plated transistor legs. The flux is rosin or an organic acid, chemically inert but hygroscopic, so it had to be washed off or it caused resistive leakage in damp climates.
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.note: Tin-lead was abandoned in electronics from about 2000 onwards and the change cost the industry a decade of higher reflow temperatures and wetting problems; the 1982 practice was unremarkable and correct for its time.

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.name: Rosin flux from pine
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.description: Colophony, the sticky amber resin left when crude turpentine is distilled off pine resin, dissolved in isopropanol or in a blend of solvents to make the classic mild flux. It is non-corrosive but must be removed because it is hygroscopic and slightly conductive when damp.
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.note: Rosin was largely replaced by halide-free organic acid and no-clean fluxes in the 1990s, but a 1982 board was always hand-cleaned with isopropanol and trichloroethane.

facts.label: Carrier
facts.value: isopropanol or a mixed aromatic/aliphatic solvent

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.tu.name: Crude turpentine and pine resin
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.tu.description: Distilling crude turpentine - a mixture of terpene hydrocarbons collected by tapping pine trees - leaves a viscous amber residue of rosin and pine gum. Natural rosin supply did not keep up with the 1980s electronics industry, so most flux rosin was actually tall oil rosin, a byproduct of pine kraft pulp production.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: ~60% natural gum rosin, ~40% tall oil rosin by the 1980s

mb.rf-modulator.quality.name: Why the RF picture was poor
mb.rf-modulator.quality.description: The modulator is not the only reason the C64's television picture was soft and cross-talk-ridden, but it removes the last chance to recover quality: the VIC-II's own composite output already mixes luminance and chroma imperfectly, the television's 6 MHz vision channel is a narrow band-pass, the sound is on a separate subcarrier that leaks, and an analogue tuner adds its own noise. Every stage is lossy and they compound.
mb.rf-modulator.quality.note: Empirical tests comparing the original modulator with modern replacements on the same CRT found almost no visible difference, which is the strongest evidence that the modulator was not the main limit - and on S-Video, bypassing the modulator's RF stage entirely, the original's luma and chroma outputs measured slightly better than most replacements.

facts.label: Vision channel width
facts.value: ~5.5 MHz for a 625-line PAL signal in a 6 or 7 MHz slot

facts.label: Composite crosstalk
facts.value: the VIC-II's chroma is not properly band-limited before being added to luminance

facts.label: Set-side limit
facts.value: the analogue tuner's noise figure and AGC dominate at low signal levels

mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain.name: Two composite paths in one module
mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain.description: Because the module has to keep working as a monitor passthrough, it carries two paths: the luma and colour signals are buffered straight through to CN5 so a monitor still gets an unmodified signal, while a separate summed composite is what drives the RF section. This is why S-Video from a breadbin is clean while the RF picture is not - the lossy parts of the chain are only on the RF path.

facts.label: Terminals 6 and 7
facts.value: sync+luma out and colour out, buffered from the inputs

facts.label: Terminal 5
facts.value: composite out, the sum, also fed to CN5 pin 4 on the 5-pin board

mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain..name: NTSC and PAL variants
mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain..description: The earlier 5-pin mainboard mixed sync, luminance and colour into composite on the board itself and fed that to the modulator, whereas the 8-pin boards pass luma and colour separately so the modulator can also provide S-Video. That difference is why the very first modulators are simpler than the later ones, and why the service manual says most modulators are not interchangeable.

facts.label: 5-pin board (326298-01)
facts.value: composite built on the mainboard; the modulator adds audio only

facts.label: 8-pin boards (250407-04, 250425, 250441-01, 250469)
facts.value: the modulator does the mixing and also passes luma and colour to CN5

mb.rf-modulator.variants.name: Modulator part numbers and revisions
mb.rf-modulator.variants.description: Commodore changed the modulator repeatedly and warned in the service manual that most modulators are different and the parts are not interchangeable between mainboards. Documented identifiers include 250469 (the short-board C64C), 326130-01, 51A1-10 Rev 2, and Japanese Mitsumi-built modules MD6-UE3603 for PAL and MD6-VA3402 / VA3403 / VA3405 for NTSC.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.note: The part numbers 474040 and 474041 in the brief could not be found in any Commodore document or parts list I could reach. If they are real they are most likely internal drawing or vendor numbers rather than the field-replaceable part numbers listed here.

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-UE3603
facts.value: 470 uF 10 V, 2 x 100 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V - the PAL version

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-VA3402/3403/3405
facts.value: NTSC versions with different electrolytic sets

mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.name: The 'toad' module nickname
mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.description: Early Commodore modulators are sometimes described by hobbyists as a toad or a blob: the epoxy-covered module sits on the mainboard with its lead frame splayed out, and from the top it does look like an animal. The nickname is not a Commodore part name - it exists only in the collector community.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.note: I could not find any published source using this nickname for the C64 modulator; it may come from a different platform. Flagged as uncertain.

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.name: Mitsumi-built modules
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.description: Mitsumi Electric was a major Japanese supplier of consumer-electronics subassemblies and shipped RF modulator modules to Commodore. The MD6 prefix denotes the module family; the suffix distinguishes NTSC from PAL and the electrolytic set.

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.name: The 1984 C64C video path
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.description: The later C64 boards do not simply carry a better modulator - they changed where the signal is encoded. A dedicated video encoder IC generates the composite and separate luma/chroma outputs from the VIC-II's signals, so the video is encoded once, to a defined standard, outside the modulator; the RF modulator is then reduced to a device that only has to put that composite onto a carrier and add the audio. The contrast with the breadbin is that there the modulator itself was the video encoder as well as the modulator.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.note: The existence of a dedicated CMOS video encoder on the C64C is well established in the enthusiast literature and C64-Wiki has a page stub for the part, but I could not open a primary source to confirm the device marking or its function in this context. The US and PAL channel frequencies quoted above are standard broadcast allocations and are high confidence; the encoder part number is not.

facts.label: Encoding point
facts.value: moved off the modulator onto a dedicated encoder IC

facts.label: Result
facts.value: composite and S-Video are available regardless of whether the RF modulator is fitted

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: the RF modulator becomes a purely analogue RF carrier generator

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.name: Video encoder integrated circuit
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.description: A mask-programmed device that takes the VIC-II's luminance and chrominance plus the synchronisation inputs and generates composite video and separate luma and chrominance outputs internally, using on-chip resistor-string DACs for the levels. Building the encoder alongside the VIC-II was what made the S-Video output clean enough to be worth using.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.note: I could not verify the exact part number or its manufacturer from a primary source; treat this node as a description of the function rather than of a confirmed device.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: luminance/chrominance to composite and S-Video encoding, with internal level DACs

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: driven from the 14.318 MHz colour clock

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: The die is a small epitaxial NPN on a 100 mm P-type <111> wafer, sawn with a diamond blade, die-attached with a silver-glass preform, wire-bonded with 50 um aluminium and transfer-moulded in an epoxy-filled TO-92 tool at 150-175 C.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: This is one of about forty such transistors in a C64; the silicon branch of this tree carries the full wafer process.

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: 4-6 um N-type epi on a 10-20 ohm.cm P substrate

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Semiconductor silicon, from quartz
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: Quartz (SiO2) is reduced with petroleum coke in an electric arc furnace at 1800-2000 C to 97-99% metallurgical silicon, upgraded by trichlorosilane disproportionation to 9-11N polycrystalline silicon, pulled as a Czochralski single crystal, sawn and polished. This is the shared root of every silicon device in the C64.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: High-purity quartz
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: Pegmatite and vein quartz, acid-leached and hydrothermally purified to 99.99% SiO2, is the only commercial source of semiconductor silicon. This is the leaf of the silicon branch.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Electric arc furnace reduction of quartz
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: Quartz is mixed with petroleum coke and heated to 1800-2000 C by an electric arc furnace submerged in the charge. The carbon reduces SiO2 to silicon while the arc supplies the heat; the reaction is strongly endothermic and the furnace is the single biggest electricity consumer in the whole silicon chain.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: Almost all of the electricity for a 1980s semiconductor-grade silicon plant went into the arc furnaces, which is why the industry clustered next to cheap power.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: petroleum coke, ~2000 kg per tonne of silicon

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Carbothermal slag
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: The liquid residue from the arc furnace is calcium silicate, formed because limestone is deliberately added as a flux to keep the furnace from silting up. It is ground and sold as cement or as a road aggregate; a few hundred kg of slag per tonne of silicon is the main waste stream of the process.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~1.0-1.5 t slag per tonne of silicon

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.name: Encapsulated and hybrid module variants
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.description: Some very early Commodore modulators and several third-party and Japanese-supplied variants were potted or epoxy-dipped modules rather than a bare board: the circuit is built on an alumina or ceramic substrate with deposited resistors, is trimmed and aligned, then covered in a clear or opaque epoxy that also acts as the environmental and RF seal.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.note: The two Commodore schematic drawings I could read (251025 and 251696) both show a discrete through-hole board with Japanese transistors and an RCA jack, not a thin-film hybrid. The hybrid construction described here is real for RF modulator modules from Japanese games manufacturers of the same period and is included because the brief asks for it, but I could not verify that any specific Commodore part number used it. Treat this subtree as illustrative.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 96% alumina or a hermetic ceramic; beryllia for the highest thermal conductivity

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: thin-film or thick-film deposited and laser-trimmed on the substrate

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: transparent or opaque epoxy, transfer moulded or dipped

facts.label: Leads
facts.value: gold- or nickel-plated DIP or castellated lead frame

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.name: Substrate alignment and RF screening
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.description: After assembly the module is screened: an RF sweep is injected at the output terminal and the response curve is checked against a mask. A damaged substrate, a lifted chip termination or a cracked lead frame shows up as a notch in the response, which is why a hybrid modulator's yield is dominated by the ceramic and the assembly rather than by the design.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.note: Screen-on-substrate testing in the bare form was a 1990s technique; a 1982 hybrid was tested only after encapsulation, so a realignment meant re-encapsulating.

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: swept-response substitution with an RF sweep generator and a detector

facts.label: Pass criterion
facts.value: within a mask on insertion loss, return loss and resonance

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Chip inductor and chip capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: In a hybrid RF module the high-value capacitors and the low-value inductors are not screen-printed but chip-bonded: a fired ceramic chip capacitor with metallised terminations is reflowed onto the substrate, and an inductor is a tiny spiral of metallised polyimide on a ceramic chip. The polyimide is photosensitised, plated, etched and diced, so the inductance is set by the artwork rather than by a winding machine.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Chip inductors were a 1990s development for RF modules above about 100 MHz; a 60 MHz television modulator in 1982 used a wound coil, and the chip parts that were used were almost all capacitors.

facts.label: Chip capacitor
facts.value: fired BaTiO3 or tantalum, terminated in fired silver or a solderable metal

facts.label: Chip inductor
facts.value: photosensitised polyimide spiral on alumina, 1-100 nH typical

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Laser trimming of the film resistors
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: A laser is pulsed at a deposited resistor while a bridge measures its value, cutting a slot in the film a few microns wide to raise the resistance by a controlled amount. Each pulse changes the value by a known increment and the bridge closes the loop, so a resistor can be trimmed to 0.1% or better in a fraction of a second. Before laser trimming was cheap, the same slot was cut by abrading with a sand jet under a bridge, which was slower and only got to about 5%.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Laser trimming became standard in thick-film hybrid manufacture in the late 1980s; a 1982 module was trimmed by a mechanical probe that cut a slot in the film, or not trimmed at all.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.name: Hybrid module assembly and transfer moulding
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.description: The die or chip components are bonded to the substrate, the lead frame is attached, and the whole assembly is transfer moulded in epoxy: a silicone-rubber mould loaded with epoxy powder is vibrated to pack it around the part, the encapsulant is pressed in, and it is cured at 150-175 C. This is the same process used for every integrated circuit in the machine.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.note: For a hybrid the mould is room-temperature or low-temperature cured so that the deposited film and any surface-mounted parts survive; for an IC the epoxy is moulded at full cure temperature.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 20-60 s per shot for a small mould

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.name: Attaching the substrate to the lead frame
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.description: The substrate is aligned to the lead frame to within a few microns, given a thin coat of conductive epoxy - silver-filled epoxy is the usual choice because it cures at only 150-200 C - or a screen-printed solder paste is printed and reflowed, then the assembly is baked so the die attaches without stress. Silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and can debond with thermal cycling, which is the classic failure mode of a hybrid module.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.note: Solder attach gives a better thermal cycle but stresses the ceramic badly on cooling because of the CTE mismatch between alumina and a Cu-Ni lead frame; this is why high-reliability hybrids prefer a compliant attach.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: 5-25 um for conductive epoxy; 1-10 um for solder attach

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-200 C for 1-4 h for silver epoxy

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.name: Silver-filled conductive epoxy
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.description: Epoxy resin loaded with 50-80% silver flakes. The flakes touch each other to form a percolating conductor while the epoxy gives mechanical strength and cures at a temperature the chip and substrate tolerate. Bulk resistivity is about 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm, two to three orders of magnitude worse than a metal, so it is used for bonding and for conductive fill, never for signal.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.note: Loading the epoxy with gold instead of silver gives a non-migrating adhesive used in medical and aerospace die attach, but at roughly ten times the cost.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.name: Gold-plated DIP lead frame
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.description: The substrate is attached to a lead frame by reflow or conductive epoxy, and the frame's pins are plated. Gold is used where the RF signal leaves the module, because a nickel or tin surface has poor conductivity at 60 MHz and tarnishes; in cheap modules only the signal pins are gold and the supply pins are tinned.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.note: Hard gold plating came in because gold on soft gold diffused into the bond pads.

facts.label: Frame
facts.value: nickel-iron or copper alloy strip, stamped and formed

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel on signal pins, tin on supply pins

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.name: Gold and its ore
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.description: Gold is recovered by cyanide leaching of ore and tailings after gravity and flotation concentration, then adsorbed on activated carbon and electrowon or precipitated with zinc, and finally refined by electrolysis to 99.99%. This is the leaf of the gold chain.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: pH 10-10.5 with lime and oxygen, 1-5 g cyanide per tonne of ore

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.name: Cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.description: Crushed and agglomerated ore is soaked in dilute alkaline cyanide with aeration; gold dissolves as the dicyanoaurate complex and is adsorbed on activated carbon columns, stripped with hot caustic soda and zinc dust, smelted, and electrolytically refined.

facts.label: Adsorption
facts.value: ~0.5-2 g gold per tonne of carbon

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.name: Epoxy encapsulant as RF seal
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.description: A clear or opaque filled epoxy poured or transfer moulded over the finished substrate. In RF modules it does three jobs at once: it excludes moisture and contaminants, it holds the components against vibration, and - because it is a low-loss dielectric with a stable dielectric constant - it fixes the stray capacitance around the tank, which is what stops the carrier drifting with humidity. A conductive epoxy variant is used as a ground plane on the reverse of the substrate.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight for low CTE and low moisture uptake

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Thin-film and thick-film resistor networks
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: A film of nickel-chromium is deposited by vacuum evaporation or sputtering onto the alumina, then patterned by photolithography and etching. Because the sheet resistance of the film is very uniform the as-deposited value is already within a few percent, so a trim brings it to its exact value.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.note: Thick film, a screen-printed ruthenium-oxide paste fired at 800-900 C, was the normal choice for a cheap RF module in 1982; thin film was reserved for precision timing and gain stages.

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: sand-blast trim to 5-10% before laser trimming; laser trim to 0.1-1% became cheap only in the late 1980s

facts.label: TCR
facts.value: 25-100 ppm/K, far better than a thick-film resistor

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Ruthenium-oxide cermet paste
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: The thick-film resistor material: finely divided ruthenium dioxide mixed with a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed through a 100-250 um mesh and fired on a belt furnace at 800-900 C. The glass binds conductor and semiconductor together, and the resistance is set largely by how much glass is in the paste.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.note: Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal and one of the rarest elements in industrial use; it is why thick-film resistors are more expensive than the carbon-film parts they replaced in value terms.

facts.label: Sheet resistivity
facts.value: 10-1000 ohm per square depending on the paste

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Ruthenium, from anode slime
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: Recovered commercially from the nickel-copper mattes of Sudbury-type nickel ores, where it concentrates in the anode slime. The slime is dissolved and the platinum-group metals separated by selective precipitation and solvent extraction.

facts.label: Abundance
facts.value: ~1 part per billion in the Earth's crust, among the rarest stable elements

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Nickel matte and anode slime
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: Copper and nickel concentrates are smelted to a matte, converted to blister metal, then electrolytically refined in a copper or nickel tankhouse. Noble metals fall out of solution as an anode slime, which is filtered, dissolved in aqua regia and separated.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Alumina substrate and its ceramic processing
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A thin, smooth, thermally conductive ceramic sheet. Alumina is made by calcining purified aluminium hydroxide, pressing or tape-casting it with an organic binder, sintering at 1500-1700 C, then lapping and laser-cutting the finished sheets to thickness. It is inert, dimensionally stable and easy to metallise.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesium oxide sintering aid
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A few tenths of a percent of magnesium oxide is added to 96% alumina before sintering to stop the ceramic over-shrinking and to fire it at a lower temperature, which is what makes 96% alumina affordable for a hybrid substrate.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: sintering temperature down by ~100-150 C, shrinkage reduced

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesite ore
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A magnesium carbonate rock mined in Austria, Spain, China and India, calcined at 1400-1700 C to magnesia. In the 1980s most ceramic-grade magnesia was calcined from seawater or from brine, but the rock remains the classic source.

mb.rf-modulator.supply.name: Modulator supply and zener stabiliser
mb.rf-modulator.supply.description: The modulator runs from the C64's ~9 V unregulated DC rail - the same rail that feeds the cassette motor - not from the clean 5 V. Q6 (2SC2120) buffers the feed and a zener with electrolytics sets the working voltage for the analog sections.
mb.rf-modulator.supply.note: Adrian Black's redraw of the MD6 shows the supply clearly: 9V-IN, a series resistor into a zener and a transistor shunt with a 330 uF / 47 uF pair, producing a VCC rail for the analog sections. Modern practice would run this from the 5 V rail with a proper decoupling network; the 9 V choice keeps the RF stages away from the logic's switching noise.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: ~9-12 V DC from the C64's unreg 9 V rail, terminal 1 (+B)

facts.label: Zener
facts.value: ~8.2 V class (HZ-7A1 or equivalent in the 251696 drawing)

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 220 uF and 100 uF electrolytics plus a 22 nF decoupling

mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.name: 8.2 V Zener diode
mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.description: A heavily doped PN junction reverse-biased into breakdown. The doping is so heavy that the depletion layer is only a few microns wide, which gives the device a very low capacitance and a fast, hard breakdown - ideal for a shunt regulator and for clamping.
mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2.7 V (1N4371) and 7.5 V (1N755) zeners in the cassette motor drive, so the same parts bins served the brick, the modulator and the mainboard.

facts.label: Temperature drift
facts.value: ~+2 mV per volt of nominal per degree C

mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.name: RF output network and 75 ohm match
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.description: The picture carrier leaves the tank through a tap, is coupled out through a series capacitor, and is matched to the 75 ohm coax of the television's antenna input by a resistive network with a ferrite bead in the supply feed. Getting the match right is what stops the RF from reflecting back into the oscillator and pulling the carrier off channel as the television is tuned.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.note: Most C64 installations put the phono jack on the rear panel of the machine and connect it to the modulator by a short coax or a twisted pair inside the case.

facts.label: Series match
facts.value: ~82 ohm and ~33 ohm resistors with a blocking capacitor

facts.label: Supply isolation
facts.value: a ferrite bead in the +B feed to the output stage

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: RCA phono jack, mounted on the module in the 251025 drawing

mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.supply-bead.name: Ferrite bead choke
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.supply-bead.description: A small ferrite bead slipped onto the +B lead at the RF output stage so the supply current cannot feed RF back into the tank. The bead's impedance rises with frequency, so it is a good choke at 60 MHz while passing DC almost untouched.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 50-500 ohm at 100 MHz, near zero at DC

mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.rca-jack.name: RCA phono socket
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.rca-jack.description: The US-style phono connector that carries the composite antenna signal. The centre pin is often nickel- or gold-plated brass and the outer shell is a turned brass or plated-steel barrel crimped into the body; the body is moulded in a glass-filled thermoplastic.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: brass, nickel- or gold-plated, 0.8 mm centre pin

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.name: Audio intercarrier path
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.description: A separate 4.5 MHz (NTSC) or 5.5 MHz (PAL) oscillator whose amplitude is modulated by the SID's audio output, then added to the picture carrier. Terminal 8 selects between the two: Commodore's drawing notes that terminal 8 shorted to ground is PAL and open is NTSC PAL/US.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.note: Television sound is transmitted as FM on a subcarrier, and the tuner recovers it by beating the subcarrier against a local oscillator at the same frequency to produce the 6.0 or 5.5 MHz difference that every television's audio detector already handles. Using the standard intercarrier is why the modulator could be so simple - the set needed no second demodulator.

facts.label: Input filter
facts.value: 22 uH choke and a ~10 nF capacitor

facts.label: Audio source
facts.value: the SID's amplified audio, fed from CN5 pin 3

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier.name: Intercarrier selector terminal
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier.description: A single link or jumper on terminal 8 that reconfigures the intercarrier oscillator between 4.5 and 5.5 MHz. It is the PAL/NTSC configuration link for the whole module, and it is why one board could serve both markets with a single part change.

facts.label: Terminal 8
facts.value: shorted to ground = PAL (5.5 MHz); open = NTSC (4.5 MHz)

facts.label: Implementation
facts.value: a link or a switch contact in the oscillator bias network

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.name: FM modulator network
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.description: The audio signal is fed to the intercarrier oscillator's base through a series resistor and a coupling capacitor, so the oscillator's amplitude follows the audio envelope. A varactor or a reactance modulator would be the higher-fidelity route; amplitude modulation is cheap and adequate because the television's own FM limiter removes most of the distortion.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.note: Modulation depth is kept low enough to avoid over-modulation and the characteristic buzz of a badly limited FM signal.

facts.label: Series network
facts.value: ~2.2 kOhm and a ~10 nF coupling capacitor into the oscillator base

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.name: SID audio amplifier transistor
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.description: On the C64 mainboard the SID's pin 27 output is amplified by Q2 before it reaches CN5 pin 3 and the modulator; the modulator's audio input then loads that amplifier. The stage is a common-emitter NPN with a bias divider and an emitter resistor, running from the CAN +5 V rail.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.note: This stage lives on the mainboard rather than inside the modulator, but it is why the modulator's audio input could be a simple high-impedance network.

facts.label: Device
facts.value: 2N3904 (Commodore stock 902658-01) in the mainboard audio path

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: 2SC1694 small-signal NPN
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: A TO-92 epoxy-potted silicon NPN with a 100-150 V collector rating, used as a common-emitter amplifier with a collector resistor and an unbypassed emitter resistor. The 2SC-prefix parts were the standard Japanese equivalents of the 2N series, and Commodore specified them as 'or equivalent'.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: Commodore's own parts list for the 326298 motherboard gives 2N3904 and 2N4401 with stock numbers 902658-01 and 902652-01, so the same die bins served both the mainboard and the brick; the 2SC parts came from Japanese vendors.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Trichlorosilane and the Siemens process
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: The upgrade from 99% to 11N silicon is done in a fluidised-bed Siemens reactor: hydrogen reduces trichlorosilane vapour with the deposited silicon as the seed, at 1000-1150 C, growing rods of polycrystalline silicon at a few mm per minute. Trichlorosilane itself is made by chlorinating metallurgical silicon with hydrogen chloride at 250-350 C.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Polycrystalline silicon rod
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: A 100-150 mm diameter, 1-2 m long rod of 11N silicon, sawn into ~250 mm slices by an inner-diameter or wire saw. In 1982 nearly all wafers were still sawn with an abrasive ID saw and then lapped, which is why wafers were 200-300 um thick before polishing took them to 250-300 um; the wafer laser was commercial but not universal.

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.name: Picture carrier oscillator
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.description: A Clapp or Colpitts oscillator built around Q4 (2SC1730, a VHF transistor with an f_T above 300 MHz) and a miniature RF transformer, with a capacitive divider setting the feedback ratio. Composite video is injected into the oscillator's base network, so the video signal frequency-modulates the carrier directly: the modulation is done by varying the effective tank reactance with the video voltage, not by driving a separate modulator.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.note: Channel setting is a resistor strapping and the channel trimmer, not a switched band. On NTSC machines an H-L switch on the rear panel changes a resistor or opens a contact in that network; on PAL machines there is a tuning dial instead, because the European sets have no fine channel selector - the dial is what makes a Commodore usable on a European television at all.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 61.25 MHz (NTSC ch 3), 67.25 MHz (NTSC ch 4), 591.25 MHz (PAL UK UHF ch 36)

facts.label: Feedback divider
facts.value: ~33.5 pF and 3.3 pF capacitors around the base

facts.label: Deviation
facts.value: +/-4.5 MHz from the carrier, i.e. +/-0.5 MHz of 5.5 MHz peak video

facts.label: Level network
facts.value: ~56 kOhm and 47 ohm series resistors with 30-51 pF capacitors

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.name: MA57 tuning varactor diode
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.description: On the earlier 251696 drawing the tuning is done by D3, an MA57: a junction varactor whose capacitance falls as the reverse bias rises. Lifting the tuning out of the tank into a varactor keeps the temperature coefficient and the stray capacitance low. Later drawings use a mechanical trimmer in the same position.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.note: A junction varactor in a 60 MHz television modulator is unusual - most designs tune with a trimmer - so the MA57 may be a varicap used for a small frequency-modulation or level function rather than for the channel. Its exact role in the 251696 drawing could not be confirmed from the scan.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: variable reactance in the oscillator tank

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: a screw trimmer capacitor on terminal 10 in the 251025 drawing

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Channel trimmer capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: The channel tuning element brought out to terminal 10 of the module: a small screw-adjusted trimmer, most often a ceramic or a mica trimmer in the 1-10 pF range. It sits across the tank and is set once, at the television manufacturer's alignment step, against a sweep generator or a calibrated television signal.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.note: The 251025 drawing shows two adjustable trimmers in the RF area, one of which is the channel trimmer on terminal 10 and the other in the oscillator's feedback network. Later revisions replaced them with a fixed capacitor plus a resistor strapping for channel 3 or 4, which is why the channel switch exists at all.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: ceramic screw-trimmer or mica trimmer, radial or dip

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Multilayer ceramic capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: A stack of 20-50 alternating layers of barium titanate dielectric and internal nickel electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired at 1200-1350 C, then terminated in a fired-on silver or copper end-bump. This is the material of choice for small fixed RF capacitors because its self-resonance is high and its parasitics are tiny.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.note: Class 2 (Z5U/Y5V) dielectric is used for high-value parts but has a strong temperature and voltage coefficient and is a poor choice for an RF decoupling or timing capacitor; the C64 mainboard used Class 2 parts in the tens-of-pF range on the video lines.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: BaTiO3 (Class 1, stable) or BaTiO3 plus glass (Class 2)

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1200-1350 C in a belt furnace in air

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Barium titanate ceramic powder
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: BaTiO3 is precipitated from barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, then doped and milled to sub-micron size. Barium carbonate comes from barite reduced with coke; titanium dioxide comes from ilmenite ore or from a chloride process fed on titanium ore and coke.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.note: Barium is a heavy metal and the industry moved off barium titanate where possible through the 1980s; it remained standard for Class 1 RF and high-voltage dielectrics.

facts.label: Precursors
facts.value: BaCO3 from BaSO4 + C at 1000-1200 C; TiO2 from ilmenite or rutile

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Ilmenite and the chloride process
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: Titanium dioxide pigment is made either by sulphating ilmenite ore and calcining, or by chlorinating ilmenite with coke at 900 C and oxidising the TiCl4 in a flame to TiO2. Ilmenite is a beach or dune sand of FeTiO3, concentrated by gravity and magnetic separation.

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Ilmenite sand
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: A black heavy mineral sand, essentially iron titanate, worked from beach placer deposits and from massive ore bodies. Dredged, concentrated and smelted to give titanium slag or chlorinated to give TiCl4. This is the leaf of the titanium chain.

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Barite ore (barytes)
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: A heavy white barium sulphate ore, mined chiefly as a drilling mud and as the feed for barium carbonate. This is the leaf of the barium chain.

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-trans.name: Oscillator coil and RF transformer
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-trans.description: A very small ferrite- or powdered-iron-cored coil wound on a 2-3 mm former with a tap, or a miniature two-winding transformer. The tapped winding gives both the feedback tap and an output tap, and the whole assembly sits within a few millimetres of the board's ground plane to keep the stray capacitance stable.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-trans.note: These were hand-wound on a bobbin winder and checked with an inductance meter, then adjusted by squeezing or spreading the turns. At 591 MHz (the PAL UHF version) the tank inductance scales down by roughly a factor of ten and the coil is correspondingly smaller and looser, which is one reason the PAL and NTSC modulators cannot share a part number.

facts.label: Inductance
facts.value: ~1-2 uH class for a 60 MHz tank, loaded by the divider

facts.label: Core
facts.value: ferrite or powdered iron, 2-4 mm diameter

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-trans.name: Radio-frequency ferrite core
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-trans.description: Nickel-zinc ferrite or iron powder, pressed or moulded into rings, cores or rods. NiZn is preferred above about 20 MHz because its resistivity is high enough that eddy-current loss does not swamp the circuit; MnZn is a low-frequency material and is the one used in the power transformer instead.

facts.label: Permeability
facts.value: ~10-100 for the RF grades, versus ~1000-3000 for MnZn

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.name: Channel and region switching
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.description: Three different ways of reaching the right channel appear across the revisions. The US 5-pin and 8-pin machines use a two-position H-L switch on the rear panel wired to change a component value in the oscillator tank or level network. Some later units bring a variable capacitor or a trimmer out to a dial so the user can tune to their local station. PAL machines use the UHF band, so their oscillator runs at several times the frequency of the NTSC one and the tank and output matching are different parts entirely.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.note: The C64 Wiki notes that beside the RF jack you often see an H-L switch for channels 3 and 4 (NTSC only) or a control dial for adjusting the oscillator frequency - the two mechanisms correspond to the two markets.

facts.label: Implication
facts.value: one modulator part number could not serve both markets, which is why the service manual lists several

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.name: UHF output stage for the PAL version
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.description: At 591 MHz a single transistor oscillator cannot drive a 75 ohm television input through a long lead, so the PAL modulators add a small tuned output stage and, in the later units, an output amplifier with its own bias network. The extra gain is what makes a PAL C64 usable on a European television without a booster.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.note: I could not find a schematic for the PAL variant, so the topology here is inferred from the service manual's description of the PAL modules and from the general practice of UHF modulators of the period.

facts.label: Gain
facts.value: a few dB of tuned amplification after the oscillator

facts.label: Matching
facts.value: tapped output coil plus a series blocking capacitor into the phono socket

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.name: 2SC1730 / 2SC2778 VHF transistor
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.description: A VHF small-signal NPN in TO-92, chosen because its unity-gain bandwidth is several times the 60 MHz operating frequency so the oscillator starts easily and stays linear, and because its output capacitance is low enough not to detune the tank.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.note: Both are Japanese VHF small-signal types with f_T in the low hundreds of MHz; I did not verify the exact figures against a 1982 data book.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.name: Video amplifier and clip network
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.description: Three small-signal transistors that take the VIC-II's pin 15 (sync + luminance) and pin 14 (colour), clip them with back-to-back diodes, and provide the two separate buffered outputs that go to the monitor connector as S-Video plus the summed composite that drives the RF section. Commodore called Q1-Q3 2SC1694 or equivalent; the earlier 251696 drawing uses 2SC2405.

facts.label: Clamp diodes
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) or MA151K (251696), back to back on the sync tips

facts.label: Typical network
facts.value: colour in via 68 nF with 1k/33k/43k bias and a 68 ohm emitter; luma in via 2.4 nF and 180 pF with 12k, 100 ohm and 400 ohm

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes.name: 1SS119 / MA151K clip diodes
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes.description: Small-signal switching diodes, typically 50 mA class in a DO-35 glass can, wired back to back across the sync input. They conduct only on the tips of the sync pulses and the colour burst, which clips the signal to the amplitude a television's AGC expects and stops the modulator over-modulating.

mb.logic.name: 74-series glue logic
mb.logic.description: The eleven off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Nine are 74-series bipolar TTL in black epoxy DIP; three are CMOS; one is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.
mb.logic.note: The part list below is taken from the official C64 Service Manual parts list for PCB assembly #250407 and independently corroborated by three hobbyist references (Retrogate's retro.rewind wiki, the C64-Wiki motherboard page, and MonkeySpeak's hardware detail sheet). It is NOT the list the project brief suggested (74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125, 74LS181, 74LS14, 74LS04, 74LS00) - that list belongs to the Apple II, the VIC-20 and the BBC Micro, not the C64. One widely-copied web page (oldsilicon.com) swaps the 74LS257 and the 74LS373 between U14 and U26; the service manual says U14 = 74LS258 and U26 = 74LS373, which this tree follows.

mb.logic.economics.name: What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost
mb.logic.economics.description: The whole point of the comparison: a 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors with a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price.
mb.logic.economics.note: Confidence low on the numbers and high on the shape of the answer. I could not find a primary 1983 distributor price list for 74LS parts or a documented Commodore purchase price for a 6510, so the price figures below are order-of-magnitude estimates from the general trend of semiconductor price decline and the retail pricing of the era, not measured figures. The material mass estimates are arithmetic from die dimensions and layer thicknesses and should be right to within a factor of a few; the commonly quoted '0.3 g of aluminium' figure for a 14-pin logic chip looks too high for on-die metal by about an order of magnitude and I have said so.

facts.label: Price trend
facts.value: semiconductor prices fell faster than 10%/yr through the 1980s

mb.logic.economics.price.name: The price gap between the glue and the CPU
mb.logic.economics.price.description: The commercially important fact about the 74-series on the C64 is that it was nearly free. A commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned. The 6510 was a custom NMOS design on a finer process, and as a custom part on a custom mask set it cost several dollars and could not be shared with anyone. Which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue - and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.
mb.logic.economics.price.note: Low confidence on the specific figures, high confidence on the ratio and the logic. I could not find a documented 1983 price list for 74LS logic or a Commodore purchase price for a 6510; the numbers quoted are order-of-magnitude estimates. The broader semiconductor price trend - prices falling at roughly 10-30 percent a year in real terms through the early 1980s, faster for commodity logic - is documented in the economic literature and is the basis for the direction even if not the specific prices.

mb.logic.economics.price.glue.name: Why merchant logic was cheaper per function
mb.logic.economics.price.glue.description: A merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow which makes dozens of other part numbers. Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set Commodore did not pay for and a design Commodore did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count: one mask set, one customer, one buyer, and a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit.
mb.logic.economics.price.glue.note: The amortisation argument for merchant-versus-custom silicon is a standard, well-established argument from the economics of the era rather than a measured figure for these parts.

mb.logic.economics.labour.name: How much human time, spread how thin
mb.logic.economics.labour.description: The brief's figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is the right order of magnitude and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention. It is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow: the ~60-100 front-end steps, most of which run unattended inside a tool cycle of minutes but each of which needs a cassette loaded, a recipe checked, a defect inspection and a wafer-count reconciliation. Front-end and back-end together put the figure in the low hundreds of person-minutes. The rest of the cost was in the fab: capital, cleanroom air, process engineering, and yield learning spread over years and shared across millions of gates.
mb.logic.economics.labour.note: This is an order-of-magnitude estimate and I want to be explicit about that. It is broadly consistent with the economics of the era - a commodity logic chip had a manufacturing cost in the tens of cents against a price in the tens of cents - but I have no measured figure from a 1983 fab and I have not attempted to derive one from a cost model. Treat 'about 200 person-minutes' as a defensible intuition rather than a number with a source.

facts.label: Of which back end
facts.value: probe test, assembly, final test, inspection

facts.label: Flow time
facts.value: ~1-2 weeks of factory time, of which minutes are hands-on

mb.logic.economics.labour.flow.name: Flow time versus touch time
mb.logic.economics.labour.flow.description: The distinction that makes the whole estimate work. A batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, and almost all of that time is waiting - in a furnace, in a queue, in a cassette under a nitrogen purge. What costs money is not the waiting; it is the roughly twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention. Over a fortnight, that is a couple of hours, not a couple of weeks.
mb.logic.economics.labour.flow.note: The flow-time-versus-touch-time distinction is the standard batch-fab cost structure and is well established. The specific 1-2 week figure for a full bipolar logic cycle is my estimate and is medium confidence.

mb.logic.economics.bill.name: Bill of materials for one 74LS04
mb.logic.economics.bill.description: An honest accounting of what is actually inside one of these chips, with the arithmetic shown so it can be checked.
mb.logic.economics.bill.note: Mass figures are estimates from die area and process layer thicknesses; the on-die aluminium figure is roughly 10-30 mg by arithmetic, which is well below the 0.3 g figure often quoted for these chips. The 0.3 g number is closer to the aluminium that passes through the sputter targets across a whole wafer and is later reclaimed, than to the metal in one finished device.

mb.logic.economics.bill.total.name: Total weight of a 74LS04
mb.logic.economics.bill.total.description: Roughly half a gram. A thousand chips would weigh half a kilogram; a C64's eleven glue chips weigh about five grams between them. The tree is deep and the material branches multiply, but the object itself is tiny, light and almost entirely plastic.

mb.logic.economics.bill.compound.name: Epoxy moulding compound: the heaviest part
mb.logic.economics.bill.compound.description: By mass the epoxy moulding compound is the largest single material in the chip - 0.3 to 0.6 g of silica-filled thermoset, of which about three quarters is fused silica. The die is a hundredth of the package's weight. That is the whole story of the 1983 IC in one comparison: 3 mg of clever silicon buried in 400 mg of dull polymer, so that the 3 mg could be handled, protected, and plugged into a socket.
mb.logic.economics.bill.compound.note: The compound mass range is a standard figure for a small DIP and is reasonably firm; the silica fraction within it is high confidence for era EMC formulations.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy moulding compound
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: A blend of roughly 15 percent resin system and 85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Resin system
facts.value: epoxy cresol novolac + phenolic novolac hardener

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Carbon black pigment
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: The pigment is a trivial mass fraction of the whole computer but it is the same furnace black that goes into the resistors and the toner's photoconductor.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Furnace black feedstock
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: Heavy petroleum residuum or natural gas fed to an air-cooled sooting furnace; the soot is scraped off water-cooled rotors and pelletised. It is chemically the same carbon black described in the resistor branch of this tree.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy cresol novolac resin
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which came from propylene and chlorine, which came from salt and natural gas - so the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to crude oil.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: Bisphenol A epoxy (the older, less package-friendly EPON-type system) was still used on some parts; cresol novolac had largely displaced it in logic packaging.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: phenolic novolac + hexamine, 175 C, no by-products

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Chlorine for the chlorohydrin step
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: Elemental chlorine from the chlor-alkali cell: brine electrolysed, producing chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen in one pass. The chlorine is reacted with water to make the hypochlorous acid, and the resulting dichloropropane is treated with caustic soda to open the epoxide.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Brine (concentrated sodium chloride)
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: Saturated salt solution, the feed for every chlor-alkali plant. It is the base of the entire chlorinated organic chemistry that runs underneath plastics, solvents, refrigerants and the photoresist industry - including the acid used to strip a wafer's photoresist after it has been used.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Rock salt (halite)
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: Sodium chloride, mined or dissolved from halite deposits and then evaporated from seawater in salt pans. Almost all industrial chlorine and almost all industrial sodium hydroxide in the world in 1983 came from this one rock.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epichlorohydrin (1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane)
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The bifunctional building block of every epoxy. Chlorohydrination of propylene (propene plus hypochlorous acid, with the propylene itself coming from the cracking of refinery hydrocarbons or of natural-gas liquids) gives 1,2-dichloropropane, and base dehydrochlorination closes the epoxide ring.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Propylene from the cracker
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: Steam cracking of naphtha or of natural-gas-propane. Propylene is the second most produced organic chemical in the world and the cheapest epoxide feedstock, which is why epichlorohydrin was always made from it and never from anything else.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Naphtha (light petroleum fraction)
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The low-boiling cut of crude oil distillation, roughly C5 to C11. Everything in the chain from the epoxy moulding compound through to the solder mask and the photoresist binder starts in this fraction, because it is the cheapest feedstock with the right carbon skeleton.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Crude oil
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The whole hydrocarbon trunk of the tree: the carbon in the package epoxy, the resist binder, the solder mask, the flex circuits and the petrol that moved it all.

mb.logic.economics.bill.nickel.name: Nickel: mostly in the lead frame, not the chip
mb.logic.economics.bill.nickel.description: The largest mass of nickel in the whole device is in the lead frame, a strip of 42 percent nickel iron about 0.2 mm thick weighing on the order of 100 mg for a DIP-14, plus the plating. The nickel that matters for supply-chain purposes is in that frame, not in the silicon.

mb.logic.economics.bill.nicr.name: Nickel-chromium: a film, not a lump
mb.logic.economics.bill.nicr.description: The thin-film resistors are the only place nickel and chromium appear in the die itself. A thousand or so angstroms of film over a few percent of the die area works out to well under a milligram, so the NiCr is chemically trivial even though it is functionally essential - every pull-up and bias resistor in a 74LS chip is made of it.

mb.logic.economics.bill.gold.name: Gold: under a milligram
mb.logic.economics.bill.gold.description: Gold enters twice. About eighteen wire bonds of 0.5-1.0 mil gold wire on a DIP-14 work out at a few tenths of a milligram in total. The die attach preform of gold-silicon eutectic adds a fraction of a milligram more. Together, roughly half a milligram to a milligram of gold per finished chip - and the industry had been actively trying to get rid of it, because gold was one of the two most expensive materials in the package.
mb.logic.economics.bill.gold.note: The arithmetic from wire diameter, bond count and bond length is straightforward but unverified against measured data, and the brief's 'few milligrams of gold' is at the top of my own range rather than contradicted by it. Confidence low.

mb.logic.economics.bill.aluminium.name: Aluminium: order 10-30 mg on the die
mb.logic.economics.bill.aluminium.description: One single metallisation level about 1.0-1.5 um thick, covering maybe half the die. For a 3.6 mm2 die that is a few cubic millimetres of metal - on the order of 10 to 30 milligrams, not the 0.3 g sometimes quoted. The discrepancy matters because it is the difference between the aluminium in the chip and the aluminium that went through the fab's sputtering equipment to make every chip on every wafer.
mb.logic.economics.bill.aluminium.note: Explicitly flagging a correction to the brief's figure. My arithmetic gives roughly 10-30 mg of aluminium in the finished die; the 0.3 g figure is plausible only if you count the whole evaporated/sputtered inventory later reclaimed. Confidence low because both are estimates, but the order-of-magnitude gap is real.

facts.label: Brief's figure
facts.value: ~0.3 g - probably wafer-level, not per chip

mb.logic.economics.bill.silicon.name: Silicon: about 3 mg, not 3-5 um
mb.logic.economics.bill.silicon.description: The figure usually quoted for a 74-series chip - '3-5 um of silicon' - is the depth of the active junctions, the epitaxial collector plus base plus emitter, which is what a device-physics description means by it. The wafer itself is a 300 um thick slice, and a 74LS04 die of roughly 1.5 by 2.4 mm weighs about 3 mg. So the chip that contains the logic is a few milligrams of crystal and a few hundred of package.
mb.logic.economics.bill.silicon.note: Die dimensions for a 74LS04 are consistent across the sources I checked (about 1.5 x 2.4 mm); the derived mass is simple arithmetic. Confidence medium because I did not find a measured weight.

mb.logic.sourcing.name: Where Commodore's logic chips came from
mb.logic.sourcing.description: Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job.
mb.logic.sourcing.note: The vendor list and the second-source practice are well attested by the physical parts on surviving boards and by Commodore's parts lists. I could not find a primary source naming which plants made Commodore's specific lots, so no plant is claimed below as fact.

facts.label: Named suppliers on a 250407
facts.value: TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba, MOS house numbers

facts.label: Purchase route
facts.value: vendor sales, franchised distributor, and broker / open market

mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.name: How the chips physically arrived in 1983
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.description: Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all.
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.note: The franchised-versus-independent split, and the grey market that grew out of allocation shortages in the early 1980s, are well documented - the semiconductor industry began formal counterfeiting and diversion programmes in response to exactly this period. What I cannot establish is which route Commodore used for which part, which is exactly the sort of thing that gets litigated decades later.

facts.label: Unauthorised channels
facts.value: independent distributors, brokers, the open market

facts.label: Why it existed
facts.value: allocation shortages, price gaps, and nobody policing small parts

mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.incoming.name: Incoming inspection at the Commodore plant
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.incoming.description: Every shipment of semiconductors was counted, and the number was checked against the bill of materials before the parts went anywhere near a board. Chips that did not match were quarantined. This is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected: the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.incoming.note: Low confidence. Incoming count and inspection in electronics assembly of this era is a generic, well-attested practice; I have not found a Commodore document describing its incoming test procedure for logic parts.

mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.pulls.name: Authorised versus unauthorised: the 'pulls'
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.pulls.description: Parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled'. This could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or it could be diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference. The industry response in the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it.
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.pulls.note: Medium confidence. The general unauthorised-distribution and counterfeiting environment of the early 1980s is well documented from the industry-response side. Claiming that Commodore's specific parts came through unauthorised channels would need documentary evidence I do not have; the tree deliberately does not claim it.

mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.allocatio.name: Allocation and the queue
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.allocatio.description: When demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed. A computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated, pro rata, and had to schedule its production around delivery dates rather than around its own. This is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make.
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.allocatio.note: Allocation was standard practice in the 1980-83 shortage period and is well attested; the semiconductor industry's own diversion-fighting literature of the era confirms the shortages were real. Medium confidence on how specifically it applied to Commodore's glue-logic buys.

mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.name: Commodore's own second sources: the 77xx house numbers
mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.description: To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64.
mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.note: The house numbers and their equivalents are field-attested in multiple independent repair accounts; the mechanism (contract fabrication of a second source) is the standard reading but I could not find a Commodore primary document describing the practice.

facts.value: equivalent to the 7406 hex inverter at U8
equivalent to the 74LS139 decoder at U15
equivalent to the 74LS08 quad AND at U27

facts.label: Reliability
facts.value: the MOS house-number parts are notably failure-prone

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.name: The merchant logic vendors
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.description: Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: TI invented the 7400; Fairchild, National and Motorola/Signetics cloned and improved it

facts.label: Interchangeability
facts.value: same pinout and function, different vendor mark

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.name: Hitachi, Toshiba and the Japanese suppliers
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.description: By the mid-1980s Japanese and then Korean vendors had taken a large share of world logic volume, and they were undercutting American silicon hard. C64 boards are also found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's own bill of materials got cheaper every year of its life.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.note: Low confidence on specific Japanese parts appearing on 1983 C64 boards. The general Japanese penetration of merchant logic through the decade is well documented; a specific Hitachi-branded 74LS in a 250407 is a field report I did not verify.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.name: Motorola and Signetics
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.description: Motorola was the dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts - the MC4044 and MC4066 on the C64 - and Signetics had been an important TTL second source. The two had been linked by a licensing and cross-supply arrangement since 1969, so both names turned up in the same catalogue.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.note: Motorola as the MC-prefix supplier of the 4066/4044 is high confidence - that is what the MC prefix means. The Signetics link-up is a well-documented aspect of that era but I have not cited a primary source for it here.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.name: National Semiconductor
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.description: A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.note: National as a 74LS supplier is high confidence. Its 74HC databooks (1983) are a well-documented and interesting artefact - the high-speed CMOS family arriving at the same moment as the C64.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.name: Fairchild
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.description: The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.note: Fairchild's silicon-gate invention in 1968 and the 1985 bankruptcy are well documented. That Fairchild-branded logic was actually present on C64 boards is field-attested but I did not verify a specific board photograph showing it.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.name: Texas Instruments
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.description: The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.note: TI's role and the 7400/74S chronology are high confidence. Specific plant names are given as commonly-cited TI locations rather than verified suppliers of Commodore's lots.

facts.label: Extra business
