facts.value: foundry / fab-forum for other semiconductor firms

mb.logic.cmos.name: The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629
mb.logic.cmos.description: Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.
mb.logic.cmos.note: Describes a 3-5 um n-well/p-well twin-tub CMOS process with LOCOS isolation, self-aligned source/drain and a single aluminium level - the mainstream logic CMOS of 1982-84, and the process behind the RCA/Motorola 4000-series and the early 74HC. TI's Micralign lines, Fairchild's and National's equivalent lines, and the Japanese and Korean fabs all ran something close to this. Two details are period-specific: LOCOS was still the isolation of choice (shallow-trench isolation was arriving but not yet dominant), and the 4000-series parts such as the 4066 and MC4044 were older designs that typically used a simpler, single-well or p-well-only CMOS rather than a full twin-tub. Confidence medium because the exact flow of a given vendor's 4000-series part is proprietary.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: n-well / p-well twin-tub CMOS, LOCOS isolation

facts.label: Minimum feature
facts.value: 3-5 um (same node as the bipolar logic line)

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: polysilicon over ~100 nm thermal oxide, self-aligned S/D

facts.label: Static power
facts.value: nW per gate vs ~2 mW for a 74LS gate

mb.logic.cmos.now.name: What CMOS became
mb.logic.cmos.now.description: The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed - shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS and finally gave way to fin-shaped gates; the gate material changed from polysilicon to metal; the number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen; the light source went from a mercury lamp to an argon fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: 436 nm mercury lamp -> 193 nm ArF -> 13.5 nm EUV

facts.label: Transistors per die
facts.value: ~10 for a 4066 switch; ~10^10 for a modern GPU

mb.logic.cmos.now.scaling.name: Shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS
mb.logic.cmos.now.scaling.description: The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer as geometries shrank. Shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide and a nitride liner, gives a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward. It is a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea described in the bipolar branch.

mb.logic.cmos.fab.name: Where the CMOS parts were made
mb.logic.cmos.fab.description: The 4066 and MC4044 were Motorola and RCA parts, made in Motorola's own bipolar-compatible CMOS lines and in the Japanese and Southeast Asian fabs that had been built to supply them. By 1983 the merchant CMOS capacity was expanding fast and much of it was in Japan and Korea, where the cost of a CMOS line was falling faster than in the United States.
mb.logic.cmos.fab.note: Low confidence on the specific plants. I have not traced which fab produced the MC4044 and 4066 in Commodore's 1983 shipments.

mb.logic.cmos.switch.name: What a CMOS transmission gate is made of
mb.logic.cmos.switch.description: The 4066's four 'bilateral switches' are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: complementary NMOS + PMOS in parallel = transmission gate

facts.label: Bidirectional
facts.value: yes - unlike an NMOS pass transistor

facts.label: On resistance
facts.value: hundreds of ohms to a few kohm

mb.logic.cmos.litho.name: The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive
mb.logic.cmos.litho.description: A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.

mb.logic.cmos.litho.positive.name: Positive photoresist and the end of negative resist
mb.logic.cmos.litho.positive.description: A positive resist is a novolac resin with a photosensitive protecting group. Exposure breaks the group off, the exposed resin becomes soluble in the alkaline developer, and the pattern on the wafer is the same polarity as the pattern on the mask - no mental inversion, no image reversal, and better control of linewidth on steps. Positive resists went from invention in the 1940s to default in the late 1970s; by 1983 they had won MOS and were displacing negative resist on bipolar. Within a decade negative resist was gone from production lines entirely.

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: NMOS from late 1970s; all production by early 1990s

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.name: Developing the image
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.description: The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.name: The alkaline developer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.description: Aqueous alkali, traditionally potassium hydroxide or, from the late 1970s, tetramethylammonium hydroxide. It dissolves the unexposed novolac resin of a positive resist but leaves the exposed, cross-linked, imaged resin alone. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.name: Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.description: The strong alkali in the developer, made by the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine alongside chlorine. It is the chemical that develops a positive photoresist.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.name: Brine feed to the chlor-alkali cell
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.description: Concentrated sodium chloride solution, electrolysed to give sodium hydroxide (the alkali), hydrogen and chlorine gas. The same rock salt that makes the epoxy precursors makes the resist developer.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.name: Rock salt (halite)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.description: The sodium chloride mined from halite or evaporated from brine. The root of both the chlorine chemistry and the sodium-hydroxide chemistry that strip, develop and etch the resist away.

mb.logic.cmos.process.name: The twin-tub CMOS flow
mb.logic.cmos.process.description: The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

mb.logic.cmos.process.thinfilm.name: Where a 4066 puts its resistors
mb.logic.cmos.process.thinfilm.description: The 4000-series CMOS parts rarely needed resistors at all - CMOS logic is naturally high impedance, so biasing resistors are sparse - but the 4066's on-resistance trimmer and some bias chains did use deposited polysilicon resistors at a value set by sheet resistance and length. Poly resistors are cheap to add because they are made at the same time as the gate, from the same film, at no extra mask.
mb.logic.cmos.process.thinfilm.note: Low confidence. That a 4066 uses on-chip polysilicon resistors is plausible from its trim and bias requirements but I did not verify a cross-section, and some 4000-series parts use no resistors at all.

mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.name: Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it
mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.description: An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.
mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.note: The relative immunity of CMOS to mobile charge is standard device physics; the specific passivation stack comparison is a reasonable generalisation rather than a cited measurement.

mb.logic.cmos.process.contact.name: Contact and aluminium interconnect
mb.logic.cmos.process.contact.description: The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.name: Aluminium metallisation
mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.description: The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.note: Single-level aluminium is exactly why bipolar logic with its large cells tolerated one metal layer so well. When bipolar shrank to compete with CMOS it needed two or three metal layers and vias, which is one reason it lost.

mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.name: The self-aligned source and drain
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.description: With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.

facts.label: Masking
facts.value: the polysilicon gate itself, plus the opposite field oxide

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.name: The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.description: The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.note: The gold-doped (Au-doped) polysilicon emitter was a real and important technique of this era, used to raise gain and suppress the emitter-base reverse conductance ('knee'). It was implemented by co-depositing a tiny amount of gold in the emitter polysilicon or dopant glass, then driving it in with the arsenic or phosphorus. Confidence medium: the technique is well documented, but I have not confirmed that a specific 74LS vendor's 1983 process used it; it was common in high-performance bipolar rather than mandatory in low-cost logic.

facts.label: Gold purpose
facts.value: suppress emitter-base reverse leakage and push-through

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.polysil.name: Polysilicon emitter (a later refinement)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.polysil.description: Instead of diffusing the emitter through a mask, a thin polysilicon film is deposited, doped with arsenic, patterned to define the emitter, and then pushed. The arsenic is confined by the polysilicon walls so the emitter comes out shallower and more uniform, and the emitter area - which sets the emitter resistance - is set by the same mask as the metal that contacts it. This self-aligned polysilicon emitter was one of the last big improvements to the classical bipolar process before CMOS took the business.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.polysil.note: Poly-emitter bipolar was widespread in analog ICs through the 1980s and 1990s. Whether a 1983 commodity 74LS used it is doubtful - it adds cost for a speed the LS family does not need.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.name: The gold in the emitter
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.description: A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.note: Gold as a recombination centre in silicon is well established physics; its use in Au-doped emitters is a documented period technique. Exact concentration is on the order of a fraction of a percent in the emitter.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.name: Arsine (AsH3) - the shallow-diffusion dopant
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.description: A very shallow-diffusing dopant, used where a junction must stop just below a thin gate oxide without drifting deeper in the subsequent hot steps. Arsenic replaced antimony for this job as the physics improved. Arcsine came from arsenic trioxide (from roasting arsenic-bearing ores) plus hydrogen.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.note: Arsenic was used on the bipolar emitters here and, on the CMOS side, for the n+ source/drain. Arsenic-bearing copper concentrates were a notorious long-time hazard in smelting, which is why arsenic control in copper works is a regulated topic today.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.arse.name: Arsenic trioxide from ore roasting
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.arse.description: Arsenic occurs in some copper and lead ores as arsenide. Roasting the concentrate oxidises the arsenic to arsenic trioxide fume, which is captured and reduced to elemental arsenic, then combined with hydrogen to give arsine.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.arse.note: Arsenic is present in metal ores from the ancient earth; the specific separation path described is high confidence as industrial chemistry.

mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.name: The source/drain anneal
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.description: After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.note: The activation anneal was around 800-900 C for an hour, or a rapid thermal anneal of a few seconds at 1000 C plus. Medium confidence on the exact numbers.

mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.name: The polysilicon gate
mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.description: A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.

facts.label: Doping
facts.value: phosphine in the deposition, or POCL3 furnace

mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.silane-source.name: Silane (SiH4) as the polysilicon feed
mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.silane-source.description: Silane decomposes on a hot surface at 700-850 C to lay down pure polycrystalline silicon. It is a cleaner and more controllable feed than trichlorosilane - no chlorine, no corrosive by-products - and by the early 1980s it was becoming the preferred source for polysilicon deposition in CMOS even though trichlorosilane still dominated for boule-grade silicon.
mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.silane-source.note: Silane was used for polysilicon deposition from roughly the mid-1970s onward. Confidence medium on the exact balance between silane and dichlorosilane in 1983 CVD; the trichlorosilane-versus-silane split for boule-grade silicon (trichlorosilane dominant) is high confidence.

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: monosilane; the gaseous form of 'silicon hydride'

chem.silane.name: Silane chemistry
chem.silane.description: Two chemically unrelated families share the name, and both come off the same silicon-chlorine-hydrogen chemistry. Monosilane SiH4 is the gas used to deposit polysilicon in CMOS fabrication. Organosilanes — silane coupling agents — are the surface chemistry that makes glass fibre bond to epoxy resin, and they end up in every FR-4 board. Both are pyrophoric, and monosilane is acutely toxic in a way that made it one of the more awkward gases to handle before the industry moved to DCS.

chem.silane.coupling-agent.name: Silane coupling agents for glass fibre sizing
chem.silane.coupling-agent.description: Organosilanes with two different ends: a hydrolysable alkoxy or chloro group that bonds to the glass surface hydroxyls, and a functional group — vinyl, amino, epoxy, methacrylate — that reacts with the resin. Aminopropyltriethoxysilane and vinyltrimethoxysilane are the workhorses. Applied to woven cloth after desizing, they are the reason epoxy bonds to glass rather than merely wetting it, and therefore the reason a C64 mainboard does not delaminate when it is soldered.
chem.silane.coupling-agent.note: Also used to size glass fibre for tyres and for printed-circuit substrates other than FR-4.

facts.label: Application
facts.value: spray or dip, then oven-dry and cure at 100-150 C

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: raises the laminate's interlaminar shear strength by 30-50% over an unsized cloth

chem.silane.monosilane.name: Monosilane (SiH4) for polysilicon deposition
chem.silane.monosilane.description: The workhorse polysilicon precursor for gate oxide, doped poly gates, lightly doped source/drain and passivation films in 1982-84 CMOS. A silicon fab in that era ran a silane or dichlorosilane plant, usually on site, because the gas is dangerous to ship and to store.

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: steel cylinders or bulk liquid at -60 C or below

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: pyrophoric in air, acutely toxic, forms explosive mixtures with air

chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.name: Low-pressure CVD deposition of polysilicon
chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.description: Silane decomposes on hot silicon wafers at 600-850 C in a diffusion tube, laying down a conformal layer. Poly gates made this way replaced the older aluminium gate, which is the change that made NMOS CMOS manufacturable at all — and the reason a 6510's logic gate is polysilicon rather than aluminium.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 100-500 nm poly-Si gate, doped P or n from the source

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: silane or dichlorosilane in N2 or Ar

chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.name: Disproportionation of trichlorosilane with hydrogen
chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.description: Trichlorosilane plus hydrogen, catalysed, yields monosilane and hydrogen chloride. This is the route most fabs used in the early 1980s because trichlorosilane was already being distilled in bulk for the polysilicon itself, so the silane plant was a small add-on to the same distillation train. The hydrogen chloride is recycled back into the chlor-alkali plant.

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 10-25% SiH4 in H2 before final purification

facts.label: Note
facts.value: SiH4 decomposes above ~400 C, which is why the CVD furnace is a cold-wall stainless tube, not a hot-wall quartz one

mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide.name: The gate oxide
mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide.description: Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.name: LOCOS isolation
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.description: Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

facts.label: Mask oxide
facts.value: Si3N4, LPCVD from silane and ammonia

facts.label: Known problem
facts.value: the 'bird's beak' - the field oxide grows sideways and eats into the active area

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.name: Hot phosphoric acid for the nitride strip
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.description: Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it. The acid was made by burning phosphorus - itself from phosphate rock - in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.note: The chemistry is high confidence; the specific tank temperature (~150-180 C) is a standard process figure but I have not verified a 1983 datasheet for it.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.p.name: Elemental phosphorus from phosphate rock
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.p.description: White phosphorus was produced by carbothermic reduction of calcium phosphate (apatite) with coke and silica in an electric furnace, then condensed to a waxy solid. Most phosphine was made by reacting this phosphorus with hydrogen or by hydrolysing phosphorus trichloride made from it.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.p.note: White phosphorus production is the deep origin of the dopant gas in every n-type diffusion in this tree.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.p.name: Phosphate rock (apatite)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.p.description: Calcium phosphate ore, mainly from Florida, Morocco, Senegal and China. Reduced in an electric furnace with coke and silica to make white phosphorus, which is the only practical high-purity source of the phosphorus dopant.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.name: The silicon nitride masking film
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.description: A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.name: Ammonia (NH3)
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.description: The nitrogen source for the nitride. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by the Haber-Bosch process: nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas, over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm. So the mask that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.name: Hydrogen for the ammonia
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.description: Steam-reformed methane, exactly the hydrogen that reduces the trichlorosilane into polysilicon. Two branches of the same industrial gas meet here: one gas becomes silicon, the other becomes the mask that patterns it.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Methane (natural gas)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: CH4, the dominant component of natural gas, the simplest hydrocarbon. It was reacted with steam over a nickel reforming catalyst at 800-900 C: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2. A shift reactor then converts the carbon monoxide to more hydrogen. This hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane into pure silicon.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Natural gas (field)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Methane and light hydrocarbons drawn from a gas or oil field. This is the geological end of the chemistry: ancient buried organic matter, converted by heat and pressure over geological time into oil and natural gas, and now drawn out of the ground.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: How natural gas formed
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Buried ancient organic sediment, compressed and heated over millions of years by the weight of overburden, cracked into hydrocarbons. Methane is the lightest and most abundant product. This is the true root of the carbon in the computer: the natural gas that made the hydrogen that reduced the silicon that every transistor is built on.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: The gas field
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: A reservoir of porous sandstone sealed under an impermeable cap, drilled vertically and produced through a christmas tree of valves, then gathered into a trunk pipeline system. This is where the chain physically ends: a hole in the ground in West Texas, the North Sea, the Dutch Groningen field or the Urengoy field in Siberia, with a gas treatment plant at the wellhead stripping out the hydrogen sulphide and the higher hydrocarbons that would poison a reforming catalyst a few thousand miles downstream.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.name: Nitrogen from the air
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.description: The other half of Haber-Bosch: air separated by cryogenic distillation or pressure-swing adsorption into nitrogen and oxygen. 78 percent of the atmosphere, liquefied at one atmosphere only at 77 K, which is why air separation plants are enormous cryogenic plants.

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.name: Air
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammo.description: 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, 1 percent argon and carbon dioxide. The raw material for every cubic metre of ammonia, and therefore of every silicon nitride masking film, in the world.

mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.name: n-well and p-well implants
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.description: Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: ion implantation (thermal diffusion still in use)

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.name: Phosphine (PH3) for the n-type epilayer
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.description: The dopant gas for the n-type collector and for the n+ isolation and emitter diffusions. A few parts per million of phosphine in the hydrogen carrier sets the resistivity. Phosphine itself is made by reacting phosphoric acid (from phosphate rock) or elemental phosphorus with hydrogen, or by burning phosphorus vapour.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.name: Boron as the p dopant
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.description: Boron came from a thin deposited glass or oxide doped with boron (B2O3, often as diborane gas) spun onto the wafer and driven in. It was the standard p-dopant for base diffusions throughout the era.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.name: Borax / boron oxide source
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.description: For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a BN wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.note: Solid-source BN and doped-oxide diffusion was the classic boron diffusion technique before diborane became routine.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.dibo.name: Diborane (B2H6) gas
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.dibo.description: Boron hydride gas used as a diffusion or implantation source. It is pyrophoric and toxic, and shipped and handled in sealed steel cylinders under inert gas.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.dibo.note: Boron trichloride (BCl3) was the other common boron gas source.

mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.name: The medium-current ion implanter
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.description: A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.note: Implanters were standard in CMOS lines by the early 1980s; diffusion was still the workhorse in bipolar logic, which is one of the more interesting differences between the two processes.

mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate.name: p-type substrate (and the tub)
mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate.description: The wafer is p-type, lightly doped. On top of it two wells are implanted: a deep n-well and a somewhat shallower p-well. The n-well holds every p-channel transistor; the p-well (or the substrate itself, on simpler parts) holds every n-channel transistor. Two tubs, two polarities, one chip - that is the 'twin tub'. The wells must be deep enough that they do not punch through into each other and short the two transistor types together.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.name: Where the silicon came from
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.description: No fab makes its own silicon. A logic fab in 1983 bought polished 75 mm or 100 mm wafers from a specialist supplier - Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo, Siltron, MEMC - who themselves bought metallurgical silicon, made it into trichlorosilane or silane, reduced that to polysilicon, pulled a monocrystalline boule by the Czochralski method, and sliced, lapped and polished it. This is the longest supply chain in the whole computer.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.diecount.name: Die-per-wafer economics
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.diecount.description: The economics of a merchant logic wafer rest entirely on this number: how many working dies of one part number come off a wafer. Multiply by yield, multiply by the cost of the wafer, divide by the dies, and you have the die cost - which for a 74LS gate is dominated not by the wafer but by testing, packaging and the fixed cost of the masks and the fab, amortised over millions of gates.
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.diecount.note: The 1,500-3,000 figure is an area calculation and is plausible for a 14-pin die on a 4-inch wafer; it is not a sourced measurement. Confidence medium.

facts.label: Yield at probe
facts.value: varies widely; the margin between good and scrap dies is what testing must find

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.sizes.name: 3-inch and 4-inch wafers in 1983
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.sizes.description: Standard wafer diameters in 1983 were 3 inches (75 mm) and 4 inches (100 mm); 5-inch (125 mm) was arriving at the leading-edge logic and memory lines. A 4-inch wafer holds roughly 1,500-3,000 of the small dies that a 14-pin logic part becomes, depending on die size and the edge exclusion the process could hold.
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.sizes.note: Die-per-wafer for a 14-pin logic die (a few square mm) on a 100 mm wafer does land in the 1,000-3,000 range by straightforward area arithmetic, but I have not verified a specific published figure for 74LS in 1983. The wafer diameters are high confidence.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polish.name: Final polish
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polish.description: A final, slow, chemically-assisted polish takes the lapped surface to a mirror finish, because every speck of damage left on the surface becomes a defect that kills transistors. A sacrificial thermal oxide is then grown on the polished surface and stripped, which anneals the last of the surface damage - the 'getter' that heals the crystal's outermost lattice layer.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap.name: Lapping and edge-rounding
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap.description: The wafers are lapped against each other in a slurry to take the bow out of the sawn surface and make them parallel to within microns, then the sharp sawn edge is rounded off with a diamond wheel. The rounded edge is what stops the wafer cracking when it is chucked onto the probe stage and spun through the photolithography coater.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap.slurry.name: Lapping slurry
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap.slurry.description: A slurry of loose diamond or alumina grit in water, to grind the wafer flat. The abrasive is the same industrial mineral as the blade.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw.name: Sawing the boule into wafers
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw.description: The boule is ground to mark where each wafer will be, then an idling saw - a thin rotating diamond-impregnated steel blade - cuts it, losing up to a millimetre of silicon kerf per cut. A 100 mm boule gave roughly 300 wafers per metre of ingot. Wafers were then lapped flat and parallel, and finally polished mirror-bright.

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: steel or resinoid with diamond grit

facts.label: Kerf
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm of silicon lost per wafer

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw.diamond.name: Industrial diamond
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw.diamond.description: The abrasive in the saw blade, the scribe and the CMP slurry. Synthesised from graphite under high pressure and temperature in a diamond press, or mined. Graphite itself is carbon, from coal or petroleum coke - another carbon branch off the crude.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.name: Czochralski growth of the single crystal
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.description: The polysilicon powder is melted with a dopant in a silica crucible at about 1420 C, just above the silicon melting point of 1414 C. A small seed crystal on a puller is dipped in and withdrawn at 1-3 mm/min, rotating. Silicon solidifies on the seed in the melt's lattice, producing a slowly tapering cylinder of near-perfect single crystal called a boule. Arsenic or phosphorus is added to set the wafer's conductivity type and resistivity.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.seed.name: The seed crystal
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.seed.description: A small, already-perfect single crystal - usually a few mm across and a few cm long - lowered into the melt to start the growth. Everything that follows inherits its lattice. The seed was itself cut from an earlier boule, so this is a lineage that goes back, crystal generation by crystal generation, to the first Ingot in 1950s.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.crucible.name: The fused-silica crucible
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.crucible.description: The melt is held in a crucible of fused quartz - amorphous silicon dioxide - because quartz melts above 1600 C and, crucially, because it introduces only oxygen and silicon, both harmless in the crystal, unlike a metal or nitride crucible. The crucible itself is made by flame-fusing pure silica in a hydrogen-oxygen flame, so even the vessel the silicon is melted in comes from the same quartz as the metallurgical silicon.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.puller.name: The Czochralski puller
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.puller.description: A tall crystal-growth machine: a graphite-heated crucible with a rotating seed shaft, a slurry of dopant, an argon atmosphere over the melt, and a diameter-control algorithm watching the melt's edge by laser/weight. It is the machine that turns dirty powder into the perfect single crystal every silicon chip in the world is cut from.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.name: Polysilicon from the Siemens process
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.description: Metallurgical silicon is first reacted with hydrogen chloride at about 300 C to make trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), which is purified by fractional distillation. The purified trichlorosilane is then reduced with pure hydrogen at 1000-1150 C in a fluidised-bed reactor, and fine polycrystalline silicon ('polysilicon') grows on silicon seed particles. The Siemens process - the reaction invented at Siemens in 1954 - is how essentially all the world's polysilicon, and so all its silicon wafers, were made in 1983.

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: fractional distillation of SiHCl3, then reverse cleaning

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.react.name: The Siemens fluidised-bed reactor
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.react.description: A steel vessel with a perforated plate, fluidised with purified hydrogen, into which trichlorosilane vapour is injected alongside seed silicon particles. On the hot (silicon-coated) walls the reaction deposits polycrystalline silicon as fine powder; the powder falls out the bottom. Twenty to thirty tonnes of polysilicon a year came out of one reactor in this era.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Hydrogen for the reduction
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: High-purity hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane to silicon in the Siemens reactor. It was made largely by steam reforming of natural gas, with a final purification (molecular sieve and cryogenic adsorption) to get to the parts-per-billion impurity levels the polysilicon needed.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: The hydrogen was mostly natural gas
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: By the 1980s the vast majority of the world's hydrogen for ammonia and for electronics was made by steam reforming natural gas - passing methane over a hot nickel catalyst with steam to give hydrogen and carbon monoxide, then shifting and scrubbing. This is the deepest tie in the whole tree: the natural gas that reduced the silicon came out of the same subsurface reservoir complex that the industry calls gas, and methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: The steam reformer is a bank of tubes packed with nickel on an alumina support. The nickel - from nickel ore - catalyses the methane-steam reaction at 800-900 C. A drop of this catalyst is one more place nickel enters the tree, alongside the NiCr resistor and the lead frame.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Hydrochloric acid (for the trichlorosilane step)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Hydrochloric acid reacts with the metallurgical silicon to make the trichlorosilane gas. HCl was made from chlorine and hydrogen, or from brine, or bought as a bulk chemical. It is the same chlorine chemistry that makes the epoxy precursors and the resist solvents.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Chlorine gas
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Chlorine for the hydrochlorination step, from the chlor-alkali cell on brine, with hydrogen from the same cell. The classic industrial pairing.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Brine
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Concentrated salt solution electrolysed to chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.name: Rock salt
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydro.description: Halite, mined or evaporated from seawater. Root of the chlorine chemistry underneath the silicon, the epoxy and the solvents.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.name: Metallurgical silicon from quartz and coke
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.description: The bottom of the silicon chain. Quartz - silicon dioxide, usually mined as high-purity quartzite - is mixed with coke and heated in a submerged-arc electric furnace at about 2000 C. The carbon reduces the oxide, and molten silicon collects at the bottom: metallurgical silicon, 98-99.5 percent pure. Every silicon wafer in the world begins here.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.quartzite.name: High-purity quartzite (the ore of silicon dioxide)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.quartzite.description: The silica must be unusually pure, because every impurity in the metallurgical silicon becomes a lifetime in the transistor. High-grade quartzite or vein quartz, low in iron and aluminium, is selected - from the Spruce Pine district in North Carolina, from Norway, from the Ural, from Brazil and China. It is crushed and reacted to make trichlorosilane, which is purified by careful redistillation before it ever becomes wafer silicon.
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.quartzite.note: The shared metal.silica node covers the deeper bauxite-to-oxide chemistry; this node covers the silicon-specific mining and purification requirement of quartz for semiconductor silicon.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.furnace.name: The submerged-arc electric furnace
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.furnace.description: A steel shell lined with refractory, with three graphite electrodes plunging into a charge of crushed quartz and coke. An arc between the electrodes melts the mix; the carbon reduces the silicon dioxide and the carbon monoxide gas burns at the electrode tips, superheating the bath to about 2000 C. Molten silicon (99 percent pure) taps off the bottom. A single furnace makes tens of thousands of tonnes of metallurgical silicon a year.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke.name: Petroleum coke (the carbon reductant)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke.description: The carbon that does the reducing. Petroleum coke is the heavy solid residue left from a refinery coker, essentially the same residuum that feeds the carbon-black furnace. It is mixed into the quartz charge as a reductant and, in the electric furnace, as a source of heat when it burns.

mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke.crude.name: Crude oil (refinery residue)
mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke.crude.description: The refinery that makes the coke is fed by crude oil. So the carbon that reduces quartz into silicon came, one step removed, from the same crude oil that made the epoxy, the resist solvents and the natural gas.

mb.logic.bipolar.name: How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)
mb.logic.bipolar.description: The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.
mb.logic.bipolar.note: This is a generalised description of the standard junction-isolated bipolar logic process as it was run in 1982-84 by TI, Fairchild, National and Motorola. Precise vendors differed: Fairchild also offered a dielectric-isolation variant, and TI ran some processes with ion implantation instead of thermal base diffusion. I have marked medium confidence rather than high because the 74LS flows are proprietary and I have not seen a period process description for a specific vendor's 74LS line. The transistor structure, the four-diffusion sequence, the NiCr resistor level and the eight mask levels are all well documented industry practice for the era.

facts.label: Diffusion cycles
facts.value: 4 thermal: isolation, base, emitter, plus the epitaxial growth itself

facts.label: Interconnect
facts.value: single aluminium level + sputtered NiCr resistor

mb.logic.bipolar.now.name: What happened to bipolar logic afterwards
mb.logic.bipolar.now.description: The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches: high-voltage, high-current, precision-analog and microwave parts, where the bipolar transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat. The two families also merged into BiCMOS.

mb.logic.bipolar.now.scaling.name: The 3-5 um feature, then and now
mb.logic.bipolar.now.scaling.description: The 3-5 um minimum feature of this logic line is unrecognisably coarse today. Modern advanced logic runs at nanometre nodes with hundreds of millions of transistors per die, whereas a 74LS gate has of the order of a few dozen transistors in total. The geometry went from the thousands of transistors that fit on one 100 mm wafer of glue logic to the billions that now fit on one 300 mm wafer of a GPU. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the DIP pin spacing changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.

facts.label: Unchanged
facts.value: DIP package, epoxy, lead frame, 0.1 in pitch

mb.logic.bipolar.now.bicmos.name: BiCMOS - bipolar and CMOS on one wafer
mb.logic.bipolar.now.bicmos.description: A process that builds CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die: the CMOS for low power and density, the bipolar for high current drive on the outputs. It was used in some gate arrays and in the output stages of older CPUs, and it was abandoned once CMOS itself could drive high current enough. It is the process family that merged the two halves of this branch.
mb.logic.bipolar.now.bicmos.note: BiCMOS was real and used through the 1980s-1990s (for example in some gate arrays and cache parts) and is now largely gone from production. Confidence medium on where exactly it was used; high that the process family existed and later declined.

mb.logic.bipolar.now.bipolar-left.name: Where bipolar still survives
mb.logic.bipolar.now.bipolar-left.description: Power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors. Bipolar transistors are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the very leading edge - the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.name: The merchant logic fab that ran the process
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.description: A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.note: Described generically. Individual vendors ran it differently - TI in Dallas, Fairchild in Mountain View and Palo Alto, National in Santa Clara, Motorola in Phoenix - and I have not traced which specific plant made Commodore's parts.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.name: Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.description: A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed. The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.note: The scale figures are order-of-magnitude for a large logic fab, not verified for a specific plant. Water intensity for semiconductors is high relative to most manufacturing; this is well documented generally.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal.name: Metallisation bay
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal.description: The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baylitho.name: Photomask bay
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baylitho.description: Coaters, developers, aligners and the inspection stations, under Class 10 and Class 100 cleanroom. This was the largest bay by machine count and the largest by electricity draw after the cleanroom air.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion.name: Oxidation and diffusion bay
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion.description: The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.name: Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.description: The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.

facts.label: Classes used
facts.value: Class 10 (ISO 4) mask bay, Class 100 (ISO 5) sub-fab and diffusion bay, Class 1000 (ISO 6) wet bays

facts.label: Wet benches
facts.value: polypropylene sinks under Class 100 laminar hoods

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.gas.name: Bulk process gases
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.gas.description: Nitrogen for purging tool chambers and for the sinter anneal, hydrogen for the metal anneal, and oxygen for oxidation and for ashing photoresist, all piped from a bulk gas farm outside the cleanroom. Dry, filtered nitrogen was also the blow-off gas for every wafer before it entered a hot tool.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.name: The wet bench
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.description: A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.name: The HEPA fan filter unit
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.description: A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.name: Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.description: A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.note: The mask set and its order in this tree: (1) isolation, (2) base, (3) NiCr resistor, (4) emitter, (5) contact window, (6) aluminium metal, (7) passivation window, plus the scribe/alignment level - about eight, ordering within the tree illustrative. Every mask is exposed once per wafer batch, and the whole flow through the diffusion and photolithography areas takes a batch of wafers roughly a week to ten days.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.bay.name: The photomask bay (Class 10 cleanroom)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.bay.description: Coating, exposing and developing happened in a 'yellow room' under filtered mercury light and then in a Class 10 (ISO 4) mini-environment with the aligners under hoods. Whole-body suits were only in the Class 100 (ISO 5) areas and the fab sub-fab; the mask bay and the diffusion bay were usually Class 1000 (ISO 6).
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.bay.note: 1980s class numbering: Class 100 = ISO 5 cleanroom, Class 1000 = ISO 6, Class 10 = ISO 4 (the mini-environment used for the most critical steps). This is the older US 'class' convention, different from the ISO class numbers used today.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.cycle.name: The full cycle, counted
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.cycle.description: One mask level's cycle, run eight times, with the non-lithography steps interleaved. Written out once: dehydrate, coat, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse, hard-bake, wet-etch, strip, clean - ten operations - then the furnace or the sputterer. Eight levels of ten is about eighty lithography-area operations, plus oxidation and diffusion pushes, plus metallisation, plus test. The brief's 'photolithography cycle count' for a 74LS chip is therefore roughly eight masks, ten steps each.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.name: Stripping the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.description: With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. The wafer goes into a hot organic solvent - historically xylene or trichloroethylene, later the piranha acid clean. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue that had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.note: Trichloroethylene was ubiquitous as a resist strip in this period and was being phased out for toxicity and ozone reasons through the 1980s, replaced by perchloroethylene and then by piranha (H2SO4/H2O2) wet strips.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.name: Piranha clean (H2SO4 + H2O2)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.description: A hot mix of concentrated sulphuric acid and hydrogen peroxide that oxidises organic residue to carbon dioxide and leaves a chemically clean, ion-free surface. Mixed in the fab at the wet bench, it is the standard clean before every photoresist coat and after every resist strip, and it is what made adhesion and ion control reliable.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.name: Sulphuric acid from sulphur
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.description: Made by burning sulphur or hydrogen sulfide and absorbing in water. Sulphur itself came overwhelmingly from recovered petroleum - the sour crude 'sour gas' processing plants removed hydrogen sulfide from crude and Claus-processed it into elemental sulphur. So the acid that cleans the wafer also traces to crude oil.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.note: In 1980s practice most industrial sulphur was recovered from oil and gas processing (Claus process) rather than mined, so this path is a strong but not exclusive claim.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.name: Elemental sulphur (recovered)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.description: Yellow solid recovered from hydrogen sulfide in oil and gas refining by the Claus process, or mined. Oxidised to sulphur dioxide and absorbed to make sulphuric acid.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.name: Hydrogen sulfide from sour crude
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sul.description: The sour-smelling hydrogen sulfide stripped from oil and gas during refining, which is the raw feed for most of the world's manufactured sulphur.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.name: Trichloroethylene solvent strip
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.description: A dense chlorinated solvent, 1,1,1-trichloroethane family, that dissolves the polymerised resist. Boiling in a hot bath it strips the wafer. It is a heavy, volatile, toxic chlorinated hydrocarbon made by chlorinating ethylene and destroying hydrogen chloride with chlorine - another chlorine branch of the tree.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.note: Trichloroethylene (CHCl=CCl2) specifically, and its 1,1,1-trichloroethane cousins, were the standard resist and degreasing solvents of the era. Being phased out by regulation through the 1980s.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.name: Ethylene from the cracker
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.description: The other half of the chlorinated-solvent chemistry. Ethylene came from the same steam cracker as the propylene that made the epoxy, from naphtha or from ethane off natural gas. The epoxy body of the package and the solvent that stripped the resist are siblings from one cracker.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.name: Naphtha feed
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.description: The light hydrocarbon fraction of crude oil distillation, cracked to ethylene and propylene. Every chlorinated organic solvent and every epoxy in this tree comes from this one feed.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.name: Crude oil
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylen.description: The root hydrocarbon: the source of the resist solvents, the epoxy, the photoresist binders and the natural gas that made the hydrogen.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.name: Etching the oxide window
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.description: The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.note: Plasma (reactive ion) etching of silicon dioxide was introduced in the early-to-mid 1980s and became standard later in the decade; a 1983 bipolar logic line used wet HF and BOE for its diffusion and contact windows.

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: etches SiO2, stops at Si and Si3N4

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) - the ore of hydrofluoric acid
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite.description: Hydrofluoric acid is made by treating fluorspar, calcium fluoride, with concentrated sulphuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C. Fluorspar is dug from hard-rock deposits, notably in Derbyshire and the Ilkley Moor field in England, Mexico, South Africa and China, and it is the single feedstock behind all the oxide etching in the entire semiconductor industry.

facts.label: Main 1980s sources
facts.value: Mexico, South Africa, Spain, China, England

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite.lim.name: Limestone (CaCO3)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite.lim.description: The acid side of the HF process, and the source of the calcium sulfate byproduct. Limestone is quarried limestone, chemically calcium carbonate, and it is one of the most widely mined rocks on earth.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.name: Aligning the mask to the wafer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.description: The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.note: Contact printing was cheapest and fastest but printed mask defects onto every die and wore the mask; proximity printing added an air gap for a small resolution penalty. 1:1 projection steppers (like TI's Micralign, and Perkin-Elmer's) were arriving in the early 1980s and gave a clean image without contact wear. Bipolar logic at 3-5 um was comfortable with any of the three.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: optical, on marks from previous levels

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: mercury g-line 436 nm or h-line 405 nm

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp.name: The mercury lamp
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp.description: A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper.name: The 1:1 projection stepper
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper.description: A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer.name: The contact/proximity mask aligner
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer.description: A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.name: Dehydration bake before the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.description: Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotpl.name: The dehydration hot plate
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotpl.description: A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.name: Spinning on the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.description: The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.negative.name: Negative (image-reversing) resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.negative.description: On a bipolar line in 1983, resist was still commonly negative: exposure cross-links the resist so it becomes insoluble in the developer, so the pattern left on the wafer after develop is the complement of the mask. This suits diffusion, where you want to open the mask where the oxide is. Positive resists, which behave the intuitive way, had taken over NMOS and CMOS from the late 1970s but lingered on bipolar.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.negative.note: By 1983 positive resists were already dominant for MOS processes (Shipley AZ-1350 and its successors), and the trend to positive resist across all processes was well advanced; negative resist on bipolar logic persisted into the 1980s. I have stated this as medium confidence on the specific mix in a given vendor's logic bay.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner.name: The coater/developer track
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner.description: A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

facts.label: Track throughput
facts.value: ~25 wafers per cycle, ~1 min per cycle

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.name: The mask set
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.description: A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.name: The mask writer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.description: A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.note: For 3-5 um logic geometries, a photographic mask stepper was adequate and much faster than electron-beam writing; beam writing was reserved for the DRAM and custom-chip masks.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.name: The reticle (1:1 mask)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.description: A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.note: The distinction: contact/proximity printing needs a full-size mask; a 1:1 projection stepper also prints 1:1 but optically; only a reduction stepper (2x-10x) needs a smaller reticle. Bipolar logic in 1983 was 1:1 by either contact or 1:1 projection. Bipolar logic generally did not use reduction steppers at this node.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.name: The opaque chrome layer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.description: A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.name: The mask blank (soda-lime glass)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.description: A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.name: The junction-isolated bipolar flow
mb.logic.bipolar.process.description: The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: n+ phosphorus, driven to the substrate

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: n+ phosphorus or arsenic, Rs ~10-30 ohm/sq

mb.logic.bipolar.process.feature.name: The resulting 3-5 um geometry
mb.logic.bipolar.process.feature.description: Put together, those four diffusions and the one resistor level put a transistor with a 0.5-1 um base and a 1-2 um emitter sitting inside an isolation island a few tens of micrometres across, wired with 3-5 um aluminium on a single level. That is the '3-5 um minimum feature' of the era's standard bipolar logic line. Compare the dynamic RAM on the same board, patterned at around 1-2 um with two or three aluminium levels and a polysilicon gate - that is where the money was, and that is why the DRAM cost more than the glue.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.feature.note: The 3-5 um minimum feature is the figure used throughout this tree for 74LS and is standard for early-1980s merchant bipolar logic. The DRAM comparison (~1-2 um, two metal layers) is a reasonable era estimate for a 4164; I have not verified a specific 4164 process cross-section.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation.name: Passivation over the metal
mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation.description: A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.name: Sintering the metal into the contacts
mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.description: After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.note: Aluminium sintering / hydrogen alloying at 400-450 C was standard in the era. Confidence medium on the exact temperature window; the purpose and the technique are not in doubt.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact.name: The contact window
mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact.description: One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: HF through the oxide to the silicon

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.name: The NiCr thin-film resistor level
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.description: A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. In a silicon-gate-era bipolar line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.note: Resistors in this class were 'thin film', not 'thick film': the NiCr was deposited in a vacuum (sputtered) to a controlled sheet resistance of order 100-250 ohm/square, then laser- or acid-trimmed to value. Low-power TTL needed relatively low resistances, so a common sheet resistance was fine. Precision analog parts moved to laser trimming and, later, to scaled 'valley' resistors.

facts.label: Trimming
facts.value: laser trim for precision; as-deposited for logic

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter.name: The RF/DC sputterer
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter.description: A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.name: The nickel-chromium sputtering target
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.description: A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.name: The Schottky clamp - the S in LS
mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.description: In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.note: The Schottky barrier itself is formed simply by touching aluminium to the lightly doped n-type collector (aluminium-silicon is 0.75 eV work-function difference against n-Si) - no extra mask beyond the one that defines the collector contact, because the Schottky diode and the ohmic collector contact are made in the same window. So the LS family costs the same number of mask levels as plain TTL. First commercial Schottky TTL was TI's 74S series, 1964.

facts.label: Barrier
facts.value: Al on n-type Si, ~0.75 eV work-function difference

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: prevents transistor saturation; 74LS gate delay ~10 ns

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: no extra mask - same window as the collector contact

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.name: The base diffusion
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.description: A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

facts.label: Why thin
facts.value: base transit time sets transistor fT

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.name: Collector-collector isolation
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.description: The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.note: The isolation junctions carry the full supply voltage between adjacent islands, so they are reverse-biased diodes and must be kept clean and leak-free. Guard rings and careful gettering protect them.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: through the n-epilayer into the substrate

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.name: Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.description: For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.note: The brief asked for the deep-trench-isolation-came-later point. Confirmed: trench isolation appeared in high-performance bipolar through the 1980s and 1990s and is gone from the logic business entirely, because CMOS with shallow-trench isolation simply won.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.name: Dielectric isolation (the alternative, and Fairchild's route)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.description: Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.
