mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.note: Dielectric isolation was used by Fairchild and a few others for high-performance analog and for some logic families in the 1970s and 1980s, but junction isolation was cheaper and dominated standard 74LS. I could not confirm which isolation a given vendor's 74LS used; most 74LS parts are believed to be junction-isolated.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.name: Guard rings around the islands
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.description: A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.name: What a guard ring physically is
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.description: Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffu.name: Diffusion into the window
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffu.description: The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.name: Growth of the field oxide
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.description: Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: mask for diffusion + isolation + field-effect control

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.name: Fused quartz tube and boat
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.description: The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.name: Deionised steam for the furnace
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.description: Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furna.name: The oxidation furnace
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furna.description: A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.name: Epitaxial growth of the collector
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.description: The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.note: The reactor also dopes: phosphine or arsine is mixed into the hydrogen stream so the epilayer comes out n-type to a controlled resistivity. This is one of only two places (the other being the isolation and emitter diffusions) where a distinct dopant chemistry is needed.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.hcl.name: Trichloroethylene-trichlorosilane vapour mix (not HCl)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.hcl.description: The epitaxial gas box fed a mixture of silane or trichlorosilane in hydrogen, with dopant gas added for conductivity. Trichlorosilane is the workhorse chlorosilane of the period; silicon tetrachloride was the older, hotter source. The hydrogen carrier is dry and ultra-pure.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor.name: The horizontal epitaxial reactor
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor.description: A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate.name: p-type starting wafer
mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate.description: A slice of p-type silicon, lightly doped so that it is a good insulator between transistor islands and does not leak much reverse current. Everything the tree contains - the transistors, the resistors, the isolation - sits on this one piece of crystal.

mb.logic.package.name: The black epoxy DIP
mb.logic.package.description: Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history.

facts.label: Row spacing
facts.value: 0.3 in (7.62 mm) for 14-24 pin; 0.6 in (15.24 mm) for 28/40 pin

facts.label: Bond wire
facts.value: 0.7-1.0 mil gold, ~20 bonds for a 20-pin DIP

mb.logic.package.marking.name: Marking the top of the package
mb.logic.package.marking.description: Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.
mb.logic.package.marking.note: Commodore bought these chips from several vendors and did not re-mark them, which is why an original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore house number, all mixed together.

facts.label: Packaging of record
facts.value: tubed, then later dry-packed and taped

mb.logic.package.marking.laser.name: Laser marking (emerging)
mb.logic.package.marking.laser.description: A Q-switched Nd:YAG or CO2 laser ablating characters into the epoxy surface, or a carbon laser removing the top layer to expose an underlying white layer. Fimeless, indelible and fast, but in 1983 it was still a premium option used mostly for military marking.
mb.logic.package.marking.laser.note: Adoption of laser marking on merchant plastic DIPs was well underway by the mid-to-late 1980s; in 1983 it was still a minority of parts.

mb.logic.package.marking.ink.name: Marking ink
mb.logic.package.marking.ink.description: A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV or by laser ablation of the mould compound. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.name: The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here)
mb.logic.package.ceramic.description: For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.note: The 74LS series exists in both CDIP (ceramic) and PDIP (plastic) forms, distinguished by the letter after the temperature grade: N is plastic (0 to +70 C), E or M is ceramic (-55 to +125 C). Commodore specified N-grade parts.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.name: Glass frit sealing
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.description: A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.note: Sealing in a continuous belt or pusher furnace at a few hundred degrees per hour rather than 700-750 C soak is the classic profile; the exact numbers vary by package. Medium confidence on the peak temperature.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid.name: Kovar lid and nickel seal ring
mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid.description: For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.name: Alumina ceramic body
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.description: A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.bauxite.name: Bauxite, the alumina ore
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.bauxite.description: Bauxite is the only commercial ore of aluminium, and alumina refined from it is both the ceramic used in ceramic packages and the feed for the aluminium metallisation on the die - two completely different routes to the same element, sitting a few centimetres apart on the same 74LS part.

facts.label: Main 1980s sources
facts.value: Jamaica, Suriname, Guinea, Australia, bauxite residue from Sines (Portugal)

mb.logic.package.probe.name: Probe test before packaging
mb.logic.package.probe.description: Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

mb.logic.package.probe.tester.name: The logic tester
mb.logic.package.probe.tester.description: An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.

facts.label: Instrumentation
facts.value: TTL pattern generator, timing analyser, DC meter

mb.logic.package.probe.card.name: The probe card
mb.logic.package.probe.card.description: A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.

mb.logic.package.probe.prober.name: The wafer probe station
mb.logic.package.probe.prober.description: A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.

mb.logic.package.assembly.name: Die attach, wire bond, moulding
mb.logic.package.assembly.description: Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

mb.logic.package.assembly.postmould.name: Post-mould cure and stability bake
mb.logic.package.assembly.postmould.description: Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature. Parts are therefore baked for hours at 175 C afterwards, which completes the cure and drives off the last of the residual stress. It was a batch operation: thousands of parts in a tray, hours in a oven, on a schedule that ran overnight.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.name: Transfer moulding the black epoxy body
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.description: A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 70-80 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 3-5 min in the mould, then a post-mould bake

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool.name: The mould cavity and ejector pins
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool.description: A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.

facts.label: Cavity marks
facts.value: the number 1 or a letter, moulded into the underside

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press.name: The transfer press
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press.description: A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.

mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.name: Gold wire bonding
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.description: A machine called a wedge bonder (or, for higher volume, a ball bonder) presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats on the other end at the pin. Each joint is an intermetallic wedge of aluminium-gold, cut with a pulled wire rather than cut. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.note: Ball bonding, with a 2.5 mil wire and ~25-50 bonds per second, was displacing wedge bonding for high pin counts in this period. Wedge bonding at ~10 bonds per second dominated merchant logic.

mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonde.name: The wedge bonder
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonde.description: A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.name: Die attach to the frame paddle
mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.description: The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.
mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.note: Organic die attach became common in the late 1980s-90s for cost reasons. In 1983 Au-Si eutectic brazing was still the standard on logic and memory.

mb.logic.package.die.name: The separated, tested die
mb.logic.package.die.description: Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.name: Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not
mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.description: A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.
mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.note: The mechanism (charge storage and refresh) is high confidence; the comparative failure rate is a well-attested field observation rather than a measured statistic.

mb.logic.package.die.passivation.name: The glass over the aluminium
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.description: After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.note: Early 1980s nitride deposition was increasingly low-pressure or plasma-enhanced CVD from silane and ammonia; furnaces using TEOS plus ammonia still ran in parallel.

mb.logic.package.die.scribe.name: Scribing and dicing the wafer
mb.logic.package.die.scribe.description: A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.

facts.label: Blade kerf
facts.value: ~0.15 mm for a resinoid dicing saw

mb.logic.package.leadframe.name: Nickel-iron lead frame
mb.logic.package.leadframe.description: A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.note: Carpenter 45 (42% Ni / 58% Fe, balance carbon and manganese) and similar low-expansion nickel-iron alloys were the standard logic lead frame material because the thermal expansion coefficient was tuned to match the alumina-and-epoxy package, so the die, the frame and the mould compound do not fight each other over temperature cycling. It was a commodity ferronickel-like alloy made in ordinary steel melts.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.name: Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983)
mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.description: A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.note: Included to mark the boundary: a C64 from 1983 contains no C4 frames. The technology existed in the late 1980s but was not standard on through-hole merchant logic.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.name: Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.description: Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.note: Matte tin plating on lead frames later became a reliability problem - tin whiskers - and the industry spent two decades fixing it. Copper-clad (C4) frames that carry a thicker, more solderable surface metal appeared in the late 1980s and 1990s, which is why the C64's successors used them and the C64 did not.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.name: Tin plating bath
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.description: A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.c.name: Cassiterite (SnO2) - the tin ore
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.c.description: Tin reached the plating tank as refined tin metal, made by carbothermic reduction of cassiterite, the tin oxide ore. In 1983 the world's tin supply came overwhelmingly from the Southeast Asian tin belt - Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand - and from Bolivia's Cerro Rico, and the price was famously volatile because the ore body was tiny in volume and the supply was political.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.c.note: Malaysia, Indonesia and Bolivia were the dominant producers of tin in the early 1980s. The famous International Tin Council price collapse of 1985-86 - triggered by the release of stockpiles and by substitution - came just after the C64's peak production years.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.name: Progressive-die stamping of the frame
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.description: The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.note: Photo-etched lead frames from copper and copper alloys were an alternative for high-lead-count parts, but the stamping route dominated through-hole logic DIPs in this period.

facts.label: Tie bars
facts.value: left until after the die is attached, to hold the frame rigid

mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool.name: The progressive die set
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool.description: A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.name: The iron half of the lead frame alloy
mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.description: Most of a logic lead frame by weight is iron, not nickel. The nickel - typically 42 percent, a little over a fifth of the mass - is the expensive part that tunes the expansion coefficient; the iron is commodity steel and was bought on the open market.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.name: Iron ore for the frame alloy
mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.description: The lead frame melt started life as steel, and the steel started life as ore. Two ores dominate: hematite (Fe2O3, the red ore) and magnetite (Fe3O4, the black ore). Both were shipped by rail and sea in bulk from the Lake Superior range, Mesabi and Labrador Trough, and the UK, and smelted in a blast furnace with coke and then converted.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.magn.name: Magnetite (Fe3O4)
mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.magn.description: The magnetic iron ore, ~72 percent iron and strongly ferrimagnetic, which is why it can be separated from gangue by a magnetic separator instead of by gravity alone. Much magnetite in 1983 came from taconite pellets shipped from the Mesabi range, a sintered concentrate rather than a lump ore.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.hema.name: Hematite (Fe2O3)
mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.hema.description: Iron in its fully oxidised state, typically 60-66 percent iron by mass, won by gravity concentration and magnetic washing of fine crushed ore. It was the dominant iron ore in world supply and the standard feed for a blast furnace.

mb.logic.package.geometry.name: Why 0.1 inch and 0.3 inch
mb.logic.package.geometry.description: The two dimensions that made the DIP work at all. The 0.100 in (2.54 mm) lead pitch was chosen so that a cheap single-row DIP socket, the same one used for the C64's own logic, could accept it. The 0.3 in (7.62 mm) row spacing was chosen so the body would just clear a 0.05 in hole-pad on 0.1 in centres and so a 14-pin part could be mounted on the older 0.6 in grid alongside the 40-pin parts. Wider bodies moved to 0.6 in rows.

mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.name: 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants
mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.description: The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.
mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.note: The 0.3 in / 0.6 in rule is high confidence; the existence of a 0.9 in (22.9 mm) row spacing in the same era is medium confidence - such spacings appear on hermetic and high-power ceramic packages, but I did not confirm one on a merchant logic part.

mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch.name: 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch
mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch.description: The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

facts.label: Lead length (DIP-14)
facts.value: ~7.6 mm from body shoulder to tip

mb.logic.not-on-this-board.name: Famous 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64
mb.logic.not-on-this-board.description: A warning about the part list. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 and 74LS181 look-ahead carry chips and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list.
mb.logic.not-on-this-board.note: Stated explicitly so the reader can trust the rest of this branch. The parts that really are fitted are the twelve listed in the sibling nodes. Which machine each wrong part belongs to is medium confidence.

mb.logic.cmos-4000.name: CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044
mb.logic.cmos-4000.description: Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.
mb.logic.cmos-4000.note: These are 4000-series CMOS, not 7400-series, so strictly they sit outside a '74-series' scope. They are included because they are the clearest demonstration that a single 1983 Commodore board carried two completely different semiconductor processes, and because the brief asked for the CMOS branch to be covered from a real machine.

facts.label: Named suppliers
facts.value: Motorola (MC prefix), RCA/Intersil (CD prefix), TI CD-prefix

mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.name: LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part
mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.description: Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.
mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.note: An analogue bipolar part, not a 7400-series logic IC. Its internal process is a linear bipolar flow (epitaxial, deep base, wide-area emitters) rather than the Schottky-clamped logic flow described under mb.logic.bipolar.

mb.logic.u31-74ls629.name: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31)
mb.logic.u31-74ls629.description: Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.
mb.logic.u31-74ls629.note: Part number, position and PLL role are high confidence and corroborated by scope measurements of the 250407 clock circuit published at tech.guitarsite.de/c64_scope.html. That the 74LS624-629 family is fabricated in CMOS rather than bipolar TTL despite the LS prefix is medium confidence: the family descends from Signetics/National designs and behaves like CMOS in pinout and power-up, but I did not find a period datasheet sentence stating the process. Some vendors did not offer it at all, which is itself suggestive.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual voltage-controlled oscillator with enable and range control

mb.logic.u30-74ls193.name: 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30)
mb.logic.u30-74ls193.description: A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.
mb.logic.u30-74ls193.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). Its exact role is low confidence: sources call it a 'binary counter', a divider, and part of the clock-generation chain, and the 250407 does share a cluster of counters and flip-flops (U29/U30) around the DRAM and raster timing that is hard to allocate from the parts list alone.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: synchronous presettable 4-bit up/down binary counter with clear

mb.logic.u29-74ls74.name: 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29)
mb.logic.u29-74ls74.description: Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.
mb.logic.u29-74ls74.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The functional description is low confidence: hobbyist references variously call U29 a 'divider', a 'dual D-type flip-flop', and part of the VIC-II raster timing, and I did not trace the 251138 schematic net by net to settle it.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual D positive-edge-triggered flip-flop with preset and clear

mb.logic.u27-74ls08.name: 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27)
mb.logic.u27-74ls08.description: Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.
mb.logic.u27-74ls08.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The specific AND terms are inferred from the topology of a dynamic-RAM controller rather than read off the schematic net by net, hence medium.

mb.logic.u26-74ls373.name: 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26)
mb.logic.u26-74ls373.description: Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: octal transparent latch with three-state outputs

mb.logic.u15-74ls139.name: 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15)
mb.logic.u15-74ls139.description: Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.
mb.logic.u15-74ls139.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). The exact set of selects it generates is medium confidence because most of the C64's address decoding lives in the 82S100 PLA at U17, and secondary sources disagree about which outputs the 74LS139 finishes off. MOS house-number versions of this decoder were a notorious C64 failure; they are more fragile than the TI/Fairchild/National parts.

mb.logic.u14-74ls258.name: 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14)
mb.logic.u14-74ls258.description: The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.
mb.logic.u14-74ls258.note: Some third-party board listings incorrectly give U14 as a 74LS373. The Commodore service manual parts list for #250407 says 74LS258.

mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.name: 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25)
mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.description: Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.
mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.note: A 74LS257 differs from a 74LS258 only in having totem-pole (push-pull) outputs instead of three-state outputs. This distinction is why U13/U25 and U14 do different jobs.

facts.label: Select inputs per mux
facts.value: 4 (A, B, and shared select per nibble)

mb.logic.u8-7406.name: 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8)
mb.logic.u8-7406.description: Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.
mb.logic.u8-7406.note: The service manual lists U8 as '7406 sub 7416'. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the MOS house-number part 7707, and those MOS-made 'equivalent' parts are notoriously unreliable - a 7406/7707 failing high is a classic cause of a dead datasette or a stuck serial bus. Confidence is medium on the exact nets driven; high on the part number and function class.

mb.discretes.name: Discrete semiconductors on the board
mb.discretes.description: The handful of non-IC semiconductors in the machine: small-signal NPN and PNP planar transistors (2N3904, 2N3906, 2N4124) for the serial/parallel port buffers, the colour-amplifier and video-driver stages and the cassette/joystick input switching; higher-voltage NPN power transistors (2N3055, 2N3792) in the power supply's regulator and short-circuit crowbar; rectifier, switching and zener diodes (1N4001, 1N4148, 1N47xx); one or two indicator LEDs; and a metal-oxide varistor across the AC input. Each of these was made in a bipolar or compound-semiconductor plant completely unrelated to the Norristown logic fab.
mb.discretes.note: Placement notes: the 1N4001 rectifiers and the 2N3055/2N3792 sit in the PSU, not on the logic mainboard - the power subsystem is another agent's tree. The exact transistors and diodes on a given C64 PCB revision vary; treat the list as representative rather than a BOM.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92 epoxy mould for small signal; TO-3 or TO-220 plastic for power

facts.label: LED colours available in 1982
facts.value: red, amber, green - no blue LED existed

facts.label: Varistor
facts.value: ZnO disc, typically 275 V AC rated

mb.discretes.epi.name: Epitaxial growth reactor for the discrete plant
mb.discretes.epi.description: After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.

mb.discretes.isolation.name: Isolation diffusion and its moat
mb.discretes.isolation.description: A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

mb.discretes.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
mb.discretes.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.
mb.discretes.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonics rather than on single-wafer wet cleans with megasonic megasonics-in-a-cassette, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

mb.discretes.litho.name: Photolithography for this part
mb.discretes.litho.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact printer in the discrete plant (diffusion and epitaxial masks), expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: epitaxial n-layer, tub isolation, base window, emitter window, metallization. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 with a hard bake, coated and developed in a bench coater/developer track

mb.discretes.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
mb.discretes.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.discretes.litho.resist.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
mb.discretes.litho.resist.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.discretes.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.discretes.test.name: Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes
mb.discretes.test.description: Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.

mb.discretes.leadframe.name: Discretes lead frame: nickel, copper, tin plating
mb.discretes.leadframe.description: A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.
inputs: nickel strip or copper alloy strip

mb.discretes.tin.name: Tin and tin-lead plating bath
mb.discretes.tin.description: Tin plating of semiconductor leads was done chemically in an acid or alkaline stannate bath over a nickel underplate, later shifting to pure tin as the industry moved off lead. The tin itself comes from cassiterite (SnO2), mined in Indonesia, Malaysia and Bolivia.

mb.discretes.cassiterite.name: Cassiterite (SnO2) concentrate
mb.discretes.cassiterite.description: Heavy, high-density tin ore from alluvial and lode deposits; the Indonesian and Malaysian alluvial placers became the dominant supply in the 1980s and 1990s, with secondary output from Bolivia's Cerro Rico and Cornwall's abandoned tinfields.

mb.discretes.to92-mould.name: Black epoxy for the TO-92 shell
mb.discretes.to92-mould.description: A discrete's package is 90% compound by mass: an epoxy or phenolic resin loaded with 60-70% silica and 0.5-2% carbon black for the black colour, injected at 150-180 C into a 3-cavity transfer tool and post-cured. A 2N3904 die is a fraction of a square millimetre inside roughly 0.1 g of this.

mb.discretes.to92-mould.silica.name: Silica filler from quartz sand
mb.discretes.to92-mould.silica.description: Ground, angular silica of 0.5-3 um mean size produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz - the same material as the IC moulding compound filler.

mb.discretes.varistor.name: Zinc oxide varistor disc
mb.discretes.varistor.description: A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.
mb.discretes.varistor.note: ZnO itself comes from zinc concentrate or from the reduction of zinc oxide; that chain belongs in the metals tree. The MOV is in the PSU, not the logic mainboard.
places: China (the dominant ZnO supplier by the 1990s)

mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.name: Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate
mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.description: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.

mb.discretes.varistor.sphalerite.name: Sphalerite (ZnS) ore concentrate
mb.discretes.varistor.sphalerite.description: The world's zinc ore: a cubic sulphide mined underground or in big open pits, floated to 50-60% Zn. The Sierra de Orueba and MIDA deposits in China became dominant suppliers in exactly the period Commodore's supply chain depended on.

mb.discretes.led.name: Indicator LED (red/green/amber only)
mb.discretes.led.description: The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

mb.discretes.led.substrate.name: GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer
mb.discretes.led.substrate.description: The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.
mb.discretes.led.substrate.note: GaAs substrate supply was treated as a strategic material in the 1980s; Japan, the USSR and the UK were the main sources.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: Czochralski from a Ga/As melt near 1250 C

mb.discretes.led.gallium.name: Refined gallium
mb.discretes.led.gallium.description: Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.
mb.discretes.led.gallium.note: Gallium is almost entirely a byproduct of bauxite refining (and of zinc), not a primary ore - this is the same trace metal that makes gallium nitride LEDs possible today.

mb.discretes.led.epi.name: Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction
mb.discretes.led.epi.description: A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.
mb.discretes.led.epi.note: High-purity phosphorus was produced by red-phosphorus distillation, and the gallium was refined by ion-exchange or by liquid-metal extraction - both expensive, which is why an LED cost tens of cents in 1982.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: quartz tube with tilting boat and zone pulls

mb.discretes.diodes.name: Rectifier, switching and zener diodes
mb.discretes.diodes.description: Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.
mb.discretes.diodes.note: Older zeners were made by alloying indium or aluminium into pits cut in the wafer surface (alloy-junction), which is why they were noisy and temperature-drifty compared with the diffused ones that replaced them by the mid 1970s.

facts.label: 1N4148
facts.value: 200 mA, 100 V, ~4 ns; N planar switching

mb.discretes.power-bjt.name: High-voltage power BJTs (2N3055, 2N3792)
mb.discretes.power-bjt.description: The 2N3055 is a 15 A, 200-300 V NPN power transistor in a TO-3 metal can or a plastic TO-220, used as the series pass element in the C64's linear 5 V power supply. The 2N3792 is a 100 V, 0.5 A NPN used in the supply's short-circuit detection, driving an SCR crowbar. Both are triple-diffused or epitaxial-base-collector designs with large dies, thick aluminium (or nickel) metallization and often a molybdenum or copper heat spreader, die-attachable with a soft solder or silver brazing.
mb.discretes.power-bjt.note: Both are in the power supply, which is outside this subsystem's scope; listed here because they are discrete semiconductors in the machine.

facts.label: 2N3055
facts.value: NPN, 250 V VCEO, 15 A Ic, 200 W Pc

facts.label: 2N3792
facts.value: NPN, 100 V VCEO, 0.5 A Ic, 1 W Pc

mb.discretes.bjt-package.name: TO-92 epoxy mould package
mb.discretes.bjt-package.description: Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.
mb.discretes.bjt-package.note: Difference from today: no 0402/0603 SMD package was on a 1982 C64 mainboard - all the discretes were radial-leaded through-hole parts.

mb.discretes.bjt.name: Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process
mb.discretes.bjt.description: The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.
mb.discretes.bjt.note: Motorola registered the 2N3904/2N3906 in the mid-1960s as a pair, which is why almost every 1982 household electronics catalog lists them as Motorola parts even when another firm made them.

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: arsenic or phosphorus, ~97% of emitter area (GEOR)

facts.label: 2N3904 rating
facts.value: 40 V VCEO, 200 mA Ic, 625 mW Pd

facts.label: 2N3906 rating
facts.value: complementary PNP, 40 V, 200 mA, ~250 MHz fT

mb.discretes.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the discrete plant
mb.discretes.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type CZ wafer, 10-40 ohm-cm, mirror polished and laser-scribed. Bipolar discrete fabs used p-type CZ with a heavy oxygen content and generally a (100) or (111) orientation; many discrete lines of the era ran 75 mm wafers because they did not need fine geometry.

mb.discretes.cz.name: CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean
mb.discretes.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium or argon, pulled on a (100) or (111) seed, boron doped to 10-40 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished, KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1. Discretes also went through a gettered or radiation-damage anneal to kill the silicon-germanium centres that degrade current gain.
mb.discretes.cz.note: The gettering anneal (in hydrogen at 1000-1100 C, or in nitrogen with a CVL nitriding cycle) was what made bipolar discrete beta usable; without it a 2N3904's hFE would be a fraction of spec.

mb.discretes.wafer.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.discretes.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.discretes.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.discretes.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.discretes.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon (same silicon, different plant)
mb.discretes.polysilicon.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by the Siemens process from 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C. Discrete makers bought the same electronic-grade silicon as logic fabs, usually from a merchant supplier.

mb.discretes.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
mb.discretes.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

mb.discretes.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
mb.discretes.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

mb.discretes.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
mb.discretes.quartz.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.discretes.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
mb.discretes.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated to remove boron.

mb.discretes.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.discretes.fluorspar.description: 97%+ acid-grade fluorspar mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the hydrofluoric acid used for the leach and for etching oxide.

mb.discretes.fluorspar-vein.name: Fluorspar vein deposit
mb.discretes.fluorspar-vein.description: CaF2 vein and stock deposits mined by open pit and underground methods, crushed and floated to acid grade.

mb.pla.name: U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS)
mb.pla.description: The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.
mb.pla.note: Correction to the brief: the part is a 28-pin DIP, not 14 or 16 pin. The 28-pin package is confirmed both by the 'C64 PLA Dissected' reverse-engineering report and by the MOS Technology products list. Also note that early C64s used a bipolar Signetics 82S100 (or Fairchild 93459 clone); the NMOS 906114-01 came later and became the standard part.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: 16 inputs, 8 tri-state push-pull outputs, 1 output enable

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: MASK programmed at wafer stage - not user-programmable

facts.label: VOH
facts.value: ~3.7-3.8 V (vs 4.2 V for the bipolar Signetics 82S100)

mb.pla.test.name: Probe, truth-table test and final test
mb.pla.test.description: A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.
mb.pla.test.note: Exhaustive truth-table testing of a PLA is standard period practice and is the reason PLDs had unusually high measured reliability despite being un-reworkable in the field.

mb.pla.failures.name: Why it fails more than anything else in the machine
mb.pla.failures.description: Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: 8 push-pull tri-state, switched every CPU cycle

facts.label: Replacement parts
facts.value: SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton, PLAtinum - all substitutes, none original

mb.pla.package.name: 28-pin 600 mil DIP package
mb.pla.package.description: A wide-body package because the array needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation, marked with the part number and date code, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

facts.label: Ceramic variant
facts.value: exists but uncommon in a C64

mb.cpu.emc.name: Epoxy molding compound from phenolic resin and silica
mb.cpu.emc.description: EMC starts from phenolic resin: phenol and formaldehyde condensed with an epoxy novolac. The resin is blended with angular ground silica (fired 0.5-3 um particles) to control shrinkage and thermal expansion, mixed with glass fibre in high-temperature grades, catalysed with a phenolic accelerator, and compounded on a two-roll mill under heat. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g.
mb.cpu.emc.note: EMC is also the material of the ABS and phenolic keyboard printed circuit boards - the same phenolic resin chemistry.
places: Nitto Denko, Japan; Sumitomo Bakelite, Japan; Dexter, USA

mb.cpu.emc.phenolic.name: Novolac epoxy resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin
mb.cpu.emc.phenolic.description: Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac (phenol-formaldehyde) resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and NaOH to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of molding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene process oxidation of benzene (mostly from coal tar until the 1980s) or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

mb.cpu.emc.benzene.name: Benzene from the coke ovens
mb.cpu.emc.benzene.description: Benzene was recovered from the light oil of the coke-oven battery that made coke for blast furnaces, and also made by catalytic reforming/dehydrogenation of naphtha. In 1982 it was overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative - the same coke-oven coke that fed the blast furnaces and (after calcining) the silicon furnaces.

mb.cpu.emc.coke.name: Metallurgical coke for the blast furnace
mb.cpu.emc.coke.description: Bituminous coal crushed and charged into a battery of coke ovens, heated to 1100-1250 C in the absence of air for 15-20 hours, then pushed out as coke and quenched with water. Coke is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace that makes the pig iron that makes the steel in the lead frame and the tin in the solder of the board.

mb.cpu.emc.coal.name: Bituminous coal seam
mb.cpu.emc.coal.description: A sedimentary seam mined by longwall or continuous miners. The coking-grade coals of the Appalachian basin (Clarion, Sewickley, Pittsburgh beds) were the premium feed in both the US and, exported, worldwide.

mb.cpu.mold.name: Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy
mb.cpu.mold.description: The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in a thermosetting epoxy molding compound: phenolic novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, plus a small amount of silicone release agent and catalyst. Typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes per cavity. Plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation.
mb.cpu.mold.note: Alternate route for hermetic parts: sintering an alumina ceramic DIP shell at ~850-950 C with a glass frit seal - slower, more expensive, but moisture-proof and used for military/aerospace grades.

mb.cpu.bond.gold.name: Bonding wire from refined gold
mb.cpu.bond.gold.description: 99.99% gold refined from ore by chlorination/electrolysis or cupellation, drawn through a die and a lubricant to 25 um. Roughly 0.3-1 m of wire per die.

mb.cpu.bond.gold.cyanide.name: Cyanide leach and activated-carbon recovery
mb.cpu.bond.gold.cyanide.description: Gold concentrate is ground to a flotation product and leached in 0.02-0.05% NaCN at pH 10.5 with lime, oxidised by air: 4 Au + 8 NaCN + 2 H2O + O2 -> 4 Na[Au(CN)2] + 4 NaOH. The pregnant solution is passed over activated carbon, which adsorbs the aurocyanide; the carbon is stripped with hot cyanide or burned and the gold cupelled to 99.99% dore, then electrolytically refined.
mb.cpu.bond.gold.cyanide.note: Wiring a computer takes a few milligrams of gold - but at 1982 C64 volumes of ~2 million machines, IC bonding alone consumed a few hundred kilograms of gold per year.

mb.cpu.leadframe.name: 40-pin DIP lead frame, FeNi alloy or copper
mb.cpu.leadframe.description: The die and its 40 leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi (C4-29) alloy in a thickness of 0.15-0.20 mm by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike, then gold for hermetic parts, then a matte tin or tin-lead surface for plastic parts. The frame is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and moulder.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: FeNi 42/58 or C4-29, or Cu-based alloy

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: Au over Ni for ceramic; Sn or SnPb over Ni for plastic

mb.cpu.leadframe.feni.name: FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy, vacuum-induction melted
mb.cpu.leadframe.feni.description: The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy (C194 with 2.3% lead) and nickel were alternatives.
places: specialty alloy strip mills, US and Japan

mb.cpu.leadframe.iron.name: Low-carbon steel from iron ore
mb.cpu.leadframe.iron.description: Electric arc or basic oxygen furnace steel from hematite ore (Lake Superior Mesabi, Carajás, Itabira) plus coke and limestone, with enough residual carbon kept very low so the frame does not contaminate the wire bonds.

mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel.name: Electrolytic nickel from sulphide ore
mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel.description: Nickel is won either by the Mond carbonyl refining loop (nickel sulfide concentrates are smelted, roasted and reduced to sponge) or by high-pressure acid leach of laterite. Then electrolytically refined to 99.8% cathode in a sulfate/chloride bath and rolled.

mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel-ore.name: Pentlandite (Ni,Fe)9S8 ore concentrate
mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel-ore.description: The world's nickel supply came overwhelmingly from sulphide ore - Sudbury, Ontario (Inco), the Norilsk-Talnakh massif (Norilnickel) and the Philippines (SLN). Ore at ~1.5-3% Ni is concentrated to 10-30% by flotation before smelting.

mb.pla.process.name: NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed)
mb.pla.process.description: The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. I am deliberately not asserting a specific figure for that line width, because no source states one for this part.
mb.pla.process.note: Explicitly low confidence and deliberately vague. The 906114-01's internal process has never been documented; inferring it from the rest of the CSG part family is an assumption, not a fact. What is not in doubt is the programming mechanism, which is the point of this branch.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: aluminium; no barrier metal in this period

mb.pla.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the 906114
mb.pla.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. The NMOS PLA was made in-house at MOS Technology's Norristown plant, so this wafer almost certainly came out of the same furnace and the same process as the 6510 and the 6526 - which is the strongest evidence for the process family, even though no 906114-01 process manual has ever been published.

mb.pla.cz.name: CZ pull and wafer finishing
mb.pla.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in this period), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

mb.pla.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.pla.crucible.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup flame-fused from acid-leached quartz sand around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed and glazed, then scrapped after a handful of pulls.

mb.pla.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
mb.pla.polysilicon.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

mb.pla.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
mb.pla.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

mb.pla.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
mb.pla.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

mb.pla.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
mb.pla.quartz.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.pla.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
mb.pla.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to strip aluminium, iron and boron.

mb.pla.quartz-leach.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
mb.pla.quartz-leach.description: Hot HF/HNO3 leach to strip surface aluminium and iron, then chlorination at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to remove boron, phosphorus and arsenic. Yield from ordinary sand is a few percent.

mb.pla.hf.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
mb.pla.hf.description: Acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead retort at 200-250 C to make the HF that leached the quartz and etched the oxide.

mb.pla.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.pla.fluorspar.description: Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity mined from hydrothermal veins and karst and flotation-beneficiated, from deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa.

mb.pla.saf.name: Submerged arc furnace
mb.pla.saf.description: Three graphite electrodes in a refractory shell maintain a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C; metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

mb.pla.economics.name: The economics of one custom mask set
mb.pla.economics.description: The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.
mb.pla.economics.note: The specific dollar cost of a mask set in 1982 is not something I found; period sources put a full 8-10 level NMOS mask set in the low tens of thousands of dollars, with mask plates alone a few hundred to a couple of thousand per level.

facts.label: NRE
facts.value: artwork + mask set + verification, once per function

facts.label: Unit cost
facts.value: trivial once masked - the die is tiny and needs no exotic process

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: single-sourced, no drop-in replacement, counterfeiting pressure

mb.pla.provenance.name: Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100
mb.pla.provenance.description: Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

mb.pla.vs-pal.name: PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads
mb.pla.vs-pal.description: The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.
mb.pla.vs-pal.note: Also worth knowing: the 906114 family covered several Commodore machines - 906114-01 for the C64, 906114-04 for the B256, and MOS 8721 (315012-01, 48-pin) elsewhere - but each is a different custom mask.

facts.label: PAL 16L8
facts.value: 10 inputs x 8 registered outputs, 64 x 32 fuse AND array, fusible, generic

facts.label: GAL 16V8
facts.value: fuse-programmed, EEPROM fuse link, generic catalogue part
mask programmed, one-off function, no equivalent catalogue part

mb.pla.mask-programming.name: The fuse pattern is one more photomask
mb.pla.mask-programming.description: This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.
mb.pla.mask-programming.note: This is the mechanical reason the 906114-01 is unreplaceable in practice: there is no second source, no substitute function, and no way to change the logic without new silicon.

facts.label: Revisions
facts.value: each logic change costs a whole new mask set

mb.pla.mask-plate.name: Custom chrome-on-glass plate for the C64 address map
mb.pla.mask-plate.description: A 1:1 chrome-on-glass or 5x quartz plate carrying the link pattern for the C64's memory map - ROM, RAM, I/O, colour RAM, cartridge and bank switching. Cut from the design database, inspected against it, defect-repaired, and stored in a mask library. One plate per unique function, like a custom printing plate.

mb.pla.chromite.name: Chromite ore for the mask absorber
mb.pla.chromite.description: Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

mb.pla.types.name: Three ways to make a programmable array, 1982-84
mb.pla.types.description: A PLD or PLA is defined by how its links are made. (a) Mask-programmed: the links are decided in a photolithography mask and are present or absent as fabricated silicon; cheapest per unit at volume, but needs a unique mask set, a long lead time and a minimum order. (b) Fusible-link: every link exists as a real wire - typically nichrome or titanium - and a programmer blows selected links with a laser or a high-current pulse. Generic catalogue parts with a wide range of functions, user-programmable in seconds. (c) Antifuse: the links start as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide layer and a pulse converts the selected ones into high-resistance insulation. Commodore's 906114-01 is (a).

facts.label: (a) Mask
facts.value: one-off NRE, lowest unit cost, 3-6 week cycle, minimum order

facts.label: (b) Fusible link
facts.value: nickchrome or titanium link blown by laser, seconds per part

facts.label: (c) Antifuse
facts.value: a-Si or SiO2 link blown open by a programming pulse

mb.pla.antifuse.name: Antifuse route, for contrast
mb.pla.antifuse.description: A link that starts conducting and is blown into an insulator. Fay's 1970 antifuse used a dielectric-coated metal; by 1982 the dominant versions were amorphous silicon and silicon dioxide films, written by a ~20-40 V pulse that punctured the film. Antifuses are tiny and need no laser, but they were slower to program and harder to test than blowing a metal fuse.

mb.pla.fuselink.name: Fusible-link route, for contrast
mb.pla.fuselink.description: The 82S100 that gave the C64 PLA its name was originally marketed as a field-programmable bipolar array: its links were real chromium or nichrome fuses, and a laser programmer burned out the unwanted ones through the package's FE/NE pin. This is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and it is why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of different functions. Commodore could not use this route for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices, so they went to masks.
mb.pla.fuselink.note: Whether early C64 82S100 parts arrived pre-programmed from Signetics or programmed in-house is not something I could establish.

facts.label: Link material
facts.value: chromium or nichrome film, 1-3 um thick

mb.pla.mask-route.name: Mask-programmed route (this part)
mb.pla.mask-route.description: The array is fabricated complete, with the links built into one of the lithography levels. There is no programming step at all: every 906114-01 off the line is already a working C64 address decoder. The cost sits entirely up front as non-recurring engineering - artwork, mask plates, mask fabrication and verification - and it is paid once per unique logic function.

facts.label: Cycle time
