facts.value: 3-6 weeks from artwork to tested parts

facts.label: Minimum order
facts.value: one wafer run's worth - tens of thousands of dice

mb.pla.array.name: What a PLA physically is
mb.pla.array.description: Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.
mb.pla.array.note: The 'FE/NE' pin on this package is used for programming field-programmable variants of the device and is left unconnected internally in the mask-programmed 906114-01 - a detail decapping shows.

facts.label: OR array
facts.value: 8 outputs, each an OR of product terms

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 16, of the 6510's address and control lines

mb.ppi.name: 6522 PPI/VIA, 40-pin DIP
mb.ppi.description: The 6522 Versatile Interface Adapter at U15 on the C64 mainboard: two 8-bit parallel ports (the user port at $D420 and the cassette port at $D800), two 1-bit handshake lines, an 8-bit shift register for the cassette serial interface, two 16-bit timers with pulse output, four interrupt inputs and an I/O port with three latched control bits. It is the same 40-pin DIP silicon-gate NMOS part as the CIAs, from the same mask-family era and almost certainly the same process.
mb.ppi.note: MOS listed the 6522 as 'VIA' (Versatile Interface Adapter); 'PPI' is Fairchild's name for the same architectural family (the 6820/6821) and is what Commodore's own documentation often called it.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

mb.ppi.userport.name: User port and cassette port wiring
mb.ppi.userport.description: The 6522's two 8-bit ports are the C64's only general-purpose parallel I/O. Port A/B appear on the 12-way cartridge edge as the user port for printers, samplers and third-party cartridges, and as the cassette port on the mainboard. Both ports are quasi-bidirectional TTL with no bus contention protection beyond a weak pull-up, so driving them from two cards at once was a hardware error, not a negotiated one.

facts.label: Ports
facts.value: 2 x 8-bit, quasi-bidirectional, 4 mA source / 1 mA sink

mb.ppi.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
mb.ppi.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.
mb.ppi.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonics rather than on single-wafer wet cleans with megasonic megasonics-in-a-cassette, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

mb.ppi.litho.name: Photolithography for this part
mb.ppi.litho.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: the same nine or ten levels as the rest of the CSG logic. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

mb.ppi.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
mb.ppi.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.ppi.litho.resist.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
mb.ppi.litho.resist.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.ppi.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.ppi.test.name: Wafer probe and final test of the 6522
mb.ppi.test.description: Probe with a 40-needle card: both 16-bit timers clocked against a reference, the shift register stepped, both ports and the handshake lines cycled, and the interrupt inputs verified. Assembled parts repeat the program in a socket on the automatic tester, then go into the C64's machined-pin socket.

mb.ppi.package.name: 40-pin DIP assembly
mb.ppi.package.description: Gold-silicon eutectic die attach at 400-450 C on a gold-plated lead frame, 25 um gold wedge bonding on a manual or semi-automatic bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, lead forming to 0.6 inch pitch, dot-matrix marking, socket test and optional burn-in. On the C64 the VIA is socketed, not soldered.

mb.ppi.assembly.gold.name: Gold bonding wire and lead frame

mb.ppi.assembly.gold.ore.name: Gold concentrate, cyanide-leached

mb.ppi.mask.name: 6522 photomask set

As with the CIAs, the process is the CSG standard flow; only the layout differs.

mb.ppi.mask.chromite.name: Chromite ore concentrate

mb.ppi.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.ppi.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.ppi.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.ppi.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
mb.ppi.polysilicon.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

mb.ppi.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump

mb.ppi.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached

mb.ppi.fluorspar-vein.description: CaF2 vein and stock deposits mined by open pit and underground methods, crushed and flotation-beneficiated to acid grade.

mb.cia.name: Two 6526 CIA complex interface adapters
mb.cia.description: CIA 1 at U17 and CIA 2 at U18 (PLA at U17 on some board revisions) provide the C64's two 8-bit parallel ports, the keyboard/joystick matrix scanning, the two 16-bit interval timers with one-shot/underflow interrupt, the shift register used for the serial (IEC) bus, and TOD (time-of-day) clocking derived from AC mains. Each 6526 is a 40-pin DIP NMOS part; CIA 1 sits at $D400 and reads port A from the VIC colour register file, while CIA 2 sits at $DC00 and drives the user port and serial bus.
mb.cia.note: TOD accuracy is entirely set by the frequency of the AC mains and by a capacitor across the TOD pin on the mainboard; Commodore trimmed that capacitor at final test, which is the documented origin of the famous 'not backward compatible' TOD behaviour.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

facts.label: Peripherals
facts.value: 2 x 8-bit ports, 2 x 16-bit timers, serial shift register, TOD clock

mb.cia.serial.name: The serial shift register and the IEC bus
mb.cia.serial.description: The CIA's 8-bit shift register is what makes the Commodore serial bus work at all. Software sets a bit, shifts it out under CIA timer control with the handshake lines driving the ATN and CLK/CB lines, and reads bits back the same way; the VIC-II's serial output is decoded separately. This is a purely digital function built from ordinary NMOS flip-flops, but its timing jitter is the reason the KERNAL's serial routines are as delicate as they are.

facts.label: Bus
facts.value: IEC/serial, 1 bit per handshake, no level shifting on the C64

facts.label: Registers
facts.value: CIA 2 at $DC00 drives the bus; CIA 1's SR is spare

mb.sid.name: 6581 SID sound chip, 40-pin DIP
mb.sid.description: The C64's sound generator at U18: three analogue subtractive-synthesis voices (two oscillators plus a noise source through a 12-bit DAC, one extra-noise-only channel for percussion), a ring modulator, a resonant multimode filter with a self-oscillating VCA, external-to-internal feedback volume routing, two pulse-width modulators and a hard sync. It is an NMOS hybrid - digital logic and poly counters driving an analogue poly on the same die - which is why it is noisy, why R4, R4AR, R5 and R6 differ, and why a 8580 (made on a newer process) sounds cleaner.
mb.sid.note: The 8580 R4 (1984) and R5/R6 (early 1990s) were moved to a later, larger NMOS process and are visually much bigger dies; the C64 shipped with 6581s until the C64C. The SID's analogue section is why the machine needs the 4066 quad bilateral switch and the 7406 inverter to stabilise it.

mb.sid.revisions.name: SID revisions as an analogue-process story

The 8580 (R4, 1984; R5 and R6, 1992) moved to a later NMOS process with a redesigned analogue section and a much larger die, and is universally regarded as cleaner and quieter. Nothing about the digital side changed enough to matter.

mb.sid.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonics rather than on single-wafer wet cleans with megasonic megasonics-in-a-cassette, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

mb.sid.litho.name: Photolithography for this part
mb.sid.litho.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: poly resistor/DAC pattern, metal, passivation. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 for the levels, AZ-1354 where the film must stand up to a deep etch

mb.sid.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
mb.sid.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.sid.litho.resist.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
mb.sid.litho.resist.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.sid.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.sid.test.name: Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581
mb.sid.test.description: Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. Final test repeated it in a socket. This is why 6581 revisions are dated and marked (R4, R4AR, R5, R6) - each was a measured change to the analogue thresholds.

mb.sid.package.name: 40-pin DIP assembly
mb.sid.package.description: Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonding with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder (roughly 40 pad bonds plus internal wiring for the analogue block), transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C / 700-1000 psi, lead forming to 0.6 inch pitch, marking and socket test. Some SIDs shipped with a ceramic (hermetic) package, which is where the 'SID in ceramic' collectors' market comes from.
mb.sid.package.note: Mould compound shrinkage over a die this large is why the SID's epoxy dome is visibly bulged and why humidity noise tracks with temperature.

mb.sid.assembly.gold.name: Refined gold bonding wire
mb.sid.assembly.gold.description: 99.99% gold from cyanide leaching and electrolytic refining, drawn to 25 um with 0.5-1% palladium for strength. The SID, with roughly 60-80 bonds, consumed more of it than any other part in the machine.

mb.sid.assembly.gold.ore.name: Gold flotation concentrate
mb.sid.assembly.gold.ore.description: Sulphide gold ore crushed, ground and floated; the concentrate is then cyanide leached, carbon-adsorbed, stripped and cupelled.

mb.sid.mask.name: SID photomask set
mb.sid.mask.description: Nine or ten levels for the 6581: n+ field, LOCOS active area, base/well, contact, polysilicon (including the poly resistor pattern that is the DAC), second diffusion, metal, passivation pad, plus alignment. Printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plates, with the grid-broken alignment scheme. The analogue poly resistor pattern was itself a mask level, and trimming it by laser was an option some makers used.

mb.sid.mask.align.name: Coburn 2400 contact printer / Micralign
mb.sid.mask.align.description: 1:1 mask printing: hard vacuum contact, or the Micralign's 100-500 um proximity gap which projected the image with a 5x optical system and so never touched the resist - the technology that removed the 'mask lifts off the wafer' failure mode that plagued pure contact printing.

mb.sid.mask.chrome.name: Sputtered chromium for the mask plates
mb.sid.mask.chrome.description: 99.5% chromium, vacuum-melted, rolled and DC-magnetron sputtered with argon onto a rotating glass or quartz plate, giving a 5-8% transmission absorber at 100-150 nm.

mb.sid.mask.chromite.name: Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate
mb.sid.mask.chromite.description: Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to chromium metal.

mb.sid.external.name: External components the SID needs from the board
mb.sid.external.description: The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 11 MHz colour clock derived from the VIC-II, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. Those are separate parts in the board and interconnect trees.
mb.sid.external.note: The 'chip-dependent' volume crackle and distortion of the 6581 was a consequence of this external network plus the internal filter threshold, which is why later revisions changed the on-board values.

mb.sid.process.name: NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly
mb.sid.process.description: The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.
mb.sid.process.note: The poly-resistor DAC and the tub isolation are standard period NMOS-analogue practice (Hitachi, Toshiba, Signetics used exactly this) but the internal details of the Norristown 6580/6581 are not public.

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: R-2R style, built from polysilicon resistors and n+ lands

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: p-type epitaxial tub around the analogue block

mb.sid.probe.name: Probe test with audio characterisation
mb.sid.probe.description: Wafer sort for the SID was as much a listening test as an electrical one: patterns stepped through the DACs and the filter and the DC output measured and sometimes listened to through a monitor speaker in the test head. Threshold voltages for the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.
mb.sid.probe.note: Functional audio testing at probe was common in 1982 for the SID but is not documented in detail for the Norristown line.

mb.sid.poly-res.name: Polysilicon load resistors
mb.sid.poly-res.description: The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.
mb.sid.poly-res.note: Silicon-barrier anodes, nitride barriers and copper lines did not exist; a 1982 IC resistor could drift several hundred ppm per year with humidity.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~+0.1 to +0.3 %/C - poor by modern thin-film standards

mb.sid.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
mb.sid.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed with a primary flat. Because the SID mixes a big analogue block with digital counters, the die is large and sensitive to oxide and substrate defects, so wafer sort did real work.

mb.sid.cz.name: CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean
mb.sid.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under helium, pulled on a (100) seed, boron doped to ~10 ohm-cm. Boule ground and laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP yet), KOH edge-rounded, and megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1.

mb.sid.wafer.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.sid.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.sid.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.sid.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.sid.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon charge
mb.sid.polysilicon.description: Silicon grown by the Siemens process: 9N trichlorosilane reduced with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

mb.sid.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
mb.sid.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus fall below 1 ppb.

mb.sid.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon from the arc furnace
mb.sid.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to 98-99% silicon with a few hundred ppm of boron.

mb.sid.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz
mb.sid.quartz.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz lump under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.sid.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined
mb.sid.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated to remove aluminium, iron and boron.

mb.sid.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.sid.fluorspar.description: 97%+ acid-grade fluorspar, mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the HF used for leaching and oxide etching.

mb.sid.fluorspar-ore.name: Fluorspar vein and stock deposit
mb.sid.fluorspar-ore.description: Hydrothermal vein and karst deposits worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and floated to acid grade.

mb.vic.name: 8562 VIC-II video chip, 40-pin DIP
mb.vic.description: The C64's video, colour and sprite chip at U19, in a 40-pin DIP. The 8562 is the C64-specific part number for the NTSC VIC-II (the 6567/6569 are the Max Machine / PAL parts); it is an NMOS silicon-gate chip of the same generation as the 6510. The die contains the 40x25 text/bitmap video matrix, the 8 sprite (hardware sprite/clogger) engine, the colour-latch RAM interface, the 6-bit DAC colour outputs, the interrupt and border logic, the ~18 colour PAL palette resistors, and the 5-bit VIC-II colour registers. It reads VIC bank colour RAM through 8 pins and does no pixel-to-PAL conversion itself.
mb.vic.note: The 8562 designation and the 'C64 is a 6567/6569' claim on early Rev 6 prototype boards are both documented; production breadbin machines carry 8562. The VIC-II in the C64 is a 2 um-class NMOS part but the die is larger and more complex than the 6510.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: 4-bit wide, 6 bits (64 levels) per RGB channel, external resistors

mb.vic.die-inspect.name: Die inspection and visual sort
mb.vic.die-inspect.description: Before die attach the diced VIC-II dice were inspected under a stereomicroscope at 20-50x for pad damage, passivation cracks and contamination, and under dark-field illumination for particles. Because the VIC-II's colour outputs and the PAL raster timing were specified tightly, late-1980s and later C64As also shipped with a socketed VIC-II and hand-selected for stable raster; in 1982 the selection was done at final test.

mb.vic.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
mb.vic.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. mb.vic.litho.name: Photolithography for this part
mb.vic.litho.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: n+ field, LOCOS, poly, self-aligned diffusion, contact, metal, passivation pad. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 throughout, AZ-1354 for the thick aluminium level

mb.vic.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.vic.litho.resist.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.vic.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.vic.test.name: Wafer probe and pattern test of the 8562
mb.vic.test.description: The VIC-II is probed with a 40-needle card and a test program that exercises the character generator, the sprite pointers, the colour registers and the interrupt logic - and, on the analogue side, checks that all six colour outputs swing the full 0-5 V and that the 18-bit colour latches all decode. Assembled parts run the same program in a socket, often while a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester's video output.

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: large relative to a 6510, so yield-sensitive

mb.vic.dice.name: Probe, dice, attach and mould the VIC-II
mb.vic.dice.description: The 8562 is one of the larger dies in the machine, so wafer sort in a Teradyne or Fairchild tester with a hand-drilled needle probe card mattered. Good dice are sawn apart, attached face-up to a gold-plated 40-pin lead frame with Au-Si eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder, transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy, formed, marked, and socket-tested.

mb.vic.dice.gold.name: Refined gold for the bonding wire
mb.vic.dice.gold.description: 99.99% gold refined from cyanide leach and cupellation, then electrolysed and drawn to 25 um. A VIC-II uses 60-100 bonds of it.

mb.vic.mask.name: VIC-II photomask set and 1:1 printing
mb.vic.mask.description: The 8562's mask set was nine or ten levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, second diffusion, metal, ROM-programming (none here), passivation pad and the alignment/test levels. A 1982 small fab of this sort typically printed 1:1 on a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner with AZ-1350, using 1 mm chrome-on-glass plates about 5x7 inch. Overlay was held to +-0.5 um by a deliberate 'grid-broken' mask design: the layout broke the grid lines over active regions and added dummy structures so the stepper could align on a broken main grid rather than a continuous one.
mb.vic.mask.note: The grid-broken scheme and the automatic stepper alignment marks are standard 1980s practice; whether Norristown used a stepper at all for this part is not documented.

mb.vic.mask.resist.name: Shipley AZ-1350 photoresist
mb.vic.mask.resist.description: The workhorse positive resist of the whole industry: a novolac phenol-formaldehyde resin with a photoactive quinone-diazoide group, dissolved in cellosolve/acetate solvents, spun to 1 um, soft baked at 90-100 C, exposed and developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. AZ-1354 (higher solids) was used for the aluminium and poly levels. Shipley was a Rohm and Haas business headquartered in Philadelphia, 30 km from the fab.
mb.vic.mask.resist.note: Negative resists were still used for a few layers needing thick-film patterning or image reversal, but positive resists had taken over by 1982.

mb.vic.mask.plate.name: Chrome-on-glass plate and its chromium target
mb.vic.mask.plate.description: 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, photopatterned in positive resist, chrome etched away in hot perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected on a Zeiss comparison tool against the design database, and defect-repaired with a gallium or indium needle where a clear speck sat in a chrome line.

mb.vic.mask.chromite.name: Chromite ore, the source of the mask chrome
mb.vic.mask.chromite.description: Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and then to chromium metal for sputtering targets.

mb.vic.package.name: 40-pin DIP assembly
mb.vic.package.description: Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame by Au-Si eutectic at 400-450 C, 25 um gold wedge bonding (about 40 pad bonds plus internal busses for the colour and sprite routing), transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy, lead forming, dot-matrix marking, and automatic socket test. A ceramic version existed for industrial customers.

mb.vic.package.ceramic.name: Ceramic DIP sintering, as the hermetic alternative
mb.vic.package.ceramic.description: For hermetic parts the die went into a 96% alumina ceramic shell, sealed with a devitrifying glass frit in a belt furnace at ~850-950 C, and the metal flange was brazed or glass-sealed to the header. Ceramic was slower and costlier, and was used for the military/industrial grades; the C64's VIC-II was plastic.
mb.vic.package.ceramic.note: Alumina powder comes from bauxite; that chain lives in the metals/packaging trees.

mb.vic.palette.name: The 18-resistor PAL palette on the mainboard
mb.vic.palette.description: The VIC-II itself does not know what colour is 'red'. It emits six 4-bit-weighted analogue voltages per colour channel; a resistor ladder and a 74LS175 shift register on the C64 mainboard combine them with the border colour to synthesise the 16-entry NTSC palette and the 20-colour PAL palette. Those resistors are ordinary thick-film or wirewound parts and belong to the passives tree, but they are the physical interface between this die and a television.

facts.label: Values
facts.value: binary-weighted 1k-10k, 1% metal film or thick film

mb.vic.process.name: NMOS front end for a large analog-plus-logic die
mb.vic.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS sequence as the CPU, with extra care because the VIC-II mixes digital logic, a 6-bit DAC and analogue comparators on one die: 2 um minimum feature, ~400 A poly-oxide, LOCOS field oxide, self-aligned n+ source/drain, single 1-2 um aluminium layer, PSG plus plasma nitride passivation. The colour DAC outputs were open-source n-channel pull-downs that the external resistor ladder on the mainboard pulled up to +5 V.
mb.vic.process.note: Exact die size and mask count for the 8562 are not published; 50-60 mm2 is an estimate from the pin count and function.

mb.vic.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
mb.vic.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, mirror polished and laser-scribed. The VIC-II is one of the largest CMOS/NMOS logic dies in the machine, so yield was lower and probe sorting mattered more.

mb.vic.cz.name: CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean
mb.vic.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, and megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

mb.vic.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.vic.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.vic.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.vic.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
mb.vic.polysilicon.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, cut into CZ charge pieces.

mb.vic.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, rectified to 9N
mb.vic.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, then fractional distillation at 31.8 C boiling point to 9N-11N.

mb.vic.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
mb.vic.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

mb.vic.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
mb.vic.quartz.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz from a pegmatite or quartzite vein, under 200 ppm Al and Fe.

mb.vic.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
mb.vic.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to strip aluminium, iron and boron.

mb.vic.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.vic.fluorspar.description: Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity, mined from hydrothermal veins and karst, converted with sulfuric acid to HF for the leach and for oxide etching.

mb.vic.fluorspar-vein.name: Fluorspar vein ore
mb.vic.fluorspar-vein.description: Vein and stock deposits of CaF2 worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and flotation-beneficiated.

mb.roms.name: 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL, 901225-01 character ROM
mb.roms.description: The three mask-programmed NMOS ROMs on the C64 mainboard, all in 24-pin DIP: 901226-01 is the 8 KB (2364-compatible pinout) Commodore BASIC V2 interpreter at $A000; 901227-03 is the 8 KB KERNAL at $E000 (901227-01/-02 in earlier lots, and 901229-0x is the 1541 drive's KERNAL, not this one); 901225-01 is the 4 KB (2532-compatible) character generator ROM at U5. Mask ROMs are programmed by deleting or adding metal at one point in the flow, which means a whole extra mask set cut for each ROM revision.
mb.roms.note: The brief said '901229 KERNAL ROM'; for the C64 the part is 901227-0x. 901229-05 belongs to the 1541 disk drive. The 901225-01 character ROM is a 4 KB part although only about 2.3 KB of it carries character data - the rest is un-decoded filler.

mb.roms.revisions.name: ROM revisions are mask revisions
mb.roms.revisions.description: Every fix to the C64's firmware cost a new mask set and a new wafer run. The BASIC ROM has exactly one version, 901226-01; the KERNAL went through 901227-01, -02 and -03, the last of which fixed a tape-loading bug and is what nearly every C64 shipped with; the character generator is 901225-01, with national variants 325018 (Swedish) and 325056 (Spanish C64C). A mask-ROM run also had to be large enough to fill the order, so a small revision could mean waiting weeks for wafers.

Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.roms.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.roms.verify.name: Verifying every ROM bit
mb.roms.verify.description: A mask ROM cannot be re-programmed, so its contents are verified twice. On the wafer, a 24-needle probe card runs a read-only pattern through the 8192 or 4096 addresses and sums the data; after assembly, the part goes into an automatic tester that reads the whole array and checks it against a resident signature and, for the C64's BASIC and KERNAL, the published checksum. Any failure meant a defective mask or a contamination particle, and the whole mask set had to be re-run.

mb.roms.package.name: 24-pin DIP: attach, bond, mould, test
mb.roms.package.description: Dice attached to a 24-pin gold-plated lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder (about 24 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires), transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked with the Commodore part number and date code, and socket-tested. In C64 assembly these were the only three chips soldered directly rather than in sockets.
mb.roms.package.note: The BASIC and KERNAL ROMs were usually soldered into the board because they cannot be usefully replaced - though owners have socketed them since day one.

mb.roms.package.emc.name: Epoxy molding compound and quartz filler
mb.roms.package.emc.description: Phenolic/epoxy novolac resin with 60-75% ground silica, transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-baked at 175 C.

mb.roms.package.quartz-fill.name: Fused and ground silica from quartz sand
mb.roms.package.quartz-fill.description: The 0.5-3 um angular silica that fills 60-75% of the moulding compound by weight, produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz.

mb.roms.package.wire.name: 25 um gold wire wedge bonding
mb.roms.package.wire.description: About 24 pad-to-frame bonds plus a few internal wires, made on a wedge bonder because gold is soft; the wedge tool presses the wire flat. Ultrasonic energy and 300-400 C tool temperature.

mb.roms.package.frame.name: 24-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel
mb.roms.package.frame.description: A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 24 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, bonding tab plated nickel-then-gold, leads later tin-plated for soldering.

mb.roms.mask.name: The ROM-only mask plate
mb.roms.mask.description: Because the ROM pattern is a physical edit to the flow, Commodore held a separate chrome-on-glass plate for each ROM number. It was cut from the ROM's bit map by the same pattern generator used for the logic masks, inspected against the database, and stored in a mask library; 901226-01 and 901227-03 each required their own.

mb.roms.process.name: NMOS mask ROM front end
mb.roms.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU - n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium, PSG/nitride passivation - with one extra mask level for the ROM programming pattern. A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.

mb.roms.programming.name: Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision
mb.roms.programming.description: An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.
mb.roms.programming.note: The brief describes programming as 'final-metal selective etch'. That is right in spirit - the pattern is defined by which bits of metal/via are present - but in 1982 the edit was usually made at the contact-cut level or in the aluminium layer itself, not by selectively etching an already-deposited blanket metal film. Either way the cost was the same: one extra mask.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 2048 words x 8 bits for 8 KB; 512 x 8 for 4 KB

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: contact / via programming done as an edit to one mask

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: each ROM revision = a new mask set cut and a new process run

mb.roms.sense.name: Bit-line sense amplifiers
mb.roms.sense.description: A masked bit line is precharged high and then a dummy word is selected to develop a voltage across the bit line; a differential sense amplifier (a latch of four NMOS transistors plus a pair of cross-coupled load devices, exactly the same topology as the 6510's logic) amplifies the millivolt difference and latches it. The sense amps were the largest block in a mask ROM die - typically 10-15% of the area - because each needed a perfect match.

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a few mV differential, amplified to a full logic swing

mb.roms.ni-cr.name: Thin-film alternatives: NiCr and Cr-SiO2
mb.roms.ni-cr.description: Some mask ROMs and PROMs of the era used a vacuum-deposited thin film as the memory element instead of a transistor array: nichrome (Ni80/Cr20) or chromium-silicon monoxide cermet resistor film, sputtered or co-evaporated to a sheet resistance of 25-200 ohm/sq, then laser- or sand-blast-programmed by burning gaps in the film. Commodore's ROMs were the ordinary transistor-array type; thin-film PROMs were more at home in TTL/PROM logic parts.
mb.roms.ni-cr.note: Included to record that 'mask ROM' and 'thin-film PROM' were two different ways to build a read-only store in the same decade.

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: pulsed laser ablation or sandblast through a photoresist mask

mb.roms.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for mask ROM
mb.roms.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. Mask ROMs ran the same NMOS front end as logic, and were often made on the same lots as the CPU.

mb.roms.cz.name: CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean
mb.roms.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped to 10 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed with a ruby laser, OD or ID saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP existed), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

mb.roms.wafer.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.roms.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.roms.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.roms.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.roms.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon charge
mb.roms.polysilicon.description: Siemens-process polycrystalline silicon from 9N trichlorosilane reduced by pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

mb.roms.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, rectified to 9N
mb.roms.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated at 300 C with dry HCl, then fractionally distilled on the 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

mb.roms.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon from the submerged arc furnace
mb.roms.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to 98-99% silicon.

mb.roms.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
mb.roms.quartz.description: Crushed and screened quartz of under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.roms.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and acid-leached
mb.roms.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove boron.

mb.roms.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar concentrate for the HF leach
mb.roms.fluorspar.description: 97%+ CaF2 acid-grade fluorspar, mined and floated, converted to HF with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead retort at 200-250 C.

mb.roms.sulfur.name: Elemental sulfur for the HF plant
mb.roms.sulfur.description: Sulfur recovered from natural gas (Claus process, H2S + SO2 -> S + 2 H2O) or from sour crude, then burned to SO3 over V2O5 and absorbed to make the sulfuric acid used in the fluorspar retort.

mb.color-ram.name: U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static)
mb.color-ram.description: The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.
mb.color-ram.note: Three corrections to the brief. (1) The part holds 1024 words of 4 bits = 512 bytes, not 1 KB; '1K' refers to the word count, and it is 4 bits wide, not 8. (2) It is not CMOS - the 2114L is explicitly 'N-channel silicon-gate technology', an NMOS cross-coupled inverter latch with a resistor load, not the 6-transistor CMOS cell of later 6264/6280 SRAMs. (3) There was no standard bipolar 4-transistor 2114; the bipolar 1K x 4 memories of the era were unrelated parts (74S287/74S288 and the 74LS189 family are 1K x 1 or 256 x 4). The 'four 256 x 4 or 1K x 4 banks sharing address pins' description does not match the real device: one 1024 x 4 array with ten straight address inputs A0-A9.

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: N-channel silicon gate, fully static, no clocks

mb.color-ram.test.name: Probe, sort and final test
mb.color-ram.test.description: Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.
mb.color-ram.test.note: Tester models and exact patterns at Norristown are not documented; the description is the standard period approach to static RAM.

mb.color-ram.package.name: 18-pin DIP package: frame, bond, mould, test
mb.color-ram.package.description: Die attach on a gold-plated 18-pin lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

mb.color-ram.vic-interface.name: How the VIC-II reads it during raster
mb.color-ram.vic-interface.description: The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the 6-bit-per-channel RGB DAC and out through the 18-resistor palette on the mainboard. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.
mb.color-ram.vic-interface.note: The VIC-II steals these cycles with AEC low; the CPU sees the colour RAM through $D800 only when the VIC is not driving the bus.

facts.label: Data path
facts.value: 4 bits direct to the VIC-II DAC, bypassing the 6510 data bus

mb.color-ram.litho.name: Photolithography for the 2114
mb.color-ram.litho.description: AZ-1350 positive resist spun to about 1 um, soft baked at 90-100 C, aligned on a 1:1 Coburn contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner through a 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plate, developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard baked, stripped in hot sulfuric acid and megasonically cleaned before the next step.

mb.color-ram.mask.name: The 2114 mask set
mb.color-ram.mask.description: Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.

mb.color-ram.chromite.name: Chromite ore behind the mask absorber
mb.color-ram.chromite.description: The chrome on every photomask in this tree starts as chromite (FeCr2O4) ore from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

mb.color-ram.process.name: NMOS silicon-gate front end for the 2114
mb.color-ram.process.description: An NMOS process in the same family as the CPU: n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 then wet H2/O2 at 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, and 1-2 um aluminium with 0.5-1% Si sputtered and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG/nitride passivation. About 2-4 um minimum feature - a static RAM has no tight-pitch sense-amplifier chain to shrink, so it could run a coarser, older, cheaper process than the 6510.
mb.color-ram.process.note: The brief suggested '~3-5 um, p-well/n-well, LOCOS, polysilicon gate, aluminium, lithium-aluminium or polysilicon depletion load'. LOCOS, polysilicon gate and single-level aluminium are certainly right. There is no p-well or n-well in an NMOS process of this era - the wells came with CMOS a few years later - and I have deliberately made no claim about a specific line width for a 2114, because none of the available sources publish one.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: single 1-2 um aluminium layer, no TiW barrier

mb.color-ram.cell.name: The six-transistor NMOS static cell
mb.color-ram.cell.description: Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.
mb.color-ram.cell.note: The 'six transistors per bit in a typical static RAM' figure is a standard period statement for NMOS SRAM; the cell topology is the classic two-cross-coupled-inverter latch plus two access transistors. Cell layout (single-ended bit line vs differential, and whether the sense amplifier was a shared latch) is not published for the 2114 and is not claimed here.

mb.color-ram.cell.access.name: Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure
mb.color-ram.cell.access.description: A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.
mb.color-ram.cell.access.note: A 32 x 32 organisation with two decoders is the natural way to build 1024 x 4 and is what other period 1K x 4 SRAMs used; I have not seen a published die shot of the 2114 to confirm the split.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 32 rows x 32 columns x 4 bit planes

mb.color-ram.cell.load.name: The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor
mb.color-ram.cell.load.description: This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. I could not establish which the C64's 2114 used.
mb.color-ram.cell.load.note: Both were standard period practice and the two are visually distinguishable on a die. The specific load device on a 2114L from 1982 is not documented in any source I could find. Lithium-doped polysilicon was used in some early NMOS logic but I found no evidence it was used here.

facts.label: Option A
facts.value: undoped polysilicon resistor, 30-100 ohm/sq, no extra mask

facts.label: Option B
facts.value: depletion-mode NMOS load, one extra implant

mb.color-ram.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
mb.color-ram.wafer.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed - the same substrate specification as the CPU and CIAs, and very possibly from the same lots, since a static RAM and a CPU need no exotic process.

mb.color-ram.cz.name: CZ pull and wafer finishing
mb.color-ram.cz.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped to 10-20 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (CMP did not exist in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

mb.color-ram.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.color-ram.crucible.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm inside diameter, holding the melt at 1420 C. Flame-fused around a rotating graphite mandrel from acid-leached quartz sand at ~2000 C, annealed, glazed inside and out, and scrapped after a handful of pulls.

mb.color-ram.polysilicon.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
mb.color-ram.polysilicon.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, cut into CZ charge pieces.

mb.color-ram.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
mb.color-ram.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

mb.color-ram.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
mb.color-ram.msi.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

mb.color-ram.quartz.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
mb.color-ram.quartz.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.color-ram.quartz-sand.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
mb.color-ram.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove boron. Also the source of the silica that goes into the package's epoxy and into the crystal puller's crucibles.

mb.color-ram.quartz-leach.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
mb.color-ram.quartz-leach.description: Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible is acid-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 at 80-120 C and chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip boron, phosphorus, arsenic and alkali metals. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.

mb.color-ram.hf.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
mb.color-ram.hf.description: Finely ground acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. The same HF that leached the quartz later etched every thermal oxide in the process.

mb.color-ram.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.color-ram.fluorspar.description: Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity, mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits and flotation-beneficiated. Large deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching and no semiconductor-grade quartz anywhere in this tree.

mb.color-ram.saf.name: Submerged arc furnace
mb.color-ram.saf.description: Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-and-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc holds a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

mb.color-ram.why-static.name: Why static rather than dynamic
mb.color-ram.why-static.description: The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.
mb.color-ram.why-static.note: The VIC-II gives about 63 cycles per character cell at 1.02 MHz, roughly 60-70 us of total screen refresh per frame, and it reads one nibble per cell during the ~500 ns the cell is on screen.

facts.label: Access window
facts.value: a few hundred ns per cell during the visible portion of the scanline

facts.label: Refresh needed
facts.value: none - 'All internal circuits are fully static'

facts.label: Power penalty
facts.value: ~225 mW typ vs ~135 mW for a 4164

mb.ram.name: Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM
mb.ram.description: The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.
mb.ram.note: The scope brief said '4x 4164 = 64 KB'. That is arithmetically wrong: 4 x 8 KB = 32 KB. A breadbin C64 has EIGHT 4164 sockets. Parts came from many Asian and US suppliers, not necessarily from Commodore's own Norristown fab.

facts.label: Organisation
facts.value: 65,536 x 1 bit = 64 Kbit = 8 KB per chip

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 8-pin DIP (pin 1 no connection; pin 8 VBB on the 16-pin -8/-10 version)

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V only; internal VBB = -5 V charge pump

facts.label: Typical suppliers
facts.value: Mosel MK4564, TI TMS4464, Sanyo, UMC, Samsung, Hyundai, Nippon Micron

mb.ram.refresh.name: RAS-only refresh and why the C64 counts it
mb.ram.refresh.description: The 4164 has no refresh counter: the address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. The C64's 6510 does the counting in software - the KERNAL's refresh routine puts a 7-bit value into $D012 and clocks the CIA's A12 line every 7 machine cycles, so all eight chips are refreshed every 7 x 256 = 1792 cycles. That is why the KERNAL must be present for the machine to run, and why a 128-cycle-refresh 4164 (not a 256-cycle part) is mandatory.
mb.ram.refresh.note: The German C64 manual states explicitly that only 7-bit-refresh 64K parts must be used - a nice example of a software workaround becoming a hardware constraint.

facts.label: Counter
facts.value: in the 6510's software, not on the DRAM

mb.ram.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
mb.ram.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.
mb.ram.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonics rather than on single-wafer wet cleans with megasonic megasonics-in-a-cassette, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

mb.ram.litho.name: Photolithography for this part
mb.ram.litho.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 4164 mask set printed on a 5x stepper, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: poly 2, bit line, metal. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1354 for the poly and aluminium levels, AZ-1350 elsewhere

mb.ram.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
mb.ram.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.ram.litho.resist.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
mb.ram.litho.resist.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
mb.ram.litho.resist.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

mb.ram.sort.name: Wafer sort and final test of the 4164
mb.ram.sort.description: Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.
mb.ram.sort.note: Specific tester models are typical of the period; the ones at Norristown or at the Asian vendors are not documented.

facts.label: Testers
facts.value: Teradyne L-200, Fairchild SICTEST, or a Voltronik 5n

mb.ram.assembly.name: 8-pin DIP: lead frame, bond, mould
mb.ram.assembly.description: The 4164's assembly is the simplest IC assembly in the machine. The die goes face-up onto a gold-plated 8-pin lead frame tab with a gold-silicon eutectic bond at 400-450 C, 25 um gold wire makes eight frame bonds plus roughly a dozen internal wires for the sense-amp chain and the cell array, and the part is transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi. About 0.1-0.2 g of epoxy per part.

mb.ram.assembly.emc.name: Silica-filled epoxy molding compound
mb.ram.assembly.emc.description: A phenolic novolac / epoxy novolac resin blended with 60-75% crushed silica filler and cured in a transfer press at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-mould-baked at 175 C. The low-alpha version used on many 4164s carried a specified alpha emission rate.

mb.ram.assembly.emc.silica.name: Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand
mb.ram.assembly.emc.silica.description: The single largest mass ingredient in the package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is the reason a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.

mb.ram.assembly.gold.name: 25 um gold bonding wire
mb.ram.assembly.gold.description: 0.5-1% palladium alloyed gold wire drawn to 25 um, spooled for the wedge bonder. A 4164 uses about 0.5 m; the VIC-II and SID use more.

mb.ram.assembly.gold.ore.name: Gold ore and cyanide refining
mb.ram.assembly.gold.ore.description: Flotation concentrate leached in dilute sodium cyanide at pH 10.5, adsorbed on activated carbon, stripped and cupelled to dore, then electrolytically refined to 99.99% and drawn through a die with a phosphate lubricant.

mb.ram.assembly.frame.name: 8-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel
mb.ram.assembly.frame.description: A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 8 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, with the bonding tab plated with a nickel strike followed by gold. Plastic-package frames get a tin or tin-lead plate over nickel so the leads solder; hermetic ceramic frames get a thicker gold plate.

mb.ram.mask.name: 4164 photomask set
mb.ram.mask.description: A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

mb.ram.mask.resist.name: Photoresist: AZ-1354 for the thick poly levels
mb.ram.mask.resist.description: AZ-1354, a higher-solids positive resist used where a thicker film was needed (poly 2, aluminium) so the etch could go deep without thinning the resist. Spun at 3000-5000 rpm to 2-3 um, hard baked at 120 C, exposed through the reticle at 30-50 mJ/cm2, developed in TMAH. As with the CPU, the process ends in Piranha and RCA SC-1 cleans between every step.

mb.ram.mask.stepper.name: 5x step-and-repeat aligner
mb.ram.mask.stepper.description: An optical reduction stepper: a mercury-doped short-arc lamp, a 5x reduction lens, an x-y stage that steps the reticle across the wafer exposing one die field at a time, automatic mark-to-mark or die-to-die alignment with +-0.2 um repeatability, and a throughput of 30-60 die fields per minute. This was the tool that made 64K DRAM economics work, because one small reticle covered the whole die and one set-up covered many wafers.

mb.ram.mask.reticle.name: 5x reticle: chrome on quartz
mb.ram.mask.reticle.description: A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

mb.ram.mask.chrome-target.name: Chromium sputtering target
mb.ram.mask.chrome-target.description: 99.5% pure chromium, vacuum-melted and rolled into a target, sputtered with argon at 1-2 kW in a DC magnetron chamber onto a rotating plate.

mb.ram.mask.chromium-ore.name: Chromite (FeCr2O4) ore concentrate
mb.ram.mask.chromium-ore.description: Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex of South Africa, the Ural chromite deposits, or the Great Dyke of Zimbabwe - the entire industrial supply of chromium metal still traces to a handful of layered igneous intrusions.

mb.ram.package.name: 8-pin DIP package, die attach, bond, mould, test
mb.ram.package.description: Dice are sawn apart, attached to an 8-pin lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, and wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder - typically 8 frame bonds plus 8-14 internal interconnect wires for the sense amps and cell array. Encapsulated in transfer-moulded silica-filled epoxy, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, socket-tested and optionally burned in.

facts.label: Pinout
facts.value: 8-pin DIP: 1 NC, 2 DIN, 3 /WE, 4 /RAS, 5 A5, 6 A2, 7 A1, 8 VDD

mb.ram.package.cover.name: Sintered chip cover over the die
mb.ram.package.cover.description: On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.

mb.ram.process.name: Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process
mb.ram.process.description: Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.

mb.ram.protection.name: Alpha-particle and latch-up protection
mb.ram.protection.description: DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.
mb.ram.protection.note: The IBM/Samsung 'HAB' (hit-point-address-bypass) and soft-error work of the mid 1980s came later.

facts.label: Alpha energy
facts.value: ~5-6 MeV from Rn-222 progeny in the epoxy

facts.label: Typical soft error rate
facts.value: ~1 FIT to 100 FIT per device, highly variable

mb.ram.photolitho.name: Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels
mb.ram.photolitho.description: The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.
mb.ram.photolitho.note: Some 64K DRAMs were still made on 1:1 proximity aligners in 1981-82; by 1984 5x steppers were standard across the industry.

mb.ram.vbb.name: Single +5 V rail and the internal -5 V charge pump
mb.ram.vbb.description: The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.
mb.ram.vbb.note: Because the 8-pin 4164 has no VBB pin, two 4164s cannot be stacked in the C128 the way 4116s were; the C64's stacked-DRAM mods all use 16-pin -10 parts.

facts.label: VBB
facts.value: -5 V, generated internally on the 8-pin -8/-12 versions

facts.label: Refresh
facts.value: 128 RAS cycles, 2 ms; RAS-only (no internal counter on most parts)

mb.ram.cell.name: The 1T1C memory cell and the 4164's three polysilicon levels
mb.ram.cell.description: Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.
mb.ram.cell.note: The brief said '3-transistor/1-capacitor cell' - that is the 1Kbit-era cell (e.g. the 1101/2102). The 4164 is definitively 1T1C; every 4164 datasheet of the period says 'single transistor dynamic storage cells'. Folded bit lines belong to the 256K/1M generation, though a few 4164 designs did use them; treat folded bit lines here as unverified.

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: charge on the capacitor, must be refreshed

mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.name: Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.description: The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.note: Difference from today: 2020s DRAM uses a sputtered AL2O3/HZO or high-k capacitor on a finFET access transistor with a deep recessed plate; none of that existed here. The capacitor area was bought by making the cell long and thin.

mb.ram.wafer.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
mb.ram.wafer.description: A 4-inch boron-doped p-type CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed with a (100) primary flat. DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content (a higher oxygen precipitate density in the bulk) because the long trapped-charge lifetime helps refresh margin.

mb.ram.slice.name: Sawing, lapping, wet chemical polish, clean
mb.ram.slice.description: OD or ID diamond saw slicing to ~0.7 mm, double-sided lapping to 300 um with colloidal silica, then wet chemical polish in hot alkaline peroxide or HNO3/HF - CMP did not exist yet. Wafers are laser-scribed for the (100) primary flat and given a rounded edge in hot KOH, then megasonically cleaned in Piranha (H2SO4:H2O2, 120 C) and RCA SC-1.
mb.ram.slice.note: Alpha-particle soft-error protection mattered for DRAM: 4164 dice were commonly lidded with a sintered alumina or nitride ceramic 'chip cover' to absorb the alpha-particles emitted by trace radon in the packaging materials.

mb.ram.cz.name: CZ crystal pull
mb.ram.cz.description: Polysilicon charge melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium; a (100) seed is dipped and withdrawn at 2-4 mm/min while rotating at 0.5-2 rpm, growing a 100 mm boule 1-1.5 m long. Boron trichloride sets the resistivity.

mb.ram.cz.seed.name: Seed crystal and dopant gas
mb.ram.cz.seed.description: A (100)-oriented 100 mm seed sliver cut from a previous ingot sets orientation; boron trichloride is dosed into the melt through a bubbler to set 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity; high-purity helium flows over the melt at 20-40 l/min to sweep away boron.

mb.ram.wafer.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.ram.wafer.crucible.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

mb.ram.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
mb.ram.wafer.crucible-sand.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

mb.ram.polysilicon.name: 9N electronic-grade polysilicon rod
mb.ram.polysilicon.description: Polysilicon grown by the Siemens process: 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, giving a 200 mm diameter, 1 m long polycrystalline rod that is diced into CZ charge.

mb.ram.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane purification by rectification
mb.ram.tcs.description: Metallurgical silicon + HCl at 300 C gives crude SiHCl3 plus boron and phosphorus trichlorides. Rectification in a batch or packed column on the 31.8 C boiling point takes it to 9N-11N, then it is stored in nickel or stainless bulk tanks.

mb.ram.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%, from the arc furnace
mb.ram.msi.description: Quartz plus petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to give grey lumps of 98-99% silicon containing a few hundred ppm of boron.

mb.ram.quartz.name: Quartz lump, 5-30 mm, under 200 ppm Al and Fe
mb.ram.quartz.description: Metallurgical-grade quartz crushed and screened from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

mb.ram.quartz-sand.name: Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2, mined
mb.ram.quartz-sand.description: Washed silica sand from a high-purity quartz deposit; acid-leached with HF and HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron before being shipped to the silicon plant.

mb.ram.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) for the HF leach
mb.ram.fluorspar.description: Acid-grade fluorspar, 97%+ CaF2, mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid to make the hydrofluoric acid that leaches quartz and etches oxide.

mb.ram.fluorspar-ore.name: Fluorspar vein and stock ore
mb.ram.fluorspar-ore.description: Hydrothermal and karst deposits worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and floated. The Xe-124 emission controversy of the mid-1980s was about elemental fluorine plants, not the mine.

mb.ram.saf.name: Submerged arc furnace, 200-400 kA
mb.ram.saf.description: Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc keeps a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

mb.cpu.name: MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP
mb.cpu.description: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.
