mb.cpu.note: MOS called its fast N-channel process 'HMOS'; here it means a NMOS process with an ion-implanted polysilicon gate, not the HMOS of later MOS parts. The exact minimum linewidth of the Norristown 6510 (2 um vs 3 um) is not published; treat the 2 um figure as medium confidence.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, depletion load (datasheet says 'HMOS')

places: Norristown, Pennsylvania, USA (MOS Technology / CSG fab)

mb.cpu.mask.artwork.name: From layout database to mask data
mb.cpu.mask.artwork.description: The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database, and written to tape. A mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks, the die boundary and a grid-broken alignment structure, and produced the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. This data-reduction step - not the exposure - was where most mask errors were caught.
mb.cpu.mask.artwork.note: Which CAD system the Norristown layout group used in 1982 is not documented; Calma and Computervision dominated the industry and Rohm and Haas/Shipley support was in Philadelphia.

facts.label: Layout system
facts.value: Calma / Computervision, magnetic tape in and out

facts.label: Output
facts.value: rectangle/trapezoid tape for the pattern generator

mb.cpu.mould-press.name: Hydraulic transfer moulding press
mb.cpu.mould-press.description: A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and an encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: press close, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail. A 40-pin DIP cavity set produced dozens of parts per cycle.

mb.cpu.dice-tool.name: Scribe-and-break or diamond-wheel dicing
mb.cpu.dice-tool.description: A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

facts.label: Coolant
facts.value: deionized water or a solvent jet

mb.cpu.fab.name: MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road
mb.cpu.fab.description: The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.
mb.cpu.fab.note: There is no well-sourced 'West Hills' Commodore fab. The documented semiconductor sites are this Norristown plant and a Costa Mesa, California plant that Commodore closed around 1985; Commodore's corporate headquarters and much of its assembly were in West Chester, Pennsylvania. Treat any West Hills attribution as unverified.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown PA 19401

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 1969 by ex-General Instrument executives John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe, Don McLaughlin

facts.label: Acquired
facts.value: 1976 by Commodore Business Machines for 9.4% of Commodore equity

facts.label: Closed
facts.value: 1992, bankruptcy protection; added to the EPA Superfund NPL in 1985

mb.cpu.fab.assembly.name: Assembly and test lines in the same building
mb.cpu.fab.assembly.description: Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.

mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.name: In-house or commissioned mask shop
mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.description: A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.
mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.note: Flagged low confidence deliberately: the existence, location and equipment of any Commodore mask shop in 1982 is not something I could verify.

mb.cpu.fab.power.name: Electricity for the fab
mb.cpu.fab.power.description: A device fab is an electricity sink, not a labour sink: 4-5 kWh per wafer per mask level for the furnaces and the aligners, plus a very large chilled-water load for the compressors and the wet benches. US industrial power in 1982 cost on the order of 5-7 cents per kWh, so electricity was a real fraction of the cost of a 6510.
mb.cpu.fab.power.note: Order-of-magnitude estimate from period fab literature; the exact Norristown figure is not published.
inputs: hard coal and natural gas generation

facts.label: Intensity
facts.value: ~1500-3000 kWh per wafer through the whole flow

mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom.name: Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration
mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom.description: Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

mb.cpu.burnin.name: Burn-in and final test
mb.cpu.burnin.description: Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage (typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part) at 100-125 C for 24-168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in - the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.
mb.cpu.burnin.note: Burn-in of consumer-grade MOS parts in 1982 was common but not universal; C64-era Commodore parts often skipped a formal burn-in step.

mb.cpu.package.name: Trim, form, marking and final electrical test
mb.cpu.package.description: After moulding, the leads are formed on a 8-16 station trim-and-form press (trimmed, bent to 0.6 inch pitch, flattened, and plated in a tin or tin-lead solder pot), the body is marked by a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with the part number, lot code and date code, and the part is inserted into a socket on a Teradyne or Fairchild automatic tester and run against a final test program.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: Teradyne / Fairchild automatic tester in a socket

mb.cpu.bond.name: Gold wire wedge bonding
mb.cpu.bond.description: A wire bonder (Orthomat, K&S 1470, or Balzer 4000) pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad to the frame (lead) and then an interconnect wire from pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than the ultrasonic ball bond used for aluminium. A single 6510 had about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 mm of 25 um gold each.

mb.cpu.attach.name: Die attach to the lead frame (gold-silicon eutectic)
mb.cpu.attach.description: The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame pad and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond (Collberg, Balzer, or Kulicke & Soffa) raises the die and frame to about 400-450 C: the gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. This both makes the mechanical bond and gives the die a low-thermal-resistance path to the lead frame.
mb.cpu.attach.note: MOS Technology shipped 6510s in ceramic and in plastic packages. In ceramic (hermetic) parts the die was attached with silver brazing or a controlled glass-frit seal instead.

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: silver-filled epoxy, or glass frit in ceramic packages

mb.cpu.dicing.name: Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw
mb.cpu.dicing.description: The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

mb.cpu.probe.name: Wafer probe (electrical die sort)
mb.cpu.probe.description: Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.
mb.cpu.probe.note: In-process testing (wafer sort) reduced assembly cost only if the yield was high; at 6510 yields in the tens of percent, a large fraction of dies were packaged and sorted after assembly instead.

mb.cpu.probe.card.name: Probe card: 40 needles on a printed board
mb.cpu.probe.card.description: A fiberglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of 40 gold-plated probe needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. 1982 probe cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated tungsten or rhenium needles; automatic stepping probe stations (handling 200-1000 pads per die) were still a 1980s novelty for 40-pad parts.

mb.cpu.front-end.name: 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack
mb.cpu.front-end.description: A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.
mb.cpu.front-end.note: Layer thicknesses for the specific 6510 are reconstructed from period NMOS design rules, not from a published process manual. There was exactly ONE metal layer - no aluminium barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP, no dual damascene.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: single aluminium level, single poly gate + poly load resistor

mb.cpu.fe.cleanroom.name: Class 10 cleanroom bay with HEPA and FFU
mb.cpu.fe.cleanroom.description: Wafer processing ran in a yellow-lit room with laminar-flow fan filter units (TAMCO, Flotronics) giving class 100 (ISO 5) work area over a class 1000 background, maintained at 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases came from a bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen distribution panel with stainless steel lines and mass-flow controllers.

mb.cpu.fe.nitrogen.name: Bulk high-purity nitrogen and hydrogen
mb.cpu.fe.nitrogen.description: Liquid nitrogen trucked in and vaporised in a bulk tank; hydrogen by electrolysis of deionized water, or delivered in bulk; oxygen as a separate liquid tank. These gases flush furnaces, run LPCVD and implant hardware, and form a large part of the process cost.

mb.cpu.fe.implanter.name: Low-energy ion implanter
mb.cpu.fe.implanter.description: A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.
mb.cpu.fe.implanter.note: If Norristown did not own an implanter, this step was done as an outside foundry service - plausible for a small internal fab, but undocumented.

mb.cpu.fe.etcher.name: Wet etch bench and plasma etcher
mb.cpu.fe.etcher.description: Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.

mb.cpu.fe.deposition.name: Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer
mb.cpu.fe.deposition.description: A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

mb.cpu.fe.furnace.name: Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces
mb.cpu.fe.furnace.description: Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/dank drives.

mb.cpu.fe.aligner.name: Mask aligner: contact/proximity printing
mb.cpu.fe.aligner.description: A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury lamp or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact (mask pressed straight down onto the resist) or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2.

mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.name: Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop
mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.description: Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.
mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.note: Contact printing at 1:1 could reach 1 um; the Micralign (Perkin-Elmer) introduced in the mid 1970s was the cheap alternative that projected the image without touching the wafer. True 10x reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire) were being installed in 1982-83 but were expensive.

mb.cpu.fe.passivation.name: 7. Passivation and pad opening
mb.cpu.fe.passivation.description: The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.
mb.cpu.fe.passivation.note: Whether the 6510 die carried nitride passivation or only PSG is not publicly documented; nitride passivation at a small internal fab in 1982 is plausible but not certain.

mb.cpu.fe.contacts.name: 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization
mb.cpu.fe.contacts.description: Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.
mb.cpu.fe.contacts.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines, and a single aluminium layer - the die simply had no room for more.

mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned.name: 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant
mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned.description: With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: self-alignment is what made 2 um silicon-gate NMOS practical in a small fab

mb.cpu.fe.poly.name: 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon
mb.cpu.fe.poly.description: Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.
mb.cpu.fe.poly.note: Dichlorosilane was cheaper per deposited atom than silane and preferred for thick films, but carried chlorine that required a careful post-deposition clean.

mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide.name: 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric)
mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide.description: After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 350-450 A (~800 A grown to allow for later poly oxidation)

mb.cpu.fe.locos.name: 2. LOCOS field oxide
mb.cpu.fe.locos.description: The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.
mb.cpu.fe.locos.note: LOCOS was still the isolation scheme in 1982; trench isolation was a few years away.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: dry O2 then wet H2/O2, 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Bird's beak
facts.value: ~1-2 um lateral encroachment - the reason a field-gate design was attractive

mb.cpu.fe.nplus.name: 1. n+ source/dank pre-diffusion
mb.cpu.fe.nplus.description: A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.
mb.cpu.fe.nplus.note: Some 1982 fabs used an arsenic implant instead of phosphorus diffusion; Norristown is documented only as an NMOS shop, not at this level of detail.

mb.cpu.mask-set.name: Photomask set, ~10 levels
mb.cpu.mask-set.description: The 6510 pattern was drawn as polygons on a Calma/Computervision layout system, converted through a mask database to mask data, and cut into 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates for a 100 mm wafer. Nine or ten mask levels: n+ S/D, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation/pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab used 1:1 masks with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982.
mb.cpu.mask-set.note: The exact level count and whether any mask was a reticle is not published for the Norristown 6510. Commodore did own mask-making capability, but I have not verified the West Hills facility mentioned in some accounts.

facts.label: Mask type
facts.value: 1:1, chrome on soda-lime glass or quartz, 5x7 inch

mb.cpu.mask.stepper.name: The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period
mb.cpu.mask.stepper.description: Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.
mb.cpu.mask.stepper.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than confirmed as sitting in Norristown.

mb.cpu.mask.inspection.name: Mask inspection and defect repair
mb.cpu.mask.inspection.description: Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles (1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame) protected final production masks from dust; Commodore bought chips on wafers or in flatpacks and cut them at assembly instead, but many C64-era NORISTOWN parts were shipped in this way.
mb.cpu.mask.inspection.note: Pellicles were in general use by 1982 but were less common for 1:1 contact printing, where the mask still touched the wafer.

mb.cpu.mask.resist.name: Photoresist for mask making
mb.cpu.mask.resist.description: Positive resists of the era: Shipley AZ-1350 and AZ-1354 (which also served as the wafer resist for most process levels), Kodak KMR-8105, and Fuji HiP resist. Resist spun at ~3000 rpm to 0.5-1.5 um, soft-baked at 90-100 C, exposed in N2, developed in dilute alkaline developer.
mb.cpu.mask.resist.note: Shipley (Rohm and Haas) was headquartered in Philadelphia, 30 km from the Norristown fab, as was the later Rohm and Haas mask-resist business - a real regional supply chain.
places: Rohm and Haas, Philadelphia; Fuji Film, Japan; Hitachi, Japan

mb.cpu.mask.plotter.name: Pattern generator driving a mask exposure
mb.cpu.mask.plotter.description: In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.
mb.cpu.mask.plotter.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, a purchased mask from an outside mask shop, or a mix is not documented in public sources.

mb.cpu.mask.plate.name: Chrome-on-glass photomask plate
mb.cpu.mask.plate.description: A 5x7 inch plate of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz coated with ~100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, then the exposed chromium etched away in hot sulfuric-perchromate or perchloric acid, washed, inspected, and defect-repaired.

mb.cpu.mask.glass.name: Mask plate glass from melted quartz sand
mb.cpu.mask.glass.description: Soda-lime float glass (most 1982 1:1 masks) or fused silica, melted from batched sand plus soda ash and lime in a continuous tank furnace and drawn into 1 mm plate, then annealed.

mb.cpu.mask.chromium.name: Sputter target of chromium
mb.cpu.mask.chromium.description: 99.5% pure chromium cathode, vacuum-melted and rolled, sputtered with argon at ~1-2 kW onto the rotating plate inside a DC magnetron chamber. Chromium's high opacity in the deep-UV and its resistance to wet cleaning made it the universal mask absorber from the 1960s to the present.
places: mask shops in California and Taiwan

mb.cpu.wafer.name: Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
mb.cpu.wafer.description: The starting substrate for the die: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished mirror finish on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat.
mb.cpu.wafer.note: P-type (100) CZ was the standard NMOS logic substrate through the 1980s; n-type epitaxial and (111) were alternatives.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 100 mm (4 inch) - 125 mm was not standard until ~1986

mb.cpu.wafer.clean.name: Pre-diffusion wafer clean: Piranha and RCA SC-1
mb.cpu.wafer.clean.description: Every wafer entering the furnace was cleaned. The workhorse step was Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C, boiling off organics and metal), followed by RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) and SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), then a megasonic rinse in deionized water and a short HF dip to strip native oxide. Megasonic (1.6 MHz sonic) cleaners and particle-count-filtered N2 blow-off were standard.

mb.cpu.wafer.water.name: Ultrapure deionized process water
mb.cpu.wafer.water.description: City water passed through sand, activated carbon, cation and anion exchange resins, a 1.5 micron filter and finally UV sterilization to reach 10-18 Mohm-cm and under 100 ppt dissolved solids. Every C64 die consumed thousands of litres of this water across its ~50 dip and rinse steps.

mb.cpu.wafer.edge.name: Edge profiling / edge chamfer
mb.cpu.wafer.edge.description: The wafer rim was rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch, removing the razor edge so later photoresist could not build up and so the wafer would not chip in handling.

mb.cpu.wafer.polish.name: Wet chemical polish (not CMP)
mb.cpu.wafer.polish.description: 1982 practice: the wafer was chemically polished in hot alkaline or acidic peroxide solution - for example hot dilute NaOH/H2O2, or HNO3/HF/acetic - which removed ~10 um of damage layer and left an atomically flat surface. Chemical-mechanical polishing with a soft pad and slurry did not reach volume production until the late 1980s.
mb.cpu.wafer.polish.note: Difference from today: a modern wafer goes through CMP in a rotary single-wafer polisher; in 1982 this step was purely chemical.

mb.cpu.wafer.lapping.name: Double-sided lapping
mb.cpu.wafer.lapping.description: Saw-cut wafers are lapped on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate using a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to ~300 um with a mirror surface but still several micrometres of total thickness variation across the wafer.

mb.cpu.wafer.slicing.name: Ingot slicing: ID or OD saw + laser scribe
mb.cpu.wafer.slicing.description: The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed (ruby or Nd:YAG) before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw (blade up to 2.2 m diameter, rotating at 2000 rpm, ~0.30 mm kerf) or, on more advanced 1982 machines, by ID saw (blade inside the crystal, ~0.25 mm kerf). The result is ~0.7 mm wafers, far too warped and marked to print on.

mb.cpu.wafer.blade.name: Diamond-impregnated saw blade
mb.cpu.wafer.blade.description: A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at 2-3 wafers a minute relies on that grit: natural or synthetic industrial diamond, 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: resin-bonded, OD up to 2.2 m; ID blades inside the boule

mb.cpu.wafer.diamond.name: Industrial diamond from graphite
mb.cpu.wafer.diamond.description: Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered into a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co, Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: kimberlite pipe, Gaborone and Kimberley, South Africa

places: Element Six (De Beers), UK; Sumitomo Electric, Japan

mb.cpu.wafer.cz.name: Czochralski growth of the boron-doped ingot
mb.cpu.wafer.cz.description: The puller melts polysilicon chunks in a fused quartz crucible at ~1420 C in a flowing helium or argon atmosphere, dips a seed crystal, and rotates and slowly withdraws it while a raw boule ~100 mm across and 1-1.5 m long grows. Boron trichloride or diborane is dosed into the melt to set the 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity. The constant rotation and the thermal gradient grow a dislocation-free, uniform cross-section with a slight oxygen precipitate peak near the seed end.
mb.cpu.wafer.cz.note: No N-type epitaxy was needed for NMOS: the transistor bodies are p+ islands diffused into the p-type substrate. Epitaxial growth in this period was done in an ATCP (Applied Technology) vertical radiant-heated reactor.

mb.cpu.wafer.he.name: Helium as the CZ growth atmosphere
mb.cpu.wafer.he.description: High-purity helium (6N) bled over the melt to carry off the intense blackbody heat and to sweep volatile boron compounds away. Argon or a helium/argon mix was a cheaper alternative and produced more oxygen precipitation.

mb.cpu.wafer.fz.name: Float zone alternative (silicon for other parts, not the 6510)
mb.cpu.wafer.fz.description: In float-zone growth a poly rod is converted to monocrystal by dragging a molten silicon zone down it in an inert atmosphere, touching no crucible at all. Yield is higher and oxygen is lower, but the crystals were narrow (<30 mm) and slow, so FZ in 1982 was for power rectifiers and some bipolar parts, not CPU wafers.
mb.cpu.wafer.fz.note: Included because it is the other way to grow a boule, and it explains why FZ silicon appears in some C64-era discrete rectifiers.

mb.cpu.wafer.seed.name: Seed crystal for CZ pulling
mb.cpu.wafer.seed.description: A short (100 mm) (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and defect-free growth of the new boule.

mb.cpu.wafer.crucible.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
mb.cpu.wafer.crucible.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm ID, holding several kilos of molten silicon and dipping into it several cm at 1420 C. It is itself grown from quartz sand in a flame-fusion electric furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel, annealed slowly to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out. Crucibles were the dominant silicon-metal loss source and were scrapped after a handful of pulls.

mb.cpu.wafer.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand melted into crucible glass
mb.cpu.wafer.crucible-sand.description: High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame/arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C into a clear annealed vitreous silica blank. Graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.

mb.cpu.wafer.polysilicon.name: 9N-11N electronic-grade polysilicon
mb.cpu.wafer.polysilicon.description: Chunky polycrystalline silicon chunks loaded into the Czochralski crystal puller. Made by the Siemens process: high-purity trichlorosilane is reduced with pure hydrogen over electrically heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C, depositing polycrystalline silicon on the hot wires until a rod ~150-250 mm diameter and about 1 m long is grown.

mb.cpu.wafer.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), 9N-11N
mb.cpu.wafer.tcs.description: The intermediate that carries silicon from cheap metallurgical-grade metal to electronics grade. Made by passing dry HCl over crushed metallurgical silicon at 250-350 C in a fluidised or bubbling bed: Si + 3 HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2. Rectified by fractional distillation to a boiling point of 31.8 C until metal, B and P contaminants are below 1 ppb.

mb.cpu.wafer.msi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
mb.cpu.wafer.msi.description: Rough grey lumps of silicon produced in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and petroleum coke at 1900-2200 C. This is the ore-like starting point: roughly 300 kg of 98% silicon per 6510-class wafer batch. Boron and phosphorus ride along at hundreds of ppm and must be removed later.

mb.cpu.wafer.coke.name: Petroleum coke as the carbon reductant
mb.cpu.wafer.coke.description: Needle coke or calcined petroleum coke from a petroleum coke calciner, used as both reductant and fuel in the arc furnace. Also the ancestor of the graphite electrodes and of the epoxy resin later on in the package.

mb.cpu.wafer.coke.calciner.name: Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke
mb.cpu.wafer.coke.calciner.description: Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours, then the green coke is calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave 0.5-2% sulphur needle coke. In the silicon industry a blend of petroleum coke and anthracite coal is used instead.
inputs: vacuum residue from crude oil distillation

mb.cpu.wafer.coke.anthracite.name: Anthracite coal as a coke substitute
mb.cpu.wafer.coke.anthracite.description: The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.

mb.cpu.wafer.coke.crude.name: Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled
mb.cpu.wafer.coke.crude.description: Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C / 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms, a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, are the feed for coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.

mb.cpu.wafer.quartz.name: Quartz (SiO2) lump for the arc furnace
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz.description: High-purity quartz, ideally with under 200 ppm aluminium and iron, crushed to 5-30 mm. Because aluminium in the metal feeds straight through to every device, silicon makers specify vein quartz or purified lump.

mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-sand.name: Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-sand.description: The geologic end of the whole tree. Sand washed from a high-purity quartzite or sandstone deposit, then purified for semiconductor use by acid leaching (HF + HNO3 to strip Al and Fe) and by chlorination, yielding quartz that can be melted into crucibles or reacted with HCl.
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-sand.note: Mined quartz of this quality is found only in a handful of districts; Spruce Pine NC is the classic North American source.

mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-leach.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-leach.description: Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible rather than the arc furnace is crushed to sand, then hot-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 to dissolve surface aluminium and iron, chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip B, P, As and alkali metals, and finally annealed in vacuum. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.
places: Spruce Pine, NC (Unimin, Quartz Corp, GE Quartz)

mb.cpu.wafer.hf.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
mb.cpu.wafer.hf.description: HF is made by treating finely ground fluorspar (CaF2) with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead/cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. It attacks glass and is the standard etchant for thermal oxide; huge quantities of it went through the same silicon supply chain.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: ~1 kg HF per wafer for oxide steps, reused several times

mb.cpu.wafer.h2so4.name: Sulfuric acid from sulfur, from pyrite or natural gas
mb.cpu.wafer.h2so4.description: Contact-process sulfuric acid: sulfur (mined as Frasch-free elemental sulfur, or roasted from pyrite ore) is burned and catalytically oxidised over V2O5 to SO3, absorbed in 98% H2SO4. Used both for HF manufacture and for the Piranha clean.

mb.cpu.wafer.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
mb.cpu.wafer.fluorspar.description: Acid-grade fluorspar mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits, beneficiated by flotation to 97%+ purity. Large deposits in Mexico (San Luis Potosi), South Africa (Plettenberg Bay) and China. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching, no quartz purification and no cleaning chemistry.
mb.cpu.wafer.fluorspar.note: Mid-1980s concern: the 1986 Chernobyl release was fluorine (not fluorspar), but fluorspar supply concentration in Mexico is genuine.

mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.name: Pegmatite / quartzite ore, mined and crushed
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.description: The actual dig: a hard-rock pegmatite or high-purity quartzite vein, blasted and jaw-crushed, then screened and hand-sorted to 5-30 mm lump for the arc furnace. Only a fraction of a deposit is white enough to be metallurgical-grade.

mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.mica.name: Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.mica.description: The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite/K-feldspar and muscovite/BIOTite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallization - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.
mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.mica.note: Biotite in particular carries a lot of iron and is a classic contaminant marker.

mb.cpu.wafer.saf.name: Submerged arc furnace, 20-40 MVA
mb.cpu.wafer.saf.description: A refractory-lined steel shell 10-12 m deep with three graphite electrodes lowered into a charge of quartz lump, petroleum coke and wood chips. Electric current (200-400 kA at 40-70 V) maintains an arc that melts the charge in the 'submerged zone' at 1900-2200 C, tapping grey metallic silicon out of the bottom every 1-2 hours. Up to 4 t/day in a modern furnace; a 1982-era unit made a few hundred tonnes per year.
mb.cpu.wafer.saf.note: Metallurgical silicon was traded globally; US and European silicon metal plants in 1982 were mainly in West Virginia, Quebec and the German Ruhr.

mb.cpu.wafer.hcl.name: Hydrogen chloride from salt and chlorine
mb.cpu.wafer.hcl.description: Dry HCl gas made by chlorinating hydrogen over a bed of rock salt, or by burning hydrogen in chlorine, then condensing and drying it with concentrated sulfuric acid. The chlorine itself comes from electrolysis of brine.

mb.cpu.wafer.brine.name: Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis
mb.cpu.wafer.brine.description: Salt dissolved in water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen; the hydrogen is what reacts with the salt to make HCl and what reduces the trichlorosilane.

mb.cpu.wafer.salt.name: Rock salt for the chlor-alkali cell
mb.cpu.wafer.salt.description: Halite mined by room-and-pillar or solution mining in the Michigan basin, Louisiana's Salt Dome, the Cheshire salt field (which is why a US chlor-alkali industry sat on top of salt), and the Zechstein basin of northern Germany. Brine is made by pumping water into the salt and pumping out saturated brine.

mb.cpu.wafer.siemens-reactor.name: Siemens wire-heated deposition reactor
mb.cpu.wafer.siemens-reactor.description: A vertical bell-jar or can reactor holding 40-80 U-shaped silicon filaments wound from vapor-grown poly. A few hundred amps of DC is passed through the filaments to hold them at ~1150 C while SiHCl3 vapour decomposes on them. These reactors were the standard ultra-purity route until the late 1980s.

mb.pcb.name: C64 mainboard ASSY 250407 - bare double-sided FR-4 board
mb.pcb.description: The unpopulated logic board of a 1983 Commodore 64. A 1.6 mm two-layer epoxy-glass laminate about 390 x 180 mm carrying 35 um copper on both faces, roughly 1200 unplated through-holes for component leads, NO plated-through holes and NO vias at all, green epoxy solder mask on both sides and a white screen-printed legend. Made by an outside printed-circuit-board house, not by Commodore.
mb.pcb.note: The board cost is the era figure quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board. A verified reverse-engineered copy of the Rev. B layout contains exactly zero vias, so no layer change goes through a plated barrel anywhere on this board.

mb.pcb.bareboard.name: Finished bare board, fab no. 250406
mb.pcb.bareboard.description: A drilled, etched, stripped, masked, legended and finished blank ready for component insertion. At 1983 commodity prices a two-layer 1.6 mm consumer board of this size cost on the order of one to two dollars.
mb.pcb.bareboard.note: The $1-2 figure is the era cost quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board.

facts.label: Etch and drill yield
facts.value: typically high; a two-layer board with no vias has few ways to fail

mb.pcb.inspection.name: Electrical test of the bare board
mb.pcb.inspection.description: Before any component goes on, the blank is checked for shorts between nets and for opens in the artwork. In 1983 this was a continuity and insulation-resistance tester plus a careful visual check under a lamp and a loupe; automated optical inspection was available but too expensive to be assumed on every commodity line.
mb.pcb.inspection.note: AOI existed by 1983 but was a line investment. Modern lines AOI every board automatically and add impedance and resistance checks as well.

mb.pcb.legend.name: White silkscreen legend and compartment boxes
mb.pcb.legend.description: Reference designators, block outlines and assembly notes are printed in white epoxy ink over the cured mask and baked. Commodore drew boxes around functional blocks, the so-called compartments, and used extra ink colours in bands and outlines to colour-code regions of the board and mark the television standard.
mb.pcb.legend.note: Coloured bands mean a second and third screen pass in a different ink, each with its own screen, squeegee pass and cure. This is a real cost and a real time step on the line.

mb.pcb.legend.colour.name: Coloured silkscreen bands
mb.pcb.legend.colour.description: A separate pass in each extra colour, with its own screen, to draw the colour bands and outlines that mark functional regions and the PAL or NTSC variant. A modern cosmetic imitation of this is a coloured solder mask; in 1983 it was extra ink passes.
mb.pcb.legend.colour.note: The exact set of colours used on the 250407 has not been confirmed here.

mb.pcb.legend.screen.name: Screen printing and bake
mb.pcb.legend.screen.description: A fine-mesh screen coated with photosensitive emulsion is stretched and tensioned over the board, epoxy ink squeegeed through, and the board then baked to cure the ink onto the mask.

mb.pcb.mask.name: Epoxy solder mask on both sides
mb.pcb.mask.description: Green epoxy ink is screen-printed over the whole board with apertures left over every pad and hole. It is the green the C64 has always been. Without it the board shorts from a fingerprint, a solder splash or a screw, and the white legend would disappear under bare copper.
mb.pcb.mask.note: Period inks were solvent-based epoxies cured in infrared or hot-air ovens. Modern liquid solder mask (LPI) is still screen-printed and cured far more cleanly; LPI plus ENIG is now the standard pairing.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: epoxy, screen-printed through a fine mesh

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: UV or thermal, typically around 150 deg C for half an hour

facts.label: Aperture allowance
facts.value: a little larger than the pad, so pads do not look ringed

mb.pcb.finish.name: Surface finish: pads and edge contacts
mb.pcb.finish.description: After etching the copper is protected, made solderable, and given a wear-resistant finish where it will be touched. On this board, because there are no plated barrels, the finish job is far simpler than on a modern via board.

mb.pcb.finish.pth.name: Plated-barrel line - NOT on this board
mb.pcb.finish.pth.description: The C64 mainboard skips the entire through-hole plating sequence a via board runs: hole desmear, electroless copper seed, electrolytic copper build, nickel, gold. This node exists to make the absence explicit, because it is a common and wrong assumption about this board.
mb.pcb.finish.pth.note: Empty branch by design. The 250407 has zero vias and zero plated barrels; anything that puts electroless copper into a C64 mainboard is wrong.

mb.pcb.finish.antitarnish.name: Anti-tarnish treatment
mb.pcb.finish.antitarnish.description: A benzotriazole-type organic protectant is applied to stop the non-plated copper from darkening in storage and handling. Cheap, invisible, and easy to skip until someone notices the boards going brown in the box.

mb.pcb.finish.selective.name: Selective plating of the edge contacts
mb.pcb.finish.selective.description: Only the edge-connector contact surfaces get a hard, wear-resistant metal. The usual route is a nickel underplate followed by electrolytic gold applied through a fountain plater or a selective rack, with everything else masked. Sometimes the entire board is immersion gold-plated instead, which is simpler and gives softer gold.
mb.pcb.finish.selective.note: On the C64 mainboard specifically these contacts are inside the female expansion, user and cassette sockets, so the gold belongs to a purchased connector; the mating plug cards carry the fingers. The plating chemistry is the same either way.

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: nickel, commonly electroless with a thin electrolytic strike

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: hard gold, roughly 1-2.5 um for a card-edge finger

facts.label: Gold bath
facts.value: cyanide-based, gold cyanide or gold sulfite

mb.pcb.finish.selective.cyanide.name: Cyanide gold bath
mb.pcb.finish.selective.cyanide.description: Gold dissolves in a cyanide complex with a fine gold anode; the cathode is the board rack. Cyanide plating baths are still the standard because they are stable and fast, and still require the same destruction-and recovery regime.

mb.pcb.finish.selective.mask.name: Selective masking
mb.pcb.finish.selective.mask.description: The board is plated overall and the gold is stripped from everywhere except the contact surfaces, or the contacts alone are exposed to the bath with the rest of the board shielded by a fountain-plater weir or a plating rack.

mb.pcb.finish.hasl.name: HASL solder level on the pads
mb.pcb.finish.hasl.description: Exposed copper is coated in molten solder by carrying the board through a wave or a drag of 63/37 tin-lead and blowing or brushing off the excess, leaving a flat solderable layer that will not corrode. This is the period default for a two-sided consumer board with no vias, and it lines up with the solder the wave machine is already using.
mb.pcb.finish.hasl.note: Modern boards use ENIG, immersion tin or OSP instead; HASL went out of fashion because its coating is soft and its thermal expansion mismatch causes failures in cycling. It was, however, ideal for a board that was going straight into a tin pot.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: a few micrometres of tin-lead over copper

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: hot enough to keep the alloy molten, several degrees above 183 deg C

mb.pcb.vias.name: How this board changed layer with NO vias
mb.pcb.vias.description: The most distinctive fact about the C64 mainboard. There are no vias and no plated-through holes. A connection that has to move from the component side to the solder side does it by passing through the hole of a component lead: every resistor, capacitor, diode and DIP pin doubles as a via. Where a layer change was needed with no component available, the board carried a short single-core tinned wire jumper, hand-fitted and hand-soldered after wave soldering.
mb.pcb.vias.note: The two jumpers appear as footprint references E1 and E2 in a verified reverse-engineered copy of the 250407 layout. The saving was real: skipping the barrel plating line removed a whole wet-chemical operation and let the board stay two-sided and cheap. The cost was longer traces and a harder time with high-speed return current.

facts.label: Wire jumpers
facts.value: 2 (E1 solid, E2 dashed on the artwork)

facts.label: What they connect
facts.value: a top-side signal to a bottom-side return

mb.pcb.vias.plane.name: Ground pour instead of a ground plane
mb.pcb.vias.plane.description: With no internal plane layer, the two signal layers carry return current on their own copper, so the layout used wide ground pours and heavy copper wherever return current had to flow. Modern boards solve the same electromagnetic problem with a dedicated plane, which is the main reason vias became universal.

mb.pcb.drill.name: Drilling every component hole
mb.pcb.drill.description: The board is drilled on a numerical-control drill for every component lead, jumper, jack and mounting hole. Because there are no vias, the drill programme is just a component position list; there is no barrel to plate afterwards.
mb.pcb.drill.note: 0.6 mm leads sat in roughly 0.8-1.0 mm holes. The oversize is deliberate: the wave has to fill the hole and a tight hole makes an unfilled, dry joint.

facts.label: Dominant diameter
facts.value: approx. 1.1 mm for DIP and leaded parts

facts.label: Larger diameters
facts.value: approx. 1.6-4.3 mm for trimmer, fuse and mounting holes

facts.label: Fit
facts.value: hole set slightly oversize so the lead drops in freely for wave soldering

mb.pcb.drill.bit.name: Carbide drill bit
mb.pcb.drill.bit.description: Tungsten-carbide or high-speed-steel bits, ground and resharpened. Laminated glass plus copper is abrasive and the hole is the one feature that cannot be reworked once drilled wrong.

mb.pcb.drill.ncd.name: NC drill and tool change
mb.pcb.drill.ncd.description: A tape-fed drill head steps through the tool table, swapping bits for the several diameters the board needs, over pinned or vacuum-held fixtures. A bit-management and drill-jig system holds sub-millimetre position accuracy; drill wander is what breaks a fine-pitch DIP row.

mb.pcb.mill.name: Routing and outline cutting
mb.pcb.mill.description: In 1983 the board outline, internal cut-outs and the edge-connector routing slot were milled mechanically on a CNC router with a carbide cutter. Laser routing existed but was not yet the commodity default for a board with no fine geometry.
mb.pcb.mill.note: Modern high-mix shops use CO2 or UV lasers for routing and depanelising because they need no tooling and leave no router burr; for this board either would be far slower than milling.

mb.pcb.mill.cutter.name: Carbide router cutter
mb.pcb.mill.cutter.description: A tungsten-carbide end mill, often with a diamond-like coating, cutting laminate that is mostly glass fibre. Glass dust is abrasive, so tool life is short and the cutter is changed on a schedule.

mb.pcb.mill.slot.name: Edge-connector routing slot
mb.pcb.mill.slot.description: The expansion-port slot is milled so that a thin projecting ear of laminate is left with copper on both faces. That ear is the board edge connector, and its copper is then selectively plated. The slot geometry sets the finger width and spacing that the case connector must mate with.
mb.pcb.mill.slot.note: Crucially, on the C64 this is a female receptacle on the mainboard, not male fingers: the board carries the socket and the expansion adapter carries the gold fingers. So the C64 mainboard has no board-edge fingers of its own.

mb.pcb.strip.name: Resist stripping and clean-up
mb.pcb.strip.description: The cross-linked resist film is dissolved away in a caustic or amine stripper, then the board is rinsed, given a mild acid clean to knock back any last residue, dried, and inspected.

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: mild acid clean and deionised rinse

mb.pcb.etch.name: Ferric chloride etching
mb.pcb.etch.description: The masked laminate goes into warm ferric chloride solution, which dissolves the unmasked copper and leaves traces, pads and ground pour standing. Copper removed along the way is recovered, and the etchant is periodically replenished or dumped.
mb.pcb.etch.note: Period text consistently quotes 42 deg Baume ferric chloride around 45 deg C. Sodium persulfate was a real alternative for some shops. Modern practice is still ferric chloride, but with tighter control and a copper-recovery loop.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: ferric chloride, commonly quoted at about 42 deg Baume, warmed to approx. 40-50 deg C

facts.label: Chemistry limit
facts.value: copper in solution poisons the bath, so it is dumped and made fresh

mb.pcb.exposure.name: UV exposure through the artwork film
mb.pcb.exposure.description: The artwork negative is laid against the resist and the board is flood-exposed. In 1983 this was a mercury-vapour or metal-halide lamp in a vacuum-frame exposure unit. Fibre-optic exposure systems that pipe collimated light into a bed of glass rods were spreading through the later 1980s and gave far more even illumination.
mb.pcb.exposure.note: An air gap between film and resist is the classic cause of a fuzzy, partly-etched trace edge on a two-sided board.

facts.label: Exposure time
facts.value: seconds to tens of seconds, set by an integrating light meter

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: film pressed into the resist under vacuum to avoid any air gap

mb.pcb.exposure.lamp.name: Mercury-vapour exposure lamp
mb.pcb.exposure.lamp.description: A quartz envelope filled with mercury vapour struck by an arc, rich in the near UV where the acrylate resists are sensitive. Needs a water-cooled jacket and a choke.

mb.pcb.exposure.vacframe.name: Vacuum exposure frame
mb.pcb.exposure.vacframe.description: A hinged platen with a rubber diaphragm. Film and resist are clamped and then evacuated so the film sits hard against the resist with no bubbles and no shadowing.

mb.pcb.photoresist.name: Dry-film photoresist, negative working
mb.pcb.photoresist.description: A dry film about 25-40 um thick, on a PET carrier, laminated onto the copper. Where the artwork film lets UV through, the acrylate resist cross-links and hardens; the hardened areas stand up to the ferric chloride. Everything else dissolves away and the copper under it etches out.
mb.pcb.photoresist.note: Period suppliers included Kodak and Dynachem. Dry film was already the default for a two-sided consumer board in 1983; modern shops more often print liquid resist, so the choice has flipped but the principle has not.

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: negative-working acrylate photopolymer on a polyester carrier

mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.name: Surface clean and tack-free prep
mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.description: Before the resist goes on, the board is degreased and dried so the film lies flat. A tack-free prep was unusual on period boards; wet resist had an easier time of it, which is one reason modern processes moved.
mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.note: Wet resist offered the no-prep advantage; dry film offered the thickness control. Dry film won on thickness.

mb.pcb.photoresist.laminate.name: Film lamination of the resist
mb.pcb.photoresist.laminate.description: The board is baked dry, the film is fed from a spool, heated, and pressed onto the copper by rubber-covered nip rollers. The rubber hardness matters: too hard and it embosses the fragile foil.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: nip rollers and a chill roll to set the film down

mb.pcb.photoresist.carrier.name: PET carrier film
mb.pcb.photoresist.carrier.description: The polyester backing the resist is laminated from. Peeled off after lamination and before exposure, leaving the resist on the copper.

mb.pcb.foil.name: Copper foil, 35 um, electro-deposited
mb.pcb.foil.description: The conductive skin on both faces of the laminate. In 1983 most consumer laminate was clad with electro-deposited foil because it is cheap and its rough surface bonds well to epoxy. Rolled annealed foil was used where thermal or dimensional stability mattered more.
mb.pcb.foil.note: The copper itself, from cathode through to concentrate, is traced by the metals subsystem; this node only follows the foil-making process as far as the laminate.

mb.pcb.foil.wind.name: Drum winding, stripping and slitting
mb.pcb.foil.wind.description: The drum winds until the foil reaches 35 um, then the foil is peeled off and slit into rolls 1.0-1.4 m wide, the width the laminator needs.

mb.pcb.foil.ed.name: Electrodeposition onto a cathode drum
mb.pcb.foil.ed.description: Cathode copper is dissolved into a sulfuric acid copper sulfate bath and electroplated onto a slowly rotating titanium or stainless drum. Brighteners and suppressors in the bath control grain so the stripped foil is a dense film rather than a powdery deposit.

mb.pcb.foil.ed.nodule.name: Nodular (peckled) deposition
mb.pcb.foil.ed.nodule.description: The final plating stage deposits fine nodules instead of flat copper. This nodular surface is what gives ED foil its grip on the resin during lamination.

mb.pcb.laminate.name: FR-4 copper-clad laminate panel, 1.6 mm
mb.pcb.laminate.description: The structural core of the board: woven E-glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin, sandwiched between two 35 um copper foils. It leaves the laminate mill as a rigid panel roughly 1.2 x 2.4 m which the PCB house cuts into working blanks.

facts.label: Core
facts.value: approx. 1.5 mm woven E-glass in brominated epoxy

mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.name: Foil bonding and copper-clad laminate
mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.description: Treated copper foil, prepreg and core are stacked and press-bonded to give the copper-clad laminate the PCB house buys. The foil is pre-treated so the epoxy keys into it during the press rather than peeling away.
mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.note: Commodore pressed none of this. It bought CCL from a merchant laminate plant and did only the imaging, etch, drill and finish itself, at an outside house.

mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.foilbond.name: Copper foil bonding treatment
mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.foilbond.description: ED foil carries a natural fine-pebble surface that grips epoxy. Rolled foil is smooth and must be deliberately roughened or given a nodular peckled treatment so the laminate does not delaminate along the copper interface. This interface is what the peel-strength test measures.
mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.foilbond.note: For a 1 oz consumer board in 1983 ED foil was the normal, cheaper choice; rolled foil was reserved for high-speed or high-temperature laminate.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.name: Hot platen press and the lamination cycle
mb.pcb.laminate.press.description: A stack of foil, prepreg, core and prepreg is pressed between heated platens. Pressure squeezes out the excess resin and forces it into the weave, and the heat completes the cure. This one step turns loose foil and cloth into a single homogeneous 1.6 mm sheet with copper bonded to both faces.
mb.pcb.laminate.press.note: Modern high-Tg FR-4 laminates press hotter (200-220 deg C) and harder. Period FR-4 at 175 deg C and 1.4 MPa is the classic cycle.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.heat.name: Press heat source
mb.pcb.laminate.press.heat.description: Steam coils or electric resistance elements in the platens. Gas- or oil-fired central steam was the norm in a laminate plant of this era.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.name: Release paper between books
mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.description: Bleached or unbleached kraft paper laid between each laminate book so resin does not bond one book to the next and the platen stays clean. Kraft paper is lignin-rich cellulose pulp.
mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.note: Also used as the cushion sheet that distributes pressure across the book.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.name: Hydraulic press pack and oil
mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.description: Pressure is applied by a hydraulic press pack with multiple heated platens so several laminate books can be pressed at once. The hydraulic oil is refined from crude.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.oil.name: Hydraulic oil
mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.oil.description: A petroleum-derived lubricating fluid circulating through the press. Traced to crude oil like almost every other lubricant on the line.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.platen.name: Heated platens
mb.pcb.laminate.press.platen.description: Cast iron platens heated by embedded steam or electric resistance elements and ground flat. The cast iron is the reason a 1980s laminate press can hold a flatness tolerance tighter than anything the component designer asked for.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.iron.name: Cast iron platen body
mb.pcb.laminate.press.iron.description: Grey cast iron, machined and surface-ground, chosen for dimensional stability and thermal mass rather than strength.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.pigiron.name: Pig iron from blast furnace
mb.pcb.laminate.press.pigiron.description: Made by smelting iron ore with coke in a blast furnace, with limestone flux. The same ore and coke that make the platen also make the drill spindles and the wave-solder machine frame.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.ironore.name: Iron ore (hematite/magnetite)
mb.pcb.laminate.press.ironore.description: Run-of-mine ore crushed and concentrated before the blast furnace. The metal backbone of every machine tool on the board line comes from here.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.orebody.name: Iron ore body
mb.pcb.laminate.press.orebody.description: A concentration of iron oxides in banded iron formation or massive hematite, mined by open pit or underground room-and-pillar, then crushed and washed.

mb.pcb.laminate.prepreg.name: B-stage prepreg and core sheet
mb.pcb.laminate.prepreg.description: Glass cloth pulled through epoxy, squeezed between metering nips to a controlled resin content and dried at 120-160 deg C until only partly cross-linked. The result is a dry, slightly tacky, board-like sheet that can be stacked and stored. The residual cure is completed under heat and pressure in the press.
mb.pcb.laminate.prepreg.note: Roll-to-roll treeline impregnation had largely displaced gap dipping by the early 1980s; it was faster and gave more uniform resin content.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.name: Brominated DGEBA epoxy resin
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.description: The diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A blended with a brominated epoxy co-resin so the cured laminate self-extinguishes. That blend is the FR in FR-4. This is the board's dielectric and its flame-retardant system, and it is where almost all of the board's non-glass, non-metal mass ends up.

facts.label: Cured glass transition
facts.value: approx. 135-150 deg C for period FR-4

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cure.name: Curing agent and cure chemistry
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cure.description: An amine or anhydride that opens the epoxide rings and cross-links them. The period laminate system was typically a bisphenol-A / diaminodiphenylsulfone blend, which is what set the elevated glass transition temperature of FR-4 sheet.
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cure.note: The curing agent is not the flame retardant; the retardant is the brominated co-resin. Keep the two straight.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.retardant.name: Tetrabromobisphenol-A epoxy co-resin
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.retardant.description: The brominated co-resin that gives FR-4 its self-extinguishing behaviour. Bromine radicals released in the gas phase quench the combustion chain, so the laminate passes the UL-94 V-0 burn test.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromine.name: Elemental bromine
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromine.description: A heavy red-brown liquid and the source of the retardant bromine. Made by oxidising bromide-rich brines with chlorine, or by blowing air and steam off seawater treated with chlorine.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromide.name: Bromide-rich brine (bittern)
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromide.description: Mother liquor left from salt manufacture, historically rich enough in bromide to strip bromine from; today also drawn from underground brines.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.epichlorohydrin.name: Epichlorohydrin
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.epichlorohydrin.description: Reacts with bisphenol A in aqueous caustic to give the diglycidyl ether liquid that becomes the binder. Made by chlorohydrin reaction of propylene, then dehydrochlorination.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorine.name: Chlorine from brine
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorine.description: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution in diaphragm or membrane cells yields chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. The same caustic soda serves the resin reaction.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.brine.name: Brine
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.brine.description: Concentrated salt solution evaporated from sea water or saline groundwater.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.halite.name: Rock salt / evaporite salt
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.halite.description: Halite mined from evaporite deposits or sun-dried from sea water, then dissolved to brine.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorohydrin.name: Chlorohydrin and dehydrochlorination
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorohydrin.description: Propylene is chlorohydrinated with hypochlorous acid at low temperature to 1-chloro-2-propanol, which is treated with caustic lime to epichlorohydrin. The caustic also does the ring-opening condensation with bisphenol A.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bpa.name: Bisphenol A backbone
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bpa.description: Condensed from two molecules of phenol with acetone under acid catalysis. This is the reaction that makes the epoxy a thermoset rather than a thermoplastic, and it is the point where petrochemical aromatics enter a material people imagine as 'plastic'.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.phenol.name: Phenol
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.phenol.description: Aromatic feedstock for bisphenol A. The cumene process alkylates benzene with propylene to cumene, oxidises it to cumene hydroperoxide, then cleaves with sulfuric acid to give phenol and acetone together.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cumene.name: Cumene and cumene hydroperoxide
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cumene.description: The intermediate whose acid cleavage is the cheapest industrial route to phenol. Benzene plus propylene over phosphoric or sulfuric acid, then air oxidation.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.propylene.name: Propylene
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.propylene.description: The C3 olefin used both here and for epichlorohydrin. From steam cracking of propane or naphtha, or as a co-product of ethylene.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cracker.name: Naphtha steam cracker
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cracker.description: Naphtha vapour pyrolysed at 800-900 deg C in coils to make ethylene, propylene and butenes. A high-temperature furnace that is the gateway from crude to the whole plastics chemistry.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.benzene.name: Benzene
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.benzene.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from heavy naphtha or made by catalytic reforming; the universal starting point for the phenol/cumene chain.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.naphtha.name: Heavy naphtha
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.naphtha.description: A mid-boiling petroleum fraction from which benzene is extracted by solvent recovery. Crude oil is the ultimate source.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.crude.name: Crude oil
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.crude.description: The hydrocarbon mixture pumped out of a sedimentary reservoir that ultimately supplies every aromatic and olefin feedstock on this branch of the tree.

mb.pcb.laminate.resin.reservoir.name: Petroleum reservoir
mb.pcb.laminate.resin.reservoir.description: Porous sandstone or fractured carbonate holding crude oil under pressure. Produced through steel casing and perforated liner into a gathering system, often by water or steam injection to hold down the pressure.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.name: Woven E-glass cloth
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.description: Continuous glass filaments woven into a plain-weave cloth that becomes the mechanical skeleton of the laminate. In 1983 the cloth would be roughly 0.1-0.2 mm thick, woven from yarn of about 9-22 tex with 8-18 filaments per centimetre. It is the structural, not the dielectric, member of the board.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.yarn.name: Glass yarn
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.yarn.description: Hundreds of continuous filaments twisted together into one yarn, then wound onto a package for the loom. Sizing holds the filaments in place so they do not fuzz or separate.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.name: Continuous E-glass fibre
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.description: The elementary filament of the reinforcement, drawn from molten glass. E-glass is a borosilicate/aluminosilicate carrying 15-19 % of non-glass oxides, mainly boron and lime, which lower the melting point enough for cheap fine-diameter drawing.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.flame.name: Flame-drawn fibre (roving)
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.flame.description: The cheaper alternative to bushing fibre: glass is remelted in a small furnace and blown through a plate with a few larger holes into 20-30 um fibres. Coarser, so it is used as a surface mat or chopped strand, not as the woven reinforcement itself.
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.flame.note: Some 1980s copper-clad laminate used a thin woven cloth with a flame-drawn mat for extra thickness and better resin flow.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size.name: Sizing and binder on the fibre
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size.description: Fresh glass fibre is slippery and fragile. Filaments are coated while hot with a thin organosilane sizing plus a film-former such as starch or PVA that holds the ribbon together and stops the yarn fuzzing. For laminate the silane is chosen to form the chemical bond to the epoxy; that interface is the classic site of delamination failure.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size.silane.name: Organosilane coupling agent
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size.silane.description: A bifunctional molecule with an alkoxy end that bonds to the glass surface and a reactive organic end that copolymerises with the epoxy. It is the molecular glue that turns a loose glass cloth into a chemically bonded laminate, and it is what makes copper-to-glass peel strength measurable.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.draw.name: Bushing filament drawing
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.draw.description: Molten glass is fed to a platinum-rhodium bushing plate perforated with hundreds to thousands of 4-9 um holes and pulled downward at enormous speed. Surface tension, not a die, forms each filament. The fibres gather into a ribbon, are cooled and wound.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.melt.name: Glass melting furnace and bushing
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.melt.description: A regenerative gas furnace melts the batch to a red-hot glass at roughly 1400-1600 deg C, with a nickel-alloy bushing plate riding on the sump. Fuel is almost always natural gas or oil.
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.melt.note: Capital-intensive, but far less so than a semiconductor fab; glass plants of this size existed in the hundreds worldwide by the early 1980s.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.batch.name: Glass batch (frit)
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.batch.description: A dry blend of silica sand, limestone or dolomite, and boron compounds, with a trace of carbon black so the glass comes out faintly green rather than water-clear. Melting the batch is what feeds the bushing.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.boron.name: Boron oxide compounds (colemanite, borax)
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.boron.description: B2O3 lowers the working temperature of the melt, which is what makes fine-diameter drawing practical on ordinary platinum-rhodium equipment.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.lime.name: Limestone / dolomite
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.lime.description: Adds lime and magnesia to E-glass, lowering the melt temperature and improving the chemical durability of the drawn fibre.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.name: High-purity silica sand
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.description: Low-iron, low-alumina quartz sand, the main glass former. Fibre-grade sand must be very clean, so deposits are washed, floated and acid-leached before melting. This is the terminal raw material of the whole glass chain.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.rock.name: Quartz sand / sandstone deposit
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.rock.description: Weathered quartz grains from unconsolidated deposits or friable sandstone, dug and screened. This is where the board's glass, and therefore a large fraction of its mass, begins as a mineral taken out of the ground.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.purif.name: Sand purification (beneficiation)
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.purif.description: Washing, density separation and flotation remove heavy mineral and clay impurities; an acid leach removes iron, which would otherwise darken the glass. Drying and sieving follow.

mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.weave.name: Air-jet or rapier weaving
mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.weave.description: Warp and weft yarn are interlaced on a loom. Air-jet looms dominate because they run fast with few picks per inch; rapier looms use a rapier to carry the weft. Some cloth for laminate is stitched rather than woven, which is cheaper and adequate for reinforcement.

c64.io-panel.name: Rear and side I/O panel
c64.io-panel.description: Everything you can plug into the machine. The back carries the 8-pin DIN video output, the 6-pin DIN serial (IEC) port, the 6-pin edge-connector datasette port, the user-port edge connector, the 7-pin DIN power input and the RF modulator's coax socket; the side carries two DE-9 control ports for joysticks and paddles; the bottom edge of the board exposes the 44-pin expansion socket. The video output is composite plus separate luma and chroma on an 8-pin DIN — which is one reason the RF modulator existed and one reason it did not need to be as good as it was.

c64.switches.name: Switches and slide potentiometers
c64.switches.description: Three human-operated controls on a C64: the mains-free power slider SW1 on the right-hand case panel, and the two slide potentiometers for volume/tone and brightness on the top surface. The power switch gates the incoming 5 V rail; the two potentiometers are wired directly into the SID audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.

facts.label: SW1 position
facts.value: right-hand case panel, between the control ports and the power socket

facts.label: Type
facts.value: single-pole slide switch, SPST, mains-rated style body

facts.label: Potentiometers
facts.value: 2 x miniature slide potentiometer, ~10 kOhm linear

facts.label: Slider location
facts.value: top surface of the case, right-hand end

c64.switches.level-sliders.name: Volume and brightness slide potentiometers
c64.switches.level-sliders.description: Two miniature slide potentiometers on the mainboard whose sliders protrude through the top of the case. One sets the audio level at the SID output; the other sets the analogue video brightness level. Both use a printed resistive track and a spring-loaded wiper.
c64.switches.level-sliders.note: I could not verify the exact resistance and taper of the two C64 slide pots from a primary source. Contemporary photographs and the schematic suggest a linear-law miniature slide pot in the 1 kOhm-100 kOhm range; treat the value as uncertain.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: printed carbon track on a ceramic or phenolic substrate

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.name: Single and ganged (twin) sections
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.description: A potentiometer is made in two or three mechanically independent sections that share a common wiper shaft, so one slider knob moves the end terminal, the wiper and the middle terminal together. A 'ganged' pair means two complete potentiometers on one shaft; the C64's two sliders are physically separate parts rather than a ganged pair, since they control completely unrelated signals in different parts of the machine.
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.note: The brief asked about a ganged twin version; the C64 does not use one. Ganging was standard on stereo audio controls, not on the C64.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.name: Self-lubricating bushing
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.description: A moulded nylon or PTFE-impregnated bushing in the chassis that the shaft runs in. Dry, it is what makes a slider pot feel smooth rather than gritty.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.name: PTFE-impregnated bushing
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.description: A nylon or bronze-impregnated bushing with a PTFE (Teflon) lubricant. PTFE is made by polymerising tetrafluoroethylene, whose monomer is made from fluorspar via hydrofluoric acid and chloroform.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.name: Fluorspar for the fluorine
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.description: Fluorspar, calcium fluoride, was the world's main source of fluorine for PTFE and refrigerant fluorocarbons. Its acid-grade material was a genuine traded mineral in 1982.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.name: Common wiper shaft
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.description: A drawn steel shaft pressed through the moulded wiper carriers, so all the potentiometer sections move together. Drawing the shaft from steel rather than moulding it in plastic is what keeps the alignment over millions of slider cycles.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.name: Steel for the shaft
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.description: Mild steel drawn bar. The chain from iron ore to drawn bar is the same one behind every other steel part on the machine.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.name: Moulded housing and slider knob
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.description: A small injection-moulded thermoplastic body with the moulded detent rails for the slider, and a moulded knob with the finger rib that protrudes through the case cut-out. The same polymer families as the switch body: nylon, ABS or a filled phenoxy.
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.note: Polymers and their moulding are expanded in the plastics file.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.name: Moulded slider knob
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.description: A small moulded knob with a moulded-in guide rib that engages the body's rails, protruding through the case cut-out. The knob and the body were often moulded in the same tool family so the fit is guaranteed.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..name: ABS for the slider knob
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..description: The knob is ABS because it has to be moulded thin, in a gloss finish, with a fine rib. It is the same polymer as the keycaps a few inches away on the same machine.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..name: Styrene for the ABS
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..description: The styrene monomer that gives ABS its rigid, gloss-forming phase.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..name: Benzene from a steam cracker
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob..description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.name: Injection moulding of the pot body
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.description: The body is injection moulded with the three terminal slots, the detent rails and the wiper guide all in one shot, in a multi-cavity tool shared with the rest of the world's miniature slide pot production.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.name: ABS or PBT housing polymer
