c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.description: Either the same ABS as the keycaps or a glass-filled PBT. Both are chosen for stiffness at a thin wall - a pot body has to hold a wiper alignment over millimetres of travel without creeping.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.name: Spring-loaded wiper
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.description: A small sprung metal clip or blade, usually a copper-nickel-plated spring steel or nickel strip, presses onto the carbon track and taps the voltage off at whatever point along it the slider has dragged it to. It must carry current through a sliding contact, so its plating and its spring force are the two design limits.
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.note: A worn carbon track is the classic reason a 1980s volume pot develops noise or drops to one end of its travel; contact cleaner and a rebuild pen were the standard fixes.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Ni-plated spring steel, or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: the carbon track is deliberately sacrificial - it wears before the wiper

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.precont.name: Pre-contact break and noise
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.precont.description: A resistive track and a sliding contact inherently generate noise, and a cheap carbon track generates a lot. C64 volume pots are a well-known source of a faint hiss or crackle in the audio output - a real consequence of the printed-carbon technology, not a fault.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.name: Plated spring-steel strip
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.description: The wiper is stamped from spring strip and plated in a nickel or precious-metal bath so that it both springs correctly and carries current across a sliding contact without galling the carbon track.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.name: Nickel plating bath
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.description: The same nickel chemistry as the resistor lead plating and the connector underplate: a sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, or electroless nickel-phosphorus where the deposit had to be hard.

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.name: Printed carbon track on a ceramic substrate
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.description: The resistive element is a track of carbon ink printed onto a flat ceramic or phenolic substrate, with metal end lands at each end. Printing is what makes a slide pot cheap: the geometry of the track, its length and its taper, sets both the total resistance and the law.
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.note: A printed carbon track and a printed cermet track are the same manufacturing route as the thick-film resistor networks on the same board; only the geometry differs. For low-level audio pots in 1982, carbon ink on ceramic was still the norm and cermet was the higher-quality option.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon/graphite in an organic binder, or a cermet (RuO2 + glass) paste

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen-printed through a mesh, cured in a tunnel oven

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: flat alumina ceramic or glass-filled phenolic

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.name: Substrate and end lands
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.description: The carbon track is printed between two metallic end lands, usually fired silver, one at each end of the travel. The wiper bridges them; the centre terminal taps the wiper. All three terminals are solder pins on the pot's tail.

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.name: Firing of the printed substrate
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.description: The carbon or cermet track is fired into the ceramic substrate in a tunnel oven at several hundred degrees, fusing the binder and the glass frit so the track cannot be scratched off by the wiper.

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.name: Carbon ink for the printed track
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.description: Carbon black ground into a binder to a printable ink, screen-printed along the substrate and cured in a tunnel oven. The track length sets the nominal resistance and its taper sets the law; the two C64 sliders are linear, so the printed geometry is constant width.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon black in an organic binder, screen-printed and cured

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.name: Furnace black in the pot track
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.description: The printed track uses a fine carbon black, finely ground so it prints smoothly and fires into a hard conductive film. The same powder, ground finer, is in the resistor film and the rubber dome.

c64.switches.power-slider.name: SW1 power slider switch
c64.switches.power-slider.description: A single-pole, double-throw or single-throw slide switch on the mainboard, actuated by a moulded slider that protrudes through a rectangular cut-out in the right-hand side of the case. Its only job in the C64 is to interrupt the incoming +5 V rail - everything else on the board runs off the switch's output side.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 VAC resistive, far beyond the C64's ~1 A load

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.name: Leaf contacts and contact plating
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.description: A pair of formed leaf springs - phosphor bronze or stainless - carry the current; one is fixed and one moves with the slider, wiping against its mate over a small spring pressure so the electrical contact area is always fresh. The wipe is the whole reason slide switches do not corrode: an oxide film is continuously displaced.
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.note: For a 5 V DC power switch the plating is silver; the gold-flashed variety was for the low-level contacts of the pots and connectors.

facts.label: Contact plating
facts.value: silver, silver-nickel, or a gold flash for low-level signals

facts.label: Contact pressure
facts.value: tens to hundreds of grams per contact

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.name: Phosphor bronze leaf stock
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.description: A copper-tin alloy with a few tenths of a per cent of phosphorus, valued for springiness, fatigue resistance and a low and stable contact resistance. Drawn strip, blanked, pierced and formed in a progressive die; the standard contact alloy of the whole electronics industry.

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.name: Copper of the bronze (from copper ore)
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.description: Refined from chalcopyrite or native copper, smelted, converted and electrolytically refined, then drawn, rolled and annealed into the contact strip. The same copper, more or less, appears in the C64's traces, connectors and windings.
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.note: The smelter and refinery chain is expanded in the metals file.

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.name: Tin in the bronze (from tin ore)
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.description: The tin that makes phosphor bronze springy and corrosion-resistant came from cassiterite, the ore of tin, worked since the Bronze Age and still a major traded commodity in 1982.
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.note: The cassiterite -> tin chain is expanded in the metals file; referenced here only.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.name: Slide mechanism, actuator and detent
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.description: The actuator is a moulded slider with ribs that engage moulded detent ramps in the body, so it clicks into a definite position at each end rather than resting ambiguously. A moulded spring or a bent leaf spring inside supplies the return force and the over-centre snap that gives the switch its tactile 'click'.
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.note: The detent geometry (moulded ramp plus leaf spring) is standard 1980s miniature-switch practice; I have no teardown-level measurement of the specific C64 switch.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.dete.name: Moulded detent ramp
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.dete.description: A stepped ramp moulded into the nylon body or actuator over which the slider rides, giving a definite position at each end. Moulding the detent rather than machining it is what keeps the part cheap at the volumes a consumer switch sold in.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.name: Return leaf spring
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.description: A bent spring steel leaf that provides the over-centre force and the return to OFF. It is the part that fatigues: after enough actuations it loses tension and the switch no longer snaps crisply.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.name: Spring steel strip
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.description: A high-carbon strip steel, hardened and tempered, cut and blanked. Blade and coil spring steel of this quality came from the same integrated steel plants as the razor blades and the automotive leaf springs.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.name: Moulded switch body (melamine / phenolic / nylon)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.description: The insulator the whole mechanism lives in. Small slide switches of this generation used a filled thermoset (melamine-formaldehyde or glass-filled phenolic) or a glass-filled nylon; both mould well in simple two-plate tools and stand a soldering iron's heat. Melamine was the industry default because its arc resistance in a mains-adjacent switch is better than polystyrene's.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.note: The C64 switch handles only 5 V DC from the external brick, not mains, so its insulation requirement was modest - but the part was bought from a mains-switch catalogue and over-specified.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.screws.name: Case screws and panel mounting
c64.switches.power-slider.body.screws.description: The switch body was riveted or snapped into the mainboard and located by the case's moulded boss. The moulded boss and its snap feature are part of the case tooling, not the switch tooling.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.name: Solder terminals and anchor
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.description: The pins of the switch are brass, either solid or a brass tube over a steel mandrel with a solder tail. Brass is used because it wets tin-lead solder reliably and does not need nickel underplate for a low-voltage contact.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal..name: Brass pin stock
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal..description: Solid brass wire or a brass tube over a steel mandrel, cut and headed. Brass is chosen because it is springy enough to survive the assembly line and soft enough to take a solder joint.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.name: Nylon-6-6 polymer (caprolactam)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.description: The base polymer of PA66, made by hydrolytic ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam, itself made from benzene via phenol and cyclohexanone. It replaced silk and nylon-6 for mechanical parts because of its moisture stability and higher melting point.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.note: The petrochemical chain from benzene to caprolactam to nylon-6-6 is real 1980s chemistry but is not expanded here; it belongs in the plastics file.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.name: Caprolactam to nylon-6-6
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.description: Caprolactam is polymerised hydrolytically, or converted to the salt and polymerised as a nylon salt, in a continuous process at ~250-280 C. The caprolactam itself comes from phenol or cyclohexanone - both benzene derivatives from a steam cracker or catalytic reformer.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.name: Benzene from the cracker
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.description: Benzene is one of the oldest commercially useful petrochemicals: it was isolated from coal tar long before 1982, but by then most industrial benzene came from the aromatics complex of a steam cracker, made by catalytic reforming of naphtha. It is the root of the styrene, phenol, nylon and epoxy trees.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.name: Glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.description: A tough, self-lubricating engineering thermoplastic used where a moving slider needs low friction and good wear resistance against the moulded track. Injection-moulded into the actuator and often into the switch's own guide body.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.note: Which of these the C64's switch actually used is not documented anywhere I could find; the materials above are the standard options for a 1982 miniature slide switch.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.fil.name: Glass filler in the nylon
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.fil.description: 30 % chopped glass fibre in the PA66, for stiffness at a thin wall and for dimensional stability against the moulded detent. The same filler as in the connector housings.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.name: Melamine-formaldehyde thermoset
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.description: A thermoset built from melamine and formaldehyde, filled with cellulose or glass fibre, and compression-moulded hot. It is rigid, arc-resistant, dimensionally stable and cheap - the standard insulator for mains switches and domestic electrical accessories of the period.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine..name: Melamine resin from urea and formaldehyde
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine..description: Melamine is made by condensing urea with formaldehyde. Urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide, both cheap industrial gases; formaldehyde comes from oxidising methanol, which comes from the catalytic conversion of synthesis gas. Both halves were pure petrochemical by 1982.

facts.label: Formaldehyde route
facts.value: methanol from CO/H2, silver-catalysed oxidation to formaldehyde

c64.keyboard.name: Keyboard module: 66 keycaps on hybrid switches
c64.keyboard.description: The C64's keyboard is a separate wired module that drops into the bezel: a steel backplate, a single-sided PCB carrying the matrix, 66 individually moulded ABS keycaps, and beneath each cap a Mitsumi-style hybrid switch - a moulded plunger with a conductive rubber pad and a metal return spring, closing a printed-circuit board contact when pressed. Legendas are printed onto the cap tops with a two-colour pad printer.
c64.keyboard.note: The service manual states 'KEYS 66 Keys total'. The 8x8 matrix covers 64 positions; RESTORE bypasses the matrix entirely (it drives the non-maskable interrupt) and SHIFT LOCK is a latching key wired to the same lines as the left SHIFT, so to the machine it is indistinguishable from pressing left SHIFT.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 66 total: 2 cursor-control keys, 4 function keys, 2 SHIFT, plus the alphanumerics and named keys

facts.label: Off-matrix keys
facts.value: RESTORE (dedicated NMI line) and SHIFT LOCK (shares the left-shift lines)

facts.label: Keyboard connector
facts.value: 24-pin header at CN1 on the mainboard, front-left edge

c64.keyboard.cable.name: Keyboard ribbon cable and connector
c64.keyboard.cable.description: A short flat ribbon or discrete-lead cable from the keyboard to the 24-pin header (CN1) on the front-left edge of the mainboard, terminating in a moulded connector housing. It carries the eight matrix rows, the eight columns, the RESTORE line and the power rails - twenty-four conductors.

c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.name: Ribbon conductors
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.description: Either a laminated flat-flex ribbon (etched copper on polyimide film) or discrete stranded wires. Ribbon is thinner; discrete leads are more flexible at the fold and are what most Commodore keyboard cables used.
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.note: Whether a given C64 keyboard cable is flat-flex or discrete is a per-run detail; both are consistent with the era and with the 24-pin connector.

c64.keyboard.body.name: Keyboard body and its fasteners
c64.keyboard.body.description: A moulded ABS body that holds the plungers, the PCB and the backplate, and carries the cable. It is retained by about twenty small gold-coloured screws, and on the shift-lock position it has a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB.
c64.keyboard.body.note: Retroleum's teardown notes that the SHIFT LOCK keyswitch is a black-backed switch with one wire soldered diagonally across the board - a small manufacturing quirk that tells you the module was hand-assembled.

facts.label: Shift lock
facts.value: black-backed keyswitch, one wire runs diagonally to the PCB

c64.keyboard.body.screws.name: Keyboard retaining screws (gold-coloured)
c64.keyboard.body.screws.description: Roughly twenty small self-tapping screws with a gold or brass finish hold the keyboard backplate and body together. The gold colour is a zinc-nickel or brass-look plating, chosen because it reads as 'quality' on a part the customer never sees.

c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch.name: Shift-lock keyswitch
c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch.description: A tiny mechanically-latching slide switch (a black plastic body with a metal leaf contact) that holds itself in the shifted position until pressed again. It is not a matrix key at all - it is a separate latch that closes the shift lines.

c64.keyboard.backplate.name: Steel backplate
c64.keyboard.backplate.description: A sheet-steel plate under the PCB with punched openings for the plungers and rolled or pressed stiffening beads. It carries the springs and holds the plungers' travel, and it is screwed to the keyboard body with about twenty small gold-coloured screws.

c64.keyboard.backplate.punching.name: Piercing and forming of the backplate
c64.keyboard.backplate.punching.description: The openings are pierced on a punch press in a single stroke across the whole sheet; the stiffening beads are then roll-formed. This is a high-volume sheet-metal process: a tonne of steel punched this way costs a fraction of a machined equivalent.
c64.keyboard.backplate.punching.note: Cold-rolled mild steel sheet is made by hot rolling a slab and then cold rolling it; the cold rolling is what gives the smooth surface and the accurate punches.

c64.keyboard.pcb.name: Keyboard PCB (matrix and contacts)
c64.keyboard.pcb.description: A single-sided PCB carrying the 8x8 matrix traces and one contact pad per switch, sitting under the plungers. The keyboard PCB plugs into a 24-pin header on the mainboard (CN1) and carries no logic of its own - it is just a switch matrix that the CIA scans.
c64.keyboard.pcb.note: The board material and the copper/gold plating processes belong to the PCB subsystem; this node exists so the keyboard's own parts are complete.

c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.name: Contact pads (gold or carbon)
c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.description: Each switch lands on a printed pad. On gold-plated keyboards the pad is gold over nickel; on cheaper sets it is a carbon/graphite coating on the copper. The contact on the plunger is the conductive rubber; the pad is the fixed electrode.
c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.note: Retroleum notes the contacts on the PCB are either gold or carbon plated and that the most common keyboard fault is dust on the backplate PCB or dirt on the plunger's conductive pads - cleaned with isopropyl alcohol.

c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.name: Matrix topology and the two odd keys
c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.description: The CIA drives one of eight rows low and reads the eight columns; a pressed key connects one row to one column. Sixty-four positions are scanned. RESTORE is wired straight to the NMI line, bypassing the matrix, which is why RESTORE works even while the CPU is jammed. SHIFT LOCK is a mechanically latching switch wired to the same two lines as the left SHIFT.
c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.note: SHIFT LOCK being on the same lines as left SHIFT is why holding shift lock in software is impossible and why BASIC sees a shift, not a separate key.

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: dedicated line to NMI, not scanned

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: latching; shares the left-shift matrix lines

c64.keyboard.switches.name: Hybrid switches (Mitsumi-style plunger, rubber dome, spring)
c64.keyboard.switches.description: The C64 does not use a rubber-dome-only membrane like a calculator, nor a mechanical switch like a typewriter. It uses a hybrid: a moulded plunger carrying a conductive rubber pad rides on a coil spring, and pressing it drives a gold or carbon contact onto a PCB pad. That gives a real click, a light touch and a definite bottom-out - which is why a C64 keyboard still feels 'mechanical' in the 1980s sense.
c64.keyboard.switches.note: Retroleum's keyboard notes describe 'Type 1' keyboards with black plungers, springs under all keys, and ~5 mm cross-points, versus 'Type 2' with white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts and a metal spring only under the space bar.

facts.label: Force
facts.value: roughly 55-70 gf at the snap peak for a typical hybrid plunger

facts.label: Life
facts.value: 10-30 million operations rated for these switches

c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.name: The snap: force-displacement curve of the switch
c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.description: The 'feel' of a C64 key is a curve, not a number. The plunger rides down the spring, then the rubber dome on the PCB has to collapse (or the contact arm has to snap over), producing a peak in force; past the peak the force drops as the dome collapses, then rises again into the bottom-out. Peak-to-valley difference of maybe 20-30 gf is what the finger reads as 'clicky'.
c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.note: These are typical figures for hybrid plunger/dome switches of this period, not measured C64 data. C64 keys are famous for a light, crisp action; the rubber dome's collapse is what gives the characteristic feel.

c64.keyboard.switches.spring.name: Return spring (music wire)
c64.keyboard.switches.spring.description: A small coil spring under each key that returns the plunger. It is drawn from music wire (a high-carbon, low-carbon-content steel with a tight tensile range) and wound on a automatic spring coiler. Type 1 keyboards spring every key; Type 2 springs only the space bar and relies on the rubber dome elsewhere.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: set so the snap peak lands at 55-70 gf

c64.keyboard.switches.music-wire.name: Music wire (patented steel)
c64.keyboard.switches.music-wire.description: A high-carbon, low-carbon-content alloy steel with very tight mechanical properties and a very clean surface - patented in the 1880s for piano wire. It is drawn to fine gauge on a bull-block or continuous wire drawer and patented through a multi-step process.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: ~0.8-0.9% (music wire is high carbon, spring wire lower)

facts.label: Process
facts.value: patenting: quench, patenting heat, over-drawing in dies

c64.keyboard.switches.conductive-rubber.name: Conductive rubber contact (carbon-loaded silicone)
c64.keyboard.switches.conductive-rubber.description: The contact is a small pad of silicone rubber loaded with conductive carbon black. The carbon particles touch each other and carry a small current across the PCB pad when the pad is pressed down, closing the switch. It needs to be conductive enough to bridge the gold contact but resistive enough not to be a dead short.

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: silicone rubber (VMQ), cured with a peroxide

c64.keyboard.switches.rubber-compounding.name: Compounding the conductive silicone pad
c64.keyboard.switches.rubber-compounding.description: Silicone rubber, conductive carbon black, a peroxide cure and a filler are mixed on a two-roll mill, then the pad is either transfer-moulded or printed as a dot on the plunger. Getting the carbon black well dispersed without overworking it is the whole trick: too little mixing leaves lumps that do not conduct, too much breaks down the carbon network and the pad stops conducting.

facts.label: Mixing
facts.value: two-roll mill or internal mixer, 60-120 C

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: peroxide or addition-cure; press or transfer mould

facts.label: Cure time/temperature
facts.value: e.g. 10 min at 150 C, or seconds in a fast cure

c64.keyboard.switches.cure-system.name: Cure system (peroxide crosslinker)
c64.keyboard.switches.cure-system.description: Silicone rubber needs a crosslinker. Dicumyl peroxide is the classic general-purpose choice for a compression-moulded pad; addition-cure (platinum-catalysed) systems came later and cure faster with less shrink.

c64.keyboard.switches.dicumyl-peroxide.name: Dicumyl peroxide
c64.keyboard.switches.dicumyl-peroxide.description: The commonest silicone crosslinker of the era. It is made from cumene: cumene is oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and then condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to give dicumyl peroxide.

facts.label: Decomposition
facts.value: gives a free radical at ~120-160 C, driving silicone crosslinking

c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-source.name: Cumene from benzene and propylene
c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-source.description: Propylene is alkylated onto benzene over phosphoric acid on silica (or a zeolite) at 300-450 C and 20-60 bar to give cumene, which is separated from its polyalkylated heavies by distillation.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: phosphoric acid on silica, or a zeolite

c64.keyboard.switches.alpha-methylstyren.name: Alpha-methylstyrene
c64.keyboard.switches.alpha-methylstyren.description: A C9 vinylbenzene used as a chain-transfer agent and as the co-reactant in dicumyl peroxide. It is made by dehydrating cumene over alumina or acid at ~300-400 C - a direct route from the same C9 aromatics that make cumene itself.

c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-oxidation.name: Cumene to hydroperoxide and alpha-methylstyrene
c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-oxidation.description: Cumene is air-oxidised in a stirred liquid-phase reactor at ~100-140 C to cumene hydroperoxide. Part is condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to make dicumyl peroxide; part is acid-cleaved to phenol and acetone, which goes on to bisphenol A and epoxy. One plant, three products.
c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-oxidation.note: This is a textbook example of how a single 1970s-era petrochemical plant feeds the whole plastics complex: phenol to epoxy and polycarbonate, cumene to rubber and peroxides.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: ~100-140 C, 4-10 bar, air bubbled through cumene

c64.keyboard.switches.two-roll-mill.name: Two-roll compounding mill
c64.keyboard.switches.two-roll-mill.description: Two counter-rotating chilled rolls nip the compound and disperse the filler. It is the oldest and still the most reliable way to get a clean dispersion, and every rubber and plasticiser maker owns one.

facts.label: Roll gap
facts.value: adjustable, often with a gauge for final nip

c64.keyboard.switches.carbon-black.name: Carbon black filler
c64.keyboard.switches.carbon-black.description: The conductive filler. Furnace black is made by feeding oil or gas to a hot refractory-carbon reactor in a stream of air at 1200-1500 C, quenching the soot, then pelletising and grinding it. It is the same carbon black family used in tyre rubber.
c64.keyboard.switches.carbon-black.note: A striking example of convergence: the tyre in a car and the switch contact in a C64 keyboard are loaded with essentially the same furnace black, from the same heavy-oil feed.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: heavy oil / aromatic residue from petroleum refining

c64.keyboard.switches.silicone.name: Silicone rubber (the matrix of the conductive pad)
c64.keyboard.switches.silicone.description: Polydimethylsiloxane. The base polymer is made by ring-opening polymerisation of octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane or by equilibration of a silanol-terminated PDMS; fillers (silica, silicone oil) tune the hardness and the tear strength.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: peroxide (e.g. dicumyl peroxide) or addition-cure platinum

facts.label: Shore hardness
facts.value: Shore A 40-70 for a contact pad

c64.keyboard.switches.silica-filler.name: Fumed / precipitated silica filler
c64.keyboard.switches.silica-filler.description: Reinforcing silica for the silicone rubber. It is made either by fuming silicon tetrachloride in a flame or by precipitating from a sodium silicate solution. Both routes end at quartz sand or silicon metal.

facts.label: Fumed route
facts.value: SiCl4 + H2 + O2 -> SiO2 + HCl at ~1000-1400 C flame

facts.label: Precipitated route
facts.value: water glass acidification, from quartz sand + soda ash

c64.keyboard.switches.silicon-metal.name: Silicon metal (from quartz)
c64.keyboard.switches.silicon-metal.description: Quartz sand (SiO2) is reduced with carbon in a submerged-arc furnace at about 2000 C to give 98-99% silicon. This is the starting point for the whole silicon chemistry, and here it ends up in a rubber pad rather than in a chip.

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger.name: Switch plunger (moulded, with conductive rubber)
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger.description: A small moulded body with a cross-post on top that the keycap clips onto, one or more arms that carry a conductive rubber pad, and a stem that slides in the keyboard body. Type 2 plungers have four prongs and carry a loose grey 'bubble' contact.

facts.label: Type 1
facts.value: black plungers, springs under every key, metal contact

facts.label: Type 2
facts.value: white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts, spring under the space bar only

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.name: Plunger polymer (acetal / filled nylon)
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.description: The plunger has to be dimensionally stable over millions of strokes and low-friction against the spring and the body. Acetal (POM) is the classic choice for its low friction and stiffness; glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate are also used. All three are moulded on small multi-cavity tools.
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.note: Which polymer each production run used is not something I could pin down; POM and filled nylon were both routine. The formaldehyde and nylon chains are documented under c64.case.other-polymers.

facts.label: Friction
facts.value: POM has a very low coefficient of friction and no 'grease needed' behaviour

c64.keyboard.keycaps.name: Keycaps (66 individual moulded ABS caps)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.description: Not a single dished sheet: 66 separate rectangular caps, each moulded in dark brown-grey ABS with a slightly concave top, each dropping through its own square opening in the bezel onto its own plunger. Some breadbin sets had tan-coloured function keys, others grey.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.note: The cross-point fitting and its shortening from ~5 mm to ~3 mm is a well-documented difference between early and late breadbin keyboards; caps from the two eras are not interchangeable. Legends on early sets are 1-3 mm down from the top of the cap; some sets use a bolder, some a thinner, font.

facts.label: Fitting
facts.value: cross-point: ~5 mm on early breadbin caps, ~3 mm on later ones

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: printed on the top face; later sets also on the front face

facts.label: Colour variation
facts.value: function keys tan on some sets, grey on others

c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point.name: Cross-point fitting and cap underside
c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point.description: The underside of the cap carries a moulded cross that clips onto the matching cross-post on the plunger - about 5 mm on early breadbin caps, about 3 mm on later ones. The two are not interchangeable. The underside also has guide ribs that keep the cap square as it travels.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded with the cap, same ABS

c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.name: Keycap colours and any colour coding
c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.description: Breadbin C64 caps are almost uniformly a dark brown-grey, with function keys sometimes a lighter grey or tan. There is no per-number colour coding on the breadbin keyboard - that idea belongs to some other machines (the C64C and later Commodore sets vary, and the VIC-20 had differently coloured function keys). What a C64 keycap has is a moulded-in colour, not a printed colour.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.note: I could not confirm any colour-coded number row or overlay on the 1982 breadbin keyboard. Where a legend colour differs between sets it tracks the cap colour, not the key function. Treat any claim of printed colour-coded number overlays as unverified for this machine.

facts.label: Number-key coding
facts.value: none on the breadbin; legends are all one colour on the cap

c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.name: Printed keycap legends
c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.description: Legends are printed on the cap top with a two-colour pad printer (pad printing / tampo printing): a soft silicone pad picks up ink from a cliche, deforms against the slightly crowned cap, and transfers the character. White legends on the dark caps; the RETURN and SHIFT caps in some sets get legends on the front face too.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.note: The ink chemistry and the pad/cliche supply chain are detailed under c64.decor. Later Commodore sets printed the whole character set on the top face only, with RETURN and SHIFT labels offset to a corner.

facts.label: Why pad and not screen
facts.value: a flat cap top with a slight crown will not lie flat under a screen; pad printing conforms

facts.label: Legends
facts.value: single character on most keys; shifted and graphic characters on the front face of later sets

c64.keyboard.keycaps.front-legends.name: Front-face legends (shifted / graphic characters)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.front-legends.description: On sets that carry the shifted and graphic characters, these are printed on the small front wall of the cap. Printing a vertical face with a pad printer needs the pad tilted and a second fixture, which is why early sets avoided it and used a bolder single top legend.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.front-legends.note: The extent to which a given run printed front legends varies; the breadbox64 write-up notes the front-side printing on later C64C sets and thinner fonts on some breadbin sets.

facts.label: Fixture
facts.value: cap held tilted in a nest

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: improves gradually across the production run

c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.name: Keycap tool (small multi-cavity, hardened steel)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.description: Keycaps are made in small high-cavity tools - 4, 8 or 16 cavities in one block - because a cap is cheap and the tool has to be small enough to fit a small press. The tool is hardened tool steel, and the caps come off a common gate so the visible faces are identical.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.note: This is the same tool steel and the same polish-and-plate route as the case tool; the difference is size and cavity count, not materials.

facts.label: Tool life
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots; replated and repolished on rebuild

c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.name: ABS grade for keycaps
c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.description: A housing-grade ABS, low rubber content so the moulded texture stays crisp and the cap does not feel gummy. Keycap ABS is usually a slightly higher-gloss, higher-flow grade than the case resin because the caps are thin and have to fill a short, tight flow path.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.note: The full ABS supply chain (cracker -> styrene/propylene/butadiene -> acrylonitrile -> emulsion graft -> compounding) is documented once under c64.case.abs-resin, because it is the same resin.

facts.label: Wall thickness
facts.value: ~1.5-2 mm, thinnest in the legend area

c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs-flow.name: Flow and fill of a thin keycap
c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs-flow.description: A keycap is one of the shortest flows in moulding: a shallow, thin-walled box filled through a single gate. It is a classic short-shot candidate, which is why keycap tools are small multi-cavity tools with a well-placed gate and a warm mould so the flow front does not freeze before the last corner fills.

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: single, on the inside wall away from the legend face

c64.case.name: Breadbin case: two-piece ABS shell
c64.case.description: The C64 'breadbin' housing is a rear shell and a front bezel, both injection-moulded general-purpose ABS in a warm beige-brown. The rear shell carries the ventilation ribs, moulded screw bosses, connector cut-outs and the rubber feet; the bezel carries the keyboard window with its square key openings, the two knurled thumbscrews, the rainbow badge and the fine 'leather' grain. A foil-on-board RFI shield sits inside over the motherboard.
c64.case.note: The case is universally reported as ABS - it is the polymer that browns under UV and can be reversed with peroxide 'retrobright' bleaching. Commodore's own 2025 C64 Ultimate copy notes the surviving tooling carries a 'period-correct 2-point flow pattern'.

c64.case.other-polymers.name: Other polymers inside the case
c64.case.other-polymers.description: The ABS case shares the machine with several other plastics. This node groups the second- and third-generation polymers in the C64's plastic parts so their feedstocks are traceable too.
c64.case.other-polymers.note: Some of these plastics belong more naturally to the PCB, connector or PSU subsystems; they are listed here so the case-side plastic inventory is complete, with a note where the detail is owned elsewhere.

c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy.name: Epoxy (potting, die attach)
c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy.description: Epoxy resin is not a case material but appears as a potting and die-attach compound inside the machine - gluing the heat sink to the regulators and, in places, encapsulating a noisy analogue section. Epoxy comes from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both aromatic-derived.
c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy.note: Epoxy potting of the PSU and die attach is really part of the power and assembly subsystems; it is listed here for completeness because the C64's plastic inventory is often described as 'ABS only' and that is not quite right.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: amine or anhydride, room temp to 120 C

c64.case.other-polymers.neoprene.name: Neoprene (chloroprene rubber)
c64.case.other-polymers.neoprene.description: Polychloroprene is used where oil and weather resistance matter - cable jackets on some Commodore leads, feet, and gasket material. It comes from chloroprene, made by chlorination of butadiene from the same C4 cracker cut.
c64.case.other-polymers.neoprene.note: Chloroprene is made by chlorinating butadiene from the cracker, so neoprene is another step downstream of the same C4 cut as the ABS rubber phase.

c64.case.other-polymers.natural-rubber.name: Natural rubber (feet, grommets)
c64.case.other-polymers.natural-rubber.description: Some C64 feet and small grommets are natural rubber, cis-1,4-polyisoprene, made by coagulating latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis. Natural rubber has excellent resilience and grip and ages to a tacky amber.
c64.case.other-polymers.natural-rubber.note: The C64's four feet are more likely SBR or soft PVC than natural rubber; natural rubber is included because grommets and small vibration parts on Commodore equipment of this era were commonly natural rubber.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: latex from Hevea brasiliensis plantations, coagulated with acetic acid

c64.case.other-polymers.hevea-latex.name: Natural rubber latex
c64.case.other-polymers.hevea-latex.description: Tapped from the rubber tree; the latex is preserved with ammonia, coagulated with acid, and the coagulum is pressed into sheets and smoke-cured. The tree is a plantation crop - rubber trees only yield for about 25 years and need a tropical climate.

c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.name: Polyester / PET film (insulation, overlay)
c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.description: Polyester film is used as thin insulation, as overlay film on some keycap legends, and as the amber capacitor sleeve material in the power supply. It comes from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, both of which come out of the aromatics and olefin chains already used elsewhere in the machine.
c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.note: PET film and the keycap-overlay question overlap with the PCB and packaging detail; see c64.decor for the overlay decoration process and the board subsystem for the PCB materials.

c64.case.other-polymers.terephthalic-aci.name: Terephthalic acid (for PET film)
c64.case.other-polymers.terephthalic-aci.description: Made by air oxidation of para-xylene over cobalt-manganese acetate at 150-250 C and 10-40 bar, in a process that is a classic example of good process engineering: the oxidation is exothermic and the acetic acid byproduct is recycled.
c64.case.other-polymers.terephthalic-aci.note: The para-xylene comes from the same C8 aromatics separation that supplies o-xylene for the phthalic anhydride in the pigment, which is a nice convergence: one unit, two products.

c64.case.other-polymers.pvc.name: PVC (cable jackets, sleeving)
c64.case.other-polymers.pvc.description: The wire jackets, cable boots and some insulators in a C64 are PVC. PVC is made by polymerising vinyl chloride, and vinyl chloride comes from the chlor-ethylene route (EDC cracking to VCM plus HCl) or from oxychlorination of ethylene. The ethylene and the chlorine both come out of the same crackers and chlor-alkali plants that feed everything else.
c64.case.other-polymers.pvc.note: The cable detail of this chain is expanded under c64.cables; this node exists so the case-side polymer inventory is complete.

c64.case.other-polymers.vinyl-chloride.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
c64.case.other-polymers.vinyl-chloride.description: Made by cracking EDC to VCM and HCl, then recombining HCl with ethylene (oxychlorination) or recovering HCl from the cracker. Then polymerised in a suspension autoclave - the classic 20-50 bar autoclave with a suspension agent - to PVC.

facts.label: EDC cracking
facts.value: ~500 C, 15-30 bar, packed or fluidised bed

c64.case.other-polymers.nylon.name: Nylon 6 / 6 (connector latches, clips)
c64.case.other-polymers.nylon.description: Nylon is the classic connector and latch material: tough, slightly elastic, and it takes a good insert or press-fit without cracking. It appears in the latch tabs and clips that hold connectors in the case.
c64.case.other-polymers.nylon.note: Nylon's high moisture uptake is why latches made of it can go slack over decades; a real reliability issue in 1980s consumer latches.

facts.label: Water absorption
facts.value: ~8% for 6,6 - it changes dimension with humidity

c64.case.other-polymers.adipic-acid.name: Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine
c64.case.other-polymers.adipic-acid.description: Both are made from benzene or cyclohexane in the chemical chain: adipic acid by nitric oxidation of KA oil (cyclohexanol/cyclohexanone), and HMDA from butadiene via the NBS route (chlorination, ammonolysis, hydrogenation). Nylon 6,6 salt is then condensed.

c64.case.other-polymers.pom.name: Polyoxymethylene (acetal / POM)
c64.case.other-polymers.pom.description: Acetal homopolymer and copolymer appear in precision mechanical parts - key plungers, small gears, latches - because POM is stiff, self-lubricating and dimensionally stable. It is made by polymerising formaldehyde from purified methanol.
c64.case.other-polymers.pom.note: Whether the C64 keyboard plungers are POM or a filled nylon is something I could not confirm; both were used for such parts in the period and both are moulded on the same 4-cavity key-plunger tools.

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: low friction, high stiffness, good dimensional stability

c64.case.other-polymers.methanol.name: Methanol (from synthesis gas)
c64.case.other-polymers.methanol.description: Made by reacting carbon monoxide and hydrogen from natural-gas reforming, a few hundred C and 50-100 bar over a copper/zinc oxide catalyst. Formaldehyde comes from methanol oxidation over silver or iron-molybdenum catalyst.

c64.case.other-polymers.polycarbonate.name: Polycarbonate
c64.case.other-polymers.polycarbonate.description: Bisphenol A polycarbonate appears in clear covers, lens and shroud parts and in some clear case variants. It is made from bisphenol A and phosgene, and from the same BPA that comes out of cumene/benzene oxidation.
c64.case.other-polymers.polycarbonate.note: Polycarbonate is much more moisture- and temperature-sensitive than ABS; any clear C64 case is noticeably more prone to stress cracking than the opaque beige originals. Full supply chain sits under the plastics subsystem.

c64.case.other-polymers.cumene.name: Cumene (for bisphenol A)
c64.case.other-polymers.cumene.description: Propylene benzene alkylation product, separated from the C9 aromatics by distillation, then oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and cleaved to phenol and acetone. Phenol + acetone -> bisphenol A -> phosgene + BPA -> polycarbonate.

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: benzene + propylene over phosphoric acid / zeolite

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: ~130 C, then acid cleavage to phenol + acetone

c64.case.other-polymers.polystyrene.name: Polystyrene (GPPS / HIPS foam, trays)
c64.case.other-polymers.polystyrene.description: General-purpose and impact polystyrene appear in the C64's plastic inventory as packaging foam and tray material rather than in the case itself. The case is ABS, not polystyrene - a common misconception.
c64.case.other-polymers.polystyrene.note: GPPS and HIPS both come from styrene; see c64.case.abs-resin.styrene for the styrene supply chain, which is shared.

c64.case.other-polymers.hips-rubber.name: HIPS (impact-modified styrene)
c64.case.other-polymers.hips-rubber.description: Styrene polymerised in the presence of a polybutadiene graft rubber, exactly the same chemistry as ABS but with styrene replacing acrylonitrile. Made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation.
c64.case.other-polymers.hips-rubber.note: HIPS is chemically the same graft architecture as ABS, one substitution away; it is what you get when you drop the acrylonitrile. It is used for the foam end-caps and trays in the packaging.

c64.case.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the case
c64.case.moulding.description: The bezel and rear shell are moulded on a large toggle or hydraulic press in a multi-cavity family tool. The ABS is dried, melted at around 250 C, injected at high pressure through a gate on the parting line, cooled against water channels, and ejected with pin marks and a visible gate vestige.
c64.case.moulding.note: A C64 case is a large, thin, textured part - the hardest kind of thing to mould without flow marks or short shots. The mould temperature control is what decides whether the leather grain comes out crisp or smeared. Note on wall thickness: a C64 case is a thin-walled part at roughly 2.5-3.5 mm, not the 6-8 mm quoted for thick structural mouldings - which is exactly why it is prone to flow marks and short shots.

facts.label: Press clamp force
facts.value: 300-600 t (C64 case is a wide but shallow tool)

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 30-60 s for a case this size

facts.label: ABS shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7%, so the tool is made oversize

c64.case.moulding.two-shot.name: Multi-shot / two-colour moulding
c64.case.moulding.two-shot.description: A second shot in a second cavity moulds a second colour or material over the first, giving a hard-wearing colour layer or a soft-touch overmould. The technique existed and was used in 1982, but the breadbin case is essentially a single-colour ABS shell: the colour comes from the pigment in the resin, not from a second shot. Multi-shot became the norm for later keyboards and for grip surfaces.
c64.case.moulding.two-shot.note: I could not confirm any two-colour feature on the 1982 breadbin case; this node records the technology that existed at the time and its realistic later use, and flags that the specific case is single-colour.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: two moulds in register on a rotating table, or a two-cavity shuttle

facts.label: Used for
facts.value: rubber feet, grip pads, hard/soft combinations

c64.case.moulding.two-shot-machine.name: Two-colour / two-material injection machine
c64.case.moulding.two-shot-machine.description: A press with two injection units and a rotating or shuttle plate so the second shot is made into the already-moulded first shot. The tooling must be indexable so the transfer happens while the part is still hot, which is why multi-shot tools are very expensive and hard to maintain.

c64.case.moulding.inserts.name: Insert moulding of metal and plastic fittings
c64.case.moulding.inserts.description: Things that cannot be moulded in - metal shields, posts, threads - are placed in the cavity before the shot and over-moulded. In a C64 case the shield standoffs and sometimes threaded metal inserts are insert-moulded this way.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: by hand or gravity feed on a fast cycle

facts.label: Used for
facts.value: brass inserts, shield standoffs, key guides

c64.case.moulding.ejection.name: Ejection, pin marks and gate vestige
c64.case.moulding.ejection.description: Ejector pins push the part off the core and off the gate. They leave small round marks, usually inside the case where nobody sees them. The gate leaves a small scar on the parting line that is trimmed or simply hidden by the two halves of the case meeting over it.
c64.case.moulding.ejection.note: The parting line, the gate vestige and the ejector pin marks are the fingerprints that prove a case was injection-moulded rather than vacuum-formed or 3D-printed - useful to anyone trying to date a case.

facts.label: Gate vestige
facts.value: a small disc or gate-cut scar on the parting line

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: a faint hairline around the seam where the two halves meet

c64.case.moulding.cooling.name: Cooling and controlled crystallisation
c64.case.moulding.cooling.description: The mould is water-cooled, or temperature-controlled, and the part is held until it has shrunk to the tool dimension. Cooling is the dominant term in the cycle time for a large ABS housing, and controlling the rate matters as much as the total: cool too fast on one side and the part distorts; too slow and the cycle stretches.
c64.case.moulding.cooling.note: Because ABS shrinks 0.4-0.7% with cooling, every dimension in the tool has to be compensated; for the key openings this is why caps fit but the plastic web between them is always slightly thinner than the drawing.

facts.label: Cooling time
facts.value: 20-40 s (major part of the 30-60 s cycle)

facts.label: Shrinkage on cooling
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear, so the tool cavity is cut oversize

c64.case.moulding.injection.name: Injection and packing under pressure
c64.case.moulding.injection.description: The mould is closed, the screw drives forward and the melt is forced into the cavity through the gate at high pressure, then held under pressure to pack the part to full density and to control sink marks. The pressure must exceed the pressure drop along the flow path, so thin, long, textured flows need very high injection pressure - this is why C64 cases show flow marks (the '2-point flow pattern' that Commodore's revived tooling still carries).
c64.case.moulding.injection.note: The visible 'flow marks' or 'weld line' on a C64 case is the frozen boundary between two melt fronts that met and did not fully knit - the two-point pattern is that boundary, now preserved as part of the tool's signature.

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: edge gate or a small sprue on the parting line

facts.label: Pack pressure
facts.value: 50-100 bar held while the gate is frozen

facts.label: Cavity fill
facts.value: must be full within a second or the ABS cools and frosts

c64.case.moulding.plasticisation.name: Melting and plasticising the ABS
c64.case.moulding.plasticisation.description: The screw melts and homogenises the pellets as it retracts. Back pressure and screw speed set the melt temperature. For ABS the barrel zones run roughly 200 (feed) to 250-260 C (nozzle); the melt must be well above the 100 C Vicat softening point but below the ~270 C where ABS starts to degrade.
c64.case.moulding.plasticisation.note: ABS is comparatively forgiving to process - unlike polycarbonate, which has to be kept dry and under 290 C - which is one reason it won home-computer housings.

facts.label: Screw speed
facts.value: 20-60 rpm typical; higher speed increases shear heat

facts.label: Residence time
facts.value: keep under ~10 min to avoid thermal degradation

c64.case.moulding.drying.name: Drying the ABS before moulding
c64.case.moulding.drying.description: ABS is hygroscopic: even a little absorbed water hydrolyses the nitrile groups at melt temperature, causing splay streaks and reduced molecular weight. Pellets are dried before use - typically 2-4 hours at 80-90 C in a hot-air, dehumidifying hopper dryer - to below about 0.05% moisture.
c64.case.moulding.drying.note: ABS is not as moisture-sensitive as polycarbonate or PET, but 1982 practice was to dry it anyway for textured visible parts. In 1982 the dryer was usually a simple hot-air hopper with a molecular-sieve or silica-gel desiccant, not the closed-loop dehumidifying type that became normal in the 1990s.

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: silver streaks (splay) on the visible surface

c64.case.moulding.desiccant.name: Desiccant for the drying hopper
c64.case.moulding.desiccant.description: Either silica gel or, better, a synthetic zeolite molecular sieve (3A/4A) that adsorbs water at low partial pressure and regenerates at 200-300 C. Zeolites are made from kaolin or from amorphous silica and alumina.

c64.case.moulding.kaolin.name: Kaolin (china clay)
c64.case.moulding.kaolin.description: A white clay, essentially kaolinite Al2Si2O5(OH)4, washed from a kaolin pit, calcined and reacted with sodium aluminate or caustic to make a 4A zeolite molecular sieve. Kaolin is a dug mineral, not a petrochemical.

c64.case.moulding.press.name: Injection press (300-600 t)
c64.case.moulding.press.description: A toggle or direct-hydraulic injection moulding machine with a screw plasticiser, a heated barrel with three or four zones, an oil or water temperature controller, and a mould base. Toggle machines clamp faster and are what most housing tools ran on.

c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.name: Hydraulic clamp unit
c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.description: Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector. A hydraulic press is the reason injection pressure reached 1000+ bar - compared with the ~500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.
c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.note: This is a mechanical node rather than a chemical one, but the press is capital equipment that traces back to cast iron, cast steel and oil.

c64.case.moulding.injection-screw.name: Plasticising screw and barrel
c64.case.moulding.injection-screw.description: A flighted screw turns in a heated barrel, conveying and melting pellets on the way back and injecting on the way forward. The screw is nitrided 33CrMoV or 40Cr steel, bimetallic-lined at the tip in later designs.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: typically 25-40 mm L/D 20-28 for this shot size

c64.case.tooling.name: Case tooling: H13 family mould with EDM texture
c64.case.tooling.description: The two breadbin case moulds are large two-plate tools in pre-hardened or hardened hot-work steel, with the leather-grain texture cut by electrical discharge machining and the cavity polished and hard-chromed. A single mould produces thousands of C64 cases; its cost is amortised over millions of parts, so Commodore could afford a 5-cavity family tool.
c64.case.tooling.note: A household-computer case is a big, shallow, textured tool - about as hard a mould as 1982 injection moulding got. Chrome plating of the cavity is what makes the texture read as a soft satin and is also what gives tool life: the chrome is harder than the polished steel and takes the abrasion of millions of shots. A C64 case was needed in the tens of millions, so a single tool had to survive tens of millions of shots or be rebuilt several times; that economics is why the tool is chrome-plated and maintained rather than run to failure.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: ~450 x 350 mm, two-plate, guided by leader pins

facts.label: Cavities
facts.value: typically 1 large cavity for a case this size; 2-4 on smaller tools

facts.label: Nickel content of plating
facts.value: hard chrome, or electroless nickel of ~5-10 um

facts.label: Tool life by run size
facts.value: large ABS housing tool 300,000-1,000,000+ shots with periodic rebuild; small high-cavity keycap tool similar; short-run and prototype tools may only see 30,000-200,000

c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.name: Mould assembly: guide pins, ejectors, cooling
c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.description: The finished plates are set into a mould base with guide pillars or bushes, an ejector-plate assembly with pins under every feature that would imprint on the visible face, and water lines carrying coolant through the cores and plates to remove the heat of plasticisation.
c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.note: Hot-runner tools avoid the runner itself as scrap but were expensive and finicky; for a big low-volume-per-cavity housing the cold runner was simply cheaper, and the runner was ground up and recycled.

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: water at 30-60 C through baffles and core channels

facts.label: Hot runner
facts.value: unusual on a large ABS housing tool in 1982; cold runner with a pressure-controlled gate was normal

c64.case.tooling.plating.name: Hard chrome plating of the cavity
c64.case.tooling.plating.description: The polished cavity is electroplated in a hexavalent chromium bath to a few microns. Chrome is much harder than the tool steel, so the tool wears far better; it is also what gives the moulded ABS its character - the gloss of a C64 case is the gloss of chrome, not of steel.
c64.case.tooling.plating.note: Modern practice has largely moved away from hexavalent chromium for environmental reasons, toward electroless nickel or PVD. In 1982 hard chrome was the standard and there was no practical alternative.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chromic acid with sulfate catalyst, 50-60 C, 6-10 V

facts.label: Hydrogen embrittlement
facts.value: a real risk; many moulds are baked immediately after plating

facts.label: Environmental cost
facts.value: Cr(VI) plating is heavily restricted today

c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.name: Chromic acid for the plating bath
c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.description: Made by roasting chromite with soda ash and limestone, leaching the sodium chromate, and acidifying. So the chromium in the plating bath comes from the same chromite that came into the tool steel.
c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.note: Chromium plating is one of the few places the same ore appears twice in a single product: once as alloying element in the steel, once as the surface plating.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: ~1000 C with soda ash and lime, oxidative roast to Na2CrO4

c64.case.tooling.polishing.name: Lapping and polishing the cavity
c64.case.tooling.polishing.description: The cavity is progressively polished - progressively finer abrasives on cloth and stone - to a mirror. On a textured tool the polish is done to the whole surface and the texture simply stays; on flat surfaces it goes to Ra 0.05-0.1 um, which is what makes the plated ABS read as glossy.
c64.case.tooling.polishing.note: This is the most labour-intensive step in the whole case tool. A large textured housing cavity takes days of hand polishing, which is why such tools cost tens of thousands of dollars and why the economics demanded millions of parts.

facts.label: Polishing media
facts.value: aluminium oxide, then chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron blocks for the final mirror; machine polish for bulk stock removal

c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.name: Abrasive polishing compounds
c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.description: Aluminium oxide for the bulk work, green chromium oxide for the final mirror. Both are made from bauxite or from chromite.

c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.name: Synthetic alumina abrasive
c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina and sintered or fused into corundum, then crushed and graded into abrasive powders. Hardness ~9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, and the workhorse of metal finishing.

c64.case.tooling.machining.name: Machining of the cavity and core
c64.case.tooling.machining.description: A 1982 tool shop would rough the cavity with large carbide or HSS milling cutters, leaving 0.3-0.5 mm, then finish-mill, then grind the critical faces flat and parallel, then EDM the texture, then lap and polish. Rough and finish were both done on machining centres or on conventional mills and grinders - CNC was normal but not universal.
c64.case.tooling.machining.note: By 1982 CNC machining centres and CNC grinders were standard in Taiwanese and Hong Kong tool shops, so this is genuinely a CNC-era tool even though the process sequence is unchanged.

c64.case.tooling.edm.name: EDM cutting of the leather grain
c64.case.tooling.edm.description: The texture is the one feature that cannot be milled: a random stochastic pattern of overlapping spherical dimples. It is cut by sinking a shaped graphite or brass electrode into the hardened, ground cavity, or by wire-EDM scanning. Sinking EDM gives a whole panel at once; wire EDM gives resolution but is slower.
c64.case.tooling.edm.note: Sinker EDM existed and was well established by 1982 - it had been commercial since the 1960s - so the texture is genuinely of its period. What has NOT changed is that the texture is a negative in the steel, not a coating.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sinker (sink) EDM is standard for area texturing; wire EDM for detail

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite, or brass for finer detail

facts.label: Rough cut
facts.value: ~0.2-0.5 mm/s removal; finish cut much slower

c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.name: Brass electrode for fine detail
c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.description: Copper-zinc alloy electrodes are used where the texture has fine features, because brass machines more accurately than graphite and can be reworked. Brass comes from copper and zinc ores smelted together.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.name: Graphite electrode for EDM texturing
c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.description: Isostatic-pressed fine-grain graphite, turned or milled to the negative of the texture panel, or a CNC-shaped graphite block. Graphite is used because it is easy to machine, wears predictably as the electrode erodes, and does not damage the workpiece the way a metal electrode would.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.name: Natural graphite flake
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.description: Flake graphite is mined in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, China and Brazil, purified by acid (or in the 1980s by chlorination) and pressed with pitch binder into tooling graphite.
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.note: China was the dominant supplier of graphite electrode and tooling graphite throughout this period.

c64.case.tooling.grinding.name: Surface grinding and the parting line
c64.case.tooling.grinding.description: The two plates are ground parallel and the parting plane is lapped. A visible flash line around the case seam is the parting line: on a housing tool it is put exactly at the joint line of the two halves so it disappears into the joint.

c64.case.tooling.tool-steel.name: Tool steel (P20 pre-hardened or H13/SKD61 hardened)
c64.case.tooling.tool-steel.description: Most 1980s housing tools were cut from pre-hardened P20-type steel (about HRC 30-35) so the tool could be finished-machined without distortion. Tools needing more polish cycles or more heat went to H13/SKD61, vacuum-hardened and tempered to HRC 44-50.
c64.case.tooling.tool-steel.note: Which grade Commodore actually used for the breadbin tooling I could not confirm; P20-class and H13-class were both routine for a case of this size in 1982.

c64.case.tooling.p20.name: P20 pre-hardened tool steel
c64.case.tooling.p20.description: A 0.38% C, 0.9% Cr, 0.4% Mo, 0.2% V steel supplied at HRC 30-35. Because it arrives hard, the whole cavity can be machined and polished with no risk of distortion from a later heat treatment, which is why it dominated housing tooling in 1982.
c64.case.tooling.p20.note: The mould texturing and polishing described below works equally on P20 or on H13.

facts.label: Trade names
facts.value: P20, 1.2311, NAK80 is the corrosion-resistant modern cousin

c64.case.tooling.h13.name: H13 / SKD61 hot-work tool steel
c64.case.tooling.h13.description: A 5% Cr, 1% Mo, 1% V, 0.4% C alloy. Chromium gives hardenability and polishability, molybdenum and vanadium give secondary hardness and temper resistance. Also sold as DIN X40CrMoV5-1, JIS SKD61 or AISI H13.

facts.label: Critical for tools
facts.value: deep hardening plus temper resistance near 250-300 C

c64.case.tooling.heat-treatment.name: Vacuum hardening and tempering of the tool
c64.case.tooling.heat-treatment.description: H13 is austenitised at 1000-1050 C, quenched in air or in vacuum, then double-tempered at 500-600 C to get secondary hardness. Vacuum is preferred because it avoids decarburisation and the distortion that salt baths cause. In 1982 salt baths were still very common for smaller tools.
c64.case.tooling.heat-treatment.note: Modern tooling shops would use a fine-grain, high-purity steel and a tighter hardness window; 1982 practice was adequate but variable, and the variation is exactly why some original C64 cases show a slightly different gloss.

facts.label: Quench
facts.value: air or vacuum; salt bath (550 C) was the 1970s norm

c64.case.tooling.nitriding.name: Nitriding of the polished cavity
c64.case.tooling.nitriding.description: A short nitriding treatment after polishing diffuses nitrogen into the surface, growing a hard, low-friction skin on the cavity that resists the corrosive effect of styrene monomer. Standard on hot-runner tools and increasingly used on ABS housings.

c64.case.tooling.vanadium-ferroalloy.name: Ferrovanadium from vanadiferous slag
c64.case.tooling.vanadium-ferroalloy.description: Vanadium is not mined as a vanadium ore at all in most of the world. It is recovered as a byproduct: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag from iron ore smelting is re-smelted, or slag is leached with soda ash, and vanadium is precipitated and reduced to ferrovanadium.
c64.case.tooling.vanadium-ferroalloy.note: The vanadium in a tool steel therefore traces back to an iron ore blast furnace, not to a vanadium mine. A nice non-obvious ore-to-tool chain.

facts.label: Main route
facts.value: byproduct of iron ore smelting (vanadiferous titanomagnetite)

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: soda ash / salt roasting then aqueous leach

c64.case.tooling.iron-ore.name: Iron ore (vanadiferous magnetite)
c64.case.tooling.iron-ore.description: The ore is smelted in a blast furnace; when it carries vanadium the slag is deliberately kept for vanadium recovery. So the same lump of ore yields the iron for the press frame and, later, the vanadium in the tool steel.
c64.case.tooling.iron-ore.note: Blast furnace coke is made from coking coal in a coke oven battery; the limestone flux is quarried.

c64.case.tooling.ferromoly.name: Ferromolybdenum from molybdite
c64.case.tooling.ferromoly.description: Molybdenite is roasted to technical molybdic oxide (MoO3) and then reduced with aluminium or in a submerged-arc furnace with coke to ferromolybdenum, which is dosed into the steel melt.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: 600-700 C, 2-4 h in a multiple-hearth furnace

c64.case.tooling.ferrochrome.name: Ferrochrome from chromite ore
c64.case.tooling.ferrochrome.description: Chromite, FeCr2O4, is smelted in a submerged-arc or submerged-top furnace with coke and lime to give high-carbon ferrochrome, then refined to low-carbon ferrochrome. Almost all the chromium in a tool steel charge comes in as ferrochrome.

facts.label: Smelting
facts.value: s submerged-arc furnace with coke, 1500-1700 C

c64.case.tooling.chromite-ore.name: Chromite ore
c64.case.tooling.chromite-ore.description: The only economic chromium ore, mined mostly in South Africa's Bushveld complex and in Zimbabwe, Kazakhstan and Turkey. Sold as a lumpy or sintered lump, or as a fines fraction.

c64.case.abs-resin.name: ABS resin, general-purpose injection grade
c64.case.abs-resin.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a SAN matrix rigidified by acrylonitrile, toughened by grafted polybutadiene and given surface gloss by styrene. Commodore bought commodity ABS pellets in 25 kg bags, compounded them with colour masterbatch in a merchant compounder, and shipped them to case factories in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
c64.case.abs-resin.note: A textured housing wants a LOW rubber content. High-rubber grades flow better but leave a soft, smeared grain; housing grades are typically chosen for a stiff, sharp texture and low sink.

c64.case.abs-resin.compounding.name: Twin-screw compounding and pelletising
c64.case.abs-resin.compounding.description: Natural ABS pellets are let down with the colour masterbatch and additives on a co-rotating twin-screw extruder, degassed, filtered through a screen pack, and pelletised - chopped strands or underwater cut. This is a 1980s standard plastic-compounding line.
c64.case.abs-resin.compounding.note: In the 1980s screen-pack melt filtration and gravimetric dosing were the state of the art; modern lines add online viscometers and inline colour measurement, but the twin-screw itself has not fundamentally changed.

facts.label: Throughput (merchant line)
facts.value: a few hundred kg/h to 1-2 t/h

c64.case.abs-resin.additives.name: Additives package added at compounding
c64.case.abs-resin.additives.description: ABS pellets as delivered are a straw-coloured, unpigmented polymer. The beige-brown of the C64 case is added downstream at the compounder as a colour masterbatch, along with stabilisers, a release agent and, in some grades, a flame retardant. A 1982 C64 case is almost certainly pigmented at the compound line, not at the moulder.
c64.case.abs-resin.additives.note: The brown-to-blonde colour shift over forty years is the classic ABS photodegradation: the butadiene rubber phase oxidises at the surface and the whole part browns uniformly. UV stabiliser and pigment loading both affect how fast it happens.

c64.case.abs-resin.flame-retardant.name: Flame retardant additive (optional)
c64.case.abs-resin.flame-retardant.description: Not all ABS is flame retardant, but electronics housings were often specified with a UL94 HB or V-2 grade, which is achieved by adding a halogenated additive - typically brominated epoxy or an aliphatic bromine-chlorine compound at 5-15 parts per hundred. It slows burning but costs toughness and colour, so a textured beige housing usually avoided it.
c64.case.abs-resin.flame-retardant.note: For a home computer case a flame-retardant grade is a 'nice to have' rather than a requirement; household-computable housings of 1982 were commonly general-purpose ABS. Included because flame retardants were a standard part of the 1980s ABS additive package.

facts.label: Common systems
facts.value: brominated epoxy resin, or chlorinated paraffin

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: raises cost and lowers Izod impact, so it is usually a trade

c64.case.abs-resin.release-agent.name: Release agent / lubricant
c64.case.abs-resin.release-agent.description: A trace of an internal lubricant such as a metal stearate (zinc or calcium stearate, or a fatty-acid ester) is compounded into the ABS so the mould releases cleanly. Too much and it bloats the surface of the textured area.

c64.case.abs-resin.tallow.name: Tallow (rendered fat)
c64.case.abs-resin.tallow.description: Rendered bovine or ovine fat, a slaughterhouse byproduct, used historically as a soap and lubricant feedstock and as a fatty-acid source.

c64.case.abs-resin.stearic-acid.name: Stearic acid
c64.case.abs-resin.stearic-acid.description: C18 saturated fatty acid, made by hydrogenating tallow (or palm stearin) or by pressing stearic acid out of beef tallow. It is the base of the metal stearate lubricants and also of many cosmetic-grade waxes.
c64.case.abs-resin.stearic-acid.note: Tallow is rendered animal fat - itself a byproduct of the meat industry. Palm stearin is the fraction of palm oil that solidifies. Both are agricultural, not petrochemical, feedstocks.

facts.label: Typical source
facts.value: hydrogenated palm stearin or beef tallow

c64.case.abs-resin.pigment-masterbatch.name: Pigment masterbatch (colour concentrate)
c64.case.abs-resin.pigment-masterbatch.description: A high-loading pellet of pigment dispersed in an ABS or PE carrier resin, let down at 1-4% into the natural ABS. The colour masterbatch is itself a compounding product, made on its own twin-screw line.

facts.label: Carrier
facts.value: ABS or PE, matched to base for colour

c64.case.abs-resin.titanium-dioxide.name: Titanium dioxide (white pigment)
c64.case.abs-resin.titanium-dioxide.description: The workhorse white pigment, present in almost every beige or grey ABS and in most white packaging ink. Rutile is the industrial grade: made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile ore to TiCl4, then oxidising it in a 1000 C flame to pure white rutile pigment.

c64.case.abs-resin.coke.name: Metallurgical coke
c64.case.abs-resin.coke.description: The reductant in the chlorinator (TiO2 + 2C + 2Cl2 -> TiCl4 + 2CO) and the fuel of the flame reactor. Coke is a by-product of coking coal in a coke oven battery, not a mined material in itself.
c64.case.abs-resin.coke.note: Coking coal is thermal-rank coal (bituminous), chosen for its caking properties. The coke oven itself is one of the great carbon-emitting industrial plants of the period.

c64.case.abs-resin.rutile-ore.name: Ilmenite and rutile ore
c64.case.abs-resin.rutile-ore.description: Titanium ore, mined from beach sands and hard-rock deposits. Ilmenite (FeTiO3) is the dominant feed; it is reduced to titanium slag, or chlorinated to TiCl4.
c64.case.abs-resin.rutile-ore.note: Beach-sand ilmenite and rutile are dredged or wet-separated; the heavy-mineral concentrate then goes to a chlorinator. This is one of the clearest 'ore -> pigment -> plastic case' chains on the machine.

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalo-blue.name: Phthalocyanine blue pigment
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalo-blue.description: Copper phthalocyanine (PB15), an intensely coloured, heat-stable, lightfast blue used for the cool grey-blue tones on some cases. Copper plus four phthalonitrile rings, assembled in a violent exotherm.

c64.case.abs-resin.copper.name: Copper for the phthalocyanine centre
c64.case.abs-resin.copper.description: Copper(II) salts, from electrorefined copper. Copper comes from chalcopyrite CuFeS2 ore or from ore sorted to a copper concentrate, then smelted, converted and electrorefined.

c64.case.abs-resin.chalcopyrite.name: Chalcopyrite (copper ore)
c64.case.abs-resin.chalcopyrite.description: CuFeS2, the dominant copper ore, mined underground or in large open pits and concentrated by flotation before smelting. The smelter's job is to strip the iron into slag so that copper matte can be converted and electrorefined.

c64.case.abs-resin.flash-smelting.name: Flash smelting and converting
c64.case.abs-resin.flash-smelting.description: Sulfide concentrate is blown with oxygen-enriched air in a flash furnace at ~1250 C, so that the sulfur burns and autogenous heat smelts the copper. The resulting matte is oxidised in converters, slagged of its iron, and the blister copper is electrorefined.

c64.case.abs-resin.flotation.name: Froth flotation of copper ore
c64.case.abs-resin.flotation.description: Crushed and ground ore is conditioned with xanthate collectors and frothers, and the copper sulfide particles are floated to the surface in a bank of rectangular flotation cells. This is how most of the world's copper is separated from its host rock.

facts.label: Cells
facts.value: dozens in series, each a few m3

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.name: Phthalic anhydride
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.description: Made by air oxidation of o-xylene over vanadia-titania catalysts at ~450 C. It is the classic route to phthalocyanine pigments and to glycidyl ester epoxy resins.

c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.name: o-Xylene
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.description: One of the three xylene isomers separated out of the mixed aromatics from the reformer by adsorption (UOP Parex-type) or by distillation. The ortho isomer is the one that gets oxidised to phthalic anhydride.
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.note: The separation of the isomers by molecular adsorption (Parex/UOP) is a good example of 1980s petrochemical sophistication: the unit separates individual isomers from the C8 cut on a zeolite molecular sieve.

c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.name: C8 aromatics separation (UOP Parex)
c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.description: Para-xylene is selectively adsorbed from the mixed C8 aromatics onto a zeolite molecular sieve, desorbed with a purge, leaving o- and m-xylene. It is a swinging adsorption unit with hundreds of adsorbent beds and rotating valves.
c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.note: Parex-type units date from 1962 and were ubiquitous in 1982 for making terephthalic acid (PET). Modern units use improved adsorbents but the process is essentially unchanged.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: mixed C8 aromatics from the reformer

c64.case.abs-resin.san-resin.name: SAN resin (styrene-acrylonitrile) matrix component
c64.case.abs-resin.san-resin.description: Most ABS is a blend: grafted rubber plus a separately polymerised SAN. The SAN is the continuous, glossy, rigid phase; the grafted rubber is the dispersed, toughening phase. The SAN is usually made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation in a separate plant and shipped to the ABS compounding line as pellets or as latex.

facts.label: Typical AN content in the SAN
Share of SAN in the finished ABS

c64.case.abs-resin.bulk-polymerisation.name: Bulk polymerisation of SAN (plug flow)
c64.case.abs-resin.bulk-polymerisation.description: A monomer mixture of styrene and acrylonitrile is polymerised thermally in a series of stirred, jacketed plug-flow reactors - classic 'prepolymerise then finish' with the reactor temperature ramped from ~130 C to ~230 C to convert 95-99% of the monomer. The SAN is devolatilised and extruded to pellets.

c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.name: Emulsion graft polymerisation to ABS
c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.description: The dominant ABS route since the 1960s and still the one that makes the resin in the C64. Butadiene is polymerised in water to a polybutadiene latex; styrene and acrylonitrile are graft-polymerised onto that latex; the graft latex is coagulated, dewatered, dried and compounded with separately made bulk-SAN resin.

facts.label: Initiation
facts.value: potassium or sodium persulfate, or an organic persulfate

facts.label: Residual monomer removal
facts.value: steam stripping in a vacuum plate column

c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.name: Free-radical initiator (persulfate)
c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.description: Potassium persulfate or sodium persulfate, thermally decomposed in the aqueous reactor to start the radical chain. Cheap, and the resulting sulphate is later washed out during coagulation.

c64.case.abs-resin.potassium-hydroxide.name: Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash)
