c64.case.abs-resin.potassium-hydroxide.description: Made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, the potassium salt crystallising from the sodium-rich liquor. It is what turns the fatty acid into the soap emulsifier and the persulfate precursor into the initiator.

c64.case.abs-resin.chlor-alkali.name: Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine
c64.case.abs-resin.chlor-alkali.description: Electrolysis of saturated brine in a membrane or mercury cell splits salt water into chlorine, sodium (or potassium) hydroxide and hydrogen. This is one of the foundational 20th-century chemical processes and it feeds PVC, solvents, and every chlorinated intermediate.
c64.case.abs-resin.chlor-alkali.note: Mercury-cell electrolysis was still the dominant technology in 1982, but was being phased out over environmental and product-quality reasons in favour of the membrane cell. This transition is one of the clean examples of where 1980s practice differs from modern practice.

facts.label: Cell type (1980s)
facts.value: diaphragm, mercury or membrane; membrane gaining share by mid-1980s

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: ~3 V per cell, but 100-150 V across a cell house

c64.case.abs-resin.halite.name: Halite (rock salt)
c64.case.abs-resin.halite.description: Sodium chloride, mined or solution-mined from evaporite deposits and dissolved to make the brine that is electrolysed. Pure salt is the raw material for the entire chlor-alkali chemical complex.

c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.name: Emulsifier (fatty-acid soap)
c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.description: The ABS latex is not made with a synthetic surfactant but with cheap soap - typically a sodium or potassium salt of a C16-C18 fatty acid, sometimes blended with a sulfosuccinate for stability. This is the 1980s process: fully synthetic surfactants were still expensive.
c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisati.note: Emulsifier choice has a big effect on the final particle size, and particle size is what sets the impact toughness. Producers who got it wrong had to agglomerate the latex or add a second, more expensive surfactant.

facts.label: Typical emulsifier
facts.value: sodium oleate / potassium oleate, or an alkylbenzenesulfonate

c64.case.abs-resin.monomers.name: Monomer triad fed to the ABS plant
c64.case.abs-resin.monomers.description: Styrene supplies gloss and mouldability, acrylonitrile supplies rigidity and chemical resistance, butadiene supplies the rubber phase that survives the drop the machine takes off a desk. All three arrive as cracker or reformer products, not as laboratory reagents.

c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene.name: Butadiene (1,3-butadiene)
c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene.description: The rubber monomer. 1980s butadiene came almost entirely from the C4 fraction of the steam cracker, extracted by extractive distillation (or by older acetylene-dimerisation routes still running in Europe).

c64.case.abs-resin.steam-cracking.name: Steam cracking of naphtha (the source of all four monomers)
c64.case.abs-resin.steam-cracking.description: Naphtha or gas oil is vaporised, mixed with steam and flashed through coils in a radiant furnace at 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second. The gas is quenched fast to stop further cracking, then fractionated into hydrogen, ethylene, propylene, a C4 cut and an aromatics cut. Almost every polymer in the C64 - ABS, SAN, SBR feet, polystyrene foam - starts as a cut out of this one column.
c64.case.abs-resin.steam-cracking.note: Modern crackers push higher severity (coils to 950-1000 C) and use more structured/elliptical coils. In 1982 the classic coiled-pipe radiant furnace was still the workhorse. The coils themselves were cast from a 25/35 nickel alloy, which is a real and expensive material choice because the coking rate falls exponentially with nickel.

c64.case.abs-resin.refractory.name: Refractory fibre block lining
c64.case.abs-resin.refractory.description: The furnace interior is lined with castable alumina and calcium-aluminate refractory or ceramic fibre blanket to hold 850 C and survive thermal cycling. It is a consumable and a real maintenance cost.

c64.case.abs-resin.naphtha-cracker-coil.name: Cracker coil casting in high-nickel alloy
c64.case.abs-resin.naphtha-cracker-coil.description: Radiant furnace coils are investment-cast from HK40 or 35Cr-45Ni alloy in twenty to forty segments, then thermally expanded into the tube supports. The nickel content is what keeps the coil from coking and creeping at 850 C.

c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene-extraction.name: Recovery of butadiene from the C4 cut
c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene-extraction.description: The C4 stream from the cracker contains butenes, isobutene and butadiene. Because butadiene boils at -4 C and its neighbours at +1 to +13 C, it is separated by extractive distillation with a heavy solvent such as NMP or furfural in a tall column, or by older acetonedimethylformamide absorption.
c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene-extraction.note: The older DDM (acetone/DMF) absorption-recovery route was still being phased out in the early 1980s; by the mid-1980s extractive distillation had won almost everywhere.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: extractive distillation (NMP/furfural) or older chemical absorption

facts.label: Challenge
facts.value: isomerise to 1,2-butene; polymerise in transit; high pressure

c64.case.abs-resin.acrylonitrile.name: Acrylonitrile (vinyl cyanide)
c64.case.abs-resin.acrylonitrile.description: CH2=CH-CN, the polar monomer that gives ABS its rigidity and resistance to solvents. Almost all of it is made by catalytic ammoxidation of propylene with ammonia and air over a bismuth-molybdate catalyst in a fluidised bed.

c64.case.abs-resin.ammoxidation.name: Sovereign/BP ammoxidation of propylene
c64.case.abs-resin.ammoxidation.description: Propylene, ammonia and air are fed together into a turbulent fluidised-bed reactor over a bismuth-molybdate-on-silica catalyst at 400-510 C and only 1.5-3 bar. Acrylonitrile comes out together with acetonitrile, HCN and COx; the gases are quenched in a countercurrent water absorber, the AN is distilled, and the residual ammonia is neutralised with sulphuric acid to ammonium sulphate fertiliser.
c64.case.abs-resin.ammoxidation.note: Originally the Sohio (Standard Oil of Ohio) process, later sold by SOHIO to BP and rebranded 'Sovereign'. An older route, acetylene plus hydrogen cyanide, was still in use into the 1980s in a few plants but was being retired.

c64.case.abs-resin.mo-bi-catalyst.name: Bismuth phosphomolybdate ammoxidation catalyst
c64.case.abs-resin.mo-bi-catalyst.description: The heart of the ammoxidation. A mixture of bismuth, molybdenum, iron, cobalt and other metal oxides, typically supported on silica or silica-alumina. It works by a redox cycle: the lattice oxygen of the molybdate grabs an allylic hydrogen from propylene, ammonia inserts, the nitrile is desorbed, and air re-oxidises the bismuth.
c64.case.abs-resin.mo-bi-catalyst.note: The bismuth-molybdate family is one of the great success stories of heterogeneous catalysis: the same catalyst family is used for the ammoxidation to acrylonitrile, for acrolein to acrylic acid, and for the butadiene to butene oxide.

c64.case.abs-resin.silica-support.name: Silica / silica-alumina support
c64.case.abs-resin.silica-support.description: The porous carrier for the bismuth molybdate, made from diatomaceous earth or by co-precipitating silica from sodium silicate. Diatomaceous earth is a filter-aid mineral mined from ancient diatomite deposits.

c64.case.abs-resin.molybdenum-source.name: Molybdenum ore (molybdenite)
c64.case.abs-resin.molybdenum-source.description: Molybdenite, MoS2, mined mostly as a by-product of porphyry copper. It is roasted to technical-grade molybdic oxide and then purified to the high-purity metal or oxidised for catalyst use.

c64.case.abs-resin.bismuth-source.name: Bismuth ore and bismuth compounds
c64.case.abs-resin.bismuth-source.description: Bismuth comes mainly as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from bismuthinite (Bi2S3) or as native bismuth in tin/tungsten veins. The oxo-nitrate is precipitated from an acid solution and calcined to bismuth oxide for the catalyst.

c64.case.abs-resin.ammonia.name: Ammonia
c64.case.abs-resin.ammonia.description: Made by steam-methane reforming natural gas to synthesis gas (CO+H2) and then Haber-Bosch synthesis over promoted iron. Every tonne of acrylonitrile needs roughly a quarter tonne of ammonia, and the byproduct ammonium sulphate goes straight back onto farmland.

c64.case.abs-resin.haber-bosch.name: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis
c64.case.abs-resin.haber-bosch.description: Nitrogen and hydrogen react at 400-500 C and 150-300 bar over an iron catalyst promoted with K2O and Al2O3. This is where the era shows: 1980s plants ran the classic packed-bed, and modern plants use much more efficient ruthenium catalysts at lower pressure.
c64.case.abs-resin.haber-bosch.note: The switch from iron to ruthenium catalysts in the 1990s cut energy use per tonne of ammonia roughly in half. In 1982 it was all iron.

c64.case.abs-resin.steam-methane-reformi.name: Steam-methane reforming (primary reformer)
c64.case.abs-resin.steam-methane-reformi.description: Natural gas and steam are burned over nickel at 800-900 C to give synthesis gas, CO plus H2. The high-temperature endothermic step is fired by burning part of the gas itself, so an ammonia plant is really a gas-fired furnace with a chemistry attached.

c64.case.abs-resin.styrene.name: Styrene monomer
c64.case.abs-resin.styrene.description: Vinylbenzene, made by catalytic dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene or by styrene monomer recovery from a cracker. 1980s ABS plants bought it at 99.5%+ into stainless bulk tanks.

c64.case.abs-resin.styrene-dehydrogenati.name: Ethylbenzene dehydrogenation to styrene
c64.case.abs-resin.styrene-dehydrogenati.description: Endothermic vapour-phase dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over shell-type alumina-iron catalysts at 600-700 C, giving styrene plus hydrogen. Modern plants add a styrene monomer recovery loop to recycle unreacted ethylbenzene; 1980s plants ran single-pass at roughly 50-60% conversion and burned the rest.
c64.case.abs-resin.styrene-dehydrogenati.note: The styrene monomer recovery loop that pushes per-pass conversion to ~65-70% became mandatory in OECD plants after about 1990. 1982 ABS resin was typically made without it.

c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene.name: Ethylbenzene
c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene.description: Benzene alkylated with ethylene (or propylene) over a solid acid to make the styrene feedstock, with diethylbenzene and triethylbenzene as the by-products that have to be separated out.

c64.case.abs-resin.benzene.name: Benzene
c64.case.abs-resin.benzene.description: A C6H6 aromatic produced either by catalytic reforming of naphtha or by hydrodealkylation of toluene. Benzene is the entry point to styrene, and via cumene to phenol, epoxy resin and polycarbonate.

c64.case.abs-resin.aromatics-extraction.name: Catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction
c64.case.abs-resin.aromatics-extraction.description: Naphtha is vaporised and passed over platinum (often with rhenium) on gamma-alumina at 450-520 C and 5-30 bar. Naphthenes and paraffins dehydrocyclise to aromatics; the C6+ aromatics are then split by extractive distillation with sulfolane or by azeotropic distillation with NMP.
c64.case.abs-resin.aromatics-extraction.note: Reformer pressure is the era tell. Low-pressure (5-10 bar) reformers dominate outside the US; semi-regenerative high-pressure units (15-30 bar) were the standard US build in 1982; continuous catalyst regeneration only arrived in earnest in the mid-1980s.

c64.case.abs-resin.platinum-catalyst.name: Platinum-alumina reforming catalyst
c64.case.abs-resin.platinum-catalyst.description: 0.3-0.5 wt% platinum with rhenium, chloride and fluoride promoters dispersed on synthetic gamma-alumina. The platinum comes from PGM ores or from spent refinery catalyst; the alumina support is sintered from calcined bauxite.

c64.case.abs-resin.bauxite.name: Bauxite (alumina precursor)
c64.case.abs-resin.bauxite.description: Hydrated alumina rock, mined and Bayer-refined to alumina. It is the source of the alumina support for the reforming catalyst, and also the ore that becomes the aluminium in the EMI shield.

c64.case.abs-resin.pgm-ore.name: Platinum-group metal concentrate
c64.case.abs-resin.pgm-ore.description: Sulfide ore mined in South Africa's Bushveld complex or Russia's Norilsk, concentrated and smelted to a matte, then leached and refined. The platinum fraction is a fraction of a percent of the ore, which is why reclaiming spent catalyst is a real industry.
c64.case.abs-resin.pgm-ore.note: Mine origin is generic. Also, note that the C64's own story and this ore are unrelated - the platinum is for the refinery, not the C64.

c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene-alkylati.name: Benzene alkylation with ethylene
c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene-alkylati.description: Friedel-Crafts alkylation over amorphous silica-alumina or a zeolite at 200-350 C and 5-20 bar, giving ethylbenzene plus polyalkylated heavies removed by fractionation.

c64.case.fasteners.name: Case fasteners
c64.case.fasteners.description: The screws that hold the C64 together: a handful of case-assembly screws plus the motherboard and keyboard mounting screws. They are cheap zinc-plated self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, with occasional brass inserts.
c64.case.fasteners.note: The common failure mode of a forty-year-old C64 is a snapped screw boss, not a rusted screw. Repro cases now mould in brass inserts to fix exactly this.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: zinc or nickel-zinc, plus a nylon patch for vibration

c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.name: Moulded-in brass insert (later practice)
c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.description: Modern repro cases and late Commodore tools mould a brass or stainless insert into the boss and use a real machine screw. The insert is placed by hand or by gravity feed and captured by the ABS on the next shot, giving a reusable metal thread.
c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.note: Original 1982 breadbins used self-tapping screws into plain plastic bosses. Inserts are the later improvement.

c64.case.fasteners.zinc-plating.name: Zinc electroplating of fasteners
c64.case.fasteners.zinc-plating.description: Small parts are barrel-plated in an acid or alkaline zinc solution, then often chromate-passivated for corrosion resistance. Zinc is chosen because it is sacrificial and cheap, and because a partly-depleted zinc coat on a thirty-year-old screw looks like rust rather than like a defect.

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or clear chromate conversion coat

c64.case.fasteners.cold-heading.name: Cold heading and thread cutting
c64.case.fasteners.cold-heading.description: Steel wire is drawn, cut to length, cold-headed on a multiple-spindle header, the thread is cut or rolled, and the head is slotted or Phillips-formed. This is one of the most automated manufacturing processes on earth: a header makes tens of thousands of screws an hour with essentially no machining.

facts.label: Thread
facts.value: cut or rolled; rolled threads are stronger

c64.case.shield.name: RFI shield: aluminium foil on a board spacer
c64.case.shield.description: The C64 needed a conductive screen over the motherboard because a 1 MHz machine with a video oscillator radiates through a plastic case. Commodore used a die-cut sandwich of aluminium foil laminated to a cardboard or plastic-fibre spacer, bent into a box and stapled or taped to plastic standoffs, rather than a full metal can.
c64.case.shield.note: Retroleum catalogues three distinct breadbin foil-shield types (Types 1, 2 and 5) which tells you the shape was not standardised across the production run. Later boards (250425) got a stamped metal shield/heatsink that doubled as a cooler for the linear regulators.

facts.label: Spacer
facts.value: thin cardboard / greyboard, sometimes a plastic-fibre core

facts.label: Attachment
facts.value: stapled or taped to moulded plastic standoffs on the case floor

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: reduce RF radiation and ingress without a metal chassis

c64.case.shield.spacer.name: Shield spacer (board core)
c64.case.shield.spacer.description: A rigidising core so the foil does not crumple and short against the board. Cheap versions use thin greyboard; better ones use a plastic-fibre or corrugated spacer. This is the part that makes the shield stand off the motherboard so it cannot touch solder joints.
c64.case.shield.spacer.note: Board core is a plausible choice because the shield only needs to hold a shape and take handling, and greyboard is the cheapest stiff sheet in existence. Stamped sheet-metal shields were the alternative on later boards.

c64.case.shield.foil.name: Aluminium foil
c64.case.shield.foil.description: Household or semi-rugged aluminium foil, 0.03-0.06 mm, slit and die-cut. Its job is not to be a Faraday cage in the strict sense but simply to be a continuous, grounded-ish conductor over the board so the radiated field collapses.
c64.case.shield.foil.note: Household foil works surprisingly well for this, which is why computer makers scavenged it off consumer rolls. It tears easily, so the real difficulty is handling, not the material.

c64.case.shield.foil-casting.name: Aluminium slab casting and rolling
c64.case.shield.foil-casting.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina, smelted to primary aluminium in a Hall-Heroult potline at 950 C, then cast into rolling ingots and hot-rolled to foil gauge. Foil rolling is astonishingly aggressive: a 600 mm slab becomes 0.006 mm sheet after thousands of reduction passes.

facts.label: Carbon anode consumption
facts.value: ~1.2 t CO2 per tonne of aluminium

c64.case.feet.name: Case feet
c64.case.feet.description: Four small anti-vibration feet on the underside of the rear shell, moulded in a soft dark rubber or a flexible PVC, that stop the machine skating on a desk and stop the moulded ABS case from ringing against the desk.
c64.case.feet.note: Whether the C64 feet are insert-moulded SBR or simply flexible moulded-in stubs varies between units and I could not confirm the exact compound. Modern restorers often replace them with stick-on silicone bumpers, which suggests the originals were not always reliable.

facts.label: Typical material
facts.value: black styrene-butadiene rubber or soft PVC, insert-moulded or pressed in

c64.case.feet.elastomer.name: Foot elastomer compound
c64.case.feet.elastomer.description: A soft, low-durometer elastomer drop-in-moulded over a small ABS boss, or a moulded-in flexible nub. The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: it is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS.
c64.case.feet.elastomer.note: Reuses the same butadiene and styrene monomers as the ABS and the SBR, which is a nice reminder that all four plastics in this machine trace back to the same steam cracker.

c64.case.logo.name: Rainbow Commodore badge
c64.case.logo.description: The seven-bar rainbow 'commodore' logo on the bezel. On the breadbin it is a raised area of the case itself, decorated by a run of coloured and metallised ink rather than being a separate appliqué; on later machines it is a flat printed decal.
c64.case.logo.note: Replicas, second-hand cases and modern reproductions disagree about whether the badge is raised mould or a bonded medallion. Surviving originals show a raised pad-printed area with the ink sitting in the texture; this is the most likely reading.

c64.case.logo.raised-area.name: Raised badge area on the bezel
c64.case.logo.raised-area.description: A shallow raised island on the bezel where the logo sits, moulded as part of the bezel tool. It gives the pad printer a flat, non-textured island so the ink sits proud of the leather grain and the colours read cleanly.

c64.case.bezel.name: Front bezel (top half)
c64.case.bezel.description: The dished front panel with the keyboard window. It is the visible part of the machine, so it carries the fine leather-grain texture, the rainbow badge recess, the two knurled thumbscrews and the moulded-in 'COMMODORE' lettering on the lower lip.

facts.label: Texture
facts.value: fine stochastic leather/pebble grain, depth 0.05-0.15 mm

facts.label: Screws to rear shell
facts.value: 6 self-tapping, plus 2 at the rear lip

c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.name: Knurled thumbscrews for contrast/brightness
c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.description: Two moulded plastic thumbscrews on the bezel that carry small metal shafts to the contrast and brightness potentiometers on the board. The caps are ABS, the shafts are plated steel, and the knurl is moulded rather than cut.
c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.note: On some breadbin boards the potentiometers were adjusted by reaching into the case with a screwdriver and the two bezel thumbscrews only appear on later board revisions; check the specific assembly.

c64.case.bezel.leather-texture.name: Moulded-in leather grain
c64.case.bezel.leather-texture.description: The fine random pebble texture on the visible faces of the bezel and the rear shell. It is cut into the hardened tool steel by EDM from a positive pattern, then the whole cavity is polished and chrome-plated so the grain reads as a soft satin rather than as sharp metal. On genuine surviving Commodore tooling the flow pattern beneath the texture is still faintly visible, which is how restorers authenticate an original mould.
c64.case.bezel.leather-texture.note: The texture is not paint or a coating: it is a negative in the steel. On parts made in a second colour or with a coating it can be partly buried, which is why grey aftermarket cases often look so much cleaner than originals.

facts.label: Cut by
facts.value: EDM from a graphite or brass electrode

c64.case.bezel.key-well.name: Keyboard window and key openings
c64.case.bezel.key-well.description: A single rectangular opening spanned by thin webs between the key holes; the caps push through and their plungers sit on the keyboard PCB below. The webs are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between 66 holes that are only about 10 mm across.
c64.case.bezel.key-well.note: Whether the bezel was a single moulding with the key openings, or a bezel with a separate keyboard frame, varies between breadbin tooling generations. Photographs of ASSY 250407 show one piece.

facts.label: Flash tolerance
facts.value: <0.2 mm, visually rejected at final inspection

c64.case.rear-shell.name: Rear shell (bottom half)
c64.case.rear-shell.description: The larger of the two mouldings. It forms the base pan, the raised side walls, the wrap-over top with its row of ventilation slots, the rear and side connector cut-outs, the internal ribs that stiffen the pan, the moulded screw bosses and standoffs, and the feet pads.

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: along the top flange, visible as a faint seam

c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts.name: Rear and side connector openings
c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts.description: Rectangular and keyed cut-outs for the cartridge port, user port, cassette port, serial port, video DIN, power DIN and the two DE-9 control ports. Cut with knife-edged steel on the tool; the moulded lip around each port also acts as a draft and a finger stop, and the mouldings carry the connector bodies as separate inserts.

c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.name: Moulded bosses and standoffs
c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.description: Integral cylindrical bosses on the pan floor that carry the four case screws, the motherboard mounting screws, the keyboard PCB screws and the RF shield tabs. Each is a thick section relative to the 3 mm pan, so the tool must be cored or cored-and-gauged to keep them from sinking, and each has a blind hole with a drafted self-tapping thread.

facts.label: Screw size
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping into 6 mm OD bosses

facts.label: Boss bore
facts.value: ~2.5 mm with a shallow helix rib

c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.steel-thread.name: Self-tapping thread form in plastic
c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.steel-thread.description: A 1980s cost trick: instead of a moulded-in metal insert, the boss is cored with a shallow single-start helical flute of the same nominal diameter as a self-tapping screw. The screw's flank cuts its own thread on first insertion, giving a metal-in-plastic thread that will not strip.
c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.steel-thread.note: Commodore's later repro cases replace these with moulded-in brass inserts precisely because the self-tapping bosses break.

facts.label: Cycle to first screw-in
facts.value: ~1 s at 1200 rpm on a hand screwdriver

facts.label: Serviceability
facts.value: poor; repeated removal strips the plastic

c64.case.rear-shell.vents.name: Ventilation slots in the top wrap
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.description: A row of moulded louvre slots in the curved top panel behind the cartridge port, letting convective air out of the case over the SID and VIC-II. They are negative features: slots cut into the tool, not separate ribs. Because they run across a thick section they leave visible flow lines and are a classic sink-mark site.
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.note: The effectiveness of the case cooling was mediocre and reviewers noted heat trapping inside; the slots are modest.

facts.label: Style
facts.value: through-slots, parallel to the long axis

facts.label: Function
facts.value: exhaust for the linear regulator and VIC/SID heat

c64.case.rear-shell.vents.rib-bosses.name: Ribs and bosses behind the vent slots
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.rib-bosses.description: Internal cross-ribs tying the top panel to the pan, moulded 1.5-2.5 mm thick at roughly the same gauge as the outer wall so the whole panel cools and shrinks as one. Where the ribs are thicker than the wall the extra melt freezes later and pulls a faint sink mark onto the visible surface.
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.rib-bosses.note: Mould-flow validation was in 1982 done by filling a clear polycarbonate or unfilled-PS prototype tool and watching flow fronts by eye or on a strobe, long before the widespread use of short-shot first-article reports.

facts.label: Design rule of thumb
facts.value: ribs capped at ~60% of the adjacent wall thickness
